I often find myself remissed that "I'm not up to date with the latest games," or that "I don't play as much as I used to."  Perhaps that's because I don't find many games like Transistor.
I recently found myself in the thralls of illness, and thus free from my daily responsibilites.  I decided to use this spare time to play the recently purchased Transistor.  In Transistor, the female protagonist (Red) is guided by an unknown familiar that is somehow trapped in the weapon that she wields: The Transistor.  You soon learn that they took her voice and she is driven, initially, by a sense of revenge and justice.  However, as the story unfolds, more questions arise as new entities are encountered and new perspectives are obtained.  Ultimately, many questions are left unanswered at the end of the story.  Even though you never truly know some of the details about Red's life before our story begins, and are left with a hazy understanding of the world that Red lives in, you gain absolute clarity of her character.
First: Transistor was great to play.  Easy to pick up and learn, lots of options for upgrading and combining skills, and a nice medium for employing different strategies in fights.  The concept of essentially pausing battle in order to carry out attacks was very heavy early in the game, and it wasn't until later that I realized that it also played as an action/rpg style combat where using the transistor for planning was optional.  It proved to be beneficial to be proficient in both types of combat as I moved through the game. It was fun, challenging, and engaging to take the different challenges and encounter new enemies with abilities that I was already familiar with using against them.
I found the story to be one of the best stories for any video game I have played.  It was compelling, it was beautiful, it filled me with sorrow and it filled me with joy.  It wasn't just the story that was compelling though; the way that they used Red's 'acquaintance' in the transistor to drive the story was a spectacularly subtle mechanism for keeping the player up to date with how Red might be moticated or directed by each event in the game.
The music didn't really stick out in this game for me.  To clarify: the music was great.  Many games really showcase the music, or to use the music to alert the player to a change in envoronment or mood.  In Transistor, the music fits seamlessly into the story, the gameplay, the entire experience of the game.  The music is a huge part of the game, helping to immerse the player into the "Transistor experience" by helping establish the setting rather than distracting from it in order to let you know that you're in a new place, or that danger is afoot!
The artwork? Beautiful.  Like the music, it seemed perfectly suited to this story to provide the most engaging, immersive experience.  It's easy enough to find the art for the game online or previews, so I won't say much more here.
Everything about this game worked together to provide a wonderful, spectacular experience that I have been encouraging others to try since I've played it.  My love for video games has been rekindled, and I hope to see more games like this.
How is the replay value?  I'm going to find out!

I would not get this game for full price, but Total War 75% sales are fairly common, so I would go for that. One thing I have to say about Rome II is that I find it harder than past Total War games. I'm going to use Empire Total War as an example. My favourite Total war playthrough was Sweden in Empire. By turn 50 of Empire, I had pretty much dominated Northern and Eastern Europe; Russia was cut in half, Poland was putting up a fight but actively losing, and the Netherlands had been invaded by me through Denmark. Meanwhile, in my first Rome II playthrough (as Armenia) by turn fifty I controlled about half a Turkey, and considering the map is the entirety of Europe and the Middle East, that's saying something. That's because you can't build a bunch of happiness buildings willy nilly and move on, you have to keep an army there to repel rebellions while you spend about ten turns converting the culture and investing in reconstruction, and I respect the game for that. It makes it more realistic if it does take away from the glamour of global conquest. Also factions are quite tightly packed and build quite large armies, with one city factions having on par army size with you early-mid game.
In conclusion this is an enjoyable game, but I wouldn't have bought it if it hadn't been on sale, but considering I only ever buy Total War games if they are on sale, that isn't saying much. This is now my tied for third with Napoleon behind Empire, and Shogun 2

This is one of the best romance Visual Novels of all time--and $20 is a steal.  If you're unfamiliar with the genre, think of this as like a "choose your own adventure" that starts at the same basic point but can branch off widely depending on your choices.  VNs like this are often erroneously called dating sims, but that's a different genre entirely.  VNs like this are more like a bundle of separate romance stories, the choices you can make in-game locking you in to one of the stories, or "routes."  Once you finish a route, you can start the game from the beginning, making different choices, and see how that changes the story.
VNs like Nekopara or the Sakura- games have probably given VNs a bit of a negative reputation around here, but this game doesn't stoop to those lows.  The story is sweet, cute, mixes in drama, comedy, and supernatural elements, and doesn't rely on fanservicey CGs to keep you playing.  This is the way the game was
to be played, too, so you won't be playing a hacked-up Steam version.

The visual novel from which my all time favorite anime is based upon, so I am hopelessly biased here.  I bought the original (unvoiced!) Japanese version of this visual novel years ago, re-bought the voiced edition when Key released it in Japan, and now I'm glad this story is finally translated to English.  If you love visual novels and love emotional rides then CLANNAD is for you.  If you loved the anime, this visual novel is for you.
The only potential issue from this superb work is that CLANNAD is quite lengthy.  Some people will find that to be a positive, others will find that it is a negative.  The story unfolds at a remarkably sedate pace (even compared to the anime) so the reader truly settles into the routine of school life.  But along the way you will be fully immersed with Itaru Hinoue's gorgeous art and Maeda's music.  From Ushio's theme that plays in the main menu to the opening and ending themes, the music of the visual novel is amazing and will be instantly familiar to those used to the anime.

The game is relatively old, but is surely classic. It goes wider and deeper than the CLANNAD animation. Many of the stories that were not clearly illustrated in the animation can be found in the game. Thanks to these playthroughs I can now fully understand the entire construct of the TV anime. Owning to the multiple 'route' mechanism which is commonly seen in visual novels, the producers must have found it difficult to convert it to an anime. But I must say they did a splendid job. Some people found the anime endings confusing. If that's the case and they still love CLANNAD, I surely recommend this game as it clearifies lots of the mysteries. Judged individually apart from the consequent anime, the game is absolutely the best of its kind and we love it as much as the anime.
The game has minor shortcomings indeed. First there are very few animations. The game is old so that's fairly acceptable. Second, Tomoya has no voice cast. I know for sure that they want the 'player' to be at the center of the stage but after watching the anime it's a little bit weird. Finally, we need fully Japanese support for subtitles and UI. There are many translations that just not fit and sounds pretty bizzare. For the game is initially Japanese, I do not see much difficulty in adding language support.
If you are new to visual novel and CLANNAD, I'd recommend the anime at first hand since it can be more appealing and vivid that the game. But if you seek a deeper dive and ask more about the detials, there you go!
P.S. Another thing great about the game is that it contains no ’エロ’ things considering its genre. Family and love in this story surely take us way beyond that :)

It's so good, I cannot recommend it enough. The story pacing is excellent, and the story length is surprsingly extensive. I've experienced two story arks (Nagisa and Kyou) so far. Both arks were joyful and had incredibly powerful and genuine moments. CLANNAD brings a lot of joy and happiness, but that also comes with heartaches that can leave you weeping for hours.
Note: I played this before watching the anime. After I completed Nagisa's story ark I decided to watch CLANNAD After Story (24 episodes) for more closure. I highly recommend doing that if you are new to CLANNAD like I was.

With no context, the options are quite arbitrary. (ex: what did "we" do at the party? You'll have to tell me, 'cause the game certainly didn't)
The requirement of typing gibberish is a nuisance.
The options are often pointless, non-descriptive (so I end up wondering what the connotation of the option is), and have practically no impact on how the game proceeds (though I read that there is a "horrible" ending where, if you treat Emily especially bad, she simply stops talking to you in the last chapter, instead of your character saying - eventually - good-bye). Other than a single line of dialogue (how Emily responds) after each choice, the rest is identical.
In terms of the story, the flow is illogical. The characters call things "weird" without explaining what they mean. They refuse to go after what they want. It is quite frustrating.
The game frequently tells you that "Emily will remember that" - that feels stolen from Telltale. In any case, it doesn't add anything. Since all dialogue is essentially the same, it's also meaningless.
By the end of it, I was quite happy to say "good-bye".

Great graphics, set design, soundtrack, atmosphere, very cinematic. Gets the feel and ambiance of the original Ridley Scott film very well. There were several times where I was startled in classic horror movie fashion. However, the gameplay tasks become repetitive real quick. The game could be great but is absolutely ruined by a horrible save system that has you repeating menial tasks over and over without progressing anywhere in the game. The alien also pops up randomly and kills you regardless of how quiet you are, which is scary and fun at first, but only highlights the horrible save system. Having to repeat menial tasks over and over with good graphics is not content. Having to stumble around in the dark trying to figure out what to do by trial and error in basically a one shot one kill darwinian environment is not content. It's just frustrating. Glad I got this on sale but still not worth the time or money. I have a library full of great games that are challenging and fun to play without needlessly frustrating you. Why would I play a game that's repetitive without much actual story? Very poor game design choice by restricting saves. Ruins what could otherwise be a great game. Will reconsider playing again if they update the save system. 5/10 If they change the save system could be 8 or 9/10.

Transistor is an Sci-Fi themed Indie-ARPG, with a kinda similar atmosphere as Bastion, even tho the general story and gameplay differ.
The strongest points in this game are the beatiful and enjoyable music, the wonderful and appealing art, a refreshing combat system, consisting of real-time as well as tactical paused and planned out combat, the flexible difficulty system, where you can change the difficulty of this game in many different ways, and last but not least the way of story-telling through narration, which  reminds me of Bastion.
The story might be confusing at first, but if you listen carefully and read all the descriptions and backstory, you're going to enjoy the amazing and interesting story line of Transistor.
The weakest link of this game is the very short length, even shorter than Bastion, but i'd much more prefer quality over quantity, and this is without a doubt a quality product.
If you enjoyed Bastion, are a fan of Indie-like game or want to experience a kinda different gameplay than usual games, Transistor is the right game for you, but you might want to wait for it to go on sale.

Think of it as Diablo 2 with an optional turn-by-turn mode in a beautiful art deco apocalypse.
To boil it down, you choose between 'functions' (which work like attacks in Pokemon: of many, you only get four at once) to mow down robots in a gorgeously-rendered future city.
The kicker: every few seconds you can pause the action, move about, and queue up a combo of attacks. When you unpause, you whoosh about the battle spitting explosions. You've got a few seconds of helpless fleeing - then you're off again, chaining up attacks.
Trust me: nothing beats laying down three consecutive damage multipliers on a high-level enemy then knocking them off in a single hit.
Difficulty can be raised with optional handicaps called Limiters.
There's a clever system around the functions themselves, too: any function can modify another or provide a passive bonus. I.e., you can add a quick-firing attack to a slower one – increasing the slower attack’s speed, but forgoing the quicker attack entirely.

Anyone that liked Bastion will find this to measure up quite nicely.
The "continue" mechanic forces you to change your approach to combat, that is quite customizable anyway.
Soundtrack is great too.

Just Cause 3 is at its best when you're role-playing a sort of jazz sociopath. Flying a plane into a silo of fuel tanks, tethering cars to a bridge and blowing it up, using modified C4 boosters on civilians. It comes alive in these moments, when you're flitting between violent, explosive acts – a rebel without a cause, just or otherwise. Just Cause 3's problem is that every one of its surrounding systems detracts from this anarchic core. There's fun to be had, once you untether yourself from the stingy unlocks, the need to liberate endless provinces, and the relentless militia. The game preaches chaos, but constantly holds you back with rules and restrictions.
Once again, you play Rico Rodriguez – former CIA operative, and a regime-change specialist. Rico has returned to his homeland, the fictional island of Medici, where he plans to overthrow dictator Di Ravello and his military, the DRM (see what they did there?). If you've played Just Cause 2, you'll be familiar with Rico's modus operandi. If not, here's a hint: explosions. Rico must destroy the red and white objects that denote Di Ravello's infrastructure. Military bases are filled with satellites, electric substations, fuel tanks, and so on. Towns and villages contain propaganda speakers, billboards and statues. Clear a settlement of all these things, and you liberate it for the resistance.
PROS:
-Beautiful
-varied environment
-Great tools for destruction and traversal
-The explosions look amazing
CONS:
-Too much repetition of objectives
-Basic features hidden behind unlock system
-An overreliance on gunplay

Disclaimer: This review reflects my free weekend experience back in April 2017 and doesn't consider the new Morrowind expansion – I am also not a MMO player to begin with - Please consider these aspect when reviewing this review as you might like the game. I just cannot recommend personally based on the review below.
Actual review:
My first experience was not convincing as I got a few annoyances right of the bat:
- First thing I noticed was what the engine doesn’t seem to display smooth image even at 60 FPS all maxed for some reason.
- Next, I got some connection lag a few times in a row out of the blue and even ended up getting disconnected later on while playing on first play session – This was a free weekend so it might have to do with it but come on its an MMO it should handle the load in particular if you want to attract new players…
- Right after that the next thing I notice - this is likely inherent to MMO’s but - other players are often in your way – I am trying to loot something from a corpse and other players pop up in from of me and I get to see an interaction menu preventing me from looting normally – annoying! P.S. I didn’t check but I hope there is a trigger button to enable the player interaction menu such as holding the ALT key (only an example) to see the menu.
- Logged back into the game and my character had an invisible body until I spawned into the next cut scene / load time (right in front of the Prophet).
- I moved on as the ambiance was growing into me and started talking to the first NPC of relative interest (Khajiit on the boat) and I am distracted by his sword floating on his left side – It is one the first encounters with the player and it is not even polished – seriously?
~ P.S. Obviously the detail above is minor but some people will be annoyed by the lack of attention to details – and I repeat that this is one of the first encounters and that his sword floats and not attached to his body… that doesn’t sound well for the things to come.
- Also noticed poor SLI scaling support – nitpicking here but it’s still the case regardless.
Personally not a fan of the MMO genre so far so I felt it was somewhat a shame that the efforts were not put on a single player game (other TES fans will likely mention this as well in their review) - even more after looking at the preview of the Morrowind DLC which looks great.
Bottom line I cannot recommend it personally as I am more of a Single player campain kind of person but I guess if you are used to MMO’s you might like it still.
P.S. I was using a gigabit internet connection at the time so it wasn’t a problem for me but the size of the game plus the multiple patches that were needed seemed to be over 85 GB worth of download so do yourself a favor and go check a video before downloading – even if it’s a free promotional event.

I only played for a short while so I can't say much about the game other than I didn't like a single second of its moment to moment gameplay. An hour of play has made me go from "wide awake" to "I need a nap". The heart of the gameplay feels off. The combat is incredibly stiff, the controls are awkward, and the game's nature as an MMO leads to an overbearing level of dissonance.
It's hard to feel like your character matters in the world when other players wait in line to "stealth kill" the plot enemy or run in from out of nowhere to instantly wreck the quest boss you're fighting. The best example of this is in the game's opening moments. You fight your way through a short prison segment, you're told by your companion to kill some important big bads for some reason or other, and then you're immediately thrown into a playpen of other level 1 players running in circles and swinging at nothing. For me personally it feels like a tonal 180° from what I like about Elder Scrolls titles. I have nothing against MMO design, I just wish the game was more instanced than it seems to be. (From the small bit I played.)
I'm sure there's a great community and a number of great features to enjoy in the game. But I just don't have the motivation to dive back in right now.

Something more need to talk about for this game. The exploitation for resources.
Lots of games nowadays, despite from open world games, are linear.
And the problem with linear games, the biggest thing is that the exploitation ratio is so low on the resources for the game, by which it can be pertained to maps, models, and objects and any other exploitable resources.
A map, you go in a maze and go all around and end up at the goal and rewards. And then, the trails you've been using are all rendered useless and ditched sideways.
A lot of games that prior to recent few years have this problem, devs designed tons of maps, tons of mazes, and rendered each one of them, putting all immersion into the environment, the visuals, the sounding, the effects et al. So if the game doesn't have much of replayability, then the trails are basically useless after players achieved the goal, on which creates a high waste ratio of the games.
I can list some examples to further clarify the subject.
Mass Effect 3, a game that is built on massive scales and a wide scope and complexity, which, in most of cases, missions, side quests, you have to run through a lot of meaningless paths to get to the final goal. And developers actually put a lot of efforts into rendering the paths
, but, you have run through them anyways.
A maze if it's a straight line to goal, add some obstacles in the path, would be dull and boring. Thus designers thought out adding more paths and side trails and more complexity of the maze to increase the playability of the game. A lot of modern games follow this rule, and even spike it. But some other studios don't think this way.
Certainly, maze is important for games, but if you can make the best use of it, the playability and replayability would certainly skyrocket for the game.
From Software has made it very clear for players. The wit of level design in Souls series has been observed by public. The maps are not only for passing use, but also a function for replayability, which is a more and more attentive subject for present and future games.
Alien: Isolation, least, did a good job on this. You'd be surprised by the massiveness of Sevastopol and the complexity for in game maps, but the best of all, the game is set in a massive station where you won't go anywhere else besides the few maps. So you have to keep passing through and using the few maps, which, makes up a high exploitation ratio for the game. And it's good. Players can discover and have more new experiences during the repetitive use of the resources. And simultaneously there's a potential, or close proximity threat for players to always keep them keens on. The game suddenly, though not saying ME3 is a bad game, exceeds the replayability and playability by using an amount of maps than ME3 using tons of rendered environments and maps and lots of works.
Hard work doesn't equal smart work, by using this method, I believe a game can be finished in less time than the original.
Horror games though, settings-wise, are based on small and sealed environments, and Isolation on a certainty, also is linear, it's partially linear. So let's say being using the model of linear plot, it did a good job on reusing/exploitation of game resources.
Things other than maps and mazes that pertains to exploitation, well, a lot could be named. Like for the immersion, adding a lot of npcs, or non-interactive npcs. The in-game objects, like pens, books, notes. And lots of more. Just how do you make use of them and smartly make the best use of them, it's upon you.

RO lovers rejoice! You'll feel right at home in ToS so stop reading now and start playing! For those who have never dabbled in RO, much fun can still be had whether you choose F2P or premium. Quite a bit of negativity going around lately but just keep in mind that it is still early days so of course improvements will be needed. Despite that, I've had a very positive and enjoyable experience so far and I don't see that changing anytime soon.
The devs are also constantly taking the voice of the community into account when releasing their frequent updates. The most recent update will alleviate the complaints on trading and team storage restrictions that you've all read about. If they continue on this path (I've witnessed no signs at all that says otherwise) then ToS will only get better and better.
Pros:
-Gorgeous art. Very unique in a saturated genre.
-Fluid combat system that works great with a gamepad.
-Tons of class choices (around 80) and even more are planned.
-Stat points to customize your unique (or cookie cutter) build to your liking, leading to many different play styles.
-Pleasant soundtrack.
-Dev team that is adamant on fighting bots and gold sellers.
-In-game bot reporting system complete with rewards and punishment for abusing the tool.
-Cash shop pay to win aspect is extremely minor so far. Mostly cosmetics.
-Good amount of crafting available.
-F2P. Premium token can be acquired with in-game currency, which has been fairly easy to accomplish thus far if you know what you're doing (a few days grinding for your average low to mid level players, even less if you're higher level or skilled).
Cons:
-Needs optimization. Very sluggish in crowded areas, especially main cities even though you may have a boss PC.
-Very linear quest system. Only a problem when you decide to make a few characters.
-Price of premium (~$18 USD) is very expensive even when compared to AAA titles and their subscriptions.
-Some premium token features (team storage, less restricted trading) are available as standard in most other games.
-The sheer amount of classes can be punishing if you take a misstep somewhere along the line so plan wisely.
-Low spawn rates (although this is always subject to change).
-Huge item market selling tax without premium token (30% vs 10%).
-48 hours to retrieve silver after selling item in market (to fight gold sellers).

Where do I start?
I have played in each and every international beta released starting in August.
Many things have changed since then be it level caps, zones, mechanics, or server side XP.
That being said I have put nearly 800 hours between the beta releases and the current early access and I plan to put many more.
If you are reading this then its likely you saw the game has "mixed" reviews right now. I implore you to actually go through the list of reviews and funnel out the massive amount of thumbs down by people who have played the game for absolutely no time considering this is an MMO. There are also people who are down voting it simply based on a mechanic they dislike rather than giving it a proper review.
Now onto the actual game review. I am currently around level 230 with the current cap being 280. I suggest you do research into the type of character you wish to build and the paths it will take.
Currently there are quest available till around level 235 and from that point on you will actually need to really grind if you wish to reach the maximum level. If you do research you will find you can reach level 200 without any grinding at all fairly easy(Don't waste cards).
At level 100 leveling gets easier as it opens up daily missions and quest which scale to your level.
The game offers controller support, keyboard support and mouse support. However I will say controller support needs to be refined a bit more to allow key mapping.
Graphical settings are fairly basic but they are now adding more to the game to help improve the experience of those who need them.
The musical score in this game is phenomenal and its fairly rare for most mmos to keep you wanting to keep the OST on rather than mute it and listen to your own music.
The game offers a wide variety of classes to play each with unique skills to make use of.
While you could very well solo in this game up to a certain point with no issues its highly recommended you try and party though content. Not only will you get through the content faster but leveling will be faster and its great to make friends at the same time.
A cash shop does exist but as of right now 4/26/2016 its in no way P2W which is great.
Cons -
The biggest con of the game currently is that there are quite a few restrictions which are getting worked on due to player feedback. I don't however believe this game deserves a bad review because of them which if you notice is where the majority of the thumbs down come from.

Bots are a problem in every mmo and just like those this game will have bots they are however publicly announcing bot bans every day and added a system so players can report the bots they see.
All in all I highly recommend if you want a new mmo to try this game out and then form your own opinion afterward on if its worth your time or not.

Let me start by saying this: If you liked Bastion you will like Transistor.
Transistor is an isometric action game with almost turn based elements. The main meat of the gameplay is centered around the planning mechanic in which you stop time and plan out a series of attacks. After hitting accept and seeing the madness unfold you must dodge enemies (and their attacks) until your planning meter refills. It feels great and during the course of the game you get several abilities that can be mixed and matched for new results.
The art is done by Jen Zee who also did the art for Bastion and like Bastion the art is sprawling, playful and stylish. Darren Korb returns to compose more tunes as well as creating the sound and nothing could be better. Logan Cunningham who played Rucks in Bastion also returns to lend his voice talent again and as does Ashley Barret. If you have no intentions of playing Transistor at least check out the soundtrack on Spotify.
The biggest flaw I'm willing to throw at the game would be the length, as it is relatively short but it ends when it should and doesn't outstay it's welcome, much like the original Portal. Finally the story is a bit vague to be sure but this leads you on as a player to discover the truth behind Cloudbank and the catastrophe that has befallen the city.
Finally, Transistor just feels more deliberate and thought out than Bastion did. Reading or listening to their development of Bastion a lot the design decisions felt more like happy accidents than actual thought choices. I really enjoyed Bastion and I think you might too, especially if you liked Bastion.

Transistor is a beautiful game - the aesthetic alone makes this game worth a playthrough. Gorgeous handpainted visuals and a brilliant soundtrack by Darren Korb easily make it worth the price of admission. The combat style works nicely, and can be surprisingly strategic - though truth be told, once you find the right combination of powers, you'll probably just spam the same strategy over and over in the main game (the optional challenges thankfully provide more of a challenge). In terms of narrative, once again Supergiant Games have employed a similar delivery strategy to Bastion, though in a completely different context. However, Transistor is far more obtuse than Bastion (which also didn't spell out everything about its world). I'm not a fan of stories that handhold you, and I love when games use their environments to support the story (it's the kind of storytelling only videogames can do well). In Transistor's case, a little more handholding and environmental interaction would have helped make the ending feel earned. The final act of the game seems rushed. With all of that being said - the experience is still exceptional, and Supergiant Games are proving themselves adepts at this particular kind of game, aesthetic, and worldbuilding. If you value aesthetic over explosions, I highly recommend.

What Call of Juarez Gunslinger inspires in me is the competitiveness of the old school arcade shooters. Gunslinger offers three modes; story mode and arcade mode and duel mode. Duel mode is mostly forgettable with a minigame style showdown.
It is the arcade mode and story mode that is the standout of the game. For me, Arcade mode alone makes this game worth it. The game is semi-fast paced point-based first person shooter. In arcade mode, shooting enemies yields points. Shooting enemies in the head, yields more points. Shooting enemies in succession yields multipliers, which yields even more points. Points galore! Yes, the arcade mode is about getting the highest score possible and this really makes the game competitive especially for those perfectionists and competitive gamers.
The story mode is an added benefit. The story itself is surprisingly good, offering a unique storytelling style. Without spoiling it, it will definitely keep you entertained and even a few chuckles along the way.
If I had a minor complaint, it would be that the arcade mode stages are all based on the stages from the Story mode. It would've been nice to have a larger variety of stages not already seen from the story mode. But this is a minor complaint, and doesn't detract from the fact that this game is such a solid shooter.
The game's gimmick is also a bullet time style power that slows everyone down. Nothing innovative in this aspect, but the gunplay makes this game highly satisfying to play. For the low price point, you will certainly get your money's worth for it.

Before I begin, if you're interested in buying this game, you might as well as get the other two games that are apart of this trilogy. You can get the bundle for cheap during a sale, which is what I did.
Now...
A lot of people compare this game to the Fallout series, and for good reason. I will also do the same.
To briefly summarize, take Fallout, remove the leveling up system with perks, and turn on hardcore mode, and you have S.T.A.L.K.E.R. Oh, and also replace every character with their Slavic counterpart.
For a game released in 2007, this game is surprisingly well detailed. Particularly on its weapons. Each weapon feels different, and you have to aim well and shoot in bursts in order to do any damage, as spraying will usually just leave you wide open as the recoil takes your gun into the sky. Don't be too slow, because before you know it, your enemy will kill you, as bullets do as much damage to you as they do to the enemy (excluding mutants, but we'll get to that later). And if your gun is old and worn, your gun can even jam in the middle of combat, forcing you to take cover and reload to clear the jam.
The Scenery is well done, and while the graphics themselves are choppy, the atmosphere the environment puts you in is nevertheless effective. The map looks exactly like what it's suppose to be; an irradiated part of Ukraine, around the Chernobyl power plant. There are even some horror elements in this game as well. Some missions lead you into dark underground facilities, crawling with mutated irradiated horrors. There have been several times where I actually feel scared to explore these facilities, because of how dark it is, and how you can hear the mutants moving around the other parts of the facilities.
The story in this game is not a strong point, but is still a good driving point to continue. Following the story takes you to knew areas in the game where you can get involved with more factions, allowing you to partake in more jobs and get better equipment.
Combat in this game is difficult, but realistically so, not infuriatingly so. This game forces you to think tactically, take cover, and actually aim. It's not like most FPS games where you can just tank bullets from 10 different guys and come out on top. Even on the easy difficulty, a single lowly Bandit can easily put down your God-tier Late Game character if you're not careful.
Some of the weaker points of this game, however, come in the AI. The AI interact well with eachother, but not at all with you. They seldom utilize their environment in combat, often standing in the open while you shoot at them (however they will scramble like mad if you throw a grenade in their direction). One time I even got the tactical edge on a group of enemies by flanking them and open fired. It took very long for them to stop walking casually and engage in combat, but by then they were already dead.
Another issue I have is the camera, which has this annoying back-and-forth sway motion whenever your character runs or sprints, but after awhile it becomes more tolerable, but still annoying. However, the later S.T.A.L.K.E.R. games fix this issue, so it's not even that big of a deal.
Overall, the STALKER games are my favorite games of all time, and on this particular one I'd have to give it a solid 8.5/10. If you're a fan of freeroam RPG-style games, I'd definitely check out STALKER.

One of the best FPS exploration oriented games I've ever played. Probably THE best.
I would HIGHLY recommend the Autumn Aurora mod, it updates graphics with depth of field and wonderful fects t subtly and realistically add to the atmosphere of the game, including damage  (edit: I don't remember if the weapon mod is included in the mod, but I'd highly recommend it to make damage more realistic both ways).
Atmosphere is paramount -- never before have I played a shooter in which I experience a sense of comradery with AI while simultaneously feeling incredibly alone and vulnerable. It's one of the few games that genuinely feels like its world operates on its own and you explore it and must respect it, rather than it being built around the player. The people you meet could be friends or could be hostile, or simply neutral, warning you to leave them alone. A seemingly straight forward raid can turn deadly in a split second all because you didn't check that last corner and a bandit happened to see you. You can reload the same firefight 10 times and the outcome can be dramatically different each time, with or without your involvement.
Atmosphere is a difficult thing to describe effectively, but the blend of hazardous environment, terrifying abominations and other people simply trying to survive in the Zone makes for a difficult and highly immersive survival shooter well worth playing.

The opinions about this game kinda crashing together.
All I can really tell you is try it for yourself. In about a week or smth this game is going to be free to play.
In my opinion the issues with botters, gold sellers and performance is real but nothing what is kinda different to other MMOs I played. And there is a patch incoming with allowing for better trade options and so on, so they are working to improve the game.
There is stuff which could be better, like the social part of this game. In most cases you walk either with a friend or alone. But the gameplay itself is very polished, there are tons of classes/builds and skills to combine, I really love that system (kinda like ArcheAge but you have to circle through 7 classes).
To give you a small sum up:
PROS:
- Tons of classes to choose and develop
- Ragnarok similar art style modernized
- Really awesome controller support (play it with a PS4 controller), feels like playing Breath of Fire 4.
- For a F2P game there is atm. not much to call it pay to win, there is actually just one item which gives you great benefits but you are able to buy it with the ingame currency from players.
- Even thou the maps are a bit linear, there are many and big one, so it fills the gap.
- "Endcontent" Earth Tower which is comparable to Sword Art Online's Castle, you have to climb up and as far as I know the highest level reached is 20 so far (I could be wrong with this information)
- No real level cap, the soft cap is at around 270 at the moment
- Stat point allocation, so many MMOs dropped that system which makes me kinda sad because I had to define my character with equipment only, but not here. There is a good balance betweet equipment stats and the ones you picked.
CONS:
- Regular performance drops. While I have most of the time 120+fps there are recent drops for like half a second to like 15fps. This really has to be fixed.
- The character customization is actually not really existent. You can choose boy/girl and one of like 6 hairstyles. That is kinda lame.
- Kill stealing. For me personally this is nothing new because I played Lineage2 for like 8 years, but it is kinda annoying in this generation of MMOs
- Bots & Goldseller. While they are annoying, bots are kinda more polite than most players, because they don't kill steal :D
- Class balance. There are few classes which really have to get more love, like the summoner for example
- Lone wolf MMO, there has to be more social stuff to care about in this game. While I like the public party system (you see parties with open slots nearby) this is not enough. I mean Ragnarok was like a freakin MMODRPG (massive multiplayer online dating role play game), but I don't see it even close here.
So why do I recommend this game?
You know I started with hundreds of new MMOs and saw how they launched, in most cases it was always chaos and stuff that should be different. Even GW2 had a crap start with hundreds of gold sellers or FFXIV with servers all the time down and queries to the moon for joining the game. With this one it does not feel much different. YES there are issues which needs to be adressed asap, but you can see and play so much content for an inofficial Ragnarok 2.5. Give this game a try and the developers some love and I'm pretty sure you might enjoy it a lot ;)

TL:DR = This is a great game depending on what you like. Do your research before getting involved.
I would reccomend this game to people, but it really depends on what you're looking for. What I will say is that there are many people on here complaining about things that the publisher cant do anything about. For example bots. There are hundreds, if not thousands of bots banned on a daily basis. But they still exist. This has to do with the detrmination of the botting community more than it does with the publisher. They honestly try, but botters are a plague to EVERY MMO. What I can say for the publisher is that they're at least trying, which is more than I can say for other games.
Character builds:
There are many character classes (upwards of 80). Which sounds like a lot, but really, the way the class system works, there are only so many paths you can go. There is more variety the higher tier you go, but makes for limited skill power. So I think it really comes down to whether you should specialize and have a few powerful skills, or diversify and have many, weaker skills. Attributes are a thing that helps with this, and at first I thought they sounded neat (pay some silver to make a skill better? Sweet!) But in reality they feel like a silver dump, and there isn't all that much variety. As for stats... I think that is where the builds are the most lacking. For most characters you just pump your main stat. Potions are cheap and easy to obtain, so you dont *need* Con or Spr. All that said: here is one thing I do like about characters in this game: You cant mess them up. Sure there are ideal builds. There always are. But if you put a few points of something somewhere less perfect, you're still going to be able to survive and advance.
Gameplay:
This is a grind fest. If that is your thing, then this game will appeal to you. If not then avoid it. I saw several people complaining about the grinding. I honestly dont know why. All I had to know about this game was that it was korean and I knew it would be grinding. That said, you can avoid much of it by doing quests and earning exp cards. Honestly, even the quests are grinding after a while. So many fetch quests. But for me, I like grinding. I feel a sense of accomplishment after putting a few hours into my character and finally seeing the level up animation. Too many people feel entitled to a high tier character with no effort. Seriously, just go play WoW people...
I've seen people complain about the repetitiveness of the combat. This is related to the grind fest nature of the game. Honestly I think its a lot of fun at times. My biggest disappointment are the bosses, but I think that has more to do with the class I play than anything. (I see videos of others taking time to kill bosses, where they die in literally seconds to my Hoplite, which is known as a boss killer class.)
The thing that I love most about this game are the things they put in for the collector in me. I feel driven to 100% every map. And to visit every map to get that 100%. Nearly every map also has a collection. Some of these are easy to finish, some near impossible. But they are worth finishing because they give small bonuses to not only your current character, but all other characters on your account as well. To me, grinding for these give me something else to do rather than just grinding away for a level. There are also achievements for various things, though I wish they were more varried. The crafting system also give me purpose to my grinding. "Oh hey, I found a recipe for a club of awesomeness... I could make that if I just went to kill some things on that map over there."
Many people complain about the trading in this game, and I guess I can see why. But to be honest, with nearly 180 hours under my belt, I never once felt like trading anyone. With most things, if you really need them, you can grind for them yourself. And you can sell things on the market easily enough. I think the biggest complaint in this department are from those too cheap to buy a token. Without a token you can only sell one thing on the market at a time. With one you can sell 5 things at a time. Without a token you cant use storage to transfer things between your characters. With a token, its no problem. I fear this complaint will only get worse with the game opening as free2play soon. Honestly, I dont care. This company needs to make money to continue to devolpe the game. Don't believe the negativity; and let me get the negatives out of the way first, this game does not have lag issues, and no it is NOT Pay2Win.
With that out of the way, Tree of Savior (ToS) is a very beautiful and fun game, very much akin to the days of Ragnarok online, it is a 2.5D MMORPG, and is literally the spritual successor to Ragnarok Online. There are so many class varieties and builds, garaunteed to satisfy anyone from softcore to hardcore gamers. Leveling speed is pretty quick, you level your physical level and your class seperately, but simultaneously. Story quests give you multitudes of items, specifically things called "Exp Cards" which give chunks of exp to both class and physical levels to help speed leveling along at a semi-casual pace, but most importantly, levels as of now, feel like they matter and took time, when I see a lvl 200+ I actually feel impressed.
The story so far (lvl 50 as of writing this) is pretty decent, nothing spectacular, etc, generic MMO story for the most part (thus far mind you)
Graphics are amazing. The watercolor paint inspired character art and graphics are amazing and breathtaking.
The sound and music are very good, especially for a MMORPG. Each area has a pretty catchy tune associated with it, and abilities, feel very heavy and hardhitting which is a very good plus, stocks sounds are at a minimum here.
Last but not least, the cash shop, it offers pay4convenience and in no way is Pay2Win (at least as of writing this review)
I hope you'll check this game out, it definitely deserves some love!

A short story about the end of an alternate sci-fi world.  I finished the game in about 6 hours and enjoyed all of it.  The gameplay is entertaining and interesting.  You have numerous skill combos at your disposal, and there's never really a "bad" combo or a forced way of playing.  Transistor isn't very challenging without turning on handicaps called Limiters (same as Idols from Bastion), but with the handicaps on things get interesting.
The main reason to play Transistor is for the story and music.  Supergiant Games does a fantastic job drawing you in and making you feel for the characters.  If you let loose and take in the story, then you will love this game and I highly recommend.  If you're just in it for the gameplay, then you might not be interested.

Yet another masterpiece from the creators of Bastion. The story, while rather vauge even after the game is finished, is still a fantastic one and with such an amazing voice actor. The combat was out of this world; mixing real-time gameplay from Bastion while having the option to use turn-based elements that made it feel like Fall-Out 1 & 2 except during the turn you were much more over-powered. The game is also about half as long as Bastion, or just as long if you don't choose to go to find the second ending of Bastion. All in all, this game is a must play, and I'd have to rate it an 8/10.

Transistor is a beautiful game - the aesthetic alone makes this game worth a playthrough. Gorgeous handpainted visuals and a brilliant soundtrack by Darren Korb easily make it worth the price of admission. The combat style works nicely, and can be surprisingly strategic - though truth be told, once you find the right combination of powers, you'll probably just spam the same strategy over and over in the main game (the optional challenges thankfully provide more of a challenge). In terms of narrative, once again Supergiant Games have employed a similar delivery strategy to Bastion, though in a completely different context. However, Transistor is far more obtuse than Bastion (which also didn't spell out everything about its world). I'm not a fan of stories that handhold you, and I love when games use their environments to support the story (it's the kind of storytelling only videogames can do well). In Transistor's case, a little more handholding and environmental interaction would have helped make the ending feel earned. The final act of the game seems rushed. With all of that being said - the experience is still exceptional, and Supergiant Games are proving themselves adepts at this particular kind of game, aesthetic, and worldbuilding. If you value aesthetic over explosions, I highly recommend.

Call of Juarez: Gunslinger, well I certainly was very surprised with this game after just an hour of playing. I remember back when this came out and a friend recommended it to me and I had little no interest in it. Well I must admit that he was certainly right with this game and I wish that I had played it a long time ago. Call of Juarez takes place back in the 1800’s during the Wild West, which was surprisingly a lot more entertaining that I had thought. I was never into westerns and was often just bored with the whole genre, but Call of Juarez actually made the genre fun for me. I don’t believe that any of the events in this game are historically accurate but who cares, it is still fun! Now many of the characters in this game are old gunslingers and outlaws such as Billy the Kid and Johnny Ringo. This game actually does a good job of altering history so that you fit right in. It doesn’t feel like the developers just bs’d the entire story. There have been so many games recently with stories that were just completely boring and pointless, but Call of Juarez actually makes a nice fictional story that is very engaging and entertaining. Some humor is also present in this game, it’s always nice to have a chuckle here and there. I was afraid that this game would have a dull story like many other low profile games currently, but Call of Juarez takes the cake in this sense.
Aside from the surprisingly good story and characterization, the graphics in the game were also much better than I had expected. Once again, this is a low profile game and I was expecting it to have dated graphics and visuals, but once again Call of Juarez proved my expectations wrong. This being said, the graphics are very well done and the maps and environments are beautiful. There were many parts that looked just like the real thing; I know this because I live in the same area.
The next thing on my list is the gameplay and mechanics. This is where Call of Juarez falls just a tiny bit short. So the actual shooting/movements/controls were perfect. I absolutely loved just how smooth it is to control your character and how smooth the shooting felt. I didn’t have to go through hell and back to learn all the controls and get used to the movements the way I did with Dead Space. This always adds a huge plus to any game. Considering the majority of games I play are shooters, it is always annoying when a shooter comes out and the controls and movements are $#!+. So call of Juarez is perfect in this category. The only part of the gameplay I didn’t really enjoy were the 1 on 1 shooting duels. These weren’t exactly poorly done, but they were just very frustrating and very unbalanced. I don’t see why I can get shot by 30 different outlaws at the same time, but when I had a duel with Johnny Ringo, I died in a instant. I would of just liked if they did this aspect of the game a little differently so that it was more balanced and less frustrating.
Next is the shooting, wow this was done perfectly! I never realized how fun it was to go on a shooting rampage with dual golden revolvers while in slow motion while chucking a few sticks of dynamite just in case! I absolutely loved how this was done in this game. Aside from just slowing down time and shooting all your enemies, you can also use your senses to lean back and fourth to dodge incoming bullets that miss your head by just a few millimeters! All of the weapons in this game are very well balanced and even though there’s not a huge variety of weapons, it’s still just non stop fun! Why can’t more shooters be like this? Instead of making more and more modern warfare shooters, why don’t we make shooters that are actually fun and entertaining? Yes I’m looking at you Call of Duty, take your thumb out of your butt and don’t be stupid/racist/and boring as a brick with a face drawn on with crayon….. Anyway, the shooting in Call of Juarez is perfect. It seems like the developers actually took into consideration all the good and bad things of previous shooters and compiled it all into a game that has some of the absolute best shooting mechanics I have ever seen! This is what a game developer are supposed to do, take out, or improve all the bad things from previous games and focus on making the good things ever better. I honestly can’t believe just how amazing Call of Juarez is! It’s only $15 and appears to have so much more work put into it than so many other games.
With all this being said, I’m afraid there always has to be a downside to every game. Unfortunately Call of Juarez has a downside as well; which is that it’s to darn short! There has been a trend recently with games being less that 10 hours (Hard Reset, Mirrors Edge, Harry Potter 7+8, Amnesia Machine for Pigs, Outlast, Burial at Sea, Sniper Elite Nazi Zombie Army 1+2, Doorways, ok you get my point) But I really don’t like how games are a lot shorter nowadays. I suppose I can let Call of Juarez slide since it was only $15, but I still wanted more fun dangit!
So what else is there to say? Overall Call of Juarez is some of the best 6 hours I’ve had in the last month or so and I would highly recommend it to somebody who is sick of the typical shooters out there. Even if you never liked westerns, Call of Juarez is a wonderful experience and you can count on me replaying it may times! 8/10

I'm giving this game a positive review, because all in all, it is a great game that has just been launched and I believe it can improve a lot more. Even though this is a positive review, I'll concentrate in giving my opinion about what's bad in the game and what needs improvement.
I think if an MMO is to succeed for many years, leveling and gaining experience needs to be extremely hard. It should be almost impossible to reach the maximum level, so that the game could be more competitive and people wouldn't get bored of it, if everyone reaches the maximum level, then what's the point? So far, from what I've seen, it's way too easy to level up and gain experience.
The game suffers from bad lagging, it's very annoying, even with a fast internet speed such as 100mbps which I am using, the game lags way too much. It's so annoying to be running through a map, and return to the same place over and over again because of the lag and server connection. Also when killing mobs this happens, and for several seconds it's unresponsive until it finally responds and it's too late and you're dead, especially when you're killing bosses.
24 hour maintenance seems like a little exagerated, no matter how much transfers they have to make, at least this was their excuse, 24 hours should never happen. Even though, I believe that if great work and improvements are being done during this time, then it's worth the wait, but if they keep making such long periods of maintenance with no major improvements, then this is a no no.
Finally, this is the point that annoys me the most... We are playing an MMO, with stunning environment and story rich, so what's with the electronic dance music? Seriously?!? I don't really write reviews as I don't see how my opinions on this game should reflect your decision on buying it, so here is my long and probably boring review of Alien Isolation!
Alien Isolation is by far one of my most favourite games in the franchise to date. It just has so many good elements to it such as the Alien's A.I. being completely random for the majority of its behavior throughout the game, while the rest in certain scenes is scripted. The immersion is nicely done too, especially at the start, the game makes you question whether you are alone. The androids seem to only exist to be a nuisance, they constantly stand in the way and once they've seen you, they will follow you around the entire perimeter until you either outrun them or blast 'em with your weapon of choice. They take a fair amount of revolver bullets to take down, until later when you'll need a fully roladed shotgun to disable them.
It wouldn't be a review if I didn't talk a bit about the graphics now, would it? Of course when you max the graphics out at 1080p or beyond; it looks truly crisp and clear (well if you turn the film grain effect off it does) and 4K looks clear as a sunny day or clear as night in this case. The story is ok, I guess lol. Pretty much self-explanatory, you follow objectives given to you by different characters...blah, blah, blah. I've played and completed the game on both normal and hard mode. Hard mode does give the game a more challenging experience as the Alien's senses are elevated a lot more, meaning there is very little room for error. Especially if you haven't saved in a long time, which I may add, after you've done about 30 minutes of the story and either the Alien or andoid(s) kill you, you gotta go right back to that lastest save point. Speaking of which, the Alien seems to love the ventilation system of Sevastopol, it spends about maybe 55% of the time up there? While the other 45% of the time it constantly wanders around like a creepy stalker.
Maybe that last sentence wasn't a great pitch for buying the game...lol. But seriously, this game is worth the price...*ahem* when on sale. For an over two year old game, it should be half the full asking price. Just saying! All in all; I'd recommend this game purely because it's the most well made game of the Alien franchise. It has my seal of approval. If you don't like it, well, that's what the Steam refunds are for. xD

Probably the best product in the Alien universe since the second movie, and the best translation of the feel of the first one to another media I´ve come across. It´s in the retrofuture enviroment which takes you back to that world without feeling a copy-paste of the Nostromo´s insides, Sebastopol really feels like something from that world, and a place of dying hope even before the alien arrived. It´s one of the most immersive enviroments I´ve ever seen in a game.
Then there´s the monster, the AI can be difficult to grasp, (I played on Hard) but that means if you know it´s around (or may be) you are never going to feel safe. Even as you get better means to distract it or (briefly) scare it away, one distraction is all it´ll take. It also translates well to computer graphics, despite the original having such an "organic" feel to it. Not that there are going to be many chances of taking the time to admire it. Other enemies are usually more of a danger because they´ll attract the alien (human, though a shot can kill you as dead as the monster) or hamper avoiding it (Joes, playing with the uncanny valley on a good way).
On the down side, the middle act of the game can feel too long, at least until you start to realize what´s going on and begins to build (even more) tension, and exploring Sebastopol besides quest objectives is kind of an immersion breaker. I can´t see why Amanda would backtrack to places she has no need to while a deadly monster she has no means to kill is almost constantly stalking her, to get some ID tags of people she never met or records from the Nostromo that really   don´t tell her anything more about what happened to her mother (especially after learning as much as she ever was going to know during the storyline).
Still, this is the best Alien experience on a screen since 1986, and  one of the best horror games  I´ve played.

No More Room in Hell, one of the very first Source engine mods to be released as a fully functional game on Steam. An 80s movie themed zombie shooter that focuses on cooperation and tactics, on the higher difficulties this game will require you and your friends to pull together to even have a chance at surviving. Overrun by hordes of the infected you'll be fighting tooth and nail against the enemy just to get to the next objective or wave of the map.
The graphics, while not anything to write home about, are more than servicable for a free game. They are similar in quality to most other Source engine games, as well as include a fair amount of effects to simulate that feel of a true movie. These effects are very similar to games such as Left 4 Dead, another game that is likely an inspiration for this one.
The balance between melee weapons, explosives, and medicinal items are all very well done. Guns however, tend to differ drastically leading to many guns being fairly weak, and in a game with fairly few weapons this can be a fair problem. However, this is a rather realistic portrayal of weapons in a zombie apocalypse. Ammo is scarce and differs between the weapons, and is often best used to share between players who need the ammo more. Medicinal supplies can be used to heal after a long time, stave off infector, or in some rare and meaningful examples; cure the infecton.
The server system is the same used in most Source games,  and you'll only ever really see a performance hit if you're on a cross continental server.
The story is virtually nonexistent, however; in an arcade style video game such as this, that is both to be expected and excusable. The biggest semblance of story you can experience is a vague history of how the infection spread, and a blurb about the maps you join.
The maps are one of my favorite parts of the game. They are single segment maps that are either about survival or objectives. Despite my previous point that the graphics are not amazing, they give you the distinct impression of enough realism that you can easily be engrossed in your situation. Assuming you are playing at lower brightnesses as intended, it can be very easy to be startled by a zombie or even another player whilst playing this game, and encourages a lovely mixed environment of both suspense and anticipation. The music in this game is quite nice and atmospheric, but is nothing to write home about.
The business model with this game is entirely free, no strings attached (unless you want the pretty cool soundtrack.)
Overall, this game is one of my favorite Source engine mods and zombie games, combining Romero style zombies with fairly realistic gun and melee play, as well as a skill based cooperative experience that encourages both cooperation and agression.

Pros:
1-It doesn't feel repetative, and it's hardly scripted. Random events and enemies, as well as a developed "life cycle" for NPCs, makes the world feel alive and dangerous.
2-Edit: Gunfights are properly deadly, and almost anything dies in 1 headshot. Spray and pray and run and gun doesn't work. You need to get low, take cover, and aim center mass until you have an accurate gun.
3-Mutants are uncommon and appropriately dangerous, if not outright lethal. Also pretty god damn scary since you find them in the lease pleasant or visible places.
4-Anamolies are plenty, making you constantly vigilent, and range from "ow that hurt" to "bloody meat chunks." They add a bit of puzzle/navigation type play now and again.
5- Edit: After finishing the game, I can safely say I found myself using almost every rifle for some time, 3 shotguns, 2 sniper rifles, half the pistols, at least 5 armors, and even a god damn RPG-7u. In the words of Gears, variety is the spice of death.
6-Immersion is great, with the zones ambience broken only be sporadically and properly placed fleeting notes of music. Turn of hud for extra immersion stalker. You will get scared sometimes, this is horror done well.
7-It unintentionally funny now and again.
8-The mod community is great, and there are plenty of great mods to not only fix some if the base games issues (if you can call them that) but also update the graphics for those who want a more modern looking game (Complete mod is a great place to begin.)
Neutral points:
1-Base game lacks the function of repairing weapon and armor. If you're like me, you will hate this. If you're not like me, you won't mind, you might actually like this as it may add to the immersion of having your weapons degree under constant use. I see it as if you get a cool and powerfull special weapon, you feel not inclined to use it in fear of degrading its durability. Easily cured with mod.
2-At the great time of 2007, surround sound wasn't exactly on point. This game very much has sound coming evenly at once from both left and right speaker, with no directionality. Not very useful for finding enemies, so much as knowing that they are indeed nearby enough. Not gamebreaking, but I normally use audio for that purpose in shooters.
3-Edit; Story is so-so. It feels a bit strung out since between getting missions and completing them, you don't get too much narration or explaining done to you until you literally beat (or almost) beat the game. The real story imo is the one you make while stalking.
Cons:
1-There are a few points in the game that are still bugged, since they never got fixed. One of them happend to be a NPC escort mission I had to redo for 3 hours to succeed and not get a bug/break in the mission(though it wasn't tied to main story progression, still annoying as hell). Needless to say, I don't believe any bugs are gamebreaking or impeed progression, but the game might work against you in a few occurences.
2-tldr; if you can't be arsed to read point 3 since it's technical babble; moding the graphics to be better will take a toll on your PC. Recommended you do so at your own risk and with a higher end rig.
3-Complete mod. Now, while it is a fully functional, non-game breaking mod that adds (in my opinion) several desired game features like a more modern look, there is one issue; optimization. Stalker doesn't run well on multiple cores and this compounds the mod; it actually took my first core hostage and ran it to 100% bottlenecking (I've got an OC'd i7-3770k 4.5Ghz processor, so not a weak CPU). This immense load is only in the modded game, since the texture overhaul is a big one. Now, disabling the first core and setting priority for the game engine to high distributes the load well among you other cores, but makes the GPU take a heavy brunt of it due to, again, optimization (I've had the game reach 70% on a few parts for my Gigabyte GTX 1080, no small feat for 2007 release). Stuttering is also an issue, but by setting the alife setting (go to steam games in your PC files, find stalker SoC, then just type alife in the searchbar) to be roughly 900, it prevent loading of things every time you move a short distance.
Verdict:
We thought the slavs only brought us the great joy of quality in the Witcher 3. We were wrong, since they've been actually doing it all the way back in 2007 with the S.T.A.L.K.E.R series.

After all this time I heard good things about it, it was about time I read it myself.
Well, people who are saying that it's among the best VN ever written must not have read a lot of them. It's not bad, but it's far from being among the best.
Little Busters, from the same studio, is better in every aspects.
Can we say that it's an overrated game? Yes, despite its qualities.
This Visual Novel can deliver good stories (Tomoyo, Fujibayashi) as well as mediocre ones (Yukine, Kappei) and the rest (Kotomi, Fuuko, Mei...) is just average in regards to others Visual Novels.
Note that if you play without following a guide, you might end on a badly written route and be left with a bad impression.
As for Nagisa, she's supposed to be the central female character. The most developped, the best written one, but she's not. She's obnoxious, her personality is boring and her way of talking too. You have to really fall in love with her to put up with her for five minutes.
It's a shame to fail such an important character in this story, since you don't care nor feel anything when she meets problems.
After that, the After Story part is not much better. It's long and often boring, to the point that anything can happen and you won't care because you have no emotional bond with the characters, especially Nagisa.
Although the psychological evolution of Tomoya follows a logical progression until
, what happens next is unbelievable, in the wrong way. It destroys the relationship between the player and the protagonist, making him do stupid actions, incoherent and
out of character. It's hard to keep relating to him when he suddenly acts like a pr!ck. I understand why the writer did it
but it's very badly written.
And above all, there's a lot of junk. What I'm calling junk is all those hours reading nothing. For hours and hours, neither the story nor the characters gain anything. There's no progression. That's exactly the kind of junk that must be cut in a real novel. There's no reason to keep it in a Visual Novel. It feels like the game has been written to boast "we've made a X hour long game with X characters!" only that it's an example of what should be cut (some characters add nothing at all) and the game would have been better without those millstones.
The other game, Side Stories, makes a better job at telling its stories because it goes straight to the point. No fillers, no useless characters. If only the original Clannad had been written like Side Stories...
I'm putting a red thumb on it, not because the game is bad, it isn't, but because for the same price and mostly for all the hours you'll spend on it, it's better to read another VN.

Depuis le temps que j'en entendais parler en bien, il était temps de le lire moi-même.
Et ceux qui disent que c'est un des meilleurs VN n'ont sûrement pas dû en lire beaucoup. Ce n'est pas mauvais, mais c'est loin d'être parmi les meilleurs.
Little Busters, du même studio, lui est supérieur sur tous les plans.
Peut-on parler de titre surcôté, overrated ? Oui, malgré ses qualités.
Ce Visual Novel est capable de proposer de bonnes histoires (Tomoyo, Fujibayashi) comme de médiocres (Yukine, Kappei) et le reste est juste dans la moyenne de ce qu'on peut attendre d'un Visual Novel (Kotomi, Fuuko, Mei...).
Du coup, si vous jouez sans guide, vous risquez de tomber sur une histoire ratée et avoir une mauvaise impression.
Quant à Nagisa, elle est censée être le personnage féminin central. La plus travaillée, la plus réussie, mais en fait, non. Elle est pénible, sa personnalité est fatigante et sa façon de parler aussi. Il faut vraiment être amoureux d'elle pour la supporter plus de cinq minutes.
C'est vraiment dommage de rater un personnage aussi important dans l'histoire, car du coup on ne ressent rien quand il lui arrive des problèmes.
Finalement, l'After Story ne relève pas vraiment le niveau. C'est long et souvent fatigant. Du coup, il peut arriver n'importe quoi, on s'en fiche parce qu'on n'a pas de lien émotionnel avec les personnages, surtout Nagisa.
Et si l'évolution psychologique de Tomoya suivait une progression logique jusqu'à
, ce qui suit juste après est illogique et détruit toute la relation entre le joueur et le protagoniste, en forçant des décisions incohérentes et stupides. Difficile de continuer à s'attacher à lui quand il agit subitement comme un♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥fini. Je comprends les raisons de l'auteur
mais c'est très mal amené.
Mais surtout, surtout, il y a énormément de déchet. Par là, j'entends toutes ces heures de lecture qui n'apportent rien, ni à l'histoire ni aux personnages. C'est exactement le genre de truc qui doit être coupé dans un vrai roman, aucune raison de le garder dans un Visual Novel.
On a l'impression que le jeu a été écrit pour dire "on a un jeu qui dure X heures et avec Y personnages !" sauf que c'est un exemple de ce qui aurait dû être supprimé (certains personnages ne servent absolument à rien) et le jeu en aurait été meilleur sans ces boulets.
L'autre jeu, Side Stories, s'en sort beaucoup mieux pour raconter ses histoires car il va droit au but. Pas de remplissage ni de personnages inutiles. Si seulement le jeu Clannad de base avait été écrit pareillement...
Je mets un pouce rouge, non pas parce que le jeu est mauvais, ce n'est pas vrai, mais parce que pour le même prix et surtout toutes les heures qu'on peut y passer il vaut mieux miser sur un autre VN.

A game that is almost ridiculously addicting, considering its rather simple mechanics. The game takes place in the ficticious country of Arstotzka, you are a worker at the border control. The main gameplay element is to check the papers of the entrants and either deny them or let them through. What sounds tedious and repetitive at first, soon develops into moral conflicts and hard decisions. Papers, Please is not just a "border control simulator", but tells a story. You have a family to feed, so you want to do your job good. Unlawfully letting entrants through leads to citations and finally penalties, you might even lose your job. But do you really want to disunite a family or change the fate of other people to the worse, just for the sake of doing a good job? Do you let a drug smuggler or terrorist through because he bribes you with money that could save your family from starving? It's decisions like these that make Papers, Please a unique experience and definitely worth its money.

I remember one of the most uneven battles I ever fought.
It was the beginning of the game, and I was Rome.  We were wiping up what little remained of the Etruscan League, when I sent a wimpy general -If you could even give him that much of a title- to fight an Etruscan army that was building up enough forces to be a considerable threat to Rome.  At the time, when I looked at that army I saw only spearmen and hoplites, the kind of thing the Hastati are good at killing.  The army made an unexpected move when it turned north, towards the barbarrians, and marched.  I, not relizing that that he could easily turn to destroy me, then marched on the city he was previously garrisoned in, hoping to take before he came back.  I laid siege for one turn, which was more than enough for him to turn back, and combine the defender armies with his own.  Now I was facing an army that had more than enough men to hold it's own against me.  I checked the odds; no chance of a victory, with the best I could hope for being 8% of my army returning home at most. 8%?  I knew I would probably have to fight him myself, unless I wanted him to kill everything I stood for.  No, I would meet him on the field of battle, and I would die honorably.
I waited for favorable weather.
After three nervous clicks of the "wait" button, I knew I had to face this man.  With the fate of my army, and possibly all of Rome, riding on my back, I positioned my javeline-men in the trees, the rest of my army out in the open, awaiting death.  I then slowly put my mouse on the on "start battle" button, and saw the enemy come into view.
The battle had begun, and it began ever so poorly.
My javeline-throwers were quickly found and sent scurrying past my horrified army.  I then ordered my men to charge, possibly into the jaws of death.  The men engaged their rival units, each outnumbered 2-1.  We did have one advantage, though.  I mentioned earlier that the Hastati were great at killing spearmen; they did manage to be the ultimate staller of defeat.  I then noticed I had left one unit unused.  one highly unlikely hero.
My general.
He may have been pathetic compared to the expensive heros we usually see conquering the battlefield, but he was definitely a determining factor in the who's-gonna-win-game.  With the backs of the enemy slingers facing him after some maneuvering, he charged.  I wonder how much of a relief it was to my men, not feeling the hard thud of rocks against a weakening armor, instead seeing that politician they grudgingly called "general" slicing down the slingers like weeds.  I then put my javelines where the enemy slingers once were, and didn't stop throwing at the enemy 'till they had nothing left throw but their melee swords.  They then bravely abandoned all caution and charged their superior foe.  In an ordinary fight, they would have been crushed by the enemy who had been focused on them.  But against heavy spearmen -already evened out by Hastati swordsmen- who had their backs to the blades, they were like a dagger on a painful wound.  Meanwhile, my general was off gloriously hacking through line after line of surprised hoplites.  The rest of my army then turned to the very heavy general's bodygaurd unit who was giving a few Hastati some trouble.
Nowhere to run, punk.
