When I think of Transistor, the first thing that comes to mind is the incredible jazz-infused soundtrack that plays throughout your journey through Transistor's Noire like atmosphere. You can easily see that Supergiant Games took a few notes from Bastion, their last game when you see the striking art style and the pastel colors used to accent each area you see in Transistor. The turn based gameplay is rewarding and challenging. The story is strong and it moves the game along well. The Transistor itself is voiced by none othere than the narrator from Bastion. This is a game that is not to be missed and in my opinion, is on the top of my list of candidates for game of the year.

Transistor is a visually stunning game from the devs that made Bastion. The amount of detail in the areas that you don't even spend much time in is incredible. Hard to really say much more about it... it's a very unique style, similar in many ways to Bastion, but  more squared townsquare types of areas as opposed to the more natural style of Bastion (which was less angles, more curves.)
Just like Bastion, the soundtrack is perfect and fits so well. It's something you can listen to outside of game and still be pleased.
The story is delivered via dialogue and in-game text via computer terminals. The story is ok, but is just incredibly shallow and vague. Character motives are never really explained, it just feels like there were a few events that were described or implied, and you just have to go, "oh okay." It seems like a very small episode of a much larger story.
The game play itself is actually fairly challenging and consists of a mixture of real-time combat and turn-based combat. Enemies appear on screen and you can attack them, but more often than not there are many of them, they're fast and disruptive. The turn-based combat is a mode you enter into, then you get to plan out your moves and attacks before having them execute in slow-motion. It's really satisfying, but is manadatory through the majority of the second half of the game. You just take way too much unavoidable damage otherwise.
The enemies themselves actually feel fairly frustrating a lot of the time. There are certain units you REALLY have to priortize, otherwise you just won't win the fights. While priortizing those targets, you're pretty much getting attacked by all the others. Later on in the game these mechanics are less strategic and just more frustrating. There is also not much variety in the enemies... so the encounters end up being X amount of these guys, Y amounts of these guys, fight. Kind of lame, as it removes some depth and strategy that could come from complex fight scenarios, and instead goes for "just throw more guys at him."
Attacks are called functions, an you unlock many, but can only equip 4 of them. The extras can be socketed into your 4 main functions to upgrade them (additional effects), or as passives that activate based on certain conditions. There's a lot of variety here, and different abilities work better in certain situations than others.
If you lose all your health in combat, instead of dying one of your functions gets overloaded and you have to continue on fighting without it. I'm pretty sure the function that gets overloaded was the last one you used prior to "death", but not 100% sure. This cycle continues until you run out of functions completely I suspect (I never had this happen though.) It's a nice way of lessening the chances of you getting stuck and not being able to get by to continue the game... which is good because sometimes you get really unlucky in a fight and it prevents you from feeling like the game hates you as much. Functions become useable again after you access a couple of switcher terminal things later on in the levels, so until then you pretty much have to swap them out with other functions or go on without 4 functions.
Overall, I think this game was pretty enjoyable. It has a very high level of thought and polish put into it. The combat system is incredibly good, but the combat scenarios are weak and frustrating at times. The game doesn't necessarily feel "fun" to play, which is the same gripe I had with Bastion, but that doesn't mean it wasn't enjoyable or not worth a playthrough. I think this mainly stems from both these games not really having "low" or "bad" points that make the great points stand out.
The game is also incredibly short... I beat it in ~5 hours according to steam, and I tried to interact with as much as I could find. This is probably the biggest "issue" with it... it just ends up sort of unfulfilling. It does however have a New Game + mode, so you can continue to level and unlock more things, as well as a lot of "challenge" levels where you can hone your skills. I think this game should have had more hands working on it, in order to really make the scope much larger in terms of gameplay and story. There is absolutely no filler in the game which is good, but like I said earlier in the review, it feels like an episode of something much bigger.... so huge amounts of potential left unexplored. Still, the amount of time, effort and detail that went into this game is really apparent in every way imaginable. For what it's worth, if you've played neither of these games, I'd highly recommend playing Bastion before this.

TOS is still a very very young game that takes note from its predecessors.

The funnest part about ToS, and also the scariest part are the character customizations. You have A LOT of freedom making your build. There is no *i'm an archer*, or *i'm a healer*. There are several jobs you can take, that altogether can make you a unique character.
If you do not think about your builds ahead of time, you WILL be punished.
I've spent at least 1/3 of my ToS time theory-building my characters. It is A LOT of fun. You aren't just grinding for gears, exp, or brainlessly questing. You are building towards a character that is yours.
There are a lot of unsatisfied, very entitled customers who have written negative reviews for ToS. While there is some truth to what they say, their anger sort of blinds them. ToS is a very young game, and they have made it very clearly that they are not just another WoW copycat game.
I've seen the staff try very hard to make sure the game is enjoyable. I've seen them implement several fixes in the last three weeks. They are quite active, which makes me feel like there is a lot of room for improvement.
There was a really really bad gigantic bot problem a week ago. The staff showed their proactiveness by decimating the bot population. It feels like 85% of them are gone. The problem isn't as bad anymore.
Though, if you do decide to play/buy this game, prepare to get frustrated from time to time.

All-in-all, 9.5/10, absolutely love this game.

This is the ultimate benchmark for how videogames based on a movie license should look and play like. Although not directly based on any of the Alien movies, it perfectly captures the atmosphere of dread and fear moviegoers have come to love about the franchise. Adding to that it also offers a near-perfect recreation of the retro-80ies-scifi look and sound from the movies, fully engulfing the player in this rich universe.
Oh and it plays bloody fantastic as well. The difficulty curve works surprisingly well, given that the player has no way to defeat his biggest enemy in the game. The game designers also do their best to not just offer a one-trick pony and vary the core challenges with each level. Once the player has mastered one technique to get around one type of enemy, it starts to mix up the core formula and throws in a stronger variant of that enemy or something new altogether - no, the one Alien is not the only enemy in the game, although it certainly is the most dangerous.
The game is also surprisingly long. In a world with so many 5-hour singleplayer campaigns, Alien: Isolation can easily take up to 20 hours to complete - 20 hours of terrific, horrifying, tense, gripping and ultimately extremely impressive horror stealth "action" in a universe that long deserved a game of this caliber. If you love the movies, then get this game. Now!

This game is good, however, you realise how it's not fully polished when you play.
GUNPLAY
First runthrough is great, most weapons can be used etc.
But when you play it in True Vault Hunter Mode, a huge chunk of the weapons is useless. In Ultimate Vault Hunter mode most weapons are trash, and this is where you notice that several characters need very specific gear to perform well. In the overpowered levels (with DLCs), you HAVE TO farm legendaries, or get really lucky with the purples to get a good loadout. So many guns are useless, a lot of skills in the skill tree is♥♥♥♥♥♥and cannot be used in any universe.
STORY/QUESTS
Story is pretty good, characters are well written for the most part. In the main game, you can easily get overwhelmed by sidequests, and a lot of them are frankly just "Go to A. Fetch X. Go to B. Fetch Y. Go to C. Fetch Z. Go to A." with the occational boss in between. You really notice this pattern once you've played through the main game a couple of times. There are some missions that are really good and interesting, but some are just annoying. During some parts of quests you also have no idea what to do because the game isn't clear enough. Some quests are clearly there for the meme and others try to be serious and fail.
DLCs:
These three DLC's are extremely boring and feel forced.
- Captain Scarlett and Her Pirate's Booty
- Mr. Torgue's Campaign of Carnage
- Sir Hammerlock's Big Game Hunt
I pretty much only play these if I need an item that can be dropped in them.
This DLC redeemes the others slightly:
- Tiny Tina's Assault on Dragon Keep
The level cap increases and the OP level dlc are pretty fun though. The Headhunter missions are often better than the three bad DLCs, which is a plus, I guess.
SECRETS/COMPLETIONIST STUFF
Finishing every quest is annoying and is not rewarding. It feels like a chore. There are also "Badass Ranks" which are kinda cool I guess, BUT there are some that clearly were added last minute, who don't add anything interesting at all.
Examples of these ♥♥♥♥♥♥ ones are "Find three hidden vault symbols in area X" or "Explore every location in area Y"
CLASSES/BALANCE
Interesting abilities,♥♥♥♥♥♥balance.
In higher playthroughs vehicles are trash due to not scaling along with everything else.
Barrels do a million damage to yourself in OP levels.
CONCLUSION
This review may seem negative but it's honestly a good gaming experience, it's only after you spend more time with it when you realise all of its flaws and a lot of them are fundimental and not fixed due to lack of polish.

Neutrals....

Negatives...

Yes, you are checking papers at a Border Checkpoint. However, you soon come to find there is more to it than the mundane stamping of passports. As days go by, terrorists attacks occur and it is clear that a more strict border regulation is needed. So, mostly each day, a new rule is implemented that you must adhere to. But then, then there are the people. Jorji... Ah, I'll let you experience this gem for yourselves. There are choices you have to make though. You must make these more decisions based on what YOU think... Will you let the wife pass with her husband even though she doesn't have proper papers? Over all, this is definitely worth the price and I would pay for it if it were more.

While it may seem like a slow-paced and droll Indie game, 'Papers, Please' is truly a work of art.
The Player (you) is just a Border Officer, working day in and day out in order to support their (your) family, but not only can they (once again, you) support their (Do you see what I'm getting at?) family, the Player is also given the choice to bend the rules for desperate immigrants, seperated families, and even
'Papers, Please' constantly tests the Player's sense of Morality, but not all good deeds for desperate immigrants are really...'good'... I've let in quite a number of immigrants whom I thought were trying to see a relative, and then they exploded outside of the gate.
I digress, so I'll just give my opinion:
'Papers, Please' is a masterpiece that will pluck at the strings of your heart, and I HIGHLY recommend that you purchase this game-no, not game, but this piece of art.
Final Verdict: 'Papers, Please' earns a 10/10, and is approved to enter Asrtotzka.

A friend and I on the cinema map. No other players, just us.
We start to wander around the spawn area equipping ourselves. Suddenly a stranger joins the game.
"Who are you?", my friend yells in his mic, pointing his gun directly at the new guy's head. I run towards them, rifle in hand. My finger is itching. Should I pull the trigger?
"My name is Luke", the stranger replies in a calm tone. "I'm a survivor just like you."
"Can we trust you?", my friend asks.
"Sure. I can show you how to get out of here."
He tells us about the epidemic and how he managed to find shelter. His voice sounds stoic. It seems like he's been out there for quite some time.
"You, grab the sniper rifle, head to the balcony, and clear the way to the entrance of the cinema", Luke tells my friend. Then he looks at me, "And us, we're going to break through. Come on!"
As we fight ourselves through the horde of the undead outside, something must have gone wrong.
"They got me! They got me!", I hear Luke screaming.
Those screams. I could not forget them. They still haunt me. And they alway will.
Luke was down. The dead were feeding upon his body.
"You have to kill me. I don't wanna turn!"
"Luke! Don't die on us!", I hear my friend shouting in despair.
"It's too late", his fading voice whispers.
Some last coughs. Then a gurgling sound. Then – nothing.
+++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++

Like with everything Korean-made that reaches our game markets, performance, balance and lag issues is a hit or miss; And for now it's a severe miss. Only time will tell if they manage to at least make it bearable.
Edit 7/21/2016:
After giving the game a serious investment, I have concluded that - while many if not all of the complaints I had to begin with remain there. - the artwork, music and customization of your character class do live up to what Ragnarok used to inspire. In fact, I can now affirmatively state it feels like an appropriate step up from it.
What makes me change this review to a positive is one grand thing most MMOs as of late never, ever apply anymore; The game actually brings challenge to you without having to reach anywhere near the middle of the game.
This actually makes someone like me, frustrated by the casualization and outburning of MMOs turning everything into a push to win simulator, actually have a blast having to use more than one neurone at a time.
All in all, if you are willing to go into this game knowing it is a gem mishandled by the publishers that will take a while to be properly polished, and keep yourself in the proper mindset for it - you will have fun.

This is the ultimate benchmark for how videogames based on a movie license should look and play like. Although not directly based on any of the Alien movies, it perfectly captures the atmosphere of dread and fear moviegoers have come to love about the franchise. Adding to that it also offers a near-perfect recreation of the retro-80ies-scifi look and sound from the movies, fully engulfing the player in this rich universe.
Oh and it plays bloody fantastic as well. The difficulty curve works surprisingly well, given that the player has no way to defeat his biggest enemy in the game. The game designers also do their best to not just offer a one-trick pony and vary the core challenges with each level. Once the player has mastered one technique to get around one type of enemy, it starts to mix up the core formula and throws in a stronger variant of that enemy or something new altogether - no, the one Alien is not the only enemy in the game, although it certainly is the most dangerous.
The game is also surprisingly long. In a world with so many 5-hour singleplayer campaigns, Alien: Isolation can easily take up to 20 hours to complete - 20 hours of terrific, horrifying, tense, gripping and ultimately extremely impressive horror stealth "action" in a universe that long deserved a game of this caliber. If you love the movies, then get this game. Now!

The short: Factorio is a fantastic game, but it takes time to admit it.
Factorio is at it heart a game about always thinking bigger. When you start you only have a few basic supplies and little applicable technology. You might get a few basic things happening but soon aliens will ruin your day. You'll be tempted to give up on it entirely.
But the problem isn't the game, you just aren't thinking big enough. Why build one lab when you can set up 4 for 4 times the price? Why only walls 1 square thick? You've built one steam engine, why not 30?
The scale is infinite, and as you build the abmition to grander and grander designs the materials that allow you to expand grow. Soon technology comes quickly, aliens become a manageable nuisance, you start planning some train lines to go for a long distance iron deposit to top up your stockpiles and oh god its 4am I'm supposed to wake up for work in 3 hours what am I doing with my life.
Its only real drawback is that with only a few core resources some people may think theres not enough complexity. But its meant to be a finely tightly tuned experience and what its doing it does well. The visuals aren't exactly next gen but they mesh well together and when you're potentially talking millions of assets at screen on once you don't want the engine grinding to a halt. The sound design is top notch and as you move about your factory you will feel like you are passing by the machinery.
If you like designing your own machines, solving spatial problems, or even the sim city experience of watching something you plan expand and grow, you will find enjoyment in this game. At the very least, I recommend running through the demo and getting a taste.

I paid 15 dollars for this game when it was on sale.  It was worth that.
DEFINITELY NOT WORTH 60 DOLLARS TO ME.
I was a huge fan of Just Cause 2 and couldnt resist this one at 75% off.
If you're like me and completely wore out Just Cause 2 then you've basically played this one.  I feel the map is a little smaller in 3 and the graphics, though great, have not seemed to improve.
The wing suit is a great added feature to get around and have fun but adds another clunky mechanic to the already sometimes cumbersome button combos.  I played this with mouse and keyboard so maybe easier with controller.
Car driving, like the prequal, is sub par if you're used to games like GTA or basically any other car driving game.  The cars all feel heavy and even the fastest and most maneuverable cars never seem to be in your control.  There is a slight lag in the driving that never fits in with going fast down a busy street or on the side of a cliff.
That mechanic seems to go away when you get into aircrafts or boats.  When you're out in the open water the waves are bigger than compared to shallows.  The water detail is the EASILY the best of any other open world game.   Zooming around in a jet ski or speed boat hitting big waves feels better than driving a car most of the time.
Aircrafts are also a big win in this game.  Helicopters are available early on and pretty handy for the smaller bases.  Jets and planes fly like they did in Just Cause 2.  The same visual stimulation and feel of vertigo when you get launched out of an exploding aircraft.
The leaderboards are a great way to keep challenging yourself.  There doesnt seem to be many people online playing this game anymore.  I seem to always be going back in forth on the leaderboards with the same few people.  But that could change.
Though I have played over 9 hours, I have only done 5 or 6 missions.  Most of the time spent blowing up enemies and doing all the side challenges.

The worst thing about the Stalker games is that they are ....  SO F******** ADDICTIVE that once you start playing - you simply can't stop. I am serious!
Even with it's outdated graphics, various bugs, with interface you sometimes will hate - still these games are MASTERPIECE. There is maybe only one other series which creates such authentic atmosphere of a post-nuclear-disaster world and these are the Metro games (btw made by some members of the crew that created the Stalker series).
Now if I have to say something useful for the potential buyers - what this game will give you:
- the different zones in the game are very well crafted and even with the out-dated graphics it creates hell of a good picture of the Frozen-in-1986 zone around the Soviet Chernobyl Atomic power plant which blew off in Spring of 1986.
- game is hard (if you play it on the last two difficulties) - which I recommend
- weapon balistics is sort of a real-life-like - i.e. it's not the COD like where you can shoot someone with a burst from AK47 from 100m and all the bullets fall in the same spot. Here you have to aim carefully and consider the gun recoil.
- Wepons breaks, armors breaks - which makes them less reliable in time
- You have limited space in your inventory so you have to plan carefully what you put in there before going to a mission unless you want to sprint back to your stash(es) or merchants
- The main story very solid and interesting so you want to dig in further and further only to see what happens. (Just read your PDA to fill in the story details)

A friend and I on the cinema map. No other players, just us.
We start to wander around the spawn area equipping ourselves. Suddenly a stranger joins the game.
"Who are you?", my friend yells in his mic, pointing his gun directly at the new guy's head. I run towards them, rifle in hand. My finger is itching. Should I pull the trigger?
"My name is Luke", the stranger replies in a calm tone. "I'm a survivor just like you."
"Can we trust you?", my friend asks.
"Sure. I can show you how to get out of here."
He tells us about the epidemic and how he managed to find shelter. His voice sounds stoic. It seems like he's been out there for quite some time.
"You, grab the sniper rifle, head to the balcony, and clear the way to the entrance of the cinema", Luke tells my friend. Then he looks at me, "And us, we're going to break through. Come on!"
As we fight ourselves through the horde of the undead outside, something must have gone wrong.
"They got me! They got me!", I hear Luke screaming.
Those screams. I could not forget them. They still haunt me. And they alway will.
Luke was down. The dead were feeding upon his body.
"You have to kill me. I don't wanna turn!"
"Luke! Don't die on us!", I hear my friend shouting in despair.
"It's too late", his fading voice whispers.
Some last coughs. Then a gurgling sound. Then – nothing.
+++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++

"What's Call Of Juarez: Cartel"?
You'll be asking yourself that after you play "Gunslinger", the absolute BEST in the series, and a very tough act to top. It's a brutally original and amazing alternate history version of the Old West, that makes great use of the truths and the half-truths that time was filled with as it came to an end in the early 20th century. The writers should get an award for such originality!
And telling it all is Silas Greaves, a whiskey-slugging, hard-bitten lone survivor of the Old West in it's heyday. You'll instantly connect with the character from the minute he sits down and begins telling his story to a bunch of saloon patrons at the game's beginning.  Greave's character is deep and multi-faceted, and couldn't be more real unless he was standing in front of the player. Such development of a game character is worthy of great praise as it's not seen in many games these days.
The keyboard-mouse controls are simplicity itself as they are reduced to a simple set of basics and not strewn all over the keyboard like most games; everything is within reach. Customizable controls too!  A gallery of historical facts about the Old West also exists, and as the player continues to pick these facts up as clues thruout the game, he can learn about Wild Western history as he goes along.  Very neat.  You'll  also be duelling at high noon with some of the West's most ornery outlaws. And with the Chrome Engine  on hand to show off the great details, you'll feel your heart beating and  the sun pounding down on you as you wait for your enemy to draw.
So, my fellow gamers, don't let the low price of $14.95 fool you-this game has a LOT to offer.  If it's true that sometimes the best is saved for last,  it dosen't get any better than this. Ubisoft and Techland have single-handedly saved a waning game franchise. And in doing so, they have created a TRUE gem in a sea of common stones.  One can only hope that their journey will continue with some equally great DLC. Ubisoft, please take note!     Final verdict- 10 out of 10

This is the ultimate benchmark for how videogames based on a movie license should look and play like. Although not directly based on any of the Alien movies, it perfectly captures the atmosphere of dread and fear moviegoers have come to love about the franchise. Adding to that it also offers a near-perfect recreation of the retro-80ies-scifi look and sound from the movies, fully engulfing the player in this rich universe.
Oh and it plays bloody fantastic as well. The difficulty curve works surprisingly well, given that the player has no way to defeat his biggest enemy in the game. The game designers also do their best to not just offer a one-trick pony and vary the core challenges with each level. Once the player has mastered one technique to get around one type of enemy, it starts to mix up the core formula and throws in a stronger variant of that enemy or something new altogether - no, the one Alien is not the only enemy in the game, although it certainly is the most dangerous.
The game is also surprisingly long. In a world with so many 5-hour singleplayer campaigns, Alien: Isolation can easily take up to 20 hours to complete - 20 hours of terrific, horrifying, tense, gripping and ultimately extremely impressive horror stealth "action" in a universe that long deserved a game of this caliber. If you love the movies, then get this game. Now!

Riding very much off the coat tails of Supergiant's previous beloved, Bastion, Transistor has at least been built with some articulation of what made the spiritual predecessor so compelling. An absolutely gorgeous hand-painted cityscape with a woozy yet full-bodied soundtrack makes it clear Supergiant knew what the first thing that came to player's minds were. Throw in another smoky voiced narrator voice to follow the antangonist through to the end of the journey, and it would seem Transitor is on to another winner.
Well... it fails in a couple of fundemental ways. Yes, we can recall the lovely artstyle, music, *that* voice actor for Bastion, but part of the universal charm was the slick, smooth combat to follow up on a compelling storyline. The former is failed with Transistor, exchanging for a slightly more clunky affair, your character taking a moment to attempt most attacks, even needing to recover from the jaunt ability. The wide variety of upgrades, potions and weapon combinations are exchanged for a universal sword, the namesake of the game, with four primary abilities where you can assign your collected powers as either secondary additions, upgrading potency, number or secondary functions of your powers, and four passive slots. It seems that this could hold a lot of potential, but for the most part those combinations don't surprise or allow for in-depth theorycrafting. You just slap what you like to your abilities, make them more powerful/numerous/have an extra projectile thrown in and mash away. The "Turn()" system also does now allow for much depth, particularly end-game considering how enemies enjoy countering or simply dodging your best laid plans.
The story starts off incredibly promising. I was anticipating a very Film Noir experience thrown in to a heavy sci-fi (Read: Not cyberpunk) universe. Alas, it mostly repeats the same apocalyptic overtones of Bastion with an unsatisfactory and, frankly, confusing conclusion that leaves far, far more questions than answers and no clear antagonist to despise, the "Big Bad" showing up very late and with not much moustache twiddling to be had.
There are a few neat little touches that I enjoyed: The slick UI and artwork is just as gorgeous as the rendered graphics, you can see other players on their adventure via Dark Souls-esque ghosts around you, and there is even a button to hold to make the protagonist, Red, hum out a lovely counter-melody to whatever soundtrack is playing at the time. There is also, apparently, a procedurally generated post-game series of challenges to experience, but... the gameplay just didn't grab me enough to really care.
I can't *not* recommend this game. The narrator, again, just about makes it, and the relationship between him and Red's conclusion enough was sweet enough. It *is* satisfying to watch said best laid plans work out just as you expect and watch a screen full of baddies die in one little turn, and the world, despite confusing and mysterious, is at least dazzling to explore. £15 though? Wait for a sale. Even taking my sweet time I easily steamrolled through this bite-sized treat in six hours.

One good thing the Just Cause franchise nails on point is sandbox f*ckery and being able to lose a few hours in just that alone. The wingsuit and grapple hook additions from JC2 are great and logical advances without taking away the core feel.
As of this review, I only have 5 hours into JC3, but feel that it's enough to have an opinion since I have obscene amounts of hours in JC1 and JC2.
Firstly, and it is said with good reason amongst every review, the memory leak and video glitches in this game are the worst I've ever encountered. i5 6600k, 16gb gskill trident, asus 1060 turbo 6gb, gigabyte mobo with pure ssd primary storage and I'm getting fps digs, force closes and rampant misc video issues (floating cities of lights in the sea that have no buildings?). Oh yeah, and its 2 years old. Inexcusable. I feel sorry for anyone that's battling this on a less spec'd system.
Foregoing all of that malarky, I still rate it subpar to my experience with JC1 and JC2. The map is insanely repetative. I am willing to bet you will find more variety in JC1 than in JC3 in terms of unique areas, which is terrible. JC2 had an incredible map, filled with diversity and flow. The vistas were insipring to investigate. This, you look over at a mountain, and you think, "well, its going to look like the ground I'm standing on here so what's the point". There's something to be said about relating the story, and I understand, but surely there are other ways of handling that. I'll also point out that I swear 2/3rds of the map is completely useless, unwalkable cliffs and mountain sides.
Controls, character movement, graphics and such are all done well. Combat mechanics are good. NPC involvement and immersion are definitely better. I've been playing GTAV lately so I feel that rating vehicle control is unfair because that game always wins that category (sadly, released twice as long ago). There are animals too which account for a hilarious time with the grapple hook :)
My biggest complaint: WHY TAKE THE MINI GAME AWAY WHEN HACKING/STEALING/INTERACTING WITH THINGS?! Sure, it was a X, Y, B, A combo that was a little hoky, but it was unique, and offered a little more resistance than just pressing y and highjacking vehicles, or waiting for a countdown hoping you don't get shot.
Anyway, long review short, avoid it. I got it on sale for $15, and I feel a little burnt by it, I'd be so angry if I spent $60 on this and can't believe they still justify that cost when they don't even fix it. Sometimes I don't know what's worse Steam, letting hoards of "alpha" titles through daily, or AAA devs port console games and give virtually no PC support.
I'll probably play it just for the explosions until that dies away. The worst part is, I'll have to go back to GTAV and not have a grapple hook :(.

To start of with the obvious this is an amazing VN, that much is clear. But there are a few things to consider if you're thinking of buying this:
1. Even by Visual Novel standards this is extremely a long read, like between 100-150+ hours to complete so be so be warned if you prefer your VN's around the normal length of 30-50 hours.
2. This VN is one of the first that made VN's popular in the West, but saying that this hasn't aged well as it did come out in 2004 and today's standards of what VN's are different.
3. Even the most diehard fan of this VN would tell you the pacing in this is snail's pace so if you want to jump in, beware its a very slow burner.
4. The Characters are all amazing.... Well expect Nagisa she is very irritating so it does affect the enjoyment of the "true route" and the After Story as she is the Canon love interest which is a shame as others like Yukine, Kotomi and Tomoyo suit so much better but oh well.
5. Despite it's age this VN is still full of heart, charm and humour that still matches up well with today's standards.
So in closing if this was 2004 I'd give this VN a solid 8/10 but now in 2017 I'd give it a more realistic 6/10 due to it being just not as good as today standards like I mentioned above. But still is one of those VN's you have to read at least once as if you don't you're just a damn casual... Haha

First off this game is early access so I undertand there is a lot of development left in the game. If you truly like to aid or be part of the development process then this game might be for you.
The idea of this game is great, but nothing is balanced. There is no sense in building a base because it will get destroyed. If you build a granary you are a fool if you think it will last. All the cool equipment you can build,  water wells, granarys, soon to be saw mills, are just pointless at the current state. You build what you feel is an impenetrable fortress, go to bed, get on, and it is gone. For awhile that was part of the fun... trying to build something that is not destroyed in 24 hours. My friends and I would grind a day out building a base and then boom its gone. Of course we want to be able to destroy bases but the seige weapons are OP at the moment. If you do build a base you better build it floating in the sky, but come on, this is not an anti gravity planet as far as I can tell. Because of the pointlessness of gathering resources, it promotes you to just go kill people and take their resources and their bases which can be fun, but really kills the ability to achieve anything great and put on any epic battles.
Fighting can be fun but once you get all that cool armor you will likely just get raided and have everything stolen in 24 hours or attacked by a group of naked people throwing javelins which is pretty funny at first. If this would be your primary interest then this game is for you. If you are wanting to build an awesome self sustaining compound where you can suit up with your friends in epic armor fighting epic battles... well its not going to happen. Also, there are frquent server wipes where all your work is wiped clean, but that is part of development so I can understand that.  On the other end of the spectrum you have the non fighting RP servers. They are great if that is your thing, but there is just no good middle ground.  It's trolls or carebares.
This game is fun for all the crazy little experiences that happen, but once you realize that it is grossly unbalanced, and its just an endless grind with no real payout, it begins to lose its luster. With this said I am excited see this game develop and I am going to revisit in a month or two to see how its evolved. I wrote this review to add my 10 cents and hopefully aid in development.

This is one of those games that I both love and hate at the same time. They capture the mood of Cold War-era paranoia and bureaucratic insanity perfectly, and most times it's relatively funny what new nonsense they come up with for me to check. The problem I have is I just don't find it fun.
Obviously this sort of thing is subjective, so I'll give my reasons why I don't enjoy this game. The biggest thing is it doesn't feel like a game. It feels like a job. I'm put under the same nerve-wracking stress I feel when I'm doing something for payment. Am I going to miss one tiny little detail and be thrown yet another violation message? Will another bomber get through and, as a result, the AGB will kick down my apartment door and gun down my entire family? Am I breathing correctly, or does my posture sitting at this border crossing booth suggest I'm a traitor?
The whole thing feels like I'm at a job. I didn't pay 10 dollars to do a job. I paid ten dollars to have fun. I know the whole point of the game is to put you under stress and make you scrutinize the tiniest details of 1,000 rules and subrules that just keep on piling up while your whole family starves and dies, but that just isn't my idea of fun. It'd be like if I bought a game where I had to answer the telephone and worry about accidentally letting a telemarketer through to my manager. It'd be like playing a game where I'm a janitor and if I miss cleaning the floor somewhere I'm reprimanded, but if I clean it and someone slips I'm reprimanded, etc.
Stress is a part of any decent slightly challenging video game. I understand that. This is work stress, though. This is something I play games to try to escape. I don't want more of it when I'm actually playing a game and not doing menial labor for menial payment. I feel like the developers should be paying /me/ for every hour I'm playing Papers, Please.
All in all, it's certainly not a bad game. It's certainly not the worst game. You might even enjoy it. This is about whether I recommend it or not, though. If you want to feel like you're at a job without the payment part, or really, REALLY like Cold War history/satire, pick it up. If you don't, buy 10 dollars worth of pancakes or something.

Yeah this game is good. Not just good but really good. There are two big parts that make this game really good. The first is just the gameplay. I'm not sure how they did it but the but checking the papers in your little booth is a very engrossing process and is very easy to learn how to point and click the varying paper work is easy and the addition of more paper work as the game progresses adds to a more challenging momentum without taking away from the game. The next strenth is the moral choices in the game. Now most games have some kind of moral choice, usually something about killing rainbow mcpuffins or not, which can easily bereplaced by a light switch at the end of the game saying what ending you want. Papers, Please makes it really hard to be a good perason. You can either reunite a couple who has been divided by the split, but you get paid by how many people you get through the booth, and if you let the wrong people in you cant pay for the food and medicine for your family. I can't even begin to describe all of the nail biting delimas that the game through me because of this small amount of context. This is a game that shows just what a small bit of context can do with a game and definitley add to the evidence that games are in fact an art form. So yes I do recommend this game over other games that have come out this year and if you have not tried it yet you should.

I’m not into horror movies or survival horror games but this game was the exception.  My review will be rather biased because I’m a huge fan of Alien (1979) and Aliens(1986) and this game really immerses me into that movie world.
For those that are seasoned players of survival horror, there are concepts within “Alien:Isolation” that aren’t new; an enemy that can’t be killed, crafting, dark spooky environment, etc.  This might not make the game unique within the game genre but I believe they excel at those concepts.
For fans of the films, you’ll appreciate the attention to detail in its’ sound design and visuals.  I’m guessing the devs had access to many, if not all, of 20th Century Fox archives.
This is not a run-n-gun type of game but a stealth heavy game; puzzles under stress.
Survivor mode DLC:
I spend most of my game time here (too much time here).  The maps are incredible and the Alien AI is at its’ most aggressive.  If you’ve competed all the Survivor mode DLCs, I highly recommend endurance mode which randomly shuffles all the survivor mode maps. You have a choice from nine characters, each with their own loadout.  Amanda has a very optimal loadout, definitely try to challenge yourself with a character that doesn’t start with a flamethrower or access tuner.
“Safe Haven” and “Lost Contact” fall under Salvage Mode; 10 stages of increasing difficulty. I’m still trying to beat my best score on the leaderboard.
Advice:
This is a “cat and mouse” game and you are always the mouse.
Listen for sounds that can save you.
The moment you think you’re safe, you’re not.
Yes, the Alien AI is unscripted and unpredictable. However, it does have observable behaviors.  Behaviors you can exploit.
Save often.
Reading terminals offer game lore and often vital information.
Answers are never far.
Cables are like bread crumbs.
Stop thinking two-dimensionally.
In conclusion:
This is a phenomenal game. There must be something wrong with me because I love the stress this game gives me.

This is the game that ruined Horror for me.
It's also one of my favorite games, for its incredible attention to detail that will absorb any sci-fi fan. And for fans of the Alien franchise specifically, this might be the best licensed adaptation since the Batman Arkham games. It is perfectly recreated in set, animations, sound design...honestly, one of the most definitive Alien products around.
But that doesn't give justice to how much this game turns horror on its head. After a certain point in the game, you are stalked by an unkillable, incredibly intelligent AI which is just unpredictable enough that you never grow comfortable. While you have a few tools to defend yourself, the Xenomorph slowly learns from your behavior and gets smarter each time you escape it. This leads to a game of cat and mouse that spans an entire campaign of twists and claustrophobic settings.
I can't enjoy other horror games I used to love, because the enemies feel dumb and predictable. So if you want an experience to end all Horror games, this is the one.

So, first things first: Transistor is not Bastion.
A lot of the criticism that Transistor gets seems to be coming from fans of Bastion who were expecting more of the same.
That's not what this game is about and i think that is a great thing.
Transistor is its own experience. It is witty, beautiful, tough and bitter-sweet all the way to the end.
It's rare that a game draws me in like this, makes me feel for its characters the way this game does and I wholeheartedly recommend it.
The one criticism I have is that it is a little short. I would not have minded a little more "grinding", for want of a better word, to get from one element of the story to the next. The combat with its endless combinations of possible moves is just that enjoyable and I am looking forward to my second playthrough.

This game is beautiful, the music is great, the voice acting is great and the combat is superb. It seems like a tradition top down action rpg, but you have to option to pause the game and issue out a chain of actions that flow out quickly, allowing you to quickly execute complicated flurries in a stylish and satisfying manner. The move system of this game is quite deep; as you progress you earn more moves (up to 20 or so), and you have up to 4 slots for combat and up to 4 slots for passives. The depth for the moves comes from the fact that each skill/move you learn can be assigned to either one of you your 4 slots, your passive, or as a modifier to another move (up to 2 for each slot) you have assigned to you main slots; I can not stress how much depth this gives and I barely scratched the surface for all the cool combos you can set up in my one play through. This combat system is quite fun, and the game does of great job keeping combat engaging, and the setting is cool and intriguing over it's 6-8 hour play through. This is a must play.

Another excellent if somewhat short game from supergiant. If you played Bastion then the art style and storytelling will be very familiar to you.
As far as the art goes its extremely well done in my opinion, the color palette is bright and vivid while the art style itself reminds me a lot of bastion in that its 2D and hand drawn. This is not to say that they look like the same game however, Transistor's art style is very strikingly different, being much more futuristic with its environments and enemies.
The combat is very fun and has nice turn based aspects to it, and there are tons of combinations with the upgrade system. Functions are your abilities, and these functions can do one of three things: be used as an active ability, augment another ability, or be a passive ability. These are all interchangeable at the various access points placed around each level and combinations are vastly different, such that for example Crash()+Breach() is not the same as Breach()+Crash().
The music is from the same guy that did the music in bastion and the vocalist is the same as well, so as you might expect it's excellent throughout.
The only real problem I have with the game, albeit a small one, is that its a bit short, clocking in at about 5-6 hours per playthrough depending on how many of the challenges you do. It does offer a bit of replayability in the recursive mode once you finish the story, however.
Overall though I can't really recommend this game enough to people that liked bastion, and if you haven't played bastion, Transistor is still a fun game with interesting combat, story, and artwork, so it's well worth the $20 in my opinion.
Also if you haven't played bastion, go do that.

(Summary points and video review also below)
Transistor is the highly anticipated release from Supergiant Games, and one thing I have noticed a lot is people comparing it to Bastion. Now, it can’t really be helped considering they share an awful lot of similarities, such as the same narrator and art style, and this is quite frankly one of Transistor’s biggest faults, because it’s NOT Bastion, but at the same time it tries to hit some middle ground between its own identity and that of riding on the former success of Bastion, and ultimately ends up becoming a very mixed experience.
This is Transistor’s main problem because it makes it become a very mixed experience, because almost everything it excels in it has an equal opposite that draws it back down that I simply can’t avoid and overall it is very much a mixed bag of qualities. The combat is incredibly enjoyable and unique, but the repetitive nature of it gets old fairly quickly. The art style is beautiful and pleasing to the eye, but the foreground obstructions and fixed perspective can get a little annoying, especially in combat. The story is fantastic and delivered in a unique way, but it means vital information can sometimes be missed if you are not paying attention. It is without a doubt an enjoyable experience that is fairly well designed, but simply misses the mark in some aspects that left me loving and hating it at times.
Summary:
+ Gorgeous art style.
+ Fantastic amount of skill customisation.
+ Combat is engaging and fluent.
+ Narrative is well written and enjoyable.
+ Incredible voice acting and dialogue.
- Fixed perspective and foreground obstructions hinder gameplay.
- Combat can quickly become repetitive.
- Vital information in the narrative is easily missed.

Call of Juarez Gunslinger is yet another in a ling of fairly good games. Nice to see that they have returned to the western theme and away from the (In my opinion pathetic) modern drug cartel from the last game.
So what is Call Of Juarez Gunslinger? Well, is a whiskey soaked, lead filled, cuss throwing, extravaganza of shooting.
The game play is fun, the levels managing to mix it up enough each time to make it fun without repeating the same old we have played before. The guns, characters, environments and mostly everything else have an large amount of detail in them making the game look lovely, however dont expect super realistic graphics. This game does have a slightly cartooney theme with it's cell shared graphics.
The characters are a bit bland and do seem to be an excuse just to unload 12 shots of lead at anything that moves. And the story is a bit cliche, but so long as you just want to shoot people and blow sh*t up then this is the game for that.
The story takes place in a tavern, the levels themselves are the story's of my Silas Greaves, you may at times find yourselves having to replay hole missions and following a different route as his somewhat exaggerated tales are set straight as he is caught by the kind folks he is telling them too. This is in no way annoying as it lets you basically add another mission to the game, and lets you explore a level from a hole new perspective.
The game is also packaged with two extra modes called Duals and Arcade mode. They let you rack up some xp and have fun trying to get the highest score you can, but they dont really add too much to the game, but are still a nice addition too see. One thing that is missed from the last Weston game, Bound in Blood, is the free roam missions. But the rest of the game makes up 10 fold.
The upgrade system is great, allowing you too upgrade weapons and unlock ability's. Also along the way you can unlock little facts about the real people in the game, interesting and a nice addition that shows the care put into the game.
The length of the game is a little short for me, I got through all the missions in about 7 hours, but for £11.99 you cant complain, this is a steal, and better than most other generic shooters around

Transistor is one of my favorite games. It provides a unique blend of Diablo-style kiting with Dragon Age Origins active pause battle mechanics, presented in a dreamy, futuristic world that takes cues from the Impressionism movement. Character customization is wonderfully addictive. You get multiple ability chips. Each of these chips can be used as an active ability, a passive ability, or a modifier for another active ability. Essentially, there are so many ways to build your character that you will not be able to resist spending a dozen hours experimenting with different builds. However, I must say that the strongest feature of this game is its instantly lovable main character, the singer Red who lost her voice and her talking sword, the Transistor. The soundtrack will also mark this game forever in your memory. Some might criticize this game as full of plot holes because it does not really attempt to explain everything. Rather, it draws you into a general dream-like feeling. And it does so masterfully. This is a short game, but it is a glorious.

I very rarely write very in-depth reviews however I have to
with a lot of the negative reviews as I rather enjoyed this. Why? Please read on if you're interested on hearing what my thoughts and feelings were after finishing all of the possible endings for this vn in particular.
Personally I found the concept of the story rather compelling as it looked at a very realistic tone to life such as things that we all take for granted; the way we perceive ourselves in society; how society works/favours some but not all and personal life decisions and how that impacts an individual's mental health. The emphasis put on the
themes were definitely seen throughout the whole game. I do however feel that the story at some points felt a little lacking. For example, parts just weren't pieced well together which left me questioning things such as did I miss out on something or what just happened or why are they introducing new ideas here when it doesn't fit in this context? As mentioned somewhere in the epilogue by the creators, one major flaw would also be the translations. Sometimes the translations just didn't make sense however I wasn't too bothered by it. I won't go into any more detail as I don't want to ruin your experience. (That's if you choose to buy this)
Overall, I feel like the story explored very complicated themes which, in my opinion, are rarely seen or explored in visual novels however I feel like the endings were either 1) too clichéd or 2) rushed/not executed well.
I know this is the 5th instalment of the series but I just felt like mentioning this. The story mainly revolved around the protagonist, Ga-yeon. It did go into side characters POV's, for example, Yunwoo a few times/I think it was Hye-na's boss (once) which was nice to see. The character development was okay. Maturity was definitely shown given the complex themes that were highlighted within this vn so good job there.
The background art was beautiful. Very. It just felt very realistic and alive to me so well done there YGGDRASIL STUDIO! A few flaws about the character art though. 1) Some sprites just weren't drawn well to others or the sprites drawings just didn't really reflect the
aspect. 2) The art for Yunwoo and Ga-yeon's ex (the doctor)... I know she got together with the doctor as he reminded her of Yunwoo but to use the
same drawings for both guys... I bet it won't bother most people but it did for me.
Other than that, the art overall was the major upside of this vn in my opinion.
I felt that the music was alright. It suit the mood at points but after awhile of listening to the same songs over and over again... Irritating. But it wasn't that bad as I just turned turn off the in-game music/sound when I could no longer bear it. So I'm giving credit to where it's due.
The animations in this I have to say...
Annoying. Very. Especially when Ga-yeon blinks or at any of the important, emotional scenes, the screen goes black all of a sudden then text goes flying by = you missing out on reading some parts. I do have to give
credit of implementing an option for faster text speeds
a log for you to check up on missed out chunks of text
an option to
the epilepsy however one downfall would be the skip button as you cannot really skip past major chunks of text but overall, I wasn't too bothered by that. Also, there are very thorough guides on the controls in the help guide. So those complaining and giving this game a bad review just because of the epilepsy warning, you can turn that off. Just saying.
As a whole, I rather enjoyed this as the themes, thoughts and feelings highlighted within this vn relates to my past experiences a lot. The art as a whole was done exceptionally well/is their major upside. Sound was okay. Technical side of things other than the whole epilepsy issue, was all spot on too. In my opinion, I do not recommend this to people who are sensitive about the themes explored in this vn; those put off by the whole epilepsy warning and bothered about how lacking this was, definitely with some parts of the story. However, I do recommend this to people willing to enjoy a short vn filled with heavy themes rarely exploited in the nature of vn's. At it's full price, no but if you're willing to pay a few bucks during sales then I suggest giving this a go.

This game only furthered my love for the Total War series. Beautiful graphics and gameplay, as well as much better AI enemies (or allies). I still have yet to conquer the world and I really suck at naval battles but this game deserves a 9/10, as my only issue being with naval battles and ramming ships was too easy. A must have for any Total War fan looking to engage in the once again brutal clashes of armies as well as anyone else looking for a perfect strategy game.

I am extremely disappointed in this game, as it should not even be mentioned in the same sentence as the original Rome: Total War. This game is utterly atrocious. From the battles to the campaign, it is just a massive bundle of crap.
Let's start with the battles; They are pathetic. The AI, which is bad on all total war games, is somehow worse on this game and it's only tactic seems to be to charge at you. The physics of the battles make no sense, for example, Cataphracts should be able to trample over, and utterly crush enemy infantry formations, but in this game, its like they slow down their charge before they hit the infantry formation.  It is also incredibly frustrating to watch your guys surround the enemy just to see them "1v1" each and every single soldier! Rome 1 physics easily defeat this game, and if you watch the comparison between the two on Youtube, you will see why I say this. I am not even going to touch on naval combat as it is pathetic as well, because transports seem to be the best naval ship in the entire game.
Next is the campaign, and boy is it a mess. They somehow streamlined a game to the point that it is more complex. I find it almost impossible to lose at all on the campaign, as the AI is a bunch of imbeciles that build armies completely out of slingers. Not only that but the AI is the most stubborn idiots I have ever seen on any game, they will not accept TRADE AGREEMENTS THAT HELP BOTH MYSELF AND THEM AT ALL! That is just the surface of the problems with the campaign, with me being lagged out by the number of trees on the map, to Farms causing squalor, it is a mess.
Finally, Let's move on to DLC. This game should be renamed DLC: Total War, as I have never seen a game picked apart into DLCs as much as this game is. This game is part of a larger trend in the gaming universe where game companies ship out half finished games for 60 dollars and charge 120 dollars worth of DLC by it is all said and done.  This is absolutely sick. Around 10 years ago, DLCs were known as EXPANSIONS and were complete add ons to the game, such as the Kingdoms expansion in Medieval II, or the Barbarian Invasion expansion of Rome: Total War. You don't see these kinda of things around anymore, but that doesn't mean they don't exist as Attila:Total War is essentially the Barbarian Invasion expansion of Rome I! Nobody should have to spend a months paycheck to get a full game with its DLC, and this is why the gaming industry is in decline right now, and Rome II is just a piece of the puzzle.
I give this game a good 0/10, It brings shame to the Total War franchise, and all the hype surrounding it came to nigh as this is a black mark on the legacy of Creative Assembly. I hope Medieval III is nothing like this one.

Pros:
Simple, familiar.  What you see is more or less what you get, and it's not hard to figure things out.
Comprehensive built-in completionist support.
Fairly varied class and playstyle options.
Individual players can be very eager to be social and party.
It really is F2P, early access aside.  People complaining about certain restricted features ignore the fact that buying access for a month with game cash is relatively cheap to anyone playing regularly.
Cons:
No PVP.  Future PVP will be unbalanced and have severe level requirements.
Does not respect your time in terms of levelling, you will never be able to try very many aspects of the game for yourself.
Full of half-measures for controlling bots and goldsellers.
Community makes the same cancerous, preteen jokes all day.
Classes scale harshly- your super-fun playstyle may not work at all at high level if you neglect classes that literally unlock later.
Overall:
It's fine.  A pretty standard package.  It really is a streamlined RO, regardless of what some hipsters say.  Differences include less loot and collectible diversity, more class diversity, and steeper level scaling in terms of overall power.
Exploiters are now receiving compensation for game errors.

------Okay, finally the GAME review!!!!!!!
(f'n developers, look how long the warning took?!!?)
theHunter is in the category of "game you need to place" if you are interested in hunting and are patient (aka like simulation/exploring/survival games). I know what your saying, more bullet points it is!!
- The enviroment of the game is perfect. Graphics are beautiful and are perfectly balanced to appear as little like a "video game forest" as possible. The sound is impeccable, the background noise is exactly like a real location and the active noises (calls, gun shot) are filtered so that you can almost get a real sense of their location.
- AI is intelligent, bam. Animals will wander around in paths that make sense, sometimes in packs sometimes not. They can hear and smell you way before you may notice them. Each animal has its own behaviors and patterns and active times and critial hit spots and on on on..... Once you get good, you can turn that intelligence against and lead them right to where you want >:)
- Maps, you will start to love the maps.... each map has its good spots and bad spots, but once your more knowledgable, you will love walking around and discovering get hunts. I live in Colorado and spend a lot of time in the mountains. This is the most realistic forest experiencei have ever seen in a game.
Alright, official review over but those that are interested, heres a simple strategy guide for your first few hunts.
- Pick a map that is one of the first four on the list and start your hunt 7-8 am.
- Walk (NOT RUN) along one of the paths, do not touch your callers.
- DO NOT follow an animal trail until you know the animal is close by (call, sight). That trail could be 30min or more old and a complete waste of time.
- Listen for a call, and note the location, give a call yourself (one), and walk towards it.
- Start looking for a good location closer to the call, preferably to the side. You can call once or twice more but no more. Calls dont stack, they will only be "refresh" if you are closer to the animal.
- Think one shot, one kill and side is always best (slightly above front leg on deer). Wait for the animal to pause, press SPACE to hold your breath, and shoot.
- Get that kill!!

In one line: Transistor is all that Jazz.
This is coming from a player who did not play the first hit of Supergiant Games. (Got my copy of Bastion right after Transistor's release)
Much like the device which the game is takes its title from, the game absorbs you into its world - its designs are woven really well to deliver that much satisfaction for an indie hit:
Art Style is superb - the city of Cloudbank is introduced to you in a mix of vibrant colors and all sorts of forms, there is an immediate sense that the city was once busy and alive. This sense is immediately taken away as you proceed with the plot. Colors are washed out in grays and all its forms reduce to blocks - lifeless and desolate.
Music is excellent. The jazz is silk - although I would probably point out that its more of trip-hop more than anything else. It's hypnotic to say the least. It's a drug inducing a heaviness, a dreaminess that sets you aback once contrasted to the fast paced combat that the game dishes out.
Game mechanics are tight. Transistor plunges you in a mix of active and turn-based type of combat. The Turn() is the Transistor's version of Bullet Time or Tactical Pause in role-playing. While enemies are suspended in freeze time, players can plan their next set of moves mixing movement (evasion & flanking), offense, defense, and utility. Encounters get overwhelming as you progress in the game, and a mastery of the Turn() will be your best friend. Outside of combat, Transistor offers a simple customization interface, where you load out all your Active Skills, Skill Upgrades, and Passive Skills. What's interesting in the skill base of Transistor is that even with a small list of skills, all skills serve out different effects in all three aspects, and make for tons of experimentation and trial. Players can hone there combat mastery via the Backdoor, where several challenges and a practice arena will be made available as the game progresses.
And what we have left is the Story - without any spoilers, the plot is basically a what-the-hell-happened-here story. Cloudbanks is riddled will terminals and files for the player to work with in order to piece out the story. An interesting feature of the game in its story telling is that part of the narrative is tucked in the combat system. The more you experiment in combat, more narrative information is available. This is not to say that you miss out on the scheme of things if you're not the experimental type. But in this game, it really is something you cannot avoid. That being said though, I think I'm part of the lot that will say that the story is floating in ambiguity. There is a lot that's open to interpretation - much as the the combat is open to a lot of approaches.
Currently down to my second run of the game, and I can say it's something hard to drop. Your money's worth is guaranteed on this one.

This game... It's nothing like you or I could have expected. When I first picked it up I was skeptical, because even though Bastion was a great game, I didn't feel like playing a clone. I'm happy to say there was no cause for concern. This game is absolutely unique and engaging in every way that Bastion was and then some. The narration, like in Bastion, is easily the best narration I have ever heard. The character progression, the world, the entire "programming" style they went with really attribute to one of the best interactive stories I've ever been told and particpated in.
The art style is mesmerizing, beautiful, and downright fitting. This doesn't just include the visuals, but the audio as well. Both of these blend really well with the story, which made the atmosphere all that much more believable. The music and sounds were perfect. This games soundtrack is probably one of the best I've ever heard as well. The vocals are powerful and chilling, and are implied to have been the vocals of the main character as far as I could tell. So you really felt like you were inside this characters mind, and it felt great.
So, for the story I rate this game a 9 out of 10. My only reasoning behind the 9 is because of the time it took, even with all the sidetracking I took. I mean, this game isn't short, at all. Don't not buy it because of its longevity. The story is one of the most impactful I've ever went through. It's just that this world could have used more world. You were given some areas to explore but for the most part it was very linear, and I found myself wanting to go back and explore some more, and I couldn't. There is a new game plus mode, however. More on that in a bit.
When it comes to gameplay I believe it's safe to say I have never done this before in my life. This was one of the most unique gameplay experiences when it comes to combat I've ever had. It really separates itself from a generic hack and slash by incorporating strategy and tactics as well as resource management into every single action your character takes. There's no free move, everything has a price. That's what this game plays like. I have to go back and say even the mechanics of this game attribute to the story so much. In retrospect however, the combat system is very unforgiving. While you are given total control over the combat style you choose, you are given permanent choices. Choices that can't be taken back in regards to what abilities you have, that is. Some casual players may encounter issues but I had none, I just figured it was worth noting. For all these reasons and then some, I'm giving this games gameplay a 9/10.
The visuals of this game are stylized, clean, isometric, and bright. They really just accent the beautiful story and are better, if not on par with Bastion's as a comparison. I am a bit biased when it comes to these style graphics as I love comic and manga artstyles. The games cinematics are represented usually with parallaxing objects, such as a character in front of a background, or Red, the protagonist on a motorcycle travelling over a bridge. The visuals are beautiful, and I give them a 10/10.
Now, for my favorite part: the audio. This is my weak spot I must admit. The audio in this game is incredible. It's so emotionally driven and relevant that it just attributes to the overall composition that Transistor turned out to be. Some of the songs are heart breaking, others are great to fight enemies with, some transition the mood smoothly, and every single piece of as engaging as the next. I find this part hardest to explain because I want to elaborate on why I love the music so much. Basically, for a character who cannot communicate, and relies on body gestures to convey herself, the music further demonstrates her mood and can really make you feel, or at least understand what is going through her mind. If that isn't powerful story telling, I don't know what is.
I am glad I bought this game. It is a masterpiece. I definitely recommend it.

So partner are you feeling lucky? I sure was feeling lucky as I got Call of Juarez Gunslinger during the holiday sale for a really low price; and it was well worth the price.  If you’re a fan of westerns and you enjoy killing lots and lots of people then this game is entirely for you.
The story was interesting at times and overall was enjoyable, but there were parts where things just seemed dull and to obvious. The character acting was done well and gave a sense of individualism to each character. The game itself progresses decently but then at times takes a Borderlands-esk turn and quickly changes into some craziness. The basic direction behind each part of the story was kill a bunch of bad guys in some heroic way and then finish off some ringleader of each gang; like I said parts can be dull. The ending itself was decent and did leave me with closure.
Overall the sound and music were good but not great as some vocals from NPCs were reused over and over. The music isn't award winning by any means and to me didn't really stand out at all. Graphically the game is good by current standards and is something that you will admire at times but not necessary be left in awe over.
Gun fighting and the actual FPS aspect to the game is done perfect and never left me feeling like I didn't know what I was doing from a mechanic point of view. The dueling mechanic is fun and original, but is somewhat confusing at times. Expect some redoes if you plan on being honorable about your dueling. The singple player gameplay  was enjoyable with the exceptions of some instances where I felt like I was getting shot by an unknown assailant. I also felt that the skill trees although interesting, felt like a waste after you got the reloading skill points.  Arcade mode is interesting until you 3 star it and then it’s basically just playing the same levels over again minus story and an added few extra NPCs to kill, unless of course you enjoy ladders.
I really enjoyed myself from both an emersion standpoint and a mindless killing game. I would highly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys a good FPS single player with some extra content like arcade mode and new game plus.

For 15 bucks, you can't really go wrong with this shooter. It looks nice, sounds nice, plays pretty well, tells a decent story, and in the middle levels (around 20 in total) it's pretty fun. Enemy variety is pretty limited, as is the range of weapons, but for a budget title that's to be expected.
It suffers a bit at the start (and also near the end) of having the action frequently interrupted / slowed down by the story they're telling, whereas in the middle they are telling that story while you're moving through the level. Not sure why there's such a dichotomy there.
However, it does suffer from one pretty big annoyance, and that's that your accuracy seems all over the place. You'll be making incredible shots from long range at one moment, and at the next, you're firing point blank at two guys that take up half your screen and inexplicably miss both of them. This happens often enough that it gets pretty damn frustrating, especially when that miss interrupts a combo streak or, even worse, gets you killed. Then in the next fight, you're hitting guys while your aim is off, and will be missing them again while you're shooting them dead center in the head. (which is especially irritating when fighting enemies with health bars, who can take rifle shots point blank to the face several times, because apparently being a "shotgunner" and carrying a shotgun also makes you bulletproof.)
The enemies, of course, suffer no issues with accuracy, as every single enemy you run across is the deadliest shot in the West, and will hit you with a quickshooter from halfway across the level.
I wasn't very enamored with the duel system, because it's poorly explained and seems to work rather haphazardly. I finally just resorted to dishonorably killing everyone by firing like mad and dodging like crazy, which seemed to get me past some of the more difficult duels. I liked Red Dead Redemptions duel system far more than this one.
Despite all this, however, it's still enjoyable to play. I recommend it because it's cheap, and it'll amuse you for the five or so hours it takes to play through. It's a definite buy when it's on sale.

Don't let the Call of Juarez name fool you: This is a very strong arcade-shooter with a unique style. Even better, though, is how the game tells its tale as a series of remembered half-truths. Hyperbole, corrections, misdirections, and other storytelling tricks are weaved through the gameplay in a way that, while not maybe groundbreaking, certainly keeps the action from getting overly predictable or repetitive. Best of all, a western game finally gets duels right!

EPILEPSY WARNING
There is a free DLC which should eliminate a potential problem for epileptics.  It is labeled "Patch for Epilepsy Patients"; if you suffer from epilepsy I urge you to download the free dlc before playing.  (The main character blinks her eyes when especially anxious, illustrated in game by having the screen flash to black at what seem to be irregular intervals.  This patch eliminates it.)
This Kinetic Novel, as it refers to itself in advertising, tells a story on a theme that is all-too-real for many people around the world.  A "Discouraged Worker" is someone who is unemployed yet is no longer looking for employment.  The description of this game refers to itself as a "satire."  Satire is not always done for laughs.
"Discouraged Workers" is about the folly of youth, the hopelessness of the seemingly unemployable, and love.  The first act offers no interaction, no choices, you as the player just watch and maybe feel the emotions of the main character. (I did.)
The rest of the game offers a few choices, branching the story.  I'd reccomend saving often.  The right choice isn't always clear.  You see the story through her eyes, not as an all-knowing third party controlling a character; to someone in her place, it is truly hard to think clearly through anxiety.
I'd recomend playing it.  I wish I could go back in time and tell myself to have played it back when I purchased it as an Early Access game. instead of letting it sit on my hard-drive.  I could have just looked up "Discouraged Workers" on wikipedia or somewhere else, but I wouldn't have felt it as I did while playing.
I should probably mention that the game itself is only aproximatly two hours long(yet longer than some movies).  The logged playtime logged is from looking for anything else to report to the very considerate Lee Yunseok of Yggdrasil Studio for the DLC patch I mentioned earlier.  What you should take into account is that what is that the playtime is less important than the time it will spend in your mind.  This is a story that I know will stay with me for a very long time.

Discouraged workers a indie adventure visul novel developed by YGGDRASIL STUDIO. It is based around popular Korean soap operas style. Which I find it intresting because i used to watch those but not anymore.
As a hospital coordinator, Ga-yeon fell in love with a doctor at the hospital she was working in and they had an affair even though the doctor was a married man. When the director of the hospital found out, Ga-yeon was fired. For over a year she tried to find another job, but her mental uneasiness eventually made her give up.
After those unfortunate events, in the spring of 2013, her younger sister, Hye-na, come to her to help her out but things just are just not going her way even with the help.
