This game only furthered my love for the Total War series. Beautiful graphics and gameplay, as well as much better AI enemies (or allies). I still have yet to conquer the world and I really suck at naval battles but this game deserves a 9/10, as my only issue being with naval battles and ramming ships was too easy. A must have for any Total War fan looking to engage in the once again brutal clashes of armies as well as anyone else looking for a perfect strategy game.

I am extremely disappointed in this game, as it should not even be mentioned in the same sentence as the original Rome: Total War. This game is utterly atrocious. From the battles to the campaign, it is just a massive bundle of crap.
Let's start with the battles; They are pathetic. The AI, which is bad on all total war games, is somehow worse on this game and it's only tactic seems to be to charge at you. The physics of the battles make no sense, for example, Cataphracts should be able to trample over, and utterly crush enemy infantry formations, but in this game, its like they slow down their charge before they hit the infantry formation.  It is also incredibly frustrating to watch your guys surround the enemy just to see them "1v1" each and every single soldier! Rome 1 physics easily defeat this game, and if you watch the comparison between the two on Youtube, you will see why I say this. I am not even going to touch on naval combat as it is pathetic as well, because transports seem to be the best naval ship in the entire game.
Next is the campaign, and boy is it a mess. They somehow streamlined a game to the point that it is more complex. I find it almost impossible to lose at all on the campaign, as the AI is a bunch of imbeciles that build armies completely out of slingers. Not only that but the AI is the most stubborn idiots I have ever seen on any game, they will not accept TRADE AGREEMENTS THAT HELP BOTH MYSELF AND THEM AT ALL! That is just the surface of the problems with the campaign, with me being lagged out by the number of trees on the map, to Farms causing squalor, it is a mess.
Finally, Let's move on to DLC. This game should be renamed DLC: Total War, as I have never seen a game picked apart into DLCs as much as this game is. This game is part of a larger trend in the gaming universe where game companies ship out half finished games for 60 dollars and charge 120 dollars worth of DLC by it is all said and done.  This is absolutely sick. Around 10 years ago, DLCs were known as EXPANSIONS and were complete add ons to the game, such as the Kingdoms expansion in Medieval II, or the Barbarian Invasion expansion of Rome: Total War. You don't see these kinda of things around anymore, but that doesn't mean they don't exist as Attila:Total War is essentially the Barbarian Invasion expansion of Rome I! Nobody should have to spend a months paycheck to get a full game with its DLC, and this is why the gaming industry is in decline right now, and Rome II is just a piece of the puzzle.
I give this game a good 0/10, It brings shame to the Total War franchise, and all the hype surrounding it came to nigh as this is a black mark on the legacy of Creative Assembly. I hope Medieval III is nothing like this one.

In this case, Gunslinger rolls with an incredibly unreliable narrator, which isn't too unfamiliar on its own... but the game goes even further by changing the world to fit the narration.  In some ways, Gunslinger reminded me of Bastion (another of my favorite small games), but in Bastion the narrator reacts to the changing world, while in Gunslinger, the world reacts to the changing narration.  I guess it doesn't hurt that I'm a huge fan of spaghetti Western drama, but I found the actual shooting mechanics and skill trees quite good in their own right.

I held out on buying this game because I'm suspicious of Early Access games--most times it seems they are just half-hearted cash grabs. A lot of YouTubers were posting fun gameplay videos so I broke and bought it.
The world is beautiful. The landscape feels like an actual land, the trees and shadows are well done, the foliage and shrubbery looks and feels great. There are ducks, sheep, chickens, elk, deer, wolves, bears, and "werewolves" (spiky mutant wolves) to fight/kill and harvest fangs, leather, wool, meat, fat, etc from. Crafting is your standard crafting: collect enough resources and pick from a menu. There is a kind of technology tree in that you upgrade your work benches from basic -> +tanning -> +stonecutting, etc. Chopping trees is strangely satisfying as they fall over then you keep chopping them to pieces. Mining is boring - there are only a handful of static nodes that respawn after a few minutes. Building is great. There are a lot of options and different materials with properties like some are more durable obviously but some others (like stone and metal reinforced wood) can only be damaged by siege equipment. I honestly really, really enjoyed harvesting resources, upgrading my tools, and planning out my little base and defenses.
That said: This game is a total piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥ You can spend hours working on a base, literally hours (hours), only to have it destroyed and lost in ten minutes. There is only one map that's just a small island that you can run across in a few minutes. The neutral wildlife AI just runs the opposite direction from you when you attack and the hostile AI is borderline ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥... they "slow motion" straight for you and swing at the air in front of them a few times once they get close enough, after they've slid down hills and gotten stuck on any minor divet in the terrain. You can hop up on a block and they can't even touch you as you poke them to death while they swipe harmlessly at your feet. Combat is abysmal - You never know if you're going to hit or miss. Even if you feel like you're going to connect, the character animations pivot and lunge weirdly as you're strafing each other and you can't really gauge the reach of your weapon. If you're decent at landing shots, a fast weapon automatically beats any powerful weapon, because hitting them first interrupts their swing. People wordlessly attack 90% of the time and a majority of my interactions were running for my life while having javelins thrown at my back. Some will give up after a short distance but a fair amount will chase you forever. Seriously. For 20 minutes. Up a mountain, into the ocean, doesn't matter. Another joy is being captured, which sounds fun until you're on the receiving end and minding your own business when suddenly your character falls helpless on the ground and someone drags you away because you weren't listening closely enough for footsteps. Now you're in a cage or some stocks and at the mercy of some 12 year old as your character slowly starves to death and you debate about using the sharp stone you've hidden in your butt (yes, really) to smash your own face in.. but you have all this stuff on you that you'll lose. IMO the king is pointless and typically ignored unless he raises the tax rate enough to irritate people. There's no reason to be king other than to be king and it's hard to get resources because people try to kill you, so you have to use the taxed resources but if you raise the tax too high they'll all band together and come to kill you. A few servers I've been on actually went several hours without ANY king because no one even cared. Hacking is also rampant, since this is a client-side game. There have been flying people throw javelins from the sky and spawning a half dosen werewolves right on top of you, invisible people one-shotting players then deleting their houses, and more.
I had a game going on a public server, until I logged in yesterday and every house on the server was gone--deleted by hackers. All of the forges, chests, workbenches, etc were still there floating in the air but the houses and structures had been deleted. So tonight after working all day I started a new game on a fresh server. Over the next 8 hours I chopped trees and tried to catch ore veins everyone was competing for while dodging person after person trying to capture me (because the admin put a "no kill on sight" rule in play but said capturing was fine). For eight hours. Until finally I had a decent little base going, made of metal reinforced wood so people would have to use siege equipment to break in, and I had the base split into three different rooms separated by strong metal doors so if they did break in, hopefully they wouldn't be able to get into all 3 areas and clean me out. I was on my way back with some resources when I discovered three guys using a ballista at point blank range to smash down just two blocks, enough room for them to squeeze into my first room. I didn't know there were three and jumped in after them swinging my swords, but ducked back out after seeing I was outnumbered. I figured that's fine, whatever, they'll get my resources, who cares... but after healing I came back again to find the one smashing my crest which gave me ownership of the area, then all they'd have to do is put down one of their own to steal the entire thing from me. I jumped in again to try to stop him but got overwhelmed again, so I took off into the mountains and this time they chased. I ended up in a 3vs1 fight, two of them throwing javelins and the other with a large axe, a hole in the side of my base, my resources gone, and soon the entire base gone. Within 15 minutes.
No thanks. I'm done. Buy this game if you want for lulz, but each time you log in, everything you had could be gone. Another thing I heard pointed out is that this is the same company that made Starforge, which they left completely screwed and failed to deliver on any of their promises. We'll see how much hope Reign of Kings has in the future. For now, I'm done.

This game... It's nothing like you or I could have expected. When I first picked it up I was skeptical, because even though Bastion was a great game, I didn't feel like playing a clone. I'm happy to say there was no cause for concern. This game is absolutely unique and engaging in every way that Bastion was and then some. The narration, like in Bastion, is easily the best narration I have ever heard. The character progression, the world, the entire "programming" style they went with really attribute to one of the best interactive stories I've ever been told and particpated in.
The art style is mesmerizing, beautiful, and downright fitting. This doesn't just include the visuals, but the audio as well. Both of these blend really well with the story, which made the atmosphere all that much more believable. The music and sounds were perfect. This games soundtrack is probably one of the best I've ever heard as well. The vocals are powerful and chilling, and are implied to have been the vocals of the main character as far as I could tell. So you really felt like you were inside this characters mind, and it felt great.
So, for the story I rate this game a 9 out of 10. My only reasoning behind the 9 is because of the time it took, even with all the sidetracking I took. I mean, this game isn't short, at all. Don't not buy it because of its longevity. The story is one of the most impactful I've ever went through. It's just that this world could have used more world. You were given some areas to explore but for the most part it was very linear, and I found myself wanting to go back and explore some more, and I couldn't. There is a new game plus mode, however. More on that in a bit.
When it comes to gameplay I believe it's safe to say I have never done this before in my life. This was one of the most unique gameplay experiences when it comes to combat I've ever had. It really separates itself from a generic hack and slash by incorporating strategy and tactics as well as resource management into every single action your character takes. There's no free move, everything has a price. That's what this game plays like. I have to go back and say even the mechanics of this game attribute to the story so much. In retrospect however, the combat system is very unforgiving. While you are given total control over the combat style you choose, you are given permanent choices. Choices that can't be taken back in regards to what abilities you have, that is. Some casual players may encounter issues but I had none, I just figured it was worth noting. For all these reasons and then some, I'm giving this games gameplay a 9/10.
The visuals of this game are stylized, clean, isometric, and bright. They really just accent the beautiful story and are better, if not on par with Bastion's as a comparison. I am a bit biased when it comes to these style graphics as I love comic and manga artstyles. The games cinematics are represented usually with parallaxing objects, such as a character in front of a background, or Red, the protagonist on a motorcycle travelling over a bridge. The visuals are beautiful, and I give them a 10/10.
Now, for my favorite part: the audio. This is my weak spot I must admit. The audio in this game is incredible. It's so emotionally driven and relevant that it just attributes to the overall composition that Transistor turned out to be. Some of the songs are heart breaking, others are great to fight enemies with, some transition the mood smoothly, and every single piece of as engaging as the next. I find this part hardest to explain because I want to elaborate on why I love the music so much. Basically, for a character who cannot communicate, and relies on body gestures to convey herself, the music further demonstrates her mood and can really make you feel, or at least understand what is going through her mind. If that isn't powerful story telling, I don't know what is.
I am glad I bought this game. It is a masterpiece. I definitely recommend it.

Its main flaws for me are in the lack of interactivity until the last quarter of the story and the artwork for the protagonist, which just seems...I don't know...physically inconsistent and clumsy sometimes. It just feels off. Also, I can't agree with the story being considered "satire" - there's nothing outrageous, cutting (no pun intended), nor that funny about it. It's actually a pretty great melodrama. If the heroine's look (not counting sprites) could be a bit more consistent and some different routes could be introduced earlier, this could be a terrific visual novel. But for the moment, it's not quite there. I'd recommend it on sale for half the price, but not for full price as it stands. Sorry. But I look forward to progress!

If you haven't played this game, you're missing out.
It's not the pretentious indie game you would come to expect. It was worth every penny and my playing time proves it. It's not some gimpy social commentary, it's a well-rounded game with a thoughtful premise and despite the outdated graphics you get something that isn't commonly seen in games today: style. Everything is sylized and despite the obvious indication that you're playing a game, you WILL be immersed after playing a few 'levels'. Like a good book, you will not be able to put this game down.  Most games will get you emotionally invested in a character after several pages of dialogue if not more, but "Papers, Please" masterfully draws you into each and every character with only several LINES. The weightiness of each situation is real, the consequence is real, and if you thought you knew who you were before this game I assure you that you will see yourself for who you really are after your first playthrough. Your choices actually have consequence, and the choices themselves are carefully constructed to test you. It's not just black and white, as you define who you are as an inspector you in turn shape your nation. It's literally nationstates: the game. I love it. I'm reccomending this game to everyone I know, it's just that good. As a puzzle game goes, this quirky thing is way up there with Meteos and Professor Layton. It can compete with the best of them. Don't play easy mode, play the way the developer intended. If you feel the time limit is too overwhelming for you, don't feel bad and drop this game. This game is great. And that's a hard thing to pull of with the shadow of it's two big brothers, Demon's Souls & Dark Souls, looming over it. The port is stellar when compared with that of it's predecessor, so much so that the smoothness of the gameplay was off putting at first for me.
However, it's success comes from a rather safe strategy, it's essentially Dark Souls with more stuff and it runs better. Which isn't a bad thing, the first game's formula was near perfect and this sequel draws from it and tweaks it (different health system, easier fast travel, healing items as consumables...) There's a huge variety of weapons and armour making for a wider range of techniques and strategies, and no GFWL so multiplayer is way better, and PvP is still going strong a year after release.
It's the same punishing game, but somehow it seems to have lost a little spark, or to be more accurate, darkness. You see the first Dark Souls felt extremely bleak, you always felt insignificant right up to the end, you were a speck of dust in a world of Gods that was crumbling to nothing, and even then your actions didn't seem to turn that tide. Here things are a bit brighter, you don't have such a dark and opressive soundtrack, in fact this game almost dares to give you hope, rather than just state that the world is plunging into darkness and nothing can stop it. The lore feels less like mythology and more like history, and in a way seems to lose some weight. On top of that the boss battles are generally much weaker than before, with most bosses being large humanoides, and very few instilling awe and fear like the giant bosses and creatures in the original.
It is fascinating though, and is as ambiguous and minimalist as ever, and does link up with the first game in a nice and  ambiguous way. (I recommend checking Youtube videos on the lore, as they tend to give a lot more depth to the battles and NPCs)
Overall this is more of the same, very nicely tweaked and with a lot more stuff, but less dark and epic feeling. The DLC is worth it too, and is much more like the original game, and a little harder too. The only thing you might want to consider is waiting for the shinier DX11 release in the form of the Scholar of the First Sin Edition this year with 6v6 multiplayer (instead of 4v4) more lore, NPCs, better graphics and all the DLC. That does sound nice actually.

S.T.A.L.K.E.R. holds a special place for me, nearly every year I finish this series again and again.
Now I will try to explain why it is simply a fantastic game:
1- Atmosphere & Story :
S.T.A.L.K.E.R. takes place in the "Zone" , an unforgiving and deadly place formed after a fictional second Chernobyl Disaster, the area is completely devastated by radiation, mutants, anomalies and valuable artifacts formed from these anomalies. Soon people who call themselves Stalker's flood the Zone for making a fortune from said artifacts. Military and Scientists ( or Ecologists ) also came to study and understand The Zone. Our character " Marked One " is an amnesiac Stalker with only one mission " Kill Strelok ".
Now, the story in my opinion is the weakest part of the game, once you start playing the game you realize you don't really care about it, it isn't bad but it's predictable.
Atmosphere on the other hand is THE strongest part of the game, developers actually went to the Chernobyl NPP and city of Pripyat to create the game's world, and it is terrific. You travel from army outposts to Stalker camps, dead cities to underground tunnels and it all feels real.
2- Weapons & Shooting Mechanics :
You have your standart assault rifles, shotguns and snipers ( and a little surprise near the end ) but each of them feels different, this game has the best shooting mechanics I have ever seen in a FPS, realistic recoil, individual ammo , scopes and silencers.
3- Factions :
In S.T.A.L.K.E.R. there are 8 factions, you can join some of them but others are sworn enemies ( Monolith , Military etc ) .
You start the game as a rookie stalker and choose who you want to help. I don't want to spoil the factions so much as they are introduced with the story so I will cut this here.
4- Artifacts & Anomalies :
Anomalies are hazards created by the disaster and almost all of them are deadly to the player, some will burn you other will shock you, but they have one good characteristic : they spawn artifacts.
All artifacts have special properties and when weared to the Stalker's belt it will grant useful abilities such as giving higher stamina or lowering radiation sickness. They also worth a lot of money.
5- Mutants :
Besides the human enemies you have mutants, animals or humans warped by radiation and experimentation. You start tangling with measly blind dogs to enormous pseudogiants. All of them are unique and drop mutant body parts which you can sell to the Ecologists. Also some more dangerous mutants have kind of introductions, imagine walking through an abondoned lab and you hear a roar, like an animal roar but something is different , then the ground starts to shake, you ready your trusty AK and...
Yeah just like that :)
Mutants do a fantastic job granting the game horror and atmosphere.
6- Fanbase & Mods :
S.T.A.L.K.E.R. just like Half-Life has the most active fanbase I have ever seen.
Still to this date there are mods coming out for it. I strongly advise you to try them as they make the game feel fresh and fun. First finish it vanilla of course.
As I finish this review I want to thank GSC for this amazing series, there is still nothing like S.T.A.L.K.E.R. . It is oozing with originality, has a great fanbase and mods and overall an amazing atmosphere.
Still waiting for S.T.A.L.K.E.R. 2 guys ;)

When I first looked at this game, I thought "Typical anime high school girl nonsense". How wrong I was. What I found was far and away the most engaging and heartfelt story I have ever experienced. I absolutely love Clannad and cannot recommend it highly enough.
Clannad is a visual novel originally released in Japan in 2004. Voices were added in a 2008 rerelease. In 2015 it was given an official English release. It is regarded by the visual novel community as a paragon of the genre and one of the greatest ever.
Clannad has several different plotlines which can be read in almost any order. These plotlines are mostly love stories. The content and quality of these are what make Clannad a legend. Rather than pander to sexual fantasies, Clannad's stories aim straight at the reader's heart. Some of these hit really close to home for me. At multiple points, I had to stop reading for a few minutes to collect myself before I could continue. Some were so good that I had to go back and reread them again just a couple of days later.
If you complete Clannad, you will cry at least once. Accept this going in. If someone tells you they completed it without crying, they're a liar.
If you're still on the fence, then consider that I was once in your position. I was unsure of if I should even give this game a shot. I took the chance based on word of mouth. Now here I am gushing over it. One of the best works of fiction I have ever experienced.

The reason why I bought the Clannad vn was that Clannad was, and still is, my favorite anime of all time. I remember that right after I re-watched it I picked the novel up on Steam. Now that I've played through every route, I can safely say that it was a great decision. I have so much more love and respect for these wonderful characters that I already loved prior to playing the Clannad visual novel. If you are a fan of the Clannad anime, or just a fan of visual novels, please buy this. It is wonderful.
A classic and gem. If you play visual novels and haven't read this you are missing out on the true quality found in this old trend-setter. 10/10

Make no mistake: This Visual Novel is worth every penny, even if you've already watched the anime.
The number of life lessons, key memorable moments and general emotional connections I have gained and treasured from this VN are incredible. As a grown man, I'm not afraid to say how much I've teared up and cried at a lot of the character paths in Clannad, and it only gets better as you continue playing, learning to understand the concept of how choices you make in your lives could lead to much bigger and better things in the future. Although the anime did an impeccable job of keeping as much content in the series as possible, the Clannad Visual Novel cannot be topped for having such a lengthy emotional rollercoaster of alternative endings.
I'm still not fully finished with all of the potential outcomes of this VN, and having currently racked up over 60 hours (currently) to this game, I can't stress enough how well worth this purchase was, even at the seemingly steep £30 price tag.
In particular I was surprised with Kotomi's Arc in this Visual Novel, which was much more detailed than shown in the anime. It is probably my favourite Arc of all, and helped me be thankful for and treasure the closest people in my life, as well as changing my perspective on how I should live. If you are even slightly interested in the concept of this franchise, I wholeheartedly and undisputably recommend this masterpiece of a story.
A key aspect of the game that set me off many a time were the soundtracks featured. These consist of some of the most beautifully crafted musical scores I've ever had the pleasure of listening to, and every time I hear them brings back events, Arcs and character quotes which made for the Visual Novel to be as memorable as it was. I applaud whoever created the "Shining In The Sky" and "To The Same Heights" Soundtracks; they are my personal favourites.
If I had to give any advice for playing the Clannad VN, I would strongly suggest that you take your time playing through it. Don't think of it as something you can speedrun through and still enjoy; treasure every moment of the Visual Novel, funny, awkward or emotional, and the events that unfold will really have a lasting impact on you, hopefully for the better.
Truly the best story I've ever read.
~
EDIT: After truly having completed all there is to this game, I feel the need to add a finishing note to my review.
Finishing the After Story, after so much pain and sadness, was such a rewarding and complete feeling. It made me finally understand what it means to love and treasure those close to you, and make the most of the short time you have on this world.
For anyone doubting continuing with the After Story as a result of it being too heartaching (I've been there) be rest assured that it's all in perfect timing to come back around and complete the missing pieces of the puzzle, allowing you to rest easy and feel blessed that you had the chance to experience something as unique as this.
Nothing comes close to what CLANNAD has done for me.

The nickel and diming of Elder Scrolls Online would put most free-to-play Korean MMOs to shame.
In the last few months, Elder Scrolls Online shifted focus from adding content to draw in new players and improve upon the experience, to adding content for the sake of purely monetizing it.
There are many examples of how the focus on purely monetizing in this PAY-TO-PLAY MMO has gotten out of hand, but here are the top ones:
The Homestead update which added player housing is designed so that acquiring a house and furniture is extremely inconvenient to entice players to spend $100+ on a furnished house for the convenience.
The most recent house added to the game can ONLY be purchased with real money for $100 to $120 USD, depending on whether it’s purchased with or without furniture.
Morrowind, the “expansion” that adds one zone goes for $40 for standard upgrade to $100 for a Collector’s Edition. It includes a new playable class, the Warden. However, there is no new character slot to accommodate the new class. Instead two character slots will be purchasable for $15 EACH. That’s right, ZOS is making players pay an additional $15 on top of the $40 or $100 spent in order to play the new class added in Morrowind. Having a new extra character slot when a new class is added in a paid expansion is standard practice in all the other MMOs.
A mount added to the store for 3 days in December went for about $40 USD.
The addition of Crown Crates, which are gamble boxes, when opened can give a costume, pet, or in almost all cases, just pure consumable junk. A pack of 15 such boxes goes for $40.00 USD, and recent player reports suggest that they are rigged to give worthless consumable experience scrolls over costumes/pets/mounts for the rarer reward tiers.
A HAIRSTYLE added to the game for 3 days went for $20 USD.
Meanwhile bots run rampant in the game, some camping in obvious areas called dolmens to the point that they are causing lag due to their sheer numbers. Others farm materials and mobs, crashing prices of crafting materials. Nothing has been done about them for months.
A year ago, the game was at its best when new zones and content were added that subscribers ($15/month) could access. It was a time when it did not feel necessary to spend hundreds of dollars to fully experience the game like Homestead did.
A year ago, the Crown Store had cosmetic purchases that could be made with real money without the astronomical prices like it does now, and it actually felt like a fun extra to the game. Now, the development of the game feels purely focused on adding the next $100 item to the Crown Store rather than on actual game content.
Until ZOS (the developers) shift their focus back to the game itself and stop treating players like bags of meat with wallets, I cannot recommend this game. Don't get me wrong though, I had a lot of fun until the nickel and diming tactics were out of control. If you can get past these issues, you could get some enjoyment out of the game.  No, the ENTIRE game is not bad, it's just overshadowed by a lot of poor PR practices and the aforementioned issues.
Reminds me of the good old days. Skyrim...

Beautiful graphics. Nice story. I'll probably play the story through 3 times before saying good-bye to this game.
Duels in the story are a bit irritating - completely different mechanic than rest of game. Figuring out the duels mechanic took me about 40 minutes to get a handle on - reading guides along the way - and there's one guy that you simply cannot outdraw - you have to dodge one way, then the other - that required dodging killed about 20 minutes by itself for me. The game runs 1 or 2 short maps of standard FPS play on interesting maps, followed by a duel that is required to progress further in the story. The duels were the only laborious part for me...that and collecting the nuggets of truth, which I recommend you ignore - they're interesting if you find them by chance, but are not worth searching for.
I guess I'm more of a fan of FPS's following the Call of Duty 1 style - just work your way through the environment, killing a limited number of enemies along the way, trying to limit the damage you take as much as possible. Call of Duty 2 introduced regeneration, and unlimited enemies if you fail to advance. No unlimited enemies here, but the regeneration is here...well I guess it's the only way they could make this game work.
Definitely worth the time and money (goes for $5 on sale) to try the story through once on normal difficulty, ignoring all achievements, etc. It's beautiful and fun, and the first run through the story should take you 6-10 hours.
There are two extra modes of play: arcade, which is all about getting a high score (killing baddies in high style with combos, rather than just killing them) and duel mode, where the duels seem MUCH harder than they do in story mode. For hardcore folks only.
A guide for story mode duels: (except for the guy you have to dodge)
A and D keep your hand near your gun, when it's placed exactly right, your draw speed slowly increases. However, you can win your duels with 0% improved drawspeed. Instead, concentrate on growing your FOCUS as high as possible.
The focus circle behaves like a big blob with a lot of momentum - it's slow to get it moving, and it's slow to stop it moving. Move your mouse to get it over the enemy.
When you get the circle over the enemy, it should turn yellow and rotate. In story mode duels you can make tight circles with your mouse to help keep it from drifting around. (In duel mode duels, this doesn't work as well.)
When you hear a heartbeat, you can draw. Or wait for the enemy to move his hand and then draw. Some people report that there's a big accuracy penalty if you draw first.
To draw, click once.
If your FOCUS was over 80%, time will be slowed enough that you can dodge right or left, but this is seldom necessary.
After you draw, wait for the red aiming cursors to appear. The moment you see red crosshairs (hugely seperated initially), you can usually fire and win the duel - there's rarely any point in waiting for the cursors to close up for better aim. One shot always seems to kill in duels.

Transistor has one of the most unique combat engines I've seen in a game, in a good way. It's got the basic hack/slash combat, but throws a spark into it by introducing a clever "turn-based" feature which might feel overpowered at first. However given the weight at which you're out numbered, the game definitely knows you've got a trick up your sleeve and feels compelled to ensure you're not allowed to run rampant with it - you will lose functions, you will be forced to strategize.
Combat aside, the game has a deep, fleshed out story that, while not completely interwoven with the gameplay, convinces you to earn it through actively combining various functions in various roles. It further pushes you to do this by not simply killing you upon death, but allowing you to continue fight with heavily relied upon functions being removed from your arsenal. The result being a stronger emphasis on reworking your strategy and further opening up more backstory.
In short: The game does a lot of new stuff while keeping fresh some of the more traditional concepts. I'd even go as far as to say that it's brilliant on everything it does new and nothing short of great on it's weaker areas, as far and few as they even are.

...what can I say about what makes this game perfect? Is it the amazing visuals of a 1920s-era style mixed with a neon cyberpunk overlay? Is it the smart and creative gameplay mechanics that allows you to slow things down, plan out your perfect sequences of attacks using moves that can be combined together in inventive ways?
Or is it that addictive original soundtrack the game has, that is like an iced coffee, that goes down smooth and cool?
How can I quantify Transistor's awe-inspiring qualities with mere words, especially from such an inexact and guttural language such as english? And after playing, how can I...transition...back to other lesser games?
I cannot recommend highly enough. GET THIS GAME AND LOOSE YOURSELF IN IT.

It surprises me that I haven't reviewed this yet.
No More Room in Hell is a standalone source engine modification set in the zombie apocalypse scenario, inspired by the likes of the "Of the Dead" Series.
From what I understand, this title goes all the way back to 2004, when the SDK for Half-Life 2 was released. While the idea was there, the original team worked, but the project died for a while, until about 2010, where another dedicated team picked this up from the ashes and pushed hard, and managed to squeeze out the first playable beta on Halloween, 2011.
I was a tad late to the party, joining in on the action when I was a wee lad in the summer of 2012. Many design choices have been made since then to make NMRiH what it is today. And for 100% FREE!
I am personally so glad that this game came to see the light of day.
If you like Left 4 Dead because of it's co-op and team mechanics, then perhaps you're looking in the right direction. If you like Left 4 Dead because of the run and gun, the arcade, the shoot em' up-- turn the other way.
This is the epitome, the cataclysm, the ABSOLUTE definition of realism. A selective HUD, where health is determined by saturation, and a weight-based inventory system, The shambling hordes of the undead are individually deadly, able to grapple you and hold you in place while they make a snack out of your humanity. Unlike L4D or most other zombie shooters, this game puts into view the mortality of the average survivor. You are not superhuman. You are not a soldier.
You are not immune.
The pathogen in question, a mutation of Encephalitis Lethargica, named 732-ZH in game lore, is unforgiving. It is indiscriminant in it's reaches for bloodthirst. When you are infected, there is no more hope for you. The average healthy survivor will have 2 minutes to either find a dose of Phalanx pills to stave off the infection for a period of time, or find peace with themselves before they fall to the horde and go after the people they used to call friends. Contact with the infected or infested waters are surefire ways to get yourself feeling a little less fine.
You can't carry everything. As an average civilian sure, you may have guns, but unless you have a quite the backpack or arms, you are not carrying more than 3 rifles EFFECTIVELY, let alone with ample amounts of ammo for each, including a possible handheld device of punishment, such as a wrench all the way to a FUBAR Wrecking Bar. Count your bullets and pack your pockets light, because travelling heavy will leave you tired and alone, easy prey for the hivemind in the streets.
Your team MATTERS. Online play is optimal and encouraged, and teamwork is borderline essential to make it out of your situation alive. You will bleed, you will scream, and you will be infected. Even with these consequences, work together, and it will all turn out alright. Stick close, because VoIP is range-based, meaning you better grab a walkie-talkie, lest you be wandering the halls, calling out to no one if you get separated. Trade ammo, guns, and other tools and gear to help each other out. Think about yourself of course, but never forget your team. They can and WILL save you later on.
Variation in playthroughs keep every map fresh and exciting through even back-to-back play. You'll go a Y-N-Y-Y route, and have the other variations ready at a throw of the dice. Let alone the spawns of gear that will beset your eyes and backpack. One run may leave your streets clean and shotguns full, while others may wall you in with the hungry and leave you scrounging for even .22 by the bullet.
Melee is simple, albeit in-depth. Shoving will keep the grabby at bay, and differences in your choice of smacking implement will decide your effectiveness. Light weaponry such as knives or carpenter tools will keep them back, but not keep them down. Your average choices of crowbars and baseball bats will surely do the average joe a service, and the Big Boys like the Fire Axe and Sledgehammer will leave you gasping for air, but with a room full of viscera from your swinging and damage.
Variations of zombies will make your treks through the zombie-infested environment a living hell, with those recently fallen running after you, flailing their arms about as if losing balance, only set on sinking their teeth into your flesh as fast as inhumanly possible. The usual longer-dead have grown stiff from their weeks of malnutrition and rest at ease, only truly making a move when food is a definite. They may be slow, but they pack a punch and can take one or two as well. The tiny beings of this earth aren't safe from the turning of dead and alive either, and sometimes among the many figures in the dark, a child will come barreling between their legs, unable to bite, but sure trying to lay waste to your being by slashing and wildly distracting you.
Take control of what you seek, being an average joe wanting out of the not-so-average situation is a guarantee, finding yourself in Objective maps where you and your team of comrades are fed up with waiting in your safe area, and decide if rescure is ever going to come, you will have to be the one to answer the phone. Ready yourself and stick close to your friends as you descend into what has spilled over from Hell, being careful in your escapade, any and all actions matter in your fight for survival, salvation only reserved for those willing to do whatever it takes. Those who aren't careful or mindful shall have an almost ensured reservation in the vast numbers of the shambling corpses. Be mindful of the barrel of your firearm, for you never know where it will be pointing in the end.
Or perhaps being the person to survive an onslaught of Hell, escaping to outskirts and lands unknown, now have an established connection with the United States National Guard. Their orders are simple:
"There are zones marked in your area. Defend them from hostiles for a defined amount of time and you will earn extraction to safety. Do your part. We are on our way."
Pack your bags and stuff everything in mother base, because things are about to get funky. Defend your zones from the stretches of the dead, using whatever tools and mechanisms available to you. Gas, traps, guns, whatever you need. Periodically, the USNG will transport airdrops for your team, beholding valuable supplies to aid your defense. Survive 10 waves of increasing numbers of hostiles and partnered hostility, and you may then leave, your struggle over and safety within reach.
Earn your keep as a true zombie killing machine; you have achievements for DAYS son! Master the craft of a bayonet, crank up the tempo with speedruns, and lock and load with the ridiculously hilarious achievements that will surely keep you busy for a while. Over 1,000,000 zombies need to die by your hands, 1,000 of the horde you'll engage in fisticuffs and must emerge victorious, 6 of your friends dominate and hold part of an elite unit by defending multiple zones with pinpoint accuracy and militant responsiveness, and redefine the definition of Tool by dispatching multiple zeds with a Blowtorch, Flashlight, or Fire Extinguisher.
And although you'll sink your life into the apocalypse, now forced to fight day-by-day, the sad fact is that no one lives forever. You'll get bitten, you'll get nicked, you'll get left behind. It is truly staggering the truly tiny amount of push you need to find yourself staring down the barrel of your own loaded gun, unsure of how or if to go on. But all you know is that either you erase your profile or come back to life in a different way.
Because when there is No More Room in Hell...

This game is great. And that's a hard thing to pull of with the shadow of it's two big brothers, Demon's Souls & Dark Souls, looming over it. The port is stellar when compared with that of it's predecessor, so much so that the smoothness of the gameplay was off putting at first for me.
However, it's success comes from a rather safe strategy, it's essentially Dark Souls with more stuff and it runs better. Which isn't a bad thing, the first game's formula was near perfect and this sequel draws from it and tweaks it (different health system, easier fast travel, healing items as consumables...) There's a huge variety of weapons and armour making for a wider range of techniques and strategies, and no GFWL so multiplayer is way better, and PvP is still going strong a year after release.
It's the same punishing game, but somehow it seems to have lost a little spark, or to be more accurate, darkness. You see the first Dark Souls felt extremely bleak, you always felt insignificant right up to the end, you were a speck of dust in a world of Gods that was crumbling to nothing, and even then your actions didn't seem to turn that tide. Here things are a bit brighter, you don't have such a dark and opressive soundtrack, in fact this game almost dares to give you hope, rather than just state that the world is plunging into darkness and nothing can stop it. The lore feels less like mythology and more like history, and in a way seems to lose some weight. On top of that the boss battles are generally much weaker than before, with most bosses being large humanoides, and very few instilling awe and fear like the giant bosses and creatures in the original.
It is fascinating though, and is as ambiguous and minimalist as ever, and does link up with the first game in a nice and  ambiguous way. (I recommend checking Youtube videos on the lore, as they tend to give a lot more depth to the battles and NPCs)
Overall this is more of the same, very nicely tweaked and with a lot more stuff, but less dark and epic feeling. The DLC is worth it too, and is much more like the original game, and a little harder too. The only thing you might want to consider is waiting for the shinier DX11 release in the form of the Scholar of the First Sin Edition this year with 6v6 multiplayer (instead of 4v4) more lore, NPCs, better graphics and all the DLC. That does sound nice actually.

One thing that is new to Dark Souls 2 is the introduction of Soul Memory which is (correct me if I'm wrong here) a sort of collection of all the souls you spend throughout the game. Soul Memory affects which players you may interract with, like COOP for example. Only players withing your Soul Memory range may be summoned by you for COOP play. The same thing goes for invasions. One thing Soul Memory prevents is the risk of being invaded by one of the same (or higher) level than you with much better gear than you, resulting in a fast defeat on your side. This is probably the only thing that Soul Memory is good for, otherwise it just feels like it shouldn't be there.
In summary: Dark Souls 2 is an experience worth remembering and it sure deserves a playthrough. It may not give out the same dark feeling as the first game, but is still a great game.

I have two main problems with Borderlands 2: first, the quests are tedious as all Hell and second, the game just doesn’t work as a single-player experience.

First things first, you will quite literally be doing the same thing over and over again during the entire course of this game. Every single quest involves you running and gunning and occasionally picking stuff up. But really just shooting at people, robots and monsters. After a while it gets old.

Second, an action RPG needs a solid single-player campaign if it’s going to stand the test of time. There’s a direct correlation with a game getting older and fewer people wanting to play it - and after a certain point you're just not going to find many takers for a coop campaign.

That’s why it sucks that the Borderlands 2 campaign is so uneven. There are plenty of times when you just repeatedly die because it’s obvious you need a coop partner, while in other other cases it’s not hard enough. For example, I don’t know if this was a glitch or what, but in the final boss fight I literally just stood on a hill taking pot shots at this guy while he kept changing the battlefield (but not my little perch) until he died. He didn’t hit me once. What’s up with that?

Yes, the game can sometimes be funny, and Claptrap remains one of my favorite video game characters of all time, but it’s not enough to rescue Borderlands 2 from its painful, repetitive gameplay.

I am going to assume that if you have found this game's page, then it is incredibly likely that you have come here having watched the rather brilliant anime done by Kyoto Animation. You are probably wondering if the source material lives up to that high benchmark. The answer is an unequivical yes. The anime focussed mostly on Nagisa's route, and interspersed the other ones as mini arcs whilst still focussing mostly on her. In the visual novel, you get the chance to see each girl's individual route properly (some of which weren't even alluded to in the anime), with all romantic elements intact, and with none of the brevity which the anime had to use in its adaptation. On top of this, unlike the anime, you are seeing all of the events from Tomoya's point of view, with his own thoughts constantly on display. This serves to make him the best developed character in the entire game, and adds new dimensions to him that are simply not there in the anime. This in turn makes every heartbreaking moment that much more poignant. Make no mistakes, although Clannad is deeply rooted in "bishoujo game" territory, Tomoya is by no means a bland self insert character. When going through the various routes, you make the decisions for him, but his personality will still dictate what happens. This is refreshing since a lot of VN protagonists can be a little one dimensional.
In terms of value for money, having played Clannad for over 30 hours (at the time of writing), I have currently completed less than half of the game, so if you are wondering whether the price of this visual novel is worth it, the answer is an indisputable yes. In terms of value, there are very few things that will give you the same bang for your buck as this gargantuan visual novel. For those unfamiliar with visual novels, they are much less interactive than a game, but more interactive than a book. The game is 99% reading text with 1% decision making, so be prepared for a good long read when you download this, since according to statistics fetched online, it has about as many words as nearly two readings of 'War and Peace' (approx 1.25m words). Just sit back, relax, and let the story wash over you. Take your time, complete the game's 12+ routes. It will make you laugh, it will make you cry like a baby, and if you're like me it will find a special place in your heart.  If you loved the anime and you are a keen reader, then this is an experience you will never forget.

S.T.A.L.K.E.R. holds a special place for me, nearly every year I finish this series again and again.
Now I will try to explain why it is simply a fantastic game:
1- Atmosphere & Story :
S.T.A.L.K.E.R. takes place in the "Zone" , an unforgiving and deadly place formed after a fictional second Chernobyl Disaster, the area is completely devastated by radiation, mutants, anomalies and valuable artifacts formed from these anomalies. Soon people who call themselves Stalker's flood the Zone for making a fortune from said artifacts. Military and Scientists ( or Ecologists ) also came to study and understand The Zone. Our character " Marked One " is an amnesiac Stalker with only one mission " Kill Strelok ".
Now, the story in my opinion is the weakest part of the game, once you start playing the game you realize you don't really care about it, it isn't bad but it's predictable.
Atmosphere on the other hand is THE strongest part of the game, developers actually went to the Chernobyl NPP and city of Pripyat to create the game's world, and it is terrific. You travel from army outposts to Stalker camps, dead cities to underground tunnels and it all feels real.
2- Weapons & Shooting Mechanics :
You have your standart assault rifles, shotguns and snipers ( and a little surprise near the end ) but each of them feels different, this game has the best shooting mechanics I have ever seen in a FPS, realistic recoil, individual ammo , scopes and silencers.
3- Factions :
In S.T.A.L.K.E.R. there are 8 factions, you can join some of them but others are sworn enemies ( Monolith , Military etc ) .
You start the game as a rookie stalker and choose who you want to help. I don't want to spoil the factions so much as they are introduced with the story so I will cut this here.
4- Artifacts & Anomalies :
Anomalies are hazards created by the disaster and almost all of them are deadly to the player, some will burn you other will shock you, but they have one good characteristic : they spawn artifacts.
All artifacts have special properties and when weared to the Stalker's belt it will grant useful abilities such as giving higher stamina or lowering radiation sickness. They also worth a lot of money.
5- Mutants :
Besides the human enemies you have mutants, animals or humans warped by radiation and experimentation. You start tangling with measly blind dogs to enormous pseudogiants. All of them are unique and drop mutant body parts which you can sell to the Ecologists. Also some more dangerous mutants have kind of introductions, imagine walking through an abondoned lab and you hear a roar, like an animal roar but something is different , then the ground starts to shake, you ready your trusty AK and...
Yeah just like that :)
Mutants do a fantastic job granting the game horror and atmosphere.
6- Fanbase & Mods :
S.T.A.L.K.E.R. just like Half-Life has the most active fanbase I have ever seen.
Still to this date there are mods coming out for it. I strongly advise you to try them as they make the game feel fresh and fun. First finish it vanilla of course.
As I finish this review I want to thank GSC for this amazing series, there is still nothing like S.T.A.L.K.E.R. . It is oozing with originality, has a great fanbase and mods and overall an amazing atmosphere.
Still waiting for S.T.A.L.K.E.R. 2 guys ;)

The short: Factorio is a fantastic game, but it takes time to admit it.
Factorio is at it heart a game about always thinking bigger. When you start you only have a few basic supplies and little applicable technology. You might get a few basic things happening but soon aliens will ruin your day. You'll be tempted to give up on it entirely.
But the problem isn't the game, you just aren't thinking big enough. Why build one lab when you can set up 4 for 4 times the price? Why only walls 1 square thick? You've built one steam engine, why not 30?
The scale is infinite, and as you build the abmition to grander and grander designs the materials that allow you to expand grow. Soon technology comes quickly, aliens become a manageable nuisance, you start planning some train lines to go for a long distance iron deposit to top up your stockpiles and oh god its 4am I'm supposed to wake up for work in 3 hours what am I doing with my life.
Its only real drawback is that with only a few core resources some people may think theres not enough complexity. But its meant to be a finely tightly tuned experience and what its doing it does well. The visuals aren't exactly next gen but they mesh well together and when you're potentially talking millions of assets at screen on once you don't want the engine grinding to a halt. The sound design is top notch and as you move about your factory you will feel like you are passing by the machinery.
If you like designing your own machines, solving spatial problems, or even the sim city experience of watching something you plan expand and grow, you will find enjoyment in this game. At the very least, I recommend running through the demo and getting a taste.

There are so many reasons why Papers Please is so appealing. It's got a typical BioWare plot, which means that there's a mystery that's so well thought out and told that everything clicks into place during the big reveal. Yet it's also a game made by sci-fi fans for those who love sci-fi. There are so many elements borrowed and culled from decades of science fiction and movies, and there are countless moments that will remind you of Star Trek or Aliens or Firefly or some early John Carpenter movie (the electronic score is very Carpenter-esque, too). There's even an effective film grain post-processing effect that makes the game feel like a 70s or 80s sci-fi movie, before digital filmmaking and CGI made everything look and feel too clean.
Here's the premise of Papers Please: Several hundred years in the future humanity has joined the galactic community after finding alien technology on Mars that opens up interstellar travel. We uppity humans are seen as too ambitious in a galaxy run by a UN-like council populated by ancient alien races. You play as The Inspector of the human Alliance military, and BioWare lets you role-play as either a male or female character. There are pre-rolled characters that you can select or you can create a custom character with a unique face.
When a rogue spectre--one of the galactic council's special agents--attacks a human colony on Eden Prime, you're tasked with hunting him down. It's not that simple, though, as invariably epic themes such as extinction on a galactic scale kick in. So you must zip around the galaxy in a very sleek starship, explore alien worlds, engage in futuristic firefights, and unearth the overarching mystery. There's also a cast of human and alien characters that can grow on you, like Wrex, a krogan killing machine with a blunt, sardonic personality. And this wouldn't be a  game without one or two romance possibilities, as well.
A fantastically visualized game with a myriad of ways to play.  The customizability in combat is simply astounding.

Not having played very many horror-esque style games before, this game certainly performs brilliantly in what it aims to do - making you a nervous wreck, who is anxious and scared for what may be around the corner, be it Synthetic, human, or worse.
This game is what got me interested in the Alien franchise, hard to believe. When I watched Alien after playing this for a few hours, I was amazed at just how much of the environment and story that this game captures, and how vividly real and eerie this game looks. When I first got this game and started playing it, I actually gave up not too far into it because I simply got too scared and intimidated by it. Recently though, I decided to buckle down and beat it, and once I got started on it a second time, I couldn't be bothered to play anything else over the next several days until I beat it. The game takes a suprising amount of time to beat, more than I anticipated - I'm sure it took me over 16+ hours at least minimum.
The graphics, gameplay, and story are all amazing, and I can think of next to nothing that I would have wanted changed to try and make the game better. I've seen complaints of how the pace of the game can vary, or how it can be too difficult on some of the easier gamemodes - I don't believe either of those to be true. It can be beat, even if for some it may take quite a few tries (though I never got stuck in any one area too many times by dying).
Concerning the DLC, I don't care very much to try and beat my own scores (or the scores of others) and see how fast I can complete a level by doing X amount of things. Others might love this, I don't particularly care for it. I liked the main game for the story and the advancement, which while the DLC missions can have a sense of story, it's nowhere near the main game in terms of concrete story. I would pass on the DLC, unless the bundle happens to be cheaper than the stand alone game.

Overall, while I'm stingy and wouldn't ever pay full price for a game, this is definitely worth a pickup if you love that scared anxious feeling, and love horror-style space games. $20 or under is a great deal.

I have had this game since its very dawn in its earliest stages on alpha, clocking in hundreds of hours. I have just recently bothered to get the Steam Key and play it through here, but here is my review from all that time. It will cover both the Pros and Cons of this game, but overall it is a good game to play.
*******************************************************************************************************
Factorio is an amazingly fun and well developed game. It has both the elements of a Strategy and that of an Action game, tied together with a Factorization / Automation simulator. There are hostile entities that will attack you and your magnificent factories, so you must retaliate and develop more technologies and destroy them. Although there is no proper "End Goal" as of yet, you can "win" by researching a very high tier technology. This makes the game feel almost endless, but the reality of it is that once you have researched that and the relatively small technology tree (it may seem large, but with good automation you can easily run through it). On the positive side it is a beautiful and artfully designed game world, that is randomly generated, as you go. Although you may not succeed on your first attempt to build a shining (and smoking) city with streets of conveyors and towering buildings on both sides, all made of Iron, and Steel to suck the planet dry, you will learn many things in each attempt.
*******************************************************************************************************
Factorio is a game in which you build and maintain factories.

If gallery shooters are your thing, Call of Juarez: Gunslinger is probably for you... sadly, they're not my thing.  I only played two levels through this game, and honestly it was so repetitive by that point that even the stellar story couldn't keep me around for more.
PROS: From what little I experienced, the game was very good in regards to a plot.  Frankly I'll probably track down a quick YouTube playthough video just to get my fix on the story (yes it is that entertaining).  Great humor and from the sample I experienced, it was well written.  The controls are relatively simple and straight forward, and if you are good at any FPS, chances are high you'll excel at CoJ:G.
CONS: Run, shoot at relatively fixed targets, run, shoot, rinse-repeat.  Every once in a while you can distribute a point to the skill tree or have a showdown with a historical western figure, but as I said it's a gallery shooter at its core.  There is no openness, rather only the illusion of such.  Weapons range from guns to guns... frankly, the only difference between the pistol, shotgun, and rifle is the rate of fire and the perception of zoom.  I just found it monotonous and boring... and that was already half-way through the first level.
Basically this game was not my cup of tea. Good story, but playability was not entertaining for me.  I'd rather digest this plot by way of a YouTube playthrough or a graphic novel.  My vote: save your money and pass on this one.

Those who brought to us this magnificent masterpiece that is Bastion fails in one thing, disappointing us. A game that only learned from it predecessor, Transistor is beautiful, immersive and brings quite the unique fighting system to the table. A gorgeous soundtrack completes the picture for a truely precious gem of a game.
Let's talk about the fighting system, shall we? Remember I said it was unique? A really savant mix of real-time action with a Turn-mode, allowing entering into a turn-based style game for a short period of time allowing for a precise, calculated burst of action. While you fight multiple enemies with your wide array of skills; all of them having active effects, synergies effect when combined with other skills, and passive effects; you must face puzzles and priorities of elemination for a truely memorable gameplay, with challenging boss battles.
Help Red find her voice as she wields Transistor, her quite talkative and only friend, her trusty USB-style sword, in this linear, but gorgeous game. Will you conquer, against the enormous adversity, in this electronic world with a feel of apocalyps?
If you loved Bastion, Transistor is for you.

I picked this up in the Steam Sale yesterday and was very happy with it on my PC until last night. I saved my game and uploaded it to the Steam Cloud, knowing that I was spending the evening at my girlfriend's house, I figured it was something I could play on my laptop. I got to my girlfriend's and ran the game, whereupon it asked me if I wanted to download the save I had. I definitely clicked 'yes' but it uploaded the laptop save to the cloud anyway.
'Fine' I thought to myself. 'I'll just start again now and load up my old save when I get home tomorrow.'
So I get home the next day and booted up my PC, only to have it automatically download my laptop's save from the cloud.
'Fine' I thought to myself. 'I'll just play from where I left off last night on my laptop.'
Alas, regardless of what day I load the save up on, it simply starts from day one. This is a great game and I know that a lot of people have had a lot of fun with it, but I honestly can't reccomend it to anyone with such a horrendous, game-breaking bug. Clannad is a fantastic visual novel in both it's storytelling and sound design. It will make you laugh, and it will make you cry but most importantly it will make you connect to at least one of the main storylines on a personal level, whether the story is about dealing with someone's death, a friend going through life threatening trouble, or family drama, Clannad has a story for everyone.

I first read this VN nine years ago when the anime was coming out, it was my first Visual Novel ever and I was not prepared for the sheer volume of content. I was overwhelmed by how much attention to detail there was in the storylines, how every day of Tomoya's life is explained to you, there are many conversations that do not even necessarily add to the plot but are just there to give you a sense of who the characters are and what it's really like to be in Tomoya's shoes. Never before have I experienced that level of intimacy with fictional characters before, I truly felt like I had lived Tomoya's life, and that made the emotional moments of Clannad feel more personally impactful than any other story I've ever read.
This was my second re-read and it was just as amazing the third time. Truly one of a kind.

Take the interactive narrator of Bastion, add the bullet time of Max Payne, simmer with the Skill Kills of Bullestorm, wrap it in a semi cel-shaded comic book aesthetic, throw in every Sergio Leone movie and spaghetti western trope, and put it all in a blender set to puree.
That's Call of Juarez: Gunslinger in a nutshell. A love letter to the spaghetti westerns of yore. It tells a simple story that doesn't take itself seriously, and has great shooting gameplay that's less about realism and more about racking up a high score while being the most badass hombre in the Wild West. Add in some excellent voice acting and music, along with excellent graphics, and you got a cheap title that's well worth playing, especially with all the unlockable skills and the highly challenging but satisfying "True West" mode, where the HUD is removed completely.
It's short, sweet, and comes with lots of fun extras. In today's obsession with modern military shooters, it's a breath of fresh air, and exactly what the franchise needed after The Cartel nearly killed it.

Having never played the prior Call of Juarez games, and hearing that this new one was pretty good after the supposedly terrible Cartel, I wasn't really too fond on getting it. I'm not a huge fan of old western movies, or games like Red Dead Redemption on consoles, though I do enjoy them. I like arcade shooters though, and when a friend gave me it I just had to try it.
The game starts with the player, an aging bounty hunter of years past named Silas Greaves, entering a saloon in a stylized comic-book/hand drawn sort of cutscene. He orders a drink (or two....or three), and begins to tell his story to the other people in the saloon, who seem fascinated by his presence. He tells wild tales of his past, each one being a level in the game, and entertains the people listening in with his crazy adventures. He narrates the story while you play through his supposed (I'll get to that in a bit) adventures, and the other people listening in chime in sometimes too.
Now, Silas is a big fat liar as it seems he's everywhere at once. First he's with the famous Billy the Kid, then next he's dueling with Jesse James, the famous bandit. Is any of what he says true? No, not at all, and the other people start to suspect him as the game goes on and it gets pretty funny. In fact, the whole game is pretty humorous as Silas is a drunken liar so he changes the story or ridiculously adds in things akin to "breaking the fourth wall" moments. He does some really silly things too and seems to always be present at every major event in southwestern USA folklore.
As I said earlier, levels consist of playing through Silas's supposed "past stories", each of which are pretty fun and fast-paced. Sometimes Silas will cause certain things to happen based on his blatant bluffing or his audience will call him out and he'll rewind to tell the story like it "really is". Gameplay consists of you moving from point to point, shooting enemies for points, and moving more. That's essentially all that the game is, but it doesn't waste its time and constantly delivers either funny scenes or action-packed scenes. I like that a lot, and it's probably what kept me going to beat it in one sitting. That may sound pretty crazy, but the game is only about 5 hours long so it's not too bad and the game kept me engaged.
I usually have a lot of problems with shooters, but this one was very solid with collectables (that included real facts of southwestern lore, which was neat to see being of the southwest myself!) littered all over the place and points to gather from killing enemies. In addition, there was also some very light RPG mechanics that were nice to see. I only wish that there were more weapons and more ways to gain points.
Graphically speaking, this is quite the good looking game and it runs very well on even slightly older machines like mine. I was surprised to see it look so good AND run so well! Textures are crisp and the animations are fairly smooth. This is essentially a AAA arcade game so you can expect it to look as good as the name backing it is popular (Ubisoft).
I can't really recall the sound or music being anything superb, but the voice acting is great and certain songs were particularly pleasant on the ears (one of the credits songs comes to mind). Everything just gives off a lovely southwestern sort of feel that you very rarely see in games nowadays.
Call of Juarez: Gunslinger overall just felt "good" to me. Nothing really stood out, but I enjoyed it a lot and would probably recommend it to others if they like shooters. However, I would not give it a huge recommendation or say it's one of the best 2013 games, no, it's not really deserving of that high in my opinion. The humor is decent and the action will keep you entertained, but even if it's one of the best Call of Juarez games it won't win any awards I think.
I give this game a: 7/10
Old west Max Payne meets Forrest Gump.

After having played the first three "Call of Juarez" games, I never really thought that they would make a fourth one, but I'm really, really glad they did and thankfully, the game has nothing to do with the previous games in the series.
In “Gunslinger” you're playing as Silas Greaves, a legendary bounty hunter, through several adventures in his life, which he tells as stories to a few people in a saloon.
That maybe sounds pretty boring, but I assure you, it isn't. It's actually one of my favorite parts of "Gunslinger". Because every level you play is currently being told as a story, things (who you fight against, whole parts of a level, ...) sometimes change, because Greaves or someone else corrects the tale.
This adds another layer of refreshing elements on top of the already solid first-person shooter gameplay. Other than "The Cartel" (which was a huge step back in my opinion after “Bound in Blood”), "Gunslinger" uses gameplay, which is similar to the second "Call of Juarez" game. And it does it well. Shooting just any gun in the game is fun and responsive. Only the shotguns I never really used, as I didn't need to. Revolvers for anything close to middle distance and lever-action rifles for anything beyond that worked fine for me. Also back again in the game is the focus mechanic from the first two games, although it works more like bullet-time now. Add to that the skills you can unlock and you have gameplay that works great, is fast and a ton of fun.
The only thing I had a really big problem with at first, were the duels you have at the end of nearly every level. I hate them in the earlier games, but after reading a bit about how the work in "Gunslinger", I had no problem with any of them. I can safely say that these are just as fun as the rest of the game and much more skill-centered than they were in the first or second game. What I also really like is the graphical side of the game. While it lacks any kind of anti-aliasing, it has a very distinctive style, that mixes somewhat cell-shading with photorealistic graphics and I would say that just overall the game looks really nice (and thanks to it using the Chrome engine, it runs great, too!). I was even able to downscale the game from a higher resolution, which somewhat provided an anti-aliasing effect.
Where I was really surprised were the controls. Many shooters nowadays have controls or gameplay actions centered on the gamepads of the consoles, but every part of the game worked flawlessly with mouse and keyboard, which is a big positive point for me.
What I also like are the voices of the different characters, especially Silas Greaves himself as he is the narrator and you hear him most of the time. The other things you hear the most are of course different guns that are going off in different directions, which also sound great. Overall sound effects are really well made and sound right.
There's also "Duel" and "Arcade" as gamemodes. "Duel" is a duel/boss-rush through all the duels in the game and "Arcade" is centered on doing highscore runs through every level. However I haven't played any of them. Also there's "New Game+" after you've finished the story.
All in all, I was really surprised by "Call of Juarez: Gunslinger". For 15€ you get a solid shooter that runs well, looks great and plays really great. I can recommend this to any first-person shooter fan and probably most action fans, too.

I'll be honest, I'm not big into MMOs and this was the first that I really wanted to and tried to get into. The first time I tried playing back during the winter sale flopped pretty hard. I was really put off by the differeces between Skyrim and ESO. So, my biggest piece of advice is not to charge into ESO expecting a normal single player Elder Scrolls game.
Once I sat back and cleared my expectations, this game has easily swept me back up and taken its slot as one of my all time favorite games. I adore it. I've only been playing regularly for a couple of months now, but I'm racking up hours pretty fast. Sometimes when first starting out it feels overwhelming with how much you can do in this game, but with the achievements and collecting titles, costumes, dye colors - just all of the things, it keeps me motivated via obsession easily.
I'm still learning how to do a lot of things in the game, I'm not terribly good at PvP, but that doesn't stop me from having fun, even in the Cyrodiil. You can play this game to be competitive or you can sit back and play for fun, both, it seems incredibly flexible. Normally I play in a group with my husband, but I also strike out and solo on occasion - but being able to play with a partner or friend(s) makes the game incredibly more fun.
The artwork, scenery, music, and so much more make this a beautiful game. It's work buying, and the free play week is a must for anyone who has any desire to check out this game. I recommend it to everyone, even those who aren't inspired by or normally shy away from MMOs.  Holiday events, DLC, interesting quests and story for the base game, there really is so much to do, it's more than worth the cost of the game when the free week is over.
I would give some additional advice to new players that I didn't understand when I first jumped in... get a mount asap, even the cheap one at the stables and start feeding it every day to level those stats. They work for all your mounts to boost your riding speed, stamina and carrying. That and make sure to put some thought into the class you pick for your character, as of now there isn't a class change option. You can always make another character though. Most of all, just have fun with the game!

This game is the next work of absolute Genius from Supergiant Games, Whose previous work was on Bastion, An amazing topdown combat game with a truckload of Charm to it. Supergiant have kept to their guns. Transistor wins in the Charm department and instead of Bastion's ' Beat em up ' Combat style, It follows more of a Strategic and tactical fashion, allowing you to take time to plan your movements in a sequence called 'Turn()' Which all takes up Action points per movement. There is even a Button which allows you to Flourish and one to Hum. BUY THIS.
STORY:
The Story is exceptional in this game, It follows the tale of a fallen city, A Girl called Red and a Sword. Sounds a little odd, it may seem that way at first glance, but trust me this is misleading. Red is a former actress/singer person, She was attacked by the Camerata with the Process in an Attempt to slay her as she got in the way of their future. The man in the Sword takes the hit for her and is now trapped in the sword. Red loses her voice in the process and remains a Silent Protaganist except for 1 moment. The sword does all the talking, Questioning her moves a little sometimes, But overall helping. I would give the story a 9/10 for being Awesome and throwing Charm around, But it can be hard to follow sometimes and one point left me thinking: 'Wait why the♥♥♥♥♥♥am I here again?' Besides that it is pretty awesome()
GRAPHICS/ART:
Well what can I say. You have done it again Supergiant! Transistor is a Beautiful adventure in a Beautiful world, The art on every aspect of the game, from the Enemies that you smash up to the Posters on the wall, all done with incredible detail and as previously said, Throwing charm around like it was going outta fashion! Everything is just so complete and amazing in the Looks department. if you are looking for awesome 3D Graphic that is here too. 10/10 for Art!
COMBAT:
The combat works very well! It is a mix of Tactical combat and Turn() Based combat, It is best to make your moves in the Turn sequence as it will allow you to Backstab, Do all your moves quickly and also clear multiple enemies! It is a whole lot of fun. I would not recommend it if you are a fan of the more fast paced combat style of Bastion. I would say to keep with that element. It is kinda Questionable! But it is my review and I say it is awesome!
ENDING [NO SPOILERS:
