It's easy to say that Clannad is one of the best VNs I ever read, considering its immense popularity. But it's true that few engrossed me as much as Clannad, that I just couldn't put them down (even when I tried). It's not flawless, of course, and I can even understand why some downright dislike it, but it's truly a remarkable experience.
As often with these kinds of things, it's largely due to the characters. Every single one, with the exception of a few purely villainous minor characters, is very likeable. Not always right away, there were some that I found difficult to like at first, but at the end I was fond of all of them. Whether they are tragic, fun or just plain sympathetic, at the end I cared about at least every major character and found myself deeply invested in their stories.
These stories are pretty diverse, with the characters having their own personal struggle. Pretty much all of them (with a few exceptions) are family-related (as that's the overall theme of the VN), like a girl trying to achieve a big goal for her brother, even when that means putting her own desires aside, a little sister seeing her brother fallen from grace, doubting that he even cares about her anymore, another one hooking up her sister with the boy she loves, deeply hurting herself in the process, and of course the daughter that is wracked with guilt, when she discovers how much her parents sacrificed for her sake.
As typical for VNs, these stories are spread out over several different routes, with the main character often (but not always) entering a relationship with the central character. While they're largely independent, it's not rare for them to intermingle with each other and finishing some routes can cause changes in others. One route even only gets fully concluded when another is played after it.
In its structure, Clannad typically follows a certain formula, in which things are pretty light-hearted and rather comedic at first, introducing and developing the characters, only for things to go wrong soon after. It's very effective, as it takes time to make you really like and care about the characters, which makes the tragedy that befalls them all the more painful. Once hooked, it's hard to stop, as you really want to see how things develop and hope that everything ends (relatively) well.
Once all the main routes are finished (and certain choices have been made), a continuation of one route gets unlocked (appropriately titled "After Story"). This isn't just a mere epilogue or extra, but an important (possibly even the most important) part, of the entire VN. It's practically composed of several "mini-routes", that follow the same pattern as before. It's here that the story hits the hardest, with the most heartrending scenes of the entire VN. Some might find it even too much, but keeping at it leads to a rewarding conclusion.
Visually, Clannad is... not impressive. The characters tend to look rather off and many might be put off by the overall style. But it's not that bad and one gets used to it after a relatively short time.
When it comes to sound, Clannad shines much more. Even without knowing language, the speech really enhances the experience with VAs all voicing their characters nearly perfectly, to the point they hard to imagine without them. The only negative is that the main character himself isn't voiced. Which isn't unusual in VNs, but very glaring here, as he has a very defined personality and even the most minor characters got voiced.
The music is just great. It's actually one of the best points of Clannad and greatly supports every scene, whether it's funny, mysterious, dramatic or (and especially) sad.
However, it's not hard to point out flaws. One of the most glaring aspects is that the plots are rather blatantly built for the sake of drama. Several things don't quite make sense, characters tend to act in rather odd ways and quite some issues could have been avoided rather easily. Depending on how much you can tolerate these things (it's hard to outright overlook them), they can hamper your enjoyment of the stories.
As typical, "gameplay" consists of several choices, some important, others not so much. It's not always obvious what's what and some routes are heavily influenced by choices that don't seem to have much to do with anything. For unlocks, several specific choices have to be made and, as mentioned before, two routes have to be played in a certain order. That makes it rather tricky to get the full story. Using guides may therefore be preferable.
And of course, Clannad is pretty expensive. As much as I like this VN and as much content as it has, it's rather tricky to defend the full price, especially considering that it's nearly 15 years old by now. Of course, with Steam having sales rather often, it shouldn't be hard to get it at a better price. It's certainly more than worth the €20 I paid for it.
Overall, while some might find it too melodramatic, Clannad is a really great VN with likeable characters and interesting storylines. I can only recommend to at least try it out.

Well, that money was well invested! Clannad managed to conquer the number one spot of my most favourite games which had forever belonged to Mass Effect 2.

I can definitely say that I have never laughed more in any other computer game before.

STALKER is a 1st person suspense shooter and adventure game. It is similar to Fallout 3 or System Shock 2, but without any super powers.  It is highly geared towards sneaking.  If you try to play like Rambo you will die and die and die alot.  STALKER is set in the Ukraine, within a cordoned off zone around Chernobyl.  The game is average at the begining, but after you get scoped rifles it becomes a blast.
The good:
1. The atmosphere in this game is one of the best of any game I ever played.  The game carriers suspense without faking it and without having to force it.
2. The sneaking action is top notch.
3. The world is an interesting place. The monsters, weapons (later on) and gear are something else.
4. The game creators tried to make this a living world. They sort of succeeded.  Your actions can make a big differince.  Factions can with your help take over certain areas.  Wild animals run wild and kill off unlucky NPCs.
5. The inventory system limits your weight and not your storage size.  It works much better than most games.  Inventory management can be a real challenge, but in a good way.
The bad:
6. Okay, so your weapns and armour degrades over time.  That is fine, but there is no-one who can fix them?
7. The humans in this game are totally uninteresting.  Sadly the game does not make a good emotional connection with the player.
The ugly:
8. The game is buggy.  Save often in multiple slots.  Some missions don't record correctly and stashes may be empty. The number of NPCs that die from walking into fires is a joke.
If you love action adventure games, I have no doubt you will love this game.  Make sure you play the secret end.  You need to do something mid-game to enable it.

A fun, shooting gallery type FPS with some nice features to distiguish it.
1.  The story of the game is told by an old gunslinger, who may not have the best memory.  Sometimes the story gets altered during the game, with amusing results.

The game also has some speed run challenges with a friends leaderboard built in, newgame+ mode and an unlockable Very Hard mode.

Call of Juarez: Gunslinger is a very good FPS for its price range. Its very well polished for a short self-contained title, CoJ:G really captures the wild west fantastically, almost near Red Dead Redemption levels. Its not just a shoot 'em up running around with a 6-shooter, there are a few game mechanics that really makes it stand apart from conventional shooters. At some points, you do get fustrated at sudden difficulty spikes and enemy AI making impossible shots, you will still have fun with Gunslingers.
The story mode of the game is surprisingly good. During gameplay, it is being narrated by Silas Greaves, a retired bounty hunter who tells you of his adventures across the Western region of America in search for the murderers of his family. During his adventure, he comes across famous gunslingers and outlaws like Billy the Kid and Butch Cassady. The whole story was pretty well written and really surprised me, especially a game made on a budget.
The gameplay has very smooth gunplay, each weapon functions differently, giving the player a way to tackle the levels the way they see fit. A double barrel shotgun to get up close and personal, a sawed-off shotgun to get VERY close and VERY personal. Or maybe a carbine repeater for those with a deadly aim. And of course, when you think wild west, you think about the tried and true, revolvers. There are about 3 different ones to use and each one fuctions differently. On top of weapons to blast your way through the game, there is a level progression and skill trees you can pick to enhance your gameplay. A gunslinger tree, for those who wish to specialize with the revolver. A ranger tree, for those that want to specialize in sniping and a brawler tree, for those want that extra buff when upclose with a shotgun or within melee ranger. However you decide to proceed with the game, those skill trees got you covered.
Aside from the skill tree, there is almost a copy of a dead eye mechanic from Red Dead Redemption. For those who don't know what it is, you can slow down the game and enemies will be colored in red, this gives you a chance to line your shots up and hit your targets with easy headshots or bodyshots. There is also a bullet dodging mechanic, in which, you can dodge a shot that would kill you. These mechanics aren't anything new, but it works for a game like this.
During the game, you will come across a traditional boss fight with a health bar and there is nothing more to be said about that. But certain bosses you have to defeat in a duel. The dueling mechanic is a little hard to get use to. You have to control your drawing speed and your focus, which determines how accurate and how fast you draw your gun. These duels are very tense and very fast pace. You can win duels honorably or dishonorably, this depends on if you draw your gun before them or after them. I have mixed feeling about this mechanic, it is very unique and very intense, but you can't help but get mad at how insanely fast the AI draws their gun at times. Maybe you might fair better then I did with the duels, it did take awhile for me to get use to it.
Outside of story mode, there is an arcade mode. It is just like how it sounds, shoot enemies and survive and try to rack up as much points as you can and compare them with your friends and others across the globe. There is also another mode call duel mode, which is a series of duels with some of the game's bosses you encounter. You only get 5 chances, use them all up and its game over. It is nice to see a low budget game putting in more for the player to enjoy, instead of just a story mode or whatever.
One thing that I rather enjoy about Gunslingers is the collectables. It sounds strange, but I rather enjoyed them. The collectables are called Nuggets of Truth, they are little factoids about people, events and locations about the wild west. Learning from a FPS, how often does that happen these days?
Overall, the game is a very good for its price range. It has a lot of effort put in the game for a low budget title. This game is nice for those who just want to play something by themselves and want to have a good time. A game worth of your attention.
On a side note, while I have not played any of the other Call of Juarez games, it is to my understanding that a previous Call of Juarez strayed away from its western roots and tried a modern and 'edgy' drug cartel story and failed, I think Gunslingers is a good way for them to get back in touch with their western roots.

This game is an irritating tonal mess with lackluster shooting and lazy filler sidequests. It has the least impressive "open world" I have ever seen in a game, in which lazy sidequests send you to revisist linear corridors that are accessed via an awful driving mechanic on an otherwise empty overworld map, making this the most pointless implementation of an "open world". There is no reason why these levels couldn't be unlocked linearly and accessed instantly a la Vermintide or Left 4 Dead. The levels respawn enemies on a timer while you are still in the level, which is a lazy way to pad gameplay time and infuriating to anyone wishing to feel a sense of accomplishment. Once again, why not use an AI director as did Left 4 Dead? Because lazy, that's why. This lazy attitude permeates the game, from level design to the writing to the aesthetic to the "RPG" elements. The game has often been praised for it's "zillion of guns" mechanic in which literally zillions of Mcdonald's Happy Meal toys masquerading as guns litter the ground at any given time. This system was stolen from Diablo, and then stolen by Destiny, and was better implemented in both those games. I must ask, why in the hell would I want a gun that provides menially extra damage but only shoots three times before reloading? Why would I want a legendary weapon that doesn't need reloading but shoots only frozen peas? I'm going to digress. The game features a serviceable class system with little variance in classes, making it a poor man's version of any other class system ever, and I extend this criticism to the shield, armor, and equipment systems. Servicable, but pointless. I'm going to talk about the writing. At best, the characters and story developments are cliches seen a thousand times in a thousand better games. At worst, the writing displays a supreme lack of self awareness on it's sleeve, which is infuriatingly ironic as the game conveys the air of supreme self-awareness. Case in point: Claptrap the annoying robot isn't annoying because he was written to be annoying. Claptrap the annoying robot is annoying because someone thought that putting an intentionally annoying robot would somehow compensate for the lackluster everything else in the game. Handsome Jack is a grating cliche, not deep, not well written. He better compelled me to uninstall the game than to chase him down and give him his comeuppance. Note to writers: why would I care if he kills off cliched vanilla nobodies you didn't take the time to make me care about? I'm going to say the one thing I appreciated about the game. I liked the lack of fall damage, although I suspect it's only there because they couldn't be bothered to put it in. In conclusion: lazy, cobbled together game with dumb writing made popular by flash in the pan gimmicks. Would have worked infinitely better as a Left 4 Dead clone than a Fallout 3 clone. Which it is.

Good game, but if you came to read a review then you have come to the wrong place. If however you were wondering how to make a potato salad, then my friend, you are in the right place. This isn't a review on Reign of Kings, but a recipie. Enjoy
Ingredients
1kg desiree potatoes, peeled, cut into 2cm cubes
1 cup fat-free mayonnaise
1 small lemon, juiced
1 small red onion, finely chopped
olive oil cooking spray
100g shaved 97% fat-free honey leg ham, finely chopped
1/2 cup basil leaves, finely shredded

Method
Step 1
Place potatoes in a large saucepan. Cover with cold water. Bring to the boil over high heat. Reduce heat to medium and cook potatoes, uncovered, for 3 to 4 minutes or until tender when pierced with a skewer. Drain. Transfer to a bowl.
Step 2
Combine mayonnaise, 2 tablespoons lemon juice, onion and salt in a small bowl. Pour half over warm potato (potato will absorb flavour while still warm). Stir gently with a plastic spatula (this prevents potato from breaking up) to coat. Cover with plastic wrap and set aside to cool.
Step 3
Heat a non-stick frying pan over medium heat. Spray with oil. Add ham and cook for 3 to 4 minutes or until golden. Set aside to cool. Add ham, basil and remaining dressing to potato. Stir gently to combine. Season with salt and pepper. Serve.

Many people hate Papers, Please. And believe me, I understand why. It's a slog, a sort of chore that you have to get through, but herein lies the genius behind Papers, Please. You live in Arstotzka, a country that you aren't certain whether it's a normal place or a facist distopia. You are a man who works at an border checkpoint. You check for discrepancies in paperwork. You stamp the paperwork with a 'Decline' or an 'approved.' Repeat. Sounds boring? Hells yeah it should sound boring, but for some strange reason, it's one of the strangest, most addictive game ideas I've ever excperienced. Every day you wake up and check a newspaper, where it might talk about sports, the weather, or something you shouldn't really care about. But every so often, if you let some suspicious person through the border, or if you witness a suicide bombing, that will appear in the paper. Then, you might read about criminals trying to flee another country, and actually meet them at the border the next morning. So this sounds interesting, right? Well that's not the best part. The best parts are the subtle things you notice or experience. The immigration offices have stories to tell, and it's really up to you whether you want to listen to them. A woman without proper indentification desperately trying to meet with her husband on the other side. A border guard who wants to help you out with finances through illicet means. A young girl fleeing from a madman who is so close to making her a sex slave. A strange and mysterious organization who want to take down the government, but must first pass through the border. This game is genius because behind a facade of boring paperwork and dull gameplay lies one of the purest forms of indirect storytelling in all of gaming history. And one more thing, this game will make you doubt yourself. Medicine is $10 for two family members, both of whom are about to die. Will you save the uncle or the mother-in-law? Moral dilemmas are abound in this game, and so are great little stories. Also, the graphics are a perfect fit for this game, and should not be overlooked in any way. I give this game a 10/10 because it is everything that I love about the gaming industry. It is a true work of art, and an achievement in storytelling that deserves this kind of praise. This gem of a game is 40 MB and $9.99. Pick it up already.

Clannad is definitely one of the best visual novels out there. More than three years after watching the anime series, I finally found the courage to face this heart-rending story again. Compared to the anime, the novel proceeds at slower pace, making you really fall in love with all the characters and enjoy their individual routes.
My three favourite routes were Nagisa's (+After Story), Kotomi's and Tomoyo's.
Overall, I have next to nothing to complain about. Due to the tons of content (easily 100+ hours), I can confidently recommend buying the game to anyone who is interested, even for the full price.
Final rating: 9/10 (my second favorite visual novel)
(Next section contains SPOILERS, so proceed with caution)
The only thing that leaves kind of a bitter aftertaste is the way the true ending in After Story is handled. First, you have to go through all the traumatic experiences of witnessing deaths of both Nagisa and Ushio. Then, you have to return to the point when Nagisa was still alive, to collect the last light orb from Akio's sidestory. That, by itself, horribly disrupts the gradation of the story. With all the light orbs, you gain access to the true ending, which is supposed to be some kind of a final closure to the novel. My problem is that the true ending basically denies all that makes After Story exceptional: devastated Tomoya getting up from the pits of despair while being saved by the gentle smile of his daughter. I feel that just brushing off all the events following Nagisa's death with some hardly explainable deus ex machina kind of spoilt my feelings about the ending. The best closure to the novel would be for the mentioned miracle to save dying Ushio and let her grow up by Tomoya's side. This is the only reason I cannot give Clannad 10/10, which I think it objectively deserves. But no matter how hard I think about it, the ending was a bit disappointing to me.

I would suggest following a guide to make it easier to complete all the routes since playing some of them in a certain order does matter in order to unlock some CGs or simply dialogues and scenes.
Just relax, put the auto dialogue on if you don't want to press any button to proceed and enjoy the story along with the game, spending the most emotional, moving and joyful 100+ hours of your life.

The stories AND the characters take exception because they're some of the most well written things I have ever experienced. They're beautifully emotional in multiple different ways, and at least one route will "hit home" for you, and I can almost guarantee one or two will make you cry. The soundtrack is absolutely wonderful, and you do get used to the art style, so getting attached to the characters and empathizing with everything they go through is a guarantee, even if they're a character you don't particularly care for, the writing is just that strong. All this time later, I no longer refer to it as playing Clannad. I call it experiencing Clannad.

Fun game, the scenery is breathtaking, hunting model is well done.  Down side is the F2P model, which is more like a demo version.  With the F2P version you can only hunt two species (mule deer and cottontail rabbits), but you only have a rifle that is legal for mule deer not rabbits so you can actually only hunt one species.  Mule deer is only on one reserve, so even though you can visit all the reserves actual hunting is limited to one (loggers point).
The best way to approach this game is to consider it as an "A" list game, figure out how much you want to spend and buy a package deal. With a shotgun and rifle you can hunt every species of game on any of the reserves (once you buy a membership or a package deal). I would recommend this game, but not as a F2P. Plan on sinking between $15-$50, depending on your budget, for one of the packages to really get the full enjoyment out of this game

A true classic!
I think it's been long enough since this game came out to say that it stands the test of time even today. In a lot ways it was a game ahead of its time, made in a simpler time before the whole zombie horror survival genre was its fullest. Furthermore, it was one of the first successful mergers of an RPG with a very skill based and action oriented FPS system. This means that if you were shooting someone in the head, you were shooting them in the head!!! This is what I can say about the game summed up in some positives and negatives:
Positives:
+ Immersive Open World RPG/FPS Experience (one of the first of this scale truly; this was huge for its time!!!)
+ Eerie and unsettling environments
+ Dangerous and pretty scary enemies
+ Fairly long and pretty decent story (just don't expect an ending that makes 100% sense, lol; Even back then horror games struggled with the bad/weird ending syndrome)
+ Interactive environment and meaningful decision (you influence the world and help people and this makes a direct effect on how they interact and respond to you)
+ Rich RP and seemless experience (big words here I realize, but what this basically means is that there are countless cases in which you will just coincidentally bump into an interesting character and can decide whether you want to help them or kill them and loot them and then find out you♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off some faction; fun times :D)
Negatives:
- Poorly optimized on more modern versions of Windows (performance issues such as crashes and even a bluescreen; COULD BE just me though)
- VEEEERY slow loading times
- A lot of glitches(if any) were not patched and fixed in the Steam version
- Never was a fan of some of the difficulty scaling and pacing in the game (sometimes you just get b*******ed by random groups of enemies, but I guess that's also part of that RP experience I described)
- Not very well dated UI, especially the map and journal system.... phew don't get me started on that! :D
- Enemies often act either completely derpy or are 360 No-scope masters of the tenth dragon legion and one shot you out of nowhere! :O
Hope this helps you with deciding if you should pick up this good ol' classic! Enjoy!

In John Ford’s classic western, The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance, a senator played by James Stewart is told by a reporter, “This is the West, sir. When the legend becomes fact, print the legend.” and in the world of Call of Juarez Gunslinger, it seems that a number of legends have been printed concerning Silas Greaves. Stumbling into a saloon in Abilene, Kansas, Greaves has a seat and the local patrons buy him drinks and as old men are wont to do, Silas begins recounting his life story in an attempt to set a few things strait that newspapers and dime novels has misrepresented.

Silas' tale is, as one would expect, a tale of revenge. He is riding in hot pursuit of Roscoe “Bob” Bryant, Johnny Ringo, and Jim Reed who managed to kill his brothers and nearly kill him as well. His quest for vengeance brings him toe to toe with the likes of Billy the Kid, Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid, the Clantons and John Wesley Hardin making Silas the Forrest Gump of the old west. His stories seem more unlikely than what the papers and dime store novels have written about him and it isn't long before the patrons of the saloon view his yarn as an apologue rather than an autobiography. It doesn't help that the old timer's memory isn't what it used to be and some details are amended in the middle of his narration. On the gameplay end, this means that your environment can change around you during the course of a missions to account for Silas' faulty memory. While these add to the game's style, they do little to affect the firefights.

Gunslinger is a competent albeit uncomplicated shooter. Enemies appear en masse and are quick to huddle behind cover. A few special enemy types are present such as enemies with wooden shields, armored shotgun toting maniacs as well as the odd desperado behind a Gatling gun. In order to more efficiently blow gaping holes in the opposition, Silas can enter a concentration mode that slows time and highlights enemies in red. This can of course be replenished by slaying foes. An arcade style combo counter multiplies the points gained from cutting down outlaws and delivering head shots, shooting through cover or taking out men on the run earns bonus points. These points grant Silas experience which can be used to level up one of three skill trees. Only a handful of abilities in each of the trees feel like substantial upgrades however and the special weapons you unlock from each tree are more ornate versions of the standard weapons with a few stat tweaks meaning they don't really feel like new weapons. Never the less, Gunslinger manages to satisfy when you are wielding two six shooters and sending torrents of  blood flying from the skulls of those who would come between you and your prey.

Almost every level in Gunslinger's campaign concludes with a duel or boss encounter. The boss encounters often require gaining ground on an enemy posted behind a Gatling gun or having a shoot out with a single shotgun wielding bullet sponge. Duels are a bit more involved as you target an enemy to gain greater focus and position your hands for greater speed so that when the time comes your iron clears it's holster and your lead decimates the body of your opposition before he can even consider killing you. Duels require some quick timing and a bit of finesse to ensure that your focus is as high as it can be and your handspeed is maxed but ultimately these become a bit repetitive.

Part of what makes Gunslinger so satisfying despite it's simple mechanics is that it drips with style. The notorious outlaws that you cross paths with are introduced through comic book panels and a beautifully detailed Boderlands style cel shaded graphical style prevents these comic panels from looking out of place. The dialogue is pulpy and seems ripped strait from a trashy dime store novel and while it can sometimes be a bit overwrought or contrived the overall aesthetic of the game makes it seem like an intentionally kitschy touch. Voice work is solid and the music plays on common western themes, employing distorted guitars to give the music a coarse tone that prevents it from conjuring quixotic images of  the west associated with 1950's western cinema culminating in a functional though not exactly exceptional soundscape.

Rounding out Gunslinger's feature set is an arcade mode that recycles sections of the singleplayer game and challenges players to string together combos and set high scores that can be compared with friends and the rest of the world on a leader board. A duel mode allows you to experience the game's duels back to back with a few added opponents. Neither of these modes will hold your attention since they do little to differentiate themselves from the game's campaign. The campaign itself will take around six hours and does have two endings. A new game plus mode and collectables add further incentive to play through the game once more.

Gunslinger is a stylish homage to the West. Fans of western cinema will find a number of references allusions to popular films and coming across some of the real outlaws whose exploits built the mythos of the West adds some novel appeal to the experience. Gunslinger masks the corners it cuts as a budget title with a rich style making it's campaign a mostly pleasant experience with repetition and simply enemy behaviors standing out as the only major blemishes. The West is somewhat of an untapped resource for video games and it's a shame that so few games have taken advantage of this period of American history. Let's hope that this new budget price point draws a few more people toward the Call of Juarez franchise and spurs the development of more satisfying western pulp.

What's the essence of good FPS shooter? Fast paced action and good shooting mechanics. "Call of Juarez® Gunslinger" is an example of how to do more than successful action game. Since Lucas Arts' Outlaws I like FPS set in the Wild West. And while I do like the Call of Juarez series (except the Cartel), Call of Juarez Gunslinger still surprised me. For 15€ you get a fun (if a bit short) arcade shooter with great sound effects and great music. The graphics engine is capable of rendering awesome and impressive environments. But the biggest surprise was the great story and the funny and noteworthy story telling (mainly because it is told by an unreliable narrator).

I love games that have style and this game has it in spades.
The game takes place in 1910. You take on the role of wild-west bounty hunter Silas Greaves, who has stopped in to the local saloon in Abilene, KS. A few patrons recognize you and invite you for drinks while they listen to your mostly embellished tales of wild-west adventures, which you play through as flashbacks while Silas narrates to his audience.
The writing and dialog is very entertaining. A skeptical listener will occasionally interrupt SIlas' narration to challenge the truth of his story, such as taking credit for killing Butch Cassidy. The game will pause while you hear Silas' humorous  backpedaling to clarify himself to the incredulous audience. This usually results in changes to the flashback while you are playing and adds a fantastically unique element to the gameplay.
Scattered throughout the game are collectible "Nuggets of Truth" that grant you additional XP and detail the historical facts behind Silas' tall tales. I thought this was a nice touch that offered a factual perspective that inspired so much of the game design.
The level design is simply amazing and reminded me of a Ken Burns documentary. The engine is the same used in Dead Island, another game that had stunning outdoor visuals.
From the dusty wooden saloons and scorched desert planes to dense forests and swampy marshland, its clear that the level designers were passionate about creating a rich environment.
The occasional high-noon shootout challenges are annoying and the game is pretty short (~6hrs on Normal), although further leveling-up and at least 2 alternate endings could stretch it out. These cons are easily pardoned by the witty characters, amazing level design and engaging gameplay that make for a great game.
Fantastic game, hits all the right notes for an enjoyable western tale.

I'll admit I had high hopes for Transistor being something fun to play.
As it is I just deleted the game and placed it in my trash category where all games go to die in my game library.
A Couple of Points.
1. Auto Save - The Auto save feature like in many games where it is not handled very very lightly is a sticking point. The game is saved when you enter an area. The Game is saved when you enter a Battle. The Game is saved when you use a terminal. And no where is it painfully obvious it's saving until you've been playing for a while and know which icons to look for.
2. Retry - I'll admit I was a dunce and "retry" on the pause menu being the button to reload the last saved point completely flew past me on my first play. Why did they change standard game menu vocabulary?
3. Break Abilities - Transistor is very much a game about losing. Please see my first two points and now think about going one save point to far after a bad battle and having most of your favored combos locked out until you level up some more.  The only rational I can offer for this is someone on the design team wanted people to play with more than just their favored combos.
4. Planning Mode - Sybil or as I like to call her "Umbrella Girl" is the first boss and for me the last boss. In a turn based system the one thing you are more or less assured of is that the attacks you make are going to get strung together very quickly and land on the person your attacking. Sybil A.K.A "Umbrella Girl" has a three out of four miss ratio sliding out of position as soon as you leave planning mode. This horrible little game mechanic was the capper that made me delete the game after beating the first boss and clocking a grand total of three hours.
5. The Music is a lie - This is the only comparison I will make to Bastion. Listening to the soundtrack was the deciding factor on my buying the game. It's very good, the same publisher, and very like Bastion's soundtrack being unique and immersive.  The soundtrack in my opinion is the only thing holding things together in a wash of stilted voice overs and Peanuts "teacher" WAh, Wah wha voice substitutes. What could have been amazingly beautiful counterpoint to the story fell flat on it's face for me at the first boss battle where it went up against a boss voice that would have made Shodan back on Citadel Station in the 90's cry in shame.
6. It's on RAILS! - It's the one unforgivable sin in my book. There may be bad portions, there might be issues, but if the player is even marginally allowed to do what they want how they want it's worth exploring. The very first training screen for the turn based planning mode actively fights you if you try to ignore it's suggestions. Once you get past the first Boss you find your first obvious one way door but there were several others prior to it. Miss a terminal and it's gone for that playthrough. Try to miss a add-on and the game will fight you tooth and nail forcing you to pick it up.
All in all Transistor IS NOT a game I would ever recommend.
The story is obtuse, the Voice Over work is only passible, the enemies are consistantly either criminally under powered or stupidly over powered, The Music is trancendant, but and it's a big but the entire game is on rails in the worst way. I will never recommend a game that is programmed to fight a players choice and force a single action.

If you liked the original you will like this. Some aspects are easier, while others are a little more challenging (Durability works differently), but overall it still feels just right. Also, the game looks beautiful. I remember the first time I visited Ash Lake in the first game. I was blown away by its eerie beauty. Many areas still capture this awe, and I love it (Aldia's keep and its successive areas come to mind). Gameplay is more or less the same, but with a few improvements, and its much more entertaining. A major issue with the last game, not too bad but still noticeable, was the voice acting. Everyone sounded off, and maybe this was on purpose to add to the overall tone, but they just sounded poor to me. Dank Souls 2, however, Has quite a few NPCs with dialogue that's a joy to listen to (Benhart and the Brotherhood of Blood Leader come to mind).
Bosses are an issue though. While every now and again you'll face something interesting, like Aldia's Keep's boss, you'll find that more often than not you'll be facing off against either a large knight or humanoid. Also, bless From's heart, but it seemed like they ran out of ideas for a few bosses. The Royal Rat Authority is Sif with minions, the Rotten is Nito, the twin Dragonriders, Ruin Sentinels, and Throne Watcher/Defender are Ornstein and Smough.
While The bosses may be dissapointing in design, they still get the job done, and that is kill you, and it's still an enjoyable game. If you're a fan of the first you should definitely give this a go, but if you disliked the first then you won't like this.
Overall I would rate it as a 8/10 game. It's a solid title and is definitely worth the money if you're a fan of the series.

I got a $20 card as a gift for Valentines Day and I pretty much have every game that I could want. I heard stuff about this and on that fateful day this was on sale so I got it. I guess it was fate that brought me here. So in that sense I kinda got this game for free.
Update:
People might be looking at the price tag and get scared of it and ask themselves why in the world you would want to grab this game when it is just a visual novel with a very scary price tag. The game is actually worth the full price. 40 hours in and I still have a lot of things to do to see the True ending. The game contains a fair amount of story arcs and depending on your reading speed and settings can last from 5 to 10 hours each story arc. Not to mention trying out different decisions and seeing how it turns out would further the game time required to finish everything the game has to offer.
So what exactly do you get for that price tag? You get a visual novel experience with multiple story arcs and I would say a fair estimation of getting all the content it has to offer can go from 80 to 100 hours. The game is not a dating sim and focuses more on the story aspect of certain people that you will meet. Playing them until the end of their storyline will give you a clearer point of view on who is who and what is going on in the world. As much as possible I would like to avoid discussing the story  since you would be doing  yourself a disservice if you wouldn't go and experience the story yourself. The game can be a hit or miss in terms of what you actually do in-game but suffice to say that the stories in the game are some of the best stories that I have ever seen in a visual novel to warrant that price tag.
As ambiguous as this review is, all I can really tell you is to take that blind leap of faith when you can and see what Clannad has to offer. I am no fan of visual novels but this game really changed all that. On one hand it made me want to try a lot of visual novels that might have stories as great as this one. On the other hand it doesn't want me to try anything else for the fear of every visual novel after this not going to surpass what clannad did.

Many people hate Papers, Please. And believe me, I understand why. It's a slog, a sort of chore that you have to get through, but herein lies the genius behind Papers, Please. You live in Arstotzka, a country that you aren't certain whether it's a normal place or a facist distopia. You are a man who works at an border checkpoint. You check for discrepancies in paperwork. You stamp the paperwork with a 'Decline' or an 'approved.' Repeat. Sounds boring? Hells yeah it should sound boring, but for some strange reason, it's one of the strangest, most addictive game ideas I've ever excperienced. Every day you wake up and check a newspaper, where it might talk about sports, the weather, or something you shouldn't really care about. But every so often, if you let some suspicious person through the border, or if you witness a suicide bombing, that will appear in the paper. Then, you might read about criminals trying to flee another country, and actually meet them at the border the next morning. So this sounds interesting, right? Well that's not the best part. The best parts are the subtle things you notice or experience. The immigration offices have stories to tell, and it's really up to you whether you want to listen to them. A woman without proper indentification desperately trying to meet with her husband on the other side. A border guard who wants to help you out with finances through illicet means. A young girl fleeing from a madman who is so close to making her a sex slave. A strange and mysterious organization who want to take down the government, but must first pass through the border. This game is genius because behind a facade of boring paperwork and dull gameplay lies one of the purest forms of indirect storytelling in all of gaming history. And one more thing, this game will make you doubt yourself. Medicine is $10 for two family members, both of whom are about to die. Will you save the uncle or the mother-in-law? Moral dilemmas are abound in this game, and so are great little stories. Also, the graphics are a perfect fit for this game, and should not be overlooked in any way. I give this game a 10/10 because it is everything that I love about the gaming industry. It is a true work of art, and an achievement in storytelling that deserves this kind of praise. This gem of a game is 40 MB and $9.99. Pick it up already.

For a simple-looking 8-bit game, the story has some surprising depth. You're a struggling poverty-stricken man working for the government border patrol. You were lucky enough to win the labour lottery to land that job. You've been placed in a run down hotel where you work for near nothing in order to support your family. You have bills to pay, your family can get sick and die, you can go to jail for going into debt. Your decisions matter and they matter a lot.
Can you catch a serial killer before he enters your country? Will you be able to stop terrorism in its tracks?
Find out if you've got what it takes to defend your homeland in Papers, Please.

If you want an excellent hunting simulator and are willing to pay for it ,you have found it.
First things first, this game is not really free-to-play. The heavy restrictions on what you can do as an non-paying player are so tight that the free experience is far closer to a demo than an a full game. For those willing to pay this game is well worth the cost but the voracious finacial model will alienate most gamers who decide to give this game a try. The most significant issue lies with the usual free-to-play nonsense that you can earn the same thing the paying players get, well no you can't. The main issue is licenses which can be bought for in-game earnable currency but cost and time limitations on their use mean that they are frustrating at best. Not having the license means that you cannot shoot at the animal, not allowing the animal to count towards a player's score would have been a better solution.
All that being said the game itself is fun for those who want a proper hunting sim instead of a shooting gallery. The horrendous payment model is the only really problematic failing that drags down the experience.

Good stuff:
The atmosphere is awesomely made, one of the best horror game - this is only game I am actually concerned for my life!! YOU WILL ACTUALLY DIE IN THIS GAME!
The scenery of Pripyat & Chernobyl is what drove me to finish it.
The story is quite rich and solid if you read into it - although I would say presentation/hinting/clues can be improved
But I still dont recommend, why?
1. The gunplay & gun balance is painful, even with mods - until you get to maybe last 30% of the game so the "good/powerful/accurate guns" start coming in waves, your guns like AK/MP5/AN94/All Pistols are horribly inaccurate and is just shooting BB bullets, well, BB bullets with ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of recoil.
I am fine with single-shot mode, but even with a scope the accuracy is completely off, you might as well run up to their face with a shotgun than single-firing 2 mags behind cover just to kill 1 enemy.
2. Locking variety of guns behind campaign - It's a shooter come on!
Why would you lock the Snipers in the last 3 levels?
Why would you lock a huge variety of Assault Rifles in the first 50% of the game?!
I get this as part of "leveling/progressing" but you can at least give me a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ sniper rifle like Mosin on top of MP5, so I get to use different guns for different situation instead of AKs for the first 10-15 hours.
3. Lack of any instructions or tutorial.
A lot of things can KILL you in seconds in this game - one of the things is Anamoly.
But the game basically never warned you about it (it's not exactly common sense) and they are TRANSPARENT!! pff.
You have to read some guides before you start the game or you dont know why you suddenly died (exactly the reason why I dropped the STALKER series in 20 mins, when I first played 10 years ago)
4. "Realism"
You are very constrained - because of realism.
Your carry weight is pathetic if you dont mod/modify it, your gun is terrible for the first 20 hours - inaccurate and low damage while the enemies have very good accuracy with the same gun!
All enemies are bullet sponse - I got the unique SPAS12 (Best shotgun in game) and I unloaded ENTIRE magazine (8 shots) into a mutant's head and it didn't die (took me 2 mags to kill) - in real life, that amount of shots and pillets will absolutely SMASH it to pieces.
In a lot of situations and missions (esp early game), you are scripted to go against groups and squads of enemies - bandits and militiary ALONE (when your equipment are completely crap as above).
The game wants to be realistic yet forcing you to be a Rambo.
5. Bugs
Mods will fix this, or the majority of it anyway.
The game can be a very solid horror shooter - but as a shooter, the gunplay and some mechanics and lack of polishing really kills the fun for me.
I really like the concept and settings and that's the only thing driving me to the end to see the scenery...

It's hard to say whether or not its the gameplay or the storytelling is to be praised the most, but the fact it's hard to tell is a sign of a great game. Combat is ridiculously fun, and has endless possibilities. You could choose to go gung-ho and play the majority of it in an action adventure style, or if you prefer strategy, you can primarily switch to the more tactical Turn() mode. Not to mention there are countless ways you can combine the many available Functions to cater to your personal offensive and defensive style. Somewhat akin to your typical RPG skill tree, but with much more freedom.
If you're worried about difficulty there's plenty of control over that too. Once reaching a certain level up, from then on, you will have the option to install Limiters to increase the strength of the enemies or decrease your advantages over them. This is also a thing to consider if you wish to gain more EXP more quickly. Another way to grind in this otherwise linear game is to visit one of many Backdoors - rooms that contain several mini-challenges that upon completion you gain EXP and soundtracks.
Just like Supergiant's previous title, Bastion, storytelling is subtle and mostly done through narration from your partner and discovering lore. You can discover lore by utilizing your Functions in varying ways. Thus, it's encouraged you mix up your combos a bit in order to get the most insight on all the pieces in the story. The deserted futuristic atmosphere only gains more charm from your narrator's personality. And, if you're a softie like me, your heart's gonna take a beating when observing the bond between the main character and the narrator.
Despite it being linear in nature to coincide well with the well-scripted storytelling, Transistor opens up several paths within its world. It's difficult to not be sucked in with the little details in the atmosphere, emotions, and simplistic yet addicting combat.

Supergiant Games set themselves one hell of a challenge coming into the market with the tagline "from the makers of Bastion". There's a lot to live up to and you don't just want to make Bastion 2.0, but you also don't want to be a one hit wonder.
So enters Transistor. With the same "narrator", the same music composer, the same isometric camera angle and the same hand-painted artstyle. But there's so much more to the game mechanics of Transistor than those of Bastion. Each Funtion has 3 options to it. You can slot it as an attack, a passive or slot in onto another attack. With around 20 Fuctions in the game, that's a lot of depth.
I did have some worries about the length, with the main story only lasting 5 hours, but then I "recurred" through the story, which randomised the combat and then I completed all of the challenges which more than made up for it.
Transistor is fantastic. A gorgeous game, as Supergiant tend to make, but they have also shown that they understand the need to improve gameplay.

This game is extremely fun and challenging, as long as you don't overlevel for your area there will usually be at least one person with a white soapstone sign to summon as a shade to help you if you are stuck.
Tips:
I would recommend starting as a swordsman to get the scimitar+1, which is a great sword early game. Melee combat is far more reliable than magic in pvp scenarios, and you will have a better time if you can master melee combat and learn to roll to dodge attacks and such, rather than luring an enemy to attack and running out of range to spam spells. As long as you learn your enemy's attack patterns and habits, a shield isnt needed either, simply rolling backward or sideways at the right time can get you out of trouble. Another tip is to buy many wooden arrows and use a bow to lure enemies out, since a fight is much easier if you can defeat enemies one by one. Lastly, if you get invaded often, you can burn a human effigy at the bonfire of that area to decrease invasion chances for a while, but at the same time stopping you from summoning allies.

Instead of making a living breathing city as in city builder games you got to manage the game not by taxes but in resources, and making a working conveyor belt factory, clearing wood and creeps to get to those resources to upgrade your research and factory size.

The game engine and mechanics of the game works really well until for an example you change from regular ammunition to piercing rounds. Now this can be done two simple ways:
Run to all your turrets and when you get to that point there will be rather lot of them and change it manually or just stop producing regular rounds and when they are have been consumed by the turrets until the new rounds can replace them.

Quick Slick Deadly reminds me of the gaming renaissance of Newgrounds, back in the early 2000s, except this was one of the bad ones. I've never heard of the engine this game was made in so I don't know what its full potential could be but I'm guessing this isn't it. The WASD sensitivity is extremely high and there doesn't appear to be any way to change this other than exiting to the main menu. It's possible to use the mouse instead but it feels sort of laggy, as if the player's sprite is slow to keep up with the mouse movement.
So far I've spent the beginning levels without doing anything other than dodging asteroids. I assume these are tutorial levels. They're implemented very poorly. It takes about 20 seconds to complete each one, they should have all been rolled into one larger level with a real goal.
The change of perspective from side-on to top-down at the most unexpected time is a very strange choice. Making every button, that doesn't perform an action, pause the game and then having ESC exit the game rather than cancel the pause menu goes against how every other game I've played is designed, forcing me to override my own habits lest I accidentally quit to level select again. It feels like I'm playing the exact same level over and over again with each stage being extended by another 2-5 seconds of content. Sometime there will be an increase of enemies and obstacles, but it's essentially the same path and layout.
I am constantly failing the Dare Devil stage with the Survivor class as I am failing to understand how it is played; I fly near enemy projectiles to consume its energy but then I can not manage to engage my shields. I make it to the end of the level without taking damage and fail. This is really discouraging, I feel the developer has not explained its mechanics well enough. There's no restart button, so failure means having to go back to level select.
I honestly feel so dumb playing this game when I'm constantly failing something so basic simply because I'm not completing each level to near perfection.

So, I had just taken a peek at the reviews for this game to see if others had been enjoying it as much as I have, and I was shocked with all the negatives there were.
A lot of the negative responses I saw were complaints on the fact that the game itself isn't really free to play or that it's pay to win. But you're playing the full game, you're just limited to what you can hunt, which is Mule Deer. Now, that doesn't sound like a whole lot, and it really isn't in comparison to what else the game has to offer. But I spent a solid 3 hours straight tracking and hunting mule deer and having a blast.
I quickly realized that this game was well worth shelling out some money for. The terrain is gorgeous, the way all of the animals behave is very realistic, the tracking keeps me very interested in the hunt and the overall experience is just amazing.
To those of you who were looking for a free hunting game with lots of guns and animals to shoot, I'm sorry to disappoint you, but this isn't it. The free part is just a demo really of the full game where you can hunt mule deer and get that taste.
But if you're looking for a great hunting game and are willing to drop 30-40 bucks on a bundle that gives you 12 months of unlimited hunting, a 12 gauge shotgun(comes with all different types of shot to hunt everything), a new stronger rifle with a new scope, a .44 and .357 revolver, some better camo'd clothes, some calls and a few other goodies, then this is definitely the game for you.
Seriously, if you enjoy the experience of just hunting the mule deer for a bit, drop some money into it and go for the full experience, it's really worth it. This game deserves to be paid for.
9/10 (Only because of microtransactions with all the rest of the items that don't come in a bundle, but none of that other stuff is actual stuff that's needed to enjoy the game and have the full experience)

Tree of Savior is a game I was very surprised by. I did not expect much going in, I assumed it was going to be another generic free to play mmo. I was wrong. So far I have been very much enjoying Tree of savior, I like its actiony feeling combat, its branching class system, its world, art, music. I have been enjoying all of it a lot.
There are 80 classes to chose from as you play, you start by picking one of  four basic core classes, wizard, cleric, archer, swordsman, and as you play these classes you unlock new classes that branch from each core class. As an example at level 15 a wizard can chose to advance into the next tier of wizard spells, or branch of into pyro, or cryomancy. In Tree of Savior you level your character and there class separately. each character level you can increase a base stat, each class level you can increase a skill level. This system I feel works really great in this game, and I am having a good time with it.
Story wise Tree of Savior does not feel too fleshed out yet, so far what it seems to come down to is one day a cataclysm occurred, and army of demons invaded mutating animals into monsters, and all the gods disappeared. You receive "revelations" from one of these goddesses  and are tasked with investigating the mystery and hopefully fixing this kerfuffle.
So far the ONLY negative I have really experienced in Tree of Savior is the bots. There are TONs of bots, they get banned every day but more just take there place, its crazy. chat is usually completely flooded with bots advertising and honestly I dont see that changing much. The devs have recently implemented an "Anti-Bot" system we can use to report bots so hopefully that works out for us players.
Tree of Savior is going  free to play some time in May as of this review. If you were a fan of early Ragnarok Online, or if you just want a quality free to play mmo, you should check out Tree of Savior.

Call of Juarez Gunslinger is a mystical fps that has entrancing arcade-like gameplay.

If you're looking for a budget single player shooter with a very distinct flavor, Call of Juarez: Gunslinger might just be the title for you. The game boasts a story mode, score-attack mode and a duel mode. The story will make any western fan feel right at home and is supposedly told by the aging Silus Greaves. Supposedly? That's right: this is a game is very much about truth and lies. People aren't who they say they are and their boasts may just be a bunch of hogwash. Although the story is very linear in going from point A to B, sometimes our narrator forgets, fibs, or flat out lies to his audience and you'll end up playing a few different scenarios until Greaves and his audience agrees about what happened.
Hidden through each level are a few 'Nuggets of Truth' which give you historically accruate facts about key people, places, and events of the wild west. I found myself collecting these specifically to learn about the outlaws and lawmen featured in the game and not just for the experience boost. The leveling system is very arcade-y, giving you bonus points for headshots, running shots, combo kills, etc. It may seem strange at first, but it really fits in well with the very, VERY, romantisized dipiction of the old west. Each time you level up, you get a skill point to invest in one of the three trees. The skills range from simple statistic increases (ex: '+ 10 damage with shotguns') to being able to have two sawed-off shotguns akimbo! If you invest a few more points, you'll unlock a legendary version of the standard weapon, giving it a nice gold trim and some more passive increases.
The graphics mimic the popular cell-shaded style, but really only to accent some fairly realistic models. It sounds confused, but it ends up looking way better than, say, Borderlands 2, which ran with the cell-shaded look 100%. The music is pretty par for the course. It sounds like a poor man's Ennio Morricone. Not distracting, but not great either.
The one caveat are the damn duels. What you're supposed to do is keep the crosshairs on your opponent while you move your hand closer to your gun -- focus too much on aiming and you'll be too slow on the draw; focus to much on speed and you'll miss every shot. Sounds great in theory, but the aiming is completely unresponsive and although it looked like my hand was in a good position, it kept telling me my speed was dropping. What could have been a really fun and intuitive minigame quickly turns into frustration. That said, by the end of the game I was starting to get the hang of it, and with the HUD off, I found myself doing better than when the game was tracking my exact speed and aim. But would I play the duel mode challenge? Hell no.

This game is a very well executed western-FPS!
The story is well put together, putting you in history with the West' most notorious cowboys and gunfighters, as you play Silas Greaves. The graphics are exceptional, more than enough to give you the feel of how it would be to be a bounty hunter in the west.
For the price (even at full, although I paid 50% off during a sale), there is very much to do in the game. 3 difficulties (unlocking the other 2 after you've finished easy mode) for story mode, artifacts or "nuggets" hidden throughout each location, arcade mode for those looking to just shoot em' up and rack up points in comparison with others, a well thoughtout dueling system which will have you on the edge of anticipation and anxiety, as well as a dueling leaderboard to compare with friends and others in the community.
Having finished the easy mode, true west mode has been an amazing experience. A minimal HUD mode which really takes out the "game" feel and puts you in a more barbaric fight-or-flight mode. It's pretty hard and I've been enjoying the progression in this difficulty the mode.
As far as weapons, there are three basic choices. More are unlocked as you progress through the game. Although few, each gun does feel different from one another, and your choice of weapon will effect your efficiency in progressing through the levels.
I recommend this game to anyone who is looking for a single-player story, western-based FPS. I really enjoyed the story, it helps you relive the tales of one Silas Greaves, and the game hardly ever feels like a grind. I've been waiting for a game like this for a long time, I'll probably be waiting a long time before such a game is made again.
Only thing that it could improve on is adding a multiplayer dueling system, or perhaps a gang vs. gang, sherriffs vs. cowboys mode. Ohter than that, it's great!

It's hard to say whether or not its the gameplay or the storytelling is to be praised the most, but the fact it's hard to tell is a sign of a great game. Combat is ridiculously fun, and has endless possibilities. You could choose to go gung-ho and play the majority of it in an action adventure style, or if you prefer strategy, you can primarily switch to the more tactical Turn() mode. Not to mention there are countless ways you can combine the many available Functions to cater to your personal offensive and defensive style. Somewhat akin to your typical RPG skill tree, but with much more freedom.
If you're worried about difficulty there's plenty of control over that too. Once reaching a certain level up, from then on, you will have the option to install Limiters to increase the strength of the enemies or decrease your advantages over them. This is also a thing to consider if you wish to gain more EXP more quickly. Another way to grind in this otherwise linear game is to visit one of many Backdoors - rooms that contain several mini-challenges that upon completion you gain EXP and soundtracks.
Just like Supergiant's previous title, Bastion, storytelling is subtle and mostly done through narration from your partner and discovering lore. You can discover lore by utilizing your Functions in varying ways. Thus, it's encouraged you mix up your combos a bit in order to get the most insight on all the pieces in the story. The deserted futuristic atmosphere only gains more charm from your narrator's personality. And, if you're a softie like me, your heart's gonna take a beating when observing the bond between the main character and the narrator.
Despite it being linear in nature to coincide well with the well-scripted storytelling, Transistor opens up several paths within its world. It's difficult to not be sucked in with the little details in the atmosphere, emotions, and simplistic yet addicting combat.

Supergiant Games set themselves one hell of a challenge coming into the market with the tagline "from the makers of Bastion". There's a lot to live up to and you don't just want to make Bastion 2.0, but you also don't want to be a one hit wonder.
So enters Transistor. With the same "narrator", the same music composer, the same isometric camera angle and the same hand-painted artstyle. But there's so much more to the game mechanics of Transistor than those of Bastion. Each Funtion has 3 options to it. You can slot it as an attack, a passive or slot in onto another attack. With around 20 Fuctions in the game, that's a lot of depth.
I did have some worries about the length, with the main story only lasting 5 hours, but then I "recurred" through the story, which randomised the combat and then I completed all of the challenges which more than made up for it.
Transistor is fantastic. A gorgeous game, as Supergiant tend to make, but they have also shown that they understand the need to improve gameplay.

Have you ever had a friendship, maybe a person you really liked during school? Maybe you talked to them a lot. Maybe you hung out. Hell, maybe you were even best friends. Now, think back to all the friends you've had in the past. How many have came and gone? How many did you stay in touch with? A single sentence, a single action could have changed who you became friends with. The words you choose have more power than you ever realise at the time. That is what Emily is Away is about, to put it shortly. It is a beautiful game where your words can drastically alter how Emily speaks to you, where your choices determine how the story flows. If you love story driven games, this is a must play for you. Hell, even if this usually isn't your cup of tea it would be criminal not to give it a try. It's short, it isn't taxing on your computer and most importantly of all it's FREE! There is no excuse to not give this masterpiece of storytelling a try, and honestly passing over this game would be a disservice to both yourself and the creator of this gem. So why are you still reading this review? Hit that download button and play it for yourself!

It's a heart breaking but realistic story about a person trying to get a long time friend's affection. The game takes place within 6 chapters, all of which will have you, the player, talking to Emily. Your choices and the things you say to her will affect how events play out in the game and how Emily herself reacts to you. It's a sad, relatable love story. The dialouge in this game is some of the most realistic dialouge I've ever seen in a game. I actually felt like I was talking to an actual person. The game, while very short, leaves you with many emotions, and a lot to think about. That's incredible for a game this short. I really liked Emily Is Away, I think it's something we can all relate to. 8/10 :)

This is an amazing game. Its that simple. Its like the Fallout games but with a COD/BF style combat system. The guns feel good. The inventory managment keeps a tight grip on the amount of ammo and weapons you can carry which places huge emphasis on ammo rationing and scavenging. You are only allowed one rifle and pistol equiped at a time which makes for more intense fire fights when you have limited ammo and have to switch to another gun.
The story is pretty cool. You play a wandering soldier in a nuclear wasteland called the Zone who is seeking to discover his past. There are mutant critters and bandits and several factions for you to beat down on, befriend, or ignore. Ultimately you are trying to make it to the north of the Zone to unravel the secrets which lie in the Chernobyl nuclear power plant.
I did have a couple frustrations with the game. The biggest is the lack of fast travel. I get that its more immersive without it, but because your stats level based on your equipment and not your character it was often easier to push on to ther next area in the zone rather than take a 10 minute trek back to another area to turn in a quest. This process is made even more frustrating by the lack of vehicles and the limit on sprinting ability. I wouldn't mind the sprinting limitations, but to  have to run back and forth across 2 or 3 areas while stopping every minute to wait for my stamina to recharge became monotonous very quickly. This did get a little better late game when I found certain artifacts which boosted endurance.
The only other issue I had with the game was the quest system. This wasnt a huge issue until late game but there were some frustrating things early on. Your PDA which contains your quests does not differentiate your main quests and minor quests. You start the game with a task to kill a certain guy and I played the whole game thinking that was the main quest only to abruptly reach the end and find out that was a super important side quest I should have done long ago and now will have to reply the game to complete. The other issue I already mentioned is the way the game progresses. You may have a quest in the starter town and have already progressed to the main hub town, but if you completed a quest for the first town you have to hike all the way back to the beginning and then all the way back to the next area. In the end it was just simpler to move on and forget quests. I would encourage new players not to look up plot lines or ending spoilers, but definitley have several saves prepared before you enter Pripyat. Otherwise you might miss out on questlines.
Altogether Stalker is a great game. There are many things it does very well and for that reason I tend to favor it somewhat over Fallout. The only drawbacks are the lack of fast travel and the confusing quest system.

My first complaint with the game is the developer logo. It's completely illegible!
Secondly, the frame rate of this game is completely bonkers. I actually couldn't find a way to find out the true FPS of the game since neither the Steam overlay or Fraps would work with it but based on my own experience it hovers around 20 to 30 FPS which is unacceptable for a PC game. Take a look at the credits and you can clearly see the text jumping while scrolling.
My third complaint is the options menu. There isn't any! I can appreciate the fact that keyboard controls are available and with the right settings they might be somewhat useful but really this game was designed to be used with a mouse and thus the movement speed is more or less a useless option which makes the options menu even more lackluster. The game only supports 1 resolution which is 1280*720 and there isn't any toggle for full screen on the options menu. There is a button command for it which is flashed when you first start the game but it disappears quickly and honestly should be listed in the options since there's tons of room for it.
You can't rebind any of the controls but mostly they're pretty logical so it's not a big deal. However the game does a pretty bad job at menu navigation. What button you need to press at the end of a level in order to continue? Test every one and you might find it's right click or escape but nowhere in the game does it tell you this.
Speaking of "bound controls", let's say you want to record some gameplay footage or put on some music while messing around in a level or at the end of it. Well too bad because you can't! The mouse is locked to the center of the screen whilst in these modes so you need to pause or quit to the menu to regain control even if you tab out. To be honest it's not a big deal but it's certainly very confusing and frustrating when it happens to you and you have no clue what the problem is since it happens on seemingly random menu screens. Another thing that happens when you tab out of the game is that the gameplay music (but not menu music) stops looping and the voiced mission briefings gets muted but doesn't stop playing.
Now to my fourth complaint about the game. The mission breifings. First of all they're way too long and convoluted. Many do have some useful info but considering the gameplay the game offers you can't be bothered to read it all most of the time. Secondly the briefing is voiced by a computer-sounding female which actually sounds pretty neat. However the things she says isn't what the text is saying. What she's saying is a condensed version of the highlighted text, but if you try to listen to her and read at the same time it's just confusing. Thirdly, there is a lot of information that would be very useful to have in the instructions of the game but I'll get back to that later.
Moving on, let's take a look at the gameplay for a bit. When you first start the game only the Fighter is available and you need to complete 5 missions before you unlock the Survivor ship. These missions are mostly just tutorial levels that let you get a handle of your ship and the mechanics which is fine. The very first mission just let's you navigate through some obstacles for 20 seconds. However there is no way to go faster, you can't gain any score and the only thing dying or getting hit does is lowering your score which starts at 0 and can't go below it so you can literally do nothing and successfully beat the mission.
That in and of itself wouldn't be too bad if the only goal was to learn how to handle the craft. However when you unlock the second craft IT'S first mission is exactly the same and as far as I can tell their speed and handling are identical. This means that there is literally zero point in having that first mission again for the second craft.
When it comes to actually handling the craft, the mechanics are in my opinion very bad. Like I said before the WASD keys are very hard to use to the point of unusable considering the overall difficulty of the game so really you're going to use the mouse for all the movement. However the ship has a maximum speed limit and if your mouse speed exceeds that, a faint shadow of your ship will indicate where your mouse is and the ship will go toward that point at maximum speed. This gives the game an inherent input lag that only makes navigating hard and unintuitive. Other games that has a similar mechanic usually use mouse acceleration to smooth out the movements to make it more natural whilst also having a slower overall speed.
Now it might not seem all that bad at first glance but consider the situation here: you have 2 enemies shooting straight from the left, another enemy moving fast in a cross pattern with fast shots aimed towards you in addition to a big boulder blocking your path and a small boulder that's almost invisible against the background. There's also a boost ring which is a sort of power up that you'd like to collect.
So basically you want to look at 5 or 6 different places that aren't your ship and steer with a method of control that basically requires you to look at the faint shadow of your ship in order to move accurately in a game that moves this fast. You feel crippled rather than challenged and whenever you do something right it feels more like luck that you happened to move your mouse to the position you wanted rather than skill.
The second mission introduces the boost mechanic. Basically you can collect "boost rings" in order to fill your boost gauge and then scroll the game faster to get a better level time. You can also combo them together in order to get more boost per ring. The first ring gives "1" something, the second gives 2, then 3 and so on. Once you reach 10 it starts over at 1 even if the combo didn't end and if it did end you also get 1.
The fifth mission for the survivor ship requires you to finish the level in "Ghost mode". In order to do that you need to gain boost level 3 and then boost to the finish. So you try it a couple times and can't seem to reach level 3. How do I keep the combo going? How long between rings can I wait? Is there a visual cue I'm missing? Do the numbers represent the combo counter or something else?
So you go to the in-depth guide PDF linked on the steam page and read about Boost and you learn that each ring gives 2% individually, the 2nd in a combo gives 4%, the next 8%. "After this, every boost ring that is reached within two seconds from the last fills the boost bar by 8%".
So in total there are 21 rings in the level. With some basic maths we find that the maximum combo we can get is 10 + 10 + 1 which gives
2*(2+4+8*8)+2= 142%
Wait hold on that doesn't look right! How much % is a level anyway? If you ignore the actual numbers and just assume a 21 ring combo you still only get
2+4+8*19=158%
That still looks wrong unless a boost level is 50% for some reason. So I don't get this mission because the game numbers your combo from 1 to 10 back to 1 and I have no clue if that resets the combo or not because it would be pretty reasonable to assume that if the number go from 10 to 1 that means the combo was reset, but the "in-depth guide" only mentions it being 2 seconds between picking up a ring as a combo breaker so I have no clue what's going on. Furthermore what is the whole deal with the percentages anyway because the numbers don't add up in any way I can make sense of.
Now you stop giving a crap about making sense of all this and try to just get all the rings in a single combo to beat the stage, which is hard because there is no indicator for when 2 seconds have gone by and you can't look at the timer because the controls are♥♥♥♥♥♥and getting killed ruins it so after some 20 attempts you finally get level 3 and beat the stage.
