As MMOs go, this particular one is notable for attempting to be the successor to Ragnarök Online. RO has held a special place in the hearts of many many generations of MMOers, being one of the first MMOs played by a new generation of gamers that weren't born in the 70s. Tree of Savior (also commonly known as Tree of Lag, Tree of Salt, and recently Talt of Savior) is not, in fact, RO. The lead director of RO is working on this game, and it does have a lot of similarities right down to the multi-tier class system and several class-specific attacks. Stats and other stuff are a one-time thing; once you dump them in, there's no way to reverse it without spending real money. However, that is where the similarities end. ToS has an even more extensive and confusing class progression, which requires extensive research BEFORE you even roll the class, let alone put points into anything. Also everyone is around level 270 now, so catching up is going to be difficult.
The market is a mess due to some brightsparks who decided to overcharge on the most useless item drops. Prices fluctuate with the sanity of a horse with chronic pain. Some people sell low, others sell the same item for stupidly high values far beyond the worth of the item. This is compounded by the fact that market participation has been limited 'to fight botting,' a phrase to strike fear in the hearts of merchants everywhere. The market problems could be felt from 'service' sales too; squires usually overcharge by a large margin, and gem roasting is a toss-up among alchemists. All in all, you will find that profiting will either consist of looking for that one very rare item, or simply ripping people off.
Guild wars erupt over minor nonsense, and bots roam the lands, pilfering, murdering, and driving people nuts. In fact, if it were more like RO people might hallucinate that they ARE playing RO, except the market limitations would bring them back to reality. This is not to say that there are no merits to ToS. There are plenty of merits to ToS, mainly for those looking to kill large blobs of things over and over again, to rip that bloodied gilt helmet from a Pawndel corpse. You could also join the SEA server for the sake of watching the saltfest that is guild wars, although it is nowhere near as extreme as WoE.
You will find that bad class choices are completely permanent; messing up requires you to reroll if you happen to screw up on your promotion choices. There is no way to change the decision once it is accepted; this applies BEFORE you actually go to the job master to get your class change quest (be warned). This also applies to stat distributions; it is usually less severe as more levels/points will fix it unless you put points in Int as any class but a caster cleric or wizard. Basically it has the same system as RO except it is less forgiving of mistakes. Plan ahead. Do not fall into the trap that is Archer C3/Scout/Rogue; PVP builds such as this are not moneymakers, and should be considered at a later date rather than early on.
Unlike RO, you do not start as a novice; you start as one of four base classes: Swordsman, Wizard, Archer, and Cleric. I will describe them to the best of my ability based off of my observations and from the experiences of others.
For those who truly wish to start the grindfest, you cannot go wrong with rolling a Swordsman. They have almost three times the health of other classes without putting points into Constitution, rendering dying less likely from normal grinding. Swordies can also live off of low level SP potions for most if not almost all their progression up to level 200, a stark contrast to SP intensive archer builds. As a swordy, you run up to people, you repeatedly bash their face in, and they die. It is not only very simple, but extremely effective. Swordsmen are hands down the most straightforward and therapeutic class to play. Swordies also get to become ninjas at Tier 7 as a secret promotion. No other class can make that claim.
This mix of wonderful attributes is inevitably dampened by the fact that high level play demand all swordsmen to be tanks. Most of their abilities do not scale as powerfully as other base classes at high levels, and DPS builds for swordies are mostly only able to keep up with established DPS builds for Wizard and Archer. In the case of the wizard, there is no competition; a swordsman at level 200+ will never be able to compete on the same level as a wizard at level 200+, assuming both are damage builds. Peltastas are in high demand, as they are the primary tanking class specialization; you can still do some damage even as a Peltasta, but nobody will accept you as a 'DPS build'.
There are many wizard builds, most of them revolving around how to creatively screw over enemies. Raw damage builds such as C3 Wiz/Ele rarely have trouble leveling due to their ability to annihilate any and all opposition with ease. Support builds are also fairly useful, and people literally worship Linkers due to their synergy; just like the Soul Linker, the Linker does basically the same thing with more tricks. As a force multiplier, Linkers are always wanted in a group unless there is already another Linker, and their ability to share buffs, damage, and force enemies to take dramatically more damage make them viable at all stages of the game. Just make sure to actually take some damage classes to make up for Linker's lack of damage-dealing abilities.
As for Elementalist builds, they deal some of the highest raw damage of any build type; even the legendary Assassin Cross stands in awe. There is no comparison to the amount of carnage a C3 Wiz/Ele can wreck upon the hordes with the help of a Linker.
Cleric is a class with some...interesting faith-related class options. They are the primary healer type class as well as having many many buffs, all doing a variety of interesting things. A cleric does not necessarily have to be played for support; their ability to do damage can be quite significant if built properly. Clerics also inherited Paladin from the swordsman, but it is completely different compared to the one you might remember. It doesn't matter because Paladins have some of the most spiffy outfits ever. For truly competitive or endgame support play, the options become more limited.
Clerics can promote to priest; a damage-orientated buff Priest is C3 Priest. You will cry tears of blood when you realise that even with your killrate you're bleeding money (literally) on reagants for your spells. You will basically always find a party though, and the chances of you being carried at level 100 and higher is fairly great. It is nowhere near as bad as playing a battle priest from RO, and you get to make the floor flash pretty colors. Also has access to one of the most powerful buff spells in the game: Stoneskin.
Clerics could also take Dievdirbys for the other support option; they are colliqually known as 'waifu carvers' due to their totem-carving abilities. They carve statues of the goddesses which all give a variety of buffs or other effects; the totems are pretty much gob-smackingly powerful and can do a lot for party play.
Cleric builds revolving around solofarming or damage usually focus on Bokor to raise a literal army of zombies to do your dirty work, or C3 Priest/Chaplain; there are many more examples not listed here.
Archers once had the short end of the stick, and certain archer classes still do.
Don't roll a rogue unless you can actually fund one. It's a trap until you hit C2, and by then you'll regret having to farm that Arde dagger. Rogues are notorious for their gear dependency and require a lot of patience and the ability to not fly into a rage when someone inevitably steals your kills.
Most other archer classes besides hunter are fine.

At this state, the game seem way more polished compared to the clusterfock that was at release. However, doesn't feel an inprovement at all with respect Rome, or other Total War games. After finishing the grand campaign here are my feelings:
-This is a couple of things that they have done better but fall into nothing
The political intrigue is more deep now than the mechanics with the shogun, the pope, or the 3 rome factions. However, is completely worthless. I have spend millions of talens to secure promotions, I have only active my family generals, and adopt and bribe any other character, and still I only have a 35% maximum of the senate control. The civil war meter hasen't move from 0 in the entire campaing.
The thing about the provinces seems like a good idea, you can also build into several settlements at a time which is nice. But doesn't seem to have a significant bonus. The province control seems rather useless other than the own satisfaction of sorting your own stuff in an arbitrary matter. You can't even interchange settlement in the diplomatic view to complete provinces.
-One thing that is actually an improvement respect Rome.
The art style is fantastic. It quite similar to Shogun 2 in regard of placing you into the historical settting. Not so much the music though; not bad, but not good neither.
-Other than than the game falls flat in many aspect.
The AI is horrible. Is worse than other TW games. Most of the naval battles are the enemy waiting there doing nothing. And the diplomatic interchange is just silly. I have multiple faction declaring war on me, only to surrender in the next turn and giving me 5000+ talens in compensation without even having a battle.
The combat seems simplify respect other titles. I remember using way more siegue weapons, archers, hoplites and lancers, and their respective special moves. In here I don't have a feeling of actually having to do anything on the battlemap. And to make things worse, the last tier lancers are replaced with swordmans preators, which are cool and nice, but albeit no sustitue for a spear wall.
Another thing that I have no idea what is for, the victory/strategy points in the battle map. Previously, if you loose the plaza, you loose the settlement. Now nothing happens. there is a flag that goes up and down but it has no consequence. The only thing that you can use it for is to capture gates and towers, but nothing else.
There are bad things with the IU. For example now you can click and draw a unit where what should happen, and what happened before is that you will make a square for multiple selection, and this is quite annoying actually. Another thing is that the tactical map in the continent view doesn't draw the icon if you zoom too much; why?? doesn't make any sense. The diplomatic view could also be mix with the tactical view, they are pretty much the same. When you click a general to figure it out the family you need to click in another 3 menu and look for him manually. The artifact bonus thing, I got 50+ extra at the end of the campaign without use. And I haven't figure it out yet how to build the coliseum. And the slums are horrible and annoying, there is no way to have a multiple settlement view to tell you where are space available and you need to look for them manually or else the slums will pop-up.
And finally, the DLC market strategy and promotion/spam aspect of the game is not acceptable. There is a constant reminder to "buy this other cool stuff" all over. Just leave me alone!
Everything is worse than earlier Total War games. The battle maps doesn't look like anything close to reality, the interface sucks, the AI is bad. Don't buy this game.

This is an amazing game, beautiful art, engaging story, capturing music, and a narration system different from its predecessor bastion but still gets the job done beautifully. This game compaired to bastion almost blows it out of the water.
The story is just as strong, the world is just as strong, and the music just as good. The gameplay however is so good with a somewhat unique planning system and interesting skill system. It makes the game something more than just a story that bastion was.
However there are two issues that hold it back a bit in my eyes. The first is that the skill trees are rather confusing at first, and after you figure them out they are innefficient and somewhat difficult to handle. This however is a minor detail. The real issue is how the turn system interacts with the world. After my first playthrough I felt slightly unsatisfied with the game and realized that this was because the turns system takes you out of the environment, it literally erases all the hand drawn background while your planning out your move.
Now in no means does this ruin the game, its just a small qualm that I have personally, and it kinda bugged me. They put so much effort into the background art but it all goes away when you plan out your moves. This kinda says something philosophically and fits with the theme of the game very well, but if you aren't really looking for it does make the game feel less immersive than Bastion was. This breaking of immersion was the only thing that held it back in my opinion just take it with a grain of salt.
Final Verdict
This is an amazing game Supergiant delivered and at least met, if not slightly exceeded, the standards set by Bastion. The gamplay is awesome and feels powerful at the sacrifice of the world for a few seconds (a damaging but kinda cool trade off that upon further reflection I kinda wonder if it was on purpose). The music is spot on but more futeristic, and the visuals are just breathtaking. The combat can feel a bit repetative but its not that bad. It is definetly worth your $20 for the game and even the $30 for the game and soundtrack.

Papers, Please Review
Papers, Please is a game about paperwork. Papers, Please is a game about 12 hour work days living life paycheck to paycheck. Papers, Please should not sound like a good game, and in theory it shouldn’t be. But Papers, Please is not just a good game, it is a great game.

You play as a border guard in the fictional country of Arstotzka, your job is to control the flow of immigrants and exterminate all who try and cheat the system. You must care for a family of 5 and your pay is very little. Mistakes are not tolerated and every error will be deducted from the small amount of money you are given. It is very easy to starve to death in Papers, Please; death and insignificance play a large part in the overall theme of the game. You are not the hero, you are not important, if you fail to live up to expectations you will be replaced in a matter of hours.
The heavy themes that Papers, Please possess are what make the experience so great, its depictions of war in the 20th century are expressed so well in the colorless background. There isn’t a single happy thought in Papers, Please. The whole game has a depressing feel to it, but this is what the creator was aiming for. He wasn’t trying to make a fantasy where everything is good and right in the world; his approach is honest and sinister.
The sensational achievement that is Papers, Please art design is not enough on its own to be worth playing, but with the addition of its intriguing gameplay mechanics and consistent challenge makes for a level of enjoyment other artistic games miss, Papers, Please is not great because of its perfection at simulating paperwork, or its ability to depict gruesome settings and artistic impurity. It is great because it can balance the two elements so well and make for an experience like no other.
Papers, Please proves that a game doesn’t need a million dollar budget and a team of thousands of developers to be good. Papers, Please was made by one man and standing up there with the biggest games of 2013. Papers, Please is the result of artistic brilliance and will be remembered and celebrated for many years to come.

Call of Juarez is a first person shooter in a western style environment.
Throughout the story you are accompanied by the narration of your protagonist, who is a unreliable story teller that mixes up facts, constantly corrects itself, which has an effect on what you are currently playing (bridges appearing out of nowhere, game 'rewinding' to a certain point because what was being told before was wrong) which is extremly funny, satisfying and keeps you interested the whole time.
I didn't find the story to have any weak spots.
Checkpoint placement is perfect, you don't have to watch some cut scenes over and over again, and right before any difficult spot there is a checkpoint.
Gun play mechanics are well implemented, you have visual feedback of hitting someone, the aiming is kinda realistic, which creates immersive gun fights..
So this game is perfect, right?
Almost, it does have a very serious flaw (in my opinion):
Graphics:
It has a comic look to it, but at the beginning or in some levels the contrast between objects and actors in the level is almost non existant.
This means it's easy getting 'lost' (which means briefly getting on the wrong path and being reminded seconds later that you can't go there), and sometimes *extremly* hard to spot enemies. Which I believe can become quite an annoyance if you're not the best FPS player in the world. This also means that sometimes everything looks the same and albeit well designed levels it might be difficult to distinguish one area from another.
This is especially annoying when you are playing on a small screen with a low resolution, where sometimes the only way for you to see an enemy is noticing being shot at from that direction. Luckily you can use concentration which paints your enemies red.
Still, after a while, with a big screen and full resolution you get kinda used to it, and it doesn't stop you from enjoying the game.
The story line itself is very short, 5-6 hours but because of New Game Plus and Arcade Mode you can easily invest twice the amount while still being entertained.
This isn't really bad considering the game is so cheap.
All in all this is one of the best single player experiences (in an action shooter) that I've had in a long time.
So, despite that one flaw mentioned I can only recommend to pick it up.

Assuming the role of the amnesiac stalker named the Marked One, you explore the various locations and areas in the Zone, an area in Chernobyl that was the site of an incident that created rifts in various locations called anomalies that have different effects when touched which ranging from a lightning, fire, to gravity-manipulation.
[GAMEPLAY]
An FPS-rpg which may be likened to games like Fallout New Vegas or Fallout 3, S.T.A.L.K.E.R Shadow of Chernobyl focuses more on the shooting mechanics such as giving the player an option to peek corners using a lean option, sprint for a certain distance which is determined by the stamina bar, and have access to different kinds of guns ranging from the common weapon categories such as pistols, shotguns, and rifles. The game features different quests given by different people of The Zone (will be discussed more later), it also contains RPG elements present in the form of quests, stats, weapon degradation, and inventory management. Stat manipulation acts more of a resistance mechanic and  can only be done through the acquisition of items called "artifacts" which can be randomly obtained in the different areas with anomalies or through containers,
PROS:
-Straightforward fps elements and simplified rpg elements that allows you to focus more on the former.
-Gun variety and implementation of the weight system forces you to be more prudent in your weapon
choices.
CONS:
- Certain stats tend to be more important to others like bulletproof, radiation, and endurance.
- The weapon accuracy of the game could be misleading at times. Even when you're using a rifle, shooting an enemy at a relatively close range will take you a couple of bullets. The game encourages the use of tap shooting instead of spraying.
- Quests are repetitive. You're given the usual get this, get that, & kill this, kill that.
- Gamebreaking quests that don't warn you of the consequences (To be discussed in the story portion)
[SOUND]
Music:
While the game's music is not something to be praised, the sound effects created when you're in an underground research facility would really set up the mood, further enforcing the idea that you're not alone and that the mutated inhabitants of the Zone may just be in the next corner.
[GRAPHICS]
The game's age shows through its textures is lackluster in terms character design and structures and confusing layouts in terms of the level design. Enemy/NPC variety is limited to a mere 5-7 designs for humans which are usually designated by armor they're wearing while there are only about 5 mutant types in the game. Building's look relatively the same with the others in the area while level design tends to be confusing as the ingame map or quest tracker sometimes doesn't specify what floor or even accurately pin points the objective.
[VOICE ACTING]
Obviously not a strength of the game, I would have preferred if the developers of the game spoke in their native tongue and had subtitles for better immersion. Although finally hearing the phrase cheeki breeki made my day any time.
Pros: Cheeki breeki
Cons: Pretty bad voice acting
[STORYLINE]
Playing as an amnesiac stalker named the Marked One who was originally thought to be dead, you are brought in by a local trader who asks you to do some work for him by running errands. You eventually get to meet the different factions in the game such as Freedom, Duty, and the Loner factions as you explore and unravel the mysteries of the Zone.
PROS: Different possible endings depending on your actions
CONS: Game-breaking quest system that could possibly deter you from progressing through the game.
[Bugs & Glitches]
The game tends to have a lot of bugs as mentioned above but can be easily avoided by saving properly or using the quick load option. Other options such as fixes or patches online can be used to address this. Some I bugs I've experienced are  getting stuck in certain areas because of trying to reach certain places and factions becoming suddenly hostile to you because of a quest.
Rating: 7/10
Rating the game as more of an fps, I rated accordingly based on its genre/s, as an fps-rpg. Although the game shines more of as a fps, the rpg elements of the game only adds to its realism while being plagued with bad-level design, few npc and enemy types, and some game-breaking bugs which are easily-fixed.

Factorio is a game about building infrastructure and completely automating everything.  You start with the basics as any building and survival game would and work your way up the ladder researching technologies and ultimately advancing to the point at which you launch a rocket into space.
What Factorio does well is keep you playing.  The map is procedurally generated and you have options to affect how it is generated at the start of the map.  There are multiple ways to play currently, a campaign, tutorial, a sandbox, and a few challenge missions where you must meet the objectives before time runs out.
From conveyor belts to UAVs, you can produce, build, and transport everything.  Locomotives are mainly used when you need to get something somewhere fast due to a vast distance between one base and another.  As you continue to mine out the resources you will be expanding and locomotives take this burden off of your shoulders.  As you upgrade technologies you get faster conveyor belts that you can simply drop down on top of the existing belt.  This same concept applies to older furnaces and chests.
The sheer amount of things you can do while trying to expand and improve your existing infrastructure is awesome.  Add mods to the game and you have even more options.  Mods are going to be what makes this game from great to awesome.
Currently, there are only a few ways to generate power until the developers add more power sources.  Solar power and steam from water are the two primary sources.  This can look a bit weird in late game when you have solar panels everywhere and steam is still powering your entire infrastructure.  At some point, I hope they add fuel/diesel generators and nuclear power.  From what I have researched, fuel generators should be getting put in.
On other topics, the music is great and the sound effects are about what you would expect from a factory style game.  Graphics obviously were not the objective in the game so the top down 2D is what you have to work with adding in zoom when you need to get a bigger or smaller view.  The various peices in which you use to build infrastructure all make sense for the most part.  They place down easily and logically and certain buildings will show you where to bring in your pipes.  The only difficult part is learning how everything works together to make the best factory system you can.
Whle building you will notice you can make cars, tanks, guns, better guns, turrets (both laser and bullet), as well as land mines and grenades.  These are to fend off the critters known as biters and spiters that expand their nests.  You can destroy their nests once you get appropriate gear but beware, this apparently makes them mad and they get even more aggressive as if the slow level of incrementing numbers wasn't already something you didn't want to deal with.
I would recommend Factorio.  It does several things well and is a throwback to what video games used to be before investors and greed took over.  While there are a few missing elements still, such as the fuel generator, nuclear power, naval, etc., I think the game is great.  Rarely will you have a game that you sit down to play and wonder where the last four hours went.
Pros:
A great expansive list of things to build and design
Great music
Large replayability due to procedural maps
Always something to do or improve
Mods
Server support, either local or off-site
Arial logistic, repair, and construction robots for when you run out of room on land
A tank
A ATV
Curcuit system for designing latches that trigger on IF,THEN statements
Cons:
Not enough energy sources yet
No naval
That I know of, no helicopters or personal arial transport
Learning curve for those that want things spoon fed to them is high

IMPORTANT NOTE: To anyone who is skeptical of my review because my playtime for the Steam version of this game is only 0.1 hours: I already finished the game before it came to Steam. I bought it on ShinyLoot:
You can find this exact review of mine there as well, which is from June 16th 2015. Also, as you can see on that page, the game was already released on ShinyLoot in July 2013.
----------
Please don't let this game slide under your radar, simply because the graphics may not catch your attention! Considering this game has been made by only 2 people whereby 1 of them did most of the graphics and the other 1 did everything else, I've been pretty impressed by it! This game is absolutely not your typical SHMUP! The 3 different classes play WIDELY different and the focus is definitely not entirely on blowing things up. Blowing things up is part of it, but there's a lot more you have to pay attention to to get good at this game.
There are some interesting environmental hazards that not only add more character to the level design, but at some points, you can actually use them to your advantage to destroy your enemies.
Then there are the boost rings, which fill up your boost meter and enable you to increase the scrolling speed of the camera. I've never seen such a mechanic in another SHMUP before and it adds so much depth! You can either focus entirely on speedrunning, or you could go for a high score. Although your time does influence your score, going just for speed requires a very different approach than going for points. It's very impressive that even though there aren't many levels, the game is highly versatile, because of all the different methods you could play a mission. Additionally, the score system is very deep and some aspects of it differ between the 3 playable classes, which adds even more character to each of them.
The way QSD handles difficulty is also worth mentioning. Overall, this game is not easy and this may put off some people. However, there are a few things that might help them have a not as much rough time. First of all, there is no lives-system. If you die, you simply return to the game right where you lost and the game continues normally. You do lose score points, which may prevent you from reaching the mission goal, which is always about reaching a specific score (except in the tutorials); but nevertheless, you get to continue until the end of the mission and thus see a bit more of it, instead of getting kicked out of the level every time you die. Second, you can pause and unpause the game by pressing literally ANY key other than the ones already assigned to an action. This makes pausing extremely easy, which can help you to "breathe" whenever you need to. Pressing ESC while the game is paused takes you right back to the mission selection screen, so you can quickly restart a mission if you so desire. Lastly, the score requirements for finishing each mission are high enough to be some challenge, but not punishing by any means. You get ranked for your score and you accomplish a mission by getting at least rank C (except for the final mission where you must get rank B). I've never managed to get rank A, which seems to be extremely difficult, but rank C can easily be received with a little practice and rank B is also achievable.
Having said all this, I must also give you some warnings. QSD is full of game mechanics and the mechanics are explained via some not too long texts at the beginning of each mission. Reading these texts carefully is absolutely essential! If you don't pay attention to these texts, you won't learn the game and easily get frustrated! It kind of reminds me of learning a board game, but the amount of text you have to read is really not much. But again, it's very, very important! If you have difficulties with a mission, make sure to check out the texts at earlier missions, in case you may have overlooked a key mechanic that can help you progress. An example is that the game clearly states that your time influences your score. A friend of mine once complained about the game being too hard, because reaching rank C would already require almost perfect play. What he was doing wrong was he never used the boosting ability, forgetting that a better completion time would boost his score, so he could allow himself some mistakes on the way. This was already explained via the text of an earlier mission, but he didn't remember.
Finally, you must be aware that the tutorial missions must be completed before you can get to the score-based missions. These tutorial missions each require a different goal to complete and a few of them are a bit tricky. Such a thing may confuse some players and there's no denying this game isn't perfect; but at the end of the day, there's a lot to this game that's not apparent at first glance and it has no doubt left me impressed. QSD is by all means a fun, addicting, and absolutely unique game, if you're willing to pay attention! Oh, and it's really cheap too!
Pros: + The three classes are WIDELY different! + Score system and boosting ability add even more versatility! + Replay value is immense! + HIGHLY addicting, once you get the hang of things! + Very cheap!
Cons: CAUTION: You MUST pay attention to the texts! - There aren't many levels (but replay value makes up for it). - Tutorial missions are not ideal (but it's worth to press on).

This game perfectly captures the original Alien. Not only the visuals and game mechanics, but the atmosphere. Space isn't a fun place. Space combines the worst aspects of a 1980s airport and a factory. Space is where blue collar workers worry about getting paid, everything's half-broken, and the company is out to ♥♥♥♥ you over every way it can. Oh, and there's an alien.
The worst thing about this game, in my opinion, is that it's too long. That's a weird complaint, these days, with so many games being only a few hours. But this game has the opposite problem - it drags on too long. There's only so many times you can restore power to pull a lever to open a door to flip a switch before all the tension is gone. There's about three times I thought the game was almost over - the first was only halfway through!
Some people dislike the ending, I think it's sequel setup, for a sequel that probably won't ever get made, as I heard this game didn't sell very well. This game has great tension, Amanda Ripley is a solid character, and it has incredible style. Just don't be afraid to take a break, it's a long haul leading to a kind of anti-climatic payoff.

The most terrifying game I've ever played. You're put in the shoes of Amanda Ripley, Ripley's daughter who's trapped in a space station with a rampaging Alien, droids that have had their programming subverted and turned murderous, and paranoid humans who shoot at you on sight. Naturally, the most dangerous (and terrifying) enemy by far is the Alien, with an AI capable of learning from player behavior. Spend too much time hiding in the vents, and the AI will figure this out and you'll find the Alien waiting for you in the vents. Brrrrrr. The game's developers had a clear love of the source material, with numerous shout-outs and callbacks to the Alien movies. The game is peppered with hacking and engineering mini-games, and while these are okay for the most part, there were a few timed sequences that were just an annoying chore to get through. There are a few dull railroad-y sections, and I hated the ending - after enduring hours of tension, give me a proper ending instead of this damnable sequel-bait cliffhanger! - but all is forgiven for the sheer pants-wetting experience of hiding in a closet, hoping the unstoppable murder machine stalking nearby won't notice your insignificant self and pass you by...
Alien Isolation is my favorite horror game.  Honestly, Outlast is the scariest game I've played, but Alien Isolation is still scary, it has better gameplay, and a lot more replayability.

Alien: Isolation is a first-person survival horror game set in the same universe as the Alien films and faithfully follows the vein of the 1979 original by Ridley Scott. It casts the player as Amanda Ripley, daughter of Sigourney Weaver's now-iconic heroine Ellen Ripley. Amanda was first introduced in the extended cut of James Cameron's Aliens, in which it's revealed that in the decades that Ellen Ripley spent in cryo-sleep following the destruction of the Nostromo in the first film, her daughter Amanda lived a full life and passed away, all without seeing her mother again.
Isolation informs us that, as it turns out, Amanda Ripley's life was not that of a normal 22nd-century civilian. She had a pretty dark event in the middle there—an event which makes up the entirety of Isolation—and at the very least must have suffered from some severe post-traumatic stress in its aftermath.
The game takes place in the year 2137, fifteen years after the events of Alien and another 42 before the start of its sequel, Aliens. Amanda is an adult, working as an engineer for Weyland-Yutani, the chilly corporation that owned her mother's ship (The Nostromo) all those years ago. Amanda has all but given up hope of finding any trace of her mother when a Weyland-Yutani higher-up informs her that the Nostromo's flight recorder has been found and is being held for safekeeping at a space station called Sevastopol.
Pros:
The Alien is terrifying, Sevastopol Station is visually appetizing and gives off the right eerie vibe. And not to mention it is the most worthy homage to the 1979 Alien.
Cons:
The story lacks much impact towards the end that it feels like its dragging on too long. Human AI is lousy.

"Free to Play" / "Pay to Enjoy"
I'd read that somewhere on theHunter's official forums and the summary resonated with me at some 30 hours played. With that said, it's incredible. Two notes on this work -- one, there are few games with better gunplay and two, it is the best hunting game (simulator?) available. theHunter has it all. Unfortunately, most of the content is gated.
Want to hunt mallards? Well, you're going to need to buy a set of decoys, a blind, and a nice shotgun in addition to the license. Win boar hunting tournaments? That demands use of a hog feeder (and the feed), in addition to a tree stand for an optimal experience. And that's the key -- optimal. You do not need anything other than the permitted gun, ammo, and license to hunt a particular animal, HOWEVER, you'll have to work much harder to win competitions or have a successful hunt.
If none of this seems like it will dissuade you, and you've some cash to make your experience easier, it's well worth the value for what you get.

The infamous Dark Souls II...
The entire 'Souls' series is well known for being quite hard to play through; or at least, hard to play flawlessly. Yes, that can be said for most games, but it seems to be the theme in this game. It's purposely not easy to get a hang of it. If you make any mistake while playing, you can expect compensation for it.
That being said, that doesn't mean this is a bad game; not by far. The difficulty of the game makes it only more satisfying when you finally learn how to play proficiently. There are many different ways to play the game and no real "wrong way". It's entirely up to you to pick what playstyle you like and shape your character to fit your needs. The game also lets you play through at your own pace, or even skip ahead. You're not forced to do anything in the game. You can even repeat the game several times, making it harder each time.
Great community as well.
I don't want to make this review too long, but there's just so much to say about this game, that I'd recommend picking it up and experiencing it for yourself. Well worth the money you pay for it.

I personally enjoy this game more than is predecessor, Dark Souls. Dark Souls II is graphically and mechanically a better game than Dark Souls. Fights are more fluid and slightly quicker than the other games in the series, which is something that's been a huge point for the Souls Series. Backstabs and parrys are more difficult to perform, but everything else works much better and feels so much smoother. Multiplayer and co op has never been better in a Souls game, connecting is mucher quicker and connections, for the most part, are more stable, I've personally never had a problem. For people expecting a lot more content or something ceompeletley different or a truly direct sequel to Dark Souls then you will most likely be very disappointed. Dark Souls II has slightly more content than, and pays homage to, Dark Souls and is very much a game of the same essence, but has an entirely different setting. Between the story and setting of the game and the slight changes to the gameplay mechanics, it is very much the same game as Dark Souls giving off the same, or at least similar, atmosphere and having very similar enemy types and bosses with next to nothing really new. For those of you who loved Dark Souls but wanted something a little different with some slight improvements, then this is the game for you or if you just absolutely love the Souls Games, then you'll still want to play this game.

It's hard to give a yes to a game with so many clunky and unfun design flaws and bugs, but it's also hard to say no when the parts that do work end up being absolutely wonderful. This is the unmodded review for 2017
The horribly nostalgic community paints a completely different picture than what I experienced and gave very wrong expectations for what the game actually is in 2017, it's incredibly hilarious watching them split when you ask about whether modding the game is a good idea, you get the purist who think it's normal for the average person to have 2 or 3 playthroughs that say do the first one vanilla and the second playthrough modded. You will get sensibile people suggesting you at least get the bug fix mods or use the overhaul complete mod.
Clearly it's all preference, I can say for certain however if you are used to modern open world games of this genre, this game will feel like a rough draft, it's easy to get immersed in, but outside of that it doesn't hold much special to it, the story isn't good, the side quests are just simplistic as can be (fetch quests, kill this, save that), and the exploration is rewarded with some loot, nothing crazy and you won't find any awesome things to see.
The combat is fairly realistic, but I found even from 10 feet away my gun was either missing or the NPCs don't react properly to getting shot in the chest, it'd be so much better if the game gave you more variety early on outside of a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ pistol or if the NPCs were more reactive to being shot, like being shot in the leg would cause limping for example, or shooting them in general caused reaction.
It's buggy, and has some very obnoxious issues, like a HORRIBLE unchangable FOV and insane shakey cam, you can edit these away in a config file only to find the shadows will break too. You will also upon looking more into the game find various gameplay features not working because of how buggy the game is.
So if you really want another game of this genre, it is a good experience for what it is, I highly suggest the STALKER complete mod, to fix a lot of the common gripes that exist. Namely combat, compatibility and visuals. The terrible quests still exist.
If you are only curious of the atmosphere and lore, I would suggest the Metro series instead.

+ One of the most genuine MC's in Visual Novels (Tomoya Okazaki)
+ Unique story where you actually SEE the married life of a couple and the relationship they had prior.
+ Easily the best OST I have ever heard in a game, each one contributing so much to the message each scene is trying to portray. Snowfield is honestly one of my favorite song in videogames, making me cry because of the beauty of the scene it was involved in.
+ Afterstory is my favorite 2nd half in a visual novel alongside Steins;Gate, evolving its themes to a much more family orientated setting as well as providing emotional heartbreak that no other game could ever provide except this one.
+ The ending is amazing and the use of the "orb lights" is one of my favorite plot elements ever, being detailed enough for hardcore analysis on the role it played in the final moments of Clannad.
+ The Illusionary World is absolutely genius.
+ Another aspect I enjoy about the themes of Clannad is that they are family orientated and could honestly help anyone in need of advice on what to do with their life, offering many unique perspectives on certain ideals that are evident in the world we live in.
- Art is charming however it is definitely not for everyone.
- The game is on average 80+ hours, being one of the longest videogame scripts EVER!!!
Overall Clannad was a 10/10 for me. I don't think I have experienced a story as great as this one since the original Steins;Gate and Steins;Gate 0. The way Clannad tells its story in such a simple but unique way, constantly evolving with time progressions is truly a thought provoking and "valuable" experience. I'd recommend this to anyone that wants to involve themselves in the "Visual Novel" medium as it is the best one I have ever played besides Steins;Gate. The game is worth every cent, 50 dollars is honestly not a bad price for one of the best games of the genre, BUY THIS and enjoy it, as it a truly profound and life altering experience!

Clannad, the Visual Novel!
The first visual novel, and best I've ever had the experience to try out! I've watched the anime, and I loved the VN! If anyone wants to support Key Visual Arts (TM), or is a HUGE, HUGE fan of the anime, this is your game!
[!SPOILERS BELOW!]
Pros:
- All your favorites characters
- You can follow your own paths, or follow the anime's path!
- More than what the anime offered
- Music like in the anime, but so much more!
- Dialogue is very close to perfection
- You'll love the characters in a matter of minutes after meeting them!
- You can make your own choices
- Multiple endings
- Supports your computer greatly; little to no lag at all!
- You get to name the main protaganist!
- Hitting 'esc' will not close the game!
- Has a encyclopedia to explain things you encounter in the game
- Get to experience the events that took place in the anime, and other events that weren't in the anime!
- Music is in High Quality, and is very memorable
- Slow build up, but keeps you intact, and interested through-out the entire play!
- Doesn't throw you into the main story right away, but lets it slowly build into it
- Nagisa! \(^-^)/
Cons:
- Sunohara (HEY!!!)
- Some dialogue can be confusing, but not greatly
- Sometimes the dialogue feels like its been drug out, but not too much to cause issues
- Have to adjust the volume settings of the music, character VAs, etc, but editing is pretty self-explanatory
- You have to play through to be able to build up your encyclopedia, b/c you aren't giving them all right away; again, this isn't a grave issue, as it's common stuff if you've been watching anime for a while
- Again, Sunohara (YOU'RE DOING THIS ON PURPOSE!!!)
- Sometimes you can't choose a dialogue choice where you feel it's necessary, which gets a little fustrating
- Japanese VAs only atm; this isn't an issue for me, but for others, eh...
- Some events are exactly the same like in the anime, but there're some things different, so don't worry!
I'm really enjoying this game, and I hope you all who're considering it enjoy it as much as I am, if not more! :D

While the term "soft drink" is commonly used in product labeling and on restaurant menus, in many countries these drinks are more commonly referred to by regional names, including carbonated beverage, coke, fizzy drink, fizzy juice, cool drink, cold drink, lolly water, pop, seltzer, soda, soda pop, tonic, and mineral. Due to the high sugar content in typical soft drinks, they may also be called sugary drinks. In Spanish, they often use the English equivalent of 'refreshment', or (given its carbonated content) also commonly called gaseosa, from agua gaseosa (literally "fizzy water"). In the United States, the 2003 Harvard Dialect Survey tracked the usage of the nine most common names. Over half of the survey respondents preferred the term "soda".

In its current state, I can't recommend the game to anyone. If you're going to play this game, be aware that you will probably run into a lot of issues. While the base foundation is there, the game is simply not ready for public access. Tree of Savior has one of the most over the top trade restriction that are built to combat gold sellers but wound up punishing its playerbase instead. Due to this games' low spawn rate and mob reward system, you're going to run into a fair amount of killstealing where you won't get quest progress or credit if you don't last hit a mob. Shout chat is still filled with gold seller shouts, and bots are running around freely in unpopulated and populated areas (granted, what free to play mmo doesn't have bots doing just that). There have been exploits, dungeon entry issues, server and channel entry issues, glitches and a lack of optimization that makes you question if IMC just wanted to push this out to make as much money as they can before it dies out.

Day 1:
- Created character with similar looks of a Potato
- Named him Spudicus
- Spawned on a beach with nothing but a handy stump and g string to cover my potato parts.
- Started hitting tree for wood but I was captured by naked man with wooden mask.
- Dragged through the ocean and across beaches onto an island and put into a cage.
Day 2:
- Forced to sing songs and play Darude Sandstorm on a flute for the tribal savages.
- Was beaten if I missed a note or skipped one.
- Every now and again they would tie me up and drag me to a pillory and begin whipping me and calling me a dirty spud.
- Soon realising I was slowly dying by starvation since they only fed me water I begged for mercy.
Day 3:
- As the tribal men were off in the woods a tiny skinny black man randomly appeared.
- I instantly got the small black mans attention and began begging for him to let me out.
- As the tiny black man was attempting to break the cage which held me a tribal man came out of no where and began fighting with the tiny black man.
- Tiny black man won the fight with wooden spears and then broke my cage.
- Soon after another tribal man appeared and began to attack us, our tools were unmatched and the tiny black man ran out of spears.
Day 4:
- After running through forrest which seemed like forever I had lost track of the tiny black man and was still being chased by the tribal man.
- Came across a knight in steel wearing a crown and wielding a mighty swirly sword.
- After one blow at the tribal man delivered by this crowned knight the savage was dead, off with his head!
- The knight introducded himself as Werthin the king of the realm.
- I pledged my life for the king and in return would always be by his side until the end.
Day 5:
- King Werthin had made me his royal knight and I shall never leave his side.
- I was given the greatest steel armour and weapons made by the King himself.
- I am now known as Sir Spudicus.
Day 6:
- Together King Werthin and I began fortifying the Ancient Thrown to keep back the relentless savages below.
- After many and endless attacks all attempts to protect the thrown seemed futile.
- The end was near and now myself and King Werthin had many spears embedded into our bodies.
Day 7:
- The raids appeared to have came to a hault for a while however we could see many lights on the bridge heading our way.
- Realising we were running out of bandages I gave my last to King Werthin.
- With the last of my strength I gave one last almighty charge towards the savages.
- Upon my first swing I beheaded one of the savages and cut down another.
- Swing after swing the savages fell upon my blade but one of them got past and through to the King.
- I chased down the savage who had now put King Werthin in ropes and hanged him from the bridge.
- I begged the savages for mercy as they relentlessly attacked me, beating me with their wooden clubs.
- As I watched my King being hung over the ledge I knew my time had come and with one last swing of my sword I beheaded the savage that held my king and plunged over the bridge to my death with the King.
Day 7:
- We survived after smashing against the mountain sides
- Killed one last savage that jumped down after us.
- He had bandages.
- We lived.
- King Werthin however is now Lord Werthin.
11/10 Would kill savages again.

It's a journey, this one. It won't let you roam free much, it won't last all that long and it will not attempt to intoxicate you with pathos, but it remains a journey all the same - with its exquisite marriage of inspired visuals and haunting soundscape clevelry used to create a reality that feels both original and enchanting. And just as the delivery is stellar, so is the gameplay - taking hints from turn-based roleplaying games of old, and expanding on their principles. As such, the game commands both style and substance, with shortcomings that are fairly few and insignificant - particularly in contrast with Transistor's many qualities. Sincere recommendation.

This is a game that does just about everything right. It is worthy successor to Dark Souls. Furthermore, the DLC is an enjoyable expansion and worth the money. The graphics are improvement on Dark Souls. The storyline is sufficiently compelling. I really enjoyed the following:
1. The fast pace action: it combines the best of rpg with action games.

3. The strategic considerations that are required to defeat tough mobs and bosses.
What I didn't like was:
1. Broken controls: Trying to execute a guard break or leaping attack was such an iffy proposition that I didn't even bother to use those maneuvers. Parrying was far more challenging than necessary and certainly more difficult to execute than in Dark Souls.
2. Player invasions could be tweaked: It detracts from the overall fun of the game when you already soloing a difficult area heavily populated with challenging mobs only to faced with an invader when your health and magic are low. In addition, the invader always had a decided advantage unless the host player is specifically spec'd for invasions. There is an option to turn off  invasions or you can play off-line but that effects co-op play and not all invasions are unwelcome.
Warning: Don't speak to the Emerald Herald when wearing poison armor. She will disappear on your next visit and you will have no way of leveling up on that playthrough.
Overall, I give the game a 9 out of 10.

I also really liked the "Nuggets of truth" thing, where you can find items which tell you the (real life) backstory to many of the characters and events and locations of the wild west. My biggest complaints would be the samey-ness and length. It's a very short game, but this is made up for by the new game+ mode and the arcade mode, which lets you replay the missions choosing from 1 of the three specialties you can pursue in the story mode in a points based system. It's fairly quick and mindless fun but it does remind you that the whole game is running around shooting people.

Let's just say that if you're not into the open world concept that Red Dead Redemption flaunted, this is likely the next best thing if you're looking for some interactive fun within the Old West.
The gunplay gives off satisfying audio/visual punches, the AI is solid (Hard and True West will give you a pretty decent challenge at the very least), the visuals are surprisingly sharp and detailed (though it's still not the prettiest game you've ever seen, exactly), and it boasts an ambitious and (mostly) successful gun duel mechanic. Hell, there's even a whole separate endurance mode catered to it. It's an excellent concentration exercise.
Equally as creative is how the great narration can alter the game in a quick pinch, even during mid-combat.
Character B: "You sayin' they were Indians?"
Narrator: "No. I said they attacked me Indian /style/."
And, with that, models are switched and your back in the game. I'll tell ya. The Old West vibe was so thick here I found myself chewing on my mouse cord like a piece of straw.
As the game draws to a close, it does tend to rely on those "breach n' clear" events (The Not So Great Train Robbery was easily the least exciting mission) and an overall scripted nature (which is normally used in moderation, thus making it enjoyable and not played out for this particular game), and the "throw dynamite from cover until he's dead" boss fights are rather dull, but it's an overall incredibly solid shooter with an infectious (albeit predictable) story and narration.

Got to say, I was very pleasantly surprised with this game.
I only picked it up because it was packaged with Blood Dragon for a couple bucks extra, and wasn't expecting a whole lot for the price. Turned out to be one of the most enjoyable shooters I've ever played, and a very refreshing change of scenery from the countless "modern combat shooter X" games that have oversaturated the FPS market.
The whole game is narrated by the main character telling the story of each level/episode, and in theory I would imagine this getting annoying after a while. The voice acting and dialogue were spot-on however, and for me at least, didn't become tiresome at any point.
Cutscenes are mostly static images inspersed with animated comic-style segments that look pretty slick. As far as style goes, CoJ hit the mark perfectly in my opinion.
Gameplay is very smooth, I haven't encountered any bugs or glitches yet, and while some segments can be a little difficult, they aren't drawn out to the point of being frustrating (and you aren't forced to listen to the same dialogue over and over if it takes you a few respawns to get past a segment).
The dueling feature was pretty well executed, and a fun diversion from the balls out gunnery.
In terms of graphics, the game is pretty beautiful. Individual textures aren't amazingly detailed if you examine them too closely, but just casually taking in the sights as you blaze along, the game looks excellent and has a gorgeous pallete of colors.
As far as cons go, the only things that really come to mind are the limited weapon selection, and that the campaign mode is a bit short (though it is very replayable, and there are a couple of other modes to mix it up).
Overall, I'd have to give this game a general score of 9/10.

I've long since been a fan of clicker/idle type games. My first adventure into this genre was with Clicker Heroes, which is still a shining example of the genre. Having played that game for well over 2000 hours, I'm always on the lookout for another idle game that I can open up and let play on its own.
Soday Dungeon doesn't disappoint.
The basic mechanic is pretty simple, buy heores, let them do the dungeons for you. You can play it move by move, if you'd like to, and there is certainly an advantage to hand picking each of your moves, to advance to the next round. The thing is, I'm the kind of player who's just too busy to sit at the computer and play round after round of games. I much prefer being able to set it up, then come back to it a while later and see what I've earned.
Soda Dungeon really shines when you start getting to later dungeons and racking up the gold. You can buy upgrades that bring new hero types to your bar, allowing you to assemble an ideal team that will bring you to ever higher dungeon levels. Add to that the loot you gain from dungeons, auto equip the strongest set, and just let the game do the rest for you.
In total, I've spent about $10 on the special heroes you can get in the game. Sure, I could probably grind my way up to unlocking them, later, but again, I like skipping at least a little bit of the grind. I feel the 1 or 2 dollars for each unlock were reasonable asking prices for extending the joy of the game.
Even if you're looking at playing the game absolutely free, there's a reason the game has been praised by so many review outlets. It's simply just a fun game to open up and let run itself. There's depth in all of its mechanics, it has a nice retro graphical charm to it, and it doesn't require you to invest any more time into it than you absolutely want to.
I strongly recommend this game to just about anyone who's a fan of fun games.

I wrote a brief two sentence review for Bastion, (which this game will inevitably be compared to) granting it a recommendation.
This game is nothing like Bastion save for sharing a voice actor (Logan Cunningham), and having beautiful artwork that sets the tone for the game. If you are playing this game looking for more of the same I suggest you watch some videos of actual gameplay before making the purchase, or you may be somewhat disappointed.
The combat doesn’t quite hit that sweet spot of being fast and frantic, nor does it seem to be wholly strategic (enemy movement outside some of the designated “planning” challenges is just too chaotic). I found myself playing with a few move combinations and finding many of them not to my liking. Much of the time in combat you spend running around avoiding enemies waiting for your turn gage to fill back up (which is not too fun).
That being said this game is brilliantly scored, with a wonderful (if less varied) soundtrack. I find the story to be passible, then slowly shifts to interesting, and then drags a bit before a bizarre conclusion that left me with more questions than answers (I thought this was a good thing, by the way).
The ending definitely left me wanting more, and a Recursion Mode (New Game +), which I have played a bit at the time of writing this, did not quite satisfy. I might stick it out and see if there are any tidbits added to the story (there seem to be) but the gameplay is not as engrossing as Bastion’s, and the limiters add more frustration than challenge (unlike Bastion’s idols).
Perhaps I have spent too much of this review comparing Transistor unfairly to Bastion, but it is a solid second effort from Supergiant Games and worth your time, if just for the visuals and story.

Transistor is a masterpiece
-The Gameplay is Great-
The beauty of Transistor's gameplay is its variability--you can play it real-time, turn-based, or even a combination of the two.  I loved Bastion's story, but I couldn't get behind the gameplay because, personally, the combat was frustrating and boring.  With Transistor, the turn-based gameplay allows for some very tactical and thoughtful planning, but allows you to button mash through it like Bastion if that's what you like.  And the highly-customizable loadout lets you tailor the game to your playstyle.
-The Story is Great-
I have heard many people bash the story, but the problem is mainly that the game makes you approach the story on its own terms.  Bastion spoon-fed you its (awesome) story, but Transistor makes you go searching for it.  The theme is, arguably, confusion, and so the story itself is very confusing.  If you are willing to go looking for the story and honestly sit down and think about things, the tale is very rewarding (and I almost want to write a guide explaining aspects I think I have figured out for those who still want answers), but I fear that too few gamers will actually be patient enough to enjoy it.
-The Art is Great-
Great Voice-Acting
Great Visuals
Great Music... Amazing music
Overall, if you are willing to sit down and enjoy the game, I highly reccomend this to you.  I knew going into it that it was short (probably my only complaint), so I took my time.  Too many games I have simply sprinted through at breakneck speed with the MMO mentality of 'get as much done as fast as possible.'  Instead, I paused at every screen, viewed the art, listened to the music (hummed with the music), contemplated the story, and thoroughly ENJOYED the game.  I think that, much like a real piece of art, you can't just rush by it and expect to enjoy it.  I could argue that the Mona Lisa is a horrible painting because it is small and I only looked at it for a few seconds, but so many people would explain that I didn't give the masterpiece a chance.
Give Transistor a chance.

Transistor is a beautiful and breathtaking experience that I'd recommend to anyone who enjoyed Bastion. For those whose first experience with Super Giant Games is Transistor, be prepared for a fantastic five hours, filled with wonderfully emotional music, a great story and plenty of replay value.

Transistor is a game with many, many great aspects, but one inherent flaw that will completely kill the game for many (particularly those who are less gaming-inclined). Let me start with the good bits:
- The soundtrack is superb. It's just a small notch below Bastion's. The vocal pieces are great as well.
- The art style is clear and concise. It suits the game, and the full-screen images and between-area cutscenes are nice.
- The difficulty curve was implemented solidly, and the game includes a "Limiter" system (identical to the Idols in Bastion) which allows you to tweak the difficulty as you see fit by adding various new strengths to the enemies.
- Combat is a bit clunky, but it makes sense within the game's premise. The Turn() system rectifies this by turning Transistor from an action game into a strategy game -- you have a "freeze time" ability which allows you to plan out your next moves and execute them afterwards.
- All of your abilities (called Functions) can be equipped as active abilities (4), upgrades for active abilities (2 each), and passive abilities (4). It can get a bit convoluted and for some reason the menus didn't play well with my XBox controller's analog stick, but other than that it was fine.
The humongous downside to this game is in death. When you die, your most powerful active ability will "overload", rendering it unusable until you have passed enough checkpoints. Essentially, this means that when you die, your character gets significantly less powerful -- and not just for the current encounter, either. Numerous Limiters cause your character to have less MEM (to equip Functions with) and cause those Functions to overload for longer. You could equip a very powerful ability that you don't plan to use to offset this -- but Functions cost MEM to equip, and your MEM is very limited until you approach the maximum value (which won't be until your second playthrough). Even with max MEM, I did not have enough to equip 4 decent actives, 4 passives and all upgrades for each active.
This can be an incredibly frustrating process, and I often found myself dying repeatedly on purpose after the first death just to restart so I wouldn't lose everything for so long -- particularly with 10 Limiters on. If you are not very good at video games in general you will get very frustrated very fast, as the game is horribly unforgiving when it comes to death. I consider myself to be pretty OK at games but I still found this a bit irriating -- tolerable during the normal game but downright ridiculous with 10 Limiters.
This game could easily be a 9/10, but I feel that dying completely soils an otherwise-wonderful experience. I'd be perfectly ok with flat-out dying and having to restart, or any other penalty really -- but not the one they chose. Not sure what they were thinking.
So, all in all,

The single-player adventures are action-packed, and filled with interesting twists and turns that keep the game from being boring (i.e. 'kill everything, kill the boss...rinse, repeat).  Flashbacks based on 'flawed' memory give a humorous angle to the storyline, as does the insertion of sometimes off-the-wall goals (chase the burning fuse before it blows the dynamite!).  Solid fun, for sure!
I can write a whole review on the quickdraw gunfights, but suffice it to say that the mechanic is unique, the situations can be heart-pounding, and speed alone will NOT determine your survival!
2. Historical Accuracy (10/10)
While the game does insert the character as the focal point of all Western history, it still adds the ability to see what 'really' happened via the 'Nuggets' system; factoids collected throughout the maps that give you the REAL story on what happened.  The flavor voice-overs also hint at the true tales (or the accepted legends), and balance out the myth that Silas (your character) pretty much wrote the book on the Wild West.  If you are a history nut, you'll absolutely love this game.  Consider popping a skill point in the skill that allows you to find the Nuggets easier, as well.  Since they give a large chunk of experience, its worth it both for character development as well as historical flavor!
3. Graphics (7/10)
Pretty standard for a shooter, with some 'Borderlands'-style paintbrushing involved on occasion.  The detail of the clothing, buildings, and firearms is eye-catching, however, and make up for any simplistic style choices made by the developers.  All in all, pretty to look at and won't have you longing for an update.
CONCLUSION
A definite 'BUY' amongst the TENtv staff!  Pick it up, and enjoy!

"Call of Juarez: Gunslinger's" central conceit of the unreliable narrator is brilliant and seems so obvious a thing for an action game to do that I'm kind of surprised it's never been done before.  Things can often get silly fast in an action FPS so it's nice to see a game find a creative way to openly acknowledge, and even celebrate, its own silliness.  The fact that the central character might very well be exaggerating his exploits is used for some really fun set pieces in which the world changes before your eyes as the narrator edits himself, alters details, and devises various absurd means of getting himself out of narrative dead ends on the fly.  Likewise, the writing, plotting, and voice acting (I think I recognized a few voices from the "Venture Brothers" in there) are all top notch and the game immediately establishes its own skewed, unique, tone in a completely confident and effortless manner that is rare for a video game.
Unfortunately, the gameplay itself never lives up to the game's narrative.  It basically plays like an old timey shooting gallery in that most action involves you standing stationary in one spot and gunning down gunman after gunman as they pop out from behind rocks or trees or bushes.  You can move around, obviously, but there's very little reason to, so must of the action is just moving from point A to point B, stopping to shoot people, then moving on to point C, and so on (with the occasional annoying QTE sequence).  It's like playing a game of whack-a-mole and it gets old fast as there's very little strategy or skill involved.  Likewise, while the game reskins the enemies for each level, there are, actually, only three or four common enemy types, which means there's next to no variety in gameplay.  Which is a shame, as if this game had a bigger budget and took more time implementing better gameplay to live up to its core ideas it could have been a truly monumental FPS.  As it is, though, it's kind of just a trifle (and its short length, just 5-6 hours, reinforces this).  Maybe worth playing for its innovative approach to narrative, but you definitely won't want to stick around very long for the gameplay.

Coming from someone who loved loved loved Dark Souls (on 360) I highly recommend Dark Souls 2. It's not nearly as amazing as Dark Souls was, but it still holds up in it's own right. It added a lot of features that I really like, and a lot of things that I really hate. Kind of have a love/hate relationship with this game...
Things I like:
-Summoning players works almost every time, it's SUPER easy to have a friend join a game by coordinating where they placed their sign, longest I ever had to wait for a friend was 2 minutes maybe, which is lightning fast compared to the first game.
-Addition of some really cool weapons/spells, there's a lot of variety in some of these things that they added, freshens up all kinds of builds you'd wanna make.
-Dual wielding + power stance, both additions are really cool. Dual wielding is viable, and power stance moves are really cool.
-Covenants. They went pretty creative this time around with covenants, espcially things like Blue Sentinels and Rat Convenant, luring other players to your world just so they get murdered by a dozen rats is classic.
-Armor looks really cool, tons of things you can do for roleplaying or just making your character look bad♥♥♥♥♥
Things I hate:
-Some bosses can be freaking impossible or are just damage sponges that you have to hack at all day, if you're coming directly from Demon's Souls, then you will be shocked at how much abuse some of these f***ers can take (Smelter Demon, Fume Knight, Burnt Ivory King...), really takes the fun out when you have to wail on the boss forever.
-Some bosses are freaking cheap (Darklurker), you know when most of the boss guides out there recommend respec'ing your build to int/faith, then that boss is broken, and the Darklurker is.
-Uninspired boss designs. You've probably heard this one before, but most of the bosses are just tall armored dudes with a sword or something, and others are just♥♥♥♥♥♥easy. Most of the time strafing around the boss leaves you impervious to damage, which isn't fun.
-Enemy attacks home in on you. If an enemy does a multiple move attack, chances are the final move will hit you, regardless if you're in front of them, behind them, or at the 7-11 down the road.
TLDR; I have a lot of problems with this game, but at it's core its Dark Souls. If you love Dark Souls, this is an obvious buy. HOWEVER DO NOT BUY THIS UNTIL SCHOLAR OF FIRST SIN EDITION IS RELEASED. If you do you'll get screwed cuz the old version won't get updated to the new version, which is a big problem I have with FromSoft right now.

TLDR: Factorio is a great game for those who love sandbox "tycoon" style games. You can build assembly lines with a great deal of complexity and automation. It's not without flaws though, the endgame is a bit lacking and there are some rough edges. But for an early access game it's surprisingly feature-packed and, more importantly, stable.
You start out with a very minimal amount of resources and armed with a mining pick you start to mine some ore. You build a smelting oven, to smelt the iron ore into plates. You build and place drills that automate the mining, powered by coal. Conveyer belts are added to take away the hassle of moving around resources manually. You add boilers and steam engines to generate electricity and to reduce the number of places you need to supply coal to. Finally you develop the machines to automate the construction of pretty much every object mentioned before. Powered by automated construction and logistics, your factory makes more and more advanced products until finally you build and launch "the rocket" to win the game.
That's Factorio in a nutshell. It's a "tycoon"-style game with a marvellous level of complexity that can be used. Starting with basic conveyer belts, you can end up with robots flying goods around and various conditions to enable or disable parts of the factory depending on, for example, the amount of a certain resource available. The complexity of the game does mean that it can be helpful to have the Factorio wiki open as a reference manual.
While the game is in early access, it's rather complete and very stable. E.A. does mean that certain systems may receive significant changes in updates. The store page has a statement that the game will not be part of a sale for the foreseeable future and that together with the rounded price (as opposed to most publishers who price their game 1 or 5 cents below a round number to appear more attractive) speaks to the no-nonsense attitude of the developers.
The game does have some rough edges. The endgame is fairly limited. Since almost all of the products produced by your factory are used to produce new machines (there are very few continuous "resource sinks"), once you have unlocked all the tech and setup assembly lines for all products, your factory will essentially only create goods that you no longer need.
There's a combat aspect where the factory is attacked by the local fauna, triggered by pollution generated by the factory, and where the player can move out to destroy enemy spawning bases. Destroying these spawners is required to obtain resources for many lategame research projects. The combat is not terribly interesting, but since attacking spawners can't be automated, it becomes a necessary lategame chore to obtain these highend resources.
Ultimately, these flaws are minor and there's more than enough gameplay to keep you going for a long time, especially if you like to optimize the efficiency of your operation. And with the game still in E.A., there's undoubtebly more to come.
Recommended.

When I started this game, I didn't know what to expect. I started running into the grassy field in front of me, and found nothing, even after 20 minutes. I questioned this "walking simulator", however crouched down, and started walking much slower. A few minutes later, I heard a deer call, and being a novice, simply walked toward it ( I didn't know yet that you are equipped with a tracker that locates where the deer was)  I pulled out my rifle and scoped in to the general vicinity that I believed the deer to be. Shortly, I saw it in my sights. I took careful aim, fired, and completely missed. The deer ran away, and I didn't get a kill that hunt.
All in all, I absolutely adore this game. The gorgeous wild beauty mixed with the enjoyable tracking and hunting of your animal makes this game incredibly fun-for me at least. See, this game isn't a game where you get kills every other minute, this is a game in which up to hours of time climaxes in one moment where you have your animal in your sights. If you blow the shot, you can expect a minimum of 20-30 minutes either tracking the same animal down, or looking for a different beast all together.
Another thing about this game that puts people off is the price tag. Although the game itself is F2P, you have to buy hunting licenses for all animals expect the Whitetail deer.  Furthermore, the only viable way to get equipment such as deer odor (to conceal your scent from the deer's) or a tent (to start your hunt at a place which you placed your tent in previous hunts) alongside rifles, shotguns, and handguns;is to pay occasionally large sums of real money. For some, this is the ultimate turn off. I believe it to be irritating that you have to pay for this content, however I am still content with the game itself.(See what I did there?)

my first opinions of this game were that it started out by trowing you in head first. yes it had tutorials, however these wre thrown straight towards the combat from square one. with that said combat is the only real mechanic of the game and it is incredibly interesting and suprisingly not aggravating to play.
the game can be played like a real-time isometric slasher or as a tactical, turn based puzzle, or both. because of this, it means that if you lose, there are thousands of other pathways you can take that will lead to success, and you need only explore them to progress through the game. the weapon system is also very creative, where attacks can also form upgrades and using unique attributes from each to give you a variety of ways of solving your recent run in with that car-sized hulk you just found.
The art style is very pleasing to the eye, and the music is a sweet mellow lullaby, which very much keeps with the games "non-intense" pace.
The story, however, falls a little short. it leaves you with very little to work with until the first boss and after that, a lot of backstory information that should be explained upront falls into the "in due time" bin. a lot of the game could very easily be compared as an analogy to actual computer directories, rahter than a real, cyberpunk city. with that said, the other points often draw your focus away from this and make the game a very good play in their own right.
especially the music.
