Factorio is a game about building infrastructure and completely automating everything.  You start with the basics as any building and survival game would and work your way up the ladder researching technologies and ultimately advancing to the point at which you launch a rocket into space.
What Factorio does well is keep you playing.  The map is procedurally generated and you have options to affect how it is generated at the start of the map.  There are multiple ways to play currently, a campaign, tutorial, a sandbox, and a few challenge missions where you must meet the objectives before time runs out.
From conveyor belts to UAVs, you can produce, build, and transport everything.  Locomotives are mainly used when you need to get something somewhere fast due to a vast distance between one base and another.  As you continue to mine out the resources you will be expanding and locomotives take this burden off of your shoulders.  As you upgrade technologies you get faster conveyor belts that you can simply drop down on top of the existing belt.  This same concept applies to older furnaces and chests.
The sheer amount of things you can do while trying to expand and improve your existing infrastructure is awesome.  Add mods to the game and you have even more options.  Mods are going to be what makes this game from great to awesome.
Currently, there are only a few ways to generate power until the developers add more power sources.  Solar power and steam from water are the two primary sources.  This can look a bit weird in late game when you have solar panels everywhere and steam is still powering your entire infrastructure.  At some point, I hope they add fuel/diesel generators and nuclear power.  From what I have researched, fuel generators should be getting put in.
On other topics, the music is great and the sound effects are about what you would expect from a factory style game.  Graphics obviously were not the objective in the game so the top down 2D is what you have to work with adding in zoom when you need to get a bigger or smaller view.  The various peices in which you use to build infrastructure all make sense for the most part.  They place down easily and logically and certain buildings will show you where to bring in your pipes.  The only difficult part is learning how everything works together to make the best factory system you can.
Whle building you will notice you can make cars, tanks, guns, better guns, turrets (both laser and bullet), as well as land mines and grenades.  These are to fend off the critters known as biters and spiters that expand their nests.  You can destroy their nests once you get appropriate gear but beware, this apparently makes them mad and they get even more aggressive as if the slow level of incrementing numbers wasn't already something you didn't want to deal with.
I would recommend Factorio.  It does several things well and is a throwback to what video games used to be before investors and greed took over. Borderlands 2 is the pinnacle of a shoot and loot game. With many classes and infinitley many guns, you will never be lost for reasons to play.
Graphics: This games art style is simply unique and well executed. The cell shaded style of the world brings out all of the best in environments and makes the world truly a joy to look at. It also helps to bring about the grit of the gameplay.
Gameplay: The way guns handle in borderlands is amazing. You can encounter everything from a regular assault rifle to a shotgun that shoots swords upon your enemies. The class system varies gameplay even more with 5+ classes and 3 skill trees each, they simply add more value to the game as a whole.
Story: Overall the story does not really grab players BUT that does not mean it is terrible. The reason you will play through the story is for the characters. With villans like Handsome Jack that are zany and insane, and playable characters like a psycho you will always want to push on so that you can hear the next quote from any of the characters.
Overall, Borderlands 2 is the perfect game for those who like interesting crazy characters, great gunplay, and not too valuable a story. It has been my benchmark shooter since its release and continues to be to this day.

What seems like a casual RPG that could quite easily milk you for money, comes a fab game with surprising depth (albeit, not in the battles- though this is not a bad thing) and you don't need to spend a penny.
Graphics can be a bit ugly, especially when shrunk down for a smaller window. Some of the SFX are un-godly, and being "retro" is no excuse.
However, once you get into upgrading, working out how to spend upgrades, finding that one item you need to make your next run better, deciding on how to build your team, and so on- you want to go further.
You can turn on auto-combat, but this only works when your fighting easier levels. You'll need to control it yourself to take on tougher levels. And, you get more money from later levels. So you can't just coast on auto-combat alone. You can grind, but the game usually gives you enough to make your grinding much shorter if you build your team smarter.
Follow some of the Steam guides to make your experience a little easier- but I'm seriously tempted to throw money the devs way for this. Great time sink.

This is a truly wonderful game with a wonderful story.
The gameplay is the easy part to talk about. It's a hybrid turn based strategy and action game, where you have a sword that charges up and lets you use a bunch of big hits. It's not terribly difficult in its base setting, but if you turn on Limiters (which are like the god statues in Bastion) as you get them then the game will keep you on your toes. The enemies aren't as deep or challenging as they were in Bastion, but you have a large variety of customizable attacks and bringing down a big pack with an innovative combo is quite satisfying.
The story meanwhile is a boldly told and rich tale. But it's a story that's going to demand that you're giving it your whole brain's attention. You have to combine what you read in the function biographies with the Transistor's ongoing narration with the little news bulletins you keep seeing everywhere. The motivations of the antagonists, along with the nature of the apocalypse that the city is going through, are secrets that the game expects you to patiently piece together. But if you give the narrative the effort it's asking you to give it, you find a really rich and well realized world. You won't really get what happened until the end, but that's what makes the game so rewarding.
Logan Cunningham is, of course, the voice of this game, but unlike the Bastion there are other characters here and I have to say that added a lot. Though really, much of the tale is told through artwork and music. The gradual twisting of the vibrant city into grey nothingness mirrors is quite striking.
In any case, this is an utterly fantastic game. Acquire it promptly.

Amazing game.  The art direction is beautiful, both in the graphics and the overall design of the game.  Even the music is amazing (so much so that I spent some time just listening to it in the various areas).  All the small attention to details in this game really shine, and help immerse a world unlike many I've seen.  They walk a line between fantasy and technology that is remarkable.  You will find all sorts of tech lingo sprinkled in - in fact your abilities themselves are called "functions" and when you pair them with other functions for augmentation, they call them "subroutines".
The gameplay is also a lot of fun, and highly addicting.  It's a lot like a dungeon crawler in the way the skills work, but the real shining point is the fact that you can plan out your attack tactically using a time-stopping function called "turn()", which allows you to setup your next moves and execute them almost instantaneously.  In addition to this, there is a surprising amount of flexibility in the way you can play.  You have 4 slots main abilities, which can be any function, and each of these main abilities can have 2 augmentation functions (again, which can be any function).  In addition, you also have 2 passive slots which can be set to any function.  Depending on the arangement, you get different effects.  This allows you to play however you like - sniping from long range, getting up close and personal, specializing in area of effect, or even charming baddies or summoning allies.
Finally, the game flows seamlessly in and out of "cutscenes" and actual gameplay beautifully.  The story is told in small, digestable chunks, rather than long winded cutscenes or forcing you to read countless pages of lore to understand what is going on.  The storytelling doesn't feel forced at all, but instead feels really natural.
Overall, this game has me hooked, and I highly recommend it for someone looking for something unique and memorable, as well as entertaining and easy to jump into.

However, that doesn't mean it's a bad story; it just gives you enough to pick your curiosity and leaves a lot to your imagination.

Interesting story/setting.  Combat plays more like a puzzle, with the puzzle being as hard as you decide to make it using optional settings (limiters) you gain through the game.  Single playthrough took me 8 hours, but you get the option for a NG+ that also changes the dialogue you experience the second time through; which gives another perspective on the narrative.  As expected from Supergiant, the art and soundtrack are excellent.  The game at times can feel like walking through the work of Gustav Klimt.  The soundtrack is a largely ambient set of aucoutic guitars and subtle electronic puncutated by vocal hums.  The game also features a couple full tracks with lovely lyrics.
The negatives for me were related to the amount of menu activity.  Pieces of backstory and character information are hidden in skills you use, and using the skills in different ways unlocks more of that information.  In order to change how your skills are arranged (to use them differently), you have to visit a menu and shuffle things around between most combat sequences.  It's not a big deal, but slows down the feel of progression and the pace of your play.  It feels tedius.  Granted, you could skip the unlocking of this information and stick to a skill arrangement your comfortable with.  Additionally, some skill arrangements work better for some fights than others, and you don't have any way to predict what the next fight will be, so you usually have to fail the combat sequence to go readjust for the fight.
When you're out of the menu's and fighting, you do appreciate the maleability of the skills.  Using any single skill as either an active, augmenting, or passive ability and over a dozen skills, you can create what feels like an endlessly diverse series of offensive arrangments.  Really cool.
Overall, a very positive experience.  Definitely worth the $19.99 price tag on release.

Factorio is a game about building infrastructure and completely automating everything.  You start with the basics as any building and survival game would and work your way up the ladder researching technologies and ultimately advancing to the point at which you launch a rocket into space.
What Factorio does well is keep you playing.  The map is procedurally generated and you have options to affect how it is generated at the start of the map.  There are multiple ways to play currently, a campaign, tutorial, a sandbox, and a few challenge missions where you must meet the objectives before time runs out.
From conveyor belts to UAVs, you can produce, build, and transport everything.  Locomotives are mainly used when you need to get something somewhere fast due to a vast distance between one base and another.  As you continue to mine out the resources you will be expanding and locomotives take this burden off of your shoulders.  As you upgrade technologies you get faster conveyor belts that you can simply drop down on top of the existing belt.  This same concept applies to older furnaces and chests.
The sheer amount of things you can do while trying to expand and improve your existing infrastructure is awesome.  Add mods to the game and you have even more options.  Mods are going to be what makes this game from great to awesome.
Currently, there are only a few ways to generate power until the developers add more power sources.  Solar power and steam from water are the two primary sources.  This can look a bit weird in late game when you have solar panels everywhere and steam is still powering your entire infrastructure.  At some point, I hope they add fuel/diesel generators and nuclear power.  From what I have researched, fuel generators should be getting put in.
On other topics, the music is great and the sound effects are about what you would expect from a factory style game.  Graphics obviously were not the objective in the game so the top down 2D is what you have to work with adding in zoom when you need to get a bigger or smaller view.  The various peices in which you use to build infrastructure all make sense for the most part.  They place down easily and logically and certain buildings will show you where to bring in your pipes.  The only difficult part is learning how everything works together to make the best factory system you can.
Whle building you will notice you can make cars, tanks, guns, better guns, turrets (both laser and bullet), as well as land mines and grenades.  These are to fend off the critters known as biters and spiters that expand their nests.  You can destroy their nests once you get appropriate gear but beware, this apparently makes them mad and they get even more aggressive as if the slow level of incrementing numbers wasn't already something you didn't want to deal with.
I would recommend Factorio.  It does several things well and is a throwback to what video games used to be before investors and greed took over.  While there are a few missing elements still, such as the fuel generator, nuclear power, naval, etc., I think the game is great.  Rarely will you have a game that you sit down to play and wonder where the last four hours went.
Pros:
A great expansive list of things to build and design
Great music
Large replayability due to procedural maps
Always something to do or improve
Mods
Server support, either local or off-site
Arial logistic, repair, and construction robots for when you run out of room on land
A tank
A ATV
Curcuit system for designing latches that trigger on IF,THEN statements
Cons:
Not enough energy sources yet
No naval
That I know of, no helicopters or personal arial transport
Learning curve for those that want things spoon fed to them is high

A disappointing regression in level design and mechanics, salvaged by having the best pvp and widest build viability of the series. Almost every argument regarding DS2's quality I've witnessed seems to come down to PVP and non-PVP players talking past each other on these two pillars. Supposedly the keyboard controls are hugely improved from the original, but I'm not crazy enough to try.
The interconnected nature of DS1's world up until acquiring the Lordvessel has given way to a more distinct and discrete method in this game. There's the Lava Level™, the Forest Level™, the Castle Level™, and so on. Combined with the bosses being Large Humanoid Wielding A Sword far more often in the previous game, there's a palpable lack of originality to be had here. From what I recall of playing SotFS on PS3, none of these concerns were addressed.
My biggest gripe with this game mechanically is that invincibility frames are now tied to a new stat (ADP) and your base i-frames are a fraction of what they were in DS1. Perhaps it was the case that dodging was too forgiving in DS1 (or at least, I always felt that long breaks from DS1 didn't hurt my timing as much as they should), but only in DS2 have I seen myself take damage from an attack that clearly did not even graze my character model. The wealth of gifs, webms, and youtube montages of this happening to people managed to hit a temporary meme-status and shouldn't be hard to find. Add in the fact that now almost every enemy has infinite stamina and can perpetually turn on a dime, and I found myself cheesing my way through the game in a way that rewarded patience for tedious playing rather than skill.
My review reads like a lot of other people's, particularly those who don't dabble in PVP, but where I diverge is that I won't even tack on a "it's still pretty good though". I didn't like Dark Souls 2 and I don't recommend playing it. I will reach for another playthrough of the first game fifty more times before giving this one another look.

Tree of Savior doesn't have the depth of most MMORPGs, however what it does offer is really well executed. The art style and soudtrack are absolutely amazing. One of the main reasons I've spent so much time playing this game is because of the environments. There are so many unique maps to explore with clever and quirky monsters throughout. The music is narrow in style but great to listen to while playing the game. I'll even listen to a playlist of the music on YouTube when I'm driving or working.
The gameplay doesn't offer a lot of variety, however the combat is very satisfying, the boss fights are plentiful and interseting, and the class customization options are second to none. It's best to think of the gameplay in ToS like an OARPG like Path of Exile or Marvel Heroes rather than an MMORPG like Rift or World of Warcraft. If you approach this game expecting the latter you'll likely be disappointed. You're not going to find the crafting systems, mini games, or large scale group content of a true MMORPG but you will find the kind of repetitve yet satisfying, combat-centric gameplay with plenty of class customization and experimentation that is so common to the OARPG genre.
I've reached level 80 on one class and played all the others at least to 20 and I've enjoyed my time playing these first three weeks since launch. I plan on continuing to play for the foreseeable future. The community has been okay- what you would expect from an MMO- and the cash shop is definitely agreeable. There's really little there that you will feel compeled to buy and you should have no problem playing for free should you chose to do so. I've purchased a few extra bank storage slots so far but that's it. Nevertheless, I will be buying more cash shop currency because I like the game and want to buy a few more convenience and cosmetic items that are offered.
Tree of Savior is a niche title that isn't going to appeal to everyone, but what the game sets out to be and do I think it accomplishes. If you like the OARPG genre but are looking for something other than grimdark and superheroes, I think this game is worth trying.

TL:DR at bottom
This is a review from someone who has not played the majority of the game and is still in the process of levelling, so if you're looking for some details for endgame content you might want to skip this review.
Review:
The game brings an odd mist of nostalgia from Maple Story where you had to pre plan your build in order to min max and had to spend tons of time grinding but yet the grind is done in a way where it doesn't feel tedious.
The class system is where the game tries to draw in its players, there are a large variety of builds created by mixing classes together so you can enjoy a play style you like however that is also a big downfall, if you specifically wanted to play a druid you would have to trudge through grinding a cleric to level 170ish just to see if you like the spells, this can cause a lot of detraction from the game as people don't want to spend 100's of hours to become the class they want. Having said that in my opinion the classes are all different enough that I can enjoy the experience of levelling just about any of them.
The combat is simply fun, I don't know what it is about it but it just feels great to fight the enemies. Once again it's kinda like a Diablo styled combat version of Maple Story.
You always feel like your progressing because your always levelling up and working towards getting to your next class or circle, rather than the end game being where the fun starts the fun is levelling.
There is a mostly cosmetic premium shop, the "token" however does give some small benefits such as more move speed and trades but can be purchased from the auction house for the standard game currency.
The OST is amazing, bosses especially have epic tracks which almost make it sad if they die too quickly as I would gladly listen to their theme all day.
The art style is one which could live like that forever its not limited by the engine it is exactly how the devs wanted it, cheerful but not distracting.
The game seems to have quite linear levelling options, all level brackets only seem to have 2 choices for maps which you can grind or quest in depending on your starting city.
As with all MMO's there are a lot of gold spammers and bots however the devs do seem to be actually working on resolving this unlike some games. (Blade and Soul)
Due to how you acquire stats / skill points which can't be reset unless you make a new character (Skills can currently be reset through premium currency) it is not an entirely noob friendly game, I had a friend who was levelling a mage and put quite a few points into Dex because he thought dodge would be more useful to him.
You can't level yourself down to help lower level characters and if you're more than 20 levels out of range of someone experience earned is halved, I understand this is to stop power levelling and such but it's annoying if you have to have a main character and a character for when friends are on due to work etc.
Rant:
I dislike having to post a review, however this game is getting a lot of unworthy negative feedback regarding the "F2P" aspect as of the moment, People don't seem to realise that you are paying to get into a beta version of the game and you are getting a month's head start along with relative premium currency. You could alternatively just wait until the 28th where the game will be free to play for all.

Combat.

progression.
CONS:
Finding a class you want to level.
Not entirely noob friendly.
No levelling down to play with friends.
Choices of areas to level in.

Transistor is an artistic cyberpunk gem that champions the expression 'less is more'. Yes, the rumours are true, this is a short game - but so was Portal, and I'll go as far to say that Transistor sits next to it on the shelf labelled 'games I cannot comapre to any other'.
Playing as Red, a singer in the cyberpunk city of Cloudbank who has had her voice stolen. Not only that, but she's been landed with the Transistor, a greatsword-like weapon that has a stranger's voice and mind trapped inside of it. With hostile, territorial enemies known as the Process taking over Cloudbank, and the mysterious Camerata seemingly behind it all - it's up to Red and the Transistor to get back her voice, and get some answers. It's story that had me gripped from the start, with charismatic voice-acting delivering me from start to finish with a smile.
Half puzzler, half action-RPG, Transistor's 'Turn()' mechanic lets players pre-plan the timing, positioning and execution of functions (skills). To compensate - the enemies aren't forgiving, making battles that are framed more like puzzles. This doesn't so much as invite the player to make tactical decisions, but straight up tells them that if they don't think before they act? Their HP is hitting 0. Still running my second play-through, and I'm still finding new and wicked ways to mix and match skills.
Is Transistor short? Yes. Should you buy it? Yes.

After playing Bastion I simply had to take a look at Transistor and let me tell you: I am not disappointed.
The story starts off quite confusing but bits and pieces of story are scattered around the game world and add up to a disturbing picture of a dystopia where no one is ever really free. As with Bastion, Transistor's story takes some twists and turns, though not as much as Bastion's.
The combat system was something completely new for me, mixing real-time and round-based gameplay elements to something extremely fun to play around with. With a controller at hand walking around and/or fighting feels smooth and quick. Effects are well animated and smashing enemies to pieces with a well placed PFUMPSHSHSHSH is very very satisfying. Level progression and combat both is well balanced and fun.
With the sound design it was a little different. While the effects and environmental sounds feel a little sterile - which seems to be intented so the music is in sync with the game world - the real beauty lies in the rich background music and songs. If you have the time, stop and listen for a moment. Also (Warning: small spoiler ahead) the main character is able to humm songs of which many are a reward to certain challenges. Again, worth listening to if you want to take the time.
As I stated above, the effects are well animated and the rest of the graphics feel just right for this type of game. I like the design as well as the sounds design for the main character and her "companion". Was a little different to what I am used to in games these days, maybe because I haven't played adventure games in a while. Having said that, Transistor is as much of an Adventure game, as it is an action game, an rpg or a strategy game. Supergiantgames tried hard to make this game stick out from the crowd and I believe they have achieved that.
If you are looking for a fazit:
Worth spending money on. Hours of gameplay, an intricate story, different yet fun gameplay, sounds design really worth mentioning and art-like graphics.
P.S.: If you haven't played Bastion yet, you should do that now.

theHunter is one of the most enjoyable and most beautiful hunting games available at this time IMO of course. The realistic aspect is not to far extreme where you find yourself waiting a whole day to bag and tag a single animal, but at the same time not at all arcade-y where you can gun down 5 deer in a matter of seconds. The pace of this game is rather rewarding is the sense of accomplishment when it come to the hunt.
The main complaint that many have is there price structure. Yes, it can get expensive purchasing all that is available for this game. In fact If I recall correctly that if you happen to buy everything all at once (not including consumables and a ammo), you are looking at about a $600 price tag.  Yes, a lot of money, but at the same time compare that to Train Simulator 2015 which holds a price tag well over double of theHunter for all of its DLC. This game should not be considered Free-To-Play, but rather Free-To-Test or simple know it as a Demo since you are only allowed to hunt 1 species of deer (Mule Deer) on 1 reserve (Loggers Point). Also some have stated this is a Pay-To-Win game. Far from it IMO. Buying the ingame equipment and such doesnt make you a better hunter than everyone else. You just have more options to hunt and hunt with. Purchasing items in this game is like buying DLC for any other game in the long run. You do get to keep them forever minus consumables, but those can even be purchased with the ingame currency, gm$ which are earned buy completing ingame missions.
At this current time, theHunter is being offered on the Steam Holiday Sale (2014) for 20% off on bundles.  If you have any  form of interest and are willing to support a game that actually works vs. the latest and greatest AAA titles that havent been, now would be a great time to purchase. The largest bundle is currently going for 39.99.  This includes an annual membership that alone cost 35 dollars during the normal time of the year, but also included in this bundle is $85 worth of gear that will allow you to hunt everything and anything under the sun within this game.  Even when the sale lets up, a price tag of 49.99 is not bad. $35 for the annual and $15  for the additional $85 worth of gear.
All and all, I recommend this game to those that enjoy a good hunt and are will to invest a little money (the bundle) into it as you would any other game title that isnt listed as Free-To-Play. After all... games dont make themselves.

I have been playing the original Rome, and Medieval 2 for some time now, those were my first 2 total war games, and I love them, but I'm fastly getting close to equal the hours I have put to those games playing Rome 2, and that is because I find this game very different to them, yet, amazing.

You can find some amazing mods made by the community, from small ones to improve your gameplay and experience, textures to improve graphics, and complex yet high quality overhauls like Divide et Impera.

I recommend this game, I don't support what SEGA did here, again, but the game in itself is great. If you can, get it on sale, because the DLC is just not worth the whole price, I just whish this evil market strategy changes in the future.

This is a sequel that such a great game as Dark Souls deserved. Locations are magnificent (sunny and peaceful little village Majula, dragons' nest in the mountains, old fortress in the middle of the sea, a castle consumed by lava, etc. - all of them are beautiful and gorgeous), the story keeps up with the first one, enemies are even stronger and still very creative (living statues, dragons and full grown viverns, giant sentinels, ciclops, even giant themselves), and Fromm finally managed to fix some major issues of DS: first of all, using a keyboard to play does not look like self-torturing anymore; maintaining humanity now makes sense not only in terms of coop gameplay - you literally lose a pretty decent chunk of health every time you die and resurrect as a hollow (and it is now not that easy to farm humanity figures); cooping is also easier because there is a new ring that allows the bearer to connect only to the ones that bear it and chose the same god and the level cap has been removed (well, not entirely, but it is enough to connect lvl 40 and 200 according to thier soul level)
The only disadvantage is that it is much easier than the first one. First of all, all the bonfires are accessible just from the start. It is not a bad change, it makes you more mobile (not mentioning the fact that you can level up only by speaking to the special NPC located in the local hub - Majula) but at the cost of the unity of the world and loss of experience of getting the teleportation perk in DS (it had been very rewarding to acquire that Soul Vessel for the first time).
Finally, in the first game, to return to human form you had to go to the bonfire. In DS2 you can use the humanity figure just everywhere. And again, while that deliveres some new possibilities, it just doesn't make sense to make a feature when you lose a chank of max health whenever you die and become hollow and then allow you to undo this everywhere you want.
Anyway, it is definitely worth playing and every fan of DS1 and Demon Souls should have it. Oh, and do not forget to get all the DLCs - they really improve an experience of DS2 (the bosses are challenging, regular mobs are tough, you even are forced to think strategically through the level, and locations are just marvellous - but i am not going to reveal too much).

Okay, first things first: I know it says I have less than two hours on this game, but that's because I usually play this game without internet. With that said, I'll get on with the actual review.
The short version:
If you like visual novels and crying, and you're fine with the giant eyes, play this.
If you've watched the anime and liked it, PLAY THIS. IT HAS SO MUCH MORE CONTENT.
The long version:
I bought CLANNAD during a sale earlier this year. I'd watched the first season of the anime, but I wanted to finish the original version in its entirety before finishing the anime.
And it was worth it.
Almost every route follows the same pattern: a bit of a rough start, then everything slowly but surely improves. But just like with a rollercoaster, right when you reach the top, a huge downward plummet. Right when it seems like there's no hope, though, a light shines through. Usually, the endings aren't perfectly happy, but that isn't how life works anyway. It might seem a bit repetitive, but somehow it never gets old. Afterstory also follows this pattern, although the plummet is even worse. Won't explain why, to avoid spoilers. Just see for yourself. I'll say this, though... they really know how to make the visual novel genre work for the story itself.
But anyway. The writing of this game is superb. The fellas at Key really know how to get you attached to a character, so that they can cause you extreme pain when they thoroughly break them. When the game isn't actively torturing you, it can also be very entertaining. There are a lot of hilarious, perverted, and usually both, scenes. I'm actually surprised at how many lewd jokes and scenes they threw into this. A lot of then weren't in the anime, so if you're here checking out the game because you liked the anime, lemme tell you, you'll find a lot of great content here. No hentai, though, (un)fortunately. There are also a lot of references to other media. Fuko's Doraemon carving, the stuffed Snoopy the gang were trying to get for Kotomi, Akio's Gundam collection... the list goes on. The art style might not be agreeable to some, but if you find it bearable, I urge you to stick with this for the sake of the story.
If there's one thing that I don't like about the visual novel, though, it's how some routes seem forever unlinked. I mean... although some characters seem to be all right even if you ignore their route, it seems some you're just abandoning. For example, the cat. It seems Misae will find out in both her and Tomoyo's route, but what about Nagisa's? Will the canon path have the cat forever unrevealed? And Kotomi.... will she NEVER meet her only childhood friend again? I just feel bad for them. I guess that's one thing the anime has over the visual novel.
All in all, though, it's a solid visual novel that knows how to get to you. Definitely recommended for anyone who likes VNs.

Interesting story/setting.  Combat plays more like a puzzle, with the puzzle being as hard as you decide to make it using optional settings (limiters) you gain through the game.  Single playthrough took me 8 hours, but you get the option for a NG+ that also changes the dialogue you experience the second time through; which gives another perspective on the narrative.  As expected from Supergiant, the art and soundtrack are excellent.  The game at times can feel like walking through the work of Gustav Klimt.  The soundtrack is a largely ambient set of aucoutic guitars and subtle electronic puncutated by vocal hums.  The game also features a couple full tracks with lovely lyrics.
The negatives for me were related to the amount of menu activity.  Pieces of backstory and character information are hidden in skills you use, and using the skills in different ways unlocks more of that information.  In order to change how your skills are arranged (to use them differently), you have to visit a menu and shuffle things around between most combat sequences.  It's not a big deal, but slows down the feel of progression and the pace of your play.  It feels tedius.  Granted, you could skip the unlocking of this information and stick to a skill arrangement your comfortable with.  Additionally, some skill arrangements work better for some fights than others, and you don't have any way to predict what the next fight will be, so you usually have to fail the combat sequence to go readjust for the fight.
When you're out of the menu's and fighting, you do appreciate the maleability of the skills.  Using any single skill as either an active, augmenting, or passive ability and over a dozen skills, you can create what feels like an endlessly diverse series of offensive arrangments.  Really cool.
Overall, a very positive experience.  Definitely worth the $19.99 price tag on release.

Transistor is an artistic cyberpunk gem that champions the expression 'less is more'. Yes, the rumours are true, this is a short game - but so was Portal, and I'll go as far to say that Transistor sits next to it on the shelf labelled 'games I cannot comapre to any other'.
Playing as Red, a singer in the cyberpunk city of Cloudbank who has had her voice stolen. Not only that, but she's been landed with the Transistor, a greatsword-like weapon that has a stranger's voice and mind trapped inside of it. With hostile, territorial enemies known as the Process taking over Cloudbank, and the mysterious Camerata seemingly behind it all - it's up to Red and the Transistor to get back her voice, and get some answers. It's story that had me gripped from the start, with charismatic voice-acting delivering me from start to finish with a smile.
Half puzzler, half action-RPG, Transistor's 'Turn()' mechanic lets players pre-plan the timing, positioning and execution of functions (skills). To compensate - the enemies aren't forgiving, making battles that are framed more like puzzles. This doesn't so much as invite the player to make tactical decisions, but straight up tells them that if they don't think before they act? Their HP is hitting 0. Still running my second play-through, and I'm still finding new and wicked ways to mix and match skills.
Is Transistor short? Yes. Should you buy it? Yes.

Factorio is a game about building infrastructure and completely automating everything.  You start with the basics as any building and survival game would and work your way up the ladder researching technologies and ultimately advancing to the point at which you launch a rocket into space.
What Factorio does well is keep you playing.  The map is procedurally generated and you have options to affect how it is generated at the start of the map.  There are multiple ways to play currently, a campaign, tutorial, a sandbox, and a few challenge missions where you must meet the objectives before time runs out.
From conveyor belts to UAVs, you can produce, build, and transport everything.  Locomotives are mainly used when you need to get something somewhere fast due to a vast distance between one base and another.  As you continue to mine out the resources you will be expanding and locomotives take this burden off of your shoulders.  As you upgrade technologies you get faster conveyor belts that you can simply drop down on top of the existing belt.  This same concept applies to older furnaces and chests.
The sheer amount of things you can do while trying to expand and improve your existing infrastructure is awesome.  Add mods to the game and you have even more options.  Mods are going to be what makes this game from great to awesome.
Currently, there are only a few ways to generate power until the developers add more power sources.  Solar power and steam from water are the two primary sources.  This can look a bit weird in late game when you have solar panels everywhere and steam is still powering your entire infrastructure.  At some point, I hope they add fuel/diesel generators and nuclear power.  From what I have researched, fuel generators should be getting put in.
On other topics, the music is great and the sound effects are about what you would expect from a factory style game.  Graphics obviously were not the objective in the game so the top down 2D is what you have to work with adding in zoom when you need to get a bigger or smaller view.  The various peices in which you use to build infrastructure all make sense for the most part.  They place down easily and logically and certain buildings will show you where to bring in your pipes.  The only difficult part is learning how everything works together to make the best factory system you can.
Whle building you will notice you can make cars, tanks, guns, better guns, turrets (both laser and bullet), as well as land mines and grenades.  These are to fend off the critters known as biters and spiters that expand their nests.  You can destroy their nests once you get appropriate gear but beware, this apparently makes them mad and they get even more aggressive as if the slow level of incrementing numbers wasn't already something you didn't want to deal with.
I would recommend Factorio.  It does several things well and is a throwback to what video games used to be before investors and greed took over.  While there are a few missing elements still, such as the fuel generator, nuclear power, naval, etc., I think the game is great.  Rarely will you have a game that you sit down to play and wonder where the last four hours went.
Pros:
A great expansive list of things to build and design
Great music
Large replayability due to procedural maps
Always something to do or improve
Mods
Server support, either local or off-site
Arial logistic, repair, and construction robots for when you run out of room on land
A tank
A ATV
Curcuit system for designing latches that trigger on IF,THEN statements
Cons:
Not enough energy sources yet
No naval
That I know of, no helicopters or personal arial transport
Learning curve for those that want things spoon fed to them is high

No More Room in Hell is a standalone Half Life 2 mod which operates on realism and cooperation. With these attributes in mind, the game is quite unforgiving yet makes for a fun experience. Players looking for a run-gun tear 'em up zombie shooter like Left For Dead and many other contemporaries will not find that in the world of NMRiH, it is far too dark and brutal in its gameplay.
The game is compromised of developer and community made scenarios, of which there are two kinds. NMO's are scenario maps which involve an objective. The players (team of 8 or less) must reach a certain extraction point by a specified time or via certain conditions to win the scenario. The converse is NMS's, which are survival scenarios based on one location where the team must defend certain tactical points.
All servers are player-based, but due to the incredible population of this game this is not an issue. There are hundreds of servers to jump into, playing dozens of maps at any given moment. This sometimes results in ping issues, as the playerbase extends from the US to China both ways around, but Americans will find no difficulty finding dozens of +/-100, 100MS servers to enjoy. Euro's have plenty as well, and for Russian/Asian players, options are more limited, but still present.
The gameplay thrives on its unforgiving nature. Like most zombie games, there are certain standards. A particular way of fighting to gurantee you never get hit once, headshots are instant-kills, your walk pace is faster than all zombies... many of the usual hallmarks of the modern zombie gaming industry. Yet even one deviation, miscalculation, or faulty key press can result in a bite leading to infection. When you start with your team, theoretically there is no reason why any player shouldn't make it to the end without a single bite.
Yet somewhere along the way you find yourself in a dark alley, surrounded by 10 zeds closing in your corner. Your gun is out, you wasted all of our ammo getting a zombie off of your teammate who ended up being bit and turning anyway. Your're getting tired, and your character can't keep swinging. One of the other survivors has a zombie on his back eating him, the other in front of you is running away from it all towards freedom. Where did it all go wrong?
With this in mind, the game has a steep learning curve. New players often times find themselves overwhelmed by the difficulty of the game, and get discouraged. Melee combat is necessary but remains tricky even for experienced gamers partially due to its bugginess and the rugged stamina system.
Guns are fun to play with and have their own interesting mechanics, same as the melee system. The inventory system is unique, and teaches resource management splendidly.
Teamplay is essential, in this regard playing with random's can be incredibly frustrating at times (especially due to the multinational nature of the community) , but playing with friends or on servers near you will help with this.
Pros:
+ Gritty, Realistic gameplay
+ Rewarding combat and weapons
+ Cooperative, play with friends
+ Enormous community
+ FREE, zero, zero, zero buy-ins!
+ Light-weight and easy to run on ANY pc
+ That quaint little HL2 engine you'll recognize
+ Loads of acheivments
+ Active developers
Cons:
- Graphics have not aged too well, the game is not for graph♥♥♥♥♥s
- Steep learning curve, combat is tough to get into, game takes high skill to succeed
- Random players on random servers
- Limited gameplay, all scenarios are linear.
All in all, get it! It's not the game for everyone, but I highly recommend it to this who have read this review and still want to try.

Imo, Total War : Rome II Emperor Edition is one of the best total war games i've ever played. The era was amazing playing as the Romans,the Macedonians,the Egyptians and many other factions. The game was pretty ambitious but I can't help but feel as if some parts were rushed.
Pros:
+Epic era
The rise of Rome,the fall of Carthage,the fall of the Egyptians,the era was great for any classical history lover.
+Decent graphics
The graphics could have been better but they were pretty decent and added greatly to the classical world feel.
+Multiple factions
The game had many great factions that I loved to try most of them. The Romans,the Carthagnians,the Egyptians,the Macedonians and others.
+Map
The map size was awesome. It complimented the huge size of Europe, North Africa and Western Asia. The new province system was pretty good with the province capital and the minor towns.
Cons:
-DLCs
The amount of "culture packs" you can buy for the game is too much. There should be no such thing as a culture pack. To play with the Spartans or the Athenians, I have to pay freakin money. The blood and gore dlc should already have been implemented, i don't know how they expect me to pay extra for blood in a
game.
-Turn times
Turn times took too long, if the turn wait is long enough that i can play a game on my phone till it finishes, that's too long.
-Poor optimisation
For the graphics, the game is really poorly optimised.
-Rushed
I felt like some aspects of the game were rushed. The civil war thing is very shallow and dumb, the internal politics were too little and had no real effect, they would have been great if CA had worked some more on them.
Tl;dr :
The game was great, but the greedy company sells half the game and half of it as DLCs. Since i love the era i would definitely recommend it but at the same time, I don't want to recommend it because of CA. Buy it on sale.

This game when if first came out was launched in a very incomplete state, the Co-op campaign was completely bugged out, many of the essential features like the ability to throw pila while stationary were completely missing and the battle ai was so damn drunk you could easily walk around them and capture the city square without them even noticing.
But now since CA did a major facelift on this game I think I can say that this game is for the most part complete.
Some of the things they added from the last iterations
-The ability to view the entire campaign and battle maps by using the tab key
-Added greater diversity of game machanics e.g. melee attack, armor penetration, health.
-It's much easier than before to keep a coherant line you can even assign subordinate ai commanders to take over and soft lock formations.
-The amount playable and non-playable factions in the game is both refreshing and even somewhat overwhelming and each one brings with it it's own unique playstyle adding months of replabiliy. Like for instance if you play a Germanic faction you must try to create a coalition in order to gain power.
-As always the graphics for this game is beyond astonishing especially if you have a decent computer. You can make out even small details like the insignias on units to the small projectiles being thrown throughout the battlefiels.
However, some cons that still need to be adressed in my opinion
-The family tree and political system in this is a complete joke, most of the things you really have to worry about is just the commander traits and army traditions.
-Compared to other games like EUIV, the diplomacy options have improved but still lack big options.
-Many of the on map resources seem to be too common to have any real value. Unlike Shogun 2, most of the buildings in Rome 2 can be constructed in about anywhere.
-For various reasons many of the major factions seem to be too passive for their own good in some playthroughs. In a playthrough of Rome, I was able to get to Carthage several times withought any real resistance. (Experience may vary).
Overall I consider this a pretty good game overall, but still shy of the level of depth of Shogun II. I would defenatly recommend this to people who want more of a variaty in unit selection and enjoy the ancient era.

Game feels too easy, players steal your kills and chest loot, feels like a typical mmo.
Though there is plenty of loot to 'steal' in dressers/barrels from nps, but you have to remember to be 'hidden' or get a bounty.
Quest npcs are voiced, though, and you can find lots of equipment from 'stealing from npcs', killing things, from quests, or crafting.
Combat system is pretty different from skyrim,
and I just kept thinking I could be playing modded skyrim and it would be more fun.
But if you're just looking for a good mmo, it's not bad at all for that, it can fill that niche.
And I wanted to elaborate more on that (now that I've played it a bit more); for an mmo, (you can tell when you play) it's  high quality.
There's that interesting skyrim steal mechanic (you see a sword/armor on a shelf, just 'hide' from all npcs and take it and use it, very cool mechanic).
The npc quests are all voiced and feel more alive than other mmos.
The customization from the start is really good (you can choose whatever race and class together), change anything about the characters appearance at the start (like body or face), use any weapon/armor with any class, and dye armor with unlockable dyes (through achievements).
The combat is interesting, and like I said it's pretty easy but it's not braindead, you still have to pay attention to what you're doing.
So yeah, it has some good things about it, if you don't mind combat being a bit easy (but not braindead press '1' to win type), or players finishing your monsters off, and compeating for the locked chests; still though, don't expect the combat to be like skyrim or skyrim level of difficulty.

Short but enjoyable game. Pretty much everything you love about Bastion is here: great storytelling, music, and art style. The combat is an interesting combination of real time and turn-based with a fair amount of variety. Each new ability you get can be equipped as either an active attack, a modifier to another attack, or a passive ability. The game provides a practice room where you can try out whatever combination of abilities you like before using it in the real game. All in all, I found it to be a fun experience. Fair warning, though: when I say "short" I mean extremely short. About 5-6 hours is more than enough to go through the game and, other than 1 more playthrough on the new game+, there's not much replay value.

I could see people saying something along the lines of 'strong contender for Indie GOTY' and I definitely enjoyed Transistor enough to not stare shame into said people's souls. I loved it enough to complete it depiste being quite anti-completionist by nature.
Personally however, as someone who's played their previous release Bastion, I felt it echoed their last game far too closely. The constant narration; the vagueness of the plot; the pseudo isometric view and colourful art style; all great, but it's all stuff we've seen before.
The gameplay makes the core difference between the two games, however it's quite simple and could use some balancing. Nothing screaming innovation there, but it's fun and creative which is enough value on it's own.
Overall a fantastic game, my only major gripe is that I couldn't play it before Bastion to truly experience it with my jaw on the floor, where it often belongs.

Transistor is a beautifully imagined world, with a colourful programming/virtual reality theming.
Pros:
- Stunning, colourful artwork and complimentary soundtrack
- Situational Narration
- Storyline and world are rich enough to draw you in, vague enough to prompt discussion.
- Fun selection of abilities to try out
Cons (I'm struggling here)
For lovers of Bastion:
- Feels little easier than Bastion
- Less freedom to return to a 'hub' area, so feels more linear?
Gameplay is a mixture of hack and slash combined with 'turns' of planned attacks. Your attacks and abilities taking the form of direct, enhancing and passive 'functions' that can be combined to give different abilities and buffs.
The situational narration from Bastion makes a return here and ties in excellently with the emotionally charged storyline.
As with its predeccessor, it's quite a linear game in which the main story can be powered through pretty quickly (for those that aren't that bothered about story or exploration), but the second playthrough and challenges give you more than your money's worth (I've put around 20 Hours into it to 100% complete it and explore as much of the story available by interacting with the terminals and world).
One of the better gameplay mechanics is that a failure leads to a temporary loss of a function, which forces you to try new combinations and really get a feel for how each function works and when best to use them. Many of the acheivements are based around this also. It's a great way to encourage you to explore all the game has to offer, rather than just sticking with what  is familiar.
It also gives you a genuine consequence for failure other than "I lost a life".
Another excellent experience from Supergiant. If you liked Bastion this is definitely worth a play.

This game when if first came out was launched in a very incomplete state, the Co-op campaign was completely bugged out, many of the essential features like the ability to throw pila while stationary were completely missing and the battle ai was so damn drunk you could easily walk around them and capture the city square without them even noticing.
But now since CA did a major facelift on this game I think I can say that this game is for the most part complete.
Some of the things they added from the last iterations
-The ability to view the entire campaign and battle maps by using the tab key
-Added greater diversity of game machanics e.g. melee attack, armor penetration, health.
-It's much easier than before to keep a coherant line you can even assign subordinate ai commanders to take over and soft lock formations.
-The amount playable and non-playable factions in the game is both refreshing and even somewhat overwhelming and each one brings with it it's own unique playstyle adding months of replabiliy. Like for instance if you play a Germanic faction you must try to create a coalition in order to gain power.
-As always the graphics for this game is beyond astonishing especially if you have a decent computer. You can make out even small details like the insignias on units to the small projectiles being thrown throughout the battlefiels.
However, some cons that still need to be adressed in my opinion
-The family tree and political system in this is a complete joke, most of the things you really have to worry about is just the commander traits and army traditions.
-Compared to other games like EUIV, the diplomacy options have improved but still lack big options.
-Many of the on map resources seem to be too common to have any real value. Unlike Shogun 2, most of the buildings in Rome 2 can be constructed in about anywhere.
-For various reasons many of the major factions seem to be too passive for their own good in some playthroughs. In a playthrough of Rome, I was able to get to Carthage several times withought any real resistance. (Experience may vary).
Overall I consider this a pretty good game overall, but still shy of the level of depth of Shogun II. I would defenatly recommend this to people who want more of a variaty in unit selection and enjoy the ancient era.

No More Room in Hell is a standalone Half Life 2 mod which operates on realism and cooperation. With these attributes in mind, the game is quite unforgiving yet makes for a fun experience. Players looking for a run-gun tear 'em up zombie shooter like Left For Dead and many other contemporaries will not find that in the world of NMRiH, it is far too dark and brutal in its gameplay.
The game is compromised of developer and community made scenarios, of which there are two kinds. NMO's are scenario maps which involve an objective. The players (team of 8 or less) must reach a certain extraction point by a specified time or via certain conditions to win the scenario. The converse is NMS's, which are survival scenarios based on one location where the team must defend certain tactical points.
All servers are player-based, but due to the incredible population of this game this is not an issue. There are hundreds of servers to jump into, playing dozens of maps at any given moment. This sometimes results in ping issues, as the playerbase extends from the US to China both ways around, but Americans will find no difficulty finding dozens of +/-100, 100MS servers to enjoy. Euro's have plenty as well, and for Russian/Asian players, options are more limited, but still present.
The gameplay thrives on its unforgiving nature. Like most zombie games, there are certain standards. A particular way of fighting to gurantee you never get hit once, headshots are instant-kills, your walk pace is faster than all zombies... many of the usual hallmarks of the modern zombie gaming industry. Yet even one deviation, miscalculation, or faulty key press can result in a bite leading to infection. When you start with your team, theoretically there is no reason why any player shouldn't make it to the end without a single bite.
Yet somewhere along the way you find yourself in a dark alley, surrounded by 10 zeds closing in your corner. Your gun is out, you wasted all of our ammo getting a zombie off of your teammate who ended up being bit and turning anyway. Your're getting tired, and your character can't keep swinging. One of the other survivors has a zombie on his back eating him, the other in front of you is running away from it all towards freedom. Where did it all go wrong?
With this in mind, the game has a steep learning curve. New players often times find themselves overwhelmed by the difficulty of the game, and get discouraged. Melee combat is necessary but remains tricky even for experienced gamers partially due to its bugginess and the rugged stamina system.
Guns are fun to play with and have their own interesting mechanics, same as the melee system. The inventory system is unique, and teaches resource management splendidly.
Teamplay is essential, in this regard playing with random's can be incredibly frustrating at times (especially due to the multinational nature of the community) , but playing with friends or on servers near you will help with this.
Pros:
+ Gritty, Realistic gameplay
+ Rewarding combat and weapons
+ Cooperative, play with friends
+ Enormous community
+ FREE, zero, zero, zero buy-ins!
+ Light-weight and easy to run on ANY pc
+ That quaint little HL2 engine you'll recognize
+ Loads of acheivments
+ Active developers
Cons:
- Graphics have not aged too well, the game is not for graph♥♥♥♥♥s
- Steep learning curve, combat is tough to get into, game takes high skill to succeed
- Random players on random servers
- Limited gameplay, all scenarios are linear.
All in all, get it! It's not the game for everyone, but I highly recommend it to this who have read this review and still want to try.

When I first looked at Transistor I thought it would be somewhat similar to Bastion. It had the same graphic style, an isometric view and a narrator (which is actually a 'character' this time; in the form of a talking sword). But, I'm happy to say that I couldn't be more wrong.
Yes, it has all of the features I just mentioned but it's not just a simple copy. There's so much more going on here. Transistor has a deep (and a little bit confusing) story and a combat system that as equally deep. The lore reminded me of Dark Souls where you have to piece things together yourself and not everything is trying to be explained.
The graphics are amazing, but are, unfortunately, this time limited to full HD resolutions and not anything higher. Despite that it all still looks like art, and it really is eye candy. Absolutely wonderful.
The narrator is doing a great job as far as the voice acting goes, even if it's a bit stiff and sometimes feels unemotional. The music and sounds are all excellent as well.
Let's get back to the combat system for a minute. Like pretty much any RPG out there, your character will level up after several battles and once you level up you're allowed to choose a certain skill and passive upgrade. When you first start it's just that, a skill. But level up a few times more and you'll have several skills. This time, however, skills can be combined to make an even more effective/deadly combination. So, for example, let's say that you chose the skill to teleport in an instant. Combine it with Charm (which temporarily transforms an enemy into an ally) and you'll be zipping across the map converting enemies, making your battles much easier. This was just a poor example, by the way (blame my memory !). Of course, this also works the other way around, resulting in entirely different skills every time. It's a blast to play with and it's even more fun to experiment with these new skills on real enemies. You'll see that certain combinations will do ridiculous amounts of damage and that others, while still being useful, need some slight tweaking in order to be effective. It's pure brilliance.
Transistor is on the short side, however, and it can easily be finished in 5-6 hours. I think I explored every area carefully in my playthrough, but I didn't do most of the (optional) challenges. So I think you can add another 2 hours to my numbers if you want to do all of those. And after that, you can start New Game+ with all your current skills intact (which will make the battles more fun right from the start).
In the end Transistor is nothing but a brilliant, deep little game. If you call yourself a serious gamer you should absolutely play this. I liked it even better than Bastion, and that's definitely saying something.

Papers, Please is one of the most Indie game ever you see (and funny).
In the year of October 1982, you have won the October labor lottery and your name was pulled. For immediate placement, report to The Ministry of Admission at Grestin Border Checkpoint. An apartment will be provided for you and your family in East Grestin. Expect a Class-8 dwelling.
You play as the Inspector, which of course you are working as a border inspector. Your job is to check their passport to make sure no expiration date, issuing city, name, picture, passport number and gender. By the time the day keeps going, there will be more papers which makes it harder to organize and match.
For stamping, "Approved" if all of the passport and papers are organized and good to go, "Denied" if some of the passport and papers are not match, forgery or false information. If you make "Approved" stamp, but saw something that is wrong, you can do second stamp for "Denied" or go for "Discrepancy Detected" to "Detain" them that it does count for that.
The citation warning will bring up what you did wrong. The first two you won't get penalty, but third and more will receive 5 credits penalty each.
There are multiple endings to choose from. Working with EZIC, brainwashed from Arstotzka, freedom, sacrifice, etc.
For me, it kinda feels relaxing and pretend to be working as an inspector which makes a whole lot of sense when I go to the airport or crossing border. Even though, I would get bribed by someone, but I wouldn't do that because the ministry won't like it (as in the game). =P
Overall, I give it 8.5/10 for this game.

While the interface is nostalgiac, and the plot
interesting, upon replaying the shallowness of the game is revealed under a spotlight. The choices do
matter in the slightest, and the ending is completely unfulfilling. It's as if the game intends for you to go after this (honestly shallow and annoying) girl, when in reality she is more pathetic than anything. If you go for the ending that I did (basically denying her attempts at a relationship with the PC), then it is meaningless. Emily's character is unbelievably clingy, and everything about her put me off.
Upon replaying and deciding to roleplay as a character that is the
opposite of myself in reality, the game threw me a curveball. The ending doesn't change no matter what you choose. Decide to ignore her and go after other girls? Lose contact, move on in life Decide to chase after her and attempt to hook up? Nope, she goes back to her d-bag boyfriend and you move on to better things. There is no difference in endings no matter what path one takes.
Now, I understand that the developer was probably going for a "some relationships are futile" philosophy, but it just comes across as angering. I felt like I wasted my time. I will admit, during the first playthrough I was intrigued, but as soon as I replayed the game it spoiled the entire experience entirely.
There is no emotional story here. There is no awesome character/relationship building. The only thing within this game is a well-designed interface, a shallow, pointless story, and sixty minutes that you could have spent playing something better.
Some of the dialogue is incredibly cringey by the way, the main character seems rather awkward. The game restricts the player from outright attempting to make advances on the girl, but also refuses to allow the player to push her away entirely.
All in all, not worth the time. Maybe one playthrough if you're really interested, but DO NOT replay it.

I purchased this game for 60 USD a year after its release, and I am glad I did.  I heard a lot about the bugs and glitches that made this game unplayable.  I was truly disappointed for the Romans interest me a lot more than feudal Japan, which my friends would try to get me to buy.  Despite all the negative reviews, I decided to trust in Rome and purchased the game for its full price.  I was glad that I did.  The game looks impressive.  The lighting on the Macedonian Shield Bearers as they march across the field of dry tall grass at dusk to face the Parthian soldiers made it seem like a movie.  The cultures definitely stand out from one another.  Romans look different than Carthage and the Hellenic factions, gallic tribes are different than the Germans and Thracians, Parthians and scythians, etc.  This makes fighting each factions much more unique than different colored samurais in my opinion.  The combat is mediocre and highly debatable.  As for me, the long drawn out battles between hoplites is an accurate portrayal of the ancient battles.  I found the campaign to be a challenge only in the beginning. As the empire expands, much of its problems becomes trivial to its power.  Also, the grand campaign doesn't have much events besides conquering territories.  Perhaps due to this, I enjoy and play custom games much more frequently.  When bored with the campaign and custom games, mods add a new level of fresh gameplay.  I don't think I'm stretching the facts when I say mods make the Total War games great.  This game has many great mods created by talented people in the community, who develop impressive mods that transform the game into something different.  So I recommend this game.  It's no longer the unplayable junk that people told me it is.  Much of my free time, I would boot this game and play a single match and go back to what I had to do.  The improvements also show that the developers do care to fix their broken game.  This game is worth buying, especially during sales when the price drops to 15 USD.

Lately I've been asking myself if it's possible that I'm just done shooting a man. I constantly find myself bored with FPS games; generally, if I finish one it's just because I was determined to see it through to the end despite the whole thing where I'm not actually having fun. About an hour into Gunslinger, I exited the game, convinced that this was actually the case. I was done with FPSes. Time to hang up my disembodied guns.
Then I loaded up this game again, mostly because I love the story conceit of this game so I wanted to see it through to the end (plus I heard it was pretty short so what the hell). Woops I was real ♥♥♥♥in' wrong. My bad. I slogged on for a bit longer, then I started getting deeper into the skill trees. Then the game finally became what it was supposed to be. I guess my impatience is showing if I feel that a game takes too long to get going after an hour, but here we are. Once you gain skills that start improving your ability to combo, the game arrives where it should have been at the beginning.
If you're feeling tl;dr, skip the next two paragraphs. They're pretty spergy. Then come back (or don't).
I made the mistake of starting with the shotgun and rifle skill trees. Who would have thought that in a game called GUNSLINGER, maybe the GUNSLINGER tree was the way to go. Imagine that. So you make your way down the gunslinger tree, your combos last longer, do bonus damage, whatever. Then you reach the last skill (this will take you like an hour if you go right for it.) It refills your concentration (bullet time) meter every time your combo reaches a multiple of 6. Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ now this is a game. You're now chaining entire multiple wave setpieces down without your opponents getting to take a shot. Maybe there's just a part of me that loves the mental image of loads of guys exploding into blood decals the second they peek their heads out from behind a wall all at once. It's incredible.
I know this is a hyperspecific way to play the game, and one size probably doesn't fit all, so I'll just go on to say that the game is probably still fun even if this doesn't tickle your fancy the way it does for me. I should probably tell you that the other skill trees are also well thought out and give you fun additional things that change the way the game plays. In the close quarters tree you gain the ability to throw back dynamite off the ground (maybe this should have been free), make your dynamite split into individual sticks in midair (with predictable results), and even skip reloading in concentration mode (this is a game changer, considering shotguns are two shot affairs). I felt like they were pretty weak until I got a couple damage boosts, but then after that all close quarters levels were handled with akimbo sawed-offs. The rifle tree is less exciting, but the rifle is already stupid overpowered so I guess that's ok. I mostly just used the pistol skills with a rifle.
----
Now that that's over... the story in this game is pretty great. You're an old bounty hunter sitting at a bar with some strangers,  telling tall tales about how you were friends with, had run ins with, or killed pretty much every single outlaw that pop culture has deemed worthy of keeping in the public conscience. You begin your first mission with Billy the Kid, end up chasing Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid, and eventually winging Jesse James. The thing that I love about this game though is the way the narrative sometimes changes midsentence. You'll play a sequence, then your narrator will inform you that that didn't actually happen, and then a totally different story will play out. I know that probably reads like lazy storytelling but it's really well done, in my opinion. Paths will open up in front of you when the story deems it necessary even though there was nothing there before. I lost my♥♥♥♥♥♥when I saw my first sky ladder.
So um, the bad. The duels are an excellent concept, but in practice can be super frustrating! I played with a controller and I feel like the analog sticks helped tremendously, so maybe that's something to consider. I actually tried doing a duel with mouse and keyboard before I wrote this and I can't say I recommend it. It's kind of a generic shooter until you get down the skill trees, but this probably isn't as big of a knock for most people as it is for me. The game is about 4 hours long. I'm not really a dollar per hour kind of guy but I can see this mattering for some people so I think it's worth mentioning. I think it has pretty good replay value but I'm the type of person that plays a game 2 or 3 times most of the time anyway.
Go buy this game. I want more old west shooters. Thanks.
(I also want to add that I think it's really funny comparing the hyper stylized comic book panels for all the main characters to the actual pictures of the dumpy looking dudes that you can find on the game's collectibles. At least wear a cowboy hat, goddamn.)

Gameplay: The way guns handle in borderlands is amazing. You can encounter everything from a regular assault rifle to a shotgun that shoots swords upon your enemies. The class system varies gameplay even more with 5+ classes and 3 skill trees each, they simply add more value to the game as a whole.
Story: Overall the story does not really grab players BUT that does not mean it is terrible. The reason you will play through the story is for the characters. With villans like Handsome Jack that are zany and insane, and playable characters like a psycho you will always want to push on so that you can hear the next quote from any of the characters.
Overall, Borderlands 2 is the perfect game for those who like interesting crazy characters, great gunplay, and not too valuable a story. It has been my benchmark shooter since its release and continues to be to this day.

Dark Souls 2 is everything as hard as I expected the first one to be with very challenging bosses and lands to explore. The fighting system and leveling is great but the developers dropped the ball in several ways making the game overtly frustrating and less rewarding than its predecessor.
The first thing is having vendors limit the amount of items they can sell. That was never a problem in Dark Souls one. I would be very happy to go out farming souls and collect enough to purchase as many items as I needed.
2nd, is the weapon durability. Its a very frustrating experience to upgrade a weapon you need to kill the enemies you need, but halfway having your weapon break or having to resort to a lower grade weapon, again, this wouldn't be a problem if you could buy as many titanite items as you needed to have a variety of weapons to make it through a boss or to the next bonfire.
The 3rd and the worst decision the developers made was the constant invasions into your world, making you lose your humanity, souls, and more importantly time. In the first dark souls you could only get invaded when you're human, but in Dark Souls 2 weather you are human or not. Every other game out there has the option of PvP like the statutes next to the bonfire after you kill the dragon knight in The Blue Cathedral, its optional to PvP if you're into that. If the developers could create a way to limit the number of invasions to one per hour or two that would be fine, but when you're constantly being invaded when you're trying to prepare and make it to the boss and you get killed it gets very frustrating, again, not to mention losing your humanity when you get killed and having a very limited amount of human effigies or having to waste an hour or two waiting to be summoned to help someone so you can regain your humanity is ridiculous, just so you can get back to where you were to kill the boss you need to in order to progress and get killed by an invading soul once again. There should be an option to stop invasions or make it optional.  Why do you NEED to be human in order to get help from someone but you can get invaded weather you're human or not, that's not balanced well at all. There are some serious updates and fixes this game needs in order to make it a great game.

These are people who are much more powerful than you--who kill you over and over, and cause you to lose your souls and humanity...and most of all, they cause you to lose time.  Not everyone appreciates losing 15-30 minutes of progress just because some 12 year old thinks it's cool to show his school buddies how bad he can kick someones butt...in a video game. More than just a good game, Transistor's social commentary is very apt for this generation.

Transistor is a beautifully imagined world, with a colourful programming/virtual reality theming.
Pros:
- Stunning, colourful artwork and complimentary soundtrack
- Situational Narration
- Storyline and world are rich enough to draw you in, vague enough to prompt discussion.
- Fun selection of abilities to try out
Cons (I'm struggling here)
For lovers of Bastion:
- Feels little easier than Bastion
- Less freedom to return to a 'hub' area, so feels more linear?
Gameplay is a mixture of hack and slash combined with 'turns' of planned attacks. Your attacks and abilities taking the form of direct, enhancing and passive 'functions' that can be combined to give different abilities and buffs.
The situational narration from Bastion makes a return here and ties in excellently with the emotionally charged storyline.
As with its predeccessor, it's quite a linear game in which the main story can be powered through pretty quickly (for those that aren't that bothered about story or exploration), but the second playthrough and challenges give you more than your money's worth (I've put around 20 Hours into it to 100% complete it and explore as much of the story available by interacting with the terminals and world).
One of the better gameplay mechanics is that a failure leads to a temporary loss of a function, which forces you to try new combinations and really get a feel for how each function works and when best to use them. Many of the acheivements are based around this also. It's a great way to encourage you to explore all the game has to offer, rather than just sticking with what  is familiar.
It also gives you a genuine consequence for failure other than "I lost a life".
Another excellent experience from Supergiant. If you liked Bastion this is definitely worth a play.
