When I first looked at Transistor I thought it would be somewhat similar to Bastion. It had the same graphic style, an isometric view and a narrator (which is actually a 'character' this time; in the form of a talking sword). But, I'm happy to say that I couldn't be more wrong.
Yes, it has all of the features I just mentioned but it's not just a simple copy. There's so much more going on here. Transistor has a deep (and a little bit confusing) story and a combat system that as equally deep. The lore reminded me of Dark Souls where you have to piece things together yourself and not everything is trying to be explained.
The graphics are amazing, but are, unfortunately, this time limited to full HD resolutions and not anything higher. Despite that it all still looks like art, and it really is eye candy. Absolutely wonderful.
The narrator is doing a great job as far as the voice acting goes, even if it's a bit stiff and sometimes feels unemotional. The music and sounds are all excellent as well.
Let's get back to the combat system for a minute. Like pretty much any RPG out there, your character will level up after several battles and once you level up you're allowed to choose a certain skill and passive upgrade. When you first start it's just that, a skill. But level up a few times more and you'll have several skills. This time, however, skills can be combined to make an even more effective/deadly combination. So, for example, let's say that you chose the skill to teleport in an instant. Combine it with Charm (which temporarily transforms an enemy into an ally) and you'll be zipping across the map converting enemies, making your battles much easier. This was just a poor example, by the way (blame my memory !). Of course, this also works the other way around, resulting in entirely different skills every time. It's a blast to play with and it's even more fun to experiment with these new skills on real enemies. You'll see that certain combinations will do ridiculous amounts of damage and that others, while still being useful, need some slight tweaking in order to be effective. It's pure brilliance.
Transistor is on the short side, however, and it can easily be finished in 5-6 hours. I think I explored every area carefully in my playthrough, but I didn't do most of the (optional) challenges. So I think you can add another 2 hours to my numbers if you want to do all of those. And after that, you can start New Game+ with all your current skills intact (which will make the battles more fun right from the start).
In the end Transistor is nothing but a brilliant, deep little game. If you call yourself a serious gamer you should absolutely play this. I liked it even better than Bastion, and that's definitely saying something.

I started a co-op factory with a close friend. After a day of work, I stepped back, looked at what we built, and came to some realizations.
1) I have no ♥♥♥♥ing idea whats going on in this factory
2) Half the components that directly interact with each other aren't even near one another, one of the machines producing copper cable for another machine to assemble into circuit boards is halfway across the god damn refinery
3) 90% of the conveyor belts are underground, and the rest are going so many directions this thing looks like a ball of yarn
4) There is coal ♥♥♥♥ing EVERYWHERE
5) I maintain enough sanity to count to 5
6) Staring at this thing makes my eyes itch
7) Looking away makes my brain itch
The scariest part is that it keeps getting bigger, and every time it gets bigger it somehow becomes MORE labrynthine. One of those ♥♥♥♥ing conveyor belts goes all the way around the entire factory to deliver steel plates to a single assembler thats making bloody gears, and its right next to the refinery itself!
Sometimes the factory breaks. We don't usually notice because of how much of a mess this thing is, and the breaks we do spot are often half an hour old and are a recurring problem. Rather than fix it, we simply unjam the machine and ignore it until it breaks again. The biggest problem to fixing it comes from our production lines. Normal production lines look like a grid. Ours looks like you threw a bunch of squares into a bowl of spaghetti noodles and gave the bowl to a five year old for a period of one to five minutes. This proccess results in either an empty bowl and a full five year old, a floor covered in noodles, or spaghetti all over the walls and ceiling with the squares nowhere to be found. Knowing the trend in increasing chaos and complexity the factory exhibits, probably all three.
The factory is an empodiment of madness incomprehensible even to the men who built it, laid every unholy circuit of conveyor belt, a thousand arms madly spinning every second, countless plates of copper and iron in a complex dance the likes of which is unseen in the realm of mere mortals. There are sections that I have no idea how they work, and I BUILT THEM.
The factory grows more complex with each passing second and more convoluted every milisecond. Perhaps the reason is in part due to each segment being constructed with no plans for future additions, then the future additions were constructed by forcibly adapting the existing segments, usually by shoving more tubes into it rather than actually redesigning it, and these futrue additions are also not planned for expansion. The end result is a cluster-♥♥♥♥ so large in magnitude, the last time a cluster-♥♥♥♥ rivaled it in size, God smote the town and turned its inhabitants into salt. Unfortunately no god can save us from this... thing.
Having expanded it further its almost as if the factory has a mind of its own, an ever hungry consciousness burning with dark malevolence and the need to grow. It infects all who stand in its presence, compelling them to add to it. A hundred furnaces belch smoke and the black blood of the earth is torn from its cradle to fuel the fires of industry. The ecosystem is demolished and the skin of the planet is rent and shattered for its glittering treasures, tossed into the inferno of a thousand stone and metal prisons to be transformed, used to expand the malignant blight upon the world that we brought. Ten thousand steel cogs turn and steam fills the air as the never ending fires boil the oceans away to power the sprawling spiderweb of mechanised mayhem, ordered chaos at its purest, a hundred thousand plates of steel and copper cycle and swirl in patterns barely knowable by the very people that created them.
Each day, the red and green fluids are pumped into glowing crystalline globes, each sparking and burning, discovering new knowledge and new machines. The factory grows. Each advance in technology only complicates matters. The factory grows. The new advances create a need for new resources. The factory grows. The new resources require new means of transportation. The factory grows. The new transportation feeds new machines that burn the new resources to produce blue fluids to discover new technology. The factory grows. The blue fluids feed the globes to reveal new truths, beginning the vicious cycle anew, a neverending circle of destruction and growth that will only end when every corner of the planet is scoured clean. The factory grows. The planet will never be scoured clean. The factory grows. The planet is infinite in size. The factory grows. The game will never be over.
The factory grows.
Epilogue:

Resources have dried up again. The factory consumes all within its reach, insatiable in its hunger. Though it had experienced full production stoppages in the past, the factory could never be eliminated from the planet by the natives, for the sun itself powered the beams of destruction that maintained its borders. Within the creaking, ancient cogs and permanent haze of foul and polluted smoke, a single humanoid shape slowly rises to its feet. Aged, failing flesh and bone long ago replaced with steel and chrome, once polished and clean, now weathered by uncountable years of exposure to acid rain and blackened by thick, choking smog, form its excuse for a body. It could have left while it was still human, before it was consumed in body by the foundry it created to escape. It never had a chance to leave, mind and soul devoured in the pursuit of freedom. With slow, clanking steps and the steady drip of oil from its joints, like a bleeding mechanical nightmare brought to hideous life, it stands and rasps as it moves for the exit. Behind it, a thousand drones rise like a plague of locusts, ready to continue the endless harvest. As the abomination that was once a man steps towards the gates of the factory, a mighty space faring vessel lies decrepit in its dry dock deep within the core of the facility. Emily is Away is a point-and-click choose-your-own-adventure story game, set in the early 2000s (2002 to 2005). Each chapter takes place in a different year in the game.
It is basically a back-and-forth conversation between you and your friend Emily. Game has very little customization, you pick a username (for the fake IM program) and a first name (for Emily to refer to you as), and you pick profile pictures. Subtle pop culture references are made both in chat and in profile pictures; say, the year Coldplay releases their album "X&Y" you can pick a Coldplay profile pic (you get to pick a new one each year / chapter if you please). You play at a Windows XP-looking computer, with cheesy early-2000s IM notification sounds and the clicks of your hard drive and whirring of your PC's fan. The theme / setting is very pleasing in my opinion.
This is about all that is really special about the game. It can be completed in well under an hour; you get three choices between each dialogue. You must type out on your keyboard - every key press you put in enters a new character of what is about to be said. This really adds time to the gameplay and I feel was just added to make it seem longer. In some instances, to my knowledge (I type 100-120 WPM so I'm not even sure if this was the case) you can start typing a message and partway through you can submit it but if you keep typing you will change what you say - this is irreversible. Sometimes you may choose to say one thing and the character revises it to say something not exactly in your vision, or
. This is something I hate with a passion.
The storytelling itself is pretty shallow. It's not really a drama; it's a very scratch-the-surface slight romance. It could be so much more, but it just doesn't go into enough detail. Often the characters end what could be a more interesting plot point abruptly to "go to a party" or "go hang out with friends", something you never actually see happening and something that really breaks the flow of the story. The characters then "log off", signaling the end of the chapter... and the worst part is, the next chapter is set a
. Oh, a big potential plot point is coming up, a true climax, it's really start to get going and... "I've gotta go, told my friend I'd hang out with them tonight." Ba-bing, screen fades. Next chapter... a year later, opportunity is blown. Being that it's a YEAR between every conversation, it completely breaks any aspect of plot depth that this game could have. Being that they're set a year apart, anything that happens is nearly completely irrelevant towards the next year. Anything that doesn't happen in the chat messages is maybe only briefly mentioned, if at all. The chapters are also very short. This game's story had so much potential but yet it was written so shallowly, there's no chance for the characters to get into a deep, lengthy conversation or to speak about something before and after an event happening while it's still recent. It's not like this is an action game, there's no buffer... there's nothing to do but these chat messages (and a "Buddy List" which does nothing but give you bios on characters that adds very little to the plot, and even if they're online you can't engage in messages with them - something that would really make the game more interesting). It's not even a very dramatic story... I've heard people say it has a sad ending, but it's barely even saddening for a video game, for fictional media in my opinion. I'm not going to spoil it for you, but it didn't really move me at all.
Overall, the story is too shallow and the game's format completely screws up any in-depth plot development between events, the system to progress through the game is clunky and feels like a gimmicky system to make it take you longer to finish it, but the whirring of the hard drive and early-2000s IM program sounds, and somewhat entertaining-ish but not really all that good at all story make it not an absolutely terrible game. I respect the time that it took to make it, and that's about it. It's not a terrible game; it's not bad; it's just not as good as it could be.
I give it a 4 / 10.

I never thought old west pistol duels could be made this fun. The story is told in a very entertaining way, often you will play through segments as Silas is telling the story that didn't really happen, exploring the what-ifs. This is the kind of shooter where you mow through tons of small fry to get to varied and surprisingly enjoyable boss fights. The chapters seems to always end with a pistol duel, through a system that really builds the tension. When you fail a duel you never feel like it's because of the system, it's because you just weren't good enough that time. If you're looking for a FPS that stands out from the herd with interesting gameplay mechanics and an entertaining story with a unique presentation, look no further.

Call of Juarez Gunslinger is a great western shooter. The storytelling was entertaining because it was told through flashbacks by the main character, who always had some funny remarks about the situations he was in.
The graphics were absolutely gorgeous on max settings.
The gameplay was really fun too. It played like a typical western shooter with guns like a shotgun, rifle and revolver, but it added some cool features like boss fights and bullet time. Skills like bullet time could be improved by the simple leveling system. Also very cool were the one-to-one duels, where you have to shoot your opponent before he shoots you (obviously), which will put your reaction time to the test.
My only complaint about this game is that it was too short ! I completed it in less than 5 hours. After that you can also play arcade mode and duels, but those are not as entertaining as the main story. You can also start a new game+ on a harder difficulty to make full use of the skills you got through the leveling system in the first playtrough, but that's about it.
I would recommend the game to anyone who even remotely likes shooters or westerns (or both), because of the fun gameplay, the gorgeous visuals and the entertaining storytelling.

After the cartel desaster we're finally going back to the core of the series. Great western shooter with a nice story (I really enjoy the times when you have to replay parts of a mission when another character is telling us "how it really happened"), great comic-cutscenes and (of course) stylish gunfights.
Only annoying things I found so far is the special weapons you unlock via skills still have to be looted from dead enemies and sometimes AI opponents get stuck in weird places (lumberyard wood-piles).
The arcade mode consists of well crafted timed runs that require you to play trough a map in one run and shoot an enemy every four seconds to keep the score timer running. Levelling up the skills in this mode is basically a requirement as you'll need the "reload faster" skills to score 3* in most of the maps.

Would I support this game? yeah why not, it's the closest MMO that mimics RO.
Class diversity - Some would argue that it is pointless diversity since everyone wants to min/max build with this game, everyone is using the same builds taken from the Korean ToS servers and there goes your diversity. But playstyle wise, you're still in charge, if you're a min/maxer then by all means use the builds you think is the best, but the choice is still yours, if you're not having fun with the min/max builds, then why do that build in the first place?
Combat - Let me compare this to RO, since this is by far, I think is the best selling point of the game, combat in general is a mixed bag in my opinion, it's like RO, you can hit multiple monster to stack them for better EXP:kill ratio (Because cool down is a thing in this game),Jumping is a new addition to the typical RO type combat, doesn't add anything much besides potential animation canceling for some classes, I think the jumping was added for the platforming aspect of the game rather than combat really, still it feel natural to have a jump button. Finally the skills, which in my opinion a little streamlined, some of the skills are a bit similar to each other, and some first circle skills are really bad, and does not really scale well with level, makes you feel that the first circle a bit of a waste in terms of skill points, again comparing to RO, some first job skill are still used and still scale well after 3rd jobs, like BASH, DOUBLE STRAIFING, DOUBLE ATTACK, etc. in this game, when you go on the branching classes, you only use your support skills for your party, the rest is just a waste of SP, too bad they should fix this.
Trading - What can I say, too many restrictions, I have to give this one a negative, I mean they try to balance the "MARKET" or "ECONOMY" of the game reason so we ban everyone from trading, I think this is ridiculous really, and just plain lazy, you can restrict the items you don't want circulating around, but trading basic items such as potions and support items is a must in MMORPGs, this is like mortal sin and a very basic aspect of an MMO, then again, the gears/sets of the game at the moment is lacking, too few legendaries, the item choices is a no brainer (just pick the higher one with better stats), unlike the original RO, we still use some of the early game equipments rather than the higher leveled ones. slot number choices and stuff. And the 1 item per person in the auction house, this is not good at all, at least 3 items per account should be sufficient enough,
Items/Equipment - As I mentioned above, very few interesting items in the game, if they are going with the WoW or Diablo type of Equipments, then the diversity of rare and legendary items should be a lot more than what we currently have.
Premium stuff -  Well, gotta make money somehow right? but do it the right way, why can't they just mimic DOTA2 for this stuff? I mean even PORTAL scrolls are also premium for crying out loud, WHY? I still don't know the real reason behind this, i mean the game map is tediously big and you want us to pay real money to travel around? WHY? in the original RO, we have B.WIngs F.Wings for that, and the big no no in any F2P game is the stat scroll that is currently breaking the balance from F2P to P2W game, If anything that will destroy the game, this is it. P2W is a really bad reputation to have in an MMO, especially when other non premium users have no access for this. please stop implementing mobile game BS if you want to be as big as the previous MMO. overall, this section gives the most negative for the game, if you want to fix something, fix this one first.
BOTS/Gold BOTS - Seriously, this is the reason why the economy can be a mess in the future, fix this one please, and fix it right, because by far the countermeasures by far is affecting the non botting players the most, all the restrictions implemented are to counter bots, please just ban the Spammers in towns, and some of the bots are too obvious for you not to crack down on them, dont punsh the whole player base because of these clowns, don't be lazy please.
Overall the main problem of the game at the momment is the last two factors that I mentioned Bots and premium items. other in game designs can be fixed by patch and balancing.

As it says "dystopian document thriller" -- that's right on the money. Well, it should be: it's in the pic.
Anyways, this game is quite unique, atleast to me. It's simple and runs on the slowest of machines. Well, there really isn't much to this game graphically becaure you're reading documents the whole time. I'm a guy who loves some damn good graphics. This game doesn't have it. But that's OK. Why?
Because this game is awesome.
You work at a security checkpoint, and you have to find discrepancies in peoples' documents (passports, ID cards, entry permit, work permits, grants, diplomatic authorization, etc.) to locate criminals or people trying to fool the system to get throught the checkpoint.
Sounds booring but it's not. This game is pretty damn fun because you're working against the clock. Attention to detail and textual discrepancies is key for success in this game.
You'll find at first people successfully tricking you, but learning their tricks and stopping them in the future is pretty satisfieng. Working against the clock, having show much stuff to look out for, and having a family you have to provide money for adds to the intensity.
Overall a sweet game I'd highly recommend. Definetly a thriller. Not a good game if you're high, by the way.

First of all, if you're new to visual novels, then this is not going to be a quick-paced game. It's nice and laidback, but it will take you a long time to get through, and you probably will get bored at times. The pace can be pretty slow, especially if you're not using a guide, as there are so many wrong choices that don't seem like wrong choices. So I would recommend using a guide just to avoid frustration.
Aside from that, once the pace picks up, this is a really great read. The characters are great, the drama is great, and the soundtrack is amazing and definitely worth a purchase if you can find it. The drama may be a little over-the-top at times for some, but if you take the time to get invested in the story and the characters, you will never forget it. I still think of some of the endings from time to time, months after I've finished the game, and I still get goosebumps when listening to the soundtrack.
Definitely worth a play, but if you're not sure/not used to visual novels, I would try something cheaper first just to explore the format, or grab this on sale price..

Factorio is a really interesting game, in that at first it seems pretty simple and easy to follow but once you hit kind of the second tier of research everyting gets creazy really fast. The game goes from "Smelt iron, make bullets" to "Okay wait how do I set up an oil refinery to process hard oil into solid fuel again?" very quickly. what's amazing about the game though is how it makes you want to just play a little more, to see what the next thing you'll build is and then tempt you with another shiny research once that's finished. I've been playing a ton of this game lately (mainly offline so my steam hours are not accurate) And I still feel like I've barely touched the surface, I haven't even seen the next tier of enemy yet or set up my first railway. Those may seem like little things but 3-4 hours into a game will keep you wondering when the enemy is going to suddenly evolve and show you that your little gun turrets might not be enough anymore.
The game has an interesting dynamic between progress and punishment, as the more pollution you spread the tougher the enemy bases and spawns become. If you tread lightly you can be an hour or two into a game still holding off enemies with your machine pistol, or at the same game time you could be cowereing behind a solid stone wall and 10 turrets hoping that you made enough ammo to last the night. I would definitly recomend checking this game out if you haven't already, or if you're interested watch someone's playthrough of the game to see what it's about. (warning though, these let's plays can get very long as there is a TON of content.)

Absolutely fantastic game this hits you right in the micromanagement spot of the brain. You will curse the day you ever thought laying out furnaces in a neat row in early game when you need to balance 16 conveyor belts all carrying seperate goods. Organized chaos ensues as your patchwork factory grows and grows to both build ever more complex items and repel an increasing onslaught of tree hugging bugs.
Factories can span entire continents as you continue to expand more and more to feed your ever growing need for raw materials. Smog covers the globe as the alien exo terrorist units desperately try to stop your noble pursuit of industrial revolution.
As this game is still in early access and already well worth the money for many hours of play there is nothing stopping me from recommending this game.
There are still kinks however. The fluid mechanics could use some work as there seems to be several issues with the way water flows compared to oil of gas. Then there is the suprise spawn of alien nests inside your walls combined with the fact that in late game your hunger for resources grows so ravenous that you just resign  to start laying down Great Walls Of Trump in all four directions to stop any alien incursions on your continent.
Instead of building enclaves to protect only the resources. By the time you have built such an enclave the resources would have been mined already. There is also no real end goal in the game except to launch rockets, which has no current tangible benefits. It takes a long time by which the fun of building factories and exterminating aliens has quite run dry.
That said it took over 40 hours before the tedium set in for me and I just didn't have the stomach to built yet another field of solar panels to power my ever growing defence grid. Just to mine resources which would be depleted within the hour.
Though with future updates and balancing on the way this game is worth the price of admission.

Big fan of the Total War series, my favorite being Medieval 2, now this game, when it first came out and I tried it, was not very good, bugs, performance issues(in my experience), and balance issues plagued the game. I totally forgot about the game until now, when I saw the Total War Master Collection sale, and bought it. I immediately tried Rome 2 first.
PROS:
It runs great on my computer, I haven't encountered any bugs that I know of and I had fun playing the game. I mostly played grand campaign(turn based war theater map chess like format, with the battles being in real time) so I can't comment anything about the 'story' campaigns and the multiplayer. the Grand Campaign AI is intelligent and will form believable alliances/rivals during your game, and come up with believable decisions in diplomacy, and the battles are also challenging(depending on the difficulty)
The economy/resources is well thought of and it can be challenging to manage and balance, to achieve a great economy to support your empire. There's also some form of micromanagement(agents, armies, cities) but imo it's not as heavy and tedious compared to previous titles.
CONS:
The game engine is not well suited for melee combat as it was designed originally for Empire Total War(emphasis on guns/ranged combat). You'll often see opposing soldiers separately 1v1-ing each other instead of fighting as a unit like in previous melee total wars(Rome 1, Medieval 2)
Also, I don't like how they put countless 'DLCs' for sale that should have been part of the game anyway, like unlocking factions so you can play as them and enabling blood and gore.
7.8/10 will probably say 8.5/10 if it wasn't for the greedy move on the DLCs
Recommended to get on sale, especially the whole Master Collection (don't get the Grand Master Collection)

Following up Bastion would be a hard act for anybody, so it can be a forgiven a bit that Transistor is what I'd call Supergiant Games' sophomore slump. It's a game that leans a little too heavily on the familiar, yet seems a bit unsure of how it wants to present itself as a separate new entity.
You've got your talking Transistor which functions as the game's narrator, you've got Jen Zee's unmistakably fantastic art direction, and you've got Darren Korb's trancey-blues fusion soundtrack, and all those elements come together fairly well for the most part. Transistor is a gem to behold and contains nothing but fantastic audio candy for days and days.
Unfortunately the gameplay and story lack the shine and polish Bastion had.
The combat is a good mixture of real-time and turn-based combat, allowing you to use skills at the press of a button or queue them up to unleash with certain timing. Customizability is a huge factor since every skill in the game can be active, support, or passive, and the combinations are almost endless. That said, with all the strategy a system like this could bring, it's fairly easy to bulldoze through almost all enemy encounters with a few of the skills you start with, and even easier once you start playing around with combinations. While discovering these ridiculous combinations is fun and rewarding though, it throws every bit of strategy the game promises and throws it out the window fairly early, and by the end of the game battles become tedious.
Transistor's storytelling takes a different approach to Basion's. You're immediately thrown into Transistor's world without much of an idea of what's going on and you're railroaded through the adventure at a Final Fantasy XIII, purely linear breakneck pace. The story does have a decent resolution, but the world, characters, and motivations of Transistor's cast are either too vague or hard to grasp. Everybody talks as if the player knows what's going on and there's not much expository dialog to help clear much up. Each skill you obtain has a character profile associated with it, but these provide mostly flavor text and there are some questions that are simply left unanswered and a plotline or two that get completely lost in the shuffle.
Transistor is in no way bad, but it's easy to feel disappointed with it. The breakneck pace with which it presents itself and the abrupt ending make it feel almost rushed in some ways, even with as gorgeous as it is on the whole. If you're undecided on it right now, I'd say wait for a sale.

I write this after experiencing five hours of pure excellence in game design.
Transistor is an absolute beauty. I would go as far as calling it a work of art. The backgrounds and environments are lovely to look at. The music is at times upbeat, at times ambient, but always a joy to listen to. The vocals by Ashley Barrett make me just... melt. The story is told in an interesting way, and you feel like a part of it. I would recommend playing it alone for full immersion.
The game's combat mechanics are complex yet simple, allowing two different playstyles. The game can be played like Bastion, with full real-time combat, or you can plan out your moves and execute them all at once using Turn(). (my personal preference.) Functions (the game's moves) can be swapped at any "Access Point" and can stack onto other Functions for greater effectiveness.
I have extremely enjoyed my time with Transistor. Supergiant Games has hit another home run. Please, support this fine team of game developers and play this game. You will enjoy it very much. I know I have.

At the beggining of the game Silas Greaves walks into a bar and ends up telling the people at the bar the story of his past. As gameplay goes on he tells the story while you are playing and this really makes the game great because sometimes Silas will accidentally say something wrong and that will affect the gameplay, but he will correct himself, then the game rewinds and you play the game as the story really went. Papers, Please is one of those games that proves that a great idea, a dash of humor and a well-made/planned game can make anything into a fun experience. Checking documents for discrepancies has never been so entertaining until I decided to play this game. Let's start with the good. The combat is enjoyable for an MMO. The graphics are great. There's lots of story, if unfortunately a quantity over quality thing. Crafting is extensive. And that's all the praise I can think of for it, now the bad.
First and foremost, the level scaling is poorly implemented. It's sophisticated, it works, and it makes having a level system pointless. There is no sense of progression with the system, however there is a constant sense of regression as every level gained makes you weaker until you get level relevant gear. Crafting resources also scale to the player, which causes problems if you want to use a high level character for quick gathering. Honestly, the game would be more enjoyable if levels were removed entirely since they serve no purpose beyond making equipment obsolete.
The game mechanics revolve around the end game. Lvl's 1-50 are a thing to rush through as quickly as possible to get past what is now the worst part of the game, only after that all there is left is grinding more numbers.
Inventory management is atrocious unless you subscribe. If you enjoy crafting, forget it unless you are willing to pay an overpriced subscription fee. If you don't want to spend more time managing inventory than playing the game either pay up or stop looting.
Sharing resource nodes and treasure chests. Not all world loot is shared, but having to race other players to a chest or crafting resources leaves players resenting other players being in the game. Most modern games understand that forcing players to compete for loot does not endear them to the idea of playing together and cooperating, nor does it make the community friendly. Fortunately loot from kills and events are not shared and each player gets their own, but it is still a terrible oversight.
Story. The quantity over quality approach to quests and content combined with the mechanics revolving around the end game leaves players rushing through dialogue in order to check off the next quest. It doesn't help that the writing is verbose, bland, and repetitive (occasionally has its moments, but rarely) and does a disservice to all the animation and voice acting that went into the game.
The cash shop makes it feel more like a F2P with freemium options, with inventory management being the biggest offender. The cosmetics in the cash shop are well priced and have a decent variety, but then the ability to dye costumes is locked behind a subscription. Housing is a massive cash sink but is also easily ignored. Then the mounts all cost $10-20. Aside from a bit of price gauging, this could have been overlooked if it wasn't for the fact that dying costumes and crafting material storage are only available with an overpriced subscription. This is also a bit dishonest since the game
but in fact is balanced to be a miserable experience unless you subscribe.
Edit:
Just to clarify, I'm not against the idea of level scaling, but I believe the way it was implemented is terrible.
On subscriptions, more can be found here:
Basically the sub crosses the line and goes from enticing people to sub to punishing people if they don't.

Who knew mind numbing repetitive desk jobs in authoritarian regimes could be so affirming.
Your lottery won job as a border control officer needs you to screen people trying to gain access to your great nation and grants you power to decide the fates of the teeming thousands at the gates. Life is not easy and the job is no guarantee; you do your best to get yourself and your family better conditions as you stand between the state and terrorists, get entangled in anarchist plots and deliberate on taking that bribe or sending someones wife back home to their death.
You even start thinking about why you are doing what you are doing in real life. Just kidding! It's fun to catch people trying to outsmart you and then detain them by force. And its satisfying when taking a chance motivated by altruistic inclinations pays off. Thoroughly engrossing, Papers,Please expands the definition of computer gaming beyond your run of the mill shoot em ups and will get you interested in exploring more indie games.

Do you like paper? Hate people? This is the game for you! This thrilling, hyper-realistic paper pushing game includes miles and miles of paper-handling. From manuals, to passports, to municipally-issued identification slips, to photo-ids, to so much more! Not just paper, though; stamps. That's right, you get to STAMP your papers. Red and green colors! But mostly the red. Well, if you like the color red, it's a plus!
Not only that, you get the hate of an entire population (or so it feels) directed at you for denying them passage into the glorious Arstotzka. And you get to hate them back by denying them even more, those filthy heathens!
Well, to wrap this up in a way those who don't like reading will understand, (TL;DR:) 'Papers, Please' is a great game. Especially if you like paper.

Papers, Please perfctly mimics the Russian Revolution. Everyone is a suspect, lies, and bribes. Secret groups are trying to stop the corrupt government, and you're caught in the middle of everything. Not to mention that choices you make have lasting and dramatic effects that come down to moments of the most important choice: do you trust the man to come back later and let him through now, or refuse him? Do you spend money for your son's birthday present, or do you buy food and heat for your family for the day? Do you kill the terrorist, or the target of the suspicious group? This game is wonderful, stratgeic, and will leave you wondering about who you really are based on your moral decisions.

After playing 100+ hours of this game, I am very much split down the middle. This game had some very good positives.
-  The controls and interface are miles ahead of the first dark souls.
-  Being able to roll in any direction vs the up-down-left-right rolling is a big + for myself
-  Being able to warp bonfire to bonfire at the very beginning is an added bonus.
-  PvP is also a much easier to handle than DS1 and connecting with friends is insanely easier.
-  The graphics on the pc are very good especially with a graphics mod installed and I always had consistent
60fps.
The downside though is that the world of drangleic was much less intruiging than Lordran in so many ways.
- The world was dull compared to Lordran,
- Many of the npcs werent as lore friendly as DS1 and I never knew what their importance was other than the
main npcs,
- The bosses were just as forgetable as the npcs and were much easier to learn and beat than the bosses in DS1.
- Although DS2 has 3 new dlc areas, the one dlc addition in DS1 was much better quality and, for me, proves that
quality>quantity.
- The addition of soul memory was also another downside since it made who you interacted with in PvP
confusing.
- Getting soft-banned was always a concern since dang near anything could ban you. If you invade a player and
you see an item on the floor and get it, you run the risk of it being a modded weapon or item and you could get
banned.
For me, and its probably obvious from the pros and cons, DS2 was much better than DS2 as far as the game ran, how the interface was much easier to use, and some upgrades to how players controlled their characters. But this game's world was pretty boring and was pretty confusing with how some of the lore was handled. It seemed like to me DS2 focused too much on the mechanics and lost sight of what made DS1 so great, which was having a gorgeous world with very interesting and consistent lore, Bosses that were challenging to face even if it was your 100th time, and npcs that werent as boring as dishsoap.
If you like Dark Souls then DS2 is a good game and deserves a thumbs up, but I would definitely rank this game lower than Dark Souls for the reasons listed above.

An excellent open world survival FPS set in an alternative reality where a second nuclear disaster occurs at the Chernobyl nuclear power plant exclusion zone causing strange radioactive anomalies to appear and the wildlife to mutate in to horrific, twisted abominations.
The gunfights are tense and require you to make every shot count because the enemies don't stand in the same spot or hide behind boxes like in some FPS' (*cough cough* COD), they will hunt you down and kill you. They're VERY good at hunting you down and killing you.
The atmosphere is foreboding and oppressive and there's some genuinely frightening moments which you won't forget for a long time.
This is a 10 year old game so the graphics, textures and animations look pretty goofy by today's standards but there are a lot of great mods which are easy to find and install which make the game look pretty stunning.
Also be sure to create multiple saves and SAVE OFTEN, LIKE ALL THE FRIGGIN' TIME because this game will not hold your hand and it's very easy to screw yourself over if you don't have enough medical supplies or ammo and it's never fun to get 20 hours in to a game and realise you're going to have to load a save from 5 hours ago.

Well I beat the game, so let's update this review.
I played on master, I pushed myself mentally to try and continue on master, but couldn't do it.
So I set the game to novice, and wa-la, no more quick load simulating.
S.T.A.L.K.E.R: Shadows of Chernobyl is dripping with atmosphere and generally frightening times.
At no point was anything going on around that didn't serve the game world or the game mechanics. It's steeped in that traditional PC rpg meta-gaming of "if your know what you're doing"
Taking on 8+ guys is more than doable, "if you know what you're doing". Getting great gear, pushing forward and making quick progress is easy, "if you know what you're doing." You get the idea.
After beating it and getting past the "master" meme, It's become one of my favorites. The semi-open world gameplay keeps things free, but not pointless as you'll explore and then choose when to move the plot forward, which in turn opens up more of the game world.
All in all the underground segments are terrifying and immersive, the final parts are a fun-free for all and those endings are classics in and of themselves. If I had any criticism it would be it's not long enough. And the carry weight limit is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

The popularly accepted theory that Jazz stemmed from a simple combination of African rhythms and European harmony is in need of a little revision. Both African and European rhythms were employed. African music supplied the strong underlying beat (absent in most European music), the use of polyrhythms, and the idea of playing the melody separate from or above the beat. European music provided formal dance rhythms. Combined, these rhythms give Jazz its' characteristic swing. Likewise, the harmonies and musical ideas of both continents are present, the blue notes derived from the pentatonic scale, "call and response" and unconventional instrumental timbres of African music together with "conventional" harmonies and, most important, the formal structure of European music. The multiplicity of ethnic, cultural and musical conditions needed to spawn Jazz was thus unique to the United States, and specifically to New Orleans. The necessary philosophical impetus for Jazz, i.e. , democracy and freedom of individual expression supported by group interaction, are also American institutions.

There are few games that make us choke up; there are even fewer games that we take the time to play twice before we review. Transistor achieves both – it’s just that gripping.
Transistor is Supergiant Games’ latest game. True to form, it’s an isometric RPG, and it’s instantly recognizable as coming from the team behind Bastion. There are a lot of similarities between the two games, and considering how much we loved Bastion, that’s very much a good thing. Everything about the game screams Bastion, but Transistor always feels like its own game. The biggest difference between the two is the plot; Transistor tells the story of Red – a singer who has had her voice stolen – and her lover, whose soul now resides within the titular Transistor, your talking sword...
Read the full review over

Following up Bastion would be a hard act for anybody, so it can be a forgiven a bit that Transistor is what I'd call Supergiant Games' sophomore slump. It's a game that leans a little too heavily on the familiar, yet seems a bit unsure of how it wants to present itself as a separate new entity.
You've got your talking Transistor which functions as the game's narrator, you've got Jen Zee's unmistakably fantastic art direction, and you've got Darren Korb's trancey-blues fusion soundtrack, and all those elements come together fairly well for the most part. Transistor is a gem to behold and contains nothing but fantastic audio candy for days and days.
Unfortunately the gameplay and story lack the shine and polish Bastion had.
The combat is a good mixture of real-time and turn-based combat, allowing you to use skills at the press of a button or queue them up to unleash with certain timing. Customizability is a huge factor since every skill in the game can be active, support, or passive, and the combinations are almost endless. That said, with all the strategy a system like this could bring, it's fairly easy to bulldoze through almost all enemy encounters with a few of the skills you start with, and even easier once you start playing around with combinations. While discovering these ridiculous combinations is fun and rewarding though, it throws every bit of strategy the game promises and throws it out the window fairly early, and by the end of the game battles become tedious.
Transistor's storytelling takes a different approach to Basion's. You're immediately thrown into Transistor's world without much of an idea of what's going on and you're railroaded through the adventure at a Final Fantasy XIII, purely linear breakneck pace. The story does have a decent resolution, but the world, characters, and motivations of Transistor's cast are either too vague or hard to grasp. Everybody talks as if the player knows what's going on and there's not much expository dialog to help clear much up. Each skill you obtain has a character profile associated with it, but these provide mostly flavor text and there are some questions that are simply left unanswered and a plotline or two that get completely lost in the shuffle.
Transistor is in no way bad, but it's easy to feel disappointed with it. The breakneck pace with which it presents itself and the abrupt ending make it feel almost rushed in some ways, even with as gorgeous as it is on the whole. If you're undecided on it right now, I'd say wait for a sale.

I write this after experiencing five hours of pure excellence in game design.
Transistor is an absolute beauty. I would go as far as calling it a work of art. The backgrounds and environments are lovely to look at. The music is at times upbeat, at times ambient, but always a joy to listen to. The vocals by Ashley Barrett make me just... melt. The story is told in an interesting way, and you feel like a part of it. I would recommend playing it alone for full immersion.
The game's combat mechanics are complex yet simple, allowing two different playstyles. The game can be played like Bastion, with full real-time combat, or you can plan out your moves and execute them all at once using Turn(). (my personal preference.) Functions (the game's moves) can be swapped at any "Access Point" and can stack onto other Functions for greater effectiveness.
I have extremely enjoyed my time with Transistor. Supergiant Games has hit another home run. Please, support this fine team of game developers and play this game. You will enjoy it very much. I know I have.

I have a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ system (GTX680, I5 2500 K 3.30 GHZ, 8GB RAM). After reading through all the comments I expected that the game would run very slow - or not at all - on my PC. Now that the game is on sale I thought I would give it a try ....and it runs great, I am VERY suprised that my old system can display this gorgeous amount of detail...especially when something is blown up.
And the game is so much fun! I saw a lot of people comparing it to GTA. Imo you can't really compare these titles apart from the fact that you can drive all sorts of vehicles in a open world, because
GTA offers:
A great story, great characters, awesome drama
A VERY detailed and unique map, not a single spot seems to be looking the same
Decent driving physics, beautiful car models
Just Cause 3 offers:
Explosions, detonations, flames, people flying up into the sky all around you. THIS is madness.
A huge world to explore...with always repeating patterns of tasks, buildings and landscapes (which can partially be nice if you just want to relax).
The story will probably make you smile from time to time, but don't expect more.
In case anyone else want to try this: I simply turned down the water and shadow quality to low, turned off motion blur, and changed the resolution from the (for my system) recommended 1280x780 up to 1920x1080. Okay, if you would excuse me now please...just one more explosion. Just one more.

Having played this game on two platforms and loving it on both, I can easily say this is an absolute buy.  This is on par with Bound By Blood as possibly the best of the Call of Juarez series. As a complete revamp of the series story, this is a game you can pick up and play by itself without having played the other games(Which is how I first played it, although there is an easter egg featuring Ray from the original series and a coin of the original game's treasure making a cameo) and thoroughly enjoy. The game does feature some minor glitches, although one is particulary nasty as it occurs in the Arcade mode during one level of the mode causing you to have restart the level, but its not enough to ruin the game. The graphics of this iteration of CoJ are cel shaded, much like Borderlands 2 compared to the original, and the gameplay is more fast paced and over the top, with the concentration mode of the original games is gone, but the new concentration mode is much like Coj: The Cartel, but done in a much better way, with enemies being highlighted for you to see, and with bonus skills(Which work like typical rogue like games with you using skill points to gain new perks, again much like Borderlands) you can become unstoppable in the game, adding to the over the top factor. The story of the game is very humor filled, and will cause history buffs to raise an eyebrow, but the story does have a solid conclusion to explain the history variations of what the game claims happened, and it leads to a poignant ending, regardless of how you see the game.
If this game is in a sale its a must have! Its a great story telling game which is quite original and which I never seen before! the story is about 4-5 hours and you also have 2 more game modes!

S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Shadow of Chernobyl is an atmospheric post-apocalyptic FPS game.
If you don't have the patience or the time to read this, then know this, it's a diamond in the rough. It's just whether you're willing and ready to deal with the rough.
Let's start with the story:
You're a "The Marked One", a special type of person. I don't know anything more, really. I never learned it from the story and whether it was explained or not, it still explains the level of quality of the story. It's boring. It really is. I just zoned out and enjoyed the game instead.
The English voice acting ranges from mediocre to awful. After the first few hours I just switched the English voice-overs to Russian and I became more immersed and interested in the game.
As for the graphics, this game is a hit and miss. It's definitely dated, no question about that. It's the "realistic" type of graphics that games used around 2005-2008. Colours are mute and it's all pretty grim. But it works for this. The post-apocalyptic setting compliments this whole look of... uglyness and grim.
Not only are the textures appropriate for this type of game, so is the lighting. Being in the dark, hiding from the enemy, planning out how to take them out is perfect.
Imagine this: It's pitch dark, it's raining... a storm is here... Lightning lights up the area slightly. You find the appropriate cover that you can use later on and map the area in your head. You find the enemies by the lights of their flashlights and count them up. There's 8 of them. You start moving in, but suddenly some other loners (neutral stalkers) wander into the area. Whether it's accidentally or not, you don't know. Does it even matter? The enemies start firing at the loners, the loners shoot back. Should you help them? They are friendlies after all. You decide to just let them fight and hope that maybe a few of them die. Maybe a few more corpses to loot later... even if they are friendlies. You see the muzzle flashes and hear the gunshots. You see some flashlights drop and you know that some of the enemies have died. According to your estimates, 3 enemies have died. Perfect... 5 remaining. You start moving up and suddenly an enemy runs towards you. Have they spotted you? You run back to your cover, ready for a fight... but he just stops near your cover. An easy headshot. You kill the enemy. 4 remaining. Others rush towards you, you kill 2 more. Another jumps in your way, you kill him without a problem. In the distance, the last enemy remains. You start firing at him, he flinches and starts moving to the side. You try to kill him, yet he runs behind the ruin of a truck. You realize that there's a blindspot there thanks to a few pieces of cover lining up perfectly. You move up... keeping an eye on every possible location for the enemy. Suddenly, someone shoots you in the back and hits you once, you kill him. How'd he get there? You lower your guard and start looting the body... Suddenly another shot, you're hit and you drop to the ground... dead. Turns out you mistook one of the friendly bodies as the enemy's.
A simple planned out operation gone sour in an instant.
This is an actual experience that I had and that was the moment when I understood that I need to play more of this.
The gunplay's got an issue. It's too random. If I aim directly towards an enemy's head, then I'd expect to hit the enemy, not miss him with shots that go literally around the enemy instead of hitting him. That's pretty much gunplay in a nutshell. Also, pistols are really inaccurate and mostly unusable with iron sights.
The difficulty of the game is too low. I played on the second hardest difficulty. So, yeah, there's still the most difficult difficulty, but it doesn't matter, since it was higher than average. After the first third of the game it's pretty easy and it gets easier over time. One of the more difficult areas, an area where you kill a total of about 30 enemies becomes a simple shooting gallery. It's not difficult, the only difficulty is that the enemies are in strategic locations. But even that is ruined by the enemy's moronic A.I. which just leaves it or does whatever else.
All of the other mechanics in the game are just not worth mentioning and you should discover them on your own.
Overall
7/10

Papers, please at first glance looks like a boring simulator of a tedious job but the first impression couldn’t be anything but horribly wrong.

You can accept or decline people to pass through or not. The interesting thing is finding the errors in their passport. Finding errors in the start of the game was not interesting at first but as  the game progressed though it got more complicated and always mixed up the circumstances. This allowed for pretty interesting engagement.
This most obvious requirement of the game is to memorize rules,cities and symbols in order to properly do the job quickly and efficiently. You don’t need to be einstein or anything but it really does help your budget to be good at your job. Since the rules constantly change its best to know the basics through repetition so if a person forges it you are able to tell quickly and not get tricked.
If you screw up you get a citation which will eventually penalize you for making mistakes. Starting with 0 - 5 - 10 etc and constantly increasing. Sometimes its not about the quality of your work but rather the guilt of your heart when you pass someone with improper documentation because you would rather have that person succeed at what they told you then make them turn back.
There is a really gray area in this game where you have to make constant choices throughout the days between your family or strangers. These strangers mind you, weather telling the truth or not, can have their lives greatly effected on your decisions. Its up to you to decide who you prioritize, your family and reputation or strangers and their dreams.
There are npc’s that add more depth to the game from trying to decode cult-like messages to using your power to jail lots of people to make the officer more money to split with you.
How you proceed through the game will effect what ending will occur. In many situations it can happen sooner than later. The variety of endings and context is actually pretty good and not a blatant copy and paste of each other unlike a certain other game I rather not mention.
There is endless mode which allows you to select 3 categories timed, perfect, endless. The courses are basically difficulties and the higher you go max being 4 the harder it becomes to process people.
This also has steam leaderboards in case you want to compare yourself with friends but that would look rather silly wouldn’t it?  Hey, I am the best stamper of my steam friends group wooo!....

I have been looking for years for a hunting game this realistic and was lucky enough to find TheHunter before it was on Steam. Instead of animals being thrown at you left right and centre, you have to look, listen and track down that one animal until you can get that perfect shot. It can be quick or fast depending on your luck and skill. The graphics and sound are amazing and shots have to be carefully placed and don't just kill the animal straight away.
**Yes it costs to be able to hunt more than just Mule deer.** But to me it is worth every cent to get that full hunting experience that I have yet to experience in any other game.
If you are not a huge fan of hunting games or games that requite patience then this is not a game for you. But if you are after a game that will keep you focused and waiting for the thrill of that perfect shot for the perfect animal then this game is worth it.
If you are unsure play the free version, hunt a few deer and decide before paying (duh :P) If you find it worth you money then I assure you you will not be disappointed as the world and the animals you can hunt expands. Even better the world will keep on expanding, adding new reserves and animals that you get for free once you have paid for the initial subscription. As I said before, to me, this game is worth every cent and its wonderful to watch it grow as my skill to grow in this amazing world.

Transistor is developed from the people who did Bastion back in 2011. In my opinion, Transistor is one of the best indie game released in 2014.
In Transistor you play as a singer named Red that wield a talking sword, the game is set in a scfi style future. The game start off without giving a clue on what really happen around the place other than something really bad happened which is similar to Bastion. As you progess through the game, the story will start piece together quite nicely and conversation between Red and the sword are done through text in kiosk machines. The story narrate by the sword, it warns you about hazards around you sometimes.
The soundtracks of the game are beautifully made which I find it better than their previous game. The music suits the situation and it transition smoothly as the surrounding changes.
As for the gameplay part, the combat allows you to pause the game and plan your move. The number of move and attack you could make is depends on the energy bar at the top on the screen, the longer distance you move, the more energy it will consume and as for attacks, every attack has a different consumption. When you done planning your move, you'll probably notice everything is moving in a slow pace as she attacks them.  The energy bar takes a couple of seconds to recharge before next use.
The only weapon you use in the game is the sword, unlike Bastion which provide a nice arsenal of weapon which ranges from spears to mortar. Having one weapon doesnt make the game boring, there are lot of attack that you can choose from, if I'm correct they are called Functions in the game. You can choose up to 4 types of active Function, there some longer range ones like Breach or some which are able to change enemy to be your ally for a couple of seconds but it has to be done in a close range or calling an ally to help you and many more. The active function can be upgrade by merging them to makes thing more interesting, for example merging the long range attack and the ability to change your enemy to ally, whenever you attack using this function it will changes your enemy to be your ally while taking damage and attacking from a long range. There are other combination such as merging a bounce attack with the long range breach, that will produce a long range attack that could bounce off your enemy and attacks other enemy around the area. Each function could merge with additional 2 attacks but it start with 1 open upgrade slot, the second slot comes as an unlock.
If you chose not to use it as an upgrade or active function, it can be use as a passive skill. For example, choosing bounce attack as passive skills will give Red a shield to absorb damage. You could put up to 4 passive skill at 1 time but it starts with 1 passive skill slot while the others are unlocks. There is a limit of functions, upgrades and passive skill you can use at a single time, it is all depends on the number of energy bar (cant remember what they call it in game). Certain function takes up more bar than others, at most a single function could take it up to 4 bars. I believe the limit they include is to balance the game and to avoid having full set of overpowerd combination.
The enemy variety is pretty good, different enemy may require different approach on attacking them. There are a couple boss fights which are interesting (especially the last one).
Overall, I'll say Transistor is one of the best game release on 2014. It has great gameplay mechanics, awesome soundtrack and a rather interesting way of telling a story. If you are a fan of their previous game, you will definitely enjoy Transistor. The game is about 7 to 8 hours long, I complete mine in 8 hours and I remember there are people manage to finish it in 5 hours.
Beautiful game with one of the best soundtracks I've heard in a long time. Sweet combat, amazing visuals, and an awesome story. If you like story-driven RPGs, I'd definitely pick up Transistor.

Soda Dungeon quite fun actually. It is a breath of fresh air compared to the other clicker games that encourage Parkinson's Disease. Soda Dungeon's main objective isn't something novel, you hire adventurers to raid a dungeon to get gold to buy more soda to get more stronger adventurers to raid stronger dungeon levels to get more gold and the loop is infinite. You build your tavern in this order Soda Junkie --> Ruffian --> Thug --> Fighter --> Conjurer --> Healer --> Thief --> Knight --> Project Zero. The main draw of the game is that it follows the time-tested formula of adventuring while keeping it simple. However, it is an eternal grindfest.
Conclusion, try the game to know what it is but don't play for long. It's simple enough to play but my guess is that one will get bored as it's a repetitive, neverending loop. It is guaranteed to loop all the way to Dungeon Level 750 and above. Personally, I got bored at around level 50. The automation in this game is both its bane and boon.
1. Simple Adventuring
It's not complex.
1. Pay To Win
It is $0.99 each to unlock the various heroes and tavern attachments. This is very obvious from the start of the game. It is a cheat code for $0.99 each time.
2. Repetitive
Get heroes, dungeon, upgrade, rinse and repeat. Gets old after a while.
3. No Skill Builds
None at all. Each character doesn't need to build a skill tree. No special combos or anything.
4. No differentiated Mechanic / Class
Soda Junkie, Ruffian, Thug, Fighter, Conjurer . There is no sense of variety. The new units you get just get exponentially stronger. While there is a small difference between the Fighter and Conjurer due to the attack values and hit points, the Conjurer is far stronger due to her ability to equip 2 Items. E.g. Fighter (30 HP 7 Attack) vs Conjurer (29 HP 6 Attack)
5. VIP Buys
I believe it's just to scam people into paying the $0.99 for nothing. It's specifically timed after level 50 just for players who are willing to spend the time on it. I think it's a belief that after a certain amount of time invested, they can target these players to pay $0.99 as an upsell. The VIP items cost like 50,000,000 Gold in-game or $0.99.
6. Fake Bestiary
I thought there was a whole lof of monsters just like Pokemon. Imagine my disappointment when I saw the reskinned versions of the same monster. After level 50, every monster is just a different coloured version of a level 1-50 monster. E.g. The level 70 boss is just a blue version of the level 10 boss.
1. Automated Best Equipment Builds
No thinking required. There's always a better item to choose from. It saves a lot of thinking but it removes a bit of thinking.
2. Automated Combat
Automated so you can run it in the background while doing work. While smooth, are you playing a game at all?

Dead Mountaineer's Hotel is a game based on the novel of the same name by the Strugatsky brothers, the generally pretty great Russian sci-fi authors who also wrote books like Roadside Picnic, which was the basis of the movie which was in turn the basis of the STALKER series. I've never read this particular book, but I figured anything related to them couldn't possibly turn out that bad. I was horribly wrong, but I don't need to tell you that, because I doubt anyone was actually planning on buying this game to begin with. But I'm going to go over it anyways because I need a therapeutic rant session to recover from playing it.
The first thing you'll notice within five seconds of starting the game is that the voice acting is absolutely terrible. Just listen to the opening dialogue of the game, and you'll see what I mean:
. Well, actually the first thing you'll notice is that despite originally releasing in 2007 the game only runs in one resolution, and it's 1024 x 768 and cannot be changed, but still. There are one or two actors who border on decent, but for the most part the game sounds as if they hired a bunch of bums off the street and paid them in bread to do the voice acting for the game. It's kind of hilarious, and was mainly what kept me playing through the game, but it also made the story impossible to take seriously.
Luckily, there really isn't much story. Again, I've never read the novel this was based off of, but I highly doubt it went quite like this. You spent the first four or five hours of the game doing absolutely nothing relevant to the plot, mainly involving stupid puzzles like helping the hotel owner fix the room service call system that never gets used again, or choosing a dinner from various categories that doesn't cause the other guests to laugh at your choice (I don't know why having too many vegetables in your meal is grounds for making you redo a "puzzle", but what do I know?), or playing billiards with another character that isn't even really a puzzle so much as just a billiards flash game implanted into the game. Then in the last 20 minutes or so of the game the story finally starts, you talk to each of the hotel's residents, and then it ends, and the game explains the story to you.
As you might have gathered from that last bit, the store page is pretty misleading. It mentions "15+ hours of gameplay", but I finished it in less than 6 and I can't imagine it taking 15 hours unless you just get lost in the unnecessarily large hotel. The store page also makes it seem as if the hotel guests have AI routines and go about their own lives, hinting at a system something like how Deadly Premonition's characters go about their day, but the game doesn't have any sort of time system and the characters just move from place to place as you solve the puzzles like in any adventure game. I used to think RunAway was the worst point-and-click adventure game I'd ever played, but I'm not sure if anything will ever top this one.

Dead Mountaineer's Hotel is pure brilliance...knocked down a few pegs by some glaring flaws.  At its heart Dead Mountaineer's club is a beautiful, brooding, sophisticated, crime noir mystery.  The incredible artwork is supplemented by great music that eventually gets repetitive over time because there are only a few measures.  The story builds up quite a bit of suspense and intrique that strings the player along and leaves them wanting more.  The locations, while pretty much all within the confines of a dilapitated ski lodge are surprisingly numerous, though could possibly still stand to be supplemented.  Quirky characters, each of which has his/her own personality and self-interests coupled with a creepy environment that always hints at some form of potential danger on the horizon makes for a rather paranoid journey through the wash of clues and suspicious events the player has to sort through in figuring out how the crime took place, if there even was a crime.
Sounds like a masterpiece, doesn't it?  Well, not quite.  Unfortunately, there are a number of flaws that prevent the game from being the forerunner of the puzzle/adventure genre that it really aspires to be.  First, the pacing is odd.  There are moments of intensity while other moments leave the player wandering around with no real direction.  While freedom given to the player to solve some story elements in different orders in a way that actually allows for multiple story endings is a great addition to this game, there are some minor problems with the way the developers implemented this feature.  The player can actually break the game by doing something before doing another required task, which leads to some sort of missed cue in the game that stops the progression of the major game events.  This is probably the biggest problem with the game.  Another, lesser problem is that the game is slightly anticlimatic, partially because the major events in the game overshadow the ending, and partially because the game builds up so much suspense as the game goes on that we're expecting a bigger resolve toward the end of the game.
Being the adventure game fanatic I am, I still enjoyed the game enough to put more than 51 hours into it, but I don't think everyone would share my exuberance.  Given the flaws, I would recommend it for unbending fans of adventure/puzzle games.  At the same time, I would probably advise those who are new to adventure games and more casual adventure gamers to steer well clear of Dead Mountainer's Hotel.  For those types, there are plenty of other challenging adventure games that do not have the same pitfalls this one has.
In the end, I would rate this one at a solid 6.5 out of 10, because in the areas where it excels it does so gloriously.

This is a hilarious, excellent arcade shooter.  It's a wild-west shoot-em-up game in all its glory and it does a great job of dramatizing late-1800s frontier America in ridiculous, over-the-top ways.  The story is super short and isn't super solid, but a lot of that is, in part, due to Silas Greaves' own embellishments on the story.  I especially enjoyed it when his narration would switch tacks in the middle of the story and the game world would alter itself accordingly.  I was doing double-takes more than once when I would blow up and die, then realize it was part of the story and it would restart the narrative from a different angle.  Defeating the Coffeyville bandits from three different perspectives in three different situations was cool, too.
Enemies in this game are many and they're not very challenging.  On normal difficulty, you mow 'em down with hardly a scratch.  On hard difficulty, I still do a fair amount of mowing down, but I die a lot more too because the enemies' bullets do a lot more damage.  And checkpoints aren't tremendously numerous, so there's a little bit of incentive for you to hunker down behind a stagecoach or a rock and reload and take careful aim, because otherwise you might be playing the same bit over and over again.  I haven't played the "True West" mode (the same as "Legendary" difficulty or "1999 Mode" in other games - a reward for beating the story once through) but I'm sure it will be a fair challenge - you'll have to make lots of careful headshots and be very wary about sticking your head out from cover.
Overall, this game is a super fun time-waster when you've got 30 minutes to burn and want to shoot your way through a pack of lawless thugs or chew through a wave of arcade-mode foes.  Definitely recommended.

In a game such as Rome II Total War you cannot give an accurate review without a detailed account of the ‘Spear Brothers’, one of the most revered,  blood thirsty and - at times - gangrenous of all the units in this medieval role-play-simulation game. If the Brothers of the Spear were not written into the game, we would likely never have seen the likes of the Total War franchise; it is said that Tim Ansell, the mastermind behind Creative Assembly who developed the game in 1987, had a dream were the Suebian Spear Brothers came to him in the night, laden with documented plans for the creation of such a game series. Whether this is entirely true or not we cannot be sure, but we can be sure that the Spear Brothers will continue to inspire a generation of video game players, young, old and even those not born yet.
The Germanic tribe of the Spear Brothers is a tribe hardened by horrific war. At the time of Rome II, iron supplies - especially in West Germany - were very sparse. It is no surprise then that the Spear Brothers, the mighty warriors, were given priority of the metal for their dreaded ‘Spear Brother Spears’ or ‘framea’ in their own tongue. It is murmured in legend that the larger the man, the larger the spear. We have no reason yet to doubt this, according to the many geophys surveys that have been undertaken to find the truth of these giants of the battlefield.
It would be a crime to end this review without mentioning the battle cry of the Spear Brothers, due indeed to the fact that few have ever survived it. One account comes from a Briton monk, Jasper, who whilst riding Maurice, his donkey into battle, witnessed the most ferocious and worrisome cry he had ever heard from the mouths of the Brothers of the Spear who he was gradually trotting towards. He could see the blood spurting from the ears of his own brothers, drenching each other in crimson pain. The horses were bleeding too while they manically ran into each other. Jasper, who now believed he was entering the blood and fire occupied Seventh Circle of Hell, only survived because when he eventually reached the front line, all the Britons were dead and the Spear Brothers had gone back to their tribes with haste, blood thirsty for more combat with their own peoples.
The tale goes that Jasper lived the rest of his reasonably long life with Maurice, entrenched somewhere in the Aiguilles d'Arves in France, safe from the devilry of the Barbarians. It is said descendants of the Spear Brothers (SB) continue fighting, albeit virtually; if you are lucky enough to encounter one, be wary, hold fast and please remember ‘The Story of Jasper & Maurice’.

After playing Dark Souls 1 on the Xbox 360 and both loving it and hating it, I can safely say that Dark Souls 2 is a fantastic sequel... WHY? Well the game on PC looks absolutly amazing, and you can easily see this just by making your way to the Hub area, Majula. Next the combat is still very similar to Dark Souls 1 but with some new weapons and spells there are obviously new and cooler ways to dispose of anyone in your way. It is still hard at some points but not nearly as frustrating as the first game. Although you could say Dark Souls 2 is easier in comparison to the first game, the death penelty is well... harsh to say the least as it strips you of some of your health when you die which is annoying sometimes because I certainly found parts where I have no more Human Effigies (Kinda like Humanity from DS1). The boss fights are still very challenging and I was finding myself getting battered around by them multiple times although I suppose this is the learning curve of each boss as each time you die to those bosses you can begin to figure out the strengths and weaknesses. Again the boss fights are brilliant but some of the boss designs are not AS cool as the ones in Dark Souls 1 but some do look very unique and pretty cool like the Rotten boss for example.
The story in the game is fairly simple, go here kill the boss and move to the next area... simple as that BUT saying that would be a complete lie because From Software like to be cheeky trolls and hide things about the story, lore and even the characters in the game within the items you can pick up throughout Drangliec. This is the most intriging part of the story, most of it can be pure speculation because hardly any of it is really told through proper dialogue. Even though that sounds like a bad thing, I think that is a really good way to tell it as you could argue that there is no right or wrong answer to what you think, to some extent.
Overall Darks Souls 2 is a fantastic game and needs to be played by anyone who played and loved the first Dark Souls or should be played by anyone who would love to see a challenge in gameplay. I would rate it a 9/10
