I have almost 800 hours on NMRIH.  It's one of my favorite games.  One of the things that has kept me coming back was the difficulty of the game.  I really like how easy it is to die.  It adds a weird, extra element of fear that you don't get with other horror games I've played.  I know this kind of dynamic exists in other games, but for some reason in this one it's more noticably pronounced.  For example, you can kill a lot of zombies with a sledgehammer, but eventually it'll become too hard to swing, and look... you've backed yourself down an alley.  Out of breath.  Looks like you'll have to wait until you can swing again.  Your arms are stubborn and refuse to move.  All those faces, though.  Emotionless like the face of a Victorian doll. You don't need to see these things grimace to know their intentions.  Always hungry, always eating, never stopping.  You swing again and two more go down!  Wow!  You're doing great!  Though in your triumph you didn't notice that more faces have turned down the alley to join the throngs of hungry mouths.  You think "♥♥♥♥ that, not today!" as you pull out your pistol and empty a clip into their rotted gaping maws.  How staggering it is to see those horrors seemingly absorb all the 22 rounds you had to give.  Always eating, never stopping!  "♥♥♥♥!" You pull out your rainy day shotgun and they start going down like they would at the end of a horrible nightmare.  Two by two you pile them up until none stand between you and your exit.  Heart racing you survey the destruction.  You can taste the smoke from the shotgun in the roof of your mouth, as well as the rotted gore coating the alleyway.  A distant moan breaks your momentary sense of securtiy, and you start to move, but you cant...  You look downwards as you feel the crawler bite into your boot.  Click.  No saving grace from your insurance policy.  No matter, you quickly reach for your sledge and swing it at the monster.  "NOTHING!?"  You attempt to get closer by bending towards it, and you're frozen!  "WHY CAN'T I BEND DOWN?!" you scream to yourself.  You see more faces turn down the alley.  Your fate sealed, you start to wonder as you're eaten feet first, "If only I could have crouched... Why was mankind broken in this way?  I wanted... I wanted to live...  I'm sorry Samantha, be strong!  Daddy's not going to be here to protect you..."

The popularly accepted theory that Jazz stemmed from a simple combination of African rhythms and European harmony is in need of a little revision. Both African and European rhythms were employed. African music supplied the strong underlying beat (absent in most European music), the use of polyrhythms, and the idea of playing the melody separate from or above the beat. European music provided formal dance rhythms. Combined, these rhythms give Jazz its' characteristic swing. Likewise, the harmonies and musical ideas of both continents are present, the blue notes derived from the pentatonic scale, "call and response" and unconventional instrumental timbres of African music together with "conventional" harmonies and, most important, the formal structure of European music. -Animations are few, your character just moves forward a tiny bit when you attack, use abilities, etc.
-The shopkeeper falls behind a little bit when you go out to the dungeons, you've already found Coral Armor, and he just now wants to start selling Turtle Shields.
-You can take the Shopkeeper, Gladiator, and the Wizard with you, you just have to hand over that $$$.
TL;DR
-Optimized from a mobile game (Best one out there so far)
-Completely free!
-Animations are a bit boring.
-Really catchy music.

A game that covers the spectrum.
I had read the reviews and wasn't expecting much, but when I saw the game on sale for less than 4 dollars I thought I would give it a go. I am glad I did.
Some aspects of this game are really great, others are awful.
The artwork is fabulous and it helps the game exude atmosphere. It reminded me of 'Evil Under the Sun' with a bit of 'Black Mirror 1' and 'Syberia' thrown in, but in the mountains. The hotel was a dream to explore as it is huge and would be a fantastic place to stay. I loved the short sections outside, with the snow falling. The artists did a fab job.
Difficulty is not too tough. I only needed to check a walkthrough once, when I couldn't fathom how to lure the owner out of his office.
Kaisa is certainly very cute.
The music is lovely for the most part, though a couple of horrendous rock pieces come in at odd moments and not just when entering the room of a particular character.
Gameplay is ok, with a clear changing cursor.
Now for the bad. The story  is a real slow boiler, which is a good thing as it sets the scen beautifully and allows us to get to know the characters. However, when the main events finally happen, the story just ends. I had the most nonsensical ending  to a game ever and though there are different endings none make a lot of sense, with an absolutely ridiculous twist at the end. So the game takes a good few hours to brew and then when something big finally happens, it ends. Crazy. It is like the developers suddenly lost interest to continue the plot.
The translation is poor, though understandable. Sometimes it appears that characters give a comnpletely different answer to the question being asked. The voicees being better than the inaccurate subtitles. It's crazy that the developers didn't get someone who can understand proper English to check the translation. The character voices range from ok (the main character, Kaisa, and Olga) to horrendously bad (Alec, for instance). Also the voices are obviously done with the actor not having a clue as to the context in which they are supposed to be said. A basic error.
So, I am going to recommend this title as parts of this game are very enjoyable indeed, though the ridiculously abrupt and silly ending ruins the experience in the end.

I got curious to play the S.T.A.L.K.E.R. games after watching Andrei Tarkovsky's Stalker movie and I have to say that it was pretty funny to see how much different in tone and aesthetic those two adaptations are.
Which is actually pretty cool, seeing how you can take a premise and create such different and distinctive experiences in different mediums.
In S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Shadow of Chernobyl you take the role of a, conveniently so, amnesiac who finds himself on the outskirts of Chernobyl, where for some reason there is a series of supernatural phenomenons occuring  and numerous factions fight against each other in what feels like a post-apocalyptic scenario. The only information you have of your former  self is a target you were in charge of killing, so you go around helping other people in exchange for his location, in an attempt to figure out who you are and what is your purpose.
In terms of gameplay and world, one cant help but notice how similar it is to the Fallout 3d games. Most of your time will be spent wandering a very dangerous wasteland being hunted down by bandits, mutated wildlife and the occasional radiation. Safe places are few and far between, with every other single point of interest in your map being for the most part filled with enemies to kill.
Unlike Fallout though, really all you will be doing in this game is killing people and not much else inbetween. The sidequests in this game really arent the most interesting part of the game like the Fallout games, and they boil down to pretty much fetch quests where you are tasked to walk to a specific area, kill someone or something, and backtrack to get your reward. So much so that I ended up not doing them because they simply werent interesting and you also do a big amount of killing in the main quest. The sidequests also have time limits which create a weird sense of urgerncy that doesnt benefit this type of game at all, making you run across a very huge map just to get your reward.
As for said killing, i have to say it's pretty satisfying and fun. You arent superman in this game, which means that enemies can kill you very easily and fast if you arent taking cover and being smart about how you approach them. Every single battle in this game is incredibly tense and demanding and I was shocked by how great the AI is. Enemies will constantly take cover and work together to flank you and surprise you from every corner, and stealth becomes a must to survive to the end in this game.
The gunplay is no Counter Strike, but that actually works in the  game's favor because it reinforces your helpnessness and how methodical and cautious you must be in this world. Call of Duty this ain't.
The game also contains a survival component, where you must fill your inventory with items like food , health packs, and medicine that cure radiation poison. Personally I found this gameplay aspect shallow, since It always felt like I was simply ticking a checkbox to prevent hunger or bleeding. There was never a point where I desperately needed a rare item to survive.
You can however ♥♥♥♥ yourself over if you arent careful with your armor, since the latter areas of the game are filled with radiation that will drop your health really fast making it impossible for you to make progress. My experience with the final quest was incredibly frustrating due to my suit being in poor condition by the end of it and every single spot in the map having high radiation that would deplete my health very fast, while having to deal with enemies at the same time.
The strongest aspect of STALKER however, is without a doubt the atmosphere. What a bleak and dreadful place this is. There is nothing more eerie than walking on an empty factory with the wind blowing and the skies filled with grey clouds.
There are certain areas of this game that feel straight out of a horror game, especially when the strange phenomenons start to happen.
It masterfully eases you into it as you get closer to the Chernobyl nuclear facility.  Trees start to get twisted, the green starts to get brownish, radiation starts to get more dangerous. It really makes you feel awful, in a good way.
While the game certainly shows its age and has some flaws, I definitely understand why people adore this franchise, and even if I found the story to be uninteresting and the sidequests dull, you should definitely try it for the combat and atmosphere, those alone make it all worth in my eyes.

“Even if I don't cry when I'm sad, I might do it when I'm happy. That's just the kind of person I am.” - Nagisa Furukawa
CLANNAD is arguably one of the most famous and influential visual novels out there. It's earned a cult following for sporting some of the saddest, most bittersweet stories guaranteed to pull your heartstrings and wring your tear ducts. Yet, it's not all melancholic gloom. The story is beautifully harmonised with cute moments of moe and romcom. The Kickstarter for CLANNAD's English translation fetched a whopping $500,000 USD, the highest on record for a visual novel as far as I know. That should stand as a testament to how many people loved the game, despite it being more than a decade since its Japan release.
The game follows a wide cast of heroines with numerous possible routes, including the soft-spoken introvert Nagisa, tomboyish prankster Kyou, studious beauty Kotomi and innocent loli Fuuko. Every character is memorable and unique in their own way.
One of the most contentious aspects of the game is its art. For most, it's something that they'll either love or hate. I'll admit that I didn't enjoy the art too much at first, having been spoiled by the anime studios of 2010 and beyond, but it eventually grew on me. If I had to describe the art I'd say that it's unpolished, but endearing, much like the art of Higurashi When They Cry.
(Random fun fact: In The World God Only Knows, Katsuragi Keima's 2D waifu "Yokkyun" was based off Nagisa's artwork from CLANNAD.)
Another controversy was raised over the price of the game upon its Steam release. Commanding a $50 price tag for a game over 10 years old?!
While the pricing is undeniably steep, what most critics fail to notice is that CLANNAD is the longest visual novel on Steam by far, with no titles coming close except perhaps Muv-Luv. The game easily takes 50 hours to complete, and I must applaud Sekai Project for coming up with a quality, error-free English translation of so much text. Also, the game was released in its entirety, and not in episodic/chapter format unlike numerous other VN titles on Steam, a practice which I'm very keen to support!
Overall, if you enjoyed the anime (or even if you didn't), consider getting this VN for a much more fleshed-out story and some unbelievably immense Niagara Feels.

Of S.T.A.L.K.E.R.:
Shadow of Chernobyl
First off I would like to address the elephant in the room when talking about this game and that is the modding community. Personally I am a big fan of the modding community for this game and I think they've done a good job at making this mess of a game look like something thats worth giving a damn. But this is a review about the base game only.
Firstly, I'm going to have to refrain anyone reading this from commenting on my review only to throw insults my way. If you are going to read on, best be prepared to argue your points against mine. Ready? Here we go!
The story of STALKER Shadow of Chernobyl is pretty simple. You wake up with no recollection of your past and with nothing to your name other than the clothes on your back and a PDA with one simple message on it "Kill Strelok". The world you wake up in is known as the exclusion zone, an area around the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant cordoned off by the government after two disastrous events occured here. The first of which was the famed meltdown in the 80's, but the second came in 2005 in the form of an explosion. Afterwards, the zone began to change in weird ways. STALKERS as they begun to call themselves began to enter the zone in hopes of finding riches in the form of artifacts, anomalous objects with incredible scientific value that also bestow subtle powers upon those who hold them. As you work your way up into this world you discover that this Strelok fellow was trying to get to the center of the zone, to the power plant itself. Rumour has it in the center of the plant is something called the wish granter, a being of great power that will grant any wish. It is however heavily guarded by the Monolith and a nefarious device known as the brain scorcher. After realizing that you are strelok and acquire some nifty psy-blocking device, you go to the brain scorcher and disarm it allowing stalkers from all over to finally get into the center of the zone. Upon reaching the plant itself there are two ending paths with a few alternate endings amongst both of them: The false route brings you to the wish granter and whatever wish you give it (based on in-game stats you've acquire) will only end up killing you. The true route will bring you to the C-Consciousness, the route of why the zone is the way it is. They are a group of scientists who have linked themselves telepathically through a large machine, altering the "noosphere" of the zone and affecting almost every facet of it. You can either destroy it or join them.
This game fails on many different levels, but let's start with the largest problem of them all which is of course, the story. I have never seen a game so heavily influenced by Atheist beliefs in my life! I've read a good amount of science fiction and I can safely say that this is the most influential piece of Atheist propaganda that I've ever seen.
- The first point I would like to make is how it straight up mocks the idea of consciousness being the product of our soul, but rather the product of some crudely explained layer around the earth that makes up our "psychic" energy. They put so much effort into trying to explain this idea that if they had a particularly charismatic speaker to pitch it to people, they could have easily created a cult of 10,000 strong and made them all drink the kool-aid. This kind of thinking doesn't belong in fiction.
- The second point is that the C-Consciousness is also tampering with the creations of god, altering their appearance to look more like demons. They are as people call it, "playing god".
The gameplay itself is relatively alright, but as much as I do enjoy a good gun I find myself wondering about the morals of my character that I am playing and the reason for why I am causing such violence. Because the narrative in this game absolutely disgusts me, I made up my own story as I went along. The game is awfully buggy however, which is why I applaud the modding community so much for fixing it up. Unfortunately they could do nothing for the story.
So that concludes my review of STALKER Shadows of Chernobyl. Thanks for reading it and I hope you enjoyed reading my thoughts. Like I said earlier, if you would like to comment on my review I ask you to be civil and respect my opinion, thanks.

I absolutely loved Bastion, so I was losing my mind while waiting for Super Giant's next game. They did not disappoint.
I expected to have a beautiful art style and a great soundtrack along with fun gameplay. The art is gorgeous and the character model for the player also looks good. That was my one complaint about Bastion, because The Kid looked strange during gameplay, despite looking cool in concept art and cut scenes. But Transistor looks beautiful all across the board. The soundtrack is also incredible and perfectly fits the game.
The gameplay is something that I have never played before. You have the option of fighting as an action game, which works well against small enemies. However, against tougher enemies, you will be killed easily fighting this way. Instead, you use a system called functions where you stop time and plan out what moves you will use. This system offers you a limited number of moves and makes this more of a strategy game compared to Bastion. While this slows down gameplay, it is still fun and tense.
All in all, I highly recommend this game to everyone. Anyone who enjoyed Bastion should absolutely give it a try.

I'm going to start this off by saying I wasn't a fan of Bastion. I had played the first hour or so of it, but it never hooked me. This game though...this game hooked me.
The art style is gorgeous with its art deco sci fi aesthetic and cyberpunk influences. The story isn't given to you all at once or in a few places with massives amounts of information. Instead, it's given to you in packages through various means, all of which is effectively delivered. Especially effective is the voice acting. Throughout the game, you are really only given one voice to listen to, that of the person inside the Transistor, but it never feels like a game empty of people. The voice is warm and treats the player as if they already know each other, and it makes you want to listen to what he has to say.
The gameplay is intriquing as well. You can play it real-time, as if it Diablo or a similar game, or you can activate Turn() mode, which pauses the game world allowing to play your actions ahead of time. It's a satisfying feeling to be able to tally the hitpoints up before hand to know that the enemy will be dead very shortly and then actually see it happen.
Overall, I'd say this is a game worth getting, and if you have doubts as to that, wait for the inevitable sale and buy it then. This game was hooked from the very beginning, kept my interest, made me want to play it again, and even made me want to revisit Bastion just so I can see what else this game developer has done.

Just finished the game.
There're a couple of small ways in which this game tries a little too much to be like Bastion, but honestly I have almost exclusively positive things to say about it.
The gameplay is based on mixing and matching a set of abilities that have different effects when used as active skills, upgrades for other active skills, or passive skills.  The sheer magnitude of options available is both impressive and carefully tuned so that it doesn't really become overwhelming.  The delivery of the story and setting is extremely varied and the devs were willing to allow the player to piece things together or his or her own with the fragments earned from how skills are used as well as the main narrative.
And as one might expect, both the music and art are absolutely phenomenal.  Not only are they amazing in their own right, but each compliments the setting and narrative of the game very effectivley.  Can't say I mind having a heavier focus on Ashley Barrett's vocals either.  Logan Cunningham's voice acting performance feels a little awkward at first, but as you get to know the character, grows to be as great as ever.
While the game feels a little shorter than Bastion was (and a little shorter than I'd hoped), the pacing is very reasonable and the experience is very dense with impressive art, music, and play.  I would have liked a bit more, though.
The only other complaint I might have is actually only partially a complaint:
There are tons of references to programming syntax in the names and descriptions of various parts of the game.  While those were really cool to me (a programmer), I feel like they could be odd or confusing to others.  Of course, I can't really speak from that perspective.
Overall, I thoroughly enjoyed Transistor and I'm looking forward to my second playthrough.  If you'll excuse me, I'm going to go buy the soundtrack.

New Total War Players; If you are thinking of getting into the total war series i would suggest Attila unless you really want the Roman era  Buy this on sale if your looking for an army management game with strategic battles.  It can be complex at first but extremely satisfying when you overcome difficult battles.  Diplomacy is in the game but it isnt complex or intelligent enough to make it seem real.   You make peace, you trade, you WAR.    Your goal in this game is to conquer the world, not build the first space ship.
Old Total War Players;   I am disgruntled that they haven't implemented any successful type of unit movement or physics system in the way units interact with eachother or the environment;  Managing units climbing castles, or on the castle walls is a nightmare.   The physics of the armies charging into eachother in Attila (and all recent TW entries) seems to have taken a step back from the Medieval 2 version where two giant armies charging into eachother would create a thunderous explosion.   Now the armies seem to stutter step their way into the opposing army and then they kind of stand around and watch eachother while a few guys kill eachother.   I enjoy these games enough to keep coming back but never until the prices are 50+% off.
Total War has an expensive DLC regime that is expensive and "unfriendly."   There is something wrong at Creative Assembly when new entries take a step back in many areas while they still can't improve on some of the weird problems that have been around for 10+ years like wall battles during seiges, general unit movement and interaction, and unsophisticated AI.  I would be more forgiving AND loyal if they didn't turn around and fleece me for DLC that doesnt really improve anything.... its just a new coat of paint

I have almost 800 hours on NMRIH.  It's one of my favorite games.  One of the things that has kept me coming back was the difficulty of the game.  I really like how easy it is to die.  It adds a weird, extra element of fear that you don't get with other horror games I've played.  I know this kind of dynamic exists in other games, but for some reason in this one it's more noticably pronounced.  For example, you can kill a lot of zombies with a sledgehammer, but eventually it'll become too hard to swing, and look... you've backed yourself down an alley.  Out of breath.  Looks like you'll have to wait until you can swing again.  Your arms are stubborn and refuse to move.  All those faces, though.  Emotionless like the face of a Victorian doll. You don't need to see these things grimace to know their intentions.  Always hungry, always eating, never stopping.  You swing again and two more go down!  Wow!  You're doing great!  Though in your triumph you didn't notice that more faces have turned down the alley to join the throngs of hungry mouths.  You think "♥♥♥♥ that, not today!" as you pull out your pistol and empty a clip into their rotted gaping maws.  How staggering it is to see those horrors seemingly absorb all the 22 rounds you had to give.  Always eating, never stopping!  "♥♥♥♥!" You pull out your rainy day shotgun and they start going down like they would at the end of a horrible nightmare.  Two by two you pile them up until none stand between you and your exit.  Heart racing you survey the destruction.  You can taste the smoke from the shotgun in the roof of your mouth, as well as the rotted gore coating the alleyway.  A distant moan breaks your momentary sense of securtiy, and you start to move, but you cant...  You look downwards as you feel the crawler bite into your boot.  Click.  No saving grace from your insurance policy.  No matter, you quickly reach for your sledge and swing it at the monster.  "NOTHING!?"  You attempt to get closer by bending towards it, and you're frozen!  "WHY CAN'T I BEND DOWN?!" you scream to yourself.  You see more faces turn down the alley.  Your fate sealed, you start to wonder as you're eaten feet first, "If only I could have crouched... Why was mankind broken in this way?  I wanted... I wanted to live...  I'm sorry Samantha, be strong!  Daddy's not going to be here to protect you..."

Fun times, with a few issues.
Gameplay-wise, the core game is excellent. Combat is really satisfying and the controls are fantastic if you use a controller.
Cash shop stuff is largely just "convenience" sort of stuff. Cosmetics & exp boosts, etc. The only mildly pay-to-win thing is an Enchant Scroll that adds a minor stat boost reforge to your hats.
The paid VIP service in the form of their Token thing feels pretty necessary to enjoy the game at its fullest, but you can buy a token for a reasonable amount of in-game currency like Wildstar or EVE.
The art style is pretty cool, and the maps and character/monster art are absolutely beautiful.
They brought on the SoundTEMP guys from Ragnarok Online for some of the BGM, and it's pretty nice.
Not a lot of the tracks are stand-out, but they create a great atmosphere and are generally pleasant.
Gold sellers continue to be an issue; there's significant gold spam in the chat, and the earlier maps occasionally have a big cloud of killstealing bots running around. They've added a "Report bot" feature to the in-game right click menu, so hopefully they can put a few interns on bot duty reviewing reports.
Gold sellers are also the direct cause of the game's other issue: considerable restrictions on player trading. You can't actually directly trade silver to another player, you can only spend it on the auction house. Non-token-users can't trade with others at all outside the market. They say they're working on improving this, and they aim to allow non-token-users to trade with token-users in the near future.
The coolest part of the game, hands down, has to be the crazy class system. As you rank up, you build your character from an increasingly large pool of different class options. There are 4 main "archetypes", and each archetype has (currently) 12-13 different classes to pick from at R7.
As you build a character, you create it from a combination of 3-6 different classes. At each rank up, you can either double-down on your current class to unlock better skills for it, or switch to a new one. The number of choices is kind of staggering. The available variety keeps there from being a single cookie-cutter "best" build for a given archetype. It's important to let go of that compulsion of "MUST OPTIMIZE" and just pick what you think you might like.
That said,
, so you may wish to plan your class progression ahead of time, based on what you want to do with your character in the endgame.
Overall, Tree of Savior is incredibly promising, and if they keep gold farmers from ruining the game I expect it to provide an excellent amount of fun character-building gameplay. Unlike lots of other MMOs, it's a lot less about "Rush to the level cap so you can do the endgame content twice a day", and more about the "journey." A lot of focus on the character building and leveling experience.

The people who criticized the game for losing the logical and physically consistent connections between areas definitively have a point. There was nothing reminiscent of visualizing the two bells you have to ring high up in a church tower and far down in the gutter below it, nothing as brilliant as when you go down the elevator in Undead Parish and realize that everything is connected and nothing as awe inspiring as climbing up the trap infested Sen’s Fortress to face the gods themselves in Anor Londo.
That being said, even without those moments, Dark Souls II is the most memorable game I have played all year and the game I have played the most (100 hours ps3 + 60 hours PC). The increased prevalence of bonfires and the early availability of free teleportation between bonfires were controversial additions, but I think there is something to be said about how these changes encouraged the player to move forward instead of turtling behind farming strategies in the early areas.
Sure, there was definitely less fear about losing your progress or being locked into an impossible situation, which made exploration less exciting compared with Dark Souls. The design in Dark Souls utilized this fear masterfully to emphasize the early well-designed areas as the foundation of the game, but also to hide the throwaway nature of some of the later areas for most players who never dared to go that far or for the other large group who hastily made it through the areas just because of the heightened tension. The design in Dark Souls II only utilized fear in compartmentalized chunks between the many safe zones, but there were more levels to explore that were still more consistent quality wise.
In a sense, Dark Souls expertly toyed with player emotions to make the world seem a bit more epic than it really was, while Dark Souls II encouraged the player to move forward and explore every detail of a truly massive world. I am not sure which one I prefer, but against the generally weak competition this year, Dark Souls II stands as the uncontested game of the year for me.

I really enjoy the core mechanics of this game but it's honestly being choked by lacking some very basic MMO features. This is caused by either cash shop nonsense, futile attempts at stopping bots, or a combination of both.
There is no trading. Not unless you use a token, which costs around $20 and only applies for 30 days. And even then, you have a finite amount of trades, and they only work with OTHER TOKEN USERS. And they DAMAGE THE ITEM'S POTENTIAL, meaning you can only trade it so many times without it being DESTROYED.
This means I, a DPS swordsman, am stuck with 3 staves in my inventory (because the loot sorting is random), while my mage friend has two scimitars. Both of which would be upgrades for the right class. But since we don't want to pony up extra money, those items are functionally useless unless you want to attempt a pseudo-trade on the market.
This is meant to stop gold traders and their bots, but the game is nonetheless full of them. You can't go into town, even on Orsha (the less populated server), without three alts standing there spamming links to a gold selling site at any given time.
THERE IS ALSO NO TRADING BETWEEN YOUR OWN CHARACTERS UNLESS YOU BUY THE $20 TOKEN. And it acts as if you're trading with another person: only allows you to trade ONE SLOT at a time (log on.. log off.. log on.. log off..), takes away from your trade limit, and ALSO DAMAGES THE ITEM'S POTENTIAL. And 'untradeable' items such as realmoney hairstyles are not tradeable between characters, as far as I know. Which means if you want to delete a character but have something valuable yet untradeable on it... you're out of luck, aren't you?
But honestly my biggest qualm isn't even the trading. It's the fact that skill resets cost realmoney and stat resets aren't even possible ingame without the $50 founder's pack (in which case you get One. Just the one). There are a TON of classes and skills and some of them are COMPLETELY USELESS right now. You chose one on accident, or just thought it sounded cool? Hope you like paying money to fix the mistake, or remaking your entire character.
Considering level cap is over 200 and this is a grindy mmo, as well as the fact that skills are constantly going to be being rebalanced, that is completely unreasonable. It is super easy to screw up your character permanently with no recourse. Skill resets only give your skillpoints back, too, they don't undo your class changes - once you swerve into Barbarian, there's no going back without remaking. I'm totally fine with skill resets costing money... but for god's sake, make it INGAME MONEY. This is a basic feature. I should not have to pay real money if a skill that defines my build gets nerfed.
A game with class diversity as a highlight should include the ability to reset and freely play with all of the different options, rather than expecting a player to carefully plot out a build beforehand and hope to god they don't get nerfed, don't you think?
The graphics are gorgeous, the game plays well and a lot of the combat is genuinely satisfying. And the class system is a really interesting concept. The staff has proven they're willing to work with the community to fix the problems, even if they're a little slow about it. But I would recommend waiting until it goes f2p at the end of the month. I can't tell anyone to spend money on this game when it has this many dealbreakers that are really simple, reasonable things to expect in an MMORPG.
We shouldn't be punished for really simple things like 'picking the wrong skill' or 'wanting to trade an item to my other character' and forced to pay money for them.

'Papers, Please' provides players with the most unique gaming experience since the launch of the PC Minecraft beta. Fascinatingly different, and surprisingly intense, 'Papers, Please' entertains in a way most games fail to even come close toward.
Simple, yet challenging, this game offers tons of replay value with new elements of gameplay being brought into the game constantly. Dark, mature and enriching, the cold war esque feel of the game is riveting and depressing. A fair amount of memorable characters make their way into a simple yet endeering plot that will captivate you. Elements of survival also help keep the tension high as the life of your family and those around you are threatened through various forces.
'Papers, Please' is unique, refreshing, grim and wonderfully cruel. You'll question your own morals as you are forced to hold the lives of strangers in your hand. Easily one of the best games of 2013. Wildly underappreciated.

Of S.T.A.L.K.E.R.:
Shadow of Chernobyl
First off I would like to address the elephant in the room when talking about this game and that is the modding community. Personally I am a big fan of the modding community for this game and I think they've done a good job at making this mess of a game look like something thats worth giving a damn. But this is a review about the base game only.
Firstly, I'm going to have to refrain anyone reading this from commenting on my review only to throw insults my way. If you are going to read on, best be prepared to argue your points against mine. Ready? Here we go!
The story of STALKER Shadow of Chernobyl is pretty simple. You wake up with no recollection of your past and with nothing to your name other than the clothes on your back and a PDA with one simple message on it "Kill Strelok". The world you wake up in is known as the exclusion zone, an area around the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant cordoned off by the government after two disastrous events occured here. The first of which was the famed meltdown in the 80's, but the second came in 2005 in the form of an explosion. Afterwards, the zone began to change in weird ways. STALKERS as they begun to call themselves began to enter the zone in hopes of finding riches in the form of artifacts, anomalous objects with incredible scientific value that also bestow subtle powers upon those who hold them. As you work your way up into this world you discover that this Strelok fellow was trying to get to the center of the zone, to the power plant itself. Rumour has it in the center of the plant is something called the wish granter, a being of great power that will grant any wish. It is however heavily guarded by the Monolith and a nefarious device known as the brain scorcher. After realizing that you are strelok and acquire some nifty psy-blocking device, you go to the brain scorcher and disarm it allowing stalkers from all over to finally get into the center of the zone. Upon reaching the plant itself there are two ending paths with a few alternate endings amongst both of them: The false route brings you to the wish granter and whatever wish you give it (based on in-game stats you've acquire) will only end up killing you. The true route will bring you to the C-Consciousness, the route of why the zone is the way it is. They are a group of scientists who have linked themselves telepathically through a large machine, altering the "noosphere" of the zone and affecting almost every facet of it. You can either destroy it or join them.
This game fails on many different levels, but let's start with the largest problem of them all which is of course, the story. I have never seen a game so heavily influenced by Atheist beliefs in my life! I've read a good amount of science fiction and I can safely say that this is the most influential piece of Atheist propaganda that I've ever seen.
- The first point I would like to make is how it straight up mocks the idea of consciousness being the product of our soul, but rather the product of some crudely explained layer around the earth that makes up our "psychic" energy. They put so much effort into trying to explain this idea that if they had a particularly charismatic speaker to pitch it to people, they could have easily created a cult of 10,000 strong and made them all drink the kool-aid. This kind of thinking doesn't belong in fiction.
- The second point is that the C-Consciousness is also tampering with the creations of god, altering their appearance to look more like demons. They are as people call it, "playing god".
The gameplay itself is relatively alright, but as much as I do enjoy a good gun I find myself wondering about the morals of my character that I am playing and the reason for why I am causing such violence. Because the narrative in this game absolutely disgusts me, I made up my own story as I went along. The game is awfully buggy however, which is why I applaud the modding community so much for fixing it up. Unfortunately they could do nothing for the story.
So that concludes my review of STALKER Shadows of Chernobyl. Thanks for reading it and I hope you enjoyed reading my thoughts. Like I said earlier, if you would like to comment on my review I ask you to be civil and respect my opinion, thanks.

Similar quality to Fallout 3/Fallout New Vegas except with a plethora of gopniks with guns instead of ghouls.  More bleak/harsh atmosphere than Fallout.  Practice your Russian as the npcs tend to blather on about I-Have-No-Freaking-Clue (but I can guess by tone).  At first the difficulty level and bullet registry will be challenging for even the most tempered fps adventurer.  Everyone is disposable, there are no women or children, no moralistic mantras being force-fed.  You're literally tossed out into this harsh environment to fend for yourself.  In soviet Russia toilet uses you.
Use your PDA -a Lot of information is there.  Don't know what this strange/weird symbol or thing is?  Search for Zone Survival Guide.  I typically like playing un-modded games however I highly recommend Zone Reclamation Project mod as an exception here.  It removes the idiotic quest time limits.  As an example:  you'll get an automated quest to save some stalkers in various areas from bandits.  You do that.  Your PDA says go pick up your reward which is 100 kilometers away, possibly in some area you've never been to before, all on foot -there is no fast travel/vehicles.  So you're supposed to hike all the way to wherever just to have some npc give you 2 bottles of vodka and a few rubles.  I play games for Fun, not time constraints.  Not like I was disarming a bomb.  So I removed those time constraints.
Additionally, I tweaked the grid size for my inventory so I didn't have to scroll way, way, way down just to eat some bread.  ZRP with minor tweaks to the vanilla game makes this Excellent.  I would avoid all the other Complete/invasive mods that totally change the game.  It will likely sap the fun out of it/make you too overpowered.
Graphics: pretty decent for when it came out  Sound/Music: really immersive/excellent  Gameplay/controls:  ASWD and very responsive  Area loadtimes/stutter:  some minor waits  Glitches: Haven't had too many occur -really stable and I'm nearing the end.
Bottomline: If you want a linear, story-driven game that holds your hand -this ain't it.  If you want an apocalyptic, Russian-themed game with tons of replay and choose-your-own-adventure, this is it.  A hidden gem worth the learning curve/difficulty.

(Don't be fooled by the low playtime on my profile. I've been playing this through Steam on Wine, so I've had to do a lot of it in offline mode.)
If I told anyone that a game made by Ukrainian indie devs on a completely custom engine was one of the best games I've ever played, they'd look at me funny.
Anyone who has played S.T.A.L.K.E.R. would immediately agree.
The X-ray engine, while quirky and strange at times, has (reportedly) the most true-to-life shooting model ever. Not that this is any solace when you try to mag dump on a mutant and die to it's melee attacks. The engine also does an amazing job with the general atmosphere of the game. It feels spooky and overbearing, like a good horror game should.
When I say this game is scary, I genuinely mean it. Everyone has been in one of those creepy basements with peeling paint, no light, and an awful dusty smell. Now you get to explore those basements with ACTUAL MONSTERS. It does an amazing job of making you panic when you hear heavy breathing.  The mutants, unlike other games which the enemies stop being a threat eventually, remain a continual threat even to the end of the game.
The story is great, while a bit ham-fisted, is a great medium for the overall experience.
The best news: The game works perfectly in Wine, so Linux/Mac users need not miss out on this fantastic game.

Overall review, 9.7/10.  Can't recommend enough, which is why I chose it for probably the only review I'll ever do.
Completely in love with this VN. I was skeptical because it was released in 2004, and is still a $50 game. but after much more hours played than shown here(I usually play in offline mode), I have come to the conclusion that I feel awful for not paying full price. The creators made so much content, and did such a wonderful job that I would consider getting it for other people. But definitely not during a sale.
My only complaint would be that there is a "True Ending", which while adorable and well written in itself, takes away from the other girls' endings based purely on the fact that there is only one you should end with. Even with this though, they do a very good job in making everyone's ending amazing, and stopping before the true ending opens will only hurt because you want more.
Art 8/10- The art is definitely dated, and artists can do much better by hand. BUT considering that it was made in '04, and it fits the feel of the game with how silly it can be, and how well it defines the emomtions of characters, I will give it a solid rating.
Gameplay 9/10 - Little kinks here and there, but most of the quirks in talk are explained in the "dangopedia"(which even the name of the in-game dictionary connects to one of the characters)
Story 12/10(or 5/7 if you're a memelord) - multiple times where I didn't get enough sleep for work because I didn't realize how much time had passed while bawling my eyes out or laughing so much. You definitely feel the full spectrum of emotions in this VN, you get a personal connection to many of the characters, and each story is long enough to be a seperate VN.
If you enjoy VNs, and are even remotely considering this game, buy it now. Don't wait for a sale, or you'll probably end up regretting buying it on sale like I did. My general standard is 1-2 hours of enjoyable gameplay per $1 spent, and even at full price, it well exceeded that.

Alright, here's a review from a jaded and critical visual novel enthusiast. If you eat up visual novels like candy, there's no reason not to think that you'll love Clannad, as most of these reviews are pointing out. But maybe you're like me and are a bit tired of outdated anime tropes taking up hours of your time for a simple misunderstanding, or because the girl is 'too embarassed'... well, honestly, Clannad has some of that too. Refreshingly though, it's really not that jarring nor frequent.
Let's get the cons out of the way first, for a big purchase like this you should know what you're getting into if you have high standards. Obviously I'm in the 'you should buy it' camp, but there is still room for some eye-rolling. If you want to get every route in the game, there's a route with a creepy over-sexualization of a minor (nothing sexual happens, but she is sexualized), not to mention that route suffers from one of those obnxious over-the-top suffering scenes, where really a teacher should have been called. It's about the worst it gets though. Besides that, there are a few repetitive jokes, and semi-overt anti-gay sentiment (mostly, they say people are gay to make fun of them), and a lot of casual Japanese-themed sexism. It's not as bad as other games, but seeing as this came out early 00's, you probably shouldn't expect it to feel very progressive. The girls are pretty diverse and interesting, but every once in a while it throws in a line like, 'you shouldn't help me because you're a boy' which is like... meh, I 100% would have helped with her sewing, I'm not scared that thread is going to suck my testosterone dry... whatever.
But on the positives, this is a really fun game. The main character is fleshed out very well over time, and is refreshingly honest and straight-forward for the most part. He is lazing about going day-to-day without any real goals or meaningful relationships. There are tons of different paths you can go on, not just with different girls, but interacting with different groups of friends depending on how to act. It's very in-depth with its ability to bring several elements together based on your previous actions. It's interface is also probably the best I've seen, very easy to use and helps with whatever you need.
It's hard to describe 80+ hours worth of story and characters, while at the same time covering mostly just a month or so of time. This game feels professional, yet it can sometimes feel like you're just hanging out with your friends. There's lots of lessons in this game that resonated with me, and a lot of jokes that make me laugh out loud. I'm usually pretty stoic when I'm reading, so it was a pleasant surprise when it was able to make me laugh and cry. If you're like me, this isn't a crazy tearjerking festival, but it cetainly went far enough to make me tear up on the route I was most invested in. This is good though, because it means this isn't melodramatic. There are difficult things that happen, but they all feel very realistic and earned.
To me, some routes felt a bit forced at parts, or maybe they appealed more to a Japanese audience, but overall the stuff that worked REALLY worked. Even characters I hated at first became dear to me in their own way. Unlike most VN protagonists, I never feel frustrated by Okazaki. He was light-hearted, easy-going, and pulled a lot of pranks. He has tons of issues to work through, but probably ended up being my favorite character of the game. It's nice to have a protagonist who's a underdog, but still feels like he deserves being admired by all these girls. I'd want to be his friend too, and it's nice to see him get off his♥♥♥♥♥and find a reason to keep going.
So tons of varied content, realistic slice-of-slife with down-to-earth problems, doesn't take itself too seriously or poke fun too much, and professional interface and voice acting. It's probably not going to blow your mind like something with sci-fi or supernatural/horror, but you'll probably remember it for a really long time, like it was a school year of your own.

This game was beautifully written and emotionally gripping. I just finished my first playthrough, and I feel so heartbroken over the events that happened. I can barely process it. But I recommend this for anyone with an interest in visual novels. Even with its high price point, it is well worth the money.

Call of Juarez Gunslinger should win some kind of an award like "Biggest Franchise Comeback of The Year". Taking a very different route from the previous games Gunslinger focuses on the fun of shooting and surviving many enemies rather than traversing long distances or sneaking. Smaller level portions gave the possiblity to add much more detail and to polish the levels. Levels are very detailed and contain additional layers of gameplay in the form of secrets, interaction with objects to earn points, and more enemies per area than before. The ai is also better than in previous games. Duels are improved and more fun. Another very important addition is the upgrades which the player has the option of choosing as they complete missions. It is a small RPG element but it adds much fun to the game.
Probably most important of all, Call of Juarez Gunslinger has excellent voice acting which is fun to liten to and which is genuinely funny sometimes. Voice actor of Silas in the old CoJ games was good, but overall it was pretty horrible. In Gunslinger all voice acting is good. I am glad the developer has chosen to focus on this.
Overall, besides being one of the best games of the year on the PC as well as on consoles, Gunslinger is easily one of the best Western themed shooters to come in 2-3 years. A must play for those who like Westerns, cowboys, and wild west shoot outs.

Let's start with the good. The combat is enjoyable for an MMO. The graphics are great. There's lots of story, if unfortunately a quantity over quality thing. Crafting is extensive. And that's all the praise I can think of for it, now the bad.
First and foremost, the level scaling is poorly implemented. It's sophisticated, it works, and it makes having a level system pointless. There is no sense of progression with the system, however there is a constant sense of regression as every level gained makes you weaker until you get level relevant gear. Crafting resources also scale to the player, which causes problems if you want to use a high level character for quick gathering. Honestly, the game would be more enjoyable if levels were removed entirely since they serve no purpose beyond making equipment obsolete.
The game mechanics revolve around the end game. Lvl's 1-50 are a thing to rush through as quickly as possible to get past what is now the worst part of the game, only after that all there is left is grinding more numbers.
Inventory management is atrocious unless you subscribe. If you enjoy crafting, forget it unless you are willing to pay an overpriced subscription fee. If you don't want to spend more time managing inventory than playing the game either pay up or stop looting.
Sharing resource nodes and treasure chests. Not all world loot is shared, but having to race other players to a chest or crafting resources leaves players resenting other players being in the game. Most modern games understand that forcing players to compete for loot does not endear them to the idea of playing together and cooperating, nor does it make the community friendly. Fortunately loot from kills and events are not shared and each player gets their own, but it is still a terrible oversight.
Story. The quantity over quality approach to quests and content combined with the mechanics revolving around the end game leaves players rushing through dialogue in order to check off the next quest. It doesn't help that the writing is verbose, bland, and repetitive (occasionally has its moments, but rarely) and does a disservice to all the animation and voice acting that went into the game.
The cash shop makes it feel more like a F2P with freemium options, with inventory management being the biggest offender. The cosmetics in the cash shop are well priced and have a decent variety, but then the ability to dye costumes is locked behind a subscription. Housing is a massive cash sink but is also easily ignored. Then the mounts all cost $10-20. Aside from a bit of price gauging, this could have been overlooked if it wasn't for the fact that dying costumes and crafting material storage are only available with an overpriced subscription. This is also a bit dishonest since the game
but in fact is balanced to be a miserable experience unless you subscribe.
Edit:
Just to clarify, I'm not against the idea of level scaling, but I believe the way it was implemented is terrible.
On subscriptions, more can be found here:
Basically the sub crosses the line and goes from enticing people to sub to punishing people if they don't.

Oh my!This is my first ever review.I havent done a review for my favourite game which is Skyrim but this game is amazing.I was looking for some good survival and horror games and after the metro series(Which were amazing) i wasnt sure if this would satisfy me.
As far as graphics goes i dont mind at all.As long as the gameplay or the story are good graphics dont matter that match but it looks good enough.
Now on to the story i havent finished the game yet so i dont know where it leads.You basically wake up in a banker and you are told to kill a mysterious guy.
But enough of that.The 10/10 of this game is the gameplay and the atmoshere.This game is really a great challenge and i am playing on Stalker difficulty(normal)out of the 4 difficulties it has and i have died so many times.I am gonna get this out of the way right now.This game has hands down the BEST ENEMY AI i have ever seen in a video game.The enemies in this game are brutal.They take cover,they prefire(i am not kidding),they coordinate with each other,they cover a person that uses a medkit,they even FLANK you from behind the walls or above.Are you tired of stupid AI that is too basic,boring or run around like idiots?Try this game and find out.You think having a good gear or good aim will let you take a base easily?You are wrong.If you are not careful while walking in the base,you will get either sniped,flanked from a shotgun guy(=dead).You need carefully trace your steps.
Now on to the atmosphere the game is less scary on the surface.The anomalies are easy to get used,the dogs are a bit scary if they are in a pack and the bandits are hard at the start but when you get better gear are a walk in the park.The milititary bases like i said above are the challenge.The underground gameplay though is terrifying.If you dont have night vision when you go in you are in for a challenge.The mutants living underground are creepy, and they can kill you pretty fast if you dont spot them quickly.I have seen 5 types of mutants and all were a challenge.
Now as far as negatives go the Gunplay while it feels realistic is a bit clunky but thats because some weapons are bad or they are in bad condition.Dont think that aiming at the head will guarantee you a kill.You need to know about zeroing to take some shots.And the other negative are some framedrops at some locations even though i can runs far better games than this.
And finally to pump you up a bit i will share with you one of the missions that led me to this review.I had to attack a bandit base so i waited out to get dark because enemies cant spot you that easily unless they spot you with the flashlights.I put a silencer on my TR301(Btw this game has many many weapons)and i killed everyone one by one.Then i entered the underground lab with only 50 bullets.Then i switched to my shotgun to deal with the creepy mutants in the dark.After i stole the the documents,a military hitsquad created an ambush on the surface to kill me,with helicopter lighting the exit so that i couldnt escape in the dark.The best part was the weather.A raging thunderstorm started while i was fighting the military out in the open.I was out of medkits,only had a few bandages left,my character was hungry and tired(out of stamina)and only 50 bullets to finish them.This was one of the coolest and most intense missions i have ever played in a video game.Props to the devs.

No, but seriously Clannad is a great visual novel. If you're in the neighborhood for a good visual novel that'll bring you both joy and sadness look no further. Key did a fantastic job with this visual novel. For those who have watched the anime, like myself, I can say you will experience deja vu since the visual novel is what the anime is based on. That being said, if you enjoyed the stories in the anime you will enjoy the visual novel even more. Full disclaimer: Clannad's entire game isn't in the anime. A good chunk is, but many of the really great routes never come to life in the anime for continuity and time issues. You can fall in love with so many characters. I recommend following a spoiler free walkthrough. I just looked up "Clannad Walkthrough" on google and used the first result. It just shows you which decisions to make if you want to play a specific route. You will need to play some of the routes to unlock the after story, but honestly to get your money's worth play them all. It took me ~50 hours to do everything. Once you've played Tomoyo's route I recommend picking up Tomoyo After: Its a Wonderful Life when you got $20 to spare. I just finished it and it's AMAZING, I'll be reviewing it as well.
There are about 14 routes I believe. There will be some similarities to routes until you really reach the bulk on the content. Each route is good in it's own regard. I will say also that one character in particular isnt in the anime at all and that person's arc is especially good.
I bought this game on an anime weekend sale on steam for $25. I know $50 is alot of money and although clannad is great it's alot of money. If you're a diehard VN fan you'll prob have no problem spending the money. I recommend wishlisting this game and waiting for a sale.
If you enjoyed the anime I recommend picking this up. If you hated the anime you probably will hate the VN. I was brought to tears by most of the routes and each route felt so great when I finished it. Clannad is an exceptional VN, probably one of the best, it's my first VN and for sure isnt my last.

I'll admit that I'm extremely biased when it comes to Clannad as a franchise. It's a very down to earth story about one person's struggle to find his place in the world. I've watched the anime countless times and still do watch bits of it every now and again. Sure, the pacing in the novel is a bit different in terms of what you choose, but at the end of the day, who really cares? Just pick a choice that appeals to you and try to pursue your favorite waifu or something. Well, for those of you who are familiar with the anime, it's very likely you know what Clannad is already, but for those of you who don't know what Clannad is, the little description at the bottom of the store page should give you an idea of what it's about. You know why I like this protagonist? Simple. He's written in a way that he is first and foremost, a human being with a believable personality. A bit of a jerk, but a respectable if not somewhat relatable human being for the most part, not like some stereotypical, whimpy nice guy or some stupidly overpowered power fantasy almost every mediocre anime has. Now it comes down to whether or not you are willing to spend a bit of dosh on a dating sim. If you have any interest in dating sims or if you watched the anime and loved it, there should be no reason for you to skip the game, unless you're a filthy cheapskate who feels entitled that they should get everything for free. Or you know, you don't like to play dating sims, and that's totally fine.

7/10
------
OVERALL: If you enjoy lots of aerobatics/acrobatics and blowing lots of stuff up using different methods and military vehicles, then this game is a chaotic, nice-looking open-world sandbox for you. I got a good 40 hours of enjoyment before I started to get a bit bored of that stuff. However, it doesn't offer much more than that, so if you're looking for something similar to GTA, look elsewhere.
I got this as a bundle (with all DLC) during the Christmas sale, and although there are a lot of things wrong with it, I feel like I've gotten my money's worth.
------
Pros:
-- THE BAVARIUM WINGSUIT (DLC).
You might as well buy the DLC too, as this became the best part of the game for me when I unlocked the jet-powered wingsuit with rockets and machine gun. It allows you to fly around Medici and wreak havoc without needing fighters or helicopters.
-- MAP SIZE.
Medici is pretty big, and there are enough bases and airports that I eventually got bored of blowing them up before I discovered all of them. The Southern islands are the nicest parts (where you spend most of the game), with a lot of caves and rock bridges to swoop in and out of with your winguit.
-- GRAPHICS.
The game looks pretty nice and is extremely colourful. Very similar to JC2, but just updated for current gen.
-- GAMEPLAY UPDATES.
What really annoyed me about JC2 was that it was so easy to escape the authorities. They were so lazy that they would just give up as soon as you were out of their line of sight. JC3 is still not perfect in that respect, but it's been improved slightly. If you hide, a timer will start and the heat will go away if they can't find you within the time limit. If you steal a vehicle, they will chase you for a lot longer, particularly if you steal a tank.  Blowing up bridges is also fun, and you get unlimited C4 explosives that you can stick to anything. Grappling hooks have a few new features, and the wingsuit challenges are a lot of fun to master.
------
Cons:
-- CAR MECHANICS.
The cars are just as bad, if not worse, than in the last game. If you're expecting GTA-style cars with a pretty, Mediteranean map, prepare to be very disappointed. The military cars are okay, but the normal civilian and sports cars still suck, and don't even try to ride a motorbike. I've ended up accidentally killing myself many times due to how difficult it is to control a car in this game. The PLANES are also just as bad. If you didn't mind the JC2 mechanics, fine, but I feel this should've been a priority in terms of progressing the series, and the developers just didn't bother.
-- MAP DETAIL.
Although the map looks nice, the towns all look very similar, and the capital city is a dissapointing shadow of the JC2 capital. Although the Southern islands are quite detailed, the main island has nothing to really get excited about. There are a few giant fortresses and air bases that are fun to battle with, but no international airport, no mile high club, and no civilisation to be found in the mountains, or anything on the North side of the island for that matter.
No point having a huge map if there's nothing there
-- OPTIMIZATION.
This is not a major issue for me personally, and it probably helps that I have a very high-end gaming PC, but even with my specs I got quite a lot of stuttering at certain times. I had to turn the settings down a bit, which made it better. Just don't buy it if you don't have the minimum requirements.
-- STORY.
Just don't buy this game expecting the story to be great. You should know by now that Just Cause has laughably bad campaigns, and the missions are relatively similar to each other. There are a few fun characters, with some cringey puns and overall cheesy dialogue, but if you treat this game purely as a sandbox for flying around and blowing things up, you won't be too disappointed.

What a masterpiece. You probably know that Transistor is made by the same developer that brought us Bastion, and you probably know about the amazing game's soundtrack. Most importantly though, this game is fun as hell and caters to a variety of playstyles through its ability customization. I've beaten the story (which is as great as you would expect from Supergiant) and am currently working through NG+ and the challenge rooms.
If you like fun, get this game.

It's difficult but try to forget that Supergiant games made Bastion; whether you liked Bastion or not is not indicative of how you will feel about Transistor.
Obvious points out of the way: sublime art and music. The aesthetics are scintillating, the backgrounds and world are meticulously detailed. The characters and enemies are well animated and designed, mirroring the world around them. There's a very strong noir vibe seeping through what often feels like cyberpunk New York as imagined by Europe. There's every chance I'm just projecting my desire for Remember Me to have been a good game, but I digress.
The gameplay is solid, provided you realise that operating outside of Turn() is very rarely the best option. Transistor gives you a lot of different skills and variety of ways to combine them allowing you to play however you want, additionally the game encourages you to mix up your skills so that you can unlock character information and the "Performance Tests" force you to improvise with randomly selected skills. Unfortunately towards the end of the game encounters become quite repetitive and even with enemies evolving it is rare that whatever combo you've perfected by that point won't be just as effective as before. New Game+ is genuinely challenging but by then you are even furthered hampered in choices and will be extremely reliant on a few exceptional skills to get you through the encounters, especially with limiters on.
It is unfortunate to say that the story and characters feel like the weakest aspect of Transistor. You're dropped into the world with no knowledge of anything, and as you progress you slowly uncovers scraps of information by way of skills and terminals. The game is quite short too, and ultimately it can be quite difficult to become truly invested in either the world or characters. After talking with people and going through the NG+, there are a few nuances that are illuminated and can be appreciated but the story never takes that final step.
Transistor is a good game. The worst thing you could say is that it is not Bastion. Regardless of who you are you should approach with caution and pay special attention to all the little details, from the art to the written and spoken dialogue.

First and foremost, for potential buyers who have watched the anime, don't assume that just because you enjoyed the anime, you'll also enjoy the game. Visual novels, such as Clannad, require a bit of a different taste, you need a fair bit of patience and also need to put up with the fact that at first glance, Nagisa looks like a skeleton, in my humble opinion, which ticked me the hell of as she is my second favorite character (Miyazawa's my favorite, obviously). For sure, playing the game is a great way to continue to immerse yourself into the Clannad universe, and it allows you to follow your own path and make friends with who you want, however, the mechanics and style of the game itself don't necessarily appeal to certain groups. I have friends who cried watching the anime, like me, however, did not enjoy playing the game. The plot of the game is fantastic, no complaints there, just prepare yourself for a bit of a different experience in how you interact with it in comparison to the anime and other video games. Just keep this in mind.
I've always personally been impressed with Key and their ability to make games that have the ability to toy with your emotions. Clannad is no different, as a player, you follow your own semi-personalised route (see below), each with their own struggles and successes that tug at your heartstrings. The plotlines are deep and engaging and allow you to feel as if you have truly connected with the characters, each of whom have a well thought out personality and background that is reflected in the way in which they interact with the player character. For me, this resulted in my getting angry a lot at Sunohara (the player character's best friend) and yelling at my screen. The point is, you'll feel the emotions that the game is meant to convey, you'll wince, you'll cry, you'll laugh, the whole story is one wild emotional roller coaster. Clannad is a fantastic example of what a visual novel should do for you.
For a visual novel, the mechanics are solid and the Dangopedia answered virtually all the questions I had about any mentions of Japanese culture within the game. At times, playing the game can feel like a chore, as is typical of many visual novels (especially if you've watched the anime, as you know roughly what will happen), but I personally didn't mind to much as I was so engaged by the characters.
The sprites, for the most part, are relatively well done for a visual novel, except for Nagisa, in my opinion, which is an incredible boon. From my experience, games with characters that look nothing like they should (for example, a human should look like a human) are a bit disenchanting and a complete turnoff. The soundtrack is incredibly well done, I cannot stress this enough, I found it to be the aspect of the game that was most beneficial to the overall quality besides the actually plotline, which is to be expected in any game. With both of these things in mind, its easy to immerse yourself into the game.
That's it for me, if you made it this far, I congratulate you and I now reward you with a joke. What do you call a funny mountain? Hill Arious. Ba dum tsh. Anyway, I hope this helped you make a decision, no doubt I missed a few things, however, so I'd recommend you read some more just to get a better feel. I encourage you to buy the game, it's fantastic and a good example of what a visual novel should do. Even if you don't like sappy stories, you should still enjoy this game. It’s October 1982 and your name is pulled from the labor lottery which makes you the newest employee of the Ministry of Admissions in Arstotzka . You are immediately assigned to a newly acquired Grestin Border Checkpoint which is not all that secure a lot of people are trying to get in and it’s your job to make sure that the right people are getting in and the wrong people are staying behind.
Although the gameplay is simplistic you will find that the difficulty ramps up very quickly as you are given more documents to sort through. This difficulties compound by the fact you are trying to earn as much money as possible by processing as many people as you can in order to feed and support your family. While this creates a lot of tension in the game it has unfortunate side effect that also makes the interface more cluttered which can have a disadvantageous effect when you are trying to juggle all the different papers, it can become very confusing and very frustrating.
This is really a minor complaint because overall the game is absolutely excellent, the story is immersive and there is a lot of interesting characters throughout but what makes this game so special is its atmosphere, from the RT soundtrack to the excellent dialogue, you legitimately feel that you are a part of a war-torn communist steep.
In conclusion, Papers,pleas is an incredibly unique game that I think everybody should experience.

Not a lot of thought was put into buying this as any survival game with building aspects gets me wilder than hormonal teenage girls on a boyband concert (it makes me sad to say this is spot-on). I don't think I even remember how much I paid for this game and quite frankly I do not care anymore, it was worth it.
Info:
Reign of Kings is a survival based medieval MMO (massively multiplayer online) game. Hunt wildlife, mine resources, craft weapons and armor to protect yourself. You may form a guild, bring war to opposition players, and seize the throne and become King! in Reign of Kings resource collection and crafting are a large part of the game. This game could best be described of a third person rust, combined with medieval aspects and a lot of content. But takes itself a lot less serious (in a good way)
First experience:
Logging into my first server I made a character called "Sir Pipsqueek", and as there is a character creator (one of those other things that gets me wild) I made a tiny little midget man (or should I say "little person"?) with giant arms and tiny tiny legs. His body proportions challenged the laws of gravity as he must have had steel legs to keep himself standing but yet brave little Sir Pipsqueek proved to be quite a handy guy. I proceed chopping some wood and becoming a chicken serial killer in order to make myself armor.
As I was done I considered I was too lazy to gather material to make a house myself and ran up into the fields where I found a person in iron armor. He was no match for the Sir Pipsqueek, the bringer of death and slayer of chickens. I beat him up with a wooden stick and killed him with it, allthough he had an iron sword. I was surprised to say the least.
I proceeded to use my findings to build myself a nice little shack and start expanding it. Sadly on my first trip into the wild I found 3 wildlings or as I'd like to call them "Dumb, dumber and dumbest". I greeted them like a polite lord of death, they danced for me and then decided to team up against me. I did not like the idea of 3 naked guys beating me with their wood against the forest while yelling especially since there was a peasant watching us go at it as wild as we can. Sir Pipsqueek fought bravely but was eventually slain by the 3 little wildlings to have all his precious possesions taken from him.
Little did I care, since that was the very way I obtained these posessions in the first place.
Verdict:
Reign of Kings is a very rewarding and pleasurable game where you can build whatever you want and have it be destroyed the next day. But somehow it's always a thrill to gather resources all over again to build your house. One thing i'd love to see is for the progress you made not to be deleted so soon, due to griefers, server refreshes, hackers, etc. The crafting system is flawless and very easy to use and the community is very nice, allthough it has it's flaws. Up till now the only major problem I have had with this game is hackers, and a lot of them. In the beginning this was a game-breaking aspect but luckily the producers keep updating and adressing the hacking issues full-time. Surprisingly enough besides the hackers keeping the developers busy they manage to add new content that makes the game a lot more pleasurable and rewarding.
Pros:
-Crafting system
-Always something to do
-Making progress is very pleasing
-New content regularly added.
Cons:
-Hackers, hackers, hackers.
-Easy to lose progress
I would definitely recommend this game, a must have for anyone who loves survival, MMO, and anything that involves building. There is always something to do in this game!

If you are the sort who will be dissapointed because you were expecting "Skyrim Online",  don't bother with this game. It is the same universe, but a totally different game.
That being said, this is IMHO, the best MMO going. If you played it within the first year and quit -give it another chance. It has undergone MASSIVE improvements.
This game has it all - deep and immersive lore (if you, like me, started this series with Skyrim, you'll be amused at some of the cross-over locations and stories - the game even features some of the same books), Crafting, PVE, a thriving PVP community/map, Dungeons, arenas, dueling, Guilds, and now - housing!
This game can most definitely be played solo, but many of the dungeons are meant to be played in groups, and frankly, the best loot comes from the group dungeons/areas.
The game does not require a subscription - though an optional one is available. The subscription is wortn it if for no other reason than the "crafting bag" it provides: a no limit inventory for raw materials. (without the subscription your inventory is capped - *including* any crafting materials you find in game. This can be frustrating when you find that piece of weaponry or armor you need, but you can't pick it up because you have too much iron ore, foods, or woodworking materials etc.) The subscription also gives you access to all the DLC for as long as you have an active subscription. (the upcomind "Morrowind" expansion is not included)
The cons about this game? The learning curve is relatively steep. If you haven't had any experience in MMO's, it doesn't do a very good job of telling you how to advance. There are some tutorials in game, but they are mainly to teach you the mechanics. There are also many tutorials online outside the game (YouTube, etc.) to get you up to speed if you need them though. It also is pretty strict about how you want to play, I.e. in Skyrim you could start as a hack & slasher, but become a mage and go back and forth as needed. Here you are required to select a class - and your advancement is partially limited to strengthening the abilities of that class.
Well worth it IMO, and constantly expanding. At three years and counting it's only getting better.
