First Up: Giving this a not recommend due to the crazy decisions around Dark Souls 2: Scholar of the First Sin & the PC version.  Will gladly reverse my stance if the PC situation in regard to this add-on/new game are changed to something more reasonable.  Not going to cover the details here, please Google it or see the Steam discussion forum if you're not aware of the situation.
Background:  130'ish hours into the game, started as pure melee until late game, have killed every boss except 1 on my first play through, no prior experience to the series before this.
Is this a good game?  By and large yes, however it can be also one of the most frustrating games _ever_.  The core game play is pretty solid.  A semi-realistic, tough as nails RPG experience.  You visit interesting places, fight interesting monsters, equipment selection and looks have lots of variations.  Some rough points, thoughts and things to be aware of before playing this game yourself:
1) The tutorial/instructional part of the game is almost non-existent.  You learn the basics, but there's so much depth to the game that you can without too terrible an effort play yourself into a corner where you have to restart the game.  Highly recommend reviewing a new character guide or some such before playing so you understand where the cutoffs are in terms of stats, how scaling bonues work, etc.  Towards the end of the game and certainly before hitting the DLC be sure you have some form of quality ranged attacks, spells or arrows.
2) Regarding online guides/fan sites be warned that much of the material online was written against earlier versions of the game.  There have been changes to the game that typically have not been reflected in the online guides/fan sites.  Generally this isn't a problem, however be particularly careful of anyone who says "this is the uberest of builds and will dominate everything".
3) Also when reading guides regarding boss fights and such be mindful that many of them were written with characters much more powerful than yourself the first time you encountered the same boss.   Guides that recommend you use a weapon you can't get until NG+2 and such.  Silly!  If watching a video to learn how to fight a boss try and use the UI elements to figure out just how much more or less powerful the person in the video is and adjust accordingly.  Unfortunately this is not something you learn to perceive well until late in the game.
4) PvP invasions are very annoying.  80% of the time I'm being invaded by someone who so outclasses me it's a joke and I just stand there and die so I can get back to the game.  I don't know if they're hacking or just that high level but outside of the first 4-5 game areas everyone I encountered pretty much killed me in one combo I couldn't get out of.  Also the folks who kill you in PVP will typically do a lot of taunting "you suck, I rule" emotes after killing you.  This is bonkers to me, the invader has all the initative in this setup.  Even if we were on equal footing they still have a leg up on the invaded!  Also it didn't make for a fun or entertaining experience to backstab some guy with my fully upgraded weapon and have him only loose ~8% of his health.  Latency (or cheating?) also has been an issue, sometimes I get backstabbed by a guy who on my screen was clearly in front of me and not within melee distance.
5) Boss fights while typically very awesome epic encounters suffer from difficulty all over the map.  Some are push overs (typically bosses that gate major progress).  There are typically NPCs you can summon to help and in some cases they're key to winning the fight and in other cases summoning them almost means a certain loss.
6) The DLC content is an inconsistent bag of good stuff and anguish.  It looks like the DLC content was targeted at players who had reached very high levels of power and perhaps completed the game multiple times.  Areas like the Iron Passage are rage inducing, thankfully it's optional, and many of the boss fights are ridiculous for someone on their first play through.  Often the rooms are so full of overpowered combinations of monsters you have to snipe them at a distance or exploit their leashes/AI to break up the groups into manageable chunks.  Charging into the room and trying to dispatch the monsters where the designers intended you to will meet with certain doom.  This just seems counter to what makes the game fun - actually fighting stuff instead of hiding around a corner!
7) This ties into the above, and I noticed this mostly in the DLC content.  The hitboxes and such for various attacks and swings are often way in the monster's favor.  The number of times I've been 1-2 feet away from a thrusting attack to be killed is maddening or the number of times I've rolled pass an attack to only be hit by some 'mysterious force' at the end of the roll is frustrating.  For a game where they're asking you to be so precise in everything you're doing it's disappointing and feels unfair when what you're fighting doesn't follow the rules.
8) If you don't have an XBox gamepad to play the game then be warned playing the game may be very difficult.
9) The developers are obviously relatively new to PC development.  There are many signs of the game being a port and some quirks as a result.  Nothing horrible as long as you're using a gamepad to play.  For example if you hit ALT+TAB to get into windowed mode it's a challenge to get back to full screen (and I really wish there was a borderless windowed mode option).  Some other rough edges:
- To quit the game you have to go back through entire login sequence, it's quicker to just kill the game in Task Manager.
- You can't recall to your last bonfire or quit the game if you have NPC summons that are still alive.
- However you can quit the game during most boss fights avoiding a death and potential loss of souls.
- If you are playing while online and disconnect there's no way to reconnect without quiting and logging back in.
10) The script/localization is pretty poor.  There are many 'quests' or things to do in the world that are very very poorly explained.  Armor sets and weapons that are only available if you do some pretty obscure sequence of events.  NPCs that 'disppear' if killed by a boss and others that don't.  The game almost requires a wiki to be opened in another window at certain parts or to make informed decisions.
11) There's very little information available to help you decided if one item is better for you than another.  I say this in particular about armor because how much benefit you gain by upgrading armor isn't easily perceived until you've potentially already made an investment to get it.  So while 'base stats' may look nice you pretty much have no idea what the final product will be.  This is made more difficult by not being able to ever see the base stats of an item once it's upgraded as well.  So I can't easily compare my fully upgraded chest peice with a base stats of a new chest peice I find and have any good sense of how the two compare.
12) Continuing from above, in late gameplay armor almost becomes worthless which is really frustrating as the amount of damage being dealt out by monsters will kill you in one or two hits regardless of your armor.  If you've invested a lot into stats to help you wear heavy armor this is a demoralizing point.  You can respec your stats a limited number of times but you can't respec all the resources that went into upgrading equipment.
12) Having a bunch of old ladies laugh at you for the first few minutes of the game really made me want to punch some old ladies.  Seriously it was so annoying I almost quit right there.  However I'm glad I didn't.
I realize this is a list of complaints and things I didn't like or thought were poorly designed.  However honestly *despite* all this the game experience is surprisingly fun once you're over the learning curve and very satisfying.

I bought this game full price a bit after release completely on the merit of Dark Souls: Prepare to Die edition. I thought it would be a great rework of the Dark Souls game with a different storyline and fun new weapons, it has both of those, but it also has different input commands. Which means the generic Radioshack ps3 controller I had for Dark Souls did a strong and normal attack for the left arm when i tried to look left or right. The game is definitely more difficult with a keyboard and mouse in my opinion, because of the whole limited rolling options and stupid stuff like that, but still managable. The game itself wasn't worth it though, it isn't that it was made poorly, or that I just can't handle it, it's that the inputs feel sloppy and slow and the movements clunky and inefficient. OVERVIEW: Honestly is a very bad addition to the Dark Souls series and gameplay possesses many of the same flaws as the first Dark Souls game. There have been minor welcome improvements and changes, but ultimately the game is lacking. The main story isn't as cohesive or filled with wonderlust, there are no Solaire like iconic characters (perhaps Dark Souls II is focusing primarily on gameplay versus any other feature). As I stated before the gameplay is very much the same with some minor tweaks, but still manages to retain a lot of previous flaws that was found in the first game. For example, being a ranged character simply makes the game 50% more easy.
PROS:
Strong combat system (Although still very flawed). Difficulty (Sense of accomplishment, but at the same time I will discuss my critiques in the CONs section).
DLC's are pretty good, and actually brings back some of the "uniqueness" of DS1
CONS:
Poor story, the main plot and all characters involved had an identity crisis. I'm not completley sure if it was trying to be its own game or simply a continuation, unless one conducts some very elaborate background research, character motivations and story design are hard to pick up.
Flawed combat, ranged+Magic users are still outrageously better than being melee (At least in PVE), as ranged one doesn't have to suffer a lot of the mechanics and can actually get a full scope of what's happening. In addition to the combat, enemy design was typically homogenous. Vast majority of enemies were humanoid creatures with the same attacks (even most bosses were humanoids with very little variance). Its unclear if the game designers were aiming to make this game as difficult as possible simply for the sense of the game being difficult or if they were trying to incorporate any sense of fairness in the game. DSII is overtly difficult and more than often the player is absolutely swarmed with enemies with absolutley unfair advantages (360 axis tilting, forcing the player to cheese instead of being able to develop a unique combat style to their liking).
GRAPHICS, this may be only on PC but honestly the graphics aren't that super fantastic or detailed. Environment design is often just the same blandness with no incredible changes between areas. There are no environmental cues either, thus adding to the outright unfairness of the game. A prime example would be burning the windmill in a certain area in order to make a boss easier, THERE ARE NOT context clues nor any kind of hint of doing an action such as that in order to simplify the boss.
STATS: With what little RPG elements DS actually has, they've somehow managed to screw up stats even worse than it was before. A lot of stats other than the core one's (STR, INT, FAITH, END, VIT), are pretty much unclear as to how they're supposed to be used. Without prior knowledge of the first game or a game guide, the stats design is truly difficult to comprehend the first time around.
RATING: 6/10. Worth a buy if its on sale, but not even worth 40$. I advise playing DS1 for a better and more unique experience into this genre

Bad:

The Turn planning system makes for a much more stategic rhythm to the game, which I enjoyed wholeheartedly. The soundtrack, done once again by Darren Korb, manages to be absolutely breathtaking, while still not feeling instrusive.
This is a game that needs to be played.

Playing through the story is something like 6 hours which I found just enough so it doesn't get stale, then there's extra game modes and challenges. While the story itself isn't anything special, it's a bounty hunter narrating his past adventures to people in a bar, employing the unreliable narrator trick which makes this game different. Gameplay elements change according to his narration and when the people listening call out his exaggerations. Listening to the non-stop monologue makes the linear maps more entertaining. It isn't really related to the previous games at all, now instead of aztec gold you're hunting famous west celebrities like Jesse James in short flashbacks. There's 3 talent paths (akimbo/long range/short range) and most maps end in a duel standoff minigame. One thing it lacks is that Bound in Blood trick where you use the gamepad right stick to simulate a revolver hammer quickfiring. Could be it's tied to a gun or skill path I didn't try, but it was my only gripe along with some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t level segments involving bullet sponges (they're few, luckily). Enjoyable game, even if it isn't anything truly groundbreaking or memorable. Funny, now that I think of it, the closest comparison game for this one is actually Bulletstorm.

Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2 (Singleplayer + Co-Operative + Multiplayer) - 7/10
NOTE: The multiplayer aspect of this game is dying, so keep this in mind.
If you are buying for singleplayer and co-operative on it's own, which is quite doubtful, keep in mind this game will only provide so much content. The singleplayer is repetitive, short and lacking, while the co-op requires a dedicated person to finish the challenging, and often irritating, nature of the missions.
I would ONLY recommend this if you have friends that are willing to play with you, and you are also interested in the multiplayer (which requires friends as well, as the community is dying).
Scoring:
-1 for lack of graphics support (FOV, fullscreen windowed, etc)
-1 for lack of dedicated server support and dying community
-1 for pricing of content (lacking singleplayer and co-op content)
Graphics: The game doesn't look horrible and it runs on almost any PC you can find. The game supports 1920x1080, various levels of detail, 4x AA and other small adjustments.
The game does NOT support full screen windowed for multi-monitor ease of use.
The game does NOT support FOV adjustments, or high level graphical changes.
Singleplayer: The sequel of Call of Duty 4 or Modern Warfare 1 (and prequel to Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 3), the game continues where you left of in COD4. I shall not go into detail of the singleplayer story, as that would result in those that haven't played having the experience spoiled. The singleplayer is fairly straightforward. Kill a bunch of enemies, press a bunch of buttons in sync with what the game says, and watch the cut scenes. The game isn't that challenging, with the singleplayer aspect taking around about 10-15 hours to complete on veteran (the hardest game difficulty) depending on your skill level. To expand gameplay amount the game has achievements scattered through singleplayer and co-op, which include finding a bunch of hidden items, passing certain missions at certain difficulties, and various other challenges such as killing chickens quickly. The singleplayer, while it may immerse some, is one of the game's weak point, with it being completed quickly and without much trouble.
Co-operative Play: You play with one other player, in which one of you hosts and you choose out of three difficulty levels, which grant you stars; 1 for easy, 2 for normal, 3 for veteran. In total there are 69 stars in all, granted by completing all 23 challenges laid out before you and your partner. Most of the levels are similar to singleplayer missions, but these can be quite interesting with two people as it changes the challenges for two people. Included in the 23 challenges are time trials, elimination of enemies, races, and stealthy missions, among others. Despite the limited amount of levels in this game area, the missions given to the party involved is quite difficult and you'll be spending several days trying to discover the most efficient way of beating the game.
Multiplayer: This is Call of Duty's main focus, multiplayer. The game starts you out at level 1 with a set of predefined classes to get you to learn the basics first. Custom classes allow you to modify your character setup the way you want it, allowing you to customise weapons to your playstyle. This game has various unlocks as a result of using weapons and completing in game challenges, and these may be beneficial to players. The multiplayer scene contains no dedicated servers, and as a result you will often run into servers that give horrible ping, as a result of the low amount of players in the game search pool. Find a group of friends that live fairly close to you (chances are if they are in the same country you'll still get great ping) and host a game between yourself in either private or try to create a lobby as a big party. The multiplayer contains no Steam achievements, although connection through game lobbies work pretty well through the Steam friends list. The multiplayer can be entertaining if you find a reliable, low ping lobby with a bunch of players that aren't 10.

If you're coming new to theHunter you should know that the majority of the negative reviews have less than 2 hours play, claim the game is pay to win (It is not. hunting as a member is no easier than as a guest), and generally moan that the entire game isn't available for free. Seriously that's what most of the negative reviews are about. The other ones complain that they don't know how to play it.
That said, theHunter is the best hunting simulator on the market today. The visuals are excellent. The environmental audio and the animal sounds are fantastic. The tracking system works very well in simulating real-life tracking with some concessions made for playability (colored domes highlight the tracks). Ballistics are accurately modelled. Skill progression is slow but rewarding - guests are limited to level 10 in skills while members cap at 20 but you have to play for more than 100 hours to reasonably reach level 10. The community is mostly good - the guest crowd has its share of trolls but this isn't a big problem with the options to restrict players by membership and/or level.
Negatives are a somewhat disappointingly limited array of weapons to choose from and a render distance that feels too limiting (230 meter radius from the player). It is easy to spend a lot of money on all the weapons and equipment available, but by no means necessary to enjoy your hunts and to bag your game. A basic three month membership gets you licenses for all animals in the game but you'll need to use the appropriate type of weapon for the animal you hunt - the .243 starter rifle is not allowed for rabbits for example. The single shot shotgun can be bought with game money and can be used to hunt anything with the right ammunition but buying a good all-around rifle is a good idea.
7/10

Papers, Please is one of the most interesting games to come from the indie circuit recently, with a fascinating premise and one of the most cleverly-presented moral choice systems in gaming. This one gets a big green stamp of recommendation.

Disabled Gamer considering buying this?  Wonder about accessibility options?  This review is for you:
I have been wanting to check out this game forever.  What’s more exciting than working the border & telling people who aren’t allowed in to bugger off?  That’s pretty much the basis of Papers, Please.  You check passports and paperwork to allow people into Arstotzka.  You need to earn enough money to support your family. But all that info does no good if we can’t play it.  So, how’s accessibility?
I can’t explain how excited I was to see this.  You can get windowed mode before you even open the game.  Thank you developers!  Windowed mode is borderless so you can access your desktop with ease. Onscreen Keyboard was a click away but honestly wasn’t needed in the first look.  So far the game is pretty point and click.  I haven’t found a way to control gameplay with the keyboard alone, but will keep trying and will definitely report back if a solution is found.  Colorblind mode is also nowhere to be found.
So far Papers, Please has been a joy for mouse only players.  The first level took nothing more than point and click or drag and drop mechanics.  The speed at which you complete each level does determine income, but during early levels I haven’t felt the need to rush thus causing fatigue.  Things may change at later levels.

Ahh, Rome II. I love you so much. I also hate you so much. Let me explain...
When I bought Rome II at launch, the game was a mess. Seriously, Total War Arena is far more polished right now and that game has not even entered open beta yet (it just finished closed beta on March 3rd). Still, there was nothing else out at the time that really appealed to me, so I continued to play it through all the patchwork and DLC shananigans that Creative Assembly seems really addicted to right now. Honestly, at the end of the day, the game is not perfect, but it works 100 times better as compared to launch and is entirely fixed as of March 2016 IF subsidized by mods such as the radious mod. I am aware that saying something is made complete or better because of mods does the developer no credit, but do not worry, I will address that elephant in the room at the end of the review. In my oppinion, I can recommend the game today in its current state if you use mods. None of the mods I use are obtained anywhere but steam workshop, where downloading mods takes no effort and is as easy as clicking "subscribe". If they required any more effort than that, my review may be different. As things stand however, they do not.
The Good:
The Setting...
The game has an extremely large scale and is a very interesting historical "what if" simulator set in the historical period after Alexander the Great's Empire disintegrated and states such as Rome, Persia (not called Persia right now, but trust me, it is) Macedon and Carthage (to name maybe 5% of the faction list in this game) made their bid for expansion in the Ancient World. The setting is really exciting and really sets a mood for expansion and ancient warfare between mighty nations where pretty much anyone could have ruled Ancient Europe, Northern Africa, the Asian Steppes and the Middle East all of the way to India. When you finally reach the end of a game you cannot help but marvel at the size of your empire and all of the epic battle symbols on the terrain and say "yeah, I built that". The setting also makes the game incredibly addictive and the feeling of "one more turn" is omnipresent. The state of diplomacy in the game is almost completely fixed, and with mods is 100% fixed so that nations respond to rationally, even if you don't see their grand strategy upfront and their actions do not make sense to you in the short term. One game, I was playing as Rome, and I sought a trade agreement with a nearby rival, Massalia, who had expanded but was diplomatically friendly to me. They refused me every time, to my bafflement. However, I later realized that Massalia had no plans of being friendly, as they launched a sneak attack on me by sea right after I became engaged in a war with Carthage, breaking a Non-Agression Pact in the process. Needless to say, things got interesting, and they behaved deviously rationally: a trade agreement with them would have made me a stronger foe in the long term, despite the short term boost in wealth. And that, as they say, simply will not do.
The Gameplay...
The gameplay, both on the campaign map and in battle are vastly improved, and immensely challenging. Enemy AI, if subsidized by mods, is capable of highly sophisticated flanking maneuvers and uses ranged units to deadly effect right where you don't want them to be. A superior force is no longer a guarantee of victory like it used to be, and this means every engagement is as tense as the last. The political and diplomacy systems are fixed even pre-mod, and make a lot of sense to me. Some people remain baffled by the political system and true, it is poorly explained. But it is not overly complicated I promise you. In short, it is a game of balancing your factions prestige and power with the other factions in the game. Become too powerful, and you will become a dictator that will be despised and subject to uprisings and schemes. Become too weak, and you will be forced out and exiled. The extreme result of either disbalance is a civil war: either from a position of the majority or minority. The catch is that maintaining a balance of power becomes increasingly difficult the larger the empire or potential pie becomes. It really is a cool dynamic when subsidied with mods like 2 turns per year or 4 turns per year that result in almost God like Generals that command the respect of tens of thousands facing off against one another in a political tug of war. Also, the Province system is a huge improvement to the system for land management  in Empire to Shogun 2, and really motivates you to expand quicker so you can control an entire province rather than just part of it in order to capitalize on the bonuses of "complete" ownership such as edicts, food bonuses, public order bonuses, and economic bonuses. It really makes me smile when addictiveness is built into a game mechanic that works well on its own already.
The Shiny Baubles...
The game looks great on higher settings. My PC is 4 years old and I cannot touch ultra on anything except unit textures, building textures, and unit sizes. The game could run better at times, but it is a thing of beuty if you crank the graphics a little bit and have a system that can do it. I am thinking of upgrading my PC soon JUST so I can see this game maxed out. The UI leaves a little to be desired though, and the unit cards are just ugly, albeit historically accurate (the unit cards look like a drawing on an ancient pot or urn). The campagin map looks beautiful though, and it is huge. Attila is a better looking game than this and is optimized better (runs smoother, better load times etc.) but Rome II is still impressive to behold.
Overall, Rome II is an excellent addition to the total war series, and becomes crazy addictive once modded out to reach its full potential. The gameplay is fun and challenging both in the campaign map and in battles. The game looks great on high end machines. The setting and sense that you are creating the story of a nation in a historical "what if" scneario is immersive and addictive in its own right, but even more so given the time period of epic ancient conquest. This game, unlike so many on the market today, is as much about being ballsy as it is about being smart and cunning. This is why I love it.
Too bad CA sucks.
The Bad:
DLC DLC and what do you know? DLC...
The DLC for this game was out of control from day one. Normally I do not mind DLC, as I believe in freedom of choice and the free market, and I honestly have no problem enhancing a product with DLC if the product is complete in its own right out of the gate. The way CA has used DLC however, has perverted the practice to the point where I am not so sure anymore, and I am very sceptical of new games nowadays. CA is certainly not the only party guilty of this in gaming (for an example of the most eggregious customer pillaging to date on consoles, see Destiny and how Bungie flogged anyone stupid enough to get that game out of the gate with shameless DLC flaunting in the season pass), but they are one of the worst. Day One DLC is an abysmal practice in its own right, but when combined with CA selling an incomplete product, using their consumers as free product testors for patchwork, AND dumping DLC behind a pay wall rather than fixing the game, the result is downright buggery on an epic scale. Again, selling DLC = not offensive. Selling DLC for an aplha build that cost 59.99 + lying to consumers  = insulting. The game was not complete until Emperor Edition (one year later), and by then creative assembly had added countless culture packs, expansions, a blood pack that should be standard but is not, and who knows what else. In the end, the game suffered, the fans suffered, and CA laughed its way to the bank. This is why I hate it: CA dropped the ball.
Conclusion: buy when on sale. A solid game with a troubled past, but if you like total war, you will like this. With mods, you will love it. Buy it instead of Warhammer TW.

Papers, Please is a true gem. An innocent looking game, using "sub-par" graphics, surprise you with its crude, and oftentimes hilarious humor. You play as an unnamed sheeple trying to make your way in this dystopian society, and every decision you make is based on information. A woman walks into the booth. She hasn't seen her son in months. Her papers are in order. You let her through. You process a man. His papers are in order. He tells you his wife is coming after him, and to let her in. Her passport is fake. You deny her access. If somebody's papers are in order, it doesn't matter who they are. Murderers, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, terrorists, you name it. If you let the poorest illegal immigrant in, you get a citation and your family starves. Dark and depressing, this will bring out the sadist, or moral compass we have in all of us.
10/10 stars.

Call of Juarez® Gunslinger is a First-Person Shooter in the Call of Juarez series. The good thing about it is that it doesn't try to be more than it is. The game doesn't pretend to have a really deep story line (although it has one). Gunslinger is a fast paced arcade shooter. Whenever I play I'll turn on some music and start blasting enemies with a shotgun. The game rewards you for killing with style, headshots, body, limbs. It is so rewarding to see all the numbers fly along side the gore fest of blood the shoots from the enemy heads. I picked up the Blood Dragon/Gunslinger pack for about $8 , and I can't recommend it enough. If you like shooting baddies and western villians; This game is a must have!

If you ever wanted to feel like a cowboy, play this game. The story is based upon the baddies of the Wild West and you're going to take everybody down in order to avenge your brother, so obviously you're going to be the biggest badass of all time.
Now there aren't a ton of guns to play around with considering the time period, but this might have just contributed to the slick gunplay. The guns fire in tremendous fashion and reloading can be quick and fluid and not break the action.
Put this gunplay with the satisfying arcade-style system of scoring, pair that with skills that you can unlock and a meter that allows you to slow down time, and you have an incredible experience.
There are some games where I only really like the feel of one of the guns. This game, I like the feel of all the guns.
It's called Gunslinger for a reason, folks.

Nice to see a decent Call of Juarez again! Doesn't take itself seriously at all, very much an arcade shooter but the style of it all is brilliant. With no real story of note and no Reverand Ray preeching, the game aims low, but Gunslinger still manages to hit the target!

Gunslinger is by far the best game in the CoJ franchise. If you want a wildly entertaining single player FPS set in the old west, this is the game for you. You're a retired bounty hunter in a saloon where people buy you drinks to hear your stories. The further into the game you go, the more drinks you've had, so the stories get more exaggerated. When bar patrons catch you in a lie, the level quickly changes as you try to adapt your story. It's pretty hilarious. The cell shaded graphics look great. The skill trees in both Story and Arcade mode really change the way you play. I got through Story mode on easy difficulty in about 10 hours, and have since been replaying on a harder difficulty as well as spending time in Arcade mode. There are more environmental traps to watch out for on the harder difficulty settings, such as mining carts flying through tunnels which will kill you if you don't get out of the way in time.

Iam a person who is not very much into the singleplayer FPSs. The notable exception is the Deus EX series, which arguably isn't so much a shooter but more an RPG.  So how do I come to recommend a simple 15 € FPS without the great freedom or RPG-elements of a Deu EX ?  Pretty simple : Smart ideas by the developer. The trick letting the maincharackter narrate the story while you are playing is genius. The game gets it's own appeal because of that, sometimes you find yourself cursing the narrator (yourself so to speak) when he's summoning some additional Apaches just because "he wan'ts to know if everybody is still listening" or make yourself play whole parts (from a different perspective) again. This and the addition of the duels in which you fight the most feared und well known Gunslingers of the time. Gunplay itself is solid, it very satisfactiory to fire the weapons, also solid are the enemys though they lack a little bit in variety. The only thing that bothered me is length which should be about 6 hours. But it only 15 € and for that price (unlike other games who cost 60 €) I can live with a gametime of 6 hours. So in conclusion its a really good game and everyone who likes Spaghetti-Westerns or the Westerngenre in general has to play this game !

Clumsy default controls, wildly varying AI, an overabundance of protect/escort missions, and intrusive online integration all conspire against a could-be-fantastic open world game.
Mission design is consistently poor, naval units seem to have laser accuracy while on the waves (even compensating for CoF increases), and the AI calls in reinforcements constantly, not even waiting for the current reinforcements to arrive.  This really messes with the flow of combat, and forces the player to do what's efficient over what might be fun or inventive or engaging.
The map is beautiful, the soundtrack is pretty good (I'm personally more of a fan of JC2's), and it performs well on my system (max settings except AA and blur effects, 1440p/60fps on a 1070).  If the battle flow was better thought out and if missions weren't variations on "don't let this pants-on-head-stupid AI die to waves of enemies), this would be a great game

After a lot of anticipation and waiting, I decided to buy and download this game.  I've been hooked on the Total War franchise since the first Rome; and I have been looking forward to Rome II only to be sorely disappointed.  I did my research, making sure my computer meets the requirements to run this game, waiting a couple of years for any bugs to be patched and kinks worked out.  After debating with myself and my wife about if we really COULD afford the $66.59 to purchase the game (I'm a rare breed of nerd who actually owns a house which I'm renovating, two cars, and holds down a full time job), my wife convinced me to spend the money and download it.  The download went fine, and I was pleasantly surprised when I clicked on 'play' and the 'Rome II' screen popped up with the standard copywrite fine print, as all the Total War games do when they first start.  But that's all that happened.  After pulling up the task manager to find that the program was not responding, I naturally chose to end task and re-try.  Well, five or six attempts later and I've given up.
I don't know if this is a Steam problem or a Total War problem, but I have just wasted good money on a product I can not use.  I could have spent this money on groceries, gas, paint or some other product for my house, or simply spent it elsewhere, but I decided to roll the dice and download a game from Steam.  What happened to the days when you went to a electronics store and purchaced software in cd or dvd form, returned home, listened to the hum of the cd/dvd reader for a few minutes after a few clicks of the mouse buttons and keyboard, then had a game you could enjoy to escape the reality of life for a couple hours when you had the time?
In the past I have been curious to know why PC seems to be a dying breed of videogame console, but I think I understand why now.  I had a couple of games on my Steam wishlist, but now they are going to be removed, and I think the next money I spend in the realm of video games will be on a PS4.  Steam is just not worth the time and bother any longer.
I know this is supposed to be a review of Rome II, but unfortunately, when I was hopping to give a great review on a new (to me) exciting recent release from this francise, I am sadly unable to do so.  Not because the game is terrible, because if it is anything like their previous titles, I'm sure it is excellent; but because I was simply un-able to play it.  If you want to roll the dice and download this title from Steam, I wish you luck on your journey, and hope you are granted many hours of relaxing escape from reality.  But my recomendation is to give up on Steam and look elsewhre for your gaming experience.

First off, don't let my hours fool you. I've completed the game using the pirated version because I did not want to spend $60 AUD on something I might not like. But after finishing, I immediately bought it from steam at full price without any hesistation. This goes to show how much I love this game.
Plot-wise, this is a romance game and is split into 2 sections: a school arc and an after story (AS) arc. I'm not gonna say anymore because that's for you to explore if you decide to give this game a try :). But be warned, the feels train has no break once it starts and you'll be crying your eyeballs out throughout the entire journey.
Graphics-wise, the art style might not suit everyone. I was taken aback at first but got used to it eventually. If you're like me, please stay with it. Don't let this stop you from playing.
Gameplay-wise, all you have to do is read and choose options. That's it. Be ready to read A LOT though. I remember reading someone's comment saying that the amount of words in this game is more than the entire Lord Of The Rings trilogy!
Sound-wise, this game has some of the most memorable, beautiful soundtracks I've ever heard. I've begun taking piano lessons just to play some of these tracks.
Length-wise, this game is very long. I think it took me more than 150 hours to complete all the major paths and reach the true ending yet there are still some hidden paths and hidden dialogues waiting for me.
Overall, I don't consider this a game. I consider it an experience. A life lesson about friends and family. This game literally changes my outlook on life. I've been gaming for more than 10 years yet never have I ever cried while playing but man this game managed to do that.
My only gripe with the game is that it's so hard to unlock AS and reach the true ending. It's practically impossible to complete this game without a guide (for me anyway). There are many guides floating around the internet which you can freely look at. I used these 2
and
. They aren't mine btw. All credit (and my thanks) goes to respective authors.
And that's it! I hope my review helps you decide. I sincerely hope that you'll give this game a try since I think it's something everyone should experience at least once in their life.
P.S. As you may know there is an anime adaption. The anime is really good however imo it's nowhere near as emotional as the VN. Therefore if this is your first time experiencing Clannad, I'd strongly recommend the VN. If you don't have the luxury of time then the anime would have to do.

Clannad starts out as a seemingly innocuous school life VN with mulitple routes but turns into much, much more.
The story touches on so many things that happen to people as they go to school and move on start their lives, jobs, and families in this case. Triumphs, tragedies, insecurities, self doubt, the meaning behind living and dealing with death. You will laugh out loud, and if you really read this story and take things seriously, it's very likely to cause you to shed tears of sadness and joy several times before the end.
Is it flawless? No, I think there are stretches that go on for a bit too long and some of the character specific routes resonate much better than others. The art is a little weak, but that can be forgiven due to the age of the title. Any complaint pales in comparison to the emotion the story can bring out in a person. It's really caused me to spend time reflecting on my life.
Anyone who likes visual novels owes it to themselves to play this story, regardless of the cost of the game.

I used to love MMORPGs and Ragnarok Online was one of my favorites. Tree of Savior definitely makes you take a trip down memory lane and brings back those nostalgic feelings. Instead of being just a Ragnarok clone, it also implements a whole lot of new ideas and features.
PROS:
+ Combat and Movement is great. You can either choose to play the game using your keyboard, controller, or a typical point and click mouse set up. When battling bosses, your movements matter as you need to manually position yourself to dodge the incoming attacks. It's not as fast paced or complicated as Tera, but it certainly freshen things up.
+ Amazing amount of classes and combinations. While the typical Tank, Healer, and DPS archetypes still exists in the game, it doesn't really stop you from exploring different types of combinations. You can have your melee cleric, your offensive tank, and as long as you're happy with your character, it's a viable class.
+Art and Music is wonderfully implemented. The game looks wonderful and sounds amazing. The art style is unique and amazing, and each of the BGM fits into the scenario perfectly.
Cons:
- Game is still basically in beta phase. Lots of known bugs and glitches are still around - primarily affecting quests.
- If you play with Mouse mode, the target click-box of many interaction items are far too small and hard to click on, while at times you have to switch over to Keyboard mode to access it
- Crafting system is very basic and bland
- Game is heavily focused on grinding, but maps are too small and there's not enough channels to support all the players
- Bots are everywhere
- Heavy restrictions on many things: market transactions, dungeons, trading, etc.
- All characters look very generic, and there's no option to dye/change your armor appearance asides from your head piece option
- Match-making for dungeons are sometimes imbalanced (I've had dungeon runs of 5 swordsmen classes)
Conclusion:
I love this game... or at least I want to say I do. It feels like the actual sequel to Ragnarok Online, but it doesn't feel like it suits being an MMORPG. The game implements questing to guide you through which zones you're supposed to be in, but because of this the game becomes very linear, and another problem with this is that all players around your level will be grinding in the same zone as well. There's not enough mobs and the respawn timers aren't fast enough to even allow more than 2 parties in the same area.
Instead of being an MMORPG, I think the game would be much more suited as an instanced based Multiplayer-RPG - like Diablo or The Division. Perhaps certain zones and towns could be shared with everyone else, but most of the maps are simply too small in size to accomodate everyone. Some zones I've visited only have 3 channels, and all three channels are filled with bots and other parties trying to KS each other. Some quests requires you to perhaps take a monster down to a certain percentage of health before using an item on them, or activating a shrine to cleanse them, and the over-crowding makes it almost impossible to complete these types of missions.
Bots are also a huge issue as they are basically everywhere. For a game like this the developers should have known that botting would become a huge issue, yet there are no protective measures against bots. Since the game already heavily restricts many things, they could perhaps implement a system where you have to verify yourself once every hour or so. Another way would be to make it so whenever you get reported for being a bot, you get a pop up timer that requires you to verify that you're actually there. Once the timer runs out and you don't verify, your character would be made immobile and invulnerable. To prevent this from being abused, perhaps a player could only be reported on every hour or 2 hours.
As a die-hard Ragnarok Online and MMORPG fan, I do enjoy the game somewhat even despite the flaws, but I wouldn't recommend the game to anyone just yet. The game has a lot of potential, but the existing issues need to be ironed out before I would suggest it to anyone. Also, the issues I've mentioned will probably become even more noticeable once the game becomes F2P and more players join in.

I don't know how to explain this game because it's hard to explain without making it sound boring.  The basic mechanics of this game are best summed up as "passport stamping simulator", but that description falls flat of the REAL heart of the game.  I'll cut to the chase.  This is a game about political intrigue and personal dilemmas.  A young woman comes up to you and gives you an invalid passport.  Naturally, your job requires you to deny her entry but she is begging you to let her through so she can see her ailing father.  Every action has consequence, and the REAL heart of the game has more to do with getting you to think critically about rules in context.  The setting is also very well established.  While the poor English might come off as a tad xenophobic, the grim mood, use of dull colors and lack of music during play segments really sets an amazingly oppressive tone.  Not to mention the way your government, who you work for, is constantly suspicious of you.  This game can be a bit of a one trick pony, but it does it SO VERY WELL that I kept playing and loved every minute.

Let me come off right the bat and say I don't normally write clean and flashed out reviews since I love myself some puns(Hah, that's a cliché way to start.) Firstly, I can't really give a definitive review since my English is bad and grammar is hard, so uh take it with a grain of salt.
Alright so we got the world reowned Visual Novel studio Key, the highly rated story of CLANNAD now available on Steam-o-roni.
tldr; this game makes you wana cry and die
(Sort of a "full(?) review down there")
While I only have completed my first route which happened to be Nagisa route, it was a rollercoaster of emotions like everyone tends to say. I'm not over-exaggerating but it is really felt something right out of the box being that my only previous experience with Visual Novels is Katawa Shoujo(Which is hands down a great Visual Novel too[Shameless Plug]), let me just tell you for now that this isn't a generic short VN you find quite a lot in the Steam Store, while I won't say their bad they sort of lack in the story department.
Righty, story then? How does it go? Well with Visual Novels the choices you make will determine which of the main heroines in the game that you'll be chasing or be chased at. Starting out with my choice I went with Nagisa the moment I layed eyes on her since the moment we were introduced at. Something about her stood out for me, and this goes without saying that she's friggin' adorable. It's hard for me to judge it's story since I started watching the Anime first then went into the game. In with the comparison there's some diferences here and there comparing the route and Anime took in the game's route.
Story: 9.5/10
Going with the flow we have the art style while isn't "modern" to keep up with the hip kids it has its charm to it since it's quite fairly old dating back all the way to 2004's. So like this is kinda 00's era. As I've stated above while I've only completed 1 route so far which is Nagisa's path. Her CG's are great and well detailed in every-way possible with vibrant colors. It can definitely do better in this deparment but hey it's from the 2000's.
Art: 8.5/10
For the music, I'm really astounded by how marvelous it is. The music really put me into the atmosphere in which scene it was depicting be it a a mundane class-lesson to a spur of the moment confession. I really don't have much else to say about this it's just great, fantastic, superb, not even words I can desribe the sound. With the most memorable sound track of mine to be "Nagisa".
Music: 10/10
Gameplay department? Well it's what you'd expect out of any Visual Novel realistically, you click, you read rinse and repeat. This ain't no triple A game where you run to Point A to Point B and blast enemies high off the earth and off to the moon with cool rockets looking guns. Standard click and read kind of thing. Did I forget to mention? The well layed out UI and settings makes it goes hand with hand.
Gameplay: 10/10
Overall I can say for sure is this is a must have for die hard Visual Novel dudes or dudette's out there. This kind of story telling, music and art style mixed so well that, well you can't help but roll up in a ball and cry the living daylight out of you. Just buy the damn game already dammit!
Overall: 9.5/10

Games are not made for free. This game uses a similar business model as most mobile-app companies do: micro-transactions are what power this game. It is a legitimate business model. If you don't like it, don't play it. You have a basic membership that gives you access to hunt all animals, gives you unlimited ammo, among some other things, but those are the basics. The memberships run at $9.99 per every three months. Without it, you're very limited on the types of animals you can hunt, so it's pretty much necessary to even play the game. In this way, yes, "Free to Play" is misleading. "Free to Explore," would be more accurate, as you can still visit all the parks and see the amazing graphics this game has to offer.
After you have paid your initial $10 for membership, there's still a few things you'd need to unlock all the basics of the game. For smaller game, like ducks and rabbits, you can't shoot those with the rifle you're given for free at the beginning of the game. You need either a shotgun, bow and arrow, or both, in order to hunt either of these. I consider calls a vital part of the game as well. While you could do without, they make getting your prey in a convenient location much easier, and it can allow you to gain a line-of-sight that you were unable to get without the calls. You absolutely will need to pay for at least two pairs of camos, as you start off with a white t-shirt and blue jeans, and prey can see you from a mile away. There's other smaller things that I personally could not do without, like various scopes and scent eliminators, but other people could quite easily enjoy the game without them.
Personally, I have paid over $100 for all my features in this game, and I don't regret it at all. The game is insanely fun and immersive. You don't need everything I purchased (like camping supplies, med kits, killer scopes, or duck blinds), and you can enjoy this game for under $50 easily.
As for the game play, I don't have many complaints. The HunterNav is basically the Normal/Hard toggle in this game. Want to play the hard way? Don't use the HunterNav. Want to play on Normal? Use it. It helps you track and locate prey on the map in order for you to hunt them down. So if you're a player who just wants to relax, play with the HunterNav. If you want to feel all the frustrations of real hunting, just put it away.
The tracking can get a little irritating at times, as the animals don't follow any kind of realistic pathing mechanisms. The game uses certain patters that animals walk in that you can pick up on after a couple dozen hours of playing the game. Since they just follow these nearly pre-set patterns, they can go some pretty odd routes, like a moose scaling down a cliff face instead of walking down the gradual slope a few meters to the left. I wish there was more AI to them.
My only other complaint would be that there's no way to purchase a vehicle in this game. Even if I had to shell out $30 to get it, even if it scared off all the animals in the area temporarily, I would kill for a vehicle in this game. The maps are gigantic and there's roads going all over the map that don't really seem to have any specific purpose at this time. I'm sure they're making money on tents, which allows you to fast travel to places you've previously been to, but I would throw money at the developers for a four-wheeler or something to use on these roads that go everwhere.
Overall, I'd say this game is an 8/10. I knocked off 2 points because it is more money-consuming than most games. Typically, you can pay $30 for a full-featured, fully-unlocked game. This one, I'd price at $50 to be "full-featured," but not "fully-unlocked," which sucks since you're already almost double the price of an average game and there's still things you want and don't have. But the gameplay is beautiful, amazing, and more-or-less realistic.

Pets covering NPCs, no way to kick players out of dungeons or find more from inside, a party matching system that is 100% random, ignores class and level, and does not guarantee a viable party... etc.
5) There is no real communication about any of this at all. Even basic information about future plans is inconsistent, at best.
It's this bad... and supposedly the game is ready to release? You kidding me? This is just awful. I could be a more viable gaming company as a one-man show hosting this out of my garage.

The Dark Souls series has become a well renowned game for a survival dark fantasy world. It has, in essence, become its very own genre that is hard to re-create. For single player experiences, it is hard to run around this unforgiving world without a little bit of help. In fact, your first achievement will likely be "This Is Dark Souls". A rude welcome as the only way to achieve it is to die. Not only can the environment be unforgiving, but monsters can, and will, be hidden. They will lure you into a false sense of security. This is best played online thanks to From Software's innovative online interaction system. Players have the ability to "summon" other players into their game by use of a sign. The cost of doing this though, is you have to be human. And if you are human, other players will invade you, and want to kill you for your souls. That is what this game is all about. The acquisition of souls. The lust for power. The greed. As a hollow, you become attracted to souls like a moth to a flame. Welcome to Dark Souls. Welcome to hell in its finest glory.

This is one of my favorite games of all time.
Steam says I've only got 16 hours clocked in on this, but I bought this on disc as a teenager when it first came out in 2007, and probably have well over +100 hours otherwise. Back then it was so horribly buggy and unoptimized at launch, that even while playing on the lowest settings it still chugged at 15 fps and the load times were God-awful. But even then, I was so absorbed in the world that was created here, it was unlike anything I had ever played before, that I was still completely engaged.
Now, ten years on, the game has so much more to offer. There are so many mods available that you can play through the game several times and get entirely different experiences every time. The combat is slow and somewhat tactical and requires patience, and the gameplay itself is clunky, and the difficulty is somewhere between challenging and outright punishing, but you'll never play a game like this again. This is Eastern European sci-fi horror/post apocolypse at its finest.

Here is my first Review of the game un-modded, well, even the Steam version of this game technically isn't actually un-modded, I checked the files & there was a mod file containing the contents of The Zone Reclamation Project Mod, to which should not be of anyone's worries as the mod is stable, changes nothing, & only fixes bugs, so for those of you new Rookies to The Zone worries about bugs, don't be, the game was mostly stable through out the game, anyways, onto the actual review, I gotta say, I love the hell out of this game, it may have been a bit rushed when it was first released, but now I consider it a masterpiece in my opinion for a plethera of many reasons,
One - The Atmosphere: The atmosphere is probably the most affective post apocalypse atmosphere's I've experienced, with Fallout 3 & METRO 2033 Redux alongside it, whether if it is night or day, you'll hear noises of mutants ahead of you reminding that wherever you are in the zone, you are not alone, that, & the gunshots sounding off in the backround at random times.
Two - The Intruiging Story & Setting: The lore itself is a bit obscure & odd as it is LOOSELY based off of the two science fiction novel's STALKER & Roadside Picnic by Boris and Arkady Strugatsky in the 1970s, to which STALKER got a film in 1979 (To which is on YouTube for free with translated subs, I recommend it), but like METRO 2033 & METRO: Last Light both being based on books, S.T.A.L.K.E.R. isn't very accurate which is fine & all that as the original STALKER story ivolved aliens, S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Shadow of Chernobyl however is very different with a story involving a very strange change in story later on in the game to which I will not spoil as you should find it out on your own, but it is very interesting to say the least if you can handle obscure stories like the original STALKER story/film, or Prometheus, as for the setting, to easily explain it, years after the events of the real Ukraine, Chernobyl meltdown, in this alternate history story, the meltdown spreaded out further than it should have, creating a bigger wasteland with people nicknaming it "The Zone" to which a emission which is basically a storm/powerful release excess of noosphere energy from the center of The Zone, but after this Emission occurred, this phenomena itself called Anomalies appeared across The Zone, what are anomalies? No one can really explain, they are random bursts of energy of many types, a vortex that pulls anyone into it before exploding, a portal that teleports you to a random area, a weird forcefield that shoots out a shockwave at you when you get too close, yeah, this game gets very strange, & as this phenomena occurred, they created these odd objects of many shapes & textues, called "Artifacts" Which held many powers, & can be used as a gameplay mechanic, for example, one such artifact can give you better strength to hold your supplies, or to make your skin harder so bullets can't easily penetrate, so STALKERS, which if you don't know is actually an acronym for "Scavengers, Trespassers, Adventurers, Loners, Killers, Explorers, & Robbers" began trespassing into The Zone to take & trade these artifacts while the Military tries to stop this operation, as all this happened, there are scientists finding out the Phenomena behind The Zone.
Three - Gameplay & Mechanics: If you know Fallout, you'll probably say "Hey! This looks exactly like Fallout!" Well, this game came before Fallout, not just that, it doesn't include an RPG system, but it does include some RPG-ish elements as I mentioned before with the artifacts holding capabilities to give you stuff like "5+ Resistance Against Fire", not just that, this game is more tactical & actually based around a more survival/realistic turn of events, well, the vanilla game isn't exactly realistic survival like DayZ, but you can look out for mods that can make it realistic, but that is up to the player whether you want a realistic experience or not, you take in heavy damage from bullets, you can take in bleeding from getting clawed by a mutated beast, & you can get radiation poisoning badly, so it's not much of Fallout 3 & more like METRO 2033 Meets DayZ, also, how is the shooting itself? Some are mixed towards this, me personally, I found my experience fine, the hit detection doesn't seem off, the guns themselves feel balances, but one thing I can say is the first few missions aren't that great & may turn off some first time players, as you are given some weak weapons & immediately shoved into a gun fight mission, but as you learn how to be a STALKER you'll get the hang of it & master the game as I did.
OVERALL FINAL VERDICT:
This game isn't exactly for everyone, but I do consider this a MUST-TRY game, Must-Try as in if you don't like your first experience you should try it again to see if you can adapt & like the game, as for Survival Game fans, this is a Must-Buy, as this is probably your Chernobyl Disaster fantasy you've been waiting to delve into.
FINAL SCORE: 8/10 ONLY MODDED WITH THE ZONE RECLAMATION PROJECT WHICH IS ALREADY INCLUDED WITH STEAM PURCHASE

I'm a long-time player of the Total War series...since the original Rome. That game, with the Europa Barbarorum mod, was a masterpiece.
I see the Creative Assembly has taken some notes from the EB team, adding depth to the non-Roman factions that was lacking in the original Rome.
Combat is decent. It's much harder to route elite enemy troops than in previous TW titles, and if one of your own units gets overwhelmed, their morale begins to drop fast, while still giving you a small window to reinforce them if you have the foresight to keep a unit or two in reserve. Cavalry seems weaker than in the original RTW, which is understandable to a point. The stirrup hadn't been invented at the time of Roman expansion, so heavy cavalry's shock value wasn't exactly what one would've expected from say, medieval knights.
I am somewhat disappointed by the lack of archers for Rome. Archers weren't a common thing for a legion in early Rome, but they could've added archers with the Marius reforms as an auxiliary unit.
Artillery seems to be significantly more accurate than in the original RTW. I can now safely place my ballistas and onagers behind my lines without fear of them bombarding my own troops.
AI is improved over the original. They will use mass charges to try and pin your front line in place, then send in heavy troops to force weak - willed units to break. Watch their cavalry too. They like to flank and/or keep your own horsemen out of the main fight.
Campaign AI is very opportunistic. Leave a town without a standing army nearby, and you'll likely find it under siege by land, sea, or both. Diplomacy is nice, especially if you start out with powerful neighbors. Generally, the AI doesn't break a treaty unless there is great profit in it, and if you play your cards right, you can form long running alliances with friendly factions.
I like the addition of the in-faction political system. Your house has to maintain something of a balance of power to keep your public order and tax revenue bonuses, while at the same time staving off civil war from gaining too much power.
Siege battles are a bit different. As with the original RTW, you have a main victory capture point, plus a number of additional, optional capture points. I'm not sure what the purpose of these additional points are, as the AI only ever seems interested in capturing the primary victory point.
Naval battles can be frustrating, especially if you're fielding a number of artillery ships. They only have a forward-facing firing arc, which is very narrow but has long range. I guess the people of the time weren't bright enough to develop a swiveling base, huh?
My one major gripe about the game is the way turns are done. You get one turn per year, with the season changing with each turn. So you'll have say spring of 170BC, summer of 169BC, and so on. This causes leveling characters to be pointless, as they never live long enough to be useful. To counter this, I highly recommend the 4 turns per year mod in the steam workshop.

When Rome II was anounced i had good intentions of buying this game, maybe not at release as nearly all games have their bug and issues, so i thought to wait until the dust settled and the game was okay to play, in the mean time i wanted to see other players reviews on this game on launch and in its current state, to my disbelief i was shocked to see many negative reviews, after watching countless youtube videos of players negetive reviews it became clear that ROME II was not the game that would be for me to buy yet.
As an RTS player who likes accient warfare and likes some of the TOTAL WAR series i was hoping this game would bring about a new generation of RTS games. Having found out this games uses the warscape engine used in EMPIRE, NEPOLION and SHOGUN 2 it seemed bezzare to use this in ROME.
The issues i found and comparing this to EMPIRE is the combat mechanics, it doesnt provide you with any sense of tention when armies clash, just dull charging.. all units would mould together into one ball, no formations, guard mode, fire at will which makes gameplay frustrating, all kills are done by kill animations and 1V1 as in empire, but seeing ROME TW all units would fight anyone and everyone.
U.I interface kind of follows on from ROME TW however, unit cards are confusing as some units like melee seem to look alike, unless you have an excellent memory of what unit is where it can be hard to remember what unit is where, also unit cards do not provide information onto one card, instead it rotates and flashs through each one as to what is happening, a bar that represents unit numbers which doesnt make any sense although you can turn this off in the game options menu.
The best improvement i can say is the Graphics of the terrain and most of the units in this game, i do think alot of effort has been put into the campaign map and battle maps giving you a sense of "waow" when seeing it on high settings, but this is an RTS game where you should have an equal improvement on all aspects of the game, again if the combat mechanics were as equal to the graphics you would see a much better quality of fighting and clashing in this game.
A.I, well we all know we cant produce the most perfect A.I that would antisipate our moves, most of the total war series do have their issues with A.I as in this game, after seeing a huge amount of patches, which i do believe is to make the A.I better to play against, still it is not enough to make this a challenge, especially in siege battles where the A.I will use their equipment to knock down the walls and leave one section left for them to use their toweres which leaves them confused as they cannot progess anywhere, in many instances this is what they will do. I do think the A.I is very primitive on a stratgy level who always commits their general to a fight, does not use any flanking or hiding units behind terrain and in forests, The AI will always charge head on into a battle regardless of what faces them which again doesnt provide any challenge to a player.
There are many more issues with this game that i can point out but personally if you want to see this then watch youtube videos from players who know what this game should be about, e.g ANGRYJOE, who points out pretty much everything in this game.
One last frustrating thing to point out is this IS NOT a complete game, SPARTA is not included in the game whereas in the previous ROME all factions are playable. I DO NOT AGREE with this at all, having a DLC for sparta and making other numerous DLC's for this game makes me believe that CA and SEGA are trying to claw back as much LOST profits as possible, you will also notice other expanions to ROME II like emperor edition, ATILLA and many more are all DLC's, other campaigns in the game are also DLC's, if you paid full price for this game at e.g £29.99 then take into account of all the DLC's you would like to add.... i will leave that to you to decide what is best for you gaming experience and wallet.
I will point out that i bought this game on a steam sale at 75% off at £7.99, personally it is not worth that, £5.99 in my opinion or less as this a basic and in-complete game which should have been recalled and customers refunded their money until CA made the game more enjoyable and challenging to play. I am very cautious towards CA as i do own EMPIRE, NEPOLION and now ROME II which  is a huge dissapointing game in my eyes, if they do make a ROME III my advice is wait until all the bug and glitches are gone and also look for a FULL content game not bits or pieces that you have to DLC.
For now folks i will be playing and STICKING with ROME TW GOLD EDITION as i do not think ROME II is  an improvement.
Cheers for Reading everyone

As many have already posted in their reviews, Dark Souls II is a game that deserves a good recommendation. While flawed in some places, the central values and mechanics that made the original Dark Souls a great game are still present in Dark Souls II, making for an engaging 60+ hours of gameplay. Unfortunately, if you play those 60+ hours on this copy of the game, you're pretty much wasting your time at this point. A new version of this game will be released, an "HD" version  that uses DX11 instead of DX9. These two games will have incompatible save files and will not allow for multiplayer between them. The short version is this: they're releasing the same game with some very minor changes, calling it the "HD edition", and charging full price for it. And if you bought the original version of Dark Soul II? You're stuck with the inferior product and a bitter taste in your mouth.Which is unfortunate, because the game itself is worth playing.
Here's the full review, in case you want my take on the original edition of Dark Souls II:
The hard thing about making a sequel, I would imagine, isn't actually making the game—after all, most of your core systems and gameplay elements are there and the backbone is ready, you just have to flesh it out. No, the hardest part must be ensuring the game is better than (or at least as good as) the first game you made. Dark Souls II, while not quite the caliber of the first Dark Souls, certainly lives up to the legend Dark Souls originally created. The combat is just as demanding and the play-styles are just as varied, making for an all around enjoyable (read frustrating/soul-crushing/lament-inspiring/awe-invoking) experience.
The only true let down for me in Dark Souls II was, in comparison to Dark Souls, the somewhat bland bosses featured in the game. There were a few bosses within Dark Souls II that I will remember (the battle against Flexile Sentry while the water rises around you and the hectic race to advance through the Executioner's Chariot fight). Perhaps I'm simply jaded after the first game, but overall I found the boss-design for Dark Souls II to lack the same gut-punching grotesqueness and tension that the original contained. Who can ever forget the sudden appearance of that second Bell Gargoyle and the lurch of dread as you dodge between them? Or the steep learning curve of Manus, Father of the Abyss, and his large, sweeping hand? Or the lunging, ground-covering strikes of Gwyn, the trail of fire arcing behind his sword and sparking through the air?
Honestly, what could possibly compare to Ornstein & Smough?
Alright, I had a bit of a thing for the bosses in Dark Souls, so maybe I'm a little bit biased. On the other hand, you can't really blame me for being disappointed when a couple of the Dark Souls II bosses are repeats of the first game. "Old Dragonslayer" will never have the same impact as the Ornstein & Smough fight, especially not when its sort of hemmed in as a weak ode to the first game. The same goes for the Belfry Gargoyles (again) and the double use of the Dragonrider boss in the game. Were they good fights? Sure, but all fights in Dark Souls games are good fights. I still can't help but feel a little cheated.
Despite that small rant, Dark Souls II is still everything you expect from it: unsympathetically difficult, with very little guidance and even less explanation.  There's still a wide array of equipment to pick from, millions of different ways to play the game, and a dozen new fantastic enemies to encounter. The new levels are equally as well done, the characters are just as dismal and complex (though I will always miss Siegmeyer of Catarina), and the plot still doesn't try to be the center focus of the game (which is how it should be, for a game whose selling point is its incomparable combat system).
Unfortunately, while Dark Souls II is a good game, the people selling it aren't. To screw over the entire playerbase who originally bought Dark Souls II by releasing an enhanced edition of the game only a little over a year after the game actually came out isn't just deplorable, it's unforgivable. Dark souls (and dark souls 2) make me remember the days when games were hard.  Times when you had to learn a monsters move set instead of just standing in front of it and loling because you were 15 levels higher than it was.  Comparing apples to apples though, Dark souls 2 isnt as good of a game as the original was.  It is a very enjoyable game nonetheless, but as someone who has played Dark souls 1, 2 and Demon souls, there is just something that Dark souls 2 lacks.   In previous games I would see a boss battle and after finally surmounting it I would want to rush to tell my friends about it, Dark souls 2 is peppered with so many mediocre boss fights that that is just not the case.
Another thing I have noticed about this game is that it feels very much like a victim of its own success.  Much of this game has been cleaned up from the previous, things like soul vessels which allow you to respec is a great quality of life improvement for the player, and yet even in doing what it feels like the players wanted (more bosses, easier spec change, etc) they seem to have lost the spirit of the game overall.  There was a primal visceral feeling about playing Dark souls 1 that just doesnt exist in dark souls 2.
To conclude, I would totally recommend this game, especially to people that havent played the previous game, as it is much more approachable than the previous game was.  That being said some of the design decisions in this game feel as though they pandered to the playerbase instead of remaining true on what was the core of what made this series so good.
