Tree of Savior is probably the most enjoyable MMO experience I've ever had. The short version of this review: It's not perfect, but it's a good start with some really cool ideas. Problems are being ironed out and IMC seems to be actually listening to the player base and changing things for the better.
Ragnarok Online was one of the first MMOs I ever played, and it is a game I'll never forget. I loved so much about the game: The art, the music, the job system. Looking back, however, the game wasn't very well-designed. Very grindy, almost no quests, and low EXP rates made the game more of a chore than anything. It was a shame to see such cool ideas go to waste.
Now, years later, Tree of Savior is the spiritual successor to RO that many of us have been waiting for. Right off the bat it's easy to see the influence RO had on this game, especially in its art direction. The game looks fantastic, blending 2D and 3D together just like RO did, to great effect. The music is also great. I'd say it's not quite up to the level of RO music, but I haven't gotten tired of the music yet and I don't see that happening any time soon.
The combat in this game is executed very well in my opinion. It's not
different from what's been seen in other MMOs, but it's different enough to make it better for me, as someone who finds combat in most MMOs very unengaging, repetitive, and boring. You have your basic attack that you can use by pressing Z, and of course a hotbar of your skills. There's also a lot of importance in moving around to avoid enemy attacks and position yourself correctly. Holding Z does make you auto attack but you still have to be aware of your surroundings and reposition yourself to hit the right enemies and not get surrounded. It's none of the standard "click an enemy and watch your character auto attack" type stuff that I see far too often in other games. Most skills either have a standard cooldown or are on the "Overheat" system. A skill that can overheat has what I'll call a "soft" cooldown. You can usually use the skill once or twice with no penalty, but if you use it too many times in a short period of time, it enters a traditional cooldown. The remaining uses are indicated by dots that get filled in on the skill icon. I like this system because it gives you some strategy. "Do I use the skill now and force myself to wait through the cooldown, or do I save it for when I'm in a real pinch?"
The job/class system is very innovative in this game.
and you'll notice that there's a ton. The way this all works is that you pick a class tree from Archer, Cleric, Swordsman, and Wizard. Once you increase your class level to 15, you can advance your rank. When you move up in rank, you have a choice. You can advance to any class in your tree that has a rank equal to or lower than yours. Choosing a single class multiple times increases the max level of most skills and also unlocks new skills for you. You can create tons of different builds this way, and just planning builds is fun on its own.
Now for all the praise I've given the game, there's some bad too. Keep in mind that right now the game is in its Early Access period, where those of us willing to shell out $10 (or more) are able to play for a month before the general public release. The game's launch was not the smoothest thing I've ever seen. It was quite common to be placed in a queue of several thousand players when attempting to login, horrible lag prevented interaction with NPCs at times, and random disconnects (the infamous "CommanderLoadFail" error) were unfortunately common. Granted this is my first time playing an MMO at launch, so I'm not sure how other MMOs have fared during their launch periods. However, I'm happy to say that these issues have been addressed. More servers have been added, weekly maintenance has been performed to increase server capacity, and these issues have pretty much disappeared.
Right at launch, RMT spammers were quick to hop on the global chat and shell out messages repeatedly. After complaints from the community, IMC stepped up and implemented a minimum level requirement to use the global chat. We've also gained the ability to report bots. The other major complaint you'll hear is about trading restrictions. At the time of writing this review, it's impossible to trade (even between your own characters) without purchasing the token item from the cash shop each month. However, IMC has stated that they are going to be removing this restriction, at least for trading between our own characters. It's nice to see the developers listening to us and making moves to better the game after we've given feedback.
The only other real issue I have with the game right now is the performance. I'm not running a top-of-the-line system: a laptop with an Intel Core i5 with integrated graphics. Even so, I'm usually able to get acceptable performance out of most games if I turn the settings down a bit. ToS struggles to give me 20-30 fps in most areas with all settings turned down as low as they go. In towns and other heavily populated areas, I drop to around 10fps. I'm hoping the game gets further optimization down the line because this performance is just plain awful.
So to sum it up, Tree of Savior, while not perfect, has some great stuff in it. It's tons of fun so far, and IMC seems to be working towards fixing everything we've complained about so far. The game has only been out for a few weeks and I'm sure it will only continue to improve.

Soda Dungeon is a mobile port, of the same name (Duh) It's simplistic and very addictive, sort of like when you become addicted to fizzy drinks, nothing satisfies you.
Follows the standard Clicker formula, get far enough, reset the world but get minimally stronger every time you reset. This game differs as it's not a pure Clicker, it's a beautiful, crisp hybrid. Sort of when you mix Fanta and Coca-Cola together. The game is a lot more interactive than other clickers, which is something I am really enjoying about it. I can't just idle it and come back to copious amounts of stuff; I have to put in a bit of input to get the rewards.
The visuals are brilliant; I wasn't aware this was a mobile port until I started looking for end-game advice and I'm normally a sucker for pointing out shoddy graphic work. The sound design? AMAZING! There's a track that plays when you get to an area called the Frozen City and it's epic, shame there's no soundtrack available.
Lastly, there are microtransactions. No beating around the bush, but this is a game where they do feel entirely optional. Though I do find it strange that the majority of them are priced at $0.99 when some are CLEARLY better than others, I feel like this should be adjusted, as I have been mad if I spent money on this, realising the upgrade was achievable in 30 minutes of gametime.
Overall, a brilliant clicker game that requires a bit of input. Solid graphics and audio with decent gameplay all for the price of NOTHING.

There's nothing really that matches quite No More Room in Hell's atmosphere and genre. It's a shooter at core, but with elements of survival horror. Roguelike sprinkled here and there.
I'll start off simple, the gameplay. It's gunplay is relatively good, every gun giving an appropriate feel of power, melee weapons having weight under each swing. It's very scarce with it's resources, and some maps not having more than 100 bullets and 5 medkits each. Teamwork is key, as even though resources are scarce, you can still fill up your inventory and leave valuables behind, especially if playing alone. More people means more things each person can carry, although more people also means health kits needed to sustain everyone. Dieing is permanent in normal mode, besides the occasional checkpoint which respawns everyone. Zombies are your typical romero zombies, impervious to body damage, but their heads are weak and the only thing that's able to deal actual damage to the zombie. Most guns kill in one to two shots to the head, and most melee kill in two power attacks to the head or five quick ones.
And now, the atmosphere. Nothing I have played matches the tense atmosphere if NMRiH. Struggling to keep that one newcomer alive by handing him pills for his infection, the despair when everyone runs out of ammo and you get overrun, the brief relief of the checkpoints, and the absolute terror of being the last one alive. Chat and voice are disabled when you're dead, as in, only other dead people can hear you if you're dead. The silence when you struggle through alone, only to see the incoming horde in front of you is terrifying, and when you reach the end while passing through all, surviving on a slither of health is probably the best feeling in the world.
The sound design is absolutely gorgeous, and morphs to your current situation, slow tunes when passing through low-zombie areas, tense music when obliterating/getting obliterated by a zombie horde, and the hopeless song when you're infected.
All in all, I'd reccomend this game to anyone.

Rome II: The Fall and Decline of Total War.

Here we go again.
Rome 2 did not have a pleasant launch, but after lots of fixes and some really lame DLC (Seriously, I have to pay to play as ATHENS? SPARTA? You have got to be kidding me), it is done. Or at least it won't be getting anymore updates despite the fact that there is still at least one thing (broken achievements) that need fixing. But with Attila out and this Warhammer thing coming soon... I doubt CA or SEGA cares about this game anymore.
Shame too since it's not bad. Since Shogun 2 got the series back on track and back into the realm of the more melee-centric combat CA is just better at doing AI for, Rome 2 generally does well.... mostly. Melee combat in this game seems rather overpowered, or rather ranged combat just does not seem to do much damage before the big melee brawl begins. This means that any faction that traditionally relied upon arrows and stuff to do much of it's work is at something of a disadvantage... unless you are the Parthians or someone else with awesome horse archers. But if you don't have speedy horses, or you play as a nation that relies more on "skirmisher" ranged units that are mainly on foot, then prepare to be eaten by the melee juggernaut that is Rome or any country lucky enough to have Macedonian-style Pikemen. That's not to say that you can't win. You can. It just will be rough.
Do I sound bitter? Well, I sort of am. And the reason for it lies in one of the game's historical battles that, because of the game mechanics I described above, is basically impossible to do as it was done in reality. Which battle do you ask? Cannae. Yes, that Cannae. The legendary victory Hannibal won by using a smaller and more lightly equipped army of ~50,000 to surround and annihilate an entire Roman army of ~80,000 men. To make that work you need to have your center, consisting mainly of lighter troops, manage to not have their morale break as they fall back until you are able to use your elite troops on the wings and your horseys to close the Romans in. Except... your center is going to get eaten alive by that giant mass of Romans. Even if you get far enough to close the net (and I did), it all went to hell once the center broke and the Romans were able to then eat their way out of this encirclement. One of the most famous battles of all time... and I had to win it by exploiting the game mechanics (which has the Roman Army march straight ahead for a while no matter where your actual troops are) and forcing all the Roman troops to chase my lighter troops all over the map until I was able to pounce on them after they got exhausted. Even then, it was a mess.
So CA messed up one Historical Battle. Who cares? Who even plays HB's anyway? Well, I do for one since they are neat and some of them have been very well done (See most of the ones in Napoleon). Even so, I concede that the campaigns are where the meat of this game lies. And in that regard... well it's mostly good. It takes times to get used to the new city management stuff in order to balance out things to make sure the people are happy, fed, and paying you the monies you need to FIGHT EVERYBODY - because you will be fighting lots of people in this game. But that isn't a problem because, well, it's Total War and all that. The whole point is to fight people. o_o
My biggest problem with the campaign part of the game lies in the AI's -very- heavy tendency to use force march to dash little armies all over the map running just out of range of the armies I have chasing after them. Unless you can corner them, the AI can just keep doing this over and over, particularly at sea, with you having great difficulty in managing to force them into a battle at all. Unless you do one of two things. First, you can deliberately weaken your own forces so the AI decides to attack you rather than flee. You still will deal with AI armies and fleets running around, but some will attack you at least. The other thing I ended up doing was to take a city/town, then leave it open and undefended to temp one of these AI roamers to attack it, and then (since you can't really move with the army that takes a city after it has done so that turn) eat them when they can't escape. I find all of this... rather annoying. >_>'
Oh yes... those victory conditions. Can't forget those. Makes every campaign game take a very long time. And there are soooo many factions to get achievements for. ;_;
The battles themselves, aside from the stuff I wrote above about how the game seems better geared towards melee combat, is fine. Lots of variety in the unit types, and the distinctions between the different cultural groups in terms of their strengths and weaknesses add quite a bit of variety to the tactics you have to fight against. The AI still does stupid AI things you can exploit, but at least they can put up a decent challenge at other times. On land at least. At sea... well. Lets just say that ramming ships very much became my tactic of choice. It made most naval battles, even when the odds were stacked against me, pretty easy. I had more difficulty with having my ships getting stuck on the wreckage of enemy ships and being unable to move than by any real opposition the enemy put up. Oh well. At least the land battles are cool.
So... overall impressions? Fairly mixed with a positive leaning, as it was with TW games during it's Empire/Napoleon days. Rome 2 does stuff right with being a competent game that has fun battles, but then annoys me with it's AI armies running all over and how the game's battles seem much more favorable to melee-heavy factions like the Romans or Greeks (unless you are the Parthians or some other horse archer country). One last negative is the volume of DLC SEGA put out for this game. Yes it's kinda neat to play so many different varied factions, but some of the factions that ended up being gated by DLC (Athens, Sparta) really should have been playable from the start. Rome 2 is a major offender when it comes to excess DLC, and SEGA seems all too happy to continue that trend into the future. ♥♥♥♥♥♥s. >_>
As for the DLC campaigns, i'll review those individually. I still need to play some of them to see how they are anyway. If nothing else, you can certainly get your money's worth out of Rome 2. There's enough stuff to do in this game to keep you playing for a -very- long time. Or at least until you get bored or aren't a crazy achievement-hunter like me.
So... this gets a "yes" from me while I frown slightly at CA for some of it's mistakes and glare at SEGA for all it's DLC. This is a competent game, but I still prefer Shogun 2 even if this game has -way- more variety with it's factions.
Get this on a sale if you want it. It seems to end up on sale often enough, and you don't want to buy all that stupid DLC for full price. Trust me on that.

Despite still beeing in Early-Access it offers a LOT more content than some AAA-Full-Price titles.
Using this you start your factory. Place the mining drill on iron and mine some coal to keep it running. But don't forget to put a chest in front of it. Where should the iron ore go otherwise? Remember to keep it fueled. But hey! Returning to the mining drill to refuel it every other minute is really annoying. Why dont play another mining drill on coal and transport the cola via conveyer belts to the other drill. Now just put the inserter before so the coal actually gets put into the drill and vóila! You just did your first automation.
You continue like this and after having stable iron and copper supply you'll have to automate the production of science packs. What is that you ask? Just the most import item in the game after iron plates. You use them to research new technologies that aid you expand your factory and make it more efficient.
But there is something out there. A threat. Danger. For the beginning your pistol and hands will be sufficent. But not for long.
After a while the ore patches you have your iron and copper plate production on are running out! Well good thing you just researched trains! With them you can transport large amounts of goods over long distances. And trust me when i say: You'll HAVE to!
After dozens of hours of automation and efficiency increasing restructuring of your factory you'll eventually reach your goal: SHOOTING A ROCKET INTO SPACE.
There is so much to write about this game and what gameplay elements it has to offer but i don't have the time to do so, nor do i want to spoil too much.

Now that I've completed the game (minus some extras) I'm going to share my thoughts. This review isn't going to be about the quality of the story itself, (other reviews have done it better then I can) but rather about the translation coming from the original fan translation for the full voice version.
Sekai I feel did a mostly good job with the translation. Those who played the original fan patch knew that the translation really fell apart as you got deeper in, with afterstory being extremely hard to understand at times. While it was a rocky start at launch, after a few patches I can happily say the translation is of great quality. While I did notice some errors here and there (the game being as huge as it is, to be expected) they weren't constant enough to really notice. For example, I only noticed one in afterstory, and given the context it might have been intentional. My only gripe is that you could tell they took a few liberties with the translation. For example “Furakawa Bakery” is translated as “Furakawa Bread”, a change from both the fan patch and the subs for the anime. (unless my memory is failing me) I also noticed “Hamburger” was changed to “Salisbury steak” as well as other small things. I can only really recall once instance where these minor changes really bothered me though and unless you're like me and have both read and watched this story too many times, you'll will prob not notice.
To me, however what really sells the 50 dollar price tag in the updated assets. While I agree that some of the CGs come off as deformed, the HD assets were still nothing short of an upgrade for me. So while some deformed CGs came of as more so, the ones that looked good already looked REALLY good. Some of them looked so good in HD to me that I felt like I was looking at them for the first time. S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Shadow of Chernobyl is a timeless classic in my opinion. I'm sure many agree with me - it was my first venture into computer gaming many years ago (2008 is when I picked it up originally, I believe). Set in and around the area of Chernobyl (obviously), the world is open for you to explore and discover your identity, as you are an amnesiac. The games' structure is pretty evenly paced for the most part, however there is a very, very steep learning curve at the beginning if you are used to run-and-gun style games (particularly the first mission, where you are outnumbered and unequipped to handle the situation if you don't use tactics). You'll encounter everything from run-of-the-mill thugs and highly trained soldiers, all the way down to mutated beasts and telekenetic monsters throughout your journey. Overall, the game is a bit buggy to this day, and most people enjoying this title won't be computer-savvy enough to iron out some of the fixes possible. However, I'd definitely recommend this game to anyone looking for a fantastic open-world adventure set within the confines of Russias' "Exclusion Zone".

In Broforce you have the ability to play as a bro-ed out version of a movie action hero, to switch to another one you have to save them from a cage and this gives you another life as well. But you can not select the one you want, you just get them randomly. And since some are noticably weaker than others this becomes a problem at the end of the game when you really want the characters which suit your playstyle and deal decent damage, otherwise you just end up losing that life.
The character design is interesting and distinctive enough to let you recognize which hero you are playing as. The very first time you play as a hero you get an introduction screen with a bro version of the hero's name. There is a pretty large selection available, and you keep unlocking new ones the more heroes you save, I think I managed to recognize every single one of them, so the developer did a great job with character design.
The levels seem to be well made, however I must say I enjoyed the earlier and middle levels much more than the later ones. Once I got to the alien infestation I just didn't find it nearly as enjoyable to shoot at aliens. The feeling that I got was that the levels were made to throw as much as they can at you without caring about pacing of the level.
Even though each hero has a unique attack and special ability it becomes really annoying that you can't choose the one you want, the game becomes kind of a slog trying to get to the next cage to change into another hero.
I also feel like they didn't go far enough with the "bro" version parodies, the enemy design could certainly be improved and it would be great if there was some ridiculous storyline with a bro version of a famous action movie villain. As it stands you're just going through the levels in order to go through the levels. Which means the game is good for a couple of hours of fun, but after that it starts to outstay its welcome.

The only reasons not to get this game would be inadequate graphics cards, lack of funds, or hating storytelling and fun.
Story-wise, the experience is essentially the same as Bastion's, though the combat and resource management is notably different.

If you liked Bastion and would play it again, then Transistor is well worth it.
If you found it to be somewhat lacking, then I don't honestly feel that the reworked combat alone will be ultimately satisfying.
Before I dive into the other parts of the game, I feel it is worth mentioning that the PC version suffers a few hiccups here and there, especially with KB+M controls. Being able to aim your attacks in Turn() is nice, but the game will often snap your attacks to enemies you're mousing over instead of the tile you're aiming for. Almost every attack is (or can have) AoE, so this is kind of a big deal. The game used to stutter hard on my rig, but no longer does so with the first update. However, that very update broke camera controls in Turn(), making it difficult to aim or move off of the screen. The game is definitely playable with a controller, and I recommend trying that.
Now, the game's individual parts are not bad-- the art direction is gorgeous, and you really couldn't ask for more from the music or Logan Cunningham. The combat system is at first pretty deep, and allows for the player to flesh out their own arsenal and playstyle, but provides little incentive for the player to actually experiment once they've unlocked all the attached lore (executed pretty neatly) and discovered their winning combos.
But there is ultimately something missing both from Bastion and Transistor. I've found that they both leave you wanting more-- not necessarily in a good way. There is little exploration or risk/reward beyond the critical path, and perhaps the addition of one or two extra mechanics might have tightened it up a bit; made it feel more substantial.
I acknowledge that it sounds superfluous, and hopefully it won't bother you as much as it did me. I really want to appreciate the sentiment of elegant game design, because the game does feel like it's pretty clean of unnecessary or tacked-on bits (aside from NG+). I think the real flaw is that you aren't really introduced to any new gameplay mechanics outside of combat, and the combat does not stay fresh forever. Again, maybe it is unnecessary and it won't bother you, but them's my two pickles.
Regarding NG+: don't bother recursing through the game for the story. All that's new is one or two lines at the start, different enemy setups, a second pair of every function (you can power up a function with a second instance of itself) and of course the achievement.

is probably one of the best visual novels I've ever played, maybe even the best, and this is coming from someone who went in knowing very little about it (I knew of one spoilery plot point and that it was apparently scientifically designed to make you come down with a bad case of the feels).
I will not include any spoilers in this review, as this game is best going in completely blind (not that spoilers will ruin the emotions, but avoiding them is best regardless), so you can rest easy.
The story is about a delinquent high schooler named Tomoya Okazaki, who has a really crappy life. He has no mother, his father is an alcoholic, and every day is miserable for him. His only friend is an annoying idiot, and he's constantly late to school. Despite all this, he still lends a helping hand to those who need it, and never expects anything in return. That all begins to change when he meets a girl named Nagisa, which kickstarts a bunch of changes in his life that (depending on the player's choices) proceed to lead him to blooming relationships with old friends, new faces, and help the people around him achieve happiness.
The other main part of the story is the "Illusionary World" which is sometimes an intermission between certain dates in the story. The Illusionary World segments focus on two characters, a single girl and a doll made out of junk, and it takes a long time (read: a lot of reading) to figure out who they are. Not every route goes through the whole thing, and some stop earlier than others.
What really drew me into this story was its world and characters. Everyone in this game feels like a real person, with very strong characterization and development. As Tomoya (and by extension the player) grows to know these people, I wanted to help them with their problems, I wanted to see them get their happy endings and overcome their hardships. The only exception to this rule is Tomoya's best friend, Sunohara. I generally found him grating, and had the serious urge to skip through most of his dialogue (which I couldn't resist doing at quite a few instances). But even Sunohara, annoying as he is, still has a lot of depth and tons of great moments.
And it's not just the story and characters that drew me into this game's world, the music and voices were a huge help to the experience. This game's soundtrack is simply phenomenal, from the calming title screen music, to the somber pieces during the emotional scenes, and the upbeat sounds of the silly scenes. The music perfectly fits whatever is happening, and I wish I had the money to buy the soundtrack, it really is that fantastic. The voices are all perfectly delivered. Everyone sounds the way they look (if that makes any sense), and they make the emotional scenes all the more powerful. The voices are only in Japanese though, but that isn't too much of a detriment, and I'm a dub person.
The visuals are okay, I wouldn't say they're anything spectacular, and it might take some time to get used to everyone's eyes being so freaking far apart. Some of the CGs also look a bit weird, especially the first one you see, but it isn't too detrimental. It can also be annoying to some that the game isn't in widescreen, but it seems every visual novel has that "problem."
Another nice feature is the Dangopedia, which is basically a helpful tool for people who don't know all the culture differences and references, which is really helpful. However...
As much as I recommend this story to people, I don't think this is a beginner's VN, especially for its price. $50 (or equivalents) is a
steep price for a game that is essentially nothing but reading with the occasional choice (Some routes have more than others) to see how the story plays out. I'd recommend trying out a freeware or at least very cheap VN (like
) to see if this kind of game is for you before considering buying this.
Granted, this is well mitigated because assuming you don't skip anything, this game is about 80-100 hours of reading, and it's a really good read.
I spent 48 on this game during the holiday sale last year, and I have no regrets about it. It may not be for everyone, but if you want a truly emotional and touching tale, then you can't do much better than

When I saw that Sekai Project and Key would release Clannad for Steam, I was excited. I had played it before, but, only a few hours or so (the not so good fan translation).
Undoubtedly, this is Key's best visual novel. It will have you laughing, crying, and thinking about things, especially relationships and the way people behave.
Its a very long VN, so, it is well worth the money that it demands. I have played many hours as you can see, and I have only finished one or two routes. Its up there in length alongside classics such as The Fruit of Grisaia.
Its fantastic that it has been upgraded to HD graphics, the translation is much better, and the inclusion of the Dangopedia is another great feature, along with achievements.
This classic VN needed a facelift, and Sekai Project have done a good job with it. Thanks to them (and Key), more people can now experience it for themselves.

First let me say this : I like CLANNAD. It's an all time favorite of mine. I own original DVD's including After Story, I bought official soundtrack available in Japan ( which was WAY too expensive to get... but I really liked the songs so it was worth it ). I was hesitant whether to buy Clannad on steam, most reviews were not helpful or honest and written by fanboys/girls. I didn't want to pay 29.99 GBP for the story that I already knew, music that I heard countless times... and yet I bought it. I bought it to support Key, I would like them to release more of their Visual Novels here on steam.
That being said I do feel dissapointed. Don't get me wrong the art style is ok albeit a bit dated but in HD. Story is the same as anime and it seems like everything is there BUT here's where the experience sucked for me.
* Small spoilers ahead *
There are some new routes and jokes that weren't present in the anime which is great BUT those that are similar to anime lack visual impact and motion. Let me explain : Tomoyo kicked some bullies on motorbike which looked awesome in anime. They added cheesy spectator view and made her look badass.
In this Visual Novel the only thing you get is Okazaki looking out of the window only to comment on what is happening. Yeah that's it.
Next example : Remember when Sunohara wanted to join the drama club? Okazaki had thought : If this was and RPG... Then in anime we had cool RPG hud displayed and all three options chosen. While in VN there is only text... yeah. It doesn't deliver the impact that anime has.
There is more examples like this so VN feels a bit poorer in that aspect.
OK,OK someone might say : OH BUT(T), VN has more content! MOAH CONTENT! More jokes and it expands a bit more of the story!
Now calm down you♥♥♥♥♥ Yelling doesn't make your argument helpfull. Yes it does have a little bit more than anime but I found out that in some routes like FUKO it doesn't really expands ANYTHING. It's the same thing that anime had! SAME FLIPPING THING. Same ending except you get LO! Two different CG... and slightly different dialogue.
I've seen it in anime. It does not add anything to my experience.
You know, I'm not caomplaining. I could look pass those points that I have stated. After all it's and old Visual Novel with a new paint on it. It's a classic so I guess I'm being picky BUT there is one thing I will not back down. CHOICES.
Yep you heard me. Choices the game gives you.
When I started playing Clannad I wanted to go with Tomoyo route. Oblivious to the fact that her route * SPOILERS * is blocked... Yep you heard me. I ended up with a bad ending. You need to do FUKO and MISAE routes first to get to Tomoyo route. WHY? I felt so angry that I have to do two routes I didn't really wanted to do... In the end you have to pretty much stick to anime's path to get in the general direction. When I started the game I didn't know I had to do Fuko and Misae first. The game DOESN'T TELL YOU. You must magically figure it out by failing...
So I went with Nagisa for a while ( in anime eventually Tomoyo shows up ) and I thought there will be a branching to Tomoyo route BUT NO. It won't show up. Instead I somehow got myself on Fuko route WTF? That wouldn't be half as bad however I didn't do everything PERFECTLY ( all the choices have to be JUST RIGHT ) and I messed up her ending... Didn't get to wedding day. Only to CG scene.
To sum it all up. WHY OH WHY, game dev's thought it would be a great idea to set up mines on players route only to watch them fail over n over again. There is around 50 + choices to make in Fuko's route. If you miss important ones YOU ARE DONE. You won't get the happy ending. Sometimes its easy to guess but other times you find yourself puzzling what the heck did I do wrong?! I wish the game valued my time a bit more. Game devs 1, player 0. GG.
I like choices but at least after failing couples of times give me hint. Highlight important choices or something. Because it will get confusing and furstrating to waste time.., trust me. Anime in that regard is just a pleasantry.
It's not a standard Visual Novel. You need to invest time and after many fails I recommend using a Walkthrough... hopefully spoiler free one.
So can I recommend the game? Yes to those who haven't seen the anime but for those who have anime WAIT for the price drop. Save yourself frustration.

I bought this game on sale, hoping that it would satisfy my pixel-art fetish until I found something more substantial. But what I thought would be a gimmicky "bargain bin" game turned out to be one of the best games I have played in recent memory. Read on to find out why…
The Good: The first thing that struck me is how slick this game is to play. The characters move perfectly across the screen. For a game like this, where you will find yourself dodging dozens of exploding enemies while trying to climb up cliffs or blow holes through walls, that tight control is essential. And they got it perfect. That same effort they put in to make the game play smooth was also present in the art and style of the game. Every single aspect of it was consistently and lovingly crafted with a specific goal in mind. They were trying to connect you to a certain sense of nostalgia about those old 1980s and 1990s action movies, and once again they completely succeeded. It was humorous but also self-conscious, not just blindly pelting you with action movie troupes but really picking out what made them fun and making the whole game about that fun. If you haven't seen the trailer for this game yet I suggest you go and take a look at it. When I first saw it I thought they were just trying to be funny (and they are). But the game actually feels exactly like that cartoon trailer. That's no small accomplishment.
The Bad: The only problem I encountered with this game is that some of the playable characters just felt weak and useless. Double Bro Seven and the Brocketeer in particular just could not pull their weight on the bro team, especially in the last third of the campaign. It took several shots from the Broketeer's pistol just to break one block or kill even the weakest bad guy. And when you have twenty bad guys on screen at once, some of them wanting very much to explode in your general vicinity, that pea-shooter of a gun was a real liability. Honestly though, I was switching between characters so often through the natural course of the gameplay that I hardly had time to feel the sting of frustration. Most of the other characters were a real joy to play, with weapons that blew the world apart in all these unique ways.
The Verdict: This game was just fun all the way around. It has all the consistent style and polish of a well-crafted game, and it also has the flexibility that makes all the best gaming "war stories" possible. There is no hand-holding, and yet the game is at just the right level of difficulty and ramps things up at the perfect pace. If the screenshots and videos look even mildly interesting to you I would definitely suggest you get your hands on this title. I don't think you will be disappointed.

S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Shadow of Chernobyl is a timeless classic in my opinion. I'm sure many agree with me - it was my first venture into computer gaming many years ago (2008 is when I picked it up originally, I believe). Set in and around the area of Chernobyl (obviously), the world is open for you to explore and discover your identity, as you are an amnesiac. The games' structure is pretty evenly paced for the most part, however there is a very, very steep learning curve at the beginning if you are used to run-and-gun style games (particularly the first mission, where you are outnumbered and unequipped to handle the situation if you don't use tactics). You'll encounter everything from run-of-the-mill thugs and highly trained soldiers, all the way down to mutated beasts and telekenetic monsters throughout your journey. Overall, the game is a bit buggy to this day, and most people enjoying this title won't be computer-savvy enough to iron out some of the fixes possible. However, I'd definitely recommend this game to anyone looking for a fantastic open-world adventure set within the confines of Russias' "Exclusion Zone".

One of my all time favourite games, Stalker SOC provides a compellingly atmospheric and challenging survival/shooter experience. An excellent game in its own right, Stalker SOC is made even better by the Stalker Complete (2009) mod, which bundles together a variety of impovements from higher resolution textures to increased variety of sounds and music, while also fixing a large number of bugs. The mod polishes and refines the game rather than drastically changing it. SOC was developed by a handful of adidas-clad slavs on a budget of four cases each of vodka and cigarettes and in the vanilla game it shows. Brilliant and ambitous in its design, but riddled with minor bugs that chip away at the player's immersion. The modded version allows players to experience the game as it could have been if the developers had more time and money.

Elder Scrolls Online or ESO is an MMO from the game series Elder Scrolls. If you haven't played a MMO but have played other Elder Scroll games just know that this is a tad bit different than what you are use to. Now if you are a MMO player but never have played Elder Scrolls then you will have no problem picking things up and noticing the beauty in the game. ESO did have a big flop upon release but that's because it was a unfinished game. The game was not polished or optimized, bugs everywhere very limited content. Now, the wonderful world of Tamriel is a marvelous place to explore and have many adventures. From Trading and selling within guilds to conquering dungeons and trials. The game keeps growing in content, convenience and community. Improvements are constantly being made. Elder Scrolls lore is fantastic and ESO brings all that is expected to the table. Economy in ESO is unlike most MMO's, there is no one Auction House but guilds bid on Guild Traders making guilds more of an importance than just a group of friends. The Dungeons in ESO will blow any other MMO dungeons out the water. From the immersive  combat and flexibility of classes to the mechanics of each boss fight to the most detailed architecture in each dungeon... did I mention the lore ? Yes, their are still some problems with the game like slow falls, farming bots, falling through the game, maybe a quest bug here and there but nothing that makes the game unbearable to play and enjoy. This game is one of the best games I've played in my life lol. I'm nervous about doing this review because I can't say enough about the game. I play this game faithful and religiously, I'm a guild leader and play this game with a passion! If you are looking for a new MMO to enjoy or never played an MMO and wanting to try one, this is it. I give this game a 10 out of 10. This one will see you in Tamriel!

This game popped up in my Steam Queue a few days ago and I downloaded it immediately after finding out it was a free to play RPG about hiring soda junkies to explore the local dungeon for you. It's all about grinding/exploring the dungeon and upgrading the tavern with the loot you bring back.
You can purchase a stall for a merchant who will collect better gear as you get further into the dungeon. You can also buy new sodas, stools, tables, and other tavern upgrades to attract new soda junkies (different classes of characters to hire.). You can even hire the merchant, tavern owner, and other local NPCs to explore the dungeon for you. I like that the game rewards you seemingly no matter what you do. By that, I mean, every upgrade you purchase feels meaningful and useful plus you can purchase a banker upgrade to earn interest on your money while not playing the game. You also get gold no matter how far your party makes it-and with the autocombat system, you can safely walk away for a bit or watch your party just rake in cash for you til they die. Then you just hire new junkies and go back in over and over again.
I'm sure it will get boring in the end, as most things tend to do with me, but I still have more than half the upgrades/soda junkies to unlock plus more than 900 more levels to the dungeon to explore. Knowing I'm collecting money even when not playing means I'll keep coming back to this in between new games that I play. The progression rate is pretty steady, too, so I'll likely play it several hours at a time without realizing it whenever i do come back. This isn't a game I can see myself binging on for days at a time (like Dark Souls, or Skyrim-games I would play all day every day for days in a row) but it is certainly a game I can see myself playing an hour or so daily or a few hours a week. Regardless, this is a game I plan on coming back to play repeatedly until I've seen all it has to offer.

Excellent game.  I don't feel that it is quite as good as Bastion, but is certainly well worth the price tag.  If you can find the spare cash I would recommend picking up the soundtrack as well.  So far the full soundtrack has been on loop every waking hour in my house for the last three days.  To break things down:
PROS
1. Excellent soundrtack as mentioned before.  It neatly ties in to the story and many of the tracks have to be discovered in game giving the music a unique relationship with the gameplay.
2. When you figure out the combat it is very tight and deep allowing for many approaches to the same problems and the method of punishing your death by taking your most invested ability forces you to see most of them.
3. Great story that I feel makes the most of the female protagonist.  Make sure to pay attention to the terminal responses as this gives great insight to the life of a singer without a voice.
4. Beautiful art although this is from supergiant so thats to be expected.
5. NG+
CONS
1. Combat can get really annoying until you get the hang of it, and as far as the PC version I didn't feel that combat outside of turn() to be smooth or intuitive forcing me to run until turn was up.
Thats about it really.  A minor quibble about the combat is all I can come up with, well worth the 20 bucks.

Its basically Rust, but with Chivalry type combat.  The map is a lot of smaller, but it evens out.  Servers are 30-60 people at the moment and the map works fine with it.
You can guild with friends and set them as family so they can open/close doors to the base.  A feature that took Rust a long time to implement is already in RoK's.  This made things a lot more group friendly at the start.  You can actually claim land with crests once you make a house/castle.  You can then upgrade the crest to take more land.
Game has a good crafting system with tiers in place.  Advancement seems pretty good at the moment.  You collect, upgrade, collect some more, upgrade, ect.  Once you place a crest in the house you can remove any blocks you placed at any time.  This makes upgrading and changing bases around really easy.  So you can make a small house at the beginning and upgrade it as you go.
Combat system is pretty good.  I have not got it down yet.  But you can block, and there are 3 types of attacks.  Left click, mouse wheel up, mouse wheel down.  Slash, Thrust, overhead attack.  You CAN hit different body parts and It does seem like protecting your head is important.  I have been 1 hit it seems a few times by lucky head shots?  I dont really know.  I need to practice more.  There is a stamina bar also that drains when you miss an attack or block.
There is a King system in place where people are constantly fighting over the throne.  You can set taxes as a king, which collects from everyone when they harvest things.  So there is always a constant end game fight over the throne giving the game a purpose other than just "raiding bases all day."  Tons of white listed servers and I am noticing a "white listed at night" server set as well so you dont get raided by hackers in the AM hours.  Also a lot of servers have no sieging in AM as well.
Game is tons of laughs, fun and lots of roleplayers.  I have been really disapointed with Rust and the "new version" however RoK is like the old rust experience but much more to offer.
9/10 so far.

Our generation was one of the first where technology played a such a huge role in our socialization into young adults.  This game succeeds not in its presentation, but in its ability to tap into the emotions of a simpler time; a time when we were developing our identities, and trying forge our futures with a sense of hopeful optimism.
The game consists of a series of instant message conversations over a 5 year period with a friend by the name of “Emily.”  Without giving away too many details, the game’s dialogue is an emotional rollercoaster that almost any American millennial will be able to relate with.  Emotions such as the the thrill of having your first “best friend” of the opposite sex, the jealousy of jilted love, and the anxiety of confessing one’s feelings are all skillfully woven into the game’s dialogue.  At the end of this game, one can’t help but empathize with the protagonist, and relate the character of Emily to someone from their own past.  It could be someone that you felt strongly about, but that for one reason or another, did not admit your feelings toward.
What impressed me about this game was not the mechanics or presentation of it.  At the end of the day, it is simply a free-to-play game, with limited content, and a relatively basic plotline.  However, it is the creative genius behind the concept itself, and the game’s ability to evoke such strong emotions in the player, that make this a memorable title.  I would really like to see this developer expand upon this title, or even create other IM-based game experiences.  This is an exploration into a new genre of gaming, much in the same way that Dear Esther, Gone Home, and Her Story charted new territory.
Give this game a try, and you might be pleasantly surprised.  The pleasure comes not from the experience itself, but from your reflection of the experience.

TLDR; GSC Gameworld deserves more credit that they get for this one.
This game has a comes with a decent storyline, multiple endings influenced somewhat by player choices and play style, standard fare of enemies (both human and mutant), side quests, and mini games.  None of this was particularly new.  What really sets this game apart is the environment.  The developer does a fantastic job of creating a post meltdown Chernobyl disaster zone.  Dynamic weather patterns and day/night really add to the setting.  Exploring the map is often a rewarding experience.  Anomolies are another interesting addition to the scenery.  The weapons physics system in the game is fantastic, though you need to mod the characteristics a bit to make things truly realistic.  This was the first game I played that incorporated tangible bullet drop and loss of energy/momentum.  I.E. you can't headshot someone on the other side of the map with a pistol that doesn't have that kind of range like you can with games like Far Cry.
There are bugs to be found, but there were a lot more at launch.  I'm normally a stickler for companies getting it polished before launch as bug are the enemy of immersion.  However, considering the size of the staff vs the depth of the game, I'll give them a little slack on the initial bug and a full pardon for doing the necessary work to hammer out the biggest grievances.
There is a plethora of mods available for this game that I would encourage checking out after the initial run through.  Some are cosmetic and may be applied even for the first run through.  Others make major changes to the game that give you a completely different experience.  Others still put features back into the game that were removed due to time/performance constraints.
Note:  The vast majority of my game time is outside of steam.  I can't really say how much time I've spend, but I've acheived 6 of the 7 endings (never did the immortality ending).  I've also played through a few mods and made a multiplayer mod of my own (never posted it).

So this has to be one of my favourite games. If you like Fallout, you'll probably like this game too. While it is known to be a bit buggy, it seems to run pretty smoothly for me, and if you find the bugs too much to handle, then you're in luck. The game has a huge modding community that I believe fixed many of the bugs and even added several improvements to an already great game. Speaking of which, I should probably say a few things as to why I think the game is good:
1. It's a sandbox game with survival elements. You're guns break and jam. You need food. And you need to find these things.
2. Decent variety of weapons. More can be added with mods
3. Gun physics. The guns aren't lasers. The bullets drop and occasionally ricochet. Also, there's a slight time delay from when you fire to when your bullet hits.
4. Amazing continuous atmosphere. The game does not revolve around you. Leave an area? When you come back, your favourite NPC in that area could have been killed.
5. While you can get better and better equipment, there is never a time when you become practically invincible. You can be walking around in an exoskeleton with a gauss rifle, and if you turn a corner and run into a bandit and take a shotgun blast point blank to the head, guess what. You're still dead.
It's a good game though it falls short in places it shoulden't and where it's succesers sucided, of the three it comes in second after a mod or two it compeats with first.

After going through this game, I can guarantee two things:
1. Clannad will make you laugh
2, Clannad will make you cry
The second point is why this visual novel is so legendary. Clannad won't just make you cry, it'll make you bawl your eyes out and sob uncontrollably. It's the hardest I've cried in 10 years. But it may take a long time to get to that point because for the most part Clannad is a lighthearted and genuinely funny VN. It's a game that you have to allow time to tell its story and enjoy it along the way.
Clannad is structured into two parts: the main story, and After Story, which is unlocked after completing the character routes in the main story. The main story is similar to a dating sim, but just saying it's a dating sim is like saying baseball is a game where you hit a ball. It goes far beyond just romance and touches on themes like loss, family, nostalgia, change and the cycle of life. Each female character has her own unique route that is the length of a visual novel by itself. This allows for exploration of each character's personality and struggles and touches on a theme unique to that character. In that way, Clannad's main story is much like a box of chocolates, each one to be savored in their own way. Some routes are very lighthearted throughout and only have a bit of sadness at the end, while others will completely rip your soul out. It's a very cathartic experience overall.
My only real gripe with the game other than having a few parts that felt dull is that some of the routes are a bit too well hidden and tough to get on your own. This makes getting to After Story, and especially its true ending, difficult and frustrating unless you consult a guide. It's a real shame because After Story is not just something that was tacked on, it's the completion of the game and the telling of its most powerful message. You'd be doing yourself a great disservice by not seeing this story to the very end. So don't feel bad if you have to use a guide, I know I had to.
One more note: this VN has an excellent soundtrack, each theme perfectly conveying the emotions they're going for. By the time you finish, Nagisa's theme (Dango Daikazoku) will move you to tears when you hear it because of the overall connection you have with this character and Clannad in general.
TL;DR - Clannad will make you feel alive. There's a very good reason why this VN is so highly-ranked and has a dedicated cult following despite being over a decade old. When people say Clannad can be a life-changing experience, they're not kidding. It's that powerful.

This is a very long and detailed review of this game which gives a fair and unbias truth about the game.
Let's begin with the outline before we go into detail about this game.
First and foremost, for a game at this level of graphics this game has a REALLY high requirement. Couple that with the density of player population in towns. Even with channels it will still lag you out.
As for UI and controls, I prefer to talk about them together. Control in this game is clunky and at times awkward. The targeting system doesn't help much either and tab targeting amongst 20 mobs where tab targeting itself is flimsy when the mob goes on and off you screen leads to much frustration.
The controls are pretty much made to work around an action RPG yet using only keyboard itself is a chore. Your only real option is to use a controller, be it Xbox/PS ones. And mouse has it's negative quirks too! Mainly due to poor UI design your spells and character will most likely move to places you do not intend it to go, and for those playing the Swordman base class, double tapping a directional key while using mouse control is annoying in itself. Isometric games like these be it Diablo, PoE, Ragnarok Online has had their controls being refined to be played with a mouse, yet strangely enough mouse is probably the worst choice among the many control types. (Especially during clutter dungeons, trying to click on something where other player and their pets are all stack up or even looking for the sweet spot which is like 4 pixels to click to interact with that Shrine of Goddess Vakarine - Orsha)
With that out of the system let us move on to artstyle. It is shiny, the art style is distinct and clearly shows that the art team wants to deviate from the standard "anime-style" art. I just can't get over the eye features and eyelashes, which sadly is main distiction of "anime-style" art which they are trying so hard to stay away from. I wouldn't put this as bad nor good. In-game sprites are well at least pleasing to look at, and brings back some memories of Ragnarok Online but that is as far as it goes in relating to what many claims as it's spiritual successor. (No skill spam, no pot spam = Not Ragnarok Online)
New player friendliness part, I guess the only tutorial part of the game was like bits of info thrown at you when you actually interact with something new. But for me the one that I clearly recognize would be the new character creation where you are shown on your screen to press your arrow keys. As one might already know, player guidance is scarce. But will it turn away players? Maybe so maybe not, but they might go down the road and only notice it like 1-2 months of play that for example you could double tap directional key to sprint as a swordsman.
I'd like to add that it is impossible to use the Auction house in the main channels in Klaipedia, due to gold spammers spamming chat now which there are so many big chat bubbles which block me from clicking the search field unless I hop over to a less populated channel.
Class and balance. As many have pointed out, stat growth in this game is so pathetic that everything you do makes no sense in the balance of things. Each of your main offensive attributes, aka STR/INT, confers to 1 point of damage in the calculation of whatever damage you do. The damage you gain from them even pouring all your stat to them can't even come close to 20% base weapon damage for the weapon tier you just arrived at (1, 15 , 40. 75, 120 etc) and on top of that the skill scales way higher than your stat could ever grow. Meaning it leaves little in the sense of build flexibility. Almost all physical based classes would go Dex and just roll the dice for critical to do decent damage, and casters will have to choose between doing paltry damage but cast more, or the other way round, or be just straight up beefy with high CON and probably just cast a few paltry spells and resume auto bolting mobs.
As for gameplay wise. I'd understand that in games there are Bots, and it is ever more common in F2P games. However, when using a bot actually makes you react faster than human, teleports you around or lets you swing invisible air blade attacks is what pushes everyone's button. An infested bot field is just impossible to contest unless you can setup damaging fields around the spot before the mobs spawn. They did well in providing as many quest on the early levels to make the game less grindy but it still requires way too much research on the players side to know when to use Exp-cards to avoid future grinding/no quest deadzones.
Publisher limitation. This is also the biggest problem in this game, the developers are trying so hard to not lose money before even making any money! The restrictions in this game is by far the WORST in the online gaming scene! With limited monthly 1:1 trading, which also counts towards same account character trade, 1 slot for inter-account item trade, losing of "potential" (item upgrade, trade flexibility) on items, longest auction house cash out wait time, super restrictive auction house prices, literally forcing people have tokens to at least make the game barely playable. (Good luck trying to get any token once the game goes F2P, even the rich people have their limit on how many Tokens they can bring into the market that it will all dry up). To put it literal, IMC is gold plating their egg baskets before there is any eggs in the basket.
In-game translation, the text on and off have grammatical errors which would only be a nuisance towards a native speaker but nevertheless will cause some misunderstanding here and there.
Community wise. There are nothing but mud flingers everywhere. Be it the common hive mind to trash talk BRs on Klaipedia, BRs not wanting to intergrate into the English community and insist on speaking Portugese, Gold selling spammers, PvP "Elitist" bragging about on shout channel. You get the jist, people just not acting their age most of the time due to the cover of being on the internet. I've gotten over it to not get my blood boiling, but to some people that state of "Zen" is not something easily achieved.
So the final question is as many would like to know I'll list it down in different criterias for different readers.
Should you play this game? If...
I have only the minimal requirements to run the game?
- No
it is F2P?
- Yes why not?
I want a good gaming community?
- Most likely not. But people are like gems and jewels you have to strike gold to enjoy your time in a F2P game which can be very much toxic in the future when the flood gates open.
I wish to invest in their Cash Shop item?
- Don't say I never warn you. 500% in favor of not supporting the publisher in the current state of the game with all it's restriction. I say this not because you cannot get good value for the stuff you paid, but those who can't will soon bleed out and you'd be left with probably a server which is void of decent people.
I want to relive my memories of Ragnarok Online?
- No. As far as succession goes, this game only succeeded in bringing back RO's sprites.
(Fun question) I wish to play a game which I probably won't throw my mouse, break my keyboard, smash my monitor and flip my computer table?
- Stay away from this game. You have been warned.

A great continuatuib if the Call of Juarez series...  My only gripe about this game is that it was too short.  I finished the game in less than a day.  If you are a fan of westerns and enjoy the look of old school graphics, then this is the game for you.

Gameplay wise, this game is decent. It has a neat level up system (with upgrades like slowing down time whenever you use iron sights) but towards the middle of the game it starts to slow down a bit. Even the story isn't anything to write home about, but it gives you reason to go from point A to point B, and for this game that's all that it needs to do. Where this game shines is the narration. The narrator is unreliable and tends to exaggerate the story, making things escalate very quickly in the heat of battle.  For example, in an intense shootout, the narrator says something along the line of "I was low on bullets", and you can see your ammo counter rapidly go from 60 to 0 in a few seconds. This kind of clever weaving between story and gameplay is really, really cool and makes it a very enjoyable experience.

Lots of fun, it really feels like you're in a gritty western. Seems incredibly cheap considering how short a time the game's been out as of writing this review, and the quality of the game.
After the first playthrough you can start again on the hardest difficulty and/or with Story Mode+ to keep your skills etc., and although the game is very story driven (more on that), the action is enjoyable and replay value is high all things considered. It also has Arcade and Duel modes where you can compete with your friends scores on leaderboards.
The story is being told by your venerable self, Silas Greaves, many years after the fact in a saloon, and the narrative constantly follows you through the game, adding well timed humour. As has been mentioned by others, the game doesn't take itself too seriously.
Fantastic scenery, I often found myself looking off over the vistas at just how realistically it's been recreated - very beautiful. They've tried to make as good a game as is reasonably possible, and I think they've done a great job. Personally I would have liked it to be a little more open world.. perhaps a choice in taking bounties etc, but that's not really in the scope of the game. It's a linear story for the main game, just so you know :)

Great game! The narrative seems similar to Bastion but I prefer Transistor's storyline and style - sort of funky minimalist sci-fi world. The combat is cool, all abilities seem useful and there are a lot of different combos to explore.
While in Bastion combat mechanic was more like a classic action/rpg hack-n-slash, Transistor is more turn-based - you have a "planning mode" where you can decide on the next course of action. Planning mode has a cooldown timer, so once you finish planning and all your actions are executed, you have to act in real-time until planning mode is available again. The game becomes more tactical but the cooldown on planning mode makes sure you do not abuse it, and helps to keep the game at a fast, challenging pace. When you run out of health, instead of seeing the typical "game over" screen straight away, your character loses one of her abilities. In my opinion, this is a very cool approach making the game less frustrating but equally challenging, as you have to master different abilities.
Oh yes, and the soundtrack is great!
If you like stylish games with fun gameplay and interesting storyline - do not miss this!!

A friend linked me this game a few days ago and I was intrigued. My initial thoughts after viewing the trailer was, "Trains? Aliens to defend yourself from? Largescale factories built within an infinite 2D world? Wow! I must buy it! Factorio has been out for years, which if I had've known it existed sooner I surely would have bought it.
Your first thoughts when looking at Factorio might be, "Another Early Access game? Ugh!" or, "The price of this 2D Early Access game seems high.." - Let me clarify: It took my friends & I 103 hours to finish the game. That includes sleeping, regular breaks, playing everyday for hours, etc. Few days ago when I bought the game until now I have over 80+ hours with still much more I want to do in Factorio. Factorio has replay value and is well worth $20+, especially how much content it has in it already.
Factorio has procedural generation (infinite random world to explore) and different biomes. With that in mind, that also includes an infinite amount of alien hives and aliens. Yes, aliens. They don't like you and you shouldn't like them. Build defenses to keep those buggers out or go out on foot on an adventure to conquer as many as you'd like! Either way, you'll have your hands tied in the process.
The basics of the game is easy to learn - never hard. Mine and chop to gain resources and craft hundreds of items to build your factory. Make your factory automatically work by logistics and/or the circuit network, that way you won't have to lift a finger again when it comes to crafting.
There's more to the game, I just summed up basic gist of the game and how great it is.
Endless possibilities, endless world, endless factory, and endless gameplay all in one 2D package.
10/10

Skyrim served as my introduction into the Elder Scrolls series. I was certainly hungry for more and the Elder Scrolls Online sated me.
While not as graphically detailed as it's predacesor, ESo offers a multitude of quests and storylines, expansive worlds, monsters and villians, crafting, skilltrees...You name it. I could certainly loose myself to this game for hours.
But don't forget that this is an MMO. In most dungeons you will be accompanied by fellow players. I don't have anything  bad to say about the community so far, as everyone I've encountered has aided me in almost every question. With that being said, there are plenty of solo dungeons. These are exciting too. I'd say that they allow you to have some intimate moments with quests. When the action picks up, these dungeons really deliver some fun moments.
Everything in the game is nicely laid out, controls are rather easy to learn, and menues are straight foreward.
I do think the response time for combat can feel a little slow. That, and I am rather irritated that you can swim underwater. But these are certainly nitpicking.
In any case, if you know that you enjoy MMOs and some nicely made quests, EOS will be an enjoyable game for you.

A gorgeous and atmospheric entry to the Alien franchise. They got this right, people.
Play with headphones, in the dark.
You might get the feeling you're in Rapture, which isn't far off as the Sevastopol Station is in a similar state of chaos, with ambiguous dangers. Other survivors may be friendly, or dangerous. Synthetics will follow you relentlessly. And the Alien cannot be killed, only discouraged for a time.
Scavenging is key, but take too long or make any noise above walking around, and you'll attract attention. The Alien may focus on other enemies in the area, especially when encouraged, so that might be a fitting distraction. Knowing what sound ques mean is very important so you know where the alien might be at any time. Conserve ammo and certain items for clutch situations. Stealth and having a hiding/exit plan will keep you alive. Don't get stuck in a dead end.
The music effects in the game are dynamic, so turning to lock eyes with a synth who just discovered you will que a musical surprise sound, giving you the feel of being in one of the films.
The Alien itself is generally trackable. Once you have the motion sensor, you can track noises in the area. However, IF the alien is around, but not spawned, you'll see it's movement pattern go all over the place. Until it spawns, it won't follow the floor plan, and you'll hear it bumping around in vents. Occasionally it will spawn to look around on its own, but a loud noise will cause it to investigate almost instantly. You can use this to your advantage.

I have previously written a bit of a joke review for this VN, but I realised this deserves much more - a proper verdict...
This VN is one of the greatst experiences of my life as a gamer - or even my life as a whole.
Every single scenario in this game is a work of art - full of huge laughs and ridiculous acts from the likes of Sunohara, touching dialogues between characters like Nagisa and Tomoya, and absolute heartbreakers from almost all of the routes that will essentially leave you crying yourself to sleep and feeling more depressed than a goth during a coffee shortage for about a week.
This game isn't just a one-time experience; much like the anime it's a life-changer. It will without a doubt change your outlook on life and have you thinking about it's events for a long time after completion. Timeless stories like that of Nagisa's and Tomoyo's are ones that will undoubtedly remain in the hearts of the players for a lifetime.
You could call this review an exaggeration - but after playing Clannad you will probably end up feeling the same way.
With a good 100+ hours available to play through-out all the routes, minigames and the after story, Clannad is worth the arguably steep asking price of £30. In fact, I would pay £500 for this game - it's a masterpiece filled with countless emotions and characters that I will never forget.

*SPOILER FREE REVIEW*
I barely know where to start with this one, but I guess it should begin with this: if you're looking for a romantic, emotional rollercoaster that goes beyond everything you expected and leaves you exhausted but hugely satisfied, buy this visual novel.  And if you're put off by the price, let me explain to you why it's totally justified.
Oh, and by the way, if you haven't seen the anime, you can play this game and still understand everything, so don't worry.  If you've seen the anime, you'll only fall even further in love with the characters and the struggles each one goes through.  I saw the anime first and found it very touching, but even having seen it, this visual novel totally blew that experience away and gave me a million new reasons to love Clannad.
What I love about this visual novel is that you can play it both casually and seriously; if you're just interested in dating a bunch of different girls and unlocking the funniest achievements, you can do that.  It has some seriously hilarious moments and hidden bonuses that are great on a casual level without you needing to get bogged down with the emotional baggage of the story if you really don't want to.  However, if you want to throw yourself in at the deep end and experience everything, you are going to be there for a LONG time.
There is SO much content in this visual novel to keep you replaying and replaying to get every CG, every hidden scene, every possible outcome, every piece of music...  it's almost endless.  Unlocking every achievement and completing the full game's true ending requires a HUGE amount of work; you'll need to play through every route until you unlock what is basically a second visual novel on top of what you just played - and then play that a few times, making little changes at the right moments to unlock that incredible ending you've been searching for.  It may sound off-putting to have to do so much, but believe me, it's worth it.  I won't expand fully for spoiler reasons, but the second you lose your heart to this story... you will not rest until you've brought happiness to that girl.  You will tell yourself that getting an okay ending is satisfactory enough and that you've played it enough times now to leave it alone...  but you'll keep coming back.
I cannot fully tell you how personally invested in the story I became, and how every time I loaded up the game, I convinced myself that I had to keep going until I found the solution to gain that ending.  I actually felt responsible.  I must have clicked over a million times and I lost count of how many times I cried, but by the time I was finally finished, I felt so happily exhausted and strangely vindicated as a human being.  'It's just a game', they always say, 'it has no bearing on real life'.  But I don't think I need to convince most of you guys that games are one of the greatest mediums for life lessons and inspiring moments that make you change your view on life, and Clannad does that.  Clannad made me realise how much I want to help people.  It made me realise that you should never give up on anything, no matter how hard it gets.  When you play this visual novel, you will feel such a yearning in yourself to make the bitterness in yourself and the people you love go away...  and you'll have the power to do it.  I know all of this will probably sound like wanky ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t to some of you, but I just can't articulate how deeply Clannad moved me as a person.
In closing, Clannad is brilliant on many levels, and if you think you can handle the feels, you should dive headfirst into it right now.  You will cry, and you will feel spiritually exhausted...  but in the end, you'll have experienced a world in which you can be the miracle somebody needs...  and have a miracle granted for yourself in return.
Soaring music.  Perfect visuals.  Spot-on translation.  Natural pacing.  Unbelievable replayability.  Engaging story.  A visual novel that goes beyond romance and dating, and touches the very core of you...  what are you waiting for?
10/10, would cry again.

Total War: Rome II - Emperor Edition is the 'definitive' edition of the much anticipated sequel to the great Rome: Total War.
This game added many new and exciting gameplay elements however from the beginning has also been riddled with major flaws.
Upon release, Rome II was riddled with terrible bugs and performance issues. Many people experienced crashes. The AI was useless both on the campaign map and in battles. There was imbalance. And of course the never ending onslaught of DLC. Fortunatlely all these problems have been improved (not fixed!) over time. The AI is still not amazing but isn't completely useless. performance has improved but it's still not amazing. Balance has improved and crashes don't seem to occur often at all.
This game introduced an improved game engine which brought the visuals to life better than ever before in a Total War game. The battles feel very responsive, although the unit cohesion is quite poor. The Blood and Gore DLC makes battles an immersive experience.
The mechanics of the campaign map are simple and easy to learn. Settlements, armies, agents and the management of public order, food etc is a simple way to summarise it. However it lacks real depth to keep it interesting. Where are family trees???
Emperor edition also added a new campaign set during the Second Triumvirate, which added to an already large amount of content. Factor in all the (overpriced) DLCs and there is an immense amount of content and replayability to be found in this game.
Summary:
Pros:
-Updated engine
-Responsive battles
-Easy to learn to play
-immense amount of content
-Replayability
Cons:
-Too much DLC
-Bugs
-Bad AI
-Somewhat simple for experienced players
-Optimisation not great
Final verdict: 6.5/10
I'd say it's best to buy this on sale, especially the DLCs, but there is a lot of fun to be had here.

So this has to be one of my favourite games. If you like Fallout, you'll probably like this game too. While it is known to be a bit buggy, it seems to run pretty smoothly for me, and if you find the bugs too much to handle, then you're in luck. The game has a huge modding community that I believe fixed many of the bugs and even added several improvements to an already great game. Speaking of which, I should probably say a few things as to why I think the game is good:
1. It's a sandbox game with survival elements. You're guns break and jam. You need food. And you need to find these things.
2. Decent variety of weapons. More can be added with mods
3. Gun physics. The guns aren't lasers. The bullets drop and occasionally ricochet. Also, there's a slight time delay from when you fire to when your bullet hits.
4. Amazing continuous atmosphere. The game does not revolve around you. Leave an area? When you come back, your favourite NPC in that area could have been killed.
5. While you can get better and better equipment, there is never a time when you become practically invincible. You can be walking around in an exoskeleton with a gauss rifle, and if you turn a corner and run into a bandit and take a shotgun blast point blank to the head, guess what. You're still dead.
It's a good game though it falls short in places it shoulden't and where it's succesers sucided, of the three it comes in second after a mod or two it compeats with first.

If you like FPS and are interested in the Chernobyl nuclear disaster of 1986 then you should definitely play S.T.A.L.K.E.R. Based on the classic russian sci-fi novel Roadside picnic. The game takes place in the exclusion zone surrounding the Chernobyl NPP affected by radiation. The zone is filled with mutants, strange anomalies and S.T.A.L.K.E.Rs who hunt for artifacts created by the radiation.
The game is an FPS with RPG elements as you progress you can upgrade your guns and gear and join various factions that suit your personal pursuits.  The guns are quite inaccurate and do break down and the game is especially difficult as you try to fight off mutants, bandits and radiation. The game's real strength is it's immersive and spooky atmosphere that carries through the game.
I heartily recommend S.T.A.L.K.E.R as a fan of atmospheric games as it's a game I reinstall more often than games like Half Life 2 and Deus Ex.
