Transistor is a great action RPG with strategy components.  The combat is highly variable due to the customizable moveset; each "function" can be equipped as an action, a modification of another action, or a passive bonus.  The system allows for many playstyles and strategies which are fun to experiment with.  You can also pause time and queue actions to be executed rapidly, the tradeoff being that most moves will be rendered unusable for several seconds.
The story here is largely told by a character who offers commentary in real time as opposed to in Bastion where a narrator is recounting the story.  Large parts of the plot are intentionally left open to interpretation, perhaps too much so, but it's a smart, multi-layered story that leaves you with lots to think about and at least a few pulled heart strings.
The amazing soundtrack is by Darren Korb who did Bastion's soundtrack so that is another huge plus.  And lastly, there's a dedicated button for humming so there's really no legitimate excuse not to play.
This game is excellent.

I would have to say that while ESO was originally pretty good to me, all of the new content since the last time I reviewed it has added so much more to the game. If I had to critique it, I'd just say that I still hate mircrotransactions, but I understand to keep money flowing in.
Considering the MMO's out there, I was getting sick of having to constantly pay for a subscription to play, but I also didn't want to compromise quality and overall enjoyment because I was playing a F2P that was s**t out from a MMO mold. I have always been a fan of the Elder Scrolls series, so I decided to avoid the negative comments and go ahead and buy the game anyway. I bought it full price quite some time ago, and had a lot of fun with my friends. We had no idea what we were doing, I think that was what most of the fun was.
Along comes the next expansion for WoW, so I left to go play for a bit and ESO went back onto the shelf. Fast forward a few months, and I come back to a lot of new content, super helpful people in the starting areas, and a lot of bug fixes for the stuff that I faced originally.
Overall? It's a good buy if you're looking for what I call a "hardy" MMO. Something different molded with something recognizable, and constantly staying fluid. I believe ESO will thrive if it continues it's no-sub and new content additions.

This game is the badass seal of approval of Creative Assembly and the redemption of Sega after mediocre and terrible games set in the Aliens (vs Predator) universe. We live in a time, when first person "hiding" horror games are popular and to be honest, this is the best gameplay mechanic that can be put behind an Alien title. Controlling Amanda Ripley I couldn't remember much games where I felt more vulnerable. I'm used to tense moments and immense horror, but aboard the Sevastopol I spent minutes sweating in lockers and under tables waiting for my courage to come back and embark on the next few meters knowing that the xenomorph is out there haunting. There were a few really scarry moments in the course of the more than 20 hours playthrough when I literally slip my mouse, because the creature grabbed me in a ventilation shaft. I appreciate that the game doesn't pause when I open a file on a computer or assemble some ammunition maintaining the tension. The phasing of the campaign is good, but there were some parts, where I felt that the developers went too far and eventually frustation overgrew fear. Luckily, on the whole Isolation is a great horror game, a real love letter to the Alien movies and fans of the franchise and the genre as well.

This is a must play if you are a fan of the Alien franchise. No question about it. Casual and hardcore fans alike will love it. The attention to detail is insane, especially when it comes to the opening level. As for the gameplay itself, the game has a healthy length to it, but it will vary depending on your skill/difficulty level. Gameplay is very intense, because if the Alien sees you, you're pretty much toast unless you've got a molotov (and you can only carry 3).
The game also has an interesting interaction mechanic that works quite well with a controller (can't speak for how it works on just a keyboard). Basically the buttons you use to do things change depending on the object, and they mimic the motion you would actually do. For instance, when using a large circuit breaker that you need to grab with both hands and pull down, you hold both triggers, and pull down with both sticks. It feels very natural and adds a tiny bit more immersion to a game already dripping with it.

The Borderlands series has become somewhat of a cult hit in the years since the original game's release, and I find it rather unfortunate as a fan of the games that it's not more spoken of the video game community. Borderlands can be summarised in several bulletpoints that act as the focus of each individual game: Guns, grinding and comedy. This review will attempt to cover each aspect of the series, and this game in particular, in enough detail to perhaps get you interested in this gem.
Firstly, guns. Perhaps the thing that this series is most well known for outside its fanbase, the guns it this game are plentiful and varied, in both design and effect. There are 4 types of elemental guns: fire, electric, explosive and slag, plus non-elemental guns. The first 3 elements are somewhat self explanatory, but slag is an element that, once it affects a foe, allows all other damage types to be more harmful. Elemental damage can also be done through special shield AOE or Spike attacks, or through the several skills that the player characters can invest in, there being 4 characters in the vanilla game and 2 extra that can be bought in DLC. Buying the DLC characters is reccomended, as each character feels much different to the rest due to the variety of skills that are given to only specific characters. The stats of all the guns in the game are procedurally generated, so even if you get two guns of the same model and make, there would be inequalities in stats, such as higher accuracy and lower damage etc.
Grinding is a rather filthy word in the gaming community, and justifiably so, making it somewhat unfortunate that it is a large chunk of the Borderlands experience. However, the game being an RPG and all, it should really be expected for it to be like that. Grinding in this game involves redoing areas with tough enemies for XP and fighting old bosses for a chance at their rarest drops of gear, the latter potentially taking hours at a time. Although it is required for completionists and the like, grinding is not needed for people who are just hoping to complete the game, as anyone who does a reasonable amount of side quests can beat the final boss with relative ease. Whether the grinding the turn-off or not for you is a matter of your own taste, so I'm just putting the facts about it out there so you can make up your opinion.
Finally, the comedy and overall style of the game. The comedy isn't really what you can call 'intelligent', but a bit of toilet humour has never hurt anyone, has it? It can feel a bit hit-or-miss at times, but fortunately the jokes are legitimately funny the vast majority of the time, the bright, cell-shaded aesthetic of the game allowing you to more easily appreciate the comedy that is delivered. Overall a solid aspect of the experience.
Concluding this review that about one person will read, anyone who enjoys collecting a ridiculous amount of loot, first person shooters, grinding, silly humour and more cartonnish aesthetic will most likely find this game to be a bit of pleasant, mindless fun. If you don't enjoy any of the above listed things, however, I doubt we will ever be very good friends.

The 2011 release 'CoJ:The Cartel' received lots of criticism.
Did Techland take notice and is this game any better?
In short: hell yeah!
*** THE STORY ***
It's the 19th century - The Wild West.
You take on the role of Silas Greaves. A bounty hunter.
The story is told by Silas himself (in exchange for some free whiskey) as he reflects on his journey.
Silas is on a quest for revenge. To right a wrong done to him. Hunting his archnemesis all throughout 'The Wild West' and meeting some notorious outlaws in the process. 'Billy: The Kid', 'Jesse James' and 'Butch Cassidy' to name a few. You'll actually get to duel them in a typical mexican standoff, but more on that later. In pursuit of your archnemesis, you''ll come across bank heists, train robberies, and what would a western be without some indians trying to scalp you.
Overall it's a pretty decent story. Nothing new, we all heard it before. Some plot twists and turns, but it's well executed. The voice acting is quite solid and the narrative style of storytelling contributes to the atmosphere of the game. I also liked the occasional story rewind of how things really went down. It seems our dear Mr. Silas Greaves tends to exaggerate a bit. Let's just contribute that to all the free whiskey he's been pouring down his throat in exchange for this story.
*** GRAPHICS ***
Graphics are great. It's a cel shaded style, which really fits the setting in this case. Some features include sun shafts, water ripples, weather effects and destructible objects. You have the ocassional low resolution textures, but nothing really disturbing. I'm usually to busy shooting people in the face anyways. Overall it looks really stunning and runs quite smooth also. I tend to favor gameplay over graphics, which brings me to....
*** GAMEPLAY ***
There are three gamemodes available: Story / Arcade / Duel
Let's begin with the story mode:
*story mode* consist out of a mission based (episodic) format.
Basically you'll move from objective to objective eliminating all who stand in your way in a linear path. At the end of the mission you will usually face a boss (in this case a famous outlaw like Jesse James) and have a true mexican standoff. Eliminating enemies will grant you with experience points. These can be used to unlock and upgrade some abilities. You have three tiers of skill categories which favor the matching playstyle (dual wielding / rifleman / shotgunner)
Maybe the best part about the gameplay is the return of 'bullet-time' we know so well from Max Payne. Slow motion gameplay, dodging bullets, lining up headshots (or crotch shots if you're into that) and keep those combo's going.
Enemies are hiding behind objects, actively taking cover.
A.I. isn't too smart though, but hey it remains an arcade style shooter and not a tactical masterpiece.
You'll also have your basic hidden secrets (golden nuggets) which, if collected, tell a bit about the background story and also net you some extra experience points in the process.
Some minor QTE's on scripted occasions are also present.
Luckily they're quite scarce and not all that annoying.
For the die-hard cowboy a 'new game+' mode is included.
This keeps your hard-earned xp and existing skills intact for the next playthrough, if you so desire. The True West difficulty only unlocks after finishing the story mode once and offers an increased challenge due to the complete absence of a HUD.
*Arcade mode* is basically a rehash from the story mode missions. Run through a parcours to the finish line, eliminating bad guys and scoring as much combo's and points as possible. Nothing really special here, but it guarantees some additional gametime.
*Duel mode* offers a mexican standoff against 15 of the in-game outlaws. 'Billy: The Kid', Jesse James, The Daltons, Butch Cassidy etc. The principle consists out of keeping two pointers simultaneously in the correct zones. One pointer resembles your draw hand and hovers above your pistol. The longer you keep it in the correct zone the faster you will draw your weapon. The second pointer is aimed at your opponent and resembles accuracy. The longer you correctly aim at your opponent the more accurate your shot will be. Furthermore, you can kill your opponents 'honorably' (which means that you react upon them drawing first) or 'dishonorably' (which inevitably means that you draw first). Statistics about reaction time and even leaderboards are available.
*** CONCLUSION ***
Gunslinger is quite a solid arcade shooter. I didn't expect this after the debacle with 'The Cartel'. Everything blends really well together (graphics, gameplay, sound and the narrative storytelling). It's an immersive experience and The Wild West never looked this good. Sure, one may claim it is too short (ca. 8-12 hours) story mode, depending on skill, rushing or finding all collectibles etc.) It's linear and not free roam and maybe has little replay value, but in the end it doesn't really hurt the game. Got this soon after getting into the Alien franchise and was not disappointed. It really captures the look and atmosphere from the original movie.
You play as Amanda Ripley, Ellen Ripley's daughter, going through Sevastopol and doing various tasks all the while hiding from and fighting off other survivors, working Joes, and of course the alien. Throughout the game you are given various blueprints so you can craft items to use as distractions and weapons for emergencies. The AI for the alien is programmed in a way that makes it very unpredictable, you will probably never have two playthroughs the exact same.
With very good graphics and atmospheric music taken from the movie, Alien: Isolation can create a very immersive experience, however, I would still recommend playing this in the dark at night with at least decent headphones so as to fully appreciate what it can really be.
However, as good as this game is, nothing is perfect. When first playing, not even ten minutes in, I encountered a bug that caused me to not be able to progress. While the solution was easy to find it was very annoying. There was also a pretty major bug in mission 14 where the next part of the level wouldn't load properly and it never registered when I completed mission 17. Also, I hate to say it, but in areas where there was no threat of the alien being around, it was honestly kind of boring, these areas don't last for too long but even still, they put me off a little bit.
All in all, a very good game, one of my favourites now actually. If you're a fan of the Alien franchise and/or want a good scare, I would highly recommend this game to you.

I have been a HUGE fan of the Alien franchise for as long as I can remember. When Alien: Resurrection was finally at the gas station we rented movies from I remember practically begging my mom to rent it for me because I had seen and enjoyed the previous films so much (I was 8 at the time, maybe?), and her caving and getting it. I've played many many hours of every game (YES, even Colonial Marines) and watched the ever living hell out of each version of each movie (YES, even AVP), and honest to Sigourney herself, this is the best thing to happen to the franchise since Aliens.
Alien: Isolation is a direct sequel and full hearted tribute to Ridley Scott's masterpiece Alien, and in multiple ways. Yes it happens before Aliens, but it also discounts nearly every aspect of the Xenomorph added to the Alien biology and mythos that has been made since the first film. For example, the Xenomorph cannot climb around on the walls and ceiling, instead using the vent systems and walks around in a bipedal manner.
In this game, you follow the daughter of Ellen Ripley, named Amanda, looking for clues to your mother's disappearance over a decade ago. The story takes you to Sevastapol Station, owned by Seegson Corp; a rival company of Weyland. When you arrive, everything is in decay and the station in total disarray. People are killing one another and they are all scared into hiding by some 'thing' that is killing everyone else on the station. But you are trapped here and you need to know the truth about what happened to your mother, and survive while you are at it...
The atmosphere in this game is absolutely perfect. They NAILED the 'space trucker/lived in but in space' look of the first film, right down to the 'drinking bird'. I mean goddamn, the vents, the lockers, the spacesuits, the ship interiors, the computers with greenscale monitors and big, clunky keyboard keys with symbols that mean who knows goddamn what and lightbulbs of all colors coming from all manner of instruments; its all there, and its all done SO WELL. And the sound, holy hell mate the SOUND! The beeps and bloops of the computers and buzzing and humming of the instruments, the hissing and screeching of the Xeno itself, the squeek of your sneakers when you turn fast while moving, the voice acting (which has original cast members!!!)-- all INCREDIBLE. Its all tied together by really good graphics that make it all seem so goddamn real.
The gameplay is great. Its superbly scary, because it does not allow you to kill the Alien, and it can very very easily kill you (If it sees you, running wont help). As noted before, there are other people aboard the station. Some are friendly, many are not, and wont hesitate to shoot you if you get too close, but they are often in the way of wherever you are trying to go, so you need to find a way to deal with them, either by trying to go around, utilizing violence and the weapons you have gathered, or -- if you are brave and kind of awful -- luring the Alien to them to do the deed for you (while you watch from a vent to make sure you still have the upper hand by way of situational awareness). There is some light crafting done in real time with a cumbersome menu, and the best cat and mouse hiding mechanics I have seen in this type of horror game ever, because this cat wises up to your behavior as you go on, without ever needing to get too many more tricks up his own sleeve. It is a long game, it took me over 30 hours to complete the story, but I never felt that the core cat and mouse gameplay had gotten stale. Speaking of the story...
The story is very well done, even though it borders on clichés within the series at some points and may go on a bit longer than some would like (I never felt it overstayed its welcome). The characters are mostly well thought out and realized, and are supported by some great voice acting work and fantastic face rendering. The story itself its not just of Amanda trying to find out what happened to Ellen, but its also the story of the Sevastapol space station, told via text and auido logs found throughout the games levels. And honestly the story of the Sevastapol and its downfall is just as gripping as Amanda's journey through it.
I'm not going to give a numeric review on this, but will say, If you like the Alien franchise, or like horror games, this is an absolute MUST BUY title.
P.S. Get the DLC. the Missions aboard the Nostromo are top notch and have voice acting by the original cast, and allow you to have a nostalgia nutty walking around the halls of one of Science Fiction's most important ships, all while trying to avoid the 'big chap'. And the survival challenge levels are actually hella fun, and great for bursts of Alien based horror.
P.P.S If you have a modern smartphone, get Trinus VR and play this game that way. Its ♥♥♥♥ing AMAZING

Just do yourself a favor and buy it, you'll fall for it from the first mission.

Soda Dungeon is, essentially, an incremental game. Like Cookie Clicker and Clicker Heroes, the game essentially plays itself, though I'd say that Soda Dungeon both requires more interaction, and rewards the player more for said interaction.
You start by hiring heroes, equipping them, then sending them to fight monsters in an ever increasing difficulty dungeon. Every 5 levels there's a miniboss, and every 10 there's a boss. Once you reach level 100 (then 200, then 300), you ascend the world, and gain a new relic, which gives you pretty big bonuses - people who've played Clicker Heroes will recognise what's happening here. Characters do not level up, instead progression is done through items and leveling relics.
And really, that's all there is to the game. Like Clicker Heroes, it's very simple, with a surprising amount of depth. It's nice to just have on in the background, checking on it every now and then. Put auto battle on and come back once an hour or so.
The art style is, like the game, simple. There's a decent amount of enemy sprites, that are all pretty well drawn. The animations are a little too basic for my liking, but that's not a big deal. I'd like a bit more variety/interesting visuals, but oh well. I really like the music, but of course it tends to get repetitive after a while.
I only really have small issues with the game. This was a mobile game ported to PC, but no keyboard controls have been added (would be nice for selecting abilities). Some of the controls are a little awkward because of this, but it's easy to get over it. I'd also like a bit more control over how the auto battle works.

Simply put. BUY IT NOW! I don't have as many hours in this game as Fallout 4, but I feel like I'm playing this game longer than it. I'm a really huge fan of Fallout 4 (yes, even though it's not as good as Fallout 3 or New Vegas, I can look past the flaws and enjoy it.) Enough about fallout 4 though.
This is the only visual novel I, personally, will play and won't stop for hours. I've tried to play the F2P ones on Steam. But their stories are kind of meh. Now, let's get going with the reivew;
Clannad is a visual novel originally made by KEY studios in Japan. Sekai Project translated it this year into english. In this novel, you play (I guess it counts as playing, i don't really know how you would catagorize it) as Tomoya Okazaki, a deliquent in his third year of high school. He skips class, falls asleep, and doesn't really care about a whole lot of things. But one day, he meets a girl named Nagisa Furukawa. From there, you can choose how the story will move on. I won't say anything else, because spoilers.
The characters in this game are very likable.  In my current play-through, I haven't met two characters, and I didn't complete one of the arcs, but that's just how I played what was given to me. Some of their personalities are very believable and EXTREMELY likable maybe even lovable. You will get very attached to all of the characters, no matter how little, or long you may speak to them.
It plays just like an other VN, so not much to say there.
There are two settings in this story; the real world, which takes place in japan (the setting for a lot of slice of life anime, vn, manga, etc. apparently) and the secon done, The Illusionary World. The real world is where most of the story takes place and where things are the best. Personally, every time I saw that the story took me to "The illusionary World" I didn't enjoy playing it as much. Now it is a neat sub-plot, but not as much fun. You don't get any choices, so you're basically just reading a book, but with nice pictures, a nice soundtrack, and on a computer.
Artstyle is nice. It's different. But nice. I like the design of the characters. Their eyes are the size of watermelons, but that's what makes them neat, and in some cases a little bit cute (not trying to be a weeb or anything).
The soundtrack is beautiful, even though there are only like 4-5 songs that you can clearly hear at every part of it. But the songs you do hear. HOLY♥♥♥♥♥♥ Soooo goood. During the emotional scenes, the song refelcts that.
All-in-all, I HIGHLY recommend this to any anime fan. ESPECIALLY those who have seen Clannad and Clannad ~After Story~. I give Clannad, a 9/10. The only downside to this game is the music, and the illusionary world segments. I just didn't enjoy those segments, now that's my opinion others will feel different. And the other downside is the music, you hear like the same 3 songs 95% of the times. 2 other songs 4% of the times. And the remaining 1% are songs you hear like once or twice, or during certain sections, certain converstions, and certain arcs, and if you don't play your cards right, you won't hear them.
Also, I HIGHLY HIGHLY HIGHLY *HIGHLY* watching the anime. It's very good. My number 1 anime.

One of the best games to come out within the last ten years. The gameplay begins to be a simple task and over time becomes more and more tedious and complex-yet you evolve with the changes as they occur and by the time you get to the end of the campaign-you will know more about the imaginary country of Arstotzka with all of it's provinces and geography than you know about your own country. What takes you by surprise however is that you may also begin to care about the imaginary people that will do anything to leave or enter. Definite Four Stars out of Four from me on this one. Lucas Pope-the designer of the game took what essentially would be considered one of the worst jobs to have and made it an exciting game.
Here is the premise of the game. You play as a checkpoint immigration inspector for Arstotzka during the height of the Cold War that must follow various rules for all immigrants that are passing through into the country. Many of these individuals are liars and terrorists that will smuggle drugs or weapons, and you may even encounter a suicide bomber or two. You primarily want to make as much money as possible because your family at home are constantly either going hungry or getting sick. Once you get used to the game and become better at it you make more money to possibly move into a better house. However things can happen where someone may offer you a bribe or ask for you to reject someone who is trying to enter you must make a choice in these cases and the depending on what you choose will either cause you to get a Game Over or continue playing. Although it seems like the game can be the same thing over and over with a lack of variety I feel that this factor is it's geatest attribute.
My only issues with the game would be the trial and error gameplay. Once one get into the game it is possible to fail in certain aspects during the initial playthrough and restart the game without saving it and fix the original errors without taking any sort of penalty. The campaign is basically a brutal presentation of this flaw as Inspectors and Superiors will harshly punish you for allowing or not allowing certain characters to pass the checkpoint as I mentioned earlier. It does offer different modes after the Campaign/Story Mode is completed which further adds to the Replay Value. When everything is said and done, this game is truly a masterpiece despite the graphics looking like they are from a Picassco NES rom. When I think of the best times I had playing Steam it would definitely include playing this one.
Final Score: 95 Out of 100

This game is brilliant!
It's a visual novel, set in a Moscow apartment complex. The protagonist is a slightly pretentious young teacher who is being slowly driven mad by his noisy neighbours. It doesn't sound like the sort of premise you could make into an involved and engaging story, but it really works. The main character is the epitome of an unreliable narrator as he slowly goes mad - you're never quite sure if his neighbours are just noisy thugs or if there is really something much more sinister going on. Without spoiling it, some of the endings are incredibly disturbing, some are strange and some are just weirdly satisfying.
It's a fairly short game and doesn't take long to get all the endings, but it's really worth playing. There are some genuinely creepy moments in the game and it overall has a really nightmarish feel to it.
We played it in English on the first play through. This game seems to be getting some negative reviews and a lot of people have pointed out that the loading screen is in Russian and has to be switched (easily done by clicking on the flag) and also that the English translation isn't perfect in areas. But it's not any worse than other translated visual novels and it's actually very well done for an indie game (with some explanations thrown in about cultural references). There are occasional random untranslated scenes (we found about three in the whole game), but it didn't really detract from the flow of the game and it's pretty forgivable.
Overall, despite a few language glitches and a few bits of awkward translation, this is a quirky little gem of a horror game with great writing, genuinely creepy atmosphere, multiple branching endings and some surprising twists and turns. 9/10

I only recommend this game to fans of the Alien or Alien vs Predator franchise. Myself being a fan, I found the game worth playing. However, there were many disappointments along the way. The game is no were near as frightening as I had hoped. There are jump scares yes, but they are more annoying than anything because this means you are dead and have to restart from your previous checkpoint (which may involve longer backtracking than you would have wished). The game has very limited combat and in most scenarios engaging in combat will get you instantly killed. That being said, Alien Isolation is a stealth driven game that involves constant sneaking and hiding to avoid enemies. The game is hard...and I mean hard. I started out on the hard difficulty setting, changed to normal about a quarter of the way through, and had to finish on easy because I was fed up with dying so often. On the plus side, however, the game is absolutely beautiful.  Space looks spectacular when it is actually shown. I found searching for items, reading datalogs, and crafting items to be fun. Every tool/item has a particular use and you have to apply that to your current situation or you will not survive! Overall, it was a beautiful and explorative atmosphere experience that was okay for me, but not for everyone.

The mechanics are solid, no unnecessary gimmicks or items or stuff like that, just a few proper guns. There isn't great variety in them, but one can imagine there wasn't, back in that day. The story has a neat twist, in that it is narrated, and sometimes the narrator "forgets" or "remembers" things, which in turn has an effect on the gameplay.
The story is short (7 hours), but has some replay value, and there's an Arcade mode which has you shooting as well as you can in set paths for highscores.
Graphically, the game is much more polished than you would expect from a relatively unknown game like this, and sometimes I just had to stop and stare at the scenery.
I highly recommend it for the current price, since it's one of the better single player FPS experiences I've had.

Well, I just finished my Recursion and can now finally review the game.
The fights are basically played in an arena - a closed area on the map - and require a lot of thought in skill preparation and use as well as character placement.
Their are two ways to wage a fight. Either you go the classic active way (like any action game), or you can use the Turn() function which allows you to stop time and plan your attacks at leisure.
While in Turn(), everyone freezes and a bar appears at the top of the screen, this bar represent the total of actions you can take (for those who know of it, imagine Legend of Legaia's system). Moving and attacking eats a part of the bar depending of the skill and isn't done right away, instead you plan all hte attack which will be carried out when you finish the Turn(). The actions are then done at lightning speed, often taking a number of enemies to the grave at once with good planning.
About the skills :
You will equip skills (which you acquire by leveling and by finding people) at savepoint, in up to 4 active slots.
Every skill is totally different from another both visually and practically. One can debuff a group of enemies in an area while the other will make you invisible for a while.
Then you can equip those skills as passives for the active skills or for yourself. A skill that makes you drop explosives packets on the ground as active will increase the damage and blast radius of another as passive. Character passives can increase your total HP, reduce damage taken, reduce cost of abilities during Turn()...
The game isn't too short, but not really long. It took me 7 hours to complete my first run and 9 hours to Recurse through the story. Recursion is basically New Game+ wherre you keep everything and replay the story while the enemies are end-game level and randomized through the areas.
The scenario can seem confused, but is very enjoyable with many things to learn.
Apart from the Sandbox - which give acces to a practice area and a number of tests as well as some miscellaneous stuff, a big one being the jukebox - there is no side content.
The art is sublime and serves very well the game. The music nicely compliments the action and events throughout the game and is a jewel to listen to.
I give a solid 9.5/10 for this well crafted game. Really enjoyed it.

What can I really say?  I love this game.
This game...is art.  Plain and simple this game is living, interactive art.  Everything looks gorgeous in an almost isometric setting and each 'cutscene' is like a beautiful painting.  The game is driven primarily by a narrative directed at the protagonist but also has little bits of lore scattered throughout the game world and in your abilities themselves (which I'll touch on briefly later) that help immerse you in the world and the protagonist's situation.  The music in the game is also fantastic, with soulful vocals and lush sonic landscapes that fit each situation.
As for the game mechanics, they are simply excellent.  You select up to 4 primary abilities out of a selection that increases as you level up and progress through the story that you then upgrade with the abilities you don't use, opening up a vast array of strategies and playstyles.  You can also use the extra abilities to provide passive buffs to you or to all your skills.  How you combine them is totally up to you...as long as you have the memory to hold the abilities you pick.
The game also encourages experimentation by letting you unlock lore as you use each skill in a different way: active, upgrade, and passive.  But plan well.  You can only change your skill sets at checkpoints and the most memory-heavy ability combinations are consumed when your health drops to 0, and don't regenerate until you reach a sufficient number of checkpoints (usually 1-2).
As for actual battles, you can use abilities in free form combat, with various charge times for each ability, or you can set up an (almost) unbreakable combo at the expense of being able to use your abilities for a brief time.  I say almost because there are combos that won't work due to things getting moved around or failing to be triggered.  Combat is quite satisfying, and you can augment the difficulty in a variety of ways to your liking.
The only downside of this game is that it is short...you might spend around 5 hours beating it.  It does have a new game plus, allowing you to fight stronger enemies with any skills you didn't get in your first playthrough, but as far as I know it doesn't lend much else storywise.  That said, if you are like me and you sometimes miss a few bits of lore because you went the wrong way, another playthough might be warrented for story!
Bottom line is this game is wonderful, oozing with quality and heart and, in my opinion, is worth every penny.

Simply put, Tree of Savior is fun as hell and it isn't a clone of World of Warcraft.
Now then, allow me to elaborate.
First of all, the music is phenomenal. The tracks are well composed, diverse, and beautiful. If that isn't enough, each area generally has multiple tracks so that you aren't listening to one song on repeat which is a really nice touch that most developers overlook.
Secondly, the graphics. While not hyper realistic or over the top, the graphics of Tree of Saviour are an interesting blend of 2D sprite components and 3D cell shading that create a gorgeous artistic style that can still be run by lower end machines.
Next, even at low levels, your skills feel powerful. Your moves have nice flashy animations that are impressive, and monsters explode on death making huge group kills ever so satisfying. Bosses are fun and interesting, scaling in challenge as you level up and progress through the story.
Moving on, the questing experience is different from other games. The NPCs that provide you with side-quests are often unmarked, so for the first time in a game in years I found myself talking to all the NPCs in an area. I learned about my surroundings, found a ton of extra quests, and enjoyed the exploration / interaction aspect that this deisgn choice creates. I do understand though that this aspect of the game isn't for everyone, so it is definitely something to be aware of.
The Cash Shop is purely costume and convenience items and steers clear of a Pay to Win environment. In fact, most of the Cash Shop items that matter at all are tradeable like the Premium Token, Tree of Savior's subscription equivalent.
Character customization may seem scare at character creation, but when you realize that the vast majority of the character customization options are both toggleable and available from the Market, Achievements, and the Class System, the lack of options during Charaction Creation kind of ceases to matter.
The Class and Statistic Systems are intense. There are over 80 Classes in the game and there are a boat load of combinations that you can build. You assign your stat points too, giving you complete control over your character.
The amount of options you have to control your character are fantastic. Want to use a Keyboard to do everything? You can. Not a fan of Keyboards and want to use your Mouse for everything? You can do that too. You like kicking it old school and want to lean back and use a Controller? Well, that's also an option. Want to switch between them? The game will just swap on the fly. You could drop your Controller and break it mid boss fight, and just start playing with the Keyboard if you knew your keybinds. That's awesome, cause Mouse and Controller batteries always seem to die at the worst times.
Finally, if you played the original Ragnarok Online, Tree of Savior feels like coming back to your house from an extended vacation. Things are familiar, you have to get used to them again, but above all, you're back home.
I would highly recommend this game. Haters gonna hate, I'm gonna play Tree of Savior.
Thanks for reading! Have a good one, and if you're gaming, may all your loots be phat!

A glance at Papers, Please might cause someone to think "Why would anyone want to play a game about checking for errors in documentation? That sounds like a job." But if there's anything that we can learn from simulation games is that they don't have to be fun to draw you in, because once you find that each document is a window into a person's private life, and that you are reluctantly given the tough decision "Should I let this person into my country?", you find that there is a dangerously comfortable flow.
This game confronts you with sequences of people who provide you documentation for immigrating to the ficticious country Arstotzka (based on the Soviet Union). You must carefully search their documents for errors and make sure that everything is in order before letting them in. But the genius behind this game soon becomes apparent. You have limited time, and the more people you let into the country before the end of the day, the more money you get. What do you need money for? Well, you have a large nuclear family who all rely on your income to take care of heating, food, medicine, and you will never be able to afford all of these things.
But you can't just let in everyone, because every time you permit a person with incorrect documentation to enter, you receive a citation, and eventually get docked pay. This creates a wonderful tension between wanting money and not loosing your job. And checking documents isn't easy, it's often tedius to compare spelling of names, or social security numbers, or expiration dates, or remembering what type of identification each person should be having, so making mistakes is a matter of a keen eye and a good memory for rules.
To make it even harder, you only have a third of the screen to place documents, so you can never see all of them at a time. But that wouldn't be stressful enough, because each person often has a story and in such a dystopian world, you find people who empathize with, but have bad documents, or people who are evil but have everythign in order. And the game will often send you reminders of decisions you made that ruined someone's life, or sometimes saved it.
And on top of all of this there is a plot about a group of revolutionaries who try to recruit you to their cause. And with the horrible bureaucracy you see around you, the revolutionaries have a good point, but you must decide whether to risk helping them, or to play it safe with a government that will hopefully leave you and your family alone.
What all this adds up to is a game that causes you to have to make the decisions that people in stressful bureaucratic jobs must make. In a way it forces you to begin to think more openly about why people at the DMV seem unhappy, or even show us how people in an authoritarian government may seem heartless, but are really trying to protect their family.
So purchase this game for your own education, if not for its compelling and intricate gameplay.
Glory to Arstotzka!

tl;dr; It's a high cost but quality visual novel.
Long version:
I won't say all that much about the contents of the visual novel itself. You either like them or you don't. CLANNAD is massive with tons of choices which matter... but it's also very expensive.
I'll rather say things about the technical aspects of the "game":
- There's a checkbox in settings, "Make this program run more slowly in order to make other programs run faster", by default it is off. The only difference I can see is that when off, the game will hog 100% of one processor at all times. When turned on... the game takes virtually no processing power. LIKE IT SHOULD AS AN IMAGE AND TEXT DISPLAYER. So, make sure to check that.
- The game seems to have massive issues with Steam Overlay at the moment. There are many resolutions and scales (the game has scaling for 50%, 75%, 100%, 150%, 200%) where the Overlay simply won't show up. If you come across this and want to use the Overlay (useful for screenshots etc.) try changing resolution and/or scaling and it might pop up... while lagging terribly. Still seems to work, at least for me.
- Otherwise, the game is rather barebones as far as settings go. It has the basics (like turning off voices per character, text window background color changing, etc.), but it lacks some stuff like being able to turn off the custom mouse cursor. Which is, to be honest, slightly infuriating, as the "click point" of the cursor is on the lower left, rather than upper left like it is just about everywhere else.
- The save system is pretty cool as it allows you to write memos on each save file, which is really useful considering how the game has - probably without exaggeration - hundreds of choices which actually matter (not just "pick this option or you get a bad end" options, but options which determine what girls you'll meet. Some girls will even interact if you've met them both, whileas some will prevent you from going to see another girl (like the class rep stopping you from skipping class, where you'd meet another girl)). However, it completely lacks an auto-save function, which would be somewhat useful... even though it'd need to record 10-20 saves to be useful. Oh, and the system also allows you to move or delete saves with ease, which always nice to see.
- The load system, unfortunately, doesn't show you any message backlog after loading a save. If you're coming back to a save after a while, you might be completely lost at what point of the game you're at because of this.
- Dangopedia is pretty cool, though if you're a complete weeaboo you probably don't need it to explain what a kotatsu or bento are. Really useful for people new to the genre. Though, chances are such people would pick a cheaper title to start with...
PS. Kyou best girl, but has the worst route. I had already played this years ago in the fantranslation, and ragequit after completing that route. Did the same here. Not sure was I even expecting anything else, really!

*sigh* I really wanted to like Clannad. I really did.
Other visual novels I had completed before this are YU-NO and the Muv-Luv trilogy (not to mention countless real novels), and I fully expected this to be superior to those two due to dealing with something as serious as family and coming-of-age themes in a realistic setting. I waited over half a year for the Steam release and instantly bought this when it arrived. Well, having reached the True End after 50 hours of reading, I have to say I was disappointed. It was extremely difficult for me to enjoy the story because it's riddled with so many dramaturgical blunders, the major ones being:
Cartoony characters and forced drama.
Most of the cast is made of generic moe/harem characters, and not very good ones at that. There's a Shy Clumsy Girl, a Tsundere, a Kind Woman, a Manchild, a Dumb Comic Relief Friend, and so on. Many of them don't behave even remotely like real, complex people do (with a few wonderful exceptions like Yoshino and Tomoyo). The worst offender is Nagisa Furukawa, who is the first girl the main character meets and the main love interest, and the likability of whom the After Story section relies on. To put it bluntly, she is an imbecile. She acts like a five-year-old, never achieves anything by herself, constantly needs support from the protagonist Tomoya, doesn't have interesting chemistry with him, and is just plain useless. The last straw for me was this: At the moment when she - who is supposed to become the president of the drama club she wishes to recreate - revealed that she had never even SEEN a play before, I instantly lost EVERY SINGLE BIT of remaining sympathy I had towards her. Hence In After Story,
The pacing is also far too slow relative to the amount of actual story content. Most of the time is spent on these so-called "slice of life" sections, which are supposed to develop the characters, but are mostly filler in actuality. The result is that the plot takes ages to get going. After Story is not much better for the first few hours: Tomoya starts life as an adult, getting a job and his own apartment and so on. Aside from an admittedly good mentor-apprentice relationship, this part is not told in a particularly engaging way, it just... happens. Slowly.
Most of the routes in School Story (first half of the VN) follow roughly the same formula: Tomoya meets a new character, many hours are spent getting to know their gimmicky personality, then Sad Stuff happens, and finally Tomoya fixes everything. Maybe we learn their parents are dead, or maybe something unfortunate is about to happen to them. Real drama comes from CHOICES: it grows naturally from elements of the plot such as the protagonist trying to attain an objective, interactions between characters with possibly differing goals and worldviews, mistakes they make due to weaknesses in their personality, and difficult decisions and consequenses. The "drama" in Clannad on the other hand usually comes from the authors forcing misfortunes onto the characters (Muv-Luv Alternative is also highly guilty of this) and appeals to the lowest common denominator, the prime example being Kotomi's backstory. I believe the problems of the drama come from the mindset the stories are made in. You see, Key, the maker of Clannad, is a company that specialises in producing these things called nakige, "crying game" - that is, games that are supposed to make you cry. There's nothing surprising about the "sad" stuff once you can fully expect it due to the genre, and it's even more ineffective when I couldn't care about most of the characters. It's just poor melodrama and feels shallow and exploitative.
One of the most famous, supposedly tear-jerking scenes happens near the end of After Story and deals with Tomoya's relationship with his father. Well, after 45+ hours of waiting for that payoff, I found that it resolved it in an incredibly contrived and anticlimactic fashion. Tomoya basically
, just like that. (And there's some crying thrown in to make it more "moving". Jeez.)
The themes and lessons taught in Clannad are safe and inoffensive, aimed at making the reader a better person. "You should be considerate of your family and the people around you." "Hard, honest work pays off." "You should accept that things don't always go the way you want and must look on the bright side." "You should search for a better solution in situations that at first don't seem to have one." And so on. I gained very little from these as they were either something I myself already had figured out a long time ago or even some cases fundamentally disagree with. In real life I've dealt with far more complex and nuanced social situations than I encountered in Clannad.
With all this this complaining, you could get the impression that I think Clannad is bad. Not quite. While I find it incredibly overrated, it does have plenty of redeemable qualities. There are well-written characters and routes (Tomoyo Sakagami's, Mei Sunohara's and maybe Kappei Hiiraki's), and there are demonstrations of good responsible behaviour and life wisdom here and there. Tomoya has beliavable, interesting relationships with Tomoyo, Yoshino and
. Youhei Sunohara is a good source of slapstick and comic relief.
In the end, I felt I had most of my time wasted and wish I had watched the much shorter anime adaptation instead, and I recommend you do just that. Or maybe you will enjoy this more than I did, who knows.
EDIT: I found these insightful articles on the Internet that discuss much more in-depth than I the weaknesses and strengths of Clannad (based on the anime version). Beware as they contain spoilers.

Yup. It's an MMO, an automatic time-suck as most MMO's tend to have the power to do.
The ups(for me): The music is fantastic, the zones are beautiful, the urge to be  a non-stop klepto is satisfied, and you'll never run out of things to do.
The downs(for me): The combat system feels unresponsive when triggering moves to get out of aoe, or firing spells. The servers have a tendency to randomly drop(though their twitter is good at updating if there's going to be unforseen downtime) Load times are LONG unless you've got it on an SSD.
Other related thoughts and things to consider:
For me, leveling has been a slow process, so if you get distracted easily by "Hey what's that thing over there..." expect to take your time reaching cap. Dungeons can be both interesting and frustrating depending if you've got people who are nice or nitwits.
Player Housing!!(This addition was a big reason why I chose to play ESO after being on an MMO merry-go-round.)
It's instanced, so you're not fighting for plots. Housing is expensive, especially coming in as a new player, though they do give you a free Inn room you quest for that you just stuff full of fish and paintings. There is an option to buy homes, and furnishings in the Crown Store(ESO's cash shop) There are definitely some cash-grab items in there which I think, for vanity's sake.. are overpriced.

That said though, the items therein are for vanity and not going to be one of those pay to win scenarios.
One last note, this game is completely playable without the need for a subscription, however if you do tend to pick up everything and horde, an ESO plus subscription may be for you, as it offers a bottomless craft bag, which holds all of your materials.
Oh! If you are a roleplayer, the roleplaying community is pretty active, but don't expect to find it everywhere, ie the cities, Inn's etc as they can get instanced. Sometimes you will stumble into it, but your best bet to make contacts if guilds aren't being advertised in zone chat, is
.

I only recommend this game to fans of the Alien or Alien vs Predator franchise. Myself being a fan, I found the game worth playing. However, there were many disappointments along the way. The game is no were near as frightening as I had hoped. There are jump scares yes, but they are more annoying than anything because this means you are dead and have to restart from your previous checkpoint (which may involve longer backtracking than you would have wished). The game has very limited combat and in most scenarios engaging in combat will get you instantly killed. That being said, Alien Isolation is a stealth driven game that involves constant sneaking and hiding to avoid enemies. The game is hard...and I mean hard. I started out on the hard difficulty setting, changed to normal about a quarter of the way through, and had to finish on easy because I was fed up with dying so often. On the plus side, however, the game is absolutely beautiful.  Space looks spectacular when it is actually shown. I found searching for items, reading datalogs, and crafting items to be fun. Every tool/item has a particular use and you have to apply that to your current situation or you will not survive! Overall, it was a beautiful and explorative atmosphere experience that was okay for me, but not for everyone.

For 5.99 this is a bargain.
Different to your average shooter. Nothing quite like spamming off a 6 shooter.
Good difficulty even on normal. Simple controls, very nice intuitive action sequences (hit the right buttons as they flash up to combo kill the enemies, fail and you have to take them out manually) and the duels are about as much fun as i've had in a shooter.
Skill trees are an interesting addition. While they are useful spec'ing into one out of Rifles, Shotgun or Pistol doesn't stop you using the other two. The skills combined with NewGame+ carrying over and allowing you to unlock all skills is a pretty neat feature for replayability.
Story is fairly well fleshed out, told in a nice style with some good humour. Pretty good if slightly predictable twist at the end.
Duel mode is vicious, trying to control your hand over the gun (left to right), your focus on the opponent (up,down,left,right), in some cases which target you want to go for first, having to react to their draw, landing the shot as quickly as possible without firing before the gun is level, etc is awesome.
TL;DR - More in depth then The Punisher game but just as fun. for a game in this price range 9.9/10, in general compared to others still 8/10

I have a really casual gamer confession to make; I never played the first Borderlands to the end enough to garner a good enough impression on it. However, when I bought the second one I was determined not to send yet another game to my backlog; especially after I heard all the good and bad about this game.
As you might have deduced from the title, Borderlands 2 is the sequel to the sleeper hit Borderlands, a western RPG with cel-shaded graphics developed by Gearbox and published by 2K Games. The game is faithful to its predecessor, and keeps canon for canons sake; but it also improves upon the graphic design as any sequel should and bridges the story forward to ensure a linear, concise story arc.
The game opens with a Skag (a type of beast found in the game) wandering around, and eventually being chained and dragged by a bandit Humvee. The midget Psycho, who is on the bandit Humvee, headbutts one of the passengers, then climbs to the hood. Shortly thereafter, the Humvee is hit by a train, and a strong cloud of dust appears. Cue Short Change Hero by The Heavy. The crew of the bandit Humvee soar into the air in slow motion, as the flaming salvage of their vehicle spins and spins until landing atop the adjacent train. One bandit exits the vehicle, but is hit by a signage and falls flat again atop of the train.
Here's where you show up (I used Wikipedia because I'm lazy)
"Five years have passed since the events of Borderlands, when four Vault Hunters, a Hunter, a Soldier, a Siren and a Berserker, were guided by a mysterious entity known as The Guardian Angel on the planet of Pandora to the Vault, a place thought to have been left behind by aliens with powerful technology. Instead, these Vault Hunters were confronted by an alien abomination known as The Destroyer inside the vault. After defeating The Destroyer, a valuable mineral called Eridium started flourishing through Pandoras crust. Handsome Jack, a member of the Hyperion Corporation, secures this new resource and makes use of it to attempt to civilize the planet. Now, Handsome Jack rules over the inhabitants of Pandora with an iron fist from his massive satellite built in the shape of an H, always visible in the sky in front of Pandoras moon. Meanwhile, rumors of an even larger Vault hidden on Pandora spread across the universe, drawing a new group of Vault Hunters to the planet in search for it."
If that large summary of text wasnt enough to dissuade you from continuing with this review, I'll start with my thoughts on the story listen, its nothing too convoluted or deep, but it definitely reminds me of Call o Duty in terms of its foregone shallowness. It abandons subjectively good storytelling for gameplay, and, depending on how much of a nerd you are, youll either see this as a positive or a negative. Thankfully, though, all four protagonists from the original Borderlands return as NPCs that are instrumental in your assault against Hyperion.
Lilith, one of the protagonists from the original Borderlands, returns as a supporting character in Borderlands 2; and she has a personality that even Anita Sarkeesian would be OK with.
Until you decide to do that, though (the game is extremely open-world; you can procrastinate the missions for as long as you want, even if youre in the middle of a mission) you are free to explore Pandora at your own leisure. Then, when you feel like it, you can go back into the main storyline. This is both a good and a bad thing, since the level scaling forces you to grind every 3-4 story missions to prevent you from speeding through the game.
Graphically, there still is the cel-shaded style from the original; but the edges are far less jagged than before, and the heads-up display is much cleaner. With the settings set to maximum on the PC, the game runs a smooth 40-60fps on mid-range specs in most places.
There are many emotional breakthroughs to be had, and despite the cringe-worthy inclusion of a few memes, the dialogue in-game is pretty fun to hear. The game remains faithful to its predecessor, and overall its a good game. It was worth the 8 bucks spent on it, anyway. I havent experienced the DLC yet, but if 2K comes through with some free games used solely for journalistic intent and not personal enjoyment I might.

Clannad takes you into the life of Tomoya Okazaki as he experiences his final year of high school. For several years now he has been a delinquent with no goal after school ends, but after a chance meeting his life begins to change. How it changes is up to you as you make the choices of his life in this massive Visual Novel.
Clannad is absolutely massive. Don't go into this VN expecting to be done in a few hours. Well, perhaps you can finish a single path in a few hours (depending on your reading speed), but if you really want to dig into the game, it's going to take you much longer than that.
I personally found Clannad extremely slow to start off, but once it got to the later parts of each story path, it really picked up. Once it does start to pick up, your emotions are going to get hammered as the story takes a lot of turns. That said, the slow ramping up parts made it really hard to read for me.
I do recommend Clannad in general, however the story does start off a bit slow. The asking price is also extremely high for most (though considering how much content you are getting, I do feel the price is justified), so if you're on the fence about getting this then you may want to just try and wait for a good sale.
Disclaimer: I was provided a key for review by the publisher.

I love the Elder Scrolls series, but let's be honest- bethesda isn't very good at making games. What they are good at is telling stories and leaving things open to modders- but with this MMO, that isn't true.
TES has always been full of glaring glitches and bugs, which modders notice and fix (you're probably one of them; I am) but getting rid of or fixing errors and/or bad game elements just isn't possible here, so you're just stuck with it.
Furthermore, the research (which is totally different from other TES games, which is fine) is pretty dumb. It takes 6 real hours (which means you can go to work or sleep and come back and its done) for a weapon/armor trait to be researched. It works similarly to Skyrim's enchantments:
-Sacrifice item with trait (like damage bonus or found loot bonus) and you can apply that affect to new items you craft of the same item type
Neat. Can enchant on top of it as well as refine, so you can get real nice stuff to a point. However, let's say you have a 1h sword with damage bonus, and another 1h sword with healing recieved bonus. Each trait takes 6 hours to research.
You research one of them.
You figure it'll take 6 hours to research the next one- but nope. Every research you do on each item type doubles the previous amount of time needed!
-6 hours
-12 hours
-24 hours
-48 hours
-96 hours
There is a skill within each crafting skill tree that lets you research more things at the same time while also slightly increasing research speed, but it takes a long time to get that high. So expect that you'll enjoy the game for a 24 hours of playtime, then only be able to functionally play for a few minutes a day as you add more stuff to research, then a few minutes a week, for the same reason.
I don't know how many months it would take to fully research everything so you can just play already.
Luckily, you can put items in the bank, and the crafting tables recognize items both in inventory and bank- so that increases useable storage. But that isn't really the point, now, is it?

3. The armies and fleet are extremely expensive to maintain. I would build 3 decent sized armies, and spend easily 4000 denaruis (Or what ever currency it is based on.) a turn for them. Usually I get capped in game at 5000-6000 denaruis so this would be 2/3 of my funding.
4. Naval battles with soldier fleets (Non-Navy ships) are somehow impossible to use in battle. You will find yourself with 5-7 soldier ships against ONE ship, the success rate is nearly 15%.
5. The nations AI is WAY too agressive; it is nearly impossible to have diplomacy. Atleast for me. Suddenly I will get indicators that a trade route has been canceled. A non-agressive peace act will be canceled, for NO reason. Even on easy there armies build REALLY fast, and you will always have to use 2-3 armies to battle one general, which is hard because usually at that moment in game you are limited to 3-4 armies, which forces you to put 2/3-3/4 of your army in one direction. With fleets sieging your harbouring cities.
6. $15.00 FOR A HISTORICAL BATTLE?! ARE YOU INSAINE?! Yes, the DLC is amazingly expensive. (And mods are not so easy to install.) The only DLC worth buying, is the blood and gore mod. I wouldn't recommend spending 15 dollars of your parents hard earned dollars or your OWN hard earned dollars on a 45 minute experience, on top of being hard as sh*t to complete even on easy.
All in all, set this aside. This game can be done casually for 30 minutes to 1 hour and 30 minutes. When the nations decide your an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, you might as well quit, or get real serious about your millitary.
This aspect makes the game easily unistallable and forgetable.
BUT it is very fun. And I play it from time to time, not a serious fan of Total War, I grew up with Age of Empires, and Stronghold 2.

I totally love this game. Played it alot when it wasnt on steam yet and i love the paying concept of this game.

What is free?
Killing mule deer in the starting area. Although this sounds like barely anything it really is quite fun!
Is this game free-to-play? No. Its more like an infinite demo that you can play over and over without any time restrictions and it keeps tracking your score.
Why pay?

Dont shoot females! Only males give you points.
Scout the other animals. If you see a group of male deers then dont shoot the first one you see. They`ll run when you shoot. Look for the deer with the biggest antler for more points!
Animals can smell or hear you! Some creatures better then others. Cant find any animals? Then stop running or move against the wind or both!
Buy an rangefinder! Is the only think i bought extra and i love it! Especially for hunting with bows.
Use the shooting range! Think about bullet drop.
Dont just kill but also collect your game! or else it doesnt add to your statistics.
Have patience! omg somethings it can really take like an hour to even find an animal you want to kill or finally find a male animal!

This game is amazing. I have played something like 18 hours in less than a week and I can't seem to stop. Having played it through in both the normal and recursion modes, with limiters on and off (including up to 10), I can honestly say that it remains interesting, complex, and as difficult (or not) as you could ask for. The combat is very strategic, and can range from just using whatever functions that you have early on, to having almost every slot filled later when you reach around level 16. I spent hours pouring over the combat loadouts, trying to figure out what could give me the most functionality and surviveability, but this is by no means required. Because of the immense customizeability everyone who plays this game will have a different playstyle and a unique experience. Beyond the amazing combat, variety of enemies (who by the way scale, becoming more interesting and dangerous as you do), and fantastic graphic style that sometimes seems more art than game, Transistor also is a treat for the ears. While listening to the soundtrack on its own is extremely entertaining, ingame the music becomes even more dynamic through the ability to have Red hum along with whatever track happens to be playing at the time. The last time you pass by the stage where you were preforming where you were attacked at the start of the story, I stood and let Red hum for several minutes, just to hear "In Circles" with her humming along. If you purchase this game, or have already done so, please do youself a favor and get the soundtrack as well. This game is an amazing experience, and is something that everyone should play. Totally worth it, even at full price.

Nowadays Post-Apocalyptic Survival Horror games tend to be multiplayer zombie fests, the sort where you are just as likely to get killed by human nature than you are by the denizens that inhabit those games. Now a select few of these games actually pull of what they attempt to do, while the rest fail horribly; but for those that want a more refined experience akin to DayZ or Rust there’s the S.T.A.L.K.E.R games.
S.T.A.L.K.E.R: Shadow of Chernobyl comes from GSC Game World in the Ukraine, home country of the Chernobyl incident and with post soviet style and estranged horror, GSC does a tremendous job at creating a truly riveting shooter.
Story:
S.T.A.L.K.E.R takes place within the Chernobyl Exclusion Zone, a roughly 30 square kilometre area that contains a plethora of locations inhabited by either stalkers, military, bandits, mutants or worse. Within the zones lies anomalies that the player must avoid; some conduct immense amounts of electricity, while others simply crush you in a vortex of force. Fortunately and unfortunately for the player there lies artifacts near anomalies that can be used to significantly increase your abilities or sell for a decent price.
You play the role of the “Marked One”, an amnesiac who just happened to find himself in The Zone. Armed with several guns and protective gear you set out to face the dangers of The Zone and hopefully gain back your memory. And that ladies and gentlemen is pretty much the story.
Now while the actual story is a little lacking, it’s the individual experiences in The Zone that I remember the most. Stories of trekking through the underground tunnels of Agroprom hearing the horrid sound of mutants lurking in the dark or wandering the wastes at night to hear distant gunshots and screams of mutants and men; this is stuff the sticks with you long after the game is done. So in that sense the story the setting has to tell is rather interesting and saves the game from being a bore to experience.
8.0/10
Design:
The bulk of S.T.A.L.K.E.R takes place within a large non-linear sandbox with varying locations with a plethora of enemies to kill. All the A.I programmed in the game is done expertly, with pack animals hunting for food while bandits and other Stalkers scout the land looking for artifacts to plunder or people to rob. The best part of the A.I is that it doesn’t stop when you enter another area of The Zone, the mutants, bandits, military and Stalkers all remain, all interacting and surviving against each other.
My only gripe with the design of the game is that it does take a little too long to load the level, nothing drastic but the self-reflection drags a bit too long.
Now the original release of S.T.A.L.K.E.R was known to be rather buggy and I’ve played the 1.0 version back in the day and I can say it was pretty buggy; thing is I’m not going to constitute the buggyness into the final score for this review because this is a review of S.T.A.L.K.E.R’s current state and the bugs are nearly gone with both official support and modding.
8.7/10
Gameplay:
The gun play in the game is more of a simulation than arcade-y feel when compared to the run of the mill shooter; while the other games you can get pumped full of bullets before you die, a stray bullet to head means you’ll hit the bucket in S.T.A.L.K.E.R. Though you might think it seems like a huge detriment to the player it only really enhances the feeling of vulnerability as it is the perfect way to completely change the mood in an instant.
One such story was in the area of The Zone known as The Garbage which is the place where the Ukrainian SSR government dumped all the radioactive debris from vehicles, buildings and bodies. I was sitting with a bunch of friendly stalkers in a large garage, just passing the time in the campfire listening to one of them play the guitar while the other tells a story; the story was is Russian so I have no idea what it was about or if it even was a story but by god does it create good atmosphere. In an instant the camp was being raided by bandits and the only way everyone knew what was going on was when the crack of an SVD (Snayperskaya Vintovka Dragunova, Dragunov Sniper Rifle) sliced through the air and hit the guitarist in the head, killing him in an instant. After a tense firefight the bandits were dead and the garage safely secure again, unfortunately the guitarist had to die but someone eventually picked up the guitar and started playing it.
And that’s what makes S.T.A.L.K.E.R so great, the never ending feeling of dread; whether in broad daylight or in the deepest, darkest tunnels of Pripyat, the feeling danger is always near.
9.4/10
Presentation:
S.T.A.L.K.E.R came out in 2007 so it’s not that old but the visuals sure look a bit dated, in a sort of lower budget Ukrainian developer sense. Ever since its release there have been numerous mods that improve the visuals significantly and some even improve the mechanics.
The bulk of the visuals consist of Soviet era architecture, muddy wasteland, swamps, abandoned labs and tunnels. It’s all rather interesting to someone who is accustomed to more “american/western european” architecture, all the soviet stuff is incredibly utilitarian and bland but it just enhances the mood of dread in a sort of “even the world doesn’t care what happens to you” sort of way.
8.6/10
Overall S.T.A.L.K.E.R: Shadow of Chernobyl is one of those gems that you might of missed amongst bigger 2007 titles like Halo 3, Gears of War, Mass Effect and Bioshock. If you have a PC that can run S.T.A.L.K.E.R (which should be any PC these days) I would highly recommend it, especially if you can last through punishing gameplay.
Overall Score:
8.7/10

TREE OF SAVIOR IS ALL BUT... RESTRICTIONS, RESTRICTIONS, AND RESTRICTIONS
Ragnarok Online was my childhood game, when I found out about the release of this game I immediately bought the highest priced Founder Access without a second thought... after 2 weeks I immediately regretted my action.
1. Trade restrictions in this game is one of the most ridiculous one I've seen in my 15 years of gaming experiences, for the very reason that it is the first of its kind which actually caused trouble for my progression in-game as I tried to transfer materials from my main character to alternate (through storage slot temporarily enabled by premium subscription) only to find that some part of my materials are unable to transfer across. To make things worse, I then realized that it was now impossible for me to transfer back the materials from my alternate to my main. The game developer has justified their poorly implemented restrictions for the glorious purpose of stopping bots and gold sellers, and yet I see endless numbers of gold sellers bot-spamming ads in the main town everyday and bots running rampant in popular dungeons.
2. Unreasonably, or I should say, utterly stupid loot system with ridiculous drop rates for some items will make you totally feel like quitting the game at days when RNG doesn't work in your favour. To craft a mid-game equipment, the recipe required me to farm for 15 materials from a group of extremely weak monsters who spawn in very few numbers. Coupling with the fact that the drop rate for the said material is 0.75%, and general low spawn rate of certain monsters including this one, I have in fact attempted to farm for the material for hours and didn't get any at all.
3. While this game succeeded in emulating the fun experiences of old school mmorpgs, they have unfortunately also retained features from the past which are obsolete and unacceptable in modern mmorpgs. Not only that, they have also incorporated some of the most despised features of a modern mmorpgs - a premium subscription option which treats non-premium players like worthless garbage with further restrictions (such as no item transfer between characters of the same account) on top of the abundance of restrictions already in existence.
4. Server lag and instability, I don't even have to mention much here.
The game, being spirit successor of Ragnarok Online, attempted to emulate the "old school" mmorpg format which many old fans including me really appreciated it much. Unfortunately many of the features from the older mmorpgs have become reprehensible in modern games such as the idea of making people grind for items with drop rate as low as 0.01%  from monsters which are slow to spawn and yield no exp gains. Worst of all, they have placed unreasonable restrictions on trading which would have helped to relax the overly stressful grinding of loots, for the very purpose which they still fail to achieve at the end of the day.

A good third of my logged hours so far have been spent waiting one one screen or another.  The issues seem to only affect the NA server as I can log in and play on the EU server without any trouble at all. Unfortunatly only the ESO Plus applies to both servers. Character bank and any other DLC isn't shared between the two mega servers. One thing that I have noticed is that the EU server doesn't seem to have many players (maybe that's why there are no server issues?).
I wish I had read more reviews before I invested in a 6 month Plus membership. The server issues make this more of an exercise in frustration waiting to play what is in fact a pretty good game.
Edit: From the time I first posted this review to now there has been dramatic improvements in server connectability - so much so that my Euro server character has been stuck at level 24 only having finished the main quest line. Since my only issue with ESO was server connectability I'm happily changing my recommendation to thumbs up!

This is really not a bad story, although short to play through even when getting all endings.  I would recommend it on sale but not at full price given the play time (with all endings I still only spent an hour on it, but I'm also a very speedy reader so others might take longer).
Keep in mind that this is a visual novel, which some people don't consider to be "games" in the strictest sense.  There are some choices to make to get different endings, but that's the extent of gameplay.  There is also an easter-egg shooter minigame that can be accessed through the main game.
Also please keep in mind that the translations in the screenshots have since been updated, and the translation is reasonably good now.  There are some minor grammatical and spelling errors, and about three lines that were missed in the translating, but the story is completely understandable.  The parts that are confusing are meant to be and that will be very apparent as the plot progresses (not going to elaborate on that to avoid spoilers).  The final ending that unlocks after completing all other endings is actually quite touching and I was pleased with it.
The minigame is a space shooter that is a little quirky in terms of controls, and some of the achievements are tied to scoring highly on that game, so if you're a 100% completionist for achievements you may want to keep that in mind.
Overall, although I wish the story was longer and had voice work rather than just music, I found it interesting and I was genuinely curious how things would turn out from choice to choice.  There are better novels out there, but this one isn't terrible and is worth a read if it can be picked up on sale.

Story: Most school life routes are enjoyable and endearing. After story is a must read. Nostalgia. Happy tears. Sad tears. Life lessons.
Art: Characters' is subpar, but you get used to it. Does its job. It has its own kind of charm.
Sound: OST is top tier. VA work is on the spot.
Characters: Sometimes subject to trope overusage, but good development. Mostly enjoyable interactions. Somehow feels more "anime" than most visual novels.
