This game is amazing. the art style is really well done and the mechanics are awesome. While the game has microtransactions, it appears to be fully playable for free. 9/10 from what i have seen so far.

I am surprised how fun this game turned out to be. It's essentially a clicker game/RPG with a lot of customisation and the possibility to play idle, active or both. You are never forced to spend any money on microtransactions and I was able to progress without paying anything. Also I didn't get the impression that portions of the game are artificially slowed down to make you pay, which is nice.
First of all you have to take care of your hub level (tavern) to attract new and stronger heroes and store more powerful items. You do this by gathering gold in dungeon runs, but you can later invest in a passive ability that gives you gold while you are away. The dungeons become increasingly difficult until your party gets defeated. If that's the case, you keep all gold/items and will return to your hub. In the meantime your tavern attracted some new adventurers, so you equip them with better gear, found or bought in the run before, and try to get a little further.
Your party can consist of up to 5 adventurers and each can have their own class with special abilities. You fight monsters in turn based battles, where you click on each adventurer to carry out your actions, be it standard attacks, magic or using items. You have an option to enable auto fighting and play the game in idle mode so you don't have to click and most of the time the AI behaves reasonable. I tend to take control myself in the later dungeons to use each hero effectively.
The overall style is simplistic but fitting and has a nice arcade vibe to it. If you want a game that offers more depth than your standard clicker games (actually hell of a lot more) get it. It's free after all and a nice little time waster.

Soda Dungeon is a very casual style RPG.  Your job is to recruit (hire) the visitors of your tavern, equip them, and send the party into the local dungeon for loot.  That loot can be spent aquiring new gear for your party, or invested into the tavern to attract new, more skilled, visitors.
It's a port from a mobile game and certainly plays that way, but it's free and worth a few hours of entertainment.

+ Better than most RPG games
+ Excellent tutorial
- Poor graphics
- Overly simplistic gameplay
- Repetitive gameplay
- A clone of so many other games
Make up your own mind with this gameplay:

A great casual RPG with a distinctive style and a sense of humour. Unlike other free-to-play games, Soda Dungeon doesn't feel as if it's trying to not-so-subtly back you into a corner to get you to pay... everything can be earned at a reasonable pace, and there are no timers or stamina. People who dismiss it because of the weird stigma attached to mobile games, which this was originally, and where I played most of it, are missing out on a game that was clearly crafted with love.

I played this game a few monts back on Android and I absolutely loved it, I'm so happy it's on Steam.  It's a great free-to-play game to add to your collection.  There are some in-app purchases but there's no ads, and the game is a lot of fun.
You start out in a tavern, and the main character is too afraid to dungeon-delve, so he hires "drunken" tavern patrons to do it for him.  As you adventure you collect gold and different gear for your brawlers, and gradually upgrade the tavern.  More tavern upgrades = more and better fighters = longer dungeon runs = more gold = more tavern upgrades.  If that equation didn't make it obvious enough, this game is a grind.  It's supposed to be.  It's a bit like a mix between a clicker game and old-school Final Fantasy turn-based games.
The game also features an auto-battle mode, which is handy for when you dont feel like doing all the clicking in lower levels of the dungeon, but you can definitely do the strategizing yourself if you want to.
This game is hella fun on mobile, and just as good on Steam.

This game, is simply amazing.
The combat is a free form turn based strategy, which means, it has but is not restricted to, turn based actions.
The story is gripping and at times dark.
The combat has a ton of variety to create exactly what you want.
Fair warning, it's short.

MUSIC AND ARTWORK:
Absolutely fantastic.  They do a wonderful job together of drawing you into this surreal world.
10/10
UI:
Flawless.  UI's in games are usually pretty bad, and I'm a UI-stickler.  However, this game's UI was clearly carefully thought-out by a professional.  It always contained all the information I needed, yet was never in the way.  There was never a time I wanted to do something and thought to myself "Crap, how do I do that again?"
10/10
GAMEPLAY:
The fighting in this game looks artificially similar to Bastion, but the ability to pause the action and execute multiple attacks in succession makes it feel completely different.  The battles end up being much more about turn-based tactics than quick reflexes.
Different powers are unlocked throughout the course of the game.  Each power can be used as an attack, an upgrade to a different attack, or a passive boost.  This mixing-and-matching opens up a wide variety of strategies for each fight; if one matchup of powers doesn't work well for a fight, you can try again with a *completely* different strategy.  This keeps the game fresh and interesting, even on subsequent playthroughs.
On the forums, many people complained about the battles being repetative, but I completely disagree; due to your ability to completely change your lineup of powers, every battle felt fresh and interesting.
My one complaint is that you only start out with three (I think?) powers, so you have to wait a short while before you can make the more interesting matchups.  And since the game is so short, "a short while" ends up being half of the game.
8/10
STORY:
This is where things turn sour.  The story in this game is very open-ended, to the point of being lazy.  It's (obviously) difficult to critique the story without giving any spoilers, but suffice it to say there are a LOT of story-elements that are never explained or even hinted at.
**Minor spoilers ahead** (but I'll keep things vague to avoid ruining the story)
All of the characters are hilariously under-developed, even (or *especially*) the main two.  It's to the point where, when you fight one of the bosses, you not only don't feel anything when they die, you don't even know why you're fighting them to begin with.  Also, one very obvious lead-up to a boss-fight ends in a very contrived, almost non-sensical Deus Ex Machina.
As for the the main two characters, you end up not caring what happens to them, because you barely know anything about them.  On top of that, the ending feels incredibly forced and out-of-place.
The whole thing reeks of lazy writing.
**End of minor spoilers**
2/10
GAME LENGTH:
The game is pretty short - only about 5 hours long, and that's *if* you complete all the side-challenges you can.  The game feels like the creators had planned on there being more content, since all of the side quest-y stuff (unlocking all the character-stories, finishing the side-challenges, the majority of the optional achievements) are impossible to complete in a single playthrough - you don't meet enough enemies or enter the "Backdoor" enough times to complete them.
It feels like at some point the developers said "I think we've worked hard enough, let's just polish and release it already," so they did.  This is corroborated by how incomplete the storyline is.
5/10
OVERALL
I don't regret my purchase, but I was expecting more.  Some people will think the gameplay and wonderful atmosphere make the game worth $20, even if it's so short and lacking on story (or, if you're the artsy type, maybe you enjoy open-ended stories).  Others will feel betrayed by the lack of content.  Depending on which type of person you are, I'd either recommend buying it now, or waiting for a sale, respectively.  But either way, I think it's worth playing.
8/10

The Borderlands series has become somewhat of a cult hit in the years since the original game's release, and I find it rather unfortunate as a fan of the games that it's not more spoken of the video game community. Borderlands can be summarised in several bulletpoints that act as the focus of each individual game: Guns, grinding and comedy. This review will attempt to cover each aspect of the series, and this game in particular, in enough detail to perhaps get you interested in this gem.
Firstly, guns. Perhaps the thing that this series is most well known for outside its fanbase, the guns it this game are plentiful and varied, in both design and effect. There are 4 types of elemental guns: fire, electric, explosive and slag, plus non-elemental guns. The first 3 elements are somewhat self explanatory, but slag is an element that, once it affects a foe, allows all other damage types to be more harmful. Elemental damage can also be done through special shield AOE or Spike attacks, or through the several skills that the player characters can invest in, there being 4 characters in the vanilla game and 2 extra that can be bought in DLC. Buying the DLC characters is reccomended, as each character feels much different to the rest due to the variety of skills that are given to only specific characters. The stats of all the guns in the game are procedurally generated, so even if you get two guns of the same model and make, there would be inequalities in stats, such as higher accuracy and lower damage etc.
Grinding is a rather filthy word in the gaming community, and justifiably so, making it somewhat unfortunate that it is a large chunk of the Borderlands experience. However, the game being an RPG and all, it should really be expected for it to be like that. Grinding in this game involves redoing areas with tough enemies for XP and fighting old bosses for a chance at their rarest drops of gear, the latter potentially taking hours at a time. Although it is required for completionists and the like, grinding is not needed for people who are just hoping to complete the game, as anyone who does a reasonable amount of side quests can beat the final boss with relative ease. Whether the grinding the turn-off or not for you is a matter of your own taste, so I'm just putting the facts about it out there so you can make up your opinion.
Finally, the comedy and overall style of the game. The comedy isn't really what you can call 'intelligent', but a bit of toilet humour has never hurt anyone, has it? It can feel a bit hit-or-miss at times, but fortunately the jokes are legitimately funny the vast majority of the time, the bright, cell-shaded aesthetic of the game allowing you to more easily appreciate the comedy that is delivered. Overall a solid aspect of the experience.
Concluding this review that about one person will read, anyone who enjoys collecting a ridiculous amount of loot, first person shooters, grinding, silly humour and more cartonnish aesthetic will most likely find this game to be a bit of pleasant, mindless fun. If you don't enjoy any of the above listed things, however, I doubt we will ever be very good friends.

Yes, Factorio really is kinda wonderful like so many people say, especially in the very beginning. Putting your factory together feels very satisfying, and I think it must speak to the core of some human trait. We just love to make stuff go.
The soundtrack and the lonely atmosphere in the game is also quite good and I fully understand people who compare the experience to being high. I felt it myself.
So in essence I wouldn't actually discourage anyone from getting this game on a general basis, and this short review shouldn't be regarded as such. When I choose to click thumbs down, it's to make a point that I feel is left out by all those understandably intoxicated reviewers that has given it such a one sided score.
This game is very simple in that it really only contains a single facet and that is working to automate your factory. There is a progression system of sorts, a hostile faction and some recource management, but they're all relatively inconsequentual. There really is no strategy, choices or fail states to speak of. It's all about putting together the puzzle that is your factory, and that puzzle really only has to be as complex as you want it to be.
Those 40 hours that I have played, consists of a single first game where I started without any knowledge. Around the 20 hour mark, I saw/understood all of the game's components and since then it's only been a matter of finishing the job and get off the planet. I got here without ever having to re-load the game or be in a situation where I didn't fully control my destiny, and now the operations have started to feel a little bit like chores.
So the game is still in development. But I have played many of these indie type management games and I honestly don't think it will ever go anywhere significant. The small dev will add pieces to the puzzle, re-structure and streamline some elements, but I seriously doubt that it will ever take on any added dimensions. What you see is basically what you get and what you get is a system where you tinker with a limited number of parts to automate a limited number of systems for a limited amount of time.
If you're the kind of person that needs a game to be about something a little more than what I have described, you may find that the price tag is a tad too high for what it is: Somewhat skeletal. I think that if the game had been about 5-10 euros cheaper, I wouldn't have written this review.

However, because of login server issues, random disconnects and 5 min to 30 min loading screens I cannot recommend this game. A good third of my logged hours so far have been spent waiting one one screen or another.  The issues seem to only affect the NA server as I can log in and play on the EU server without any trouble at all. Unfortunatly only the ESO Plus applies to both servers. Character bank and any other DLC isn't shared between the two mega servers. One thing that I have noticed is that the EU server doesn't seem to have many players (maybe that's why there are no server issues?).
I wish I had read more reviews before I invested in a 6 month Plus membership. The server issues make this more of an exercise in frustration waiting to play what is in fact a pretty good game.
Edit: From the time I first posted this review to now there has been dramatic improvements in server connectability - so much so that my Euro server character has been stuck at level 24 only having finished the main quest line. I have put over 80 hours into this game in order to 100% eveything in-game and complete all Steam Achievements. There are a lot of things that I genuinely love about this game, but man there are some things that just aren't great. I know I'm reviewing a game thats over a year old, but if you're thinking about buying, I have some thoughts.
I think this game does a fantastic job on expanding some of the things that were so wonderful about JC2. I spent countless hours in JC2 using the parachute and reining terror on the towns and settlements below. The parachute in that game is one of my all time favorite modes of transportation in any open-world game. The parachute in this game is... lackluster, but I soon realized that's because the new appeal of this game is the wingsuit. Like the parachute of JC2, the wingsuit in this game took a few hours of gameplay for me to finally 'get', but once I did, I didn't want to look back. I adore the wingsuit in this game, especially once I unlocked the 'Bavarium Wingsuit' of the Sky Fortress expansion (I bought the game + all DLC during previous winter sale). You're probably going to spend a lot of time using the wingsuit if you put any time into this game, so I think it's worth talking about. The real game-changer here for me was using the Steam Controller. Having gyro assisted aiming and camera movements, plus the back pedal buttons mapped the way I wanted made the whole experience really unique. I pretty much tailored it specifically for flying with the wingsuit, and I wouldn't trade that experience for a keyboard/mouse or any other gamepad out there. If you've got a Steam Controller, I highly recommend it for this game.
The story is laughable, and that's not really a bad thing. I found myself skipping every cutscene because I just didn't care, and that's totally fine. It really didn't diminish my enjoying of the game at all. Like the games before it, JC3 draws on bad B-tier action movies for its plot and dialogue. If its your cup of tea than great, but I was more interested in skipping the cutscenes so I could continue to play the game.
The destruction is really great in this game, and they've made the grappling hook SO much more functional than before. Having multiple tethers and being able to upgrade their strength really made for some fun moments. It also helps greatly in the destruction of bases and settlements. It added a lot of variety to my gameplay which is great, because you get tired of liberating the same settlements really quickly. That's one major complaint I have about this game: liberating settlements can be fun, but after a while it really felt like a chore. Just nailing one after the other became a little too easy.  And that's pretty much the meat of the game. Everything you do depends on how much chaos you cause, by liberating settlements.
The DLC expansions are all a bit silly, a don't provide too much in story content, but they do give you some fun new tools to play with: The fully upgraded Bavarium Wingsuit is by far my favorite, literally making me feel like Iron Man while I play, which is going to keep me coming back to this game for years. The Mechs are ♥♥♥♥ing rad, I really love driving them, but that whole dlc felt like the biggest chore to get through. Same with the Sea vehicle expansion. The Lochadore is fantastic, but the story and missions are boring. None of it feels super essential except for maybe the sky fortress expansion, the rocket wingsuit probably should have just been in the game to begin with. Hell, all of it could have been in the game to begin with.
My #1 gripe with this game: DRIVING. Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ in my opinion, they really ♥♥♥♥ed up the whole driving part of this game. Getting into any random vehicle and trying to drive it usually made me very angry very quickly. The handling of vehicles is almost non-existent. There are a few vehicles in the game that drive like the vehicles in JC2, or other open-world games like GTA, but it takes a while to find them. Nothing feels as responsive as it should, the motor cycles are absolute garbage, I don't think there is a single motor-cycle that is actually drivable (good ♥♥♥♥ing luck on the challenges that force you to use them). The planes are alright, though really feel unchanged from JC2, and the sea vehicles I'd say are actually an improvement on past games, where there is actually a reason to use them sometimes. But the land-vehicles... man I cannot tell you how much getting into cars and cycles really impacted my enjoyment of the game. Its not so bad during general gameplay, but it really shines during the land-vehicle challenges when you need them to be fast and handle excellently. I probably spent hours on whole challenges with cars and motor-cycles.
My second biggest gripe is the optimization of the game. Its not great. It's not horrible per say, but I've seen way better. Options are basically non-existent. It takes a lot of user leg-work upfront to really get the game going and playing well, especially if you've got older specs. I'm running fairly decent hardware (GTX 1060 6gb mem) and 8 gb RAM, on a 1TB Samsung SSD with an i5 Skylake processor. Nothing top of the line but just decent enough. Making the game run at a smooth frame-rate all the time took a few hours of researching USER-GUIDES to make it work. What the hell? That's not ok! I should be able to play the game 'out of the box'. I shouldn't have to put in as much time into making the game run well or at all. The simple fact is the devs really didn't care as much about the PC release, as usual with these giant games that are made primarily for the console crowd. Nothing wrong with consoles, but for those of us on PC, we are all pretty used to this treatment. Not being able to change the FOV was a really noticeable problem, and after googling, I discovered everyone is upset about this. I even was tempted to try modding the game to fix it, but didn't because even the available mod didn't run the way I would have wanted (it was just for moving the camera to take decent screenshots.)
*sigh*
FINAL VERDICT: I think if you loved JC2 like I did, you will find tons to love in this game as well. I can say that I'm glad I didn't pay full price for this game. I think if I had I would have been a bit dissapointed. So if you can wait till it's on sale, I highly recommend it. It's not perfect, nothing really is. The wingsuit and grappling hook are top-notch, but the driving will make you miss GTA a lot. Despite all the flaws, I really enjoyed playing this game. I want it to be better, though I know this far after release that's not going to happen. IT SHOULD! But it won't. If you've got the patience and the know-how to make it work for you, then I think you will find there is a really enjoyable open-world action game full of silly and epic moments alike.

I previously played and loved Just Cause 2, despite some things that irritated me about it. I was hoping that Just Cause 3 wuld improve on those and at least for the most part, it has.
JC 3 has the same ridiculous physics as JC 2 and adds the wingsuit. The wingsuit is fast and quite tricky to get used to but once you are used to it, its a fantastic and fun way to get around. The tethering system is back and the number of tethers and their strength improves further in the game.
The challenges are back too (such as time trials) and are as fun as they were last time. Unlike last time, completing challenges also unlock upgrades to things such as vehicle boosts, the wingsuit and the tethers, giving an added incentive to play them.
For me one of the most irritating partsd of JC 2 was spending ages trying to find the last item I needed to destroy to liberate a settlement. This time around you can just switch to map view and it will show you.
But JC 3 isn't perfect. The vehicle handling is easily among the worst that I have ever come across in a game- it's unrealistic but also not always easy, a terrible combination, I think. The voice acting isn't great, the story itself isn't great and the missions aren't great either- there are too many similar missions. Even liberating settlments, which is one of my favourite bits, gets quite repetitive after a while.
But JC 3 makes up for its flaws with a massive and beatiful open world and the ability to destroy massive structures using imagination and tethers. It won't win prizes for replayablilty or its innovative story, but its a blast to play and will take a good chunk of your time.

Alien: Isolation is an action-adventure game developed by Creative Assembly and based on the Alien film series with a strong emphasis on stealth and survival horror elements.
The story in Alien: Isolation is set 15 years after the events of Ridley Scott's 1979 Alien film and follows Amanda Ripley, daughter of Alien protagonist, Ellen Ripley, and her efforts to investigate the disappearance of her mother. In due course, Amanda learns of a discovered flight recorder of the Nostromo stored on board of a space station, Sevastopol, and, with a small team, journeys there to recover the missing recorder. Not long after she sets foot on the station, things do go horribly wrong, as you might expect, and is forced to survive through various situations. At large, the plot takes some inspiration from the Alien film, which is a must-watch before playing this game, but a lot of the backstory, behind the station and its habitants, is filled in by tape recorders or diary logs stored on computers which can be accessed by the player at their leisure.
In terms of gameplay, the player must explore the space station and complete numerous objectives while evading, outsmarting or overcoming adversaries like human occupants or hostile androids. You can hide into lockers, behind boxes or under desks and even equip various weapons (revolver, shotgun, flamethrower, Molotov cocktails, etc.) or tools for self-defence, although the best and most useful item which you will be using throughout the majority of the game is the motion tracker, which not only helps keep track of nearby enemies (only when moving), but it is also a useful tool for guiding you to your objectives. On the other hand, when you are pitted against the Alien, about 6 hours into the game, all alone in the dark, it turns into a big game of cat and mouse. Unless you have sufficient fuel for the flamethrower or a handful of Molotov cocktails, all your other weapons are rendered useless against the Alien. While you cannot kill it, you can certainly make it temporarily run away from you if you expose it to fire, giving you a gap to resume your journey towards the objective. Early on in the game, these moments with the Alien can cause heart palpitations.
One praiseworthy addition to the gameplay in Alien: Isolation is the simple crafting system which allows the player to collect scraps, components or schematics scattered around the environments and turning them into (upgradable) items which can range from medical kits, distraction devices or weapons such as bombs. With the fear of always running low on health or ammunition, this encourages exploration and ultimately avoids creating a strictly linear experience.
The level design is satisfactory and packed with nice visual touches that stay true to the Alien films. Some levels, or sections for that matter, are fairly big in size and can occupy up to four floors, while others can be very small with relatively tight corridors.  Usually, each section is composed of a set of rooms and corridors separated by doors. Some doors require certain tools, obtainable by the player as they progress into the game, before granting access. When it comes to accessing or hacking computer terminals, sometimes the player has to solve easy minigames to proceed. Furthermore, the inclusion of accessible ventilation systems allows for shortcuts to be taken which can also provide good sneaking spots to briefly hide, escape from a chase or access a restricted area. Admittedly, certain level assets do seem to be reused from time to time, causing a loss in level design uniqueness.
Visually, not only it remains faithful to the aesthetics of the original film, Alien: Isolation is absolutely a beauty to look at. It vaunts some of the best lighting, particle and smoke effects I have seen in a video game to date; possibly since the Metro series or any recent game on the CryEngine. Some of the most unforgettable backdrops will no doubt be outside the space station while wearing a spacesuit, especially in the second half of the game. On top of that, Creative Assembly has managed to pull off a fantastically optimised port on PC where you can crank up lots of videos settings to maximum even on medium-ranged PCs while still maintaining a high and stable framerate performance.
For such a type of game, the sound design plays a key role in the immersion and credibility of the atmosphere and is safe to say that is it unquestionably phenomenal, especially if you own high fidelity headsets. Certain sound queues play out during specific moments which give the player an indication of what is about to happen. Moreover, the soundtrack has a very distinct Alien-like vibe to it which is more than enough to please any person well accustomed to the Alien franchise.
However, Alien: Isolation is plagued with evident flaws as you progress through its overly long +20-hour story. In actual fact, that is one of its main problems as result of inconsistent pacing and lots of avoidable padding. It gets to a point, later on in the game, where you begin rolling your eyes every single time you complete something like a story arc while thinking you are near the end of your journey, but the game keeps throwing you new information right near the end and thus forces you to investigate new locations to see what is happening over there. Likewise, this does not help in creating a consistent scary and tense atmosphere in the long term as it gets same-y halfway through the game. Rinse and repeat.
Another notable issue is the backtracking as you will be revisiting the same locations at times, even when you have to travel to a totally new location in the space station. Even in the context of completing objectives, the game forces you to travel back and forth within a section quite a lot, which can be dull every now and then.
Admittedly, the saving system in this game has an interesting twist to it. To save your progress, the player needs to trace a specific terminal and manually insert an access card in it. There is no such thing such as quick-saves, conventionally saving from the menu or reaching checkpoints (except in three or so instances – which in their respective context make sense). Consequently, even at normal difficulty, this can lead to many downright frustrating moments where you either get caught by the Alien in a one-shot kill or taken down by androids (which are more of a nuisance than scary) and have to start a huge chunk of the section all over again. Some terminals are located way too far. It would have also been nice being able to actually outrun the Alien without being caught, but realistically, the Alien would be the fastest here.
The trial-and-error nature of the gameplay will most likely rub some people up the wrong the way, especially those not looking for a challenge. Connoisseurs of the stealth genre should, technically, feel right at home in Alien: Isolation, although even for them it might feel a bit unfair and irritating due to the very smart AI. There is no denying that there is a lot of trial-and-error in this game, even for my own tastes.
In conclusion, despite some very glaring issues, Alien: Isolation is by far the best Alien game to date for anyone craving for that true Alien experience of the original film, but it is also far from the scariest game out there, as it sadly loses some of its scary charm in the long run. It does, however, require a specific type of player to fully enjoy the entire experience; someone who is a fan of the franchise, in addition to being patient and methodical. At the end of the day, what Alien: Isolation accomplishes is in creating a strong concept and solid foundation for a sequel which at the very least should easily outshine its predecessor. Ironing out all the aforementioned issues will indisputably make it not only the ultimate Alien experience, more so than Alien: Isolation, but also one of the most frightening games out there.

Alien: Isolation is challenging, thrilling, and totally immersive. The Alien universe, in all of its clunky, 1979 glory, is fully realized here. The aesthetic and graphics reflect painstaking detail and immense dedication put forth by Creative Assembly. Many of the game's sounds are pulled directly from the original film, and the others are so thoughtfully inspired by it so as to make it difficult to tell they do not originate from it. This is to make little mention of the outstanding sound design and implementation -- both of which do their job of filling the player with dread and fear admirably -- nor the soundtrack which both takes nostalgic cues from Jerry Goldsmith's original and forms its own memorable well of frightening music. Isolation, from beginning to end, is a game made for and by Alien fans, and it, to incredible effect, transports you to that grounded vision of the future originally put forth by Alien where things cannot help but go terribly wrong.
The gameplay is solid, with responsive and simple movement mechanics coupled very well with and intuitive crafting system and a large arsenal of improvised weapons and tools. The craftable items feel like the natural next step in the horror game genre. They add an additional layer of gameplay that, in any given situation, has the potential to be immensely rewarding or go horribly wrong. This kind of tension is what makes the horror genre tick, and it results in countless terrifying situations throughout your trek through Sevastapol, the game's principle location. Pressing through the endless space station, you will be treated to surprising vistas and remarkably realized locations. It all feels lived-in and used, and when you run into the station's desperate and paranoid human inhabitants, its ghostly android attendants, or its terrifying unwelcome guest, the environment often becomes your biggest ally.
The story of Alien: Isolation is well told. It is neither too simple nor overly convoluted. Its characters are interesting and its mysteries exciting. Isolation's protagonist, Amanda Ripley (who boasts an outstanding voice performance by Andrea Deck) is easy to become invested in and a character whose hopes you want to see realized nearly as badly as she does. She is effectively used to reflect the player's feelings and elaborate upon objectives. Fortunately, despite her being well written and brilliantly voiced, she is scarcely given dialogue outside of cutscenes or the occasional hub or character-heavy encounter, and as such never becomes an annoyance. The supporting cast is also largely well acted and contains one familiar in William Hope, who played Lt. Gorman in Aliens.
The star of Isolation, of course, is the titular beast itself. The Alien is a monstrous thing, its nightmarish qualities brought to life through a terrifying level of interactivity. Its AI has received countless accolades by now, and rightfully so. The Alien hunts aggressively, lurks patiently, and stalks relentlessly. When you hear that furious, inhuman scream at the end of a dark corridor and you realize your mistake, there is often little you can do but scramble desperately to get away before coming face to face with the perfect organism. Isolation and its Alien have come under fire in the past for being too difficult or unfair, but, over the course of one hard playthrough, not one death felt undeserved and neither did any situation seem unwinnable.
Alien: Isolation is difficult, unforgiving, and terrifying, and in this way it evokes the original film better than anything else since. However, it is also extremely rewarding; the succesful completion of each trial providing a sense of achievement seldom felt in gaming. When the astoundingly crafted and utterly harrowing journey finally comes to a close, it is hard not to feel accomplished.

Id like to preface this review by saying I maybe a tad bit bias in this as I absolutely love Clannad, I have the Manga, the Blurays, the 10th anniversary art book and even a boxed copy of this VN, so yeah just keep that in mind while reading this ;)
Now, I have been waiting for a long time to get an official English release of this VN and my patience has finally been rewarded, though Clannad has a high price tag I hope in the following words I can convince you that it is worth every cent, for Clannad is much more than a simple story you grow attached to every character, and with the huge amount of choices there is so much replayability; anyway lets get started shall we.......
In my humble opinion Clannad is the best representation of life, friendships, love and loss. It shows purpose, fulfillment and satisfaction can be attained and at the same time it teaches people that the most unexpected things can sometimes come from the most unexpected person. It will show just how far an ordinary man will go just to help his friends and family.
Clannad has many different arcs that are just as good as the last, the choices you make throughout Clannad can alter your entire experience, it has a beautiful story and many touching moments, those who are looking for drama, romance and slice of life genre look no further for Clannad is exactly what you are looking for.
What truly sets Clannad apart from other visual novels is its clear representation of emotions. I would highly recommend this VN to anyone, it is well worth the money and has a very enjoyable story, it has excellently designed characters which are so incredibly believable; specifically with their personalities, as you keep reading the VN you will notice changes with each character, and you will come to love each and every one of them.
Overall to be honest this VN is a must own, I believe that most people will be able to relate greatly with Clannad.
I hope that this review has helped you in your decision in getting this VN and I hope you will enjoy the whole experience as much as I have; there is also a second VN that you should check out if you enjoy this one that being
I have also done a review on it if you wish to read my thoughts on it.
I will finish by saying; Clannd is not only my favorite thing on steam but the anime adaptation is my favorite anime of all time, if you are so inclined I'd recommend you go check that out too; happy reading :3
p.s. Im very passionate about Clannad and thats the reason I have so many hours.
(Like all my reviews I do not put a score as it is my belief that games like all forms of art are subjective and therefore it is impossible to afix a number to them)

CLANNAD
, and finally is available in Steam. While the translation from Sekai Project is far from perfect, it is more polished than the fan translation that is available on Internet*. And Sekai Project really made an effort to make this the best CLANNAD release ever, including extras not available in the original PC release like voices, HD asserts, Dangopedia and Archivements.
*: Sekai Project seems to have fixed most translation problems in the original release. I didn't personally replayed this game yet (again), so I can't say for sure, however it seems that Sekai Project really wants to make the best release of Clannad ever.
Is it worth the $50? Yeah, it is a step price for a visual novel. However, visual novel are more like books than games, and the word count number for CLANNAD script
. So I think it is a good price, considering the effort to translate everything. Just FYI, this is my second playthrough of this VN (the first one was using the fan translation). I finished all routes and did all archivements, using a walkthrough so I wouldn't waste too much time going nowhere in the story, and my reading speed is pretty average. So around 100 hours is a good average of time that you will spend reading through everything.
And like lots of reviews already said, yeah, you're going to cry. However, not only about the sad things, but from small piece of happiness that occurs in the progress of the story. This is a VN for everyone, it does not matter if you're a man or women, child or adult. This is my second time playing it (the first one was the fan translation 3 years ago) and I still cried for different reasons.
If you never heard of CLANNAD before, just play it. Don't bother watching the anime or reading the manga adaptations first. It is not that they're not good, the anime at least is very good (I never read the manga), however it does miss some of the small details that makes this work awesome. I do recommend you to watch the anime from Kyoto Animation (forget about the movie, it is bad, really bad) after playing the VN though, since there is some scenes that simple are better animated.

7.5/10 A game with a lot of potential.
If you're looking for a game you can play casually (at least I do), then this is a nice option! Perhaps not as stable (yet), complex, or vast as other mmos (looking at you WoW).
However, it is complex enough to have you travel back to the same maps to look for treasures, hunt items, or even hunt monsters. It's class diversity is vast enough to still have me unsure about other people's capabilities, strengths, and weaknesses.
I have 70 hours put into the game with a main of level 84 (Wiz 3, elementalist 1). I've done my best to minimize afk time for an accurate gauge of "time playing." It's very easy to stay a little too long in town digesting what the market has to offer...
Personally, the "grind" has been easy, AT LEAST SO FAR (I hear it picks up). Quest exp. will have you above the recommended level for your map, but not by much.  Recently monsters are doing enough damage for me to die! Phew! Thought it was going to be a cake walk! I shall consider partying more or perhaps even plate gear, Haha! (On a mage!? Complexity!),
The element system could be a little more visually clear about when you do advantageous or disadvantageous damage; maybe point out the enemy element to you somehow.
Skills are very interactive, you can easily mess them up or miss. "Smoothness" was a huge issue in this game's spiritual predecessor, Ragnarok Online, specifically in the form of "cell glitches," and I am glad to see this game is much smoother. (They still use a grid system though!)
They are constantly improving, soon coming out with guild vs. guild, bot reporting features, and revisions to the economy / trading systems. The game is pretty good for what it is(7.5). It has a lot it could improve on, but remains charming in it's current state. Very easy to relax and escape for a bit, beautiful soundtrack, and fun. The uncertainties are a part of the game / adventure.

(This is an Early Access review and as such is prone to changes in accuracy. This review was made on the 8th of the 4th, 2016.)
Factories, industry, manufacturing; steel and iron stacks pouring the smoke of industry from the fires of progress. This is a sight a player will come to recognize and love in Factorio. And Factorio is, exactly as the name suggests, a game about factories. Actually no, it's a bit more complicated then that, but at the core of it Factorio will have players developing and constructing automated assembly lines, foundries, smelters, and mining rigs for the efficient exploitation of an alien world.
You start off as the lone survivour on an uninhabited alien planet with nothing more than an engineering rig, a weapon, and some designs for construction of basic machines. This is the same basic concept as Minecraft, Subnautica, Rust, and half a million other games. Where Factoria differs is with it's main concept adn gimmick: You can automate EVERYTHING.
No, seriously, everything. Make it so that you have conveyor belts, smelters, and arms taking fuel and materials from damn near every source, put through machines, creating components, and reassembiling it as complicated machinery for other devices to use. The amount of possible automation is obscene, and has resulted in a convulouted mess of conveyor belts, mechanical arms, and smelters to create three different devices requiring no less than twelve components to make. Decives which were then carted off to another factory to be assembled into a singular device which was then taken to a single building to be used for research, all requiring no imput from me. Simply push a button, and everything was taken care of.
Factorio is a 2d isometric top down viewed game with simple 3d vectored graphics. The game is played with WASD keys and a mouse, and has tight, responsive controls. Vehicles can be built, but the driving controls are more problemactic as Factorio's world is not well suited to driving as convoluted and tight areas are extremely common and driving long distances can be very hazardous due to cluttered facories, refineries, trees, and rocks. This is not to say that the driving controls are bad, just that Factorio is not well suited to cars.
Another aspect of the game is tower defense, because what open world crafting game isn't complete without defense. At seemingly random intervals swarms of small biting aliens about the size of a dog will attack you and your factory, favouring your more comlicated and advanced machines as targets over low tech designs. Again, automation is possible and building turrents with autoloaders that recive munitions straight from the factory is possible. Of course, attacking Alien nests in an attempt to stop the oncoming swarms requries a more personal touch, but with work power armor, exoskeletons, tanks, and even combat robots are all possible to build. Unfortunately, human input is still required, and robots are not capable in independent action beyond following the player.
As the game is still in Early Access the game has flaws. First and formoest is the UI. Although the UI is quite easy to use with practice, the Ui is lacking in areas which makes conveying information difficult although this will most like be corrected with time.
Despite being Early Access Factorio is also very stable. Amazingly, Factorio is more stable than some AAA games, as I have not once encountered a bug, crash, or loss of data.
Like many games, the true joy of this game is setting up an amazing network and construction of devices and then watching it all work smoothly. Unfortunately, mass automation can take things away, and after a while the player just runs out of things to do once the end goal is reached. There is nothing more to this game than construction and factories, and the game can quickly run dry as a result.

Transistor is a beautiful piece of art, worthy of sitting next to the narrative masterpiece that was Bastion, Supergiant Games previous title. I wholly recommend the game to anybody that stumbles across it.
The gameplay is smooth, and combat picks up where Bastion was lacking. Customization of your ability loadout, passives, and upgrades is wholesome and fairly deep. While the game has no difficulty settings, it does have a set of 'Limiters' to amp up the difficulty by warping some of the core gameplay mechanics, making it increasingly difficult to survive and move through the story with each one activated.
Darren Korb once again provides a masterful score of music, along with Ashley Barrett representing the protagonist, Red, in the vocals. While the total score is a masterpiece, listening to it pre-emptively can and will spoil much of the symbolism and plot of the game, so I don't recommend it. However, the game itself is worth playing just for the music.
The art style is gorgeous, and is one of the game's defining features. Coupled with the narration which one of the main characters does throughout the entire storyline, voiced by Logan Cunningham - the same narrator from Bastion! - the game never feels empty or alone. With a silent protagonist, and one who won't shut up and describes everything that happens in Mr. Cunningham's beautiful and skilled voice, you learn to fall in love with the characters.
Overall, I one-hundred-percent recommend Transistor to any and all. It's a 10/10, and the only flaw is that it's short, and ends abruptly - despite this, the plot fits perfectly to end here, and it creates a more artistic, and complete piece with the ending.

From the get-go, Transistor thrusts you into a world of mystery and artistic brillance with a technological city back-drop. The game itself is similar to that of its older sibling "Bastion" but with added Turn-based RPG elements which are nice gives a breath of customization to your moves and abilites. Where Transistor really shines is its story which, while confusing at first, is worth the effort of discovering through listening to dialog and reading through decrypted data. Transistor is overall a very solid game much like its sibling while making a few changes to make the game feel resfreshing and worth playing again in the harder difficulties, and is one of the few game I bought as soon as it was released.
Oh, and did I mention the music is fantastic? The music is fantastic.
Fantastic - SuperGiant has done it again (and I've gone and bought the soundtrack, again).

Call of Juarez Gunslinger is refreshing admist all the modern military shooters, it's got a arcadey style, mixed with RPG elements (Sharpshooter, Close-range and Gunslinger, focusing on revolvers) it has a hollywood wild-west vibe to it with action set-pieces that are not overly convuluted like "Call of Duty".
It also features a regenerating health system that while may be seen as too forgiving at first, (regenerating health as a rapid pace) you'll find out soon enough that enemy's can kill you just as fast (I've only played on hard mode, which is what I recomend) which in practice makes the gameplay fast-paced, no need to having to hide behind a rock for half a minuite, keeping you admist a raging gun fight.
As a quick side note: The gun sounds for this game are brilliant, very hollywood-esque.
With the fast-paced action and along with more challenging enemy variant's later in the game, the game demands that you build up you skill and reflex's for both score and survival, getting headshots, that said, you do have to take cover in the game as again you can be killed quickly, thrown dynamite is a tactic that will be used against you to try and flush you from cover as to keep you on your toes but you can shoot them down (preferably while they are still out of the blast radius)
Finally the one big flaw to this game (which is sad to say) is the dueling, dueling occours when it's just you and a "boss" character, it's mini-game more or less but I found it fustration because the whole premise is basicly you vs the control's, you constalty try to percisely adjust two value's: "Focus" and "Speed", Focus is represented by a contant wavering reticle (your aim) that you battle to keep on your target (with the least ammount of adjustment in the right area) and Speed is represented by your hand above the revolver (the delay to draw your gun), you have to position the hand left/right, getting the palm right above the gun's handle, as with the reticule, it's constantly moving and adjustment slows the process down, you only get a limited amount of time to get as much speed and focus as you can before the target draws.
Your hand, the reticule and your speed/focus statistics are the only visual aid's you get, you have to feel for the sweet spot and try to keep it at that point as best you can but don't forget about your opponent alltogether, you let a moment to breathe, you won't get the chance and die instantly, I personally feel that it's more fustrating then fun and ended up killing dishonourably (drawing before your target does).
Personally though this flaw is no where near game ruining and they are far long between, which is good.
In summary: Buy it if you like westen's like Red Dead Redemption or if not, it makes a refreshing break from shooting communist soldiers or aliens.

Don't let the expensive price haunt you. Though $50 is a lot of money for game, much less a visual novel, it is definitely worth it. Clannad is one of the greatest visual novels of all time. If it helps you, go see the anime if will help make up your mind wether this is worth the buy (anime only covers one route).
Plot - 5/5 The plot can be slow as sometimes one single day in the visual novel can take half an hour or more to finish. But it is worth it, as it has an amazing plot. Especially After Story. Anyways, the visual novel has many routes, and if you've watched the anime, basically every girl has a route of her own. There are also some other routes other than the waifu routes. There is also unlocking After Story, which takes a lot of time. So this visual novel isn't a quick 3-10 hours - it will probably take over 100 if you want to finish all routes and clear the game. You will also get many choices throughout, not leaving you to just watch without actually doing anything. Many choices are important, and can sometimes lock you into certain routes.
Art - 4/5 Some may not like Clannad's unique artstyle. At first I was unsure but quickly got used to the interesting artsyle. Sekai Project also did a great job of improving the quality of the overall game. Backgrounds are great, as they actually include people in them and there is some variety to some backgrounds. (e.g classroom has a few backgrounds depending on the time of day)
Sound - 5/5 The soundtrack for Clannad is amazing. Each song can easily fit the mood and current scenario. It is also a pleasure to listen to. It was also a nice bonus for Sekai Project to get the original voice actors from the anime (excluding Tomoya).
Characters - 4/5 Each character gets their own moment to shine. Almost all characters have a route, and each character has a unique personality. Most are very likeable as well.
Overall - 5/5
Get this game if you are a fan of Clannad, or if you want a nice visual novel to play. Highly recommend. If you are not able to get it at the price it is at, it is definitley worth getting the game on sale.

As a fan on anime, manga, light novels, and visual novels, I'm well versed in many forms of these Japanese mediums.  But playing through Clannad will always be one of my most precious memories.  With an incredibly well-balanced plethora of genres, this VN has something for everyone.  Comedy, tragedy, mystery, romance, action, drama, etc..  On top of that, the visuals are stunningly beautiful, and the voice actors and actresses did a fantastic job.  The storylines are amazingly deep and interesting, and you can't help but fall in love with all of the characters.  And you can never go wrong with Jun Maeda being in charge of the musical direction.  The only bad thing I can say about it is that there are a few minor spelling and grammar mistakes.  Other than that, it is a flawless work of art.
Key Studios is famous for their visual novels, and by playing through Clannad, you will understand why.  Whether you've played hundreds of VNs or you haven't played a single one, I highly recommend Clannad to anyone and everyone.

I'm really enjoying this game. The characters are great, and their stories are emotionally heavy and beautifully told.
I don't have a lot of prior experience with visual novels, but this feels like more than just a Choose Your Own Adventure book. It feels like there's stuff going on in the background no matter which areas of the story I choose to explore for any given playthrough. For example, I'll play through one game, and catch a glimpse of something another character I'm not spending my time with is up to. Then I'll play through a second time, focus on that character, and get their backstory. Then I'll play through a third time, do stuff with another character, and see, yet again, another facet of that first character's story. It's really interesting.
A lot of people complain about the $50 price for a visual novel. I do expect that price will go down after a while and agree that it should, But for me, it was worth it to pay $50 to ensure this beautiful localization even exists (I got it through the kickstarter). If you're impatient to try it out and can afford it, just drop the full price. You won't regret it.

The mechanics of the game are simple and plain, however the entire package  is a cluster of emotions raging from unfathomable sadness and loss to genuine happiness. I would HIGHLY recommend following the Clannad walkthrough guide on the Kazamatsuri web site. Without it, you may be hard pressed in figuring out what it is you're supposed to do. This game is basically like reading a book with added audio and soundtrack. Also, you must complete the game numerous times (while altering your choices) in order to experience all the routes. The first route for me (baseball route) was nothing special imo but it works as a good introduction for all the characters in the game. The proceeding routes from there are impactful personal stories of each of the characters. It is also important to note that while the game is not exactly a fantasy genre, it does employ fantasy elements such as the orbs of light that you collect as well as the Illusionary World (all of which become relevant in After Story). After Story is considered to be the "main" story and is unlocked after collecting 8 light orbs obtained throughout different routes. (The skip diolouge function makes this much faster to get through).
I personally loved the story telling of the game and the emotional ride was unforgettable. If you don't mind reading, I would highly recommend this game.

An amazing, solid, and fun Early Access game that offers a lot of features with very little bugs or annoyances.
For an Early Access Title, Factorio may be one of the best. The developers have been working on this game for about 4 years now (as of 2016), and from what it looks like, will improve as time moves forward.
What Factorio is is a survival, strategy, RTS, puzzle game where you attempt to create a factory off the resources of the land while fending off the dangerous local alien life. It reminds me a bit like some Zachtronics games, but more accessable for a wide audience.
If you're into RTS, management, or even survival games, this game is worth a look. Heck, there's even a demo version that apparently runs you through the tutorial long enough for you to get a good idea of what the game is.
After the demo/tutorial there is more to explore, a survival mode, and more in game toys and techs to explore and play with.

Holy crackers! I'm having fun! Most of the other reviews have said a lot already so I'll try and list out what I like in particular.
Pros:
Addictive, but not in a bad way like an incremental game. I don't feel like I'm sitting here playing it due to some basic animal instinct where I like seeing numbers get bigger. I'm having a good time while doing it. There's always little things I can do to improve my factories. It's hooked me, and it's earned it.
Very well designed! Most things feel pretty intuitive and it seems like everything I've come across so far in the game has a reason for being there. The interface seems like it was designed to stay out of the player's way as much as possible. Little things like being able to upgrade storage areas/furnaces/etc. without having to remove the contents or implicitly crafting items required to build something saves a lot of unnecessary tedium.
Fairly easy to figure out. Once you figure out the basics you shouldn't be hitting that many roadblocks where you can't figure out what to do.
Figuring out a way to automate something that's been wasting you a lot of time is a pretty good feeling.
Cons:
Graphics are pretty ugly. They serve their purpose well enough and maybe the grittiness was intentional but even the entirely natural areas that I'd usually expect to be beautiful (like lakes and forests) seem pretty drab.
Seems like some campaigns are only available to a certain "tier" (furnace attendant). I'm assuming this is some Kickstarter stuff, along with having odd names for train stops/labs/etc. A very minor annoyance but I figured I'd mention it anyway.
Another minor annoyance is some of the writing in the game is in awkward English ( like "Press T to start a new research"). It's nothing a good proofread or two coudn't handle, though.
The music isn't all that great. It's there. It's just... not really what I was expecting. I figured it'd be something more hectic or mechanical but it's mostly just ominous strings. Definitely not worth eight dollars just to get it seperate.
The main campaign feels really short and a lot of unexplained stuff is thrown at you. Like I said earlier, it's fairly intuitive, but it would've been nice if stuff like trains or the oil industry was a little more gently introduced. I think at least half of the items in the game never make an appearance. They seem to have plans on adding more to the campaign though.
Quite a few of the upgrades are just faster/more efficient versions of previous items. I guess this is fine and it'd make sense that improved versions of already existing things would come out but it's all very boring.
--------------------
I've played it over 40 hours and I still don't feel like I've wasted my money. I think that's a good sign.

I have put over 80 hours into this game in order to 100% eveything in-game and complete all Steam Achievements. There are a lot of things that I genuinely love about this game, but man there are some things that just aren't great. I know I'm reviewing a game thats over a year old, but if you're thinking about buying, I have some thoughts.
I think this game does a fantastic job on expanding some of the things that were so wonderful about JC2. I spent countless hours in JC2 using the parachute and reining terror on the towns and settlements below. The parachute in that game is one of my all time favorite modes of transportation in any open-world game. The parachute in this game is... lackluster, but I soon realized that's because the new appeal of this game is the wingsuit. Like the parachute of JC2, the wingsuit in this game took a few hours of gameplay for me to finally 'get', but once I did, I didn't want to look back. I adore the wingsuit in this game, especially once I unlocked the 'Bavarium Wingsuit' of the Sky Fortress expansion (I bought the game + all DLC during previous winter sale). You're probably going to spend a lot of time using the wingsuit if you put any time into this game, so I think it's worth talking about. The real game-changer here for me was using the Steam Controller. Having gyro assisted aiming and camera movements, plus the back pedal buttons mapped the way I wanted made the whole experience really unique. I pretty much tailored it specifically for flying with the wingsuit, and I wouldn't trade that experience for a keyboard/mouse or any other gamepad out there. If you've got a Steam Controller, I highly recommend it for this game.
The story is laughable, and that's not really a bad thing. I found myself skipping every cutscene because I just didn't care, and that's totally fine. It really didn't diminish my enjoying of the game at all. Like the games before it, JC3 draws on bad B-tier action movies for its plot and dialogue. If its your cup of tea than great, but I was more interested in skipping the cutscenes so I could continue to play the game.
The destruction is really great in this game, and they've made the grappling hook SO much more functional than before. Having multiple tethers and being able to upgrade their strength really made for some fun moments. It also helps greatly in the destruction of bases and settlements. It added a lot of variety to my gameplay which is great, because you get tired of liberating the same settlements really quickly. That's one major complaint I have about this game: liberating settlements can be fun, but after a while it really felt like a chore. Just nailing one after the other became a little too easy.  And that's pretty much the meat of the game. Everything you do depends on how much chaos you cause, by liberating settlements.
The DLC expansions are all a bit silly, a don't provide too much in story content, but they do give you some fun new tools to play with: The fully upgraded Bavarium Wingsuit is by far my favorite, literally making me feel like Iron Man while I play, which is going to keep me coming back to this game for years. The Mechs are ♥♥♥♥ing rad, I really love driving them, but that whole dlc felt like the biggest chore to get through. Same with the Sea vehicle expansion. The Lochadore is fantastic, but the story and missions are boring. None of it feels super essential except for maybe the sky fortress expansion, the rocket wingsuit probably should have just been in the game to begin with. Hell, all of it could have been in the game to begin with.
My #1 gripe with this game: DRIVING. Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ in my opinion, they really ♥♥♥♥ed up the whole driving part of this game. Getting into any random vehicle and trying to drive it usually made me very angry very quickly. The handling of vehicles is almost non-existent. There are a few vehicles in the game that drive like the vehicles in JC2, or other open-world games like GTA, but it takes a while to find them. Nothing feels as responsive as it should, the motor cycles are absolute garbage, I don't think there is a single motor-cycle that is actually drivable (good ♥♥♥♥ing luck on the challenges that force you to use them). The planes are alright, though really feel unchanged from JC2, and the sea vehicles I'd say are actually an improvement on past games, where there is actually a reason to use them sometimes. But the land-vehicles... man I cannot tell you how much getting into cars and cycles really impacted my enjoyment of the game. Its not so bad during general gameplay, but it really shines during the land-vehicle challenges when you need them to be fast and handle excellently. I probably spent hours on whole challenges with cars and motor-cycles.
My second biggest gripe is the optimization of the game. Its not great. It's not horrible per say, but I've seen way better. Options are basically non-existent. It takes a lot of user leg-work upfront to really get the game going and playing well, especially if you've got older specs. I'm running fairly decent hardware (GTX 1060 6gb mem) and 8 gb RAM, on a 1TB Samsung SSD with an i5 Skylake processor. Nothing top of the line but just decent enough. Making the game run at a smooth frame-rate all the time took a few hours of researching USER-GUIDES to make it work. What the hell? That's not ok! I should be able to play the game 'out of the box'. I shouldn't have to put in as much time into making the game run well or at all. The simple fact is the devs really didn't care as much about the PC release, as usual with these giant games that are made primarily for the console crowd. Nothing wrong with consoles, but for those of us on PC, we are all pretty used to this treatment. Not being able to change the FOV was a really noticeable problem, and after googling, I discovered everyone is upset about this. I even was tempted to try modding the game to fix it, but didn't because even the available mod didn't run the way I would have wanted (it was just for moving the camera to take decent screenshots.)
*sigh*
FINAL VERDICT: I think if you loved JC2 like I did, you will find tons to love in this game as well. I can say that I'm glad I didn't pay full price for this game. I think if I had I would have been a bit dissapointed. So if you can wait till it's on sale, I highly recommend it. It's not perfect, nothing really is. The wingsuit and grappling hook are top-notch, but the driving will make you miss GTA a lot. Despite all the flaws, I really enjoyed playing this game. I want it to be better, though I know this far after release that's not going to happen. IT SHOULD! But it won't. If you've got the patience and the know-how to make it work for you, then I think you will find there is a really enjoyable open-world action game full of silly and epic moments alike.

I previously played and loved Just Cause 2, despite some things that irritated me about it. I was hoping that Just Cause 3 wuld improve on those and at least for the most part, it has.
JC 3 has the same ridiculous physics as JC 2 and adds the wingsuit. The wingsuit is fast and quite tricky to get used to but once you are used to it, its a fantastic and fun way to get around. The tethering system is back and the number of tethers and their strength improves further in the game.
The challenges are back too (such as time trials) and are as fun as they were last time. Unlike last time, completing challenges also unlock upgrades to things such as vehicle boosts, the wingsuit and the tethers, giving an added incentive to play them.
For me one of the most irritating partsd of JC 2 was spending ages trying to find the last item I needed to destroy to liberate a settlement. This time around you can just switch to map view and it will show you.
But JC 3 isn't perfect. The vehicle handling is easily among the worst that I have ever come across in a game- it's unrealistic but also not always easy, a terrible combination, I think. The voice acting isn't great, the story itself isn't great and the missions aren't great either- there are too many similar missions. Even liberating settlments, which is one of my favourite bits, gets quite repetitive after a while.
But JC 3 makes up for its flaws with a massive and beatiful open world and the ability to destroy massive structures using imagination and tethers. It won't win prizes for replayablilty or its innovative story, but its a blast to play and will take a good chunk of your time.

Short review:
It's a good horror game and video game in general. It is different the way it inspires fear in you.  A truly intense experience. Recommended 8/10
Personal Experience:
I am given a simple task to go find a keycard in San Cristobal Medical Bay.  Seems simple enough, but while in the medical bay sirens start going off. A voice on the P.A. system says "Medical Quarantine in effect, unidentified biological material in medical bay.  I exit the office I'm in and start running down the hallway when the vent cover on the ceiling pops right off. Fog starts to hiss from the vent as I quickly hide under a hospital bed with a mutilated corpse on it.  Then out in all of it's glory, sinks down, the Alien.  I can see the individual muscles and its vicious clawed hands on the floor. It screechs and clicks, while I am in the mean time literally shaking with fear.  It doesn't notice me and starts to slowly walk down the corridor.  Each footstep making a loud thumping noise. Proceed to find an escape from the medical ward, and an escape from the monster.  That level was the most intense and scary experience I have ever had.  It truly does a great job of giving you a real sense of survival out of fear.
Long Review:
I am not a fan of horror games at all.  But this game is easily one of my favorite singleplayer experiences I have ever played.  I will admit that halfway through the game it begins to lose appeal.  But with that said, the first 10 hours may be the most intense singleplayer experience in a video game you'll ever have.  The Alien is absoultely terrifying and intense, and the fact that 90% of its actions are non-scripted makes it even more frightening.  Although there are a substantial amount of glitches, the game has been refined since it was released.  I recommend this game even if you are not a fan of horror games. This is a game that you do not want to miss out on. Also if you are craving for a nostalgic trip to something like the very first Alien movie this is it.  The atmosphere and enviroments just captures the 1978 Ridley Scott world of Alien.  Alien Isolation does have excellent world building, to the level of Dishonored in my opinion. The clunky space aesthetic mixed with retro DOS technology makes for a very immersive world.  The graphics are very impressive if you are running on ultra settings.  4K Alien Isolation is one of the best graphical games I've played on PC.  Textures can sometimes be a little muddy even on Ultra settings.  8/10

OK, let me start off by saying this to anyone who is reading....  First off, THIS GAME IS NOT FOR EVERYONE.  This is one of those MMOs that is enjoy a type niche like grindfests, loot centric or w/e the case.  That being said, here we go:
This is by far the closest you can get to a good successor of Ragnarok Online.  Being as I come from the usual KR grindfest games, this is definitely up my alley when it comes to sitting down and enjoying the feel of the game.  It has various classes to choose from and you are placed into a usual META if you don't want to.  This game is very open on ideas people can come up with while still holding a foundation for what it really is.  Music, Visuals and story are all very good.  It has a lot of variety and I must give credit where it is due.  My only opinion is saying this to new players who are jumping in, be ready for a traditional MMO sense from 'the day' that everyone reminisces about.
That being off my chest, for all others who are used to being given it all and don't have much attention span.  This is a game that requires you to get a reward for what you put in.  Sometimes its fast, others it is slow.  If you are from WoW or other MMOs nowadays which cater to handing out things, this game won't necessarily do that for you.  You got to earn it and it makes the game that much more valuable for it since you treasure the character more.

A glance at Papers, Please might cause someone to think "Why would anyone want to play a game about checking for errors in documentation? That sounds like a job." But if there's anything that we can learn from simulation games is that they don't have to be fun to draw you in, because once you find that each document is a window into a person's private life, and that you are reluctantly given the tough decision "Should I let this person into my country?", you find that there is a dangerously comfortable flow.
This game confronts you with sequences of people who provide you documentation for immigrating to the ficticious country Arstotzka (based on the Soviet Union). You must carefully search their documents for errors and make sure that everything is in order before letting them in. But the genius behind this game soon becomes apparent. You have limited time, and the more people you let into the country before the end of the day, the more money you get. What do you need money for? Well, you have a large nuclear family who all rely on your income to take care of heating, food, medicine, and you will never be able to afford all of these things.
But you can't just let in everyone, because every time you permit a person with incorrect documentation to enter, you receive a citation, and eventually get docked pay. This creates a wonderful tension between wanting money and not loosing your job. And checking documents isn't easy, it's often tedius to compare spelling of names, or social security numbers, or expiration dates, or remembering what type of identification each person should be having, so making mistakes is a matter of a keen eye and a good memory for rules.
To make it even harder, you only have a third of the screen to place documents, so you can never see all of them at a time. But that wouldn't be stressful enough, because each person often has a story and in such a dystopian world, you find people who empathize with, but have bad documents, or people who are evil but have everythign in order. And the game will often send you reminders of decisions you made that ruined someone's life, or sometimes saved it.
And on top of all of this there is a plot about a group of revolutionaries who try to recruit you to their cause. And with the horrible bureaucracy you see around you, the revolutionaries have a good point, but you must decide whether to risk helping them, or to play it safe with a government that will hopefully leave you and your family alone.
What all this adds up to is a game that causes you to have to make the decisions that people in stressful bureaucratic jobs must make. In a way it forces you to begin to think more openly about why people at the DMV seem unhappy, or even show us how people in an authoritarian government may seem heartless, but are really trying to protect their family.
So purchase this game for your own education, if not for its compelling and intricate gameplay.

This is what I think are the good and the bad of Dark Souls 2...
Pros:
1. Great combat system; it feels authentic
2. Innovative online co-operative system, allowing me to team up with others or for them to team up with me
3. Non-linear
4. Each enemy is unique and awesome in design
5. Lots of different cool spells, gear, weapons, etc
6. You can see the spirits and bloodstains of other players playing the same level as you
7. You can read tips from other players (or write them yourself) about the environment and nearby enemy
8. Great game design, sound and voice acting adds to the immersion
9. You can create many different characters like bandits, swordsman and mages
10. You can challenge other players to fight in an arena (using a statue at a convenent) or within a level (using a soap sign)
Cons:
1. Lack of a story to immerse you (this may annoy some)
2. No easy mode. Can be very frustrating at times; you will die a lot! (It is definitely a challenge unless you look on youtube for hints)
3. You can get invaded by others when you are fighting many enemies
There is definitely replay value as you can create various characters and try beating the game in a different style. You don't have to play online but it makes it more fun. If there was a better story element to this game, I would have rated it higher. But maybe that is what the developers intended I don't know.
To play it on PC it is recommended to use a controller for the best experience. It makes fighting much easier, especially against other online players who have very quick reflexes (some of them anyway!).
Overall, I love the game and have spent many hours playing it (it took me around 40 hours the first playthrough to complete).
