Call of Juarez Gunslinger is something of a hidden gem. It's a dumb, visceral, shooting gallery that pits an omnipotent death dealing protagonist against legions of nameless inept goons, but it doesn't pretend that it's anything else and it does what it does incredibly well.
In the game, you play as aged bounty hunter Silas Greaves, a narrator of dubious reliability, recounting the stories of his youth as a feared and deadly bounty hunter to a small audience in an old saloon. As old Silas tells the story in narration, you enact the story as his younger self. Typically, these tales tend to involve gratuitious amounts of lead, but as you play through, different characters may remember events differently, or Silas will suddenly reveal a detail that he was holding back to build narrative tension. Doing so causes the game world you play in to change, sometimes opening up a new path or restarting the level from a completely different perspective. This is done seamlessly, with almost no confusion, and it just plain works.
While all of the events are pure historical fiction, they are all based on real world tales and legends about the American West. Throughout many of the levels, you can collect "Nuggets of Truth" that will explain the stories and real-life figures associated with the current level and their historical significance. As an avid history buff, I fell in love with these. Rather than detract from the main gameplay as secrets often do, they helped me appreciate the story and the setting even more.
The gameplay is very well polished. Gunplay is weighty and powerful, and killing enemies grants you skills and upgrades that tend to have an immediate impact on your playstyle. The satisfying gunplay is occasionally broken by Gun Dueling minigames, which will be a hit or miss for most players. These are quite sparse compared to the meat of the combat, however, and they are a definite upgrade over Call of Juarez: Bound in Blood's duels.
Perhaps the weakest part of the game is the presence of a handful of arena-style boss fights. They are not particularly fun and tend to break the flow of combat, but, like duel mode, they are in no way the core focus of the game.
The game has three modes: A story mode with XP, upgrades, and multiple NG+ options (including a HUD-free hardcore mode), an arcade-style Score Attack mode with multiple upgradable classes, and a Duel mode devoted to the Dueling minigame with a 15-boss ladder. The Duel and Arcade modes are both supported by worldwide leaderboards. Between all of this, you can easily squeeze countless hours out of this game. For anyone looking for a mindless but entertaining and satisfying first-person shooter, I would definitely recommend this game.

I recently spent 36 hours awake a couple weekends ago, playing Factorio. I kept glancing at the clock, and thinking about sleep... but there was just a bit more I could improve in my resource processing. Then one of my queues backed up and started misrouting material. Then I researched some improved belt layouts on the forums. Then I had to go out and clear out a bug infestation that had spawned near my base. Then one of the mining locations had petered out so I had to migrate the miners to a new lode. But before I could do that I had to manufacture ammo for the tank so I could clear out a big nest near the new copper mine. And then...
Well. Let's just say that the game throws a lot of problems at you, and leaves the solution up to you.
Factorio is a game that is deceptively passive. Build a base, mine some materials. No big deal, right? But it throws more and more complex problems at you, at the same time as it provides the tools you need to surmount those difficulties. And while in theory at the end of all this work you have a base that does everything for you, by the time you get close to that goal you realize that there are so many ways you could do it better and you start ripping out what you have built to redo it more efficiently, more compactly... and another 36 hours pass.
In the beginning, you hand mine some coal, iron, and rock. You build a few coal powered tools, and perhaps connect them directly to each other. Soon you may add belts and carry the material where it's needed, like from the coal field to your smelters next to your iron mine.
But the complexity ramps up. Early crafting requires only one or two ingredients, but later items may need four or more. Processing Oil requires pipes... unlike belts, pipes block movement and thus require more forethought in how they are laid out. Advanced items may need both parts and liquids to craft, necessitating more ingenuity in moving resources to where they are needed.
You also get access to fun tools that reduce some of the tedium of moving parts around as you advance through the tech tree. Expensive parts that require you have a comprehensive and efficient setup already to be able to afford to use.
Finally, the last thing I would like to note is that the graphics are only meh. But with an interesting caveat... while the sprites and graphics are dated, they are surprisingly effective at conveying information. Sound is used to great effect, providing subtle cues to how hard your engines are working. Small touches like the speed of bubbles moving in a pipe provide clear and immediate feedback on how your infrastructure is working... it's not just window dressing. And the User interface does a laudable job at conveying all the information you need to make accurate decisions, including very well done historical graphs for crafting and power.
Mod support is also excellent, with an active community of modders and well done steam integration.
The one bad thing though is very bad: multiplayer support. The networking code is horrible. Due to the nature of the game, it's possible it will never become good. If you are envisioning playing this game with your 10 friends on the same map turn around and leave now because anything beyond two player support requires a LAN connection to work reliably. This might get fixed in the future, but it's a big if, so if online multiplayer is your bag just pretend the game doesn't support it yet because the support it has is laggy, buggy, and unpleasant all around.

good multiplayer support. I have a group of friends, and building things together is one of our favorite activities (we met on Minecraft). We can't yet play a game of Factorio together, and that makes me very sad. I really hope this gets fixed.
But other than that... if single player is your thing, crafting bases gets you
engaged, and you love the idea of a game where optimizing your resource strategy is an involving and enjoyable task, then Factorio is probably the game for you. It might be early access, but it's already filled with dozens, if not hundreds of hours of gameplay.

Then you unlock Roboports and have an army of hundreds or thousands of little robots running around moving things between crates, loading and unloading, repairing damaged walls, and bringing you requested materials.
Play the tutorial. It will help get you started. Then just play the game. Don't start over if you feel you could have done better, because you can always do better. Just keep going and you will learn very quickly from your mistakes.
Finally, the only thing about this that's Early Access, is they are still adding content after 4 years. To me, this feels like a completed game.

Short review:
It's a good horror game and video game in general. It is different the way it inspires fear in you.  A truly intense experience. Recommended 8/10
Personal Experience:
I am given a simple task to go find a keycard in San Cristobal Medical Bay.  Seems simple enough, but while in the medical bay sirens start going off. A voice on the P.A. system says "Medical Quarantine in effect, unidentified biological material in medical bay.  I exit the office I'm in and start running down the hallway when the vent cover on the ceiling pops right off. Fog starts to hiss from the vent as I quickly hide under a hospital bed with a mutilated corpse on it.  Then out in all of it's glory, sinks down, the Alien.  I can see the individual muscles and its vicious clawed hands on the floor. It screechs and clicks, while I am in the mean time literally shaking with fear.  It doesn't notice me and starts to slowly walk down the corridor.  Each footstep making a loud thumping noise. Proceed to find an escape from the medical ward, and an escape from the monster.  That level was the most intense and scary experience I have ever had.  It truly does a great job of giving you a real sense of survival out of fear.
Long Review:
I am not a fan of horror games at all.  But this game is easily one of my favorite singleplayer experiences I have ever played.  I will admit that halfway through the game it begins to lose appeal.  But with that said, the first 10 hours may be the most intense singleplayer experience in a video game you'll ever have.  The Alien is absoultely terrifying and intense, and the fact that 90% of its actions are non-scripted makes it even more frightening.  Although there are a substantial amount of glitches, the game has been refined since it was released.  I recommend this game even if you are not a fan of horror games. This is a game that you do not want to miss out on. Also if you are craving for a nostalgic trip to something like the very first Alien movie this is it.  The atmosphere and enviroments just captures the 1978 Ridley Scott world of Alien.  Alien Isolation does have excellent world building, to the level of Dishonored in my opinion. The clunky space aesthetic mixed with retro DOS technology makes for a very immersive world.  The graphics are very impressive if you are running on ultra settings.  4K Alien Isolation is one of the best graphical games I've played on PC.  Textures can sometimes be a little muddy even on Ultra settings.  8/10

This title, like Rust is a sandbox survival game. That is, gather resources, gear up, build your base of your dreams, and fight other players.
The core concept is fun, the game can be too, but there are issues. As I previously reviewed, "You can spend hours building a house, only for it to be destroyed faster than you built it while you sleep." this game punishes those who either don't have a large, active clan, or those who have other responibilities. IE: School or work.
Playing solo, to build a respectable building and start upgrading can take 1-3 hours, depending on pace, and threats (Players or monsters). The fact that you can log off for dinner, and come back to have all your work destroyed in under an hour is defeating.
Essentially, the game's design punishes players unwilling, or unable to put forth greater time and effort to build an impenetrable base. Rest assured, even at your best, your base can still be breached and destroyed by a top tier player with time and a lock pick.
While hackers numbers have lowered, they're still an issue as well.
If you're a casual gamer who doesn't mind getting murdered, and struggling to build, this game can be for you. But if you're with alot of friends or have a tremendous amount of time on your hands, this game was made for you.

text:
Where to start?
Positive
Game is pretty, if you like the animu style it's right up your alley, gorgeous drawn environments, abilities generally look pretty good as well.
Lots of classes, really interesting as well and a good diversity of classes and abilities, sadly the game doesn't tell you much about them or what they do, so it's almost hard to put this in the plus column. And there is no respeccing, so if you mess up, better reroll.
My friend plays it, no really my friend likes it, that's the main reason I play this game.
Negatives
Well the community on the games forums are completely horrible people, so don't bother going there for help when you need to find out the information about the game which should be included in the game but is not. Not only that but they take pride in the fact that their game tells you literally nothing about how abilities work, or actively tells you the wrong thing. They see nothing wrong with the game telling you an ability does one thing, but it does another, or Nothing at all.
Stats are pretty meaningless, they don't matter much at all. abilities scale so poorly with stats it's humorous, you'll have maybe 300 in a stat if you dump most of your points in it by the time you hit the cap, most abilities will do X + stat damage or so, of course in the later levels X is usually about 3-4 thousand. so your 300 in your stat is about 10% scaling. Not very useful, dump points in either DEX for crit, spirit for mana, or con for HP.
There continue to be huge problems with optimization, control, and server stability.
The "translation" is actually a fan translation, no literally the company made their text available and said hey translate this for free. They didn't bother to hire a professional localization team, and it shows, it really shows.
The information transparency is TERRIBLE, just plain awful, You can't really learn what abilities do, there is some nebulous stat called "aoe factor" which does something to do with AOE, it looks like it should increase the size of your AOEs, but going from 2 to 7 did literally nothing to my abilities/circles. Not to mention that it is a completely useless statistic that is 100% arbitrary and has no comparison to what people already know. Incredibly poor design.
You cannot join a guild until the end of the game, and only if you are the correct class to make a guild, yes making a guild is a class decision, so I hope you didn't want to be the other class at that tier.
The cash shop is the worst kind of garbage I've ever seen. It's beyond even pay to win ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, it's pay for features that should just be part of the damn game. Combined with Draconian lockdown on gold sellers which of course haven't stopped gold sellers at all but have screwed all the regular players. 30 trades a month, IF you buy a subscription. 5 auctions if you bought a sub. It's ridiculous.
There is no respeccing, if a class doesn't play the way you thought it would, better respec. This is fine if it's a tier 1 class or w/e but if it's a tier 5 class that's like a week of playtime right down the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Of course you only have the most vague of ideas of how a class will play because of the complete lack of information or help you will receive. The response from the community is "just reroll it's fine" ♥♥♥♥ that, seriously. I don't mind rerolling if I want to try something new, or I had a cool idea, but rerolling because the game is garabage at conveying information that should be conveyed is just not acceptable. I'm not even asking for respecs, I just want some idea of what to expect. (if I have to look something up on a wiki about the basics of the game, then the game has failed.)
Overall this game is pretty, it wants to be ragnarok online, but holy♥♥♥♥♥♥is it just a completely half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥attempt to gouge you for 10-50 bucks.

Given that I speak from experience ranging from iCBT2 and, as of this time of writing, the early access my views of this game is pretty limited. But here goes:
The game is, despite the staggering amount of people throwing down 10 dollary-doos or more, a work in progress. We got in early to both actually play the game and to see if IMC can handle the numbers we're currently throwing at thim. Needless to say, its been...rocky. CommanderLoadFail and his gang have not been kind to us but given past experiences, what MMO has had a flawless launch? Not too many.
Still with little than less of a month left to go IMC has been dealing with the rampant issue of RMTs, Bots, and possibly the developer's curse of fixing 1 bug and spawning 99 others in its place. As a player I'm generally patient, I don't entirely understand or pretend to know the inner workings of a company when it comes to managing an MMO, so I put my hopes in the team to know what they're doing and not entitle myself to anything. I don't particularly hold this game up to other standards as, again, experience has shown me that I can't expect Game Y to be like Game X, otherwise why not play Game X.
Give this a shot if you have money to spare, if you don't then feel free to wait until Free to Play to give it a dip, Tree of Savior's experience is reminiscent of Ragnarok Online and hitherto vastly different from the MMOs in the current market. Which may in fact be one of the factors that drew so many into this game.
Just keep in mind that it's early access, it basically means an open beta so you're bound to see bugs galore and run into trouble every once in a while.

Some pros and cons
Pros
+great visual style
+amazing music with tons of tracks
+smooth gameplay that isn't too simple or too complex to grasp
+tons of options to build your character
+friendly people who like to help
Cons
+some system mechanics need improvement (such as trading, selling items on the market)
+limited on inventory space and diffucult to transfer stuff between characters (but not impossible)
+while the community can be helpful also a small fraction of unhelpful players (that's any online game really)
+lots of customization for character builds but choices are permanent so expect trial and error and do research (however there are skill and stat reset potions)
*EDIT* IMC recently announced they are expanding item storage and updating trading mechanics*
In the end, if your willing to get over some flawed system mechanics the game is absolutely worth it. These problems are mostly to fight against gold sellers and botting so it's not completely unwarranted. If it helps the ecomony then is worth it to me and they are working constantly to improve it and actually listen to feedback from the fans which is a must in a community driven game.

One of the most original games I've played in a long time.  You work at border checkpoint in a 1984 stylized world where you examine the paper work of individuals trying to make their way into the country.  Its kind of strange to think that looking at paper work can be even remotely fun but when you find that descrepency its incredibly satisfying to deny them entry.
Papers Please has a ton of surprises sprinkled about it and has a very dark humor which does a great job at keeping it entertaining.  The story lines throughout your time at the border present someone in your position with some tough choices that can really only happen in a game like this.
One of the side plots had a guy ask me to allow a murderer through the border even if his papers were wrong because the man killed his daughter.  He wanted me to let him through so that he can kill him himself later on. But If I were to do that I would get a deduction from my pay which means I might not be able to pay for the medicine my son needs.  So you can see this game can be pretty damn dark, and that darkness isn't always accompanied with humor.
There are many more side plots that are best experienced for yourself so I won't say much more but Papers Please is completely original almost to its core and should be played by all.

I found myself digging underneath enemies to get around them, and while that feels inventive to do at first, it becomes a tedious way to play the game. And while running forward guns blazing is the more fun way to play the game, the barrage of explosions and camera shake makes it hard to see what's even happening. Carefully walking forward and dealing with enemies one by one is a lot safer, but also kinda dull.
The game's fun, it just feels like it outstays its welcome. I played it in coop, and it's possible it feels more managable in singleplayer. The game really tries real hard to be funny, but aside one good gag near the end of the game, it feels like the game keeps repeating the same jokes over and over. If steam allowed a score somewhere between thumbs up and down, I would lean more towards a sideways thumbs up.

Your populations wil starve despite your developing food resources.

At the end of the day you need to decide if you want to play an imbalanced time wasting nuisance of a game.
Cetainly Rome was more powerful than this game tries to simulate.
ETW and ETWN are far superior game experiences.

EDIT: Okay, I wasn't really satisfied with the quality of my prior review, and although this review probably won't be read, I still want to express my thoughts on the game.
CLANNAD is a heartwarming story about finding love despite a tragic past and depressing life, and the game puts you in the protagonist's shoes. Prepare for the feels--snickers at the witty and sarcastic humor, "aww"s at the cute moments scattered throughout, and the waterfalls of tears during some of the sad moments (but being the manly man I am, I managed to make it through without crying. Yep. Nearly 40 hours without shedding a single tear...am I even human?) It's probably going to be one of the longest games you play, with about ~1.29 million English words. Granted, this number might not mean much but here are some other works for comparison:
Grisaia no Kajitsu: ~1 million
The entire Harry Potter Series: ~1 million
4 book Twilight series: 591,434
4 book LotR series: 550,147
Witcher 3's script: ~450,000
So basically what I'm trying to say is this: CLANNAD takes you for a ride on a rollercoaster of emotions for a long, long time. Out of anyone else I know, I have the shortest playtime with around 33 hours of actual playing. It's also praised as being one of the best visual novels of al time. I think I've made my point pretty clear, but the only obstacle stopping most people from buying is the steep $50 pricepoint. However, this game will probably take you 50+ hours to complete (I mean every route, every achievement) and paying less than a dollar for each hour you enjoy doesn't seem like too bad a deal.
Hopefully I convinced you to buy this game, or at least consider it! If you're still on the fence about this game, feel free to add me as a friend or message me any questions about CLANNAD/suggestions for my review! Cheers!

COJG does a great thing. It utilizes a narrative mechanic that I feel deserves more time: the unreliable narrator.
You play Silas Greaves, an aging cowboy telling stories of his life. You frequently paint yourself into a corner and then the game world morphs as you frantically backtrack and try to fix your completely insane bragging.
Sometimes everything rewinds, sometimes the environment changes. Either way, fun is had by all.
It's smart, it's lean, it's good. It knows exactly what it wants and it achieves it with such ease, you wonder why any game ever screws up.

For any western-lover or plain FPS fan, this game is ESSENTIAL to your library of games. The game is completely linear but don't let that put you off as it's been crafted perfectly in terms of set-pieces, level design and just the look. Talking of the look, this is a beautiful game. (even with the kinda cell-shaded look around everything) It's highly stylized, colourful, and authentic. The game pulls you into this rich world and doesn't let go, it oozes style and personality.
The weapons look, sound and most importantly; FEEL fantastic in this game. The gunplay is satisfying as hell. The recoil in each weapon is strong and the kick gives you the visual feedback you need to place your shots on target correctly. As you get more skilled with your weapon of choice you'll get used to the recoil and later on through levelling up you can obtain a higher-performance version of your weapon.
There is a small variety of guns in the game but don't see that as a negative point. Each gun has a unique purpose and aren't watered down unlike other games where there are about 30 guns and they all roughly feel the same. As the game progresses you'll probably find a few favourite weapons that fit your play style and stick with them though you can mix and match as you please.
Same goes for the skills. You can unlock abilities/skills through levelling up. (which is fast and fun in this game, not a chore) You can put a point into the skill you believe fits your playstyle best in one of the three trees, but you can also put points into the others to make your original skills more effective! Ranging from accuracy to faster combo-chaining.
This game is arcade-like in terms of being able to earn combos, you're rewarded for trick shots (Headshots, Piercing shots, Long-Range shots etc) and as well as being fun as hell they will bag you a lot of points which will move you higher up the leaderboard if you're into that kinda thing, if not, simply ignore it! Points also go towards filling up your Focus gauge, which allows you to go into slow-mo when in emergencies and will highlight enemies in red. Use it wisely as it runs out fast, though you can turn it on and off anytime you wish.
The story in this game actually surprised me with its quality. There are a twists and turns along the way, you'll meet some of the most notorious people in the West along the way as allies and enemies. Gunslinger also has a BRILLIANT sense of humour! From the characters relations with each other, to the occasional 4th wall breaking.
This game it utterly fantastic and although you may complete it within anywhere from I'd say... 7-10 hours. The game has a lot of replay value. Going back to finish off the skills/abilities I missed, messing around with new playstyles, completing the harder difficulties, a completely seperate arcade score-attack mode with its own seperate leaderboards, the dueling challenge and last but not least the collectibles!
Which are ACTUALLY good in this game, to which I was immensely surprised. Usually a collectible is some useless piece of junk you pick up for the sake of it being hidden. But in Gunslinger the collectibles are a Poker card. Each one has a little slice of history from the West with photos and theories behind some of the more mysterious ones which made me genuinely give a damn about collecting them! Not too hard to find and rewarding for finding them!
This game is a STEAL for £12!! ($20-25ish?? lol) I would of happily bought if for more! Don't miss out on this! This game has been overlooked by a lot of players but definitely deserves a chance! Get the demo first if you don't feel confident enough, I guarantee you'll fall in love with this game. I recommend this game to everyone!
P.S. - The dueling is badass. (couldn't find anywhere else to say that!)

How the Old West was Lost
As Silas makes his way to the saloon, a car nearly runs him over, or so we are led to believe through the graphic novel cutscenes. Gunslinger is a blending of the old and the new, fact and fiction; Gunslinger tells a story about storytelling.
Silas’ story is presented through the original tradition of storytelling: by word of mouth. As Silas tells his story the truth becomes blurred: he embellishes his story, challenge history, and is challenged by other patrons of the saloon and his own memory. All of these elements make a well-worn, classic story feel fresh again, and make for some interesting turns in the gameplay. At one point Silas mentions that some men attacked him and they were like Apaches, at which point Apaches surround the player as he fights for his life, but then Silas corrects the story by emphasizing that the men attacked like Apaches, but were in fact just the bandits mentioned earlier.
The gameplay synthesizes with the idea of blending old and new. The action of the game has a very distinct arcade feel. There are explosions everywhere, combo kills, frantic firefights, and cartoonish blood spurts. Coupled with this are the modern gun and health mechanics: carrying only one gun from each category of weapon, regenerating health over time, and three skill trees to invest in after level ups.
The slick art style and presentation fit perfectly with the game. Every character in the game is introduced with a small Sergio Leone inspired sequence. Add to the style is The duel mechanic that makes you feel like a cowboy: slowly inching your hand closer to your gun as your eyes focus on your target, and you have to draw second if you want to kill your opponent honorably.  Old West fans and history buffs will appreciate how crowded this game is with famous figures and “Nuggets of Truth” that detail some of the history that the game touches on.
Gunslinger shows just how good Westerns can be. Adding to the style, interesting storytelling, and great action is the replay value. You can try your hand at a various arcade levels, duels, and Silas Greaves may be old, but he still has a story tell and a good fight in him.

Ah, post western America. As the good ol' U.S of A comes from it's glorious 19th centuary antics and into the 20th centuary. A violent, legendary and styish period for sure, but is it an over played time period?
Story- Call of Juarez The Gunslinger starts in the early 20th centuary (unlike the hiddeous excuse for a modern shooter CoJ The Cartel was) and focuses upon the huskey voiced fictional character of Silas Greaves. Most of the game is played through hilarious and outlandish dialouge that passes between Silas and patrons of a local saloon to whom his story is told. This means that most characters in the story aren't voice acted, however the narration from Silas and script work colabirates well to keep the player constantly informed of exposition and characters who otherwise say nothing. One or two players may have just cringed in their chairs, but fret not, for the comedic lines and voice acting fails to break pace and is a unique, snazzy way of communicating setting to the player directly. The script is genrally as fluient as your standard FPS script, whilst maintaining that classic western feel that you would expect from a tale such as this. The humor is brief, but therefore never outstays its welcome meaning that inbetween shooting and slow motion dueling, you'll be laughing and mostly having a real hearty time with The Gunslinger. The tale is strong within itslef, however serves as a sort of current with which the player will sail through hectic gunfights and various other great western senarios, but really The Gunslinger boils down to arcade-dy shoot 'em up with fun story sequences to hold the whole whiskey-soaked cake together.
Gameplay- The Gunslinger isn't your typical first person shooter. Sure you can aim, shoot and move- but The Gunslinger will make sure you do it with a more than satisfying kick and a certain degree of style. Every shot shows Silas' hand shoot up with recoil, smoke and fire errupts from your weapons when you fire and- if well placed- a delicious splash a crimson blood splats from your enemy. Its the little weapons in Gunslinger's that catch the eye the most. Sure: the game may make you feel over-powered at times, in the gatling gun segments at least, but that's how a good western should feel. If you want a challenge you choose to play a different game, if you want a hyper-active, high-octane, super badass shooter with explosions and bullets galore: look no further. The game may be short, (you could easily finish in under ten hours) but every step of the way you feel like a director of an action movie; gliding your actors around, building the actions and shouting at the... Oh waith, that's something else. Further adding to the short play time are challenge modes for both the exceptional shooting and the rather unresponsive dueling. I mention the dueling now because Ubisoft have created a new dueling system from Bound in Blood (the actual previous game) and they serve as some of the game's 'boss fights'. All of these boss fights offer seperate mechanics however some of them feel lazy and out of hand. For example the gatling guns boss fights and the dueling boss fights. Neither requires any amount of skill as much as; wait for the appropriate que and fire, hoping that your bullets are faster than the enemy's. This issomething that is sorely missed and I feel would have made the game 'that' much better.
Graphics- Look at the screenshots. Do it! Now, look my profile picture in the eyes and say that those graphics aren't glorious... I know they are, aren't they? Suffice it to say, The Gunslinger looks and feels like one of the most unique games this year. Performance is rarely an issue with the game playing pretty much smoothly, provided your PC can handle it. If your laptop can... Well done! Stunning is simply not enough to describe each enviroment, ever character model and every incy weensy detail that Ubisoft has so cunningly detailed. Epic are the environments. Epic is the sense of scale. Epic... Is The Gunslinger.
9/10
Definatly a step on the right trail for the franchise, and for games to come. With only a few sloppy bos fights to nit-pick about, Call of Juarez The Gunslinger is worthy of a rightous score.

Russian Horror Story is a visual novel based on a true story. It follows the miserable life of a man named Ivan as he deals with his downstair neighbours (a voluptuous lady and her child) and all the trouble that it brings him.
The game features gorgeous hand drawn scenery, an incredible soundtrack that makes the Witcher soundtrack sound like Caillou and an open ended story with incredible choice and consequense. Bare minimum use of pop culture reference make the player symphatize with Ivan while still keeping his descent into madness as the main star of the story. The only weakness of Russian Horror Story is how short it can be at times, as it leaves players craving for more and more.
Russian Horror Story is a hidden gem worth every penny, and brings every tenants fear into the accessible form of a visual novel. All in all? A must have for everyone that appreciates fine literature and artwork.

FOR NEW PLAYERS TO THE GAME: this review is for you, as it is my experience from being a completely new player with no idea what is going on.  Bullet points of review after intial intro, to keep things short and sweet for those looking to buy.
After being a WoW veteran since beta and playing various other MMOs (FFXIV, SWTOR, EQ, EQ2, etc.), I wanted to test this game out after it had the initial terrible reviews and then the ravingly good reviews after the rework patches.  I also was playing a LOT of skyrim special edition and wanted to expand upon that universe.
THIS GAME is decent.  For a new player it is immensely confusing, the world is not very linear to begin with and I really had no idea what I was doing when I made my initial character.  The tutorial and messages for new players as they play the game are lengthy, but not much time is given to read them.  Since the world is "do whatever you want and play", it sucks for new people since there, of course, is a best and worst of what you can do in certain situations.
That being said, this game is NOT skyrim.  You can't get away with wearing leather armor as a caster, as it really provides no benefit.
BULLETS:
- Extremely confusing to start, as the game has SO MUCH depth
- Alliance doesn't really matter (from what I can tell), but there are WAY more people on Aldmeri Dominion
- The combat system is awesome, but takes some getting used to (active combat, blocking, interrupting, etc.)
~MUCH better combat than other games where you just press the buttons to do the dmg
- Racial aspects DO MATTER A LOT.  It will effect your end-game if you want to be an elitist
- The only thing you can't "reset" is your class, so choose wisely at the start for class-specific abilities and passives
- You are NOT LIMITED by your class, as weapons dictate abilities (i.e. resto staff = you can heal as any class)
- Addons are slightly more annoying to use and there is a specific amount of memory given to them, which is a bad thing.
- Crafting is rather interactive and much better than other games, however without an ESO PLUS membership it sucks.
- ESO PLUS membership is almost NEEDED due to the crafting bag and general access.  ALMOST
- CROWN STORE is NOT worth it AT ALL.  Items are WAY overpriced.  Excessively so.  Watch youtube for crown purchases
~Crown crates are random loots and can contain stupid stuff such as potions and general worthlessness
- FORUM accounts are SEPARATE from regular accounts, when you buy the game pay attention to an email for them
- Armor shown at character creation doesn't matter, you can get a style motif in the game to make the other races' armor
- You have two skill bars (one being gained at level 15) so you can swap between two weapons if you want
- Side quests are sometimes hard to find, there are addons that can help you.
- There are damage meters for this game (Addons)
- I am still confused for a lot of the UI (isn't just social, guild, inventory, character tabs - much much more).
- breaking items apart at crafting stations is often better than selling them, be sure to check the attributes of the item
All that being said, I recommend this game on the FREE-TO-PLAY version, but I HIGHLY RECOMMEND you watch youtube videos for beginners BEFORE purchasing.
I DO NOT RECOMMEND the CROWN STORE, many things on there are already available to you and you can be literally throwing your money away.  IGNORE that entire aspect unless buying UPGRADES or DLC (like imperial race upgrade)
Play around with character creation, class testing, crafting, and weapon interaction before seriously committing to anything.
NOTE: If you get a sub, you get 1500 crowns per month you sub.  ESO plus of 3 months can provide you with the DLC and upgrades you may want and be cheaper/more beneficial than straight purchasing crowns.
All in all it gets better over time :), and it is a good deal to take it on descount.

Emily Is Away is a nice little game about a boy and his high school friend Emma. And to be honest, it's a pretty sad one. It starts off happy, with Emma inviting you to a party. Then from every chat you have with her after that, it all goes downhill, only to go a bit up right after. You make some choices which are either pretty good or pretty bad, depending on whatever you said to Emma during your chats. The part that really got to me was the ending. And don't worry, I won't spoil it. All I'm saying is that it was so sad, it nearly made me cry a bit. And I'm a 14 year old teen boy, for crying out loud!.
The game takes place during the years from 2002-2006, and it does an excellent job in making you feel as if you were actually living in that point in time. You can change your Instant Messenger Buddy Icon to a Green Day, or hell, maybe even do a Mean Girls or High School Musical icon as well(yes, I am a straight teen boy who likes to watch Mean Girls and High School Musical, bite me).
Overall, this is a game that I would definitely recommend. This game is probably especially built for you 20-something year olds looking to get a little throwback to that beautiful time before the 2010s. Back when Fillmore was still on Disney Channel, and Panic! At The Disco was on the radio. A time when Cartoon Network had one really good Teen Titans cartoon on, and Spongebob was still good.
A beautiful time before Scotter Braun met Justin Bieber.

I'm writing this game as fan of the Alien(1979), Aliens(1986), and Prometheus(2012) movies.
Alien:Isolation is awesome game that has very scary and interesting early game, however that's when the fun stops.. after progressing to mid-end game the story turns into a slog. I was so frustrated with the attempts to extend the game every time you were about to "complete" it.
Sevastopol is great piece of junk, it looks great. I did love and hate it at the same time. The Space station feels like old claustrofobic soviet vessel, i did hate every part of beign on the ship.. wanting to get out. I think thats the right feeling developers were after.
Lack of windows make it eaven worse, i were often wondering how horrible it would be to actually live on the station (before the alien outbreak)
The best moment i had in the game was to see this horrible piece of junk burn and explode into the planet. I was cheering the whole cutscene.
* Graphics, Sevastopol looks great! It's just like in Alien movies.
* Sound & Atmosphere
* Sounds of the alien lurking in vents and nearby is very scary
* Minigames are fun and intense if there is alien nearby
* Sevastopol is very claustrofobic and MAKES you want to get out of it as soon as possible.
* Visiting the Engineer ship was one of the best parts of the game!
* Parts where you operate outside the station
* Story has so many silly excuses to continue when you are so close to completing it, dragging the story for way too long.
* Game loses it's scare factor after Alien dies.
* You enter alien Hive but never encounter the Queen.. i was expecting her from this point to the last cutscene.
* Alien is not scary after a while, it's incredibly frustrating when you have to play same 30min part over and over again.
* Game is long because you will die a lot and play the same part so many times you want to stop playing
* Aliens can live outside the station in space, what?
* The Story elements were too much similar to events of the movies
* I was sometimes just standing behind the alien and laughing as it just stood there doing nothing (the part when you wait the ambulance capsule to open)

Review:
[Gamplay and Performance]- Over all, its clean cut, killing monsters is very satisfying, leveling up is not a chore. The Questline is a story you experience and is very enjoyable. The game is very engaging and there are lots of bosses to fight in the game. The gameplay is simple its easy enough for beginners to start playing RPG games yet complicated enough for the competetive player to have the resources they need , to go far PVE and PVP wise.
[Visuals and Music]- Have you ever played, " Final Fantasy: Crystal Chronicals", some time in your life? The visuals and initial feel of the game has a very artistic and familiar feel to FFCC, it's very pleasant and very fitting. The Art style used in the game can be very compelling and give you sense of peace and then do a 180 and pump you up with great Power Metal Electro beats when doing a dungeon. It's hard not to be moved by the game on your first time playing it.
[Game Mechanics] The game is a meta breaker, it changes the way you view class progression as a whole, usually class progression is linear But this game is very diverse. Slapping down money on the game can be a nice little luxury but is not required it is entirely just for your own pleasure.
[Consistency] The game dose a good job making it easy when you start off but then progresses to become a bit more difficult. If you don't like a game that can get difficult then you need to go back to Wizzard 101 with the rest of the babies.

This review was written pretty much hot off the presses of finishing the game, and as such everything below is expressive of my raw impressions of the game after completion. Let that say what it will of the quality of my review.
--------------------------------------------
Supergiant Games has hit the ball out of the park yet
with their second game. As I've made apparent, I liked Bastion,
this game is substantially different from Bastion in many ways. So if you didn't like Bastion (I hope you at least liked the music and narration), don't let that put you off of Transistor.

is entirely different, replacing a weapon-based combat system with an ability-based system with
depth. As you proceed through the game, you gain new abilities either through leveling up or encountering certain points, and each of these abilities is equipped in one of four slots (1-4 are their hotkeys). However, each of these slots has one open subslot and an additional unlockable subslot, and beside the four base slots, are two slots on each side that are passive slots.
As I said, very impressive depth, because each ability operates differently based on whether it's equipped primarily (in the four slots), complementarily (in one of the eight subslots), or supplementarily (in one of four passive slots).
is likewise in its differences. You're no longer in a fantasy-esque setting in Transistor, and you don't have to worry about falling off floating platforms anymore. You're grounded, but in a world as far out there as Bastion's. It's a fascinating modern, sci-fi styled world full of mysteries to try to grapple with, not unlike Bastion. Yet, these mysteries aren't resolved like Bastion's, not laid out for you by anyone. If you want to understand Cloudbank, you're gonna have to get digging for yourself. Fortunately, you'll probably want to after exploring the place and its characters.
is as dynamic as Bastion's, if not more so. There's more detailed background on the much larger casting this time around, and there's more chatter occurring. This isn't to say you're frequently stopped for conversations and the like, you're definitely not, and all the background is entirely optional to look into. You can play the game ignoring the characters as much as you like, and still enjoy it as much as if you were to pay attention, much as in Supergiant's previous title.
is as vibrant as ever in this game. It's also as vital to the atmosphere as in Bastion, and while there are equally energetic tracks in Transistor's soundtrack as in Bastion, it's of a very different styling. It's softer, of an electronic jazz vibe, compared to some of Bastion's harder, folksy tunes. If you didn't enjoy Bastion's soundtrack, don't worry, Darren Korb has outdone himself in making Transistor's soundtrack distinct from Bastion's, something you can't necessarily say for many musicians.
is fantastic...If you don't mind a story that won't hold your hand. The plot will keep you moving forward to figure out what happened to Red, as well as who acted against her and why, but perhaps even more compelling than that is understanding the world she lives in. Every part of the story from the characters to the setting to what led up to your adventure is a mystery for you to solve, and personally, I loved that. Even after having finished the game, I have questions, and I doubt there are answers, but I like being left with room to imagine on top of their world.
If you don't like that, you may not enjoy it, but there's so much more to the game than that to enjoy if you can look past your discomfort with it. The gameplay and music and art are all lovely to experience and behold.
is of a different stripe than Bastion's. It's a mixture of darkness and brightness, in a bit of contrast to Bastion's primarily bright, varied color palette. Transistor has a harsher, darker color scheme, seemingly set mostly at night, but is broken up by bright lights throughout and a transition into a lighter color scheme as the game proceeds. This isn't dark grays accompanied by muddy browns as seen in other games by any stretch of the imagination, but it is something of a darker color scheme if you're coming from Bastion.
Not to mention it's also in an urban setting with more futuristic and interestingly styled buildings. That also serves to differentiate the artwork drastically in its own right, having you ascending stairs along the edge of towering structures and taking elevators here and there amidst buildings serves as a different experience than Bastion would have you expecting.

If you're looking for a unique scifi styled game with a complex cast of characters with splendid voice acting, music, gameplay,  and artwork, you can't find much better than Transistor right now. Frankly, if you have to decide between this and Watch Dogs, coming out tomorrow as of this writing, I'd say save your money and buy this. While I have nothing against Watch Dogs and intend to get it myself, I think you'll find a far more compelling experience in Transistor, in essentially every way.
Thanks for reading! I hope this helped inform you of the game, and led you to pick it up. It's absolutely worth it.

Probably one of the best shooters I've played in a long time. It's built entirely around the tall tales of the wild west, and the many legends which circulated from this era, many of which erroneously.
The game is framed by Silas Greaves, a bounty hunter who wanders into a bar, and tells stories about his life to the patrons in exchange for drinks. As the story is told, the gameplay is built around exactly what he says, rather than what actually happened. And so, all the exaggerations he includes to impress and excite his audience, you get to play yourself, in all it's slow-motion running-and-gunning bullet-dodging glory. It may not be entirely true, but it's certainly exciting.
Historical facts from this era are hidden throughout the game as collectable secrets, called 'nuggets of truth'.  I've heard they aren't 100% accurate in some places, but they do well to separate the legend from the reality. Billy the Kid's introduction in the story as told by Silas boasts he had "21 killed by age 21", while his historical note mentions he only killed between 4 and 9 people. It's exactly this distinction between historical fact and legend which is at the heart of this game, making it so thoroughly enjoyable.

While some of the other games I've reccomended have done some aspects of storytelling better, Call of Juarez: Gunslinger's story is unique in that it is told from an "unreliable narrarator". I've always hated game stories that are told in past-tense, but this game makes a great case for it's usage. Often, revisions, depictions, and plot details are inserted mid-game, changing the environment as the player traverses through them. The plot itself only really becomes interesting in the second half, but when it does, it's quite enthralling.
The gameplay itself feels like something common on the Chrome engine - the same engine that Far Cry 3 utilizes. There's a similar RPG progression, though it's dialed back for a much smaller game. Early game, it's not much fun, but as abilities are unlocked, the game feels much more fleshed out. It certainly makes the iron-sight-and-recharging-health gameplay easier to swallow.

Almost a perfect game.
Great action, decent humor, and fairly original mechanics.  For the price, it's a great game.  The only serious flaw is at the end of the game... Most of the levels can be completed in well under five minutes.  Complete roughly four levels, and you've reached a savepoint, so you can quit and resume later.
At the end, you have to complete at least ten levels, plus boss fights before the end of the game - without savepoints.  Instead of 15-minutes to a save, it can take hours, depending on how long you fight the multiple bosses.
If the game had more savepoints toward the end, it would be perfect.  And to add insult to injury, you can't go back and re-play earlier levels without resetting the whole game (or starting a new profile).  Whenever I load it up, it's the same gruelling 10+ level multi-hour slogfest that usually ends with me quitting.
The BroForce "Expendables" freebie was welcomed, as it allowed me to play more levels without having to go through the stupid-long finale process.
Hoping this shortcoming is fixed someday.

An amazing, solid, and fun Early Access game that offers a lot of features with very little bugs or annoyances.
For an Early Access Title, Factorio may be one of the best. The developers have been working on this game for about 4 years now (as of 2016), and from what it looks like, will improve as time moves forward.
What Factorio is is a survival, strategy, RTS, puzzle game where you attempt to create a factory off the resources of the land while fending off the dangerous local alien life. It reminds me a bit like some Zachtronics games, but more accessable for a wide audience.
If you're into RTS, management, or even survival games, this game is worth a look. Heck, there's even a demo version that apparently runs you through the tutorial long enough for you to get a good idea of what the game is.
After the demo/tutorial there is more to explore, a survival mode, and more in game toys and techs to explore and play with.
I got this game as a gift from a friend for my birthday, and for an essentially free game for me. It's now one of my favorites.

(I'll be updating this review as I think of more things to add or as things get added or changed in the game)
Holy crackers! I'm having fun! Most of the other reviews have said a lot already so I'll try and list out what I like in particular.
Pros:
Addictive, but not in a bad way like an incremental game. I don't feel like I'm sitting here playing it due to some basic animal instinct where I like seeing numbers get bigger. I'm having a good time while doing it. There's always little things I can do to improve my factories. It's hooked me, and it's earned it.
Very well designed! Most things feel pretty intuitive and it seems like everything I've come across so far in the game has a reason for being there. The interface seems like it was designed to stay out of the player's way as much as possible. Little things like being able to upgrade storage areas/furnaces/etc. without having to remove the contents or implicitly crafting items required to build something saves a lot of unnecessary tedium.
Fairly easy to figure out. Once you figure out the basics you shouldn't be hitting that many roadblocks where you can't figure out what to do.
Figuring out a way to automate something that's been wasting you a lot of time is a pretty good feeling.
Cons:
Graphics are pretty ugly. They serve their purpose well enough and maybe the grittiness was intentional but even the entirely natural areas that I'd usually expect to be beautiful (like lakes and forests) seem pretty drab.
Seems like some campaigns are only available to a certain "tier" (furnace attendant). I'm assuming this is some Kickstarter stuff, along with having odd names for train stops/labs/etc. A very minor annoyance but I figured I'd mention it anyway.
Another minor annoyance is some of the writing in the game is in awkward English ( like "Press T to start a new research"). It's nothing a good proofread or two coudn't handle, though.
The music isn't all that great. It's there. It's just... not really what I was expecting. I figured it'd be something more hectic or mechanical but it's mostly just ominous strings. Definitely not worth eight dollars just to get it seperate.
The main campaign feels really short and a lot of unexplained stuff is thrown at you. Like I said earlier, it's fairly intuitive, but it would've been nice if stuff like trains or the oil industry was a little more gently introduced. I think at least half of the items in the game never make an appearance. They seem to have plans on adding more to the campaign though.
Quite a few of the upgrades are just faster/more efficient versions of previous items. I guess this is fine and it'd make sense that improved versions of already existing things would come out but it's all very boring.
--------------------
I've played it over 40 hours and I still don't feel like I've wasted my money. I think that's a good sign.

Dark Souls 2 is the second game in the series Dark Souls. Much has changed in a few years. (perhaps too much) It is again time to die many, many times and to experience creative game art.
Overall, I'm very happy with Dark Souls 2 and I feel that everything is done very carefully, and there is almost nothing that could have been different. What I perhaps most pleased with is how the game begins. Both stories are told and the two places that you very first meetings gives me a very good feeling, and it could not have been any better way to start the game.
The story revolves around a undead man or woman known as "carrier of the curse." The carrier thus whoever plays must travel to Drangleic, who is rumored to be home to powerful souls who can help Immortal regain their humanity and prevent this cruel fate. The support of the curse find their way to Majula where they meet an enigmatic woman known as Emerald Herald, which acts as the player's guide. She asks the player to search for four ancient beings with enormous souls: the old Iron King, the Rotting, the abandoned sinner, and the giant spider called Duke Dear Freja. Herald also tells the player to seek Flip Rick king of Drangleic.
One thing that is okay to say at once is that the game's action is very complex with many details that are not always easy to detect and requires that one is a good listener. For some it might be nice with a research after you are finished with the game to find out what really happened. It can sure seem like a minus that it is difficult to perceive the game action, but for me this is really a big plus. It may seem that it is intended that the game should have a little complicated action. It may be up to each player, one decides really even how the story should be interpreted and how much will be heard by the while playing, and it is for me a very creative concoctions. Some mysteries of Dark Souls are never resolved.
The game has that game before taking a very poor control setup. It has been improved a lot so you can at least be able to play it with mouse and keyboard, but it is still much nonsense with it. Especially when playing in PvP (player versus player) will be much worse than what you really are, because of a hopeless position. Now, one can of course change to their own control setup, but it is not exactly less hopeless because of it. I recommend HIGHLY playing with an Xbox control if you play on PC, but on other platforms is it really okay. Xbox controller makes it more comfortable to play on PC so there is no point in holding on to the money once you have purchased the game. Camera can also be a bit wobbly at times, but this can be fine tuned on settings.
Dark Souls 2 has a high level of both Gameplay and AI (Artificial Intelligence) that really takes the game far up in the right direction. NPCs (unplayable characters) has a major role in Dark Souls series and is highly prized. Door an NPC, he can never come back. Some NPCs sell or upgrading things that you need, someone gives hints, someone can help you with a boss, someone can unlock a trophy also on, and so on. All NPCs have a pretty creative look, but I'm a little disappointed voice acting is somehow not very much empathize, but it is not the greatest necessity rather then.
In Dark Souls 2 have much to choose from. One of these things is partly what direction you should go first of all, you can usually choose between two roads leading to the same thing, but that is a bit different. It also happens that you have to take the other way not initially chose to move on. Objects contains a medium amount of enemies and insanely annoying obstacles Dark Souls is certainly no dear mother. But all will be rewarded if you like I fail to see the creativity and charm behind it all. For if this game was only supposed to be bloody against you had not exactly been very exciting to play it.
Summary:
Dark Souls is a game with amazing creativity that shows what games really are. There are usually no unfinished scenes to see some places and the whole game sparkles of cursing and obstacles everywhere. The way the game joking with you is an ingenious way to make you totally mad , yet it gives you an irresistible desire to try again and again, after all then it's your own fault.
The graphics are absolutely stunning and fits well with the game. Sound effects are good and the game's music is simply a gorgeous masterpiece, but unfortunately voice actors a bit relax in his voice. Focus on "Artificial Intelligence and" Gameplay "matched game well and helps to make Dark Souls for something unique. The game has a bit wobbly camera and a poor ability to control the player with the mouse and keyboard. Xbox control is STRONGLY recommended for the PC version .
PvP (Player vs. Player) and Online collaboration (Co-Op) is a great opportunity and certainly entertaining. Some rings can make it easier for you to play with friends. The game has a jocular sense of humor as well as a large online community that both want to troll you greatly! It may at certain times be long snow loading screens.

This review was written pretty much hot off the presses of finishing the game, and as such everything below is expressive of my raw impressions of the game after completion. Let that say what it will of the quality of my review.
--------------------------------------------
Supergiant Games has hit the ball out of the park yet
with their second game. As I've made apparent, I liked Bastion,
this game is substantially different from Bastion in many ways. So if you didn't like Bastion (I hope you at least liked the music and narration), don't let that put you off of Transistor.

is entirely different, replacing a weapon-based combat system with an ability-based system with
depth. As you proceed through the game, you gain new abilities either through leveling up or encountering certain points, and each of these abilities is equipped in one of four slots (1-4 are their hotkeys). However, each of these slots has one open subslot and an additional unlockable subslot, and beside the four base slots, are two slots on each side that are passive slots.
As I said, very impressive depth, because each ability operates differently based on whether it's equipped primarily (in the four slots), complementarily (in one of the eight subslots), or supplementarily (in one of four passive slots).
is likewise in its differences. You're no longer in a fantasy-esque setting in Transistor, and you don't have to worry about falling off floating platforms anymore. You're grounded, but in a world as far out there as Bastion's. It's a fascinating modern, sci-fi styled world full of mysteries to try to grapple with, not unlike Bastion. Yet, these mysteries aren't resolved like Bastion's, not laid out for you by anyone. If you want to understand Cloudbank, you're gonna have to get digging for yourself. Fortunately, you'll probably want to after exploring the place and its characters.
is as dynamic as Bastion's, if not more so. There's more detailed background on the much larger casting this time around, and there's more chatter occurring. This isn't to say you're frequently stopped for conversations and the like, you're definitely not, and all the background is entirely optional to look into. You can play the game ignoring the characters as much as you like, and still enjoy it as much as if you were to pay attention, much as in Supergiant's previous title.
is as vibrant as ever in this game. It's also as vital to the atmosphere as in Bastion, and while there are equally energetic tracks in Transistor's soundtrack as in Bastion, it's of a very different styling. It's softer, of an electronic jazz vibe, compared to some of Bastion's harder, folksy tunes. If you didn't enjoy Bastion's soundtrack, don't worry, Darren Korb has outdone himself in making Transistor's soundtrack distinct from Bastion's, something you can't necessarily say for many musicians.
is fantastic...If you don't mind a story that won't hold your hand. The plot will keep you moving forward to figure out what happened to Red, as well as who acted against her and why, but perhaps even more compelling than that is understanding the world she lives in. Every part of the story from the characters to the setting to what led up to your adventure is a mystery for you to solve, and personally, I loved that. Even after having finished the game, I have questions, and I doubt there are answers, but I like being left with room to imagine on top of their world.
If you don't like that, you may not enjoy it, but there's so much more to the game than that to enjoy if you can look past your discomfort with it. The gameplay and music and art are all lovely to experience and behold.
is of a different stripe than Bastion's. It's a mixture of darkness and brightness, in a bit of contrast to Bastion's primarily bright, varied color palette. Transistor has a harsher, darker color scheme, seemingly set mostly at night, but is broken up by bright lights throughout and a transition into a lighter color scheme as the game proceeds. This isn't dark grays accompanied by muddy browns as seen in other games by any stretch of the imagination, but it is something of a darker color scheme if you're coming from Bastion.
Not to mention it's also in an urban setting with more futuristic and interestingly styled buildings. That also serves to differentiate the artwork drastically in its own right, having you ascending stairs along the edge of towering structures and taking elevators here and there amidst buildings serves as a different experience than Bastion would have you expecting.

If you're looking for a unique scifi styled game with a complex cast of characters with splendid voice acting, music, gameplay,  and artwork, you can't find much better than Transistor right now. Frankly, if you have to decide between this and Watch Dogs, coming out tomorrow as of this writing, I'd say save your money and buy this. While I have nothing against Watch Dogs and intend to get it myself, I think you'll find a far more compelling experience in Transistor, in essentially every way.
Thanks for reading! I hope this helped inform you of the game, and led you to pick it up. It's absolutely worth it.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.
Eat.

While some of the other games I've reccomended have done some aspects of storytelling better, Call of Juarez: Gunslinger's story is unique in that it is told from an "unreliable narrarator". I've always hated game stories that are told in past-tense, but this game makes a great case for it's usage. Often, revisions, depictions, and plot details are inserted mid-game, changing the environment as the player traverses through them. The plot itself only really becomes interesting in the second half, but when it does, it's quite enthralling.
The gameplay itself feels like something common on the Chrome engine - the same engine that Far Cry 3 utilizes. There's a similar RPG progression, though it's dialed back for a much smaller game. Early game, it's not much fun, but as abilities are unlocked, the game feels much more fleshed out. It certainly makes the iron-sight-and-recharging-health gameplay easier to swallow.
A better-than-average game with some pretty neat tricks up it's sleeves. I'd say that's worth picking up.

I had high hopes for Gunslinger. A series of good reviews gave me the impression it was a well constructed return to old-fashioned shooters, with a good chunk of humour and innovation thrown in for good measure. But it's only nearly those things.
There's a lot to like; great visuals, engaging combat, a humourous but exciting plot, and lots and lots of shooting. But, for me, a number of things just ruin it beyond repair; the insta-death QTEs, the stupid black border, the hideously low FOV, the duels, the poorly integrated bullet-time, the constant stopping and breaks in gameplay, and the stupidly distracting HUD elements and key-press reminders. Yes, I know there are hacks to remove the borders and fix the FOV, and these fixes allowed me to progress further than five minutes into the game, but I'm reviewing the game in its vanilla state (as I did with Far Cry 3), and it's disappointing how these games still treat everyone like 6 year-olds without giving me the option to TURN THEM THE HELL OFF. Does that make me picky or elitist? Then so be it. Maybe other people are too easily pleased because they've been spoon-fed this console crap for so many years. Seriously; screw this nonsense. Screw it all the way back to 2005.

So you are a borders control officer in this simple looking game.
To begin you are checking passports - yeah that guys face matches his picture, passport number mhm... simple enough.
Daily you are assigned new tasks, soon immigrants require further paperwork which all must be checked and stamped so you know it isn't a forgery.  Then they require proof of vaccines as polio hits the country... then there are faces of the country's most wanted you must watch out for as well as doing your job.
The game becomes a test of your scrutiny and vigilance towards the documentation and dialogue as you approve or decline individuals and hope as you call "next" that a little print out doesn't appear on your desk telling you why the last person's checks were incorrect.
You are monitored!
To add further problems, you encounter various characters coming through your booth.
There is the chap who seems nice enough with his hand drawn passport but no you cannot just let through anyone!
Then there is the guy who dumps a bomb at your window!
Then there is the ever elusive order.  It is up to you how you deal with this vigilante group.  Do you support them with their promises to keep you safe or do you maintain your honesty and deny them their requests.
At the same time there is corruption and you are ordered by your superiors to let certain individuals through against the rules.
At the end of every day you go home with whatever scrapings you made from bribes, rewards and efficiency at your work.  You can save money by denying your family heat and food but they will get sick and you must pay for medicine.
This game for whatever reason is addictive!  I enjoy playing it and am curious to discover all 20 endings and somehow unlock the endless mode.  People complain about the price but for the hours you get out of it, it is not to be sniffed at.

Overall, I had a great time with Alien Isolation. It's based on the movie
rather than
, which is a welcome change. As such, this game focuses more on survival and stealth rather than combat.
As I worked my way through Sevastopol, my heart was racing as I was being stalked by the Xenomorph. Every blip from my motion tracker made me nervous, knowing that any of those blips could be the vicious and undefeatable Xenomorph on the hunt. Whenever I came across a synthetic or a Human, I had to ask myself "is the Xenomorph in the area" before firing my weapon. I had to be mindful of the noise I generated and always had to be on the lookout for places I could hide if the Xenomorph turned up.
I loved the art direction in this game. It's all based on the original 1979 movie. You've got CRT displays complete with curvature and distorted picture, incandescent lights, tape players, and old style keyboards like you would've seen in the movie
.
I thought the story was pretty good. When you first turn up on Sevastopol, you have no idea what's happening on the station. You're thrown into a nightmare and you have to move forward from there. Much of the story is told through a combination of dialogue and messages that you find on computer terminals and on tape.
My one complaint is that the Xenomorph's tendency to stick close to the player in some parts of the game means that you have to skip reading what's on some of the computer terminals. Spend too much time on a terminal when the Xenomorph is lurking nearby and you could be impaled by its tail. As a result, you miss some of the backstory, which is a shame since the game has a great story.
In closing, I would definitely recommend this game to fans of survival and stealth games as well as fans of the Alien movies.

Possibly the best game I have ever played (and i have played many in 20+ years of gaming....) The design is absolutely beautiful in a convincing retro style and very close to the first alien movie. The fact that you can only save here and there really makes the enemy encounters so much more horrifying. I was never so scared playing a game ever!! It really keeps you on the edge of your seat constantly. Sound design is stunning and supports the atmosphere a lot. Here too one can see that the dev team pulled in some original creators from the first movies props and sounds etc. The whole setting is just unbelievably charming in its own way. Alien AI is great as well and it's a ballsy and great decision to make the Alien unkillable (at least with the weapons you can get), this adds much to its terryfing nature. I couldnt think about one thing i would have changed on this game, its propably as close to a perfect alien game as we will ever get. Also, this is a rather long game. You will get a lot of fun (or rather terror), missions and playtime with this game.
I am usually not too keen on survival games but this has just the right amount of it without ever getting boring and you can also be creative in the way you use your arsenal of weapons and tools. Especially an absolute must for any fan of the Alien franchise!
My heartfelt thanks go out to the devs and all the ppl that made this game possible for giving me some of the most scary but fun hours of my gaming life :) and please continue to make such ballsy and quality games!!!!

Alien: Isolation comes across as a project that had a very clear direction from the start.  The Alien franchise has been mis-treated but Creative Assembly "gets it" and their focus paid off for the player.
What you get with Alien: Isolation are beautifully crafted 70's sci-fi environments, a single antagonist alien that really does terrify and gameplay mechanics that really do serve to both stay consistent to the franchise elements and help the player survive.  I understand what the developer was going for with the save system (no quick save, just terminals you have to find) and the alien behavior can be more predictable in certain situations, but this is splitting hairs on an overall excellent title.
I was engaged with the story and sincerely hope Creative Assembly have the opportunity to do similar titles in the future.
Highly recommended!

I recently spent 36 hours awake a couple weekends ago, playing Factorio. I kept glancing at the clock, and thinking about sleep... but there was just a bit more I could improve in my resource processing. Then one of my queues backed up and started misrouting material. Then I researched some improved belt layouts on the forums. Then I had to go out and clear out a bug infestation that had spawned near my base. Then one of the mining locations had petered out so I had to migrate the miners to a new lode. But before I could do that I had to manufacture ammo for the tank so I could clear out a big nest near the new copper mine. And then...
Well. Let's just say that the game throws a lot of problems at you, and leaves the solution up to you.
Factorio is a game that is deceptively passive. Build a base, mine some materials. No big deal, right? But it throws more and more complex problems at you, at the same time as it provides the tools you need to surmount those difficulties. And while in theory at the end of all this work you have a base that does everything for you, by the time you get close to that goal you realize that there are so many ways you could do it better and you start ripping out what you have built to redo it more efficiently, more compactly... and another 36 hours pass.
In the beginning, you hand mine some coal, iron, and rock. You build a few coal powered tools, and perhaps connect them directly to each other. Soon you may add belts and carry the material where it's needed, like from the coal field to your smelters next to your iron mine.
But the complexity ramps up. Early crafting requires only one or two ingredients, but later items may need four or more. Processing Oil requires pipes... unlike belts, pipes block movement and thus require more forethought in how they are laid out. Advanced items may need both parts and liquids to craft, necessitating more ingenuity in moving resources to where they are needed.
You also get access to fun tools that reduce some of the tedium of moving parts around as you advance through the tech tree. Expensive parts that require you have a comprehensive and efficient setup already to be able to afford to use.
Finally, the last thing I would like to note is that the graphics are only meh. But with an interesting caveat... while the sprites and graphics are dated, they are surprisingly effective at conveying information. Sound is used to great effect, providing subtle cues to how hard your engines are working. Small touches like the speed of bubbles moving in a pipe provide clear and immediate feedback on how your infrastructure is working... it's not just window dressing. And the User interface does a laudable job at conveying all the information you need to make accurate decisions, including very well done historical graphs for crafting and power.
Mod support is also excellent, with an active community of modders and well done steam integration.
The one bad thing though is very bad: multiplayer support. The networking code is horrible. Due to the nature of the game, it's possible it will never become good. If you are envisioning playing this game with your 10 friends on the same map turn around and leave now because anything beyond two player support requires a LAN connection to work reliably. This might get fixed in the future, but it's a big if, so if online multiplayer is your bag just pretend the game doesn't support it yet because the support it has is laggy, buggy, and unpleasant all around.
I
good multiplayer support. I have a group of friends, and building things together is one of our favorite activities (we met on Minecraft). We can't yet play a game of Factorio together, and that makes me very sad. I really hope this gets fixed.
But other than that... if single player is your thing, crafting bases gets you
engaged, and you love the idea of a game where optimizing your resource strategy is an involving and enjoyable task, then Factorio is probably the game for you. It might be early access, but it's already filled with dozens, if not hundreds of hours of gameplay.
Just try to keep your 36 hour marathons confined to your days off.

Everything about this game can be made your own. You can spawn a world with the exact resource specifications that you want, down to specific resource quantity and quality. You can have enemies more numerous or more sparse, and can even make them passive to only defend if you attack them.
