I've only played two arcs of the visual novel prior to this release, but I'm a huge fan of the anime, so take that into account with this review.  CLANNAD is a long-form visual novel that primarily details the life of delinquent high-schooler Tomoya Okazaki during his last years of school and his interactions with the people in the small town he lives in.   It's a comedy and drama mix, full of a hilarious and endearing cast of characters that you'll love to laugh and cry with.  It remains a poignant and enduring work today as a testament to the importance of "family," the impermanence of life, and the consequence of choice.  Great, upbeat songs that can get easily stuck in your head, accompanied by glorious somber pieces that encapsulate the feelings on screen. The art style is a bit of a turn-away for me personally, but it still has great backgrounds and is at least consistent in what it depicts.
On a more technical level, this game is a fairly traditional branching-path bishoujo game.  On a surface level you would expect this to be a very fanservice-heavy, "compliment girls to advance relationship" kind of setup, but for CLANNAD the dating sim elements are very toned down, there are no sex scenes, or really even any fanservice.  Certain routes even follow some of the male characters, who in my opinion are by-and-large much more interesting than some of the more archetypical/tropey female cast members.  Thankfully the more important characters seem to have the most screentime and longest routes.  "Gameplay" exists solely to continue the story in various directions, based on a few small options that lead the main character in a certain direction (for instance one involves simply going to talk to someone you see outside a window).  Most of the actual character interaction is done without player input, so don't expect much heavy moralizing on choices. Specific to this English version of the game is the "Dangopedia," which explains some of the more culturally-specific aspects of Japan, namely things like food, holidays, school life, etc. that us Westerners might not immediately understand.  And finally to those worried about the steep price, please note that CLANNAD is the eighth largest video game script in the world, and clocks in at 1.4 million words, almost a time and a half that of the ENTIRE Harry Potter franchise.
If you like to laugh, cry, and overall become emotionally attached to a great cast of characters, CLANNAD is a great entry into the visual novel genre, and works well in distancing itself from the more questionable aspects that could keep people away from them.  Though if I could recommend anything to you, it would be the anime. :)

I think it's about time for a fair review of this game.  Let me start by saying that I almost agree with the way it is marketed as a F2P.  I would recommend that the game should be put out as a FREE DEMO.  That would at least stop all these childish "Reviews" done by kids who don't have any money to support the developers.  Within the first 10 minutes of exploring this game you can tell that a lot of people put a lot of hard work into the amazing details of the enviornment.  Even the details in the audio are spectacular.  The gunshots sound LOUD and realistic.
You start off with a handheld device that maps your hike and allows you to identify various animal trackings such as hoof/paw prints and droppings as well as audio callings.  You can track one animal at a time by finding these track domes throughout the wilderness.  Once you started tracking one of these animals you will follow a brighter traking dome trail with the freedom to switch trails whenever you wish.  A lot of times, while you're tracking a mule deer, you will hear a different deer calling as you get closer to them and you have the option to switch tracks and start tracking this closer deer.  That is a nice feature to the hunt, because I have spent hours tracking a single deer, determined to get this specific deer only to find that I've made a mile long circle through the woods.  That can happen in real life though, so I'm not too frustrated with it.
My advice is, check it out and track a couple mule deer.  You may really like the layout of the game.  If you do, great, find an upgrade package that works for you or just explore the vast wilderness and keep tracking mule deer for free, or track other animals and take pictures of them instead of killing them.  I wouldn't mind paying $50 to play this massive game for a single year.  If you try the game and don't like it, what did it cost you besides some time and hard drive space?  Chances are you will enjoy this game if you're really looking for a good hunting game.  Just look at it as a DEMO, not a F2P.

As a big fan of the Alien movies, I was so excited to follow this game during development. There has been many alien games but none of them has really caught my interest until I saw this game.
If you are a fan of the Alien movies, you can stop reading this already and just buy the game. You will not be disappointed. In case you want to know why, or if you are not familiar with the Alien movies then by all means read on.
Remember that first time you saw Alien by Ridley Scott? A space vessel in the vast void of space, and the claustrophobic and terrifying experience that followed? The nightmarish Xenomorph and his hunt for the crew of the Nostromo?
This game takes us back, everything that this game presents is done by love for the original movie. That isolated and claustrophobic feel of space, the terror, the music, the feel and even the props used in the movie. This is as close to the original movie you can get, but with a uniqe story that even ties together with the Alien movies.
Without going too much into the story, you play as Amanda Ripley. The daughter of Ellen Ripley from the Alien movies. For a long time she's been searching for her missing mother, and it finally seems like a strong lead has come to her attention. She's being informed by a co-worker named Samuels that a commercial vessel named "The Anesidora" has recovered what they believe is the flight recorder unit of the Nostromo. The towing vessel where Ripley, Amandas mother was one of the crew.
The unit has been taking to Savastapool station, and a courier ship by the name of "USCSS Torrens" is heading there. Ripley is being invited to tag along, and from here on the story begins.
I'm having trouble puting into words how best to describe this game, where to start? First of all, there's a reason why It's so hard. It just needs to be experienced. To be completely honest I have never had a similar experience with any other game in the survival horror genre, this game is terrifying.
It's a game that just combines so many aspects of horror that it gives you such an intense immersion into the game. The atmospehere, the surroundings, the isolation, music that builds up suspense at the perfect moments. Everything is in perfect harmony to give you the best Alien expereince you could ever dream of.
When the end credits started rolling, I was completely exhausted. It's a rollercoaster ride of emotions, and It's one of the few games that has been able to scare me and make me sit on the edge of my seat as much as I did during this insane ride.
Like I said, if you are a fan of the first Alien movie, just buy this game. If you have never seen the movie but like horror survival in general, just want to get scared ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, and have a true horror experience, then buy this game. If you have a love for space, than that's just a plus.
+ Wonderful graphics, ambience and immersion.
+ A new unique story that ties together very well with the Alien franchise.
+ A perfect harmony of horror elements, to such a degree that I have never experienced anything like it.
+ A music score that stays completely true to the original movie.
+ Sound that makes u feel immersed in every single way, plays with your head, and that alters depending on what kind of situation you are experiencing in the game.
+ Very smart AI, that is scripted very well and which will react to you in unpredictable ways. (Especially the Alien itself).
+ A good amount of game-mechanics - crafting, blueprints and items that all have a purporse and usage.
+ Elements of immersion that takes you into a isolated space (Where no one can hear you scream) and gives you a TRUE Alien horror experience.
+ I bought this game at release at full price, and It was worth every penny. Getting this on sale is an epic win.
+ List goes on.
- Not the same experience with a bad Headset (I started playing in 2014, when I had a pretty bad headset and the game still scared me to death. With my new headset the effect is 100x better, and this game must be experienced with a decent headset.)
- The last 2 missions felt a bit dragged out, but it might be because of my total exhaustion. Could have been slightly shorter, and that's nothing I say too often. I enjoyed every second of the game though.
- A bit of annoying backtracking that could have been worked around, most of the times the backtracking works perfectly ok though. But I do think that some parts are a bit overwhelming.
- Some of the DLC is a bit of a luckluster, and tied to the survivor mode. I wish there were a tiny bit more expansions to the actual campaign. But that's just a minor thing.

Okay I make an exception here and write a review about Alien Isolation even though I have not finished it yet. But this game... holy cow.. okay, where to begin. This here is the very first game that TOTALLY catches the Alien spirit. It's a survival game, no shooter, no action Alien-vs-Predator stuff. You know it could be anywhere, it could wait for you behind each corner, often you even hear it move in the ventilation shaft, and you know very well that you are pretty much dead if it spots you. The game looks fantastic, the textures could have been taken from the original sets. From what I know, many of those actually are based on original movie stuff. The music too, oh the music is just as merciless as the alien itself. This is one of the few games that really make you feel scared if you ain't completly numb. Call me a wuss, but I personally only play from one checkpoint to the next in one go cause after that I just need a break! But in the end this space wuss is gonna blow the alien to kingdom-come!

The community for this game is extremely passionate with many guides and documentation it's nearly impossible not find a solution that isn't listed on the internet. Overall, this is a game that is extremely solid with a passionate community. So if you're looking a game with nearly unlimited replayability and want conquer alien nests for oil, this is the game for you!

I enjoyed Alien: Isolation as much as I have enjoyed the first Alien film. They are similar in so many ways that sometimes it feels the whole game is just fan service - but that would be wrong. The game stands out on its own and I'm sure people that are unfamiliar with the Alien universe are going to enjoy the game as much as the others.
It's survival horror without unnecessary complicated crafting systems (you can build tools like the Noisemaker, Molotovs, Medkits and Flashbangs that are all used on specific enemies and in specific situations), with enjoyable gameplay mechanics (you pretty much have to rely on the radar in order to stay alive), gorgeous art and sound design and an overall feel of great attention to detail - it seems the devs really gave their best to create a game that captures the Alien film's look and feel but at the same time make an enjoyable game, which rarely happens, especially with movie to game adaptations.
The game does things poorly on a couple of instances - sometimes the Alien's AI seems overly aggressive and it finding you seems unfair - there is a particular level where you have to evade humans, androids and the Alien at the same time and the number of times I died made me take a break and come back later. The game seems a bit too long (it took about 20 hours to finish the main campaign) and several levels could have been removed without damaging the overall quality of the game - they just felt tacked on and unnecessary.
However, the number of things Alien: Isolation does right makes it, in my opinion, a must buy for a) Alien fans (Scott Ridley's version of it, that is) and b) anyone else who enjoys horror games (though not that scary after the first deaths). The DLCs are basically scenes from the movie but there are some extra nuggets of lore in the form of audio logs / dialogues not in the movie (most of the cast comes back, except for Ash and Dallas).

The xenomorph is an iconic, popular horror figure.  Having been the titular monster in countless films, games, comics, and books, the sleek, black, slimy, acid-blooded perfect killing machine is as recognizable a slasher as the likes of Jason Vorhees, Freddy Kruger, and Michael Myers.  Being lumped in with that new class of terrors, it's easy to look at the nightmare from the mind of H.R. Geiger and forget why it was a thing of pure panic; we watched colonial marines mow them down by the dozens, it's been literally cloned into some stupid albino thing, it's fought Predators on more than one occasion... but that towering, silent, spiny stalker that can get into the walls and abduct you from the ceiling... Alien: Isolation gets it.
Continuing the tradition of “Alien” means a Ripley must be involved, Isolation ties directly into the first film with you playing as the daughter of Ellen “One Shot Swish” Ripley, Amanda.  You're coaxed into accompanying an investigation on the space station Sevestapol with the promise of answers to the disappearance of the USS Nostromo.  Using the time period and nepotism as a convenient excuse for fan service, most of the technology and environments look like they're ripped stripped straight out of the 1979 sci fi/horror classic.  CRT monitors display black and green text, there are plenty of giant red buttons and ducts that probably serve no purpose, and you save your game on a giant, corded phone.  It's part art asset museum, part “what if...” sequel, and it works incredibly well to set the tone.
Of course things go downhill almost immediately once you arrive at the station; things break and explode, communications are predictably cut off, the locals have turned into crazed survivalists, and the security androids do what A.I. tends to do in these stories.  Luckily Ripley is a master class engineer and born survivor like her mother, so you're tasked with breaking things that need to be broken and fixing things that need fixin'.  From a gameplay standpoint this means Metroidvania-like objectives that require you to find and upgrade tools to progress or unlock optional areas, and plenty of smart mini-games to hack into '70s future computers.  The game is really good about presenting you with screens and challenges that initially look like gobbledygook, but make sense after poking around and understanding the mechanical language of the station.  It's certainly true to form for the genre, where people just hit buttons and pull levers while a countdown is happening... you'll do that more than a few times in Alien: Isolation.
Stealth is your best option for survival as you navigate around hostile humans, droids, and maybe something more dangerous... spoiler: I mean the ♥♥♥♥ing alien.  The early hours of the game have you observing patrol patterns of enemies, hiding under desks and in lockers, hoping they don't spot you and murder you in a few shots or a robotic stranglehold.  Avoiding the humanoid threats is okay, serviceable first person stealth; it's fairly predictable and can be cheesed rather easily.  You do get weapons to defend yourself eventually, but direct combat is either a last ditch resort or a special case scenario.
So the game is a slow burn at first.  Then a wild xenomorph appears... and holy♥♥♥♥♥♥  The entire game seems built for the sole purpose of being a♥♥♥♥♥♥your pants as you're being hunted by the alien simulation, because it works so well.  You've seen the thing a thousand times before, but from a first person perspective, knowing any noise you make can send it pouncing for a brutal one hit kill, seeing the back spines rise from above a desk or it's goo dripping from a vent above... it's seriously terrifying.  It also helps that they made it incredibly loud, too.  You'll hear it stomping around in the vents like an elephant, screeching like nails against a chalkboard if it spots you... even when you don't see it, you know it's a constant threat.  Even closing an elevator door or waiting for a save to register doesn't guarantee your safety, and it's this ever-present, singular monster that's seemingly playing it's own game in tandem with yours that elevates Alien: Isolation into something special.  It's a horror game that's actually horrifying.

A lot of you are probably like me and heard about how bad this game was when it first came out.  A couple of months ago, however, I heard from some friends that the developers have been working hard on fixing a lot of the launch issues.  Then finally, "One Tamriel" update came out, and I thought I would finally give this game a shot.
This game, in my opinion, is one of the best MMORPGs you can play in this day and age.  It effortlessly merges some of the best designs and elements of other popular MMORPGs together yet stands in a unique untouched area that sets it apart from anything else on the market.  Let me break it down.
1) Exploration: 10/10
This is, by far, the strongest point of this game to me, and it is my reason for why this game is unique.  With the One Tamriel update, this game now uses a fancy, balanced, yet intuitive level scaling system that is similar to Guild Wars 2.  The game now feels like a proper Elder Scrolls game (but a lot better in the level scaling than stuff like Oblivion).  You can go anywhere, do anything, and attempt any danger.  This both encourages exploration but also allows high level players to revisit old zones, help with their friends, or explore other starting zones.  All in all, this added tons of gameplay and strengthed the community.
2) Combat/Classes/Builds
The action combat in this game is a blend of Guild Wars 2, Tera, WoW, and Elder Scroll games.  It's flash at times, yet realistic in others.  It is both simple to learn yet complex to master.  While there are "metabuilds" each classes can adhere to, for 99.999% of the game, you do not need to follow cookie-cutter builds.  As long as you do your research and have a good understanding of the game, the flexibility and incredible arsenal of skills you can use to customize is truly incredible.  Any classes can be any builds, and there are diversity on top of that.  Even the way they incorprated the classic Tank-Healer-DPS is interesting, and all of that is further boosted by the interestingly designed dungeons, worldbosses, and events.
3) Payment model, community, and others
You pay the game once, and you do not have to pay for anything else.  The ESO-Plus subscription is nice to have, but it is not at all necessary.  All the stuff you can buy with real money are cosmetics, as they should be, and most of them can be aquired through in game currency.  Unlike games like Black Desert, you are still able to fully customize and create some very cool "fashion" outfits without paying a single cent after purchasing the game.
With the One Tamriel update, the game has steered hard into friendly co-op mode, and you can see this in the community.  People are generally very kind to each other, and since there are no competition in exp or quests, players are often happy to see another running by.
tl;dr-
If you want a world worth exploring, diverse and flexible classes, incredible pvp (which I didn't get to touch on), and well designed group content, this game is for you.
Especially considering how cheap the buy to play price is, this is a steal for anyone who like Elder Scroll games, MMORPGs, or even just exploration/immersive worlds.

Finally, the wait is over! After a year of anticipation and throwing almost all my money at the Kickstarter campaign, our beloved Clannad is here! All you VN lovers should already know that Clannad is a universally-acclaimed masterpiece. But for those who don't know much (or anything) about it, know this: it's one hell of a rollercoaster ride. Clannad will have you laughing, crying, happy, angry, and a whole slew of other emotions. In fact, Clannad (both the anime series and the VN) is the only story that has truly made me empathize with the characters and relate to it in my own life. I dare say it to be a life-changing experience if you open your heart.
While Clannad is almost always described as a romance game, there is so much more than that. While there is a lot of romantic material, Clannad offers an endless ocean of life lessons around family, friends, overcoming hardship, making excruciating decisions, dealing with change, and much more. Clannad really made me take a deep look into my own life and helped me overcome many personal barriers relating to my own family and friends. It has positively influenced my outlook in many areas of my life and I will forever be grateful for it.
Even if you don't think you would enjoy it much, do yourself a favor and pick it up. And if you already previously played it, buy it on Steam! Compared to the original Full Voice version, it has so many new enhancements that warrant playing it again (as if the story alone wasn't enough!). The HD assets, Steam achievements, and Dangopedia are all big bonuses to me. The only things missing are trading cards and emoticons.
And lastly, join the Clannad steam group for all your Clannad needs! We're active and very friendly and love discussing all things Clannad (as well as other games, anime, etc.). You could say we're Steam's very own Big Dango Family! Also, if you ever want to talk about Clannad, feel free to friend/message me! ( ' ' )
Here we go again...

Not only is CLANNAD one of the most memorable visual novels I have ever had the pleasure of reading, it is also what really got me hooked on the entire medium itself. If you are a fan of the drama/slice of life & romance genre I recommend you give CLANNAD a go, you will smile, you will laugh, you will love & you will cry.

Call of Juarez Gunslinger
I loved the first Call of Juarez games, I remember the day the first game came out, I just sat and played it for hours until I finished it,
It was amazing! I just loved the western feel, and I also loved the second one :)
but... after the cartel... I was afraid they lost it, until I saw this game! and I knew they're back!
Story
The story is about this old bounty hunter named Silas Greaves, it all begins when Silas enters a Saloon and starts telling his story...
Silas's story is how he met\dueled\killed real outlaws from the Wild West, outlaws like Billy The Kid, Jesse James and more... all in the sake of revenge...
Graphics
I loved the graphics, it's not BF4 or Metro, it's more like Borderlands 2, they tried to make it like a cartoon, since the whole game is being told by Silas,
The cut scenes are like comic book pages, anyways, the game got really sweet graphics, for me, it worked!
Gameplay
Gunslinger is a FPS with touches of RPG, set in the Wild West, so you know what you'll get... and they deliver it!
The game is packed with gun fights, where you run in the old wild west towns, deserts, moving trains, mountains, mines and more,
the RPG part is that you have 3 trees that you can choose from, Desperado, Trapper and Ranger, The Desperado class focuses on two revolvers, Ranger uses his Lever-Action rifle and the trapper uses Shotgun and dynamites,
each level you get a point you can spend to each class, after 6 skill points invested in each class you get a legendary weapon, which is just a better revolver\shotgun\rifle
each chapter you face a boss which is an historical figure as i said above, for instance, in the first mission you face off Pat Garret,
when you face those bosses, you enter a duel, which is pretty cool too, they've made it really nice!
they also have a bullet-time effect, where you gain concentration after killing your enemies just like the old Call Of Juarez games.
Ok, so I'll just summarize this, the gameplay is just great! i mean, the shootouts are great, it's full of action, and if you love the wild west like i do, this is the game for you!
Conclusion
I hope they'll make more like this!
The game is just amazing, well made, bug-free, full of action and fun, they deliver the atmosphere of the wild west, from the narration to the scenery and to the guns and foes.
the game is pretty short actually, about 10 chapters, and it took me about 7 hours to finish it, but hey, it's 15$ so for that price is a steal imo,
there is also an arcade mode that you can play which has 10 levels, the arcade mode is another game that you need to make combos to reach high score and compete with friends.
So, after they made the Cartel game and failed big time, they redeemed them self with this great game imo, I can't wait for them to make more games like this!
and if you didn't play this one yet, but it now! and play it now!

This game, what can I say.
It shows great promise. It could be an amazing sandbox game that's totally player driven. There is definitely a place for roleplay. It has great graphics, especially for early access, the textures are nice, the block placement system works, the progression is good. There is room for some awesome content to make the game even better.
But it has a problem. A glaring problem. A game breaking issue.
Hackers.
There is no protection against hackers. You could dump hours and hours into this game, you could convince your friends to join you, start a guild, build a castle, become king, then boom. All those hours are wasted, because a hacker decided to join the server and destroy all your hard work for a laugh and there's nothing you can do about it. I had been having fun with the game for the most part, but each server I went to ended up the exact same way. With a hacker teleporting into your base and killing you from behind, insta-killing you, chaning your color to fluorescent ones, making your character fat, spawning a trebuchet in front of your base and destroying you and your hard work. On and on it goes, ever server is the same way. It's pointless. There's no such thing as an RP server, unless you manage to get into a whitelisted one, good luck.
I cannot in good conscience recommend this game to anyone as long as hackers can easily get in and destroy everything. I wouldn't have a problem with someone legitimately beating you in battle and destroying your castle, that makes sense. That's expected. But this game has the same issues as every other sandbox mmo, and that is the community itself.

Russian Horror Story is a true story made into a visual novel, but will you want to experience it ?
Russian Horror Story follows on a man named Ivan, he finds his downstairs neighbors making too much noise and when he investigates he finds out they are plotting to kill him.
I could keep this review short and call this game a piece of garbage and leave it at that, but I think I should explain a bit more.
The art style is really weird. While I don't love it, I don't hate it as well. It's okay-ish.
Now I was intrigued by the concept because of the true story aspect and not to mention some truly messed up stuff happened in Russia ( like the granny killer).  I tried digging around  to find the true story it was based on and my research led me to a web series named Russian Reality. I have no idea what the videos are about since all of them are in Russian, but I believe it's highly controversial ( I'm not entirely sure so don't hate me for this), because of the massive amount of reaction videos.
The story does have choices you can choose and it affects the story. Now the game has 8 endings in total. 2 of them being good endings and 6 being bad endings. Now the endings end up being normal to incredibly over the top.
The reason the game is terrible is the horrific English translation. It's the worst translated game I have seen period. The story makes no sense at all, not to mention the entire game the terrible translation will haunt you. Unless you speak Russian and can experience the game in the native language otherwise just don't even bother.
There's also a really poorly made space shooter, but you rather stay far far away from that. The horrible controls make it really hard to play.
In the end Russian Horror Story is only for people who speak Russian. If you don't speak it stay far away from this disaster.
UPDATE:
Recently the developer added an updated translation and guess what ? IT ACTUALLY MAKES SENSE.
It's amazing that the developer listened to the community and fixed it, but this still has the negative review for the story as it's still very mediocre and not really worth the asking price.
UPDATE 2:
Turns out I was wrong, the developer only fixed the main endings and left a few of the other ones unfixed. So that means only 50% of the game is fixed. Big thanks to virotti for poiting this out.
Final Rating:
3/10 - Terrible

Have you ever wanted to build a city-sized factory spewing out pollution from all that burning coal? One with turrets to shoot any natives trying to attack your pollution-spewing strip mines?   Of course, you have!
Factorio is a building / crafting / logistics management game. Despite being listed as Early Access, it is complete and bug-free.
To give a tiny flavor of gameplay, one early task many players perform is to automate the production of green science packs. To make one, you need to find some iron ore which is extracted (possibly with an electric drill), smelted (possibly with a steel smelter), turned into a gear wheel, and combined with another plate to make a transport belt (you probably used a bunch to move all that ore and plate around). Oh, you also need copper ore to turn into copper plate to turn into copper wire to turn into electronics (with yet more iron plate) to make an inserter (very handy device). The inserter combines with the transport belt to make a green science pack. Now connect a bunch of factories and converyers and inserters together so you can make a pack per second since research needs a lot of them.  Oh, and you can also make plastics from petroeum gas, electric engines for flying robots, a tank to drive around, power amour, trains, ....
The game is under active development; the developers have weekly blogs giving hints of what they are up to. But even if the developers decided right this second that Factorio would never receive any more updates, it is worth the money for anyone that likes crafting / base building / sandbox kinds of things.

Factorio is a thinking man's game. From the time I've spent with it, I can immediately see why there are so many positive reviews. There is always a better way to do what you're trying to accomplish, and the tools to do so are always at your disposal. It's a learning process that doesn't seem to cease nearly as quickly as in other games of these genres you could say this game taps into. If you're reading this review, my guess is that you will be happy you spent 20 bucks on this game no matter how much time you spend with it. This game is worth it

Another masterpiece by Supergiant.
Darren Korb may have just created the best soundtrack to any game. Add to that one of the best combat mechanics I've experienced in a long time, and the incredible visuals and story, and you've got what can only be described as a perfect game.
YES.

A wondeful combination of 2D Isometric art style with an emotive sound track. It's a game that a great experience to have. Unlike some other "art games", it also have really good gameplay. Almost similar to Bastion, it has action slashy-smashy gameplay, but also the unqiue mechanic of "Planning".
Pause time an plan your next moves. Movement on the battlefield and executing abilities eats up alloted "Turn Time". You can undo any actions and replan at any point during the pause. When you're happy, execute your plan. The whole world will mostly wait as you stab and wreck at hyper speeds. After, simply wait for your "Turn Bar" to recharge before "Plan"ning again.
The narrative is around you. The exposition isn't heavily in your face. It's drip fed to your nicely through the environment. If you want to know more about the personalities of the world, you can read an expanding biography of them. But it's not crucial. You can get a statisfactory story experience playing through.
This game is heavier on the RPG than Bastion was. You can switch in and out abilities in up to 4 ability slots. Other abilities can be attuned as "Passives" that affect one of your skills (kinda like Runes in Diablo 3 or World of Warcraft) or as a Passive for yourself (More damage. Chance when you enter Planning Mode to Transcend gaining the ability to deal heavy AOE damage or taking less damage passively. Each Active ability has a maximum of 2 Passive slots. You also have a limited about of "Memory" that caps how many skills you can equip at once. Levelling up gives you access to more Abilities and choosing if you want to increase your Memory's capacity or unlocking more Passive slots.
If you enjoyed Bastion, you will enjoy this game.
If you haven't played Bastion, but enjoyed playing Dragon Age 1, you will probably enjoy the game. I felt the Planning Mode was similar to pausing during Dragon Age 1. It lets you review the battlefield at your own pace and strategically plan your moves. Later on in the game, it benefits you to enter planning mode at the right time, as opposed to entering it when ever it's off cooldown.
Otherwise, maybe watch some lets plays to decide if it's the game for you.

Another game by the creators of Bastion. You have no idea how hyped I was. It has the same hand-painted 2D-looking isometric art style as Bastion, but it's set in a futuristic cyberpunk setting. The game looks absolutely beautiful the whole way through. Everything is stylized so nicely, even the HUD and menus. Again, they managed to get a lot of emotion and power in a relatively simple narration. The ending is sad, but simultaneously beautiful and heart warming. You also get thrown into the game without getting explained much of the story and world in the beginning. Actually, throughout most of the game I didn't really properly understand what was going on in this plot. But this only adds mystery to it, and makes you want to continue. This also makes it impossible to describe the plot without spoiling anything. It's basically about a robotic force called the Process, and they're corrupting the city. Your goal is to stop the organization behind this, to save the city from corruption but also for other personal reasons.
The gameplay is similar to that of Bastion, yet it isn't as much of an action RPG anymore. You can still run around and use skills in real time, but it's far less effective than entering planning mode, which freezes time and lets you plan moves which are then executed quickly when you leave planning mode. But some builds or specific skill actually work better when used in real time, or before entering planning mode to amplify one or several of the skills you will use then. Using the planning mode will put your skills in a cooldown for a few seconds, which can be very disadvantageous. Overall it's a very good and refreshing combat system. The skill system in this game is really awesome and offers a lot of freedom. In Bastion you could upgrade each weapon a few times and have a special ability. Here you can choose from about 20 abilities, which can be used in three different ways. You can have a skill on your active hot bar, or as an upgrade to another skill, or as a passive skill. In each of these ways of use, they will have a different effect, but it will still be in the same category. I love this skill system, and you can really do what you want with it. It gives you potential for so many crazy combos. There is a memory limit which you can't exceed though, so you can't go overboard unless you're a high level.
If you want to get better at this gameplay or try skills in a different way, you can try doing challenges which test your planning, speed and survival skills. They're located in an area which reminded me of the Bastion. Your pet goes there, you can do these challenges, interact with things, or just mull some thoughts while laying in a hammock. It's your own little place.
The music in this is amazing too, which was to be expected. In both Transistor and Bastion, the music fits the theme perfectly, but Transistor's music is better in general if you'd listen to it without having played the game. A design choice that's just genius is that your character can hum. She used to be a singer, but she lost her voice, and thus can only hum now. Best part of this, is that it's always in sync or in a rhythm fitting the song which is currently playing in the background. A simple feature like this gives her character so much soul already. But Supergiant Games have always been really good at making compelling stories and likable characters with little things like this.
If there's ANYTHING negative I can say about this game, then it's that it's too short. I completed my first playthrough in six and a half hours, while also doing a bunch of the challenges already. But every amazing game is too short.

Warning: Disliking this game (and this review) is punishable by death.
Methods of execution include being kicked out of a tall building by Tomoyo, being forced to listen to Kotomi playing the violin until your head explodes, run over by Kyou's scooter, and eating nothing but Sanae's bread for the rest of your life. However, if you do not wish to die, you can instead be allowed to live and make a happy life for yourself. But instead of execution, your punishment will be to have your happy life collapse around you, with you being forced to watch those you love and care for most die before your eyes without being able to do anything to help them.
So dislikers, what will you choose as your punishment?
Anyway, CLANNAD is one of those classic VN's that, until now, has never been officially translated. It did recieve a critically acclaimed anime adaptation, and if you have seen that you can basically look at this game as being the "unabridged version". This game is quite old now (2004), so some might find the art a little odd, but the story itself is superb and at the core of why this game, and the anime that spawned from it, are considered among the best ever made.
As for the price tag... it is pretty damn steep. Too steep some would say for a VN, and I'll respect the decisions of those who decide that the current 50$ cost is just too much for what is essentially a story game with some voices and anime drawings. But there is one thing I do have to say about the cost: This is one of the largest game stories ever created. I don't know for sure, but around 80+ hours is the generally accepted figure given for how long it takes to beat this game. That means, at a price of $50, you will be recieving ~96 minutes of game for every dollar you spend. It might be a visual novel, but that is still a hell of alot more bang for your buck than most Triple-A game releases these days.

This is without a doubt the pinnacle of romantic visual novels. Clannad tells a deep story that unlike 90% of visual novels on Steam, doesn't value fanservice more than story and character development.
In terms of presentation it's great. The artstyle may be hit and miss to some people, however there is a charm to the aesthetic, even if it's a bit odd at first glance. The music is really good and helps to set the mood of the scenes being shown and the voice acting is very good, even if the protagonist isn't voiced like he was in the anime.
Clannad is an incredibly long visual novel, in fact it's one of the longest visual novels available. Each route in the first half of Clannad takes around 5-12 hours to complete, depending on the route and reading speed.
The second half of Clannad, which unlocks after completing all the routes of the first half, is easily the greatest part of the visual novel, even if mostly because most of the impactful moments happen during that half. In total Clannad probably takes around 100+ to complete fully.
I will say that it probably wont be everyone's cup of tea. There isn't much violence or sexual innuendo in Clannad, as it's focused primarily on telling a captivating romance story. It's a very family oriented story, as that is the main theme of the visual novel.
if you are interested in Clannad, there is also an anime adaptation that faithfully follows most of the routes (although omitting some of them completely, even omitting an entire character.)
Overall if you enjoy visual novels, I can highly recommend Clannad. It's incredibly long, but none of the story routes are particularly bad, so it shouldn't be a chore to read.

Clannad was and still is one of the best visual novels even after 10+ years since its original release. Clannad blends a fun slice of life school setting with emotional drama and romance. Combined with a stellar soundtrack and pretty CG this makes the formula for a great game and a lot of tears. Those looking to only complete a couple of arcs might see that the high price isn't justified and should wait for a sale as I don't see 8 hours of gameplay is worth. Those who are commited to reading everything the game has to offer will be rewarded with one of best stories ever written with about 100 hours of content.
Clannad is about Tomoya Okazaki, (or whoever you name the MC) a teenage boy who is struggling to find meaning in his life with his high school days slowy disappearing. One day on his way to school, he meets a strange girl, Nagisa. He sees her attempting to motivate herself to go to school and keep moving through life as well as talking to herself, asking herself how to move forward when everything changes. Tomoya befriends her and the visual novel revolves around Tomoya and his adventures with him and his friends in this slice of life novel. I really don't want to spoil anything and recommend you play if without any spoilers. If you didn't watch the anime I highly recommend playing this first and then watch the anime after.
Clannad has one of the best original soundtracks ever, beautiful art and CG, and one of the bests characters and stories for a game. If you're looking for a waifu game you'll like this game, but the game gets more deep than that after multiple arcs and playthroughs. Each main arc generally revolves around a girl and each arc has it's own story and not a variation of the same story. You can pour about 100+ hours into this game just to experience every arc and every arc is different with different characters focused on and the main plot and driving action being different. This is almost like 10 novels in one, so there replay value after you finish an arc is huge. I recommend this for anyone looking for a visual novel or want to start reading visual novels
-The characters are extremely lively and unique. From your best friend, to the the boys dorm manager. Most of the characters you will end up liking by the time their arc is over. Some of the character arcs are lively fun and full of laughter and some will ultimately make you sob. The overall story is beautiful and I think everyone should experience every arc including the After Story arc which is unlocked after finishing every arc. Even after finishing the main After Story, you'll need to play it a couple more times. And every time you do you'll need more tissues.
-Gameplay is you basic visual novel gameplay. There are very few interactables and even those are simple. You get to make A LOT of choices though. These choices aren't your typical go hang out with waifu B to end up with her in the end. The choices you make impact the game a lot and some arcs require specific actions to complete and you might get a "bad ending" as a result which might turn people off. I recommend a guide if you get stuck because it'll be fustrating to get "bad endings." But try to play the game without spoilers. If you watched the anime then go ahead and use a guide. The anime grazed through the arcs pretty fast so there's still a lot unexplored content for you to go through even though you know the main plot. At it's best, you're laughing at all the shananigans and hi-jinks you and you're friends get into. You'll also be crying because the writing allows you to connect with almost all of the characters and you'll generally feel for them. At it's worst which is rare, you'll be reading long passages where nothing significant is happening or you're reading over a passage you already read. (Skip previously read text feature, helps a bit with this) Overall, reading this novel is enjoyable and I found myself changing who's my favorite girl each time I finish an arc.
-The music sets the tone for the game very well. Each track sets the mood of the situation almost perfectly and it intensifies the experience. Clannad is has one of the best OST in video games and is up there with TWEWY and Persona 4
Clannad changed my life. I got into visual novels when I was about in middle school and this novel helped me find meaning in life. I recommend this novel to anyone who was like me, who went to a new school and didn't know anyone and anyone who struggles to find a reason to keep going or don't know what they're going to do with their life. I generally recommend this game to everyone. I gaurentee it will affect your life in some small way.
Overall I give this game a 10/10. The beautiful music and CG along with a well written story make this one of the best visual novels ever.

No, this is not a game featuring an Irish band. Or Enya.
CLANNAD is a popular Japanese visual novel that was originally released in 2004, developed by a company called Key. Having been translated to English by fans in the past, this is the first official English release, courtesy of a Kickstarter started by Sekai Project in 2014. This iteration includes HD visuals (which I believe are from the PS3 version), Dangopedia (to explain Japanese terms, culture etc.) and Steam achievement support.
I am not going to say very much about the story at all because it is extremely spoiler heavy, so beware of looking up almost anything to do with the series if it is new to you. It is difficult to specify an exact genre, but drama, romance, slice of life and supernatural all fit rather appropriately.
The Steam tag of “Story Rich” could not be more apt. The word count of CLANNAD surpasses a number of books (combined) in classic literature. That does not automatically make it great, but this volume of text feeds and gives flavour to the many rich and different story arcs and endings that are available within the game. This means there is well in excess of over 100 hours if you want to read and see absolutely everything. CLANNAD is not a kinetic visual novel so this means gameplay requires you to make many decisions throughout the game which will impact the story.
The story is an emotional rollercoaster like no other and never falls short in the ‘feels’ department. As a result, I would struggle to see how the game and story could not have an impact on your future outlook in life. Yes, it’s that good.
Character development is of the very highest calibre and you can simply not help but admire and love all of the different characters; feeling and sympathising for them as they suffer through various trials and tribulations. There are of course, some stereotypical characters traits, but character individuality is strong and always shines through.
The graphical style is excellent with plenty of variation in computer graphics (CG) throughout the game. Environments are colourful and vibrant which fit well to the various settings and key points in the game and some are nothing sort of stunning. Having said that, I do personally still prefer the art style from the animation by Kyoto Animation in comparison to the art in this game; even though it is the original source material.
CLANNAD is lavished by a soundtrack which, in my opinion, is the best feature of the game and one of the greatest soundtracks of all time. Jun Maeda crafted some of the most beautiful music ever written to fit both the ups and downs of the game. There are so many wonderful tracks, with outstanding piano pieces such as 同じ高みへ (To The Same Heights) and 小さなてのひら (The Palm of a Tiny Hand). There are many other great tracks composed by other staff at Key, such as 空に光る (Shining in the Sky) and 潮鳴り (Roaring Tides), but again – a big warning about spoilers when seeking these out, because the Internet and YouTube in particular, is flooded with them.
I spotted a review online once which quoted: “CLANNAD is the greatest story ever across all genres and media”. I couldn’t agree more with this and the fact that the Kickstarter smashed its stretch goals is no coincidence.
Visual novels are (finally) breaking through and gaining popularity in the west so I can understand some people might stumble across this and be highly apprehensive given the price point and type of minimalistic gameplay that a visual novel usually involves. Therefore, if you are not convinced enough to buy the game then, please; at least do yourself a favour and go and watch the animation (the one by Kyoto Animation). After 40+ episodes your transformation will be complete and you will then come back to buy and enjoy the game.

Let's just start off by getting this out of the way. YES, the English translation is very bad. To the point of being indecipherable at times. However, these jumbled messes add a bit of charm to this game. At times it can be hard to understand certain references if you're not familiar with Russian culture. If you spend a little time you can usually understand the just, of what the translator had intended to say.
Now to move onto what I enjoyed about this game. It does do some very interesting things for all it's faults. The way it potrays the dreary, decaying, atmosphere and seedy characters, makes you think of Moscow itself as the real monster in this horror story. It's obvious your character has very strong feelings for Soviet era. Longing back to what he perceives as the pinnacle of societies. Only to awaken everyday to face a totally alien and modern nightmare. The game uses psychology instead of cheap parlor tricks to create a constant sense of uneasiness. Big budget horror games could actually learn a lesson or two from this rather simple game.
I like the art style but the music is nothing to special. The game is very short as well. I managed to unlock all the endings in about 30 or 40 minutes.
This game is supposedly based on certain true events. It's hard to tell how much if any of this is true. Although it just kind of adds to the interest an mystery by trying to dig up the real truth.
If you can get past the translation faults, I would recommend buying this game. Especially if you're looking for something a little more bizarre and unusual than what you'd normally find in a horror visual novel.

At its core, its a hack and slash mixed with some tactical elements into it.  A solid base, if rather simplistic.
The reason WHY you need to play this game?
Art.
Narrator.
Music.
Mood.
Art:  Not graphics, but ART.  The visuals just set this apart in a way that is rare in games.  There are no FMVs, realistic 3d graphics, or even a next-gen graphics.  Instead, the scenery and design of ... well everything is just wonderful.
Narrator: This is simply a rarity in games, a spoken narrator and a good one at that.  The ONLY game that beats this and Bastion in this is Quest for Glory IV, and its tough to beat John Rhys-Davies as your Narrator and some improv jokes in it.  Just ... just turn up the volume or put on headphones and Listen as you play the game.
Music: ...... Get those Headphones or Turn up the Volume even further.  The musical score is wonderful and sometimes when you get to a nice spot to look at, Hold TAB and enjoy.
Mood:  Not story, which is kinda simplistic and predictable to be honest, but the MOOD.  Dark, Melancholy, Hopelessness hidden by bravado and dreams.  Its a lovely setting that fits the emotions it evokes as you play along.

It's hard to describe this game without using the word "beautiful" at least several hundred times, along with other adjectives, such as "amazing", "addicting", and "magnificent". I'm shocked how some people don't realize its true intentions as rather a story you are thrown into to experience first hand. I'll try to explain this further with no spoilers:
The beginning throws you straight into the game; no main menu, no background story, nothing. I had to YouTube the game just to make sure I hadn't accidently skipped an intro cutscene, but sure enough, what I was seeing was the way it was intended to begin. Already, I was impressed.
Gameplay felt comfortable. No stretching my tiny, feminine fingers out to reach oddly specific keys. Mouse controls were smooth and responsive. I never had a problem getting stuck on anything or walking into walls. My first time playing through I obviously relied on the Turn() aspect of the combat quite a bit, but towards the end and on my second time around, I realized the benefits of using both styles of combat, using the real time more for specific enemies that either evaded the effects of Turn() or were not of importance to waste it on. The key feature of applying Functions as a normal active function, an upgrade, or a passive stat was genius and allows for any person's unique fighting strategies. With how flexible the combat is, I'm surprised people have complaints about it.
The characters and dialogue of the entire game were enthralling and immersive. I felt highly connected with Red's character, and knew so much about her despite her ailment. That never stopped her character from shining through. Her sassy yet proper attitude was visible in her actions, not to mention how weak and afraid she truly was. She didn't have the amazing super strength to lift such a giant sword all the time. It would constantly dragged behind her, but she would gather her little strength to unleash amazing attacks, usually having to lift herself and the sword back up off the ground afterwards. She was constantly playing with her hair and adjusting herself, but obviously was not too absorbed in her looks, seeing that she tore such a beautiful ball gown to shreds for the sake of being able to run. Mr. Nobody, as he titles himself at an early point and what I prefer to call him since, no, he is not the Transistor itself, still shines through despite not even having a body. His voice acting is absolutely amazing. Every word meant something. Some lines made tears well up in my eyes. He had attitude as well, much more sarcastic and joking, but he was just as believable as Red.
The story, while I won't say much, was just beautiful. It's never what you expect, but not hard to follow along with. I will say the trailer gives false ideas and practically lies about the true story. Playing this blind is an amazing experience. Do me a favor and when Mr. Nobody starts talking, don't cut him off. Let him speak. All the dialogue means something in the story and if you cut him off, you could lose so much of the true story and not understand things in the future. A lot of playthroughs on YouTube do this. Don't cut off the experience for yourself. Take the extra time to sit there and just listen.
The music is just fantastic, and the little hum you can play for each track gives it a new spin and practically makes it a different song. All the music is addicting and plays perfectly along side the gameplay. The music is mellow and slow, so you never feel rushed in a battle, making the combat feel smooth and relaxed rather than frantic. The music is meant to calm you in the fray of battle and does so quite well. The art speaks for itself. Even if you hate the game, you can't deny its beauty. Everything looks hand painted. The 3D models are high definition, to the point where Red's facial expressions are visible. I'm simply obsessed with the artistic style they chose.
Final boss and ending sequence brought me to tears. I sobbed like a little girl, but for good reason, so don't judge. I had been near tears for most of the game due to its music and voice acting and the end pulled the final strings to my heart. It has been a very long time since a game has done this for me. I will ask you all again something here; if you beat it, when it asks you to play the recursion, at least watch the intro again. If the slight secret difference in the intro does not compel you to play more, than I'm not sure what will.
To be blunt, I'm kind of an expert on this game. I've been tracking it since its announcement at E3, watched all the demos and trailers, received it on the release day, have the soundtrack on my phone, and at the time of posting this I have racked up about 14 hours on the game. I will say if you're expecting a casual game of the typical demographic of 13-17 year old boys, this has no time for you. This game requires patience, attention, and heart. It is not the game's fault if you do not feel the need to provide it with these then seek to trash it for "not being good enough". Before you judge it, follow my suggestion of listening to all the dialogue and at least attempt to finish it. The game should take someone who is not rushed about 10 hours; not long at all. This game is a story and an experience, not something you can mindlessly blow through.
My final rating is 10/10, simply because it brought me to tears not once, not twice, but three times, and I'll happily cry again just to play through it once more to immerse myself in its beautiful story.

was my favourite game of 2011. So you could say I was highly anticipating
next release -- which was revealed to be
in 2013. After a long and patient wait, I've completed Transistor and I would like to share some of my thoughts and perhaps answer how it stacks up to Bastion.
The story revolves around a character called
, who seems to be a singer superstar in the city of Cloudbank. After Red wakes up from an assassination attempt by a sinister group of high ranking public figures known as
and realising her voice was also stolen... Red pulls The Transistor out of a mysterious body next to her, and attempts to unravel what exactly happened to her. Little does she know though, that The Transistor can talk, and actually seems to know her. As Red starts to make her way out of the district, she is attacked by an army of robotic intelligences known as
, who seem to be controlled by The Camerata.
The story is more abstract, subtle and darker this time. I would say the story is not as immediatetely likeable as Bastion's story -- as the narrator for Bastion basically narrated and spelled everything out for you in a clearer way. In Transistor, the narrator is also your companion,
. You are more encouraged to explore the world this time to find out more about Cloudbank's lore instead of relying on the narrator.
What is amazing is how the story also mechanically ties into the gameplay . You come across various slain characters in the story that you absorb into The Transistor, gaining new abilities. Abilities are multifaceted, so each ability can be used as an active/upgrade/passive and can be mixed and matched for some cool possibilities. You unlock character lore by using each ability in one of the 3 types of slots. It's quite a brilliant and elegant way of doing lore if I must say so myself.
You have 4 ability slots which can be upgraded (via leveling up) to have 2 upgrade slots each and you can also unlock 4 passive slots. As you can imagine, this gives Transistor much more depth and customisability this time around compared to Bastion. You can play the game in real time like any normal ARPG... but Transistor also adds a layer of strategic depth with it's new feature called the planning stage -- letting you pause, queue and plan your attacks (with a short global cooldown for all your abilities as a penalty).
There is no overworld hub this time like in Bastion, but you do come across back doors -- taking you to a mini oasis of sorts. Here is where you can access all of the challenges known as
. Beating each test unlocks a track for you to listen to. Supergiant also added a feature where if you press tab, Red can hum to every track in the game. I love and appreciate this small attention to detail. You can also gaze up at the stars on your hammock and listen to what the Transistor has to say on your current situation and also play with your process dog named Luna (Dota reference?).
The idol system from Bastion also makes its return, but in the form of limiters in Transistor. Limiters can be toggled on and off making the game harder but also granting more experience with each limiter you enable (up to 10 limiters). Limiters also have their own lore to be unlocked by using them at least once. The game becomes VERY CHALLENGING with 10 limiters enabled and is not for the feint of heart.
The music for Transistor is also incredible once again. It has a bit more of a jazzy and eery sci-fi vibe this time compared to the more upbeat tunes of Bastion. In only 2 games, Darren Korb has cermented himself as one of my favourite game composers of all time. Instant classics, and I can't wait to hear more from this very talented man.
Now, I'm praising this game to the high heavens, but what are some of my
? Every time you are taken to 0 health, one of your abilities will be overloaded, and can't be used until you reach the next checkpoint. It is a unique way of handling failure, but I didn't really like the idea of having your skills being stripped from you as it can basically ruin the idea of your build if you make a mistake. It also seems random on what skill you will lose -- which is
punishing -- especially when you are trying to complete some of the later performance tests where if you lose 1 crucial skill, you basically have no hope of finishing the test without restarting the whole test and playing flawlessly. The developers also forgot to add a restart test option to the menu which was frustrating when you are attempting them over and over. Frankly, I also didn't think the tests/challenges were as well designed as they were in Bastion.
Transistor is another monumental achievement by Supergiant Games. It shows they are maturing as a developer. Some people probably thought Bastion's narrator was a bit of a gimmick, and that the story was all it had going for it. Transistor shows that Supergiant also understand how to craft a more mechanically deep and subtle game this time, while still sticking to their strengths of unique story-telling via narration and music.
SuperGiant Games does it again. I finished the game with my heart in my throat and my brain wanting more...

Tree of Savior is a really great game with a lot of serious (but ultimately fixable) flaws. I'm just gonna do some bullet points on it quick.
- The gameplay is fun and addictive and if you like action RPGs at all you will probably have a blast with it. It sort of harkens back to games like Secret of Mana, Legend of Mana, and Seiken Densetsu 3. And, of course, Ragnarok Online. My only gameplay-related complaints are that it's really really unforgiving when it comes to your character's build so it's easy to make mistakes that will haunt you later on, and also that around level 30-35 and again around 70-75 it's easy to get lost and confused and lose track of what you're doing.
- The artwork and the game world is beautiful and colorful. The characters are well-animated. The portraiture is just awesome. The skill and spell effects are pretty cool. There is some flickering going on with things like fog and lighting and foreground objects (pillars, trees, and so on), and there are some clipping issues with the character's hair while jumping, but overall the game is really kind of gorgeous and I'm sad that I don't see more art like this in modern gaming.
- The game's music is super milquetoast and there are a limited amount of sound channels so sometimes when there's a lot going on sounds can sort of abruptly cut off and it's kinda messy.
- It's one of the most poorly optimized games I've ever seen in my life. I have an i5 4460 CPU and a GTX 960 video card (not impressive, but not terrible) and Tree of Savior chugs like crazy in towns and in maps with a lot of people. I'm talking 5-10 frames per second, here.
- The game is plagued by an ever-increasing number of bots and RMT spammers. There are literally dozens of bots camping out in popular farming zones using hacks to attack enemies at long range with melee weapons. It's a growing problem, but IMC seems to be aware of it, at least. They've taken a few steps in the right direction WRT the chat-spammers, so let's hope they keep moving in that direction.
- On the other hand, IMC has also taken a bunch of ABSURD measures to combat botting and RMT that are entirely ineffective and ultimately cumbersome to legitimate players. Trading is restricted to premium accounts and players cannot trade money. The auction house takes a 30% (!) cut of any money you earn from sales, ON TOP OF the normal posting fee. When you sell something on the auction house, you are forced to wait a full 48 hours until you can retrieve your money. AND you cannot trade items between your own characters (although they recently posted about this and might be changing it). Unfortunately there's no right click > report function in the game, which kinda boggles my mind a little since it's a pretty standard feature in modern mmos.
- There aren't many hairstyles or costumes in the cash shop yet, so after level 90 people all basically look the same.
- In stark contrast to the beautiful artwork, the game's story and dialogue looks as though the localization team just ran the korean script through google translate and cleaned it up a little. It's bad. It's really bad, and I hope they fix that someday.
- There's a non-optional profanity filter in TOS and it's the worst and most invasive/annoying I've ever encountered. It checks words, it checks parts of words, and if you have a flagged word or syllable in your message, the entire message is deleted. Words like class, encumbrance, titan, etc are flagged because they contain ♥♥♥♥♥, ♥♥♥♥♥, and ♥♥♥♥♥, respectively.
- People in the game aren't very social, and on the NA servers there are a lot of non-english speakers. Which isn't a bad thing necessarily, but it can make it hard to make friends with anyone or find a group.
- Even now, before the official F2P release, the game's cash shop has some pay to win items in it. Enchanting scrolls allow players to enchant their cosmetic head items, and the stats on the enchantments (despite what the game's die-hard fans would have you believe), can be quite significant. Enchanting can add 20-40 attack power or magic potency to a hair ribbon, which is the equivalent of dumping 17-34 levels worth of stat points into your strength or intelligence. To put it a different way, 40 attack power or magic potency is around 15% of the stat on an endgame item. It's a severe advantage that you can only buy with money, and it has to go.
In spite of all this crap, I still love the game. I have almost 100 hours in it already as of the time I wrote this review, and I'm still having fun. So I totally recommend it, but I do want to stress that it is a flawed game. I am hopeful for the future, though!

No, this is not a game featuring an Irish band. Or Enya.
CLANNAD is a popular Japanese visual novel that was originally released in 2004, developed by a company called Key. Having been translated to English by fans in the past, this is the first official English release, courtesy of a Kickstarter started by Sekai Project in 2014. This iteration includes HD visuals (which I believe are from the PS3 version), Dangopedia (to explain Japanese terms, culture etc.) and Steam achievement support.
I am not going to say very much about the story at all because it is extremely spoiler heavy, so beware of looking up almost anything to do with the series if it is new to you. It is difficult to specify an exact genre, but drama, romance, slice of life and supernatural all fit rather appropriately.
The Steam tag of “Story Rich” could not be more apt. The word count of CLANNAD surpasses a number of books (combined) in classic literature. That does not automatically make it great, but this volume of text feeds and gives flavour to the many rich and different story arcs and endings that are available within the game. This means there is well in excess of over 100 hours if you want to read and see absolutely everything. CLANNAD is not a kinetic visual novel so this means gameplay requires you to make many decisions throughout the game which will impact the story.
The story is an emotional rollercoaster like no other and never falls short in the ‘feels’ department. As a result, I would struggle to see how the game and story could not have an impact on your future outlook in life. Yes, it’s that good.
Character development is of the very highest calibre and you can simply not help but admire and love all of the different characters; feeling and sympathising for them as they suffer through various trials and tribulations. There are of course, some stereotypical characters traits, but character individuality is strong and always shines through.
The graphical style is excellent with plenty of variation in computer graphics (CG) throughout the game. Environments are colourful and vibrant which fit well to the various settings and key points in the game and some are nothing sort of stunning. Having said that, I do personally still prefer the art style from the animation by Kyoto Animation in comparison to the art in this game; even though it is the original source material.
CLANNAD is lavished by a soundtrack which, in my opinion, is the best feature of the game and one of the greatest soundtracks of all time. Jun Maeda crafted some of the most beautiful music ever written to fit both the ups and downs of the game. There are so many wonderful tracks, with outstanding piano pieces such as 同じ高みへ (To The Same Heights) and 小さなてのひら (The Palm of a Tiny Hand). There are many other great tracks composed by other staff at Key, such as 空に光る (Shining in the Sky) and 潮鳴り (Roaring Tides), but again – a big warning about spoilers when seeking these out, because the Internet and YouTube in particular, is flooded with them.
I spotted a review online once which quoted: “CLANNAD is the greatest story ever across all genres and media”. I couldn’t agree more with this and the fact that the Kickstarter smashed its stretch goals is no coincidence.
Visual novels are (finally) breaking through and gaining popularity in the west so I can understand some people might stumble across this and be highly apprehensive given the price point and type of minimalistic gameplay that a visual novel usually involves. Therefore, if you are not convinced enough to buy the game then, please; at least do yourself a favour and go and watch the animation (the one by Kyoto Animation). After 40+ episodes your transformation will be complete and you will then come back to buy and enjoy the game.
