Clannad Official English Release, Published on steam by Sekai Project Developed by Key, who has also developed visual novels like Kanon, Air and Little Busters and many more. Through the course of the visual novel Clannad with over 8 heroines for you to choose from to build a relationship with However, there are also 3 other characters, one of which doesn’t appear in the anime those three aren’t really relationship choices but it is more about finding out more about whats going on in the world of Clannad. In total, there are over 11 routes in Clannad. Being themed around family, friendships, bonds, and relationships.
Clannad starts off in a dream like world where everything appears to be covered in snow. This world is called the Illusionary World. There is no life in this world, except for one young girl and a robot made out of junk.
The story quickly shifts to the real world and get to see the world of Clannad through the eyes of Tomoya Okazaki an emotionally distant delinquent student, a student at Hikarizara Private High School. After losing his mother in an incident and subsequently falling victim to an abusive, alcoholic father. Unable to play basketball after that fight, Tomoya becomes a student that just hate the thought of school, showing up late to class and not trying in the classes he does show up to become a “normal” thing for him. He spends most of his time at Youhei Sunohara’s dormitory. Tomoya Okazaki who have a friend, provably his only friend, Sunohara, a blond and is very energetic who is also a delinquent, that is Tomoya’s best friend. Together, the two scrape by school, coming to class only during lunch break, and then sleeping through all of his other classes, and on some days just outright skips school all together.
One day, being late for school, Tomoya comes across a girl who wears the same uniform as him. She is standing at the bottom of the hill leading to the school trying to motivate herself to go to school. Together, Tomoya and the girl, who we find later is named Nagisa Furukawa who is repeating the year due to a severe illness, enlists Okazaki to help revive the school’s drama club. With nothing much else going on in his life, Okazaki agrees to help, making friends with many other students in the school along the way, and overcoming all of the different problems and challenges that they face. From there, the story branches out into many routes.
All of the routes in the main part of the game are balanced very well with humor matched with strong drama, the routes/characters are well written. Kyou is brash, loud, and quick to anger often flinging a dictionary as a weapon. She mirrors Tomoya in many ways as she does show a softer side with how she treats her twin sister, Ryou, and her pet, Botan. Fuko is hilarious with her love of star fish and her suspicion that Tomoya is, “a strange person”. Kotomi, a genius, is very innocent and harbors an obsessive fear of bullies. Those are just a few of the colorful and interesting personalities you will come across while reading Clannad. And finally Nagisa
The comedy in Clannad is hilarious, the drama is what makes it an unforgettable experience. Many characters have experienced death or suffered emotional trauma in the past, or might be struggling to carve out a new identity. Kotomi’s route, and Fuko’s route stand out in the first part of Clannad as two of the strongest stories. Both deal with heavily with the family theme, and coping mechanisms to tragic events. (I can’t say much here because spoilers..)
We also learn more about the Illusionary World and the two inhabitants of it. by playing through Clannad. The story of the Illusionary World is advanced slowly, and in the After Story, it finally plays a very important part of the story as a whole.
Without After Story, Clannad is a cute, bittersweet visual novel with some very good moments and a great story. With After Story, Clannad becomes something different. It becomes a valuable experience that you will never forget.
The character development is probably ONE of the best I’ve ever seen in a story, the pacing is not too fast or too slow, and the emotions that this story extracts out of you are just unbelievable. As you play through the Visual Novel, you will get attached to the characters very easily because of the character development that Clannad brings to the table. Most of the characters are dealing with issues and many times you will be able to relate to them.
Overall it is a very memorable experience, with all the build up that the Visual Novels offers and then after some time you will start to feel many emotions that the characters in the Visual Novels and… Tears will start flowing down your face. Unless your heart is ice.
What makes Clannad great is, the soundtrack. The soundtrack list is very huge, having over 45 different music, 4 of them are vocal pieces. All of the soundtracks are memorable and are perfect in setting the mood of the game having the ability to alter your mood just through music and making you shed a tear. Ranging from from silly to energetic music, to slow, atmospheric songs, that will make you feel time around you has slowed down to a standstill and you’re just indulging in the beautiful music. For those who have watched the Anime, when you start the Visual Novel with the in game menu you will be hit with nostalgia in an instant because that is what happened to me, it’s like everything replayed in my head in that instant just by listening to the soundtrack.
Among all my favorite is, Roaring Tides, I really love it so much it is a really a beautiful soundtrack very outstanding.
There are new features to clannad 1 of them being a HD Upgrade: All visuals have been upgraded to 1280×960
Dangopedia that is exclusive to the english version, the Dangopedia is a Encyclopedia that is a handy refrence tool for understanding aspects of Japanese tradition and pop culture.
Achievements, Clannad has achievements that are steam supported! There’s also an in-game menu to review your achievement progress.
I would highly recommend anyone to read this Visual Novel because giving this a miss means you are really missing out. In fact you are missing a very valuable experience, it will change how you view your world completely. Clannad has a story with a message, a message of showing the importance of family, friends and more.
The Art, The Story, The Music, The Characters in this Visual novel is just amazing. The characters surpass any Visual Novels in terms of growth, complexity, and how I am able to connect to them. Clannad is a masterpiece(kamige) in both story telling and character development. A thing i did not mention is that Clannad also changed how I viewed people around me in fact it changed me quite a lot it, because it teaches me to be appreciative to people and appreciate the things you have because no matter how bad you think your situation is there is always someone is out there alone and lonely suffering in a situation far worse than you. It also showed me that people, no matter the ambitions or situation, can live a happy life. It showed a simple yet happy life, it showed that everyone has issues they need to learn from and overcome. Clannad showed me the strength of family, and the weaknesses of it at the same time. It’s a story that everyone can relate to.

For the past 10 years, I’ve been a fan of the (popular) anime adaptations of Key’s various work including Kanon, Air, Clannad, Little Busters, and Angel Beats. Although I was aware that both Kanon and Air started out as games (Visual Novels), I actually never bothered to play them, especially since they were in Japanese. Even in the recent years, with fans releasing English patches, I never had an interest on playing their respective visual novels. However, having the opportunity to play my first visual novel ever, I figured it would be best if I give it to what gave birth to one of my favorite series of all time—Clannad.
Clannad originally released in Japan on April 28, 2004, becoming Key’s third visual novel. Since then, the game quickly turned into one of the most notable series in the company’s lineup of visual novels. Following the wave of Visual Novels officially releasing in North America, the company decided to work with publisher Sekai Project and finally bring the game to the west via Steam for many fans of the Visual Novel community to enjoy.

CLANNAD is one of the most well-regarded visual novels in the world, boasting an epic 80-120 hours of content; about twice the size of the Lord of the Rings trilogy. It starts off at a very slow pace with lots of light-hearted comedy, but once you begin getting involved with each of the characters' individual conflicts, the story ramps up into some gripping emotional storytelling, sometimes sprinkled with a tinge of supernatural intrigue. The character routes are very worthwhile in their own right, but the true value of CLANNAD is to be found in its final route: After Story. It doesn't matter how emotionally hardened you think you are; After Story will hit you like a sledgehammer with its relentless emotional impact, and you won't come out unscathed.
So, yeah, CLANNAD is kinda cool. Changed my life / 10.

At its core, its a hack and slash mixed with some tactical elements into it.  A solid base, if rather simplistic.

Art.

Music.

Art:  Not graphics, but ART.  The visuals just set this apart in a way that is rare in games.  There are no FMVs, realistic 3d graphics, or even a next-gen graphics.  Instead, the scenery and design of ... well everything is just wonderful.
Narrator: This is simply a rarity in games, a spoken narrator and a good one at that.  The ONLY game that beats this and Bastion in this is Quest for Glory IV, and its tough to beat John Rhys-Davies as your Narrator and some improv jokes in it. It's hard to describe this game without using the word "beautiful" at least several hundred times, along with other adjectives, such as "amazing", "addicting", and "magnificent". I'm shocked how some people don't realize its true intentions as rather a story you are thrown into to experience first hand. I'll try to explain this further with no spoilers:
The beginning throws you straight into the game; no main menu, no background story, nothing. I had to YouTube the game just to make sure I hadn't accidently skipped an intro cutscene, but sure enough, what I was seeing was the way it was intended to begin. Already, I was impressed.
Gameplay felt comfortable. No stretching my tiny, feminine fingers out to reach oddly specific keys. Mouse controls were smooth and responsive. I never had a problem getting stuck on anything or walking into walls. My first time playing through I obviously relied on the Turn() aspect of the combat quite a bit, but towards the end and on my second time around, I realized the benefits of using both styles of combat, using the real time more for specific enemies that either evaded the effects of Turn() or were not of importance to waste it on. The key feature of applying Functions as a normal active function, an upgrade, or a passive stat was genius and allows for any person's unique fighting strategies. With how flexible the combat is, I'm surprised people have complaints about it.
The characters and dialogue of the entire game were enthralling and immersive. I felt highly connected with Red's character, and knew so much about her despite her ailment. That never stopped her character from shining through. Her sassy yet proper attitude was visible in her actions, not to mention how weak and afraid she truly was. She didn't have the amazing super strength to lift such a giant sword all the time. It would constantly dragged behind her, but she would gather her little strength to unleash amazing attacks, usually having to lift herself and the sword back up off the ground afterwards. She was constantly playing with her hair and adjusting herself, but obviously was not too absorbed in her looks, seeing that she tore such a beautiful ball gown to shreds for the sake of being able to run. Mr. Nobody, as he titles himself at an early point and what I prefer to call him since, no, he is not the Transistor itself, still shines through despite not even having a body. His voice acting is absolutely amazing. Every word meant something. Some lines made tears well up in my eyes. He had attitude as well, much more sarcastic and joking, but he was just as believable as Red.
The story, while I won't say much, was just beautiful. It's never what you expect, but not hard to follow along with. I will say the trailer gives false ideas and practically lies about the true story. Playing this blind is an amazing experience. Do me a favor and when Mr. Nobody starts talking, don't cut him off. Let him speak. All the dialogue means something in the story and if you cut him off, you could lose so much of the true story and not understand things in the future. A lot of playthroughs on YouTube do this. Don't cut off the experience for yourself. Take the extra time to sit there and just listen.
The music is just fantastic, and the little hum you can play for each track gives it a new spin and practically makes it a different song. All the music is addicting and plays perfectly along side the gameplay. The music is mellow and slow, so you never feel rushed in a battle, making the combat feel smooth and relaxed rather than frantic. The music is meant to calm you in the fray of battle and does so quite well. The art speaks for itself. Even if you hate the game, you can't deny its beauty. Everything looks hand painted. The 3D models are high definition, to the point where Red's facial expressions are visible. I'm simply obsessed with the artistic style they chose.
Final boss and ending sequence brought me to tears. I sobbed like a little girl, but for good reason, so don't judge. I had been near tears for most of the game due to its music and voice acting and the end pulled the final strings to my heart. It has been a very long time since a game has done this for me. I will ask you all again something here; if you beat it, when it asks you to play the recursion, at least watch the intro again. If the slight secret difference in the intro does not compel you to play more, than I'm not sure what will.
To be blunt, I'm kind of an expert on this game. I've been tracking it since its announcement at E3, watched all the demos and trailers, received it on the release day, have the soundtrack on my phone, and at the time of posting this I have racked up about 14 hours on the game. I will say if you're expecting a casual game of the typical demographic of 13-17 year old boys, this has no time for you. This game requires patience, attention, and heart. It is not the game's fault if you do not feel the need to provide it with these then seek to trash it for "not being good enough". Before you judge it, follow my suggestion of listening to all the dialogue and at least attempt to finish it. The game should take someone who is not rushed about 10 hours; not long at all. This game is a story and an experience, not something you can mindlessly blow through.
My final rating is 10/10, simply because it brought me to tears not once, not twice, but three times, and I'll happily cry again just to play through it once more to immerse myself in its beautiful story.

was my favourite game of 2011. So you could say I was highly anticipating
next release -- which was revealed to be
in 2013. After a long and patient wait, I've completed Transistor and I would like to share some of my thoughts and perhaps answer how it stacks up to Bastion.
The story revolves around a character called
, who seems to be a singer superstar in the city of Cloudbank. After Red wakes up from an assassination attempt by a sinister group of high ranking public figures known as
and realising her voice was also stolen... Red pulls The Transistor out of a mysterious body next to her, and attempts to unravel what exactly happened to her. Little does she know though, that The Transistor can talk, and actually seems to know her. As Red starts to make her way out of the district, she is attacked by an army of robotic intelligences known as
, who seem to be controlled by The Camerata.
The story is more abstract, subtle and darker this time. I would say the story is not as immediatetely likeable as Bastion's story -- as the narrator for Bastion basically narrated and spelled everything out for you in a clearer way. In Transistor, the narrator is also your companion,
. You are more encouraged to explore the world this time to find out more about Cloudbank's lore instead of relying on the narrator.
What is amazing is how the story also mechanically ties into the gameplay . You come across various slain characters in the story that you absorb into The Transistor, gaining new abilities. Abilities are multifaceted, so each ability can be used as an active/upgrade/passive and can be mixed and matched for some cool possibilities. You unlock character lore by using each ability in one of the 3 types of slots. It's quite a brilliant and elegant way of doing lore if I must say so myself.
You have 4 ability slots which can be upgraded (via leveling up) to have 2 upgrade slots each and you can also unlock 4 passive slots. As you can imagine, this gives Transistor much more depth and customisability this time around compared to Bastion. You can play the game in real time like any normal ARPG... but Transistor also adds a layer of strategic depth with it's new feature called the planning stage -- letting you pause, queue and plan your attacks (with a short global cooldown for all your abilities as a penalty).
There is no overworld hub this time like in Bastion, but you do come across back doors -- taking you to a mini oasis of sorts. Here is where you can access all of the challenges known as
. Beating each test unlocks a track for you to listen to. Supergiant also added a feature where if you press tab, Red can hum to every track in the game. I love and appreciate this small attention to detail. You can also gaze up at the stars on your hammock and listen to what the Transistor has to say on your current situation and also play with your process dog named Luna (Dota reference?).
The idol system from Bastion also makes its return, but in the form of limiters in Transistor. Limiters can be toggled on and off making the game harder but also granting more experience with each limiter you enable (up to 10 limiters). Limiters also have their own lore to be unlocked by using them at least once. The game becomes VERY CHALLENGING with 10 limiters enabled and is not for the feint of heart.
The music for Transistor is also incredible once again. It has a bit more of a jazzy and eery sci-fi vibe this time compared to the more upbeat tunes of Bastion. In only 2 games, Darren Korb has cermented himself as one of my favourite game composers of all time. Instant classics, and I can't wait to hear more from this very talented man.
Now, I'm praising this game to the high heavens, but what are some of my
? Every time you are taken to 0 health, one of your abilities will be overloaded, and can't be used until you reach the next checkpoint. It is a unique way of handling failure, but I didn't really like the idea of having your skills being stripped from you as it can basically ruin the idea of your build if you make a mistake. It also seems random on what skill you will lose -- which is
punishing -- especially when you are trying to complete some of the later performance tests where if you lose 1 crucial skill, you basically have no hope of finishing the test without restarting the whole test and playing flawlessly. The developers also forgot to add a restart test option to the menu which was frustrating when you are attempting them over and over. Frankly, I also didn't think the tests/challenges were as well designed as they were in Bastion.
Transistor is another monumental achievement by Supergiant Games. It shows they are maturing as a developer. Some people probably thought Bastion's narrator was a bit of a gimmick, and that the story was all it had going for it. Transistor shows that Supergiant also understand how to craft a more mechanically deep and subtle game this time, while still sticking to their strengths of unique story-telling via narration and music.

The Debate:
"The game is extremely grindy"
Rebuttal:
So far, I have only done quests and dungeons, and have never at any point had to resort to mindlessly killing creatures to level. The quests are moderately innovative. While many quests are simply kill quests, others involve things such as disguising yourself as monsters to lure other monsters to their death. Dungeons are similar to other modern MMOs, in that they are instanced, and are queued through a party finder. I would argue that this is far less of a grind than any other Asian MMO.
EDIT: It should be metioned, that when you start the game you choose to start in one of two cities. If you find yourself out of quests, you simply go to the other city and follow the quest chain there. I have heard however, that a wall appears in the mid-100s where there are insufficient quests and grinding becomes necessary. More on this when I hit it, if I hit it.
"The storyline is terrible"
Rebuttal:
Although it is in no way unique, the storyline isn't terrible. I've found myself actually reading the text more often than I have in other games. Rather than droning on and on and forcing the story down your throat, ToS delivers the story in short succinct dialogues, which I find far preferable to having to read about every NPC's life story.
"The gameplay sucks"
Rebuttal:
The class variety of ToS is amazing, and allows you to change your class every 15 class levels. Instead of changing your class you can rank it up, to a maximum of rank 3. You retain your class skills every time you change classes, and thus your character becomes a specific blend of what classes you choose to fit your play style. This allows for an immense amount of customization: from your chosen classes, to which skills you decide to invest in within these classes. The gameplay is fluid and engaging, and lets the player create interesting combinations that other people may not have come up with.
"Everything is locked behind a pay wall"
Rebuttal:
Although the game requires the premium token to utilize numerous functions, the premium token is tradable, and can be purchased from the auction house using in game currency. Premium tokens last for 30 days, and are the only necessary purchase to unlock all of the features of the game. In a way then, this game functions as a subscription game, that can still be played while not subscribed, at the cost of features until a token is purchased using real or in game currency.
EDIT: 4/11 ToS has issued a statement that due to the overwhelming outcry against trade restrictions to non-premium characters, they are actively working to create a system that will allow for trade for non-premium members. They also are working on a bot/gold-farmer report option to help circumvent current issues.
"The game is full of bugs and lag"
Rebuttal:
I have encountered very few bugs so far, and I honestly wouldn't expect any MMO to be completely bug-free. There are however, issues with lag, and the game seems to devour computer resources in ways it should not. The launch was only a week ago however, and there is plenty of time for the developers to fix these key issues.
OVERALL: Tree of Savior brings to the table something that feels a lot like Ragnarok Online, only far more refined. The art and music are excellent, and the storyline pulls the player through the game rather than leaving them grinding on the same mobs for hours. The class system allows for an immense level of playstyle customization, and gives each player an individual experience. Although the game virtually demands subscription in the form of premium tokens, paying real money for these becomes less essential in the long run.

The PC version of Dark Souls II is the definitive one to own. It’s a good step up in the graphics and performance departments, annoying load times are drastically reduced, and players can even opt to play with the mouse and keyboard if they so desire. It shows that From Software spent a considerable amount of time attempting to come up with controls that would feel natural on the PC.This game is art in the good and bad sense of the word. It represents some of the best things that video games have to offer:
732-902-1093
at its most immersive, it offers a beautifully and thoughtfully rendered world to be explored that reveals itself not just through what is seen on the screen, but through the brutal and challenging experiences the player guides the in-game avatar through. The negative part of that is that the story of the game and the motivations and reasoning behind what is happening are obscure and unclear. A lot of the onus is on the player to piece things together. This is a kind of experience that is not necessarily designed to appeal to a broad swath of people, but its pitch perfect execution and strict adherence to its draconian design principles earn it a place in the pantheon of great games.

If you love high risk high reward models and have the patience to actually take the emotional pain behind it.

I've had a pretty long history with this game. I've played since the Beta, and have had an on and off again sort of experience with it, at times enjoying it, and at times hating it with a passion. First off, to anyone interested in this game, it's free to play and decent enough that you should download and try it at the very least. Plus, with soon to be 91 different gods and goddesses to choose from, pretty much any playstyle is available.
Now as for my actual thoughts on the game, that's another matter.
There are a few significant problems that make this game frustrating at the very least to play, let alone get really in to. The first is bugs. Hi-Rez tries and tries to prevent them, but with added content and mechanics, and constant changes to effects and play testing amounting often to "Hey if you really like the game, you can play what we are releasing in a week early" which literally anyone can do. Crashes, errors, disconnections, incorrect explanations, all of these happen regularly around SMITE. I had a laptop I enjoyed playing games on that could run plenty of games that look far better graphically than this, but I wasn't able to play SMITE on it because of how poorly optimized this game seems to be. Either that or something on it for whatever reason wanted to fight with it.
The second problem is the gems system. Yes, a free to play game with micro-transactions, no surprise there. The reason why it's a problem though? Chests. Similar to other games wanting to add an element of randomization in rewards, chests can give you anything from skins, to small icons for your account. This in and of itself isn't really that big an issue, until you find that almost half the skins in the game, most of them being any of the good looking ones, all are in chests. That each range from two to four hundred gems, which are already an extremely expensive in-game currency which only increases in price with having to pay multiple times for chests in attempts to get the one thing you might want. It's just not worth it. Granted, this is about cosmetics, so it's not necessarily a huge thing, but it should be noted that many of the skins that make the characters interesting or funny all can cost dozens of real world dollars.
The final big problem is the balancing. Try as they might, Hi-Rez just doesn't seem to get how to make characters more balanced against each other. Granted, they do look at the competetive seen and high levels of play, and try to balance around that. However they often miss the mark on what changes are needed, and most of the player base isn't skilled enough at the game to make the changes made around high levels of play actually do what they want. My favorite example is when this last season (year) started for SMITE and they released an item named Bluestone pendant. This item made abilities do a bit more damage from the beginning of the game, giving several gods and goddesses new options. Chief among them was Sun Wukong, a god that was very underpowered for a long time, now thrown to the top of most people's tier lists for the lane he usually plays in. He wasn't the only one to become much stronger, but his change was the biggest, as he was near the bottom and shot near the top with the addition of this item, since now he could easily clear the lane where before he would have to use 2 abilities for a third of his mana. This created an imbalance in the game, so what do you think should happen? A) Change the item so that it's still a good choice but not a must buy, by changing the damage and/or cost of the item. B) Change Sun Wukong so that he can clear minions with 1-2 abilities without spending most of his mana every time, but not have as much aggressive poking damage, or C) Nerf the crap out of Sun Wukong so that he falls back to the bottom of god picks. If you chose C then congrats, you can work at Hi-Rez's balance team. Another example, an item, named Golden Bow, hasn't been a viable choice for almost every character in the game, except for a couple niche characters where it's a must-have item. Someone suggests buffing it, it goes through, and now you find that every hunter in the game is building this item and doing insane damage because of it. Do you A) Change the item back to how it was to re-evaluate what changes it needs to be less niche but not overpowered B) Make it so that this item that is now extremely strong is also much harder to get, so that it's still available for the niche characters, but also less appealing for the other characters that were using it until very late into the game or C) Remove the item and never re-introduce it with any changes whatsoever, just abandon ship on it. Guess which one was picked.
That's not to say SMITE is bad, it's still plenty of fun, but these problems make it very frustrating to play for long periods of time, and that's without mentioning the toxic player base, lack of attention to other modes outside of conquest (the typical MOBA style mode), and recent implementation of voice features built in that is unable to be turned off, only muted. There's good in there though, with stellar voice work for many of the skins and the gods themselves, content creators that make plenty of fun videos on the game, plenty of fun characters to try and master, a "mode of the day" match mode that puts fun twists on the game, and while it may be misguided, there is at least effort being put into making the game more fair, even if it makes the game wildly more unfair at times.

Following the horrid "Cartel" episode Call of Juarez returns to its roots.
Gunslinger at first glance appears to be offering less in every respect: game length, characters, story, locations and even weaponry. In truth it doesnt aim at being a worthy successor to the legend of a game that is Bound in Blood. Being its funny little brother it takes the player to a very fast paced and colourful warped Wild West and grandiose encounters with famous figures from the history books. There even is a dedicated arcade mode in which to compete for high scores by chaining up head shots and multikills. And once accepted for being what it is it proves to be very capable in just that.

Best arcade-FPS fun I've had since Bulletstorm. There's a keen sense of style, there's just enough of that wild west atmosphere, there's solid gunplay with just enough features to keep it interesting. Not a whole lot of guns(think about three revolvers with different speed/damage, the ever so classic lever-action rifle and the two-buckshot shotgun everyone loves, in regular and sawed-off flavors). There's slow-mo shooting- and dodging bullets! -, there's shooting dynamite in the air, there's combos for how fast you are on the trigger... the game could use some more "skillshots", though. Still fun to put a bullet to a head and watch the oh-so-satisfying red splash fly.
Duels can be a finicky thing. If you can get the hang of them, they can be enjoyable, but myself I always had to switch mouse sensitivity to play them. Most of the story duels have some sort of gimmick to keep things fresh.
Story is not a whole lot to talk about. The way the narrative entwines with the level design, though, is great. Think playing a level only for the whole thing to rewind as Silas recalls his story. "No, no, kid, that's not how it happened." It's new, and while not revolutionary, it is enough to warrant a chuckle.
Sound is nothing to write home about. It does it's job well enough, with most of the classic sounds like the lever action from your rifle or the wild-west trademark of bullets whizzing by. Guns sound a bit alike, however.
All in all, a pretty good arcade fun with an enjoyable campaign and just enough ways to play to keep you interested and maybe bring you back to beat your record on those arcade missions.

The Call of Juarez  franchise started out as a first person Wild West shooter and the first two games were much appreciated by the fans. With the third game, The Cartel, Ubisoft most likely pushed Techland to develop a modern-day version of the game to appeal to a wider audience. Suffice to say, The Cartel got torn into pieces both by fans and the press because of its shortcomings in regards to visuals, story, character design, AI and, of course, because they dumped the entire Wild West theme in favor of a Drug Cartel War theme taking place in the modern-day Los Angeles.
With Gunslinger, Techland finally went back to the roots of the franchise and provided fans of the series with some more smoking Revolvers and Wild West action.
The story is fairly simple and as Wild West cliché as it can get: You end up in a saloon and tell the story of how an outlaw killed your brothers, so you became a bounty hunter seeking for revenge and came across many other famous outlaws such as Billy the Kid, Butch Cassidy, Sundance Kid or the Dalton - who all stood in the way between you and your Nemesis.
While the story isn't exactly innovative, the storytelling itself definitely makes up for it as it is told in voice-over manner and makes up for some funny dialogues and actual game changing effects when the remaining crowd in the saloon questions details of the story. For example, 'you' tell them about how you've fought a hundred Indians all by yourself. The barkeeper thinks you're lying and couldn't have survived this, so the majority of Indians disappear from the level so that only a handful is left and then you reply something like 'Yeah, well, maybe it was a couple less...'. I can't recall I've seen a narration like this in another game, but I definitely liked it a lot.
The game is based on Techland's own Chrome Engine 5, which was also used for The Cartel and both Dead Island games, and makes use of a mix of both realistic and Cel-shaded graphics. While Gunslinger does look fairly decent on max settings, the lack of any AA option whatsoever makes for some really ugly jaggies around the edges of pretty much everything, so unless you force AA on in your graphics drivers or through a 3rd-party tool such as SweetFX, you will have to live with that.
Being a first person shooter, there aren't any surprises in regards to controls or movement. Everything feels smoth and precise and the hit feedback is also pretty satisfying, so you always know if you've hit an enemy with any of the, unfortunately, few weapons in the game - among them revolvers, a rifle, a shotgun and their sawn-off counterparts. Additionally, by killing enemies and racking up combos or by finding collectibles, you earn XP which you can spend on a variety of character upgrades.
My biggest gripe with the game, though, is the linearity. While the first two games basically had on open world where you could saddle your horse and just roam around, Gunslinger has a relatively narrow level design where a horse wouldn't even make sense, so they removed the horse riding aspect entirely from the game, which is a huge shame IMO.
With around 4.5 hours for the main story on normal difficulty, the game is fairly short but if you want to spend more time with it you can replay the story in the New Game+ mode, which will preserve all your previously unlocked upgrades and provide for some additional challenge. On top of that there is an Arcade mode with 10 levels where you can fight your way to the top of the leaderboards. Lastly, there is a Duel mode where you have 5 lives and  face 15 enemies one after another until you either win or run out of lives.
Call of Juarez: Gunslinger has some minor flaws, but for a budget game like this I'm extremely surprised by its quality, so if you're a fan of the original CoJ games or just want a decent Wild West experience, give Gunslinger a shot (heh) and check the game's store page for the Demo download button.

Elder Scrolls Online is a game that takes you into the shoes of a traveller in the civil war torn remains of the once great empire of Tamriel. Three factions; The Aldmeri Dominion, The Daggerfall Covenant, and the Ebonheart Pact are vying for control over the ruby throne to rule over Tamriel as its new emporer. But little do they know that their war is fueled by a greater evil.
You start off by selecting your race and faction. Each faction is made of three races;
-The Aldmeri Dominion is made up of the Altmer (High Elves), the Bosmer (Wood Elves), and the Khajiit (Cat Elves... Wait...)
-The Daggerfall Covenant is made up of Orismer (The orcs), Bretons, and Redguard.
- Last, but definately not least, the Ebonheart Pact made of the Dunmer (Dark Elves), Nords, and Argonians.
Certain expansions allow you to a) play any race in any alliance, for instance I could play an Argonian in the Daggerfall Covenant, and b) play as an imperial, which is the only race without use of the adventure pack to play all three factions.
This game will certainly grasp at you with its iconic soundtrack and stunning visuals, (play this on full graphics if your computer can handle it. You will NOT be disappointed.) rather captivating storylines and quests specific to each faction, and intriguing PvP action in the frontlines of Cyrodiil. The Gold edition allows you to get all of the currently available DLC at a rather discount price (I will NOT say free because you are still paying more for this version)
(I would also like to add that this is probably one of the best communities among MMORPGs that I have found thus far)

The saying "don't judge a book by it's cover" translated into video games would read something like "graphics don't mean♥♥♥♥♥♥quot;. Despite the idiotic masses of pathetic adrenalin junkies, some games are still investing more into storytelling, atmosphere, emotion, and less into the shallow Hollywood formula of gratuitous explosions and lens flare.
Papers, Please is by far one of the greatest games ever made, if only for the amount of emotion and story packed into its simplistic 8-bit art style and text dialog. You are a citizen of Glorious Arstotzka, a communist regime that's just finished fighting for control of half a major city. The border is to be opened for immigration, and you've been chosen at random to be the border inspector.
The game is literally a job, but done in such a way that you really give a damn about doing it right. You must compare documents, check expiration dates, watch for forgeries, catch wanted criminals, be on the lookout for contraband, and juggle the excessive bureaucracy building up above you, while dealing with all the hazards of being the point where the rubber meets the road.
You view the world through your immigration booth; a small window into a much larger and more complex society existing on its own with you caught up somewhere near the eye of the storm. Not only do you have to worry about the increased crime rates in the Altan district requiring closer inspection of the local citizenry, but you're constantly struggling to keep your family alive and healthy with your meager commission wage.
Corruption plays a large part, as you can try to line your pockets with some under the table deals, or sacrifice a penalty to do a good deed. The game keeps you on your toes as documents and requirements keep changing, every day carries the risk of a terrorist attack, your family expenses keep shifting as life happens within the walls, and you're given the chance to help or hinder each person coming through your station, a fleeting moment in their lives that can change it forever. But for you, it's Tuesday.
10/10 - GLORY TO ARSTOTZKA

Dystopian document thriller may be the most apt description for a game that defies genre as much as this one does. While at its barest it can be called a game of spot the difference all the various pieces combine to turn it into so much more. The washed out pixilated aesthetics give off a somber and oppressive mood. The audio provides crisp sounding paper noises that make you feel like you’re actually shuffling papers, a satisfying ka-chunk when the stamp comes down and the ever nerve racking noise of a citation slip being printed that will haunt you for days to come.  Then there’s the narrative which gives the game its tension and stakes. It creates interesting moral quandaries that you have to deal with and doesn’t come off as judging the player or having a right way to play.  No karma meters, no paragon/renegade points, just your decisions and their consequences and whether you can live with them or not.  All these turn a game which should feel like work into a tense, nerve racking, and wonderfully cohesive experience that’ll stick in your mind.  It’s a harsh game, in tone and gameplay, so expect to lose a few times as you get the hang of it but thanks to the games day save system you’ll never lose a lot of progress and it should be easy to start back up where you died/left off last.  This may not be the game for you if you’re looking for something quick and relaxing to pass time, but it’s an experience that should be experienced and I’d highly recommend it.

Papers Please delivers a one-two punch of addictive gameplay and moving storyline that's sure to be a knockout.  The drab, retro art style creates an oppressive atmosphere that compliments the rushed tedium of the game mechanic.  That combination peppered with the huge cast of NPCs ranging from pitiful to hilarious and the hard decisions one must make to keep their family alive is a recipe for deep emotional impact and hours of fun.  It is rare for a game to be so addictive on a shallow mechanical level and also have a story as compelling as a good dramatic film.  Cart Life awakened that possibility in my mind, but where Cart Life stopped as a beautiful-yet-buggy experiment, Papers Please delivers a polished simulator with a fantastic story and a decent amount of replayability.  If you are ready to challenge your memory and observational skills, if you are ready to question your moral compass and empathy, if you are ready to experience the bleak and utter hopelessness of the Arstotskan border and love every minute of it, pick up your "Approved" stamp and download Papers Please.

I took the time to get all of the achievements in the game before writing this review. I'll sum it up right here for you. Should you buy this game? Yes. Is it worth $19.99? It really depends on how much of the game you go out of your way to experience.
Transistor is, as most of you know, the second game from Supergiant Games. There are a lot of similarities between Bastion and Transistor (music, art, challenges), but overall it's a fresh idea from a great company. The tactical combat, known as Turn(), was fantastic. At first I thought the game was going to be rough because getting attacks in seemed difficult. Once the game introduced Turn(), everything changed for the better.
What I Liked:
Tactical addition to combat
The music. It's absolutely fantastic and there are different versions of each song (normal, humming, processed).
Attention to detail. This goes along with the music. You can have Red hum along with the current song.
Losing functions. If you die while Turn() is charging, you lose your highest-cost function. While it seems horrible, it forces you to experiment with other functions and makes the game really fun.
Having to find the story. Between the terminals and having to use the functions to learn about the world and its people, I had a great time piecing together what was going on.
Recursion Mode. Minor things change but you also get new sets of enemies that weren't necessarily grouped together in any other run you've played through.
The computer/programming theme. Functions, The Process, functions like Breach(), Crash(), Mask(), and finding minor things like "NaN" and "Struct: Not Allocated" really made the game grab my attention.
Planning tests. Seriously, these were the most fun of all of the tests for me.
What I Didn't Like:
The game is short. My first run was about 4.5 hours after doing 3-4 tests, reading all of the terminals, and interacting with everything that was able to be interacted with. My second run was probably about 2 hours because I skipped everything, but I spent about 6 hours beating my head against the wall for some of the tests you can do.
While emotionally engaging after reading everything about all of the characters, I still didn't get that connection like I did in Bastion. I'll just mention Zulf and Mother, I'm Here. Those of you that played Bastion will understand what I'm getting at and I was really hoping for that kind of situation in the game.
Fantastic, worthy successor to Bastion. Good buy for sure.

Let's put it this way: you should only buy this game if you like your games to be "work" more than "fun".
DS2 certainly doesn't look bad - it's miles and miles ahead of its predecessor in terms of visuals. There isn't much story to it unless you are willing to read every item's description - apparently then you can find out a lot more about lore, but the gane certainly doesn't go out of its way to present it to you. At the end of the day, you've been dropped in a post-apocalyptic kingdom and your only goals are to kill your way from point A to point B while dying the least number of times in between.
Some things you should be aware of:
1. At the end of the day, it's still a console port, with a lot of resulting wonkiness. My biggest gripe is the lock-on mechanic. It is inconsistent to say the least - sometimes, the game refuses to lock on to the nearest enemy, sometimes you'll have a guy literally ten steps ahead and the lock-on just doesn't happen, etc. And without lock-on, any kind of ranged combat is nearly pointless (you might land one in four hits or so).
2. Enemies do not play by the same rules. They can stagger you far more frequently than you can stagger them. They gleefully fall off the same heights that would kill you, and keep on coming.
3. There is the everpresent threat of limited resources breathing down your neck. Every time you die, your maximum health is reduced, and you must use a certain item to undo this. But this item is in limited supply, so sooner or later you're screwed.
4. A lot of mechanics are very MMO-ey. This isn't a living world, it's a fixed-time-of-day series of rooms where enemies stand motionless waiting for you to come. Kill them, and after you rest, they respawn again (though not indefinitely). You can farm - in fact you SHOULD farm to improve your stats and get a leg up  on things - and farming involves killing the same guys over and over and over again. Just like your friendly neighbourhood MMO.
5. Oh, and there is unwanted PvP as well. Sooner or later, someone will drop by your "world" to screw with you. That's right - you may be in the middle of the toughest fight, and some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ will join you with the express purpose of ruining your day. There's no way to opt out of it other than: disconnecting your Internet or expending the same item that reverses the effects of death.
Yes, combat has its charms. Yes, it's old-school (as in, you can get permanently screwed old-school; as in, missing creature comforts such as a map old-school). Yes, if you beat it, you can join the leet club of the leetest doods evah. But at the end of the day, it's "kill your way from point A to point B with the fewest deaths and restarts in between."
You decide if it's worth your cash.

The game itself is fun and action packed with each class feeling like it has its own flavor and play style and the variety of every class is certainly a bonus. The sheer amount of customization options via stats and class combinations through out the rank system and the circle system give the game a fresh feel and the grinding isn't too bad with quests and exp cards making the trip to 100 and beyond quite enjoyable. The art style is gorgeous and the difficulty curve is just right with challenging bosses and monsters as you advance through the areas but it never feels unfair or like a crazy gear or difficulty spike. Exploration is rewarded with small caches of treasure that include recipes for weapons, armor and hair accessories and from what I saw the story was actually quite interesting.
Unfortunately; the game has some glaring issues not with the content itself but with the management and implementation of things within the game. Firstly, the premium token system is what you would expect of such, more exp, move speed, faster stamina regen and things of that nature so you think you don't need it until you realize you can't trade with any non token users nor can you buy tokens for your friends and trade with them. If it weren't bad enough that trade is restricted to premium members the amount of times you can trade in a premium period is restricted as well. You get 30 trades for every 30 day token you use so don't expect to be trading with friends or others. On top of that you cannot trade the in-game currency of silver with friends or with other players for goods and services you have to go through an auction house that makes you wait upwards of 2 days real time to get your hard earned silver.  There is also a team bank where you can trade equipment and other items through between your characters but it's restricted by your trades remaining, potential(the number of times a piece of equipment can be traded, fail an upgrade or be socketed) drops by one and you CAN'T trade TP items between your characters this includes tokens, costumes, TP potions or enchant scrolls. This to me just screams of greed and money gouging.
It's truly disheartening that such a promising game is behind such incompetent management and put behind so many paywalls and arbitrary road blocks to true enjoyment based on nothing more than corporate greed. I only wish I realized this sooner so I could have gotten a refund for all my friends and myself.
Bottom line: Tree of Savior would be an amazing spiritual successor to RO were it not for IMC games and their insufferable greed. My advice would be to wait for private servers to truly enjoy this gem because you will -not- have a pleasant experience in the official version.

First things first I'd like to say that I'm WoW veteran with my whole high school life wasted on it.
I bought this game because I was looking for something fresh and I couldn't really justify paying for gametime in WoW while playing couple hours a week.
After downloading this YUUUGE thing I was hyped to get in and play but that was not the case. I actually spent over 5 hours trying to get this game to run.
First I had to install it in safemode so I'd get past the javascript error.
Then I was getting blackscreen everytime I tried to run the game which I ended up solving by redownloading and repatching the entire game(!!!)
Then when I finally got to log in screen I got an error that game is not running through steam and cannot login(!!!!!)
At this point I was ready to refund but fixed it quite easily by changing settings in compatibility mode of steam.exe and steamoverlay.exe. Basically it all had to be set for admin rights and I was good to go.
After surviving this ordeal and actually getting in-game I spent 8 hours straight playing till 5am turning it off only because of exhaustion.
Seriously there is so much stuff to do. I never really cared about lore in mmo's since I was always grinding hard to get to the endgame  content. This is different though. Quests are actually narated and you can get really emerged into the story.
My plan was to grind to level 50 as fast as possible and get a decent PVE build but now after 40 hours I still find myself wondering around the map doing quests even reading freaking BOOKS I find around the world.
So far I have encountered only one bugged quest and it solved itself just by doing other quests and returning to it later.
If I don't take into account the horrors I had to go through to get this game started it runs really well and most of it release problems have been polished.
I'd recommend this game to casual MMORPG players as well as to hardcore endgame players.
I haven't really tried PVP yet since I haven't reached max level but PVE is great and actually challenging.
I went into normal dungeon with a group of people and we wiped like 11 times on one boss before learning the mechanics and actually cooperating together to get him down.
It was so much more rewarding then WoW dungeons where at this point you just spam spell rotations unless you actually go for a mythic raid.
The combat of ESO is very unique unlike any other MMO I played. And I must say I love it. It actually makes you move around and engage into combat instead of just TAB targeting and spamming your spell rotations.
I'll be updating this review as I go through the game but as of now I have nothing bad to say about it except: FIX THE FREAKING INSTALLATION!!

Call of Juarez: Gunslinger is a first-person shooter which heavily trives on old Westerns tropes and cliché to tell the story of Silas Graves, a bounty hunter on a quest for revenge, without taking itself too seriously.
The game actually encourages the player to take precise shoots and off the various enemies in the most unortodox ways: given the score mechanic, the more points you can earn for a series of stylish kills the more experience you can gain, the more abilities/perks/unlocked weapons you can secure for your character and the longer you can use the bullet time feature (Concentration). The gameplay is rendered even more fun by a great enemy variety and a pletora of combat techniques. There is even a dedicated arcade mode with the purpose of achieving the highest score possible out of waves after waves of enemies.
Gunslinger's plot is told in a "story within a story" fashion, with Silas telling his tales to a bunch of costumers in a saloon. The game actually takes advantage of this by using unexpected turns of events justifyed by how Silas is actually reporting the story, with paths often appearing out of thin air because Silas just remembered about them or the time being rewinded to tell the tale in a different light. Such events are always amusing.
All in all, Call of Juarez: Gunslinger is a cheap and charming title. There is no harm in trying it. Not at all.

Overall, I'd give this game a 7.1/10. It was hard to run for the first few hours, but then ran mostly smoothly from then on.
Pros
- Great fun: gunplay, explosions. This is the Michael Bay of video games
- Wingsuit, parachute and grappling device are very fun and easy to use

- Excellent visually
- Huge map with decent diversity
Cons
- Frame drop, as mentioned before this didn't plague me but I did experience it from time to time
- Frustrating: sometimes a checkpoint takes forever to get to. There were numerous times where I destroyed 90%+ of a base, then died to a stupid debris hit or something else uncalled for.
- Repetitive: I could not play more than 3 hours of this game a day. And while it kept me coming back, I have to be real and say that the game can get boring after a single sitting.
- Poor driving: planes and boats were great, but car handling was pretty awful
In summary, if you liked the first 2 Just Causes and want more interesting ways to blow things up you will love this game. That is assuming it runs well on your rig, it's worth $40 or less. If you haven't played a Just Cause before, think of this game as a sandbox with explosions and addicting gameplay. For you guys, I cannot recommend this game for anything over $30.

Bottomline Upfront:  Its worth dropping some coin to get a membership starter pack.  This is the game for you if enjoy first person shooters, but need something laid back to play after work to unwind on, prior to going to bed and getting up early the next morning.  Absolutely gorgeous, runs on a wide range of machines.  Pacing is excellent for what it is.  The least arcadey of the hunting simulators, but certainly one of the most polished.
Note: If you do see my low hours, that's a bit deceptive... I've put many more hours on it prior to it going on Steam, and only recently crossed it into my Steam account.
Lastly... for those that criticize the game for being deceptively marketed as "free-to-play", I say "nuts!"  If you're going to be critical towards a single game, you're going after the wrong target.  The whole industry should move away from the term "free to play" because nothing is free... to include the player's time as well as the player's private information.  Free-to-play these days is too often synonymous with getting a fully loaded game that you & the developer are expecting the die-hards to drop enough cash to cover the expense of making and maintaining it.  Nothing wrong with that... that's a viable model for many games, but that is not "free" either.  Let's be clear.

Papers Please delivers a one-two punch of addictive gameplay and moving storyline that's sure to be a knockout.  The drab, retro art style creates an oppressive atmosphere that compliments the rushed tedium of the game mechanic.  That combination peppered with the huge cast of NPCs ranging from pitiful to hilarious and the hard decisions one must make to keep their family alive is a recipe for deep emotional impact and hours of fun.  It is rare for a game to be so addictive on a shallow mechanical level and also have a story as compelling as a good dramatic film.  Cart Life awakened that possibility in my mind, but where Cart Life stopped as a beautiful-yet-buggy experiment, Papers Please delivers a polished simulator with a fantastic story and a decent amount of replayability.  If you are ready to challenge your memory and observational skills, if you are ready to question your moral compass and empathy, if you are ready to experience the bleak and utter hopelessness of the Arstotskan border and love every minute of it, pick up your "Approved" stamp and download Papers Please.

I never got the chance to play Bastion (i know, for shame), but considering all the poistive publicity surrounding it, I had high hopes for this title. And even after playing only 30 minutes into the game, I knew I would not be dissapointed.
The game follows the story of renowned singer Red who has lost her voice, and a sword known as the Transistor that is inhabitted by the soul of the man who saved her life. They embark on a journey to quell the incursion of The Process, an army of machines bent on wrecking everyone's day, and to discover the motive behind Red's attackers.
The story isn't ham-handed to you like other RPG's, but neither is it dull or few-and-far-between. The commentary of the sword is all the upfront, situational context you'll need, and if you want more, each function and limiter unlocked in the game comes with it's own attached codex on people intrinsic to the story. There are also occasional electronic info kiosks to keep up to date with the news and various other happenings occuring around the city.
Combat is incredibly fluid. It's a semi-isometric action adventure OR strategy romp. Though it may take a while to get used to the "turn()" mechanic, it delivers strategic capabilities few other systems can match. To assist through combat are functions, which are universally customizable as active abilities, passive abilities, or upgrades to active abilities, increasing their utility or power, such as causing a dash to draw in opponents, and then finish them off with a devistaing upward slash that can steal health. After a certain point, the game offers an "inbetween zone", focusing on challenges and for practicing new function set-ups before you head out into the field, allowing for experimentation. The game also offers limiters, which upgrade the difficulty of the progress while offering bonus exp boosts. These can range from giving the progress shields to doubling their damage and so many more.
The atmosphere drowns the senses. The phenomenal soundtrack gives a brand new vibe to a world that's both futuristic and vintage. The artwork, inspired by the art nouveau movement, is vibrant eye-candy. It almost makes we wish for a bit more explorability of the city just to see more of it.
This game is definetly worth the purchase. And it keeps the player entertained even after the ending with a new game+ mode, allowing for replayability while retaining you're functions and limiters. All in all, Transistor is a more-than-worthy edition to the 2014 game lineup, and a definite contender for Game of the Year.

I took the time to get all of the achievements in the game before writing this review. I'll sum it up right here for you. Should you buy this game? Yes. Is it worth $19.99? It really depends on how much of the game you go out of your way to experience.
Transistor is, as most of you know, the second game from Supergiant Games. There are a lot of similarities between Bastion and Transistor (music, art, challenges), but overall it's a fresh idea from a great company. The tactical combat, known as Turn(), was fantastic. At first I thought the game was going to be rough because getting attacks in seemed difficult. Once the game introduced Turn(), everything changed for the better.
What I Liked:
Tactical addition to combat
The music. It's absolutely fantastic and there are different versions of each song (normal, humming, processed).
Attention to detail. This goes along with the music. You can have Red hum along with the current song.
Losing functions. If you die while Turn() is charging, you lose your highest-cost function. While it seems horrible, it forces you to experiment with other functions and makes the game really fun.
Having to find the story. Between the terminals and having to use the functions to learn about the world and its people, I had a great time piecing together what was going on.
Recursion Mode. Minor things change but you also get new sets of enemies that weren't necessarily grouped together in any other run you've played through.
The computer/programming theme. Functions, The Process, functions like Breach(), Crash(), Mask(), and finding minor things like "NaN" and "Struct: Not Allocated" really made the game grab my attention.
Planning tests. Seriously, these were the most fun of all of the tests for me.
What I Didn't Like:
The game is short. My first run was about 4.5 hours after doing 3-4 tests, reading all of the terminals, and interacting with everything that was able to be interacted with. My second run was probably about 2 hours because I skipped everything, but I spent about 6 hours beating my head against the wall for some of the tests you can do.
While emotionally engaging after reading everything about all of the characters, I still didn't get that connection like I did in Bastion. I'll just mention Zulf and Mother, I'm Here. Those of you that played Bastion will understand what I'm getting at and I was really hoping for that kind of situation in the game.
Fantastic, worthy successor to Bastion. Good buy for sure.

I've had a pretty long history with this game. I've played since the Beta, and have had an on and off again sort of experience with it, at times enjoying it, and at times hating it with a passion. First off, to anyone interested in this game, it's free to play and decent enough that you should download and try it at the very least. Plus, with soon to be 91 different gods and goddesses to choose from, pretty much any playstyle is available.
Now as for my actual thoughts on the game, that's another matter.
There are a few significant problems that make this game frustrating at the very least to play, let alone get really in to. The first is bugs. Hi-Rez tries and tries to prevent them, but with added content and mechanics, and constant changes to effects and play testing amounting often to "Hey if you really like the game, you can play what we are releasing in a week early" which literally anyone can do. Crashes, errors, disconnections, incorrect explanations, all of these happen regularly around SMITE. I had a laptop I enjoyed playing games on that could run plenty of games that look far better graphically than this, but I wasn't able to play SMITE on it because of how poorly optimized this game seems to be. Either that or something on it for whatever reason wanted to fight with it.
The second problem is the gems system. Yes, a free to play game with micro-transactions, no surprise there. The reason why it's a problem though? Chests. Similar to other games wanting to add an element of randomization in rewards, chests can give you anything from skins, to small icons for your account. This in and of itself isn't really that big an issue, until you find that almost half the skins in the game, most of them being any of the good looking ones, all are in chests. That each range from two to four hundred gems, which are already an extremely expensive in-game currency which only increases in price with having to pay multiple times for chests in attempts to get the one thing you might want. It's just not worth it. Granted, this is about cosmetics, so it's not necessarily a huge thing, but it should be noted that many of the skins that make the characters interesting or funny all can cost dozens of real world dollars.
The final big problem is the balancing. Try as they might, Hi-Rez just doesn't seem to get how to make characters more balanced against each other. Granted, they do look at the competetive seen and high levels of play, and try to balance around that. However they often miss the mark on what changes are needed, and most of the player base isn't skilled enough at the game to make the changes made around high levels of play actually do what they want. My favorite example is when this last season (year) started for SMITE and they released an item named Bluestone pendant. This item made abilities do a bit more damage from the beginning of the game, giving several gods and goddesses new options. Chief among them was Sun Wukong, a god that was very underpowered for a long time, now thrown to the top of most people's tier lists for the lane he usually plays in. He wasn't the only one to become much stronger, but his change was the biggest, as he was near the bottom and shot near the top with the addition of this item, since now he could easily clear the lane where before he would have to use 2 abilities for a third of his mana. This created an imbalance in the game, so what do you think should happen? A) Change the item so that it's still a good choice but not a must buy, by changing the damage and/or cost of the item. B) Change Sun Wukong so that he can clear minions with 1-2 abilities without spending most of his mana every time, but not have as much aggressive poking damage, or C) Nerf the crap out of Sun Wukong so that he falls back to the bottom of god picks. If you chose C then congrats, you can work at Hi-Rez's balance team. Another example, an item, named Golden Bow, hasn't been a viable choice for almost every character in the game, except for a couple niche characters where it's a must-have item. Someone suggests buffing it, it goes through, and now you find that every hunter in the game is building this item and doing insane damage because of it. Do you A) Change the item back to how it was to re-evaluate what changes it needs to be less niche but not overpowered B) Make it so that this item that is now extremely strong is also much harder to get, so that it's still available for the niche characters, but also less appealing for the other characters that were using it until very late into the game or C) Remove the item and never re-introduce it with any changes whatsoever, just abandon ship on it. Guess which one was picked.
That's not to say SMITE is bad, it's still plenty of fun, but these problems make it very frustrating to play for long periods of time, and that's without mentioning the toxic player base, lack of attention to other modes outside of conquest (the typical MOBA style mode), and recent implementation of voice features built in that is unable to be turned off, only muted. There's good in there though, with stellar voice work for many of the skins and the gods themselves, content creators that make plenty of fun videos on the game, plenty of fun characters to try and master, a "mode of the day" match mode that puts fun twists on the game, and while it may be misguided, there is at least effort being put into making the game more fair, even if it makes the game wildly more unfair at times.

Dark Scavenger is an odd game. It's like you mixed together a turn-based first person perspective RPG, an adventure game, and Dungeons & Dragons in a sci-fi setting. By that, I mean that the combat is like Dragon Quest in terms of perspective, but you use items, weapons, and allies/summons with limited uses per area, when regen after completing a chapter, even if fully exhausted to zero, and every room/screen has things to inspect which trigger events where you can attempt to save someone, hide from enemies, obtain a hard-to-reach item, etc. Attempting to just naturally succeed without using an item/weapon/item/something you found is almost guaranteed to fail, as best I can tell, so using the items that you dislike the most is the most profitable way to handle events.
Each event will typically lead to you obtaining a crafting material, and you have 3 persistent allies who you can have craft items/weapons/allies out of the objects you find in each room/area. I believe my only serious complaint about the game comes from their descriptions of what they will make. They're incredibly vague. The weapons guy is typically easy to understand, but the items guy is basically insane and rarely makes sense about what he's saying, and the allies guy tries to act out what he'll make for you. He chased me around at one point, and he made a tiger for me as a summon. How the hell was "chases you around the room" supposed to let me know it was a tiger? For all I know, it could've been a child wanting to play tag. Since you don't get do-overs with a crafting material, this is problematic.
Like I said, though, that's literally my only real gripe about the game. The music is pretty nice; especially some piano music at the very beginning, and the artwork really worked for the game. I only played a little bit into the second chapter, but it seems to be a well-made game, and the D&D-like events are pretty nice. I won't deny that the game does have a definite "one-note" quality in regard to how it is played. You are in a room, you click on every thing, make choices on what item/weapon/ally to exhaust a use to have success, hopefully get crafting components, maybe do a turn-based battle, leave the room, craft 1-3 objects, then repeat forever.
For me, that did make me get bored with the game, but I'm pretty demanding when it comes to being kept entertained. It's a fine line between me feeling like a game was genuinely boring to the point that I felt tortured, and simply being a little less exciting/interesting than others so that my own desire for entertainment got me amped up for playing something different. I feel like Dark Scavenger was more the latter sort of experience. I do not plan on completing the game, but it has my blessing, for what it's worth. I disagree with people saying $4.99 not on sale is too high a price, though. I had a fried chicken sandwich the other day that cost almost $7 USD, and it was absolutely terrible. I could grab a McChicken and this game for less than that hauntingly awful nearly $7 sandwich and be far happier.

After looking at the store page and the reviews for
, I wasn't sure what to make of this game so I never came around to buying it. When my friend
from
had a spare key, I was happy I could give
a try.
The developer describes
as "a bizarre point-and-click RPG adventure", which is quite accurate.
plays like a fully-illustrated 'choose your own adventure' game based on the 'choices matter' principle with old school turn-based RPG-like combat and even a loot system, so it does seem to be an RPG at its core.
It's a unique game, that's for sure. If you think you may be interested in the type of game described above, I certainly recommend picking up
, especially if it's on sale. It'll provide at least 4 hours of fun for one playthrough, and more if you make use of its replayability. Or you can pick up the demo version on Steam to check out the first chapter of the game. If you decide to purchase the game after that, your save file will carry over so you can simply continue your adventure after the demo.
At the start of the game, you find yourself adrift in space and attacked by a shapeless blob that's both enormous and intelligent. After that encounter, a group of strange creatures who call themselves 'dark scavengers' pick you up with their spaceship. Problem is: the ship urgently needs refueling. There's a planet nearby but it might be a dangerous place and the dark scavengers tell you they're lousy fighters so they send you down to the planet to go scavenge for any source of energy that can be used as fuel.
The dark scavengers are uniquely strange creatures. The planet you'll explore looks pretty normal at first sight (I mean, you'll see grass, trees, lakes and ruins and they're all the 'right' size and colours and such) but by contrast, the creatures that inhabit the planet are out of this world – if you'll pardon the pun. This makes for weird but interesting encounters as you go adventuring through this unknown place.
The game is divided into five chapters, although the last chapter consists of little more than the final boss fights. In each chapter, you'll explore a different part of the planet you're on. To you, the player, this looks as follows. You see a scene with several interactable objects. Clicking on such an object triggers an event. Each event may lead to finding an item, encountering an npc to talk to, getting into a fight, and so on.
When you're done with the current scene, you choose where to go next by clicking on an arrow pointing north, south, east or west, if available. At any time you can access a map that keeps track of the scenes you visited and shows where you are now, which makes finding your way around the game world effortless.
If you gathered any loot from a scene, before entering the next scene you'll find yourself back on the spaceship where your shipmates can craft useable items from the loot you found. The crafted item can be a weapon, a summonable ally or a consumable item that'll buff or heal you. You only get a vague description of the kind of item each of your shipmates can make from any given piece of loot, so you'll need to try to choose wisely.
Combat takes place through a tactical interface and is turn-based. Each turn you can use one or more consumable items and you need to use one of your weapons or your summonable allies to attack the enemy. Each weapon, item and ally has very distinct effects and has limited uses, making the combat quite strategic and the possibilities legion. At the start of each chapter, all your items' uses are replenished. So the choices you make about which items to craft have a long-term impact on the game, as well.
During your adventures on the planet, you'll also be required to make choices in all sorts of situations. You really get the feeling that these choices matter. Not every decision you make has a huge impact, of course, but most of the time you do notice an immediate consequence to your actions. And the other times, the consequence may or may not become clear later on in the game, depending on which way you choose to handle things in future situations.
Often, you can't help but wonder 'What if I had chosen one of the other options?'. This adds replayability to the game. Also, after you finish the game a new option called 'New game +' appears in the game menu. This allows you to start a new game with all the items you gathered in your previous playthrough, allowing you to craft different items from the loot this time around.
The graphics are pretty basic and mostly static, but they're decent enough to serve their purpose. It's clear a lot of heart and talent went into the creature design. Almost all of them look truly unique and interesting. I would have liked to see some more creature
during combat, though, but I do realise things like that are very time-consuming and we are talking about an indie production here.
The music is strange but characteristic because it fits the strange atmosphere of the game, and it sounds very original.
Sound effects are okay but I would have liked more of them. A lot of actions that are described to the player and some combat actions that you see happening would have been so much more impressive if they had been accompanied by a fitting sound effect. I suppose this also shows the time and budget restrictions of an indie production.
