Wow! 100/100. One of the best games I have ever played.
What an exquisitely executed game. There are a huge amount of things I could say about how wonderful this game is, and the very much nothing that I dislike so far. I will touch on a few of the things that stand out the most concerning how amazing this game is.
The first is the overall game feel. It may be early access, but it plays like a complete and polished game, with very few bugs appearing. The only potential bug I have experienced is trivial, and comes about when you have two different materials going through the same furnace. This could be intentional, however. Aside from that, it is truly engaging and challenging, while also easing you in properly and without seeming too overwhelming right at once. It also makes you step back and appreciate how some polish goes a long way towards creating beautiful worlds out of minimal graphics packages.
The game has a wonderful combination of mechanics, with a sort of amalgamation of Minecraft, Command & Conquer, Sim City, and a few RPG elements tossed in. The balance of base building, resource management, incredible tech tree depth, combat, creativity, and strategy is phenomenal, and you have very little down time in this game while you're just waiting for things to happen, which is one of the best parts of the game. The crafting tree, which is integral to the gameplay, is very quick and doesn't feel like it drags on. That being said, you're crafting such a large quantity of things that it ultimately takes quite a while. You just don't get stuck doing nothing while its happening.
I love the crafting mechanics and tech tree, as well as the way the game doesn't punish you for moving buildings around, but encourages you to rearrange your base with some regularity instead. All the negative side effects of destroying and moving buildings in RTS games is erased, and so you can freely try over and over to arrange things to your liking or functional necessity. In this sense, you get a great way to explore what the game can do without having lost a bunch of money or resources on useless items that you don't know how to use yet.
It is hard to describe how engaging this game is on so many levels until you start to play and see the depth for yourself. I have rarely come across a game of such high quality and balance, while being completely flexible and customization. It is engaging from start to finish. If you're the kind of person who likes to fill out tech trees in any game you play, you will be quite ecstatic about the sheer breadth of options and progressions to the technology this game contains.
Like most open world games, this is also an excellent game for exploring and just doing whatever the hell you want. While a lot of the gameplay focuses on the automation of large scale production and complex infrastructure, you also will start to see some of the more creative and goofy things you can do with this technology, and have ample opportunity while playing a standard campaign mission or a skirmish map to futz around with a silly idea you have to design your train schedule so that once an hour all your trains line up on the tracks and spell the word "1337" or some other such ridiculousness. The possibilities are endless, and get more endless the further through the tech tree you progress.
All in all, this game takes some of the best elements from a fair number of game genres and combines them with perfect balance and execution, and really has demonstrated what is possible without insane fancy graphics, extreme AI, and heavy lifting engines. It has a tiny footprint compared to most games, but offers more in its tiny package than most games I have ever played. You will not be able to get bored with this game, though you might start wondering what happened to all your friends, or the sun, or your job, as you sink deeper and deeper into this immersive game. Worth every penny you could spend on it.

"Yeehaw, ye gunslingers, wanna take a ride in the ol' wild west?"
Hehe, really enjoyed this wild west shooter.
The narration is pretty good and very well implemented.
Silas Greaves, a bounty hunter, comes into bar and tells his story of how he took revenge to the men who killed his brothers and also nearly himself.
Throughout the story you'll eventually end up playing the same part of the level again, because he remembers it being different. So instead of duelling Pat Garret after entering a barn, you'll have a fast reward and then he just punches you unconcious as you enter it.
These narrative tricks keep the game interesting and surprising.
The shooter part is pretty straightforward, nothing groundbreaking but it's fun, especially the "bullet time", where you can dodge bullets and see everything in slow motion, while the enemies are highlighted.
You can also upgrade some skills for your shotgun, rifle and revolver which will give you slight improvements in zoom or reload time etc.
All in all it's a pretty neat, straight wild west shooter with a well done narration.

Factorio is exceptionally fun to play. Learning all of the ins and outs of how to most efficiently build things has left me playing this game for hundreds of hours. The only major downside to this game is that once you realize your base is pretty adequately safe, and the only factor preventing you from finishing the game is collecting the final resources for the rocket launch, it gets kind of pointless. I've played through the game once and on my second play through after building the rocket silo and the satellite, I just didn't see a reason to finish. I knew I'd be able to eventually collect enough resources to build the rocket... it was just a matter of time. Playing the waiting game... building more factories for rocket parts. There wasn't any challenge left. I almost feel like the whole rocket assembly process isn't necessary. Let me build the satellite and rocket silo and call it a day.
The only other thing I can say is I wish there were more interesting campaigns to play. Hopefully in the future there are different ways to win the game also. I wouldn't mind focusing entirely on military and just eradicating all of the enemies on the planet as a win condition. Also, some form of bridge making or flight transport would be a big bonus.
I also found little use for railways or robots due to playing the game with rich resources... I'm not really sure I'd be too excited to play the game on normal settings as collecting resources would require far too much effort only to have them run dry quicker.
Overall I highly recommend the game though. You'll get far more play time out of it than most games so the value is amazing. I played it through twice and that's more than I can say about 99% of games I've ever played.

I hated playing The Evil Within. I quit after two or three passes with the first encounter and its unfriendly checkpoints.  It felt tired and forced, and held back vital mechanics from the player in favor of cheap scares.  It annoyed me and did not value my time.
I reminded myself of this the 10th time I tried to make it through the medical section in Alien:Isolation.
Directed and linear to fault, Isolation has enormous issues, especially in the last third of the game which are offset magnificently by the first third of the game. Playing as Amanda Ripley, the grown daughter of the still vacu-frozen Ellen Ripley from Alien, the story takes place on a near derelict space station that is being decommissioned.  With art and sound direction that feels like the original Alien was rubbed up and down over the developer’s bodies, mood and tone are established quickly and retained for the most part.
The Sevastopol station leans heavily on the design of the refinery towed by the Nostromo in Alien, with towering spires and spikes sticking out of everything. On in the inside, inexplicably large open holes dot the ceilings and the walls are lined with circular vents that iris open.  Wall-grids are backlit creating the illusion of light against massive negative spaces of shadow. In short it looks great. It looks right.
The station thrums and pulses with the film’s atonal sounds that create tension on their own, delivering inescapable claustrophobia, like an empty active auto factory. Machinery is alive everywhere but little else is. Sparse human survivors run or attack when they see Amanda, desperate to hold on long enough for a rescue that is never coming.
In survival horror tradition, resources are thin though there are crafting materials everywhere if you take time to look.  Amanda picks up blueprints throughout the game, expanding the repertoire of jury rigged defenses that as much distraction as weapon.  Early on,  a locked door hints at a specific kind of torch i.e. the one she didn’t just get, that is needed to cut through the lock. Backtracking through environments is a thing.
Man is it a thing.
The opening hours are tense and exciting, as Amanda works her way deeper into the station, trying to reconnect to the ship orbiting outside that brought her here.  All of the enemies on the station are revealed, average loud dumb gun toting humans, ultra creepy near invulnerable androids and finally the titular alien.
Revealed in a cut scene and soon followed in gameplay in the dreaded medical section I was immediately terrified by the Alien’s presence.  Booming footfalls or rumbling vents announced it and drips of drool would hint at why lie ahead. I was riveted.
I was riveted until I died or backtracked through medical enough times to memorize it and really watched the Alien’s behavior.  It thumped past me and I drank in the detail and I died enough that I stopped caring. I stopped being afraid of the plodding Alien and hid and crouched and kept quiet, so much so that by the time I had completed what I thought was the ending I was barely annoyed.
I realized then I wasn't even halfway into the game. There would be pointless side missions that could be replaced with a cut scene and lose nothing.
More and more I backtracked and had a sudden realization that it seemed like sequences were created from a cool visual concept and reverse engineered to create that moment, and thus were impervious to subversion by the player.
Isolation betrays its own conceit late in the game, having abandoned the Alien as enemy, placing hordes of androids instead, only to reintroduce the Alien. But by then it’s too late. Amanda has enough weapons and tools to keep her out of harm’s way.  The Alien has been effectively neutered as a threat as have the androids.
When it ends, when it finally ends, it betrays the conceit of the film so spectacularly one wonders why the slavish devotion in all other areas. It falls to the same pitfalls Alien: Colonial Marines fell to in trying too hard to retro-fit canon when it isn’t completely ignoring canon. (ie. Why name her Amanda if Aliens is outside the source material, but then why ignore Aliens if her name is Amanda?)
Isolation is ambitious and visually stunning, often incoherent and in love with its set pieces, and too long by half.

TLDR:
MOBA of all time
I've played thousands of hours combined of DotA, DotA2, LoL, etc. and none of them even comes close to the level of fun and gameplay diversity SMITE provides.
The 3rd person perspective alone is enough to beat off the competition as it adds several more layers of skill-based gameplay and immersion (such as: every basic attack is a skill-shot; you can't see behind you; juking is key; you can bodyblock attacks; sound effects matter).
But what really makes SMITE shine is its fun factor and fast pace. The mythology theme never gets old; the variety of game modes is extraordinary (heck, there's even PvE events); and the voice commands and emotes system is unrivaled and incredibly amusing to use.
On top of everything, the devs listen closely to feedback, go out of their way to please the community and give away freebies like no other (which means with enough dedication you can unlock virtually everything in the game for free, including cosmetics).
Sure, there are community and matchmaking issues that need fixing, but which competitive multiplayer game doesn't have them?
About as balanced as a fat guy on a tightrope. However, it's still very fun and satisfying to play, especially when you get a pentakill :)

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

It's an MMO based of The Elder Scrolls Series; lore and mechanics are heavily inspired by previous games, so there may be a similiar feel when playing the game. Emphasize on 'may', because as a standalone game, it is also very different.
The environment isn't as good as the main games, due to multiplayer limitations. Everything is placed to help players fulfill quests easier as opposed to 'enjoying' the view or atmosphere. As a result, gameplay feels rushed as you try to get good gear and level up quicky.
As a Skyrim player, the UI takes some time to get used to, as well as the menu bars. Even then, some features still feel off and uncomfortable. Luckily, the game supports mods so use them to enhance your experience.
Additional note: I usually play solo since whenever I try to party with other, I discovered the lag makes cooperation difficult. This may be my fault and not the server's fault, as I was using a relatively slow connection at the time.
Overall, it's good if you are a fan of the Elder Scrolls Series, but not worth in its full price in my opinion. Wait for sales, watch gameplay videos and read reviews before buying this game. I would recommend the Imperial edition, as you get a mount early on and this significantly helps travel, instead of walking from one end of the map to the other.

Zenimax is doing a pretty damn good job here. This is probably the closest we'll be getting to an "updated" Ultma-Online(player freedom as the primary goal), It has it's short-comings though it gets major props for actualy trying to break the generic MMO mold.

______
+ Game is Buy-2-Play and, the Cash Shop avoids breaking the experience very nicely.
+ One Tamriel update unlocked leveled zones, letting players go anywhere, quest anywhere.
+ Combat is smooth and responsive, each hit has weight to it's swing making each weapon feel different from the next.
+ The Champion system rewards multiple characters and, with the amount of calsses/skills, building a new character doesn't feel like a chore.
+ No Cooldowns on Skills/Spells, everything works off a pooled resources stamina and/or magicka, with very few skills having cast times.
+ All quests are fully voiced, making them feel more personal with a total of four campaigns (Vestige and, the Alliances) and everything inbetween.
+ The Vestige story here is the best in the Scrolls series since TES:Oblivion, Molag Bal remains a persistent Antagonistic force.
+ Probably the most rewarding crafting/gathering experience I've had in a MMO in a long time, the economy is also controlled by the player-base with personalized trading guilds.
______
- Customer support's automated e-mail response♥♥♥♥♥♥is very dodgey, and can get very annoying.
- Game client is ♥♥♥♥ing "Yuuge"!
- Equipment loadouts need reworked, as of now a "double 2-handed weapon loadout" gets gimped loosing out on a potential 2/5/5 monster set(So, DW/1H&Shld are almost a required meta slot). The MSA weapons are out there, but they just don't compare to the effects on the MS's, and having two 5's active at ounce.
- Right now, Cyrodiil feels empty outside the Imperial City/Sieges. I just wish there was more out there then just bouncing from ruins and skyshards.
- Mounts are disappointing for me, I thought there would be racing at some point. They instead strapped the riding skills on the character and, then threw upgrades in the damn cash shop...meh.

This game is laugh-out-loud freedom and explosions.  There is quite a bit of satire involved in the overall theme of the game, but it's not overwhelming or trying to shove a political opinion down your throat.  Mostly it's poking fun at the 80's and 90's action movie genre, while delivering some solid gameplay.
The game has sort of a modern Contra-like difficulty to it.  You get one hit per life, and your Bro changes every time you die.  There are a few difficulty spikes, with certain bosses or some of the challenge levels, but the only real complaint you can make with the game is that it has bugs, and they aren't going anywhere.  Controllers sometimes freak out and have to be moved to a different port on your PC in order to start functioning again.  Also, some of the transition scenes like for bosses entering another stage of the fight can stick, and there isn't anything you can do but start the level over.  If you can deal with the bugs and you like a challenge, then this game is totally worth it.

So there is an amazingly cool game here.  It's one of the most fun MMORPGs I've played and I've literally sampled hundreds of different ones.
There are a lot of boss fights that are really interesting.  The combat is overall very fun to do with each class playing differently.  There even are all sorts of hidden areas in the game that you start to find out about later.  Even all the side quests usually have a bit of extra story you can choose to read about or not which I enjoy reading.
There is a crazy amount of ways to do class builds.  At first you choose one of a few base classes but each line has at least 15 other classes under their line with other hidden classes too.  You mix and match what you want to do, you can take some of a lot of classes or fully master up a few.  The class system is easy to mess yourself up on though so I highly suggest planning out what you want to do outside the game through some websites first.  There is no resetting back to base to choose again.
When you first start it will seem too easy, but as soon as you open your first instanced dungeon you'll understand that the game doesn't stay easy all the way through.
So if it's that good, why the mixed reviews?  Launch issues for one.  They haven't even been that bad compared to a lot of popular MMORPG launches, but there are a lot of players here that have never experienced a popular MMORPG launch and think everything is supposed to go smooth.  So basically newbies are downvoting because of launch issues.
Next is that people have issue with certain things that aren't going to be free.  They'll absolutely love the game, plan on playing it many many hours, but dislike how something is being done with the trade system so downvote the game because of it.  All I can say is watch the play hours of the people downvoting.  If they continue to go up, they obviously don't dislike it that much.
Free players are going to have fits once they start to play and downvote because not everything is given to them free though too.
Are there some things that could use tweaking in the game system?  Absolutely yes.  Does that spoil the entire game and make it so it's not recommended?  Absolutely no!  Sure some things need changing but the overall game is still great.

THERE IS A TUTORIAL. If you can't find it yet still somehow start a hunt, don't play it. You clearly don't have the chops for this game, sorry.
Let me open this up by saying if you're under 16 or have some kind of attention deficit disorder, stay away. If you're the kind of person whom while playing MMOs jumps on your mount to run 10 meters and tries to hit max level on the first day\week, stay away. If you're the kind of person who thinks games like the ArmA franchise are 'boring' stay away. If you're the kind of person who thinks 'Free to Play' should mean: "Give me everythig in a week so I can move on to the next game like a ravenous locust" stay away. If you can't take the time to read a few pages of text, stay away.
This game requires an insane amount of patience, forethought and time. It requires you to learn animal behaviours, how to use lures. It'll teach you how to stalk, stay down-wind and it'll teach you to ease off the trigger and wait for that pefect shot. But it won't beat it into you. If you don't learn, you'll never kill anything, and you'll blame the game for your own hysterical ineptitude.
The game is your typical huting style game, you enter a range with a few buddies, gear up and go looking for game. If you're an idiot and run around everywhere, you'll hear nothing and see less. See my point above: Go low, go slow. Follow the trails the animal has left. Spot it's calls and get yourself in range for a quick, clean effcient and ethical kill. Simple right? It's an especially enjoyable just chilling in a tower or a hide with a few buddies catching up.
Now let's talk about the pay wall, shall we? Yes the game is hardly playable as a free to play game. Is it prohibitivly expensive? Only if you're an idiot with no idea how to take advantage of bundles. There are a selection of bundles on the store that offer 3, 6 and 12 month subs respectivly alongside a whole boat load of gear. If you drop the £30 on the top end back you get:
12 Month Sub
Around £50 worth of consumables
A weapon from each catagory and a high powered pistol, as well as ammo and equipment for it.
Gear
Hides
Stands
Tents
This is as much conent as if you'd bought the game normally. CRAZY I KNOW. It's almost like the company wants to stay in business with such a small demograph. (Let's hope these kids never spot Flight Sim after market prices, eh?)
Yet the people knocking this game are more than happy to drop £60 on the latest CoD Map Pack while shouting about this games payment model. It is MORE than possible to buy a single 3 month sub and complete the missions in a few days, giving you around 100,000 GMS (In game currency) which is enough to buy liscences and hunt for free for around a year and a half.)
Make no mistakes though, the Free to Play in this game should be considered a pretty hefty, unlimited demo, much like WoWs Free to Play model.
If you've ever wanted to actually hunt or want a realistic representation of what it could be like, this game, some buddies and a few hours to kill will be a rewarding and satisfying experience. If you want to have a collection of 30 deer pelts and wrestle a bear all within 10 minutes, don't waste your time, or my time when you come crying to the forums.

Call of Juarez Gunslinger is a linear fps based in a western setting. Although not directly connected to the previous games in the Call of Juarez series, this feels very similar to Bound In Blood (in terms of atmosphere at least)
There’s a decent story in Gunslinger about a famous bounty hunter as he tells bar patrons about his famous adventures. This allows for some interesting and at times, comical, gameplay elements. One second you’ll be fighting dozens of Indians only to have the story paused and rewound having to replay the same part but with a different scenario. It’s because of this that the story kept me interested and by the end of it, I was genuinely surprised.
The gameplay is arcade-like with scores, combos, and multipliers that build up depending on the way you kill enemies. It’s really satisfying to pull off different kills and see the points stack up. There’s even a focus meter that slows down time and lets you make very precise shots (a lot of fun). At certain points in the story, you have to showdown against famous outlaws in the form of “duels”. They’re basically boss fights where you have to maintain focus and draw your weapon at the right time in order to win. I really enjoyed these moments because there’s a reasonable learning curve, and I found myself getting better at the duels as the game progressed.
There’s also a level up system with upgrades that improve your three different weapon classes, pistols, shotguns, and rifles. Most of the upgrades make significant changes to your character’s abilities. You can even unlock unique weapons after upgrading a weapon class to a certain level. There are 2 unique weapons for each class making for a total of six unique guns to unlock. Aside from the unique guns there are plenty of other weapons to use. In case you don’t unlock all the guns/upgrades in your first playthrough, there’s a New Game+ option with a higher difficulty level to keep the challenge up.
In addition to the single player story, there’s an “Arcade” mode and “Duel” mode. “Arcade” takes levels from the story and focuses on gaining the highest amount of points using the multipliers. “Duel” mode is all about reliving the famous duels from the campaign and trying to get as far as possible on a certain number of lives. Both are fun accessories to the main missions that can give you a few hours of extra gameplay.
Overall I’m very impressed with Call of Juarez Gunslinger. The game is relatively short, but so much fun to play. It’s certainly one of the best western themed games I’ve played.

Super Giant flexes it's art muscles again and delivers some of the best 2D artwork in a game. It is truly a piece of art in motion. In addition to the top notch visuals, Transistor boasts one of the best gaming soundtracks. I find myself listening to the cd over and over while at work.
The combat is a unique blend of strategy and an action game where the player can freeze time and plan out their attack on the "Process". As with Bastion, there are game modifiers that make this game tougher, making the need for this planning mode essential.
I cannot praise this game enough. A run through of the story may be a brief 6 hours but it does not over stay its welcome and feels complete in almost every way. The game does not hold your hand and expects you as a player to dig into the world to get the most out of it.

Transistor is something of a tactical RPG by Supergiant Games. The player is thrust into a vague situation as the famous singer Red, whom has had her voice "stolen" from her, as she removes a sword-like object from a corpse. It's insinuated that you knew this person, Mr. Nobody, and they protected you. The sword acts as the narrator of the story and as the majority of the player's insight into the world.
Red uses the sword, the titular "Transistor", to fight off mysterious white invaders known as "The Process". The sword begins with a few attacks and has the ability to stop time (called "turn) to plan attacks, and then execute the qued attacks. This can only be done once every few seconds, depending on how many actions were lined up, and this is the main method of playing. The player can attack outside of combat when they aren't regenerating their "turn" ability or when an ability is upgraded with a specific augment, but it's very slow and inaccurate. There's a multitude of skills (called "functions"- 18 in total) which can also be used to augment other skills or Red herself. Functions are multi-purpose: not only do they act as Red's skills system, but they also unlock fragments of backstory for the game while using them in one of the three different capacities (ability, ability upgrade, personal upgrade), but the backstories are focused on the person related to the ability.
The skill system is very interesting and can lead to some creative builds, but ultimately the goal is still to do gross amounts of damage, and there's only a handful of skills that will help you reach those levels. While many of these functions have interesting properties and uses, Transistor's combat doesn't really lend to using some of them more than once to unlock background story. An example of this is the function "Get", which pulls an enemy toward you. Due to the nature of combat, Get often is redundant or, at worst, a detriment. When executing a turn, time isn't stopped anymore- it's slowed. Faster creatures will begin to move away from your planned abilities and Get can sometimes miss or pull the wrong one. This doesn't require faster enemies to mess up, either, as the game's readout of potential damage often is misleading. When stacking attacks, the game will caculate how much damage will occur to enemies. Often it'll drop out enemies if there's too much information on the screen, but it also poorly handles damage over time and momentum knocking enemies out of range. Some monsters, like Jerk 3.0's, are able to rotate so quickly that by the time you're done buffing and debuffing, they have rotated and you can no longer backstab. This is frustrating considering that the two most simple solutions are: A, stop time entirely for the turn function, or B, remove the damage readout.
Despite being flawed on many fronts on its own, the mediocre combat isn't the only thing to blame. Enemies in Transistor focus on ten different enemies. These enemies start out basic, and get "upgrades" as the player continues through the story. These upgrades are denoted by a 2.0 or higher designation beside the name. Despite the intent that the player needs to deal with these enemies in different ways, none of these enemies force the player to think differently. The answer is always the same: use a turn and do as much damage as possible in one go, preferably by way of AoE damage. This is absolutely true for every enemy, from hulking Jerks to artillery Cluckers. There are some attempts to break this up, such as the Snapshot's obscuring effect, but many of the abilities in the game already force the player into melee combat, so they are often inconsequential. In the later stages of the game, the player merely need to wait until an enemy is no longer stealthed to unleash flurry of void debuffs and a final cull swing.
The game is rather short, and it takes somewhere in between two to six hours for a playthrough, depending on if the player does everything (interacting with spots and terminals, doing challenges, etc) or not. The player is thrust into the story as soon as they start the game for the first time, and it really never becomes much clearer. Transistor takes something of a "Dark Souls" approach to telling a story by having it dispersed through strings of text on functions and difficulty increasing "limiters". The Transistor, whom is inhabited by someone Red knows that remains nameless, is the main source of off-hand information during the game, usually to excess. The problem with this story is that nothing is ever divulged, nothing is ever expanded upon, and most information presented through functions are about people that either aren't important to the story or provide nothing concurrent that puts things into context. The game is absolutely full of plot holes to an incredible degree and it's presented in a way that would be lost on a lot of people, as it expects the player to use all abilities in all capacities and sift through the text. It's terrible storytelling, which is a shame. The story is interesting, but inaccessible unless subtitles (for Sybil, Royce and Mr. Nobody) and with some extra reading and conjecture. Conjecture is not a basis for storytelling, though; you're just witnessing an event without any context. It's like if you've witnessed a UFO beaming up some farm animals in the distance. Without the rest of the story, the game focuses on Red and Mr. Nobody's extremely obvious relationship as lovers, and Mr. Nobody talks at great length in regards to this when he's not busy filling your ears full of nonsense otherwise. "Sea Monster's the only real choice here," indeed. The relationship stands somewhere around "puppy love" on the devotion spectrum until the end of the game, but there's really no development at all. There's no back story, outside of a few obscure references and some images during the credits.
The majority of the game is spent trying to get to the Camerata in their tower, and then backtracking through some of the early areas to an M.C. Escher area (which contrasts to the Gustav Klimt inspired "golds and shapes" artwork through the rest of the game). The areas, while beautiful, are exceptionally similar and the game's areas bleed into each other. While there's plenty of polish, there's plenty of little things I wouldn't expect at this level of polish, like how OVC terminals are pretty much just inverted when facing the other way, including the giant "OVC" markings. These things become very apparent when the environments aren't differentiated, and when you're doing the same things over and over.
Supergiant Games had a lot to live up to for their second game, and I can't really hold them to those expectations; they were just astronomical considering Bastion was their first fare, which was both refreshing, innovative, and honed in just about every category. Something about Transistor feels rushed, or hollow. It's hard not to compare Transistor to Bastion with all the similarities and outright references to it; a silent protagonist with a narrator voiced by Logan Cunningham battles to save what's left of their city using a deus ex machina device, all whilst encountering a few survivors and an eventual "betrayal" that leads the character to seek greener pastures. The only differences here are story elements, which are even more vague in this offering, and the well meaning but ultimately poor combat. I'm pressed to say that this game would be amazing for a first entry as a studio, but, it's not.

This game is amazing, and one of the few that I regard as "full price worthy" even years after its release.
Artwork, Atmosphere, Feel:
The artwork is spot on and a real love letter to Ridley Scotts Alien movies. Every room feels authentic and is full of detail but never feels cluttered or overloaded. And it is not just the bigger areas, even those little dead end hallways that are only there to make the level layout more believable are rich with atmosphere.
Gameplay:
At its core it is a hiding and sneaking game but you also get weapons to fight back. You can't kill the Alien but pretty much everyone else. On top of that is a light crafting system that lets you build distractions, bombs and other little helpers that allow different solutions to a problem. But resources are rare and require additional exploration = more risk to gather.
Another great aspect of the gameplay and this ties in very well with the lvl design is the obfuscation of the engagement areas. A lot of similar games make the mistake that they send you down a linear path with no hiding spots or dark shadowy corners and then all of a sudden you see a room full of them which makes it a clear tell that an enemy will show up and breaks the game apart into safe exploration areas and dangerous engagement spots. This game does it differently, you will often find rooms with conveniently placed hiding spots that would allow a safe route from one shadow to another, a clear tell that an enemy encounter is up, huh? But nope, no one is there. This might sound like a minor detail but it adds so much immersion.
The alien itself doesn't use a fixed patrolling route, rather some sort of clever AI which works pretty well. Only downside to this, and this took me a while to get used to is that you will see it a lot. I would have preferred if it would stay more often in hiding and only come out when it sees a good opportunity to attack you directly, like in the movies.
Overall I would score it a solid 9.5

I haven't dumped a lot of hours into this one yet.  But the keyword here is "yet".  This game captures one thing impeccably well: going through the daily grind over and over and over.  Definitely recommend a mouse and not just a trackpad for this one as each day is time sensitive.
Another really great aspect is the ability to choose personal morals over the morals of the state.  Do you buy the sob story and let the lady pass, or do you send her back to her war torn country because her stamp is invalid.  Will that affect how much you can feed your family?!
As to your family: you make a certain amount of credits each day based on how many people you correctly allowed to immigrate.  Each day the rules get a little harder.  Each day you make a little less.  At some point, you have to use money management to decide if, with the pittance you just made, you are going to: heat your house, buy food for your family, purchase medicine or upgrade your booth.  If you can't pay rent, the game is over.
If given the chance would I buy it again?  Absolutely, even if I had to pay full price for it.

It's an MMO based of The Elder Scrolls Series; lore and mechanics are heavily inspired by previous games, so there may be a similiar feel when playing the game. Emphasize on 'may', because as a standalone game, it is also very different.
The environment isn't as good as the main games, due to multiplayer limitations. Everything is placed to help players fulfill quests easier as opposed to 'enjoying' the view or atmosphere. As a result, gameplay feels rushed as you try to get good gear and level up quicky.
As a Skyrim player, the UI takes some time to get used to, as well as the menu bars. Even then, some features still feel off and uncomfortable. Luckily, the game supports mods so use them to enhance your experience.
Additional note: I usually play solo since whenever I try to party with other, I discovered the lag makes cooperation difficult. This may be my fault and not the server's fault, as I was using a relatively slow connection at the time.
Overall, it's good if you are a fan of the Elder Scrolls Series, but not worth in its full price in my opinion. Wait for sales, watch gameplay videos and read reviews before buying this game. I would recommend the Imperial edition, as you get a mount early on and this significantly helps travel, instead of walking from one end of the map to the other.

One of my all-time favorite games. After five years there are only two words that describe this game: Replay Value.
It's timeless (and timely, if you're following the script).
What keeps me coming back: It's a narrative masterpiece. Outstandingly well written. The voice acting is on point, and the dark, layered humor of the script never gets old. I care about the characters and each one has such a personality.
Visually, it's stylized and stunning. The music is so good that it's a character on its own that keeps you company, like a best friend along the way.
All these elements put together makes me feel wrapped up in a warm, zainy blanket.
It's linear. It doesn't bother me because I'm always swept up in the story and it's something I want to be apart of. So, I do feel taken care of in the game. Just bouncing straightforward from quest to quest is a ton of fun and makes the learning curve less steep. Very low barrier of entry into this game.
The FPS gameplay is medium-paced, simple and straightforward. The different makeup of skill trees satisfies those with a desire to further customize their character. There are clear roles that each character falls into, and can be utilized to create a proper group with the right teamwork. Or it can be a free-for-all and everyone can kind of bounce around and have fun that way. It's like a casual, narrative-driven, linear First Person Shooter RPG.
Pub community is where it's at. Being able to hop on and matchmake is a strength that adds to the replay value. I get satisfaction in simply accompanying someone else in their game for awhile. And, if I get lucky, they're new and on their first playthrough. That keeps things fresh for me. I shut up and enjoy the ride.
I come from a background of intense gaming. Power gaming. Spending hours/days online until my body hurt. I grew up playing Valve games and mods, Quake, all sorts. These days I prefer to remove the glued-to-your-seat adrenaline junky aspect.... and instead play for pleasure, feel good about myself and actually take breaks/get things done throughout the day (tales of an aging gamer).
This is sort of the light version of games I grew up addicted to :) Best thing is, while I can really invest it, I also feel like I can walk away from it. Like a good book. I can set it down and I look forward to picking it up later. The story will always be there.
I highly recommend this game. For those who've tried it in the past but were bored, I hope my review inspires you to take a second glance. You might think, really? BL2? It doesn't take itself seriously at all! ... And that's the point. I think it's video games as an artform and social commentary at its finest. Comedy is a dignified way of dealing with pain. Comedy unlocks it. BL2 is like one giant key.
Good game not PW2

Okay, so here's the thing. I'm currently level 134, I really enjoy playing this game and I'm going to continue to play it. So giving this game a negative rating would be dishonest and hypocritical, and I say this to anyone else rating this game poorly while continuing to sink hours into the game.
There's problems.. Yes, very annoying problems holding it back..
Such as bots running around leveling automatically and stealing kills, and the developers don't seem to be doing anything about it. There's no way to even report these bots.
The slight B2W advantages you get, like the enchantment scrolls, token benefits, and some other things I'm sure I'm missing. You can buy tokens in-game, though for a hefty price, so that's not a big deal to me. It's mostly the enchantment scrolls. Yes, you can get those in-game, too.. but they're extremely rare.
There's also dramatic stuttering and performance issues even on my high-end PC in heavily populated areas. This one is a little disheartening as it questions the ability for events such as sieges in the future.
I also think the game would be better if only certain classes could use pets. Everyone having a pet, all of which look pretty much the same given that there's only 3 types of pets, is a bit obnoxious regardless of what they look like. The fact that you can take them into PvP with you, too is a bit silly. They also don't help the lag.
Overall though, despite all that, I'm still really enjoying this game. It has an incredibly deep class customization system, a really fun combat system, and the difficulty scaling is on par. The game can be pretty challenging which I really admire.

Slow and steady progress with the updates and IMC doing something about the bots. Devs take time to take action on problems but they do listen to feedback. As for the game:
Gameplay
- Classes
It is necessary to read up on your preferred class and their higher ranks you want to play because this game contains a ton of classes including hidden ones you need to unlock. This game contains so many classes it gives players a lot of builds to experiment on.
- Controls
I have only ever used the keyboard because of the two classes I've rolled (Cleric and Swordsman). All I can say is it is very intuitive for melee classes. Positioning yourself to use skill couldn't be easier. Felt awkward at first because I imagined ToS as RO.
For wizards and Archers, they can use mouse to target and keyboard to move their characters and use skills. For Clerics and Swordsmen, it's all keyboard. You can of course use mouse for the melee classes and keyboard for the long range ones but is really not recommended. Controllers can also be used to play.
- Quests
Diverse enough that you don't get bored (Similar to GW2 quests)
- Grinding
You're probably going to spend your time grinding around levels 160 and 200+. The time it takes to reach those levels alone isn't very long. I have a Level 129 Priest and Level 182 Fencer at this time. There are a lot of ways to level up, dungeons, daily quests, story quests, bounties (killing a certain amount of enemy on a map) and map completion. You get a lot exp cards for doing quests which you can use to get tons of exp.
Graphics
My processor is an i5-6500. I have no video card (waiting for AMD Polaris), I can run this game at an average of 30 fps, but dips to 12-17fps in cities. This game uses only a single core and is badly optimized. IMC is currently working on optimization. Take note that the characters you see on screen are 3D models designed to look 2D. This game looks gorgeous! Fair warning though, this game drops in FPS if there are a lot of people on screen, even if you have a decent video card. IMC is working on this currently.
Music
Somewhat of a mixed bag for me. You'll be missing the nostalgic music of RO, but there are quite a few good bgm here. Most of the maps have multiple soundtracks so you won't be listening to only one track while you're questing, farming or grinding.
Premium Tokens
This is given to founders and is sold on the cash shop. This gives a reduced market commision fee (from 30% to 10%), increased market listing to 5 (default is 1), increased movement speed (from 1 to 3), simultaneous attribute training (from 1 to 2), increased exp from monsters +30% (exp from exp cards do not count), allows you to trade up to 30 times, increased buff count by 1, able to use premium gestures and + 1 dungeon and mission entry.
This is untradable but can be listed in the marketplace. This is currently priced 350k - 500k but I imagine this is going to go higher once F2P releases. Buying this at this price is easy. One can make around 80-100k in an hour from loots and silver drops alone if your level is high enough. I saved enough money doing quests alone for two tokens. Using two or more of these will extend the effect (1 token is 30 days - your number of trades will add up).
Bots and Gold Sellers
This is what the majority of players cry about. It's hard to remove this from the game and in an attempt to minimize the number of bots and sellers, IMC put heavy restrictions in-game (3 day no marketplace selling for new accounts), minimum and maximum price limit for items in the marketplace, trading 1:1 only for token users. We have a report bot option and IMC regularly bans bot accounts which you can see in the forums. The heavy restrictions will likely be changed as soon as there's a better way to stop bots. Help IMC stop them by reporting these bots in-game.
**Don't get scared about the mixed reviews. Most of the clowns who put in negative reviews are crybabies complaining about every changes made to the game but they still currently play.

I recommend getting this game, but definitely not at 7€ price, rather around-below 3. It would be a superb deal for 1€,  as the game is a little bit crude, but it was made with a lot of love and care.
The game is a little weird mix of visual novels, point and clicks and choose your own adventures. Basically the game goes on a ~top-down map where certain locations can trigger choose your own adventure-type parts where depending on your choices can fight, avoid it sometimes, and/or find new items. Every time you move on from a smaller location (like a meadow with 3-4 hotspots) you're taken back to the ship where your 3 companions can craft an item from each piece of the loot you got. You'll get an overly scientific description for a weapon, a crazy one for a usable item, and a mute alien will play charades to explain what a summon would do. A golden axe can get sharper, can get reforged into a shield or made into a summon. The writing of this part outstanding, and there are a lot of weird items to get, like an item that stuns stupid enemies. Or enemies who have more than 10 words in their descriptions. There are maybe 5? type of resistance and weakness in fight, and in many story parts you'll need fire weapon to make light, sharp one to cut something, etc.
The story has two warring factions + wild animals, corrupted enemies, sidequest-like unique NPCs, recurring boss-characters with whom you'll get some story - in some fights you can get adventage if you halt the enemies with talk.
I don't think I'll try new game+, but while the game lacked the gameplay variety, it had a nice little campaign going on with enjoyable fights and interesting events inbetween (For example I used Your Mother to weight down a chair on a trapdoor :) ) - maybe I'll swing a few people to get this game during a discount, or if it will get bundled again.

Ce pot să spun? Un joc extrem de atrăgător, atât din punct de vedere grafic, cat si din stilul de joc.
Da, dai rage ca in lol, dar... aici e ceva mai interesant.
Poveste:
Ca in ori ce alt joc de lupte, practic iti iei propiul tău zeu, si incepi să te lupti cu altii, luându-ti arme sau armuri(nu vizuale) si potiuni.
Povestea mea a inceput acum 1 an(baza practic) cand am văzut mai multe video-uri la IHP.
M-a atras stilul de joc si grafica.
Da, si eu am spus la inceput că seamana cu LoL-ul, dar nu e adevărat. Jocul ăsta este mult mai bun decât gunoiul ăla de lol. E un joc atrăgător, prin simplul fapt că are zei.
Ce zei? Toti zeii antici; de la Loki, la Thor, pana la He Bo sau chiar Neith.
Gameplay:
Este ca LoL-ul, sau Dota. Iti selectezi un campion/zeu si te duci la luptă.
Fiecare are o putere specifică, exact ca cele reale. Spre exemplu, Loki: Loki este fratele lui Thor, iar el cu Thor sunt fii lui Odin. Loki are niste abilităti geniale, atât strategice cat si din punct de vedere al DMG-ului. Loki, era un clown(măscărici) care a făcut multe ''prostioare'' ;). In mitologia antică, se spune că Loki, avea puterea de a se transforma in diferite animale, păcat că aici nu se aplică.. :(.
Concluzia:
Nu prea am cuvinte. Cand intrii in joc, ai un tutorial ca să te obisnuiesti cu gameplay-ul, ceea ce mi se pare destul de ok. Da, poti să si plătesti, dar nu prea iti da un avantaj, decât in skin-uri, in rest... nu prea ai nevoie să bagi bani in joc. Poti aduna diamante destule, doar din timp. Intr-un an, poti ajunge la 9-10k diamante(fără să le folosesti, desigur).
Este un joc bine pus la punct, fiind locul 6 in top-ul jocurilor de acest gen.
Desi pare un joc care nu dispune de update-uri, din luna in luna( sau 2 luni, depinde) se face cate un update la patch, ce constă in rezolvarea unor bug-uri si adăugarea unor zei noi.
Recomand acest joc, fiind si free si cu o grafică genială si gameplay pe măsură!

I almost put this game down early in the piece. In the beginning, for a very long time you will explore the space station in uninterrupted solitude, with a gradually rising feeling of dread. It's an important sequence that does a brilliant job of establishing a sense of place, allowing you time, without fear of attack, to read the text on highly detailed posters, and generally poke about to get an idea of what life on the Sevastopol might have been like prior to the catastrophe that has recently been visited upon it. But you know the game has more. The title promises us an Alien to complement this Isolation.
When the Alien eventually enters the picture it makes up for the time not spent harrassing you by following you around at a distance that suggests it may well be physically magnetised to your person, for about three missions straight. It all becomes insufferably tedious. Despite adoring the game's atmosphere and attention to detail, I felt that the titular Alien, the intended drawcard of the whole affair, was a blight on the experience, because its tenacious nature had transitioned me from admiring the form of the environment to analytically considering no more than its function, and had slowed my progress into new environments to a crawl. After reloading some checkpoint for the nth time, I was ready to just uninstall the thing. But then the alien unexpectedly went on holiday for a while, and I realised that the pacing of the game had been deliberately structured into a series of troughs and peaks, and I thought 'Okay, I can live with that'.
During its hefty playtime you will find times for exploring, times for hiding, times for running, and times for killing. It does a good job of mixing things up to prevent the alien's presence becoming too oppressive.
In addition to the alien, you will encounter two other types of foes: humans, and androids of limited intelligence designed for performing mundane tasks, however something has gone very wrong in their programming. It was this latter enemy that I actually found the most creepy - their body shape is just human enough, and their movement just robotic enough that they venture deep into the uncanny valley. All three enemies require different approaches, however it is a constant that although there are limited combat options available, you are encouraged to avoid violence as far as possible. The alien is so sensitive to sound that if it hears a shot or blast anywhere in the level it will instantly make a beeline to that location, and for the majority of the game your firearms consist of The World's Worst Shotgun And Revolver (I played on hard, and these things emitted the noise of a jet breaking the sound barrier and delivered the force of a flicked pea). The quieter melee option of a maintenance jack to the face is viable, but only situationally as it is slow and only suitable for one-on-one engagement.
Instead of shooting things, you are encouraged to turn various spare parts and salvage into the items you find on blueprints scattered throughout the game. Throw a noisemaker into the corner and make for the exit while the alien investigates the diversion. Lay down an EMP mine to shock a group of androids before smashing them with the jack. Slip through a room of humans with the aid of a smoke bomb. Even though I detest crafting, I found its presence here relatively benign because you will so seldom have need of many of these objects to begin with - I went through the entire game without chucking a single smoke bomb, molotov or flashbang, and used the other items only a scarce handful of times, because the alien is completely impervious to most. The crafting system seems a pointless addition, included only to be trendy, but it could have been so much worse.
The game has a reputation for difficulty, however I can't really agree with it. This may seem an odd thing to say, given the frustration I described earlier, but hear me out. Alien: Isolation requires no twitch reflexes, no combo inputs, no aptitude for puzzle-solving, no resource management, no direction of units, nothing by which we measure the difficulty of a game on any given metric. The only abilities Alien: Isolation requires of the player are the capability to identify clearly designated hiding spots, and the patience to wait within them before resuming their journey to a point marked on their map. I believe the perception of difficulty comes from players' eagerness to progress at a pace out of keeping with the game's rhythm. And to be fair, the game itself encourages this lack of synchronisation.
From the moment you receive it you are told by every second loading screen that the motion detector is your life and to consult it regularly. When I adhered to this advice, I played timidly, looking for a hiding space whenever I saw a blip. That's what I was meant to do, right? The game itself told me as much. As I grew more experienced I realised that that timidity is what had been getting me killed time and again in the early game. The motion detector only works on a horizontal plane, meaning that the alien could be very proximate, yet also oblivious to your presence due to travelling in the overhead network of vents. Therefore, by hiding every time you see a nearby dot on the detector, you may just be giving more time for the enemy to find you. Not a great strategy for self-preservation. A more useful mantra is simply: Keep moving! Around the halfway point I used the motion detector less and instead relied on intuition - sounds in particular provide a reliable indicator of a threat's position.
Alien: Isolation is a very aural experience. You will come to dread the creaking of vents, and feel relief when the familiar repetitive beep of a save point (which I actually found amply portioned, despite others' criticism to the contrary) comes into earshot. Much of the game's scare factor comes not from things you can see per se, but from an expertly crafted atmosphere rife with tension.
Though I felt it struggled to hit its stride at the beginning and dropped the ball towards the conclusion, with a deeply unsatisfying ending and a couple of instances of backtracking for no purpose other than padding, I enjoyed the substantial majority of my time with Alien: Isolation, once I had keyed into what sort of experience it intended to offer me. If you are a fan of the Alien universe, and the first film in particular (the best by a mile in my opinion), I'd encourage you to give this game a look for its production values alone - so much care has gone into doing the source material justice, creating a deliciously retro vision of the future, and providing a cinematic experience that doesn't wrest control of the proceedings away from the player. If you're simply a fan of the genre then it's still worth a play, though it goes without saying that you'll get less from it, because even though the story is self-contained, there are elements of assumed knowledge which will enrich the experience. Alien: Isolation is a fine effort by any measure, however the fact that it's Creative Assembly's first foray outside of the strategy genre makes it exceptionally remarkable.

I purchased this game for three reasons:
1: Love the Alien franchise
2: it was cheap via Humble Bundle and came with all the DLCs
3: Creative Assembly have a reasonably good reputation/track record when it comes to quality, I say reasonably if you take Rome 2 as a diabolical dross of a game.
However what put me off buying this initially was that I am not a stealth player, I love to run, shoot and blow stuff up, if thats what your expecting then this game is not for you. However if your willing to look past that, then this game is excellent. Not completed the Isolation game as of yet, but slowly getting there, and slowly is right. Unlike other Alien based games like Colony Marine or even the AvP games, the Aliens (or Alien in this case) are the feared monsters from the movies again. Stealth is a must and the game plays out very very slowly as a result. The game reminds me a lot of two games specifically, the first is Fallout 4, with the crafting element. Being able to scavange scrap items etc and make tools, tricks and weapons works really well in this game. The other game it reminds me of is Doom 3. I have never soiled myself so much as playing Doom 3 in the dark and using headphones. This game has matched that feeling. There are moments in the game when you know the alien isn't about, or is it? The sound effects and the shadowy effect of the enviroment make this game intense.
I have found very few negatives in the game so far, the main technical one I have is that the game randomly crashes, with no obvious explanation.
The main in game issue I have is the story itself. I like the idea of playing Ripley's daughter, however the game plays out on the backdrop of WY and their decision to close down a long range space station. That story offers no feeling and it slowly becomes annoying. Not sure if this is a bug, but there is a scene were there are a group of armed men and the Alien bypasses them to hunt you down, a slight WTF moment if I ever saw one.
These issues however have not really ruined the game as it might in other gaming experiences, and its fair to say the positives outway the negative. This game brings back the terror of Alien and it reminds the player why Alien is still a movie that has been difficult to beat or better.
In my opinion the game rates a solid 8/10, the niggles take the score down a few notches but considering that Creative Assembly were making an Alien game in the shadow of the controversial Alien: Colonial Marine, they have done an amazing job.

The Elder Scrolls Online.
The title itself should be reason enough to buy this game.
Now into the more serious reasonings:
The game feels and flows like skyrim with better graphics and it does not really strangle your computer either.
The UI and skillbar is very adaptable for your playstyle and preferences, so is also character creation and shaping (lvl up system), there are so many good points about this game I can't list them all due to space limitations.
Now, let's talk about Crown store and what you can buy in the game. First of all, there is no pay to win model at work here, it is all vanity items with one exception, the EXP scroll which very marginally boosts xp gain, for a whopping 10%. This is not enough to warrant constantly buying them. Still, you do get some crowns to spend if you buy the game nontheless, and quite a good sum if you got the gold edition (700 crowns, enough to buy a good looking mount!).
Still, there are certain important things to know of in this game.
The community is helpful, RP players don't need to worry much, most people just ride along and enjoy the fun with you in public (which is rare!). There are also guilds with functionality for flavour, but since you can join up to five guilds, the special feeling of beloning to a guild could be ruined.
Still, if you do join a roleplaying guild, there are a lot of fun PVE and PVP content to ride along with your friends.
Massive trading guilds with 400+ members are always a option if you want to find certain items for your lategame gear, with no need to leave your RP'ing guild. Just take what you can with the options available to you! If you don't like the roleplaying guilds, there are even more options for you.
This game is a blast, you can enjoy it solo and/or with friends in the way you prefer to do it. Dungeon finder will demand multiplayer but you could simply ignore those and walk the lonely path of solo quests instead if you wish.
Elder scrolls can be what you want it to be. An open mind with a happy attitude will most likely find many friends here.
Angry gamers with no tolerance for RNG and who has high demands on everything they do, won't enjoy this game as much. Especially if they are going to buy crown crates and expect to win the lottery, take it for what it is, sometimes the ticket will win you a cool mount. Most often you shall not win one...  - It's optional and wont bring any kind of advantages over any other player.
I highly recommend this game.

This is a very nice game. It's basically a choose your own adventure gamebook type of game with interesting and quite unique mechanics. It is very heavy on text, so you'll have to read a lot while playing it. The game asks you questions from time to time to check if you actually payed attention or just clicked through everything without reading. Like in a gamebook, the text is really the whole point of the game, so that would be quite pointless indeed. What is very unusual for a computer or video game is that apart from very few typos the writing is absolutely excellent. Neither childish, nor deliberately opaque, the author has a very enjoyable and literate writing style. The orthography and the grammar were also excellent. Why can't every adventure game be like this? The story is original and refreshing, and the game has a subdued kind of humour that mainly comes across in the quirky graphics rather than in the text. Playing through Dark Scavenger takes a couple of hours, somewhere between 5 and 10 typically. Having done this once, I don't think it is very replayable. You can always try to do better to collect all items and solve all the puzzles, but apart from this the story is very much linear. When you play it for the first time, a large part of the fun in Dark Scavenger is the fact that you often don't have the slightest idea what is going on. Once you finished it, you will surely have figured that out, so this excitement is also lost on later playthroughs.
If you like adventure games at all, I really recommend buying and playing Dark Scavenger, especially if you can get it in a bundle or a sale for one or two euros.

Dark Scavenger puts you in the roll of a human(or something like that, game doesnt say) "lost" in space and you are being saved by 3 aliens who then sent you on a dangerous mission to help them out (what a save!!). Game combines Point-and-click exploration, text-based adventures and RPG turn-based combat and decision making but the main thing that grab me is the variety of tools given to you.
While the writing is top notch, its focused on the moment so there isnt that big plot to follow( its just stuff given at the start of the game and then at the end) so you can just focus on your exploration. During your adventure you will get help from your 3 alien allies :  Kamaho - weapon crafter and fills the role of the generic NPC you often meet in the games( always serious!!!) ; Falsen - the master of puns( bad or good its all up to you) ; Gazer - alien without mouth but always seems that he is trying to talk. With the help of the gang( by making stuff for you while you do the fighting) you need to find a fuel source(well they found it but you need to get it) so they can survive in SPACE. The source is on a planet near you so they beam you down and you start your adventure.
Gameplay consists of Exploration, "Crafting"/Equipment and Combat.
The funniest part of the game. Now lets see what steps you can take while exploring : First you are in a room with several objects to interact with . Always be careful how you pick them because it matters at times ( Example : I crushed a cage with a bird inside because it bit me but on the next object I clicked I found bird food so I ended up losing an item). Once you click on an object you will enter the text adventures which often leads to decision making which includes dialogues or actions.
For actions you will be mainly asked how to proceed : use your bare hands/body, use weapon/item/ally or go back.  Using the right KIND of equipment always lead to success while using yourself mainly leads to harm.
Dialogues are weird because well... cant say really... it's just that often make no sense. Sometimes there is logic sometimes is completly random.
Once you interact with all objects you found(some can be well hidden) you have to go to another room by clicking on an arrow(you dont need to interact with all objects if you dont want to risk it). But before you are send to the next room you will have to use the items you found which leads to
making new tools for your adventures. Now lets start with equipment(or you can call them items/tools w/e you want since you dont really equip them as in other games) . There are 3 kind of tools on your disposal : Weapons, Items(consumables) and Allies. Each one of them got durability . Whenver you use them(combat or exploring), the items lose 1 durability unless its stated otherwise.
I dont think I need to explain how to use them since each one of them got short and well written description though it needs sometime to get used to how the game plays itself but lets get on the more important part: how you acquire this stuff. Well, you give them to your allies on the ship.
Kamaho can make weapons, Falsen can make items and Gazer makes you allies(dont ask how because I have a bit of a hard time imagining). You can use them only once per visit(aka you cant use 2 items to make 2 allies in 1 visit) so you have to pick wisely what you want out of each item(dont do like me where I decided to turn a sacred amulet into a weapon and ended up with a pointless stick). This trick gives quite high replay value to the game if you want to see what kind of items the devs got prepared for you. And once you are done crafting lets start fighting.
Combat is generic turn-based system. You need exploit the weaknesses of your enemies or die trying. One thing worth noticing is that not every item you use ends your turn(its show in the right bottom corner in a box if it ends your turn or not). I found the combat to be quite challenging because of the durability system so it requires some thinking in case you end up needing a tool for later. But stay calm, at the start of each chapter you will get back all the charges and items back to use so feel free to use them as much as you want.
Save system is quite nicely made since it saves after each interaction so if you die during combat you will be put at the start of the fight unless the enemy got forms.. then it will restart from the last form( example : boss has 2 forms, you were able to reach 2nd form and you died so game will restarts from 2nd form).
As said the game has a decent replay value ( 4-6 runs or a lot more if you want to find everything) and the lenght is able to allow that ( average 3 hours). There is a New Game+ that I'm yet to try so cant talk about it.
Answer this questions:
Do you like text-based adventures?
Do you like silly/random writing?
Do you like challenging turn-based combat?
Do you like replaying games?
If you have 3 yes then go ahead and buy it. If not... you can still buy it and give it a whirl but I can say that its worth every penny ..

Wow! 100/100. One of the best games I have ever played.
What an exquisitely executed game. There are a huge amount of things I could say about how wonderful this game is, and the very much nothing that I dislike so far. I will touch on a few of the things that stand out the most concerning how amazing this game is.
The first is the overall game feel. It may be early access, but it plays like a complete and polished game, with very few bugs appearing. The only potential bug I have experienced is trivial, and comes about when you have two different materials going through the same furnace. This could be intentional, however. Aside from that, it is truly engaging and challenging, while also easing you in properly and without seeming too overwhelming right at once. It also makes you step back and appreciate how some polish goes a long way towards creating beautiful worlds out of minimal graphics packages.
The game has a wonderful combination of mechanics, with a sort of amalgamation of Minecraft, Command & Conquer, Sim City, and a few RPG elements tossed in. The balance of base building, resource management, incredible tech tree depth, combat, creativity, and strategy is phenomenal, and you have very little down time in this game while you're just waiting for things to happen, which is one of the best parts of the game. The crafting tree, which is integral to the gameplay, is very quick and doesn't feel like it drags on. That being said, you're crafting such a large quantity of things that it ultimately takes quite a while. You just don't get stuck doing nothing while its happening.
I love the crafting mechanics and tech tree, as well as the way the game doesn't punish you for moving buildings around, but encourages you to rearrange your base with some regularity instead. All the negative side effects of destroying and moving buildings in RTS games is erased, and so you can freely try over and over to arrange things to your liking or functional necessity. In this sense, you get a great way to explore what the game can do without having lost a bunch of money or resources on useless items that you don't know how to use yet.
It is hard to describe how engaging this game is on so many levels until you start to play and see the depth for yourself. I have rarely come across a game of such high quality and balance, while being completely flexible and customization. It is engaging from start to finish. If you're the kind of person who likes to fill out tech trees in any game you play, you will be quite ecstatic about the sheer breadth of options and progressions to the technology this game contains.
Like most open world games, this is also an excellent game for exploring and just doing whatever the hell you want. While a lot of the gameplay focuses on the automation of large scale production and complex infrastructure, you also will start to see some of the more creative and goofy things you can do with this technology, and have ample opportunity while playing a standard campaign mission or a skirmish map to futz around with a silly idea you have to design your train schedule so that once an hour all your trains line up on the tracks and spell the word "1337" or some other such ridiculousness. The possibilities are endless, and get more endless the further through the tech tree you progress.
All in all, this game takes some of the best elements from a fair number of game genres and combines them with perfect balance and execution, and really has demonstrated what is possible without insane fancy graphics, extreme AI, and heavy lifting engines. It has a tiny footprint compared to most games, but offers more in its tiny package than most games I have ever played. You will not be able to get bored with this game, though you might start wondering what happened to all your friends, or the sun, or your job, as you sink deeper and deeper into this immersive game. Worth every penny you could spend on it.

Factorio is exceptionally fun to play. Learning all of the ins and outs of how to most efficiently build things has left me playing this game for hundreds of hours. The only major downside to this game is that once you realize your base is pretty adequately safe, and the only factor preventing you from finishing the game is collecting the final resources for the rocket launch, it gets kind of pointless. I've played through the game once and on my second play through after building the rocket silo and the satellite, I just didn't see a reason to finish. I knew I'd be able to eventually collect enough resources to build the rocket... it was just a matter of time. Playing the waiting game... building more factories for rocket parts. There wasn't any challenge left. I almost feel like the whole rocket assembly process isn't necessary. Let me build the satellite and rocket silo and call it a day.
The only other thing I can say is I wish there were more interesting campaigns to play. Hopefully in the future there are different ways to win the game also. I wouldn't mind focusing entirely on military and just eradicating all of the enemies on the planet as a win condition. Also, some form of bridge making or flight transport would be a big bonus.
I also found little use for railways or robots due to playing the game with rich resources... I'm not really sure I'd be too excited to play the game on normal settings as collecting resources would require far too much effort only to have them run dry quicker.
Overall I highly recommend the game though. You'll get far more play time out of it than most games so the value is amazing. I played it through twice and that's more than I can say about 99% of games I've ever played.

TL;DR - If you can get it running, you can have massive fun. Genuine "put a huge smile on your face" fun.
Right. It took me ages to get this game working properly on PC. My RX470 & FX8350 rig struggled to run this with any competence, but since upgrading to i7 & GTX1080, I came back to it, and it now runs much better.
Except...
You can't use a controller as there is a memory leak or something that causes it to stutter when you do. I have yet to find a fix for this, so had to abandon playing with my Xbox 1 controller.
So mouse and keyboard it is. Except the default FOV is ridiculously small for mouse/keyboard, which requires modding to adjust.
BUT, with all of those things solved, I am actually enjoying the game itself.
Sure it begs the question as to why whoever put out the software can't fix these issues. And, yes, there is still a little bit of that feeling of frustration so familiar in JC2, when you're just wandering around trying to find that last billboard/gas tank/[insert other generic destructible that you've destroyed like 200 times already].
But the world is STUNNING. The acting is top notch and the characters and story are way more involving than the anonymous wreck-fest of JC2. But, most importantly, the possibilities for just having pure, truly open-world, sandbox fun are unparalleled.
The moment when you order a rebel drop that includes a helicopter but it hits a partially destroyed satellite dish on the way down, brings a ton of debris down with it, pops open while spinning in mid air sending a helicopter flying through the air amid the debris, only to explode. I genuinely laughed out loud.
Awesome, proper fun, and that, for me, is what gaming is about.
