Short Version:
Does this game generally objectively fulfill perceived goals: Yes.
Should you buy this game: Yes.
How does it chalk up to Bastion?: They have similarities, but Transistor stands on its own. In some ways, it is superior and more mature than Bastion, while in other ways, Bastion has an edge in storytelling.
Long Version:
Transistor is beautiful. Transistor is inspired by Bastion in many ways, and that's abundantly clear from the get-go. From the similar ever-present voice of Logan Cunningham, to the angled top-down approach, Supergiant is definitely playing to their strengths.
Transistor, visually, has a great feel. Pre-rendered maps have stunning detail and effort. While Bastion in places had a pieced together, stylized look in the Calamity-stricken ruins of Caelondia, the city of Cloudbank is fully fleshed, and takes on strange and interesting changes as the enemies of the game - "The Process" - make their mark on the city.
Transistor is linear. That's okay. Linear is not always bad, though your adventure feels more or less on rails throughout the entire game. Some may consider this a flaw. People coming from Bastion, however, probably are not expecting much here. It is, however, worth noting that Transistor does -not- have different endings.
Transistor's soundtrack is breathtaking - the music alone easily justifies half the cost of the game. The music played in various scenarios takes on different variations depending on circumstances, and the world becomes muted and quiet while the haunting voice of the protagonist - Red - takes center stage during the Turn(). Musically inclined peoples want this soundtrack, if not the game too.
Transistor is short. People generally expect to get more hours from a video game than they can realistically play in a day without a binge session. If it were full price, that might be a problem. Fortunately, the nice low price of 20$ means that a 6-8 hour playthrough (assuming you do not rush through content) will strike a sweet spot. The game values your time and effort, and nothing in the game feels like "busy work", nor does anything feel like filler. The game, contrary to what some claim, feels like pure substance.
Transistor is a bargain - the game is effortlessly worth more than it costs.
Transistor's combat is varying shades of complex. In time, you will find that some abilities may feel somewhat superfluous and certain abilities like Void() become more or less necessities in gameplay with highest difficulty settings enabled - "limiters" in game. The game does an admirable job of respecting the intellect of its player - there are very few tutorials or listed instructions in actual gameplay, and you are encouraged and rewarded with bits of story and background when you experiment with the various "Functions" that are made available to you throughout.
Transistor leaves a lot to interpretation. If you prefer a story where everything neatly ties up in the end, and you are left satisfied and ready to move on to the next big thing in your day, Transistor will leave you unsettled. The game offers a peak into a dire moment in Cloudbank's story, and as you play a mystery unfolds that descends into chaotic circumstances that few could possibly predict. Because the game is short, there is ultimately only so much that can be done to lend clarity to some of the events of the story, and you will likely be left with questions that will leave you scratching your head for days to come.
That's not to say the game is pointless, absurd, or nonsensical. It is simply the sort of game that seems more or less designed to haunt you, be that good or bad.
The game, despite it's great strengths also suffers from limitations of the developers. Transistor's probably largest flaw is that the story is TOLD to you, and not SHOWN as well as some may like. Earned story tidbits more or less being fed in the form of static images and a few paragraphs of vague background information begin to feel like a substitute or a placeholder where something better could have been implemented - brief cutscenes or playable intermissions where we can watch events unfold in other places. It feels like a missed opportunity to elevate the methods used to tell the story. Why it's done this way, I can only guess - this is the first title that Supergiant Games has self-published, and only their second game. They're a very small name in gaming for now, and that means that a lot of the things we may expect and take for granted in other games are not options to them.
All that said, I can wrap it up. It's a gorgeous, fun, interesting and expressive game that is presented at a price so low that you really can't lose. It's flaws are minor enough that it becomes easy to forget about them and simply bask in the enjoyable combat mechanics and the sultry tones of the sword in your hands as you explore the computer-like city of Cloudbank.

S.T.A.L.K.E.R. is one of those special games that punches way above its weight class. It seeks to be an open-world, open-ended FPS/RPG with fluid relations between characters, emergent behavior in the wilds, and a compelling story and setting underpinning the whole thing. Those are lofty goals for any game, much less one from unproven developers back in 2007. What's shocking, then, is just how much it gets right even by modern standards.
In the world of S.T.A.L.K.E.R., the Chernobyl disaster spiraled outward to create the Zone, a harsh land ruled by mutated creatures, spatial anomalies, and mercenaries seeking to capitalize on the chaos. You play one such S.T.A.L.K.E.R. sans memories, sent back into the Zone to kill a mysterious figure close to the epicenter of it all. Along the way you'll forge alliances with other wanderers, discover threats far worse than mutated wildlife, and maybe come face to face with the source of the disaster itself. I wouldn't bank on that last one without some serious effort, though.
Instead of discreet levels, S.T.A.L.K.E.R. is made up of maps that connect to form one contiguous world. Starting near the border of the Zone, you'll journey through radioactive swamps, underground bunkers, ghost towns, and more as you complete jobs for the other inhabitants. Sometimes that'll mean finding a stash of bizarre artifacts, and other times it'll mean gunning down a band of killers in their hideout. There's plenty to do in the Zone even without a specific mission, as you can loot corpses, hunt hidden stashes, and locate artifacts by navigating the treacherous anomalies that can crush, shock, or maim you with little warning.
All of this is accomplished from a first-person perspective, but don't expect the run-and-gun action of... anything, really. The combat in S.T.A.L.K.E.R. is very much its own thing, a perpetually harrowing affair of dancing around cover, emptying magazines to only land one shot, and pumping dozens of bullets into charging beasts. Weapons in the Zone are inaccurate, difficult to use, and seemingly do no damage until you land a headshot that kills in an instant. I imagine it's more like real-world firefights than anyone would admit, but that doesn't necessarily make it fun to be eaten alive by wild dogs who dodged or shrugged off a dozen rounds.
You'll want to avoid combat as much as possible, at least at first, and luckily there's a robust and effective stealth system to make use of. This system tracks your light level, posture, noises made, and even gives you bolts you can toss to cause distractions (or trigger anomalies). There's a pretty big emphasis on stats across the board, really. Your character has resistances to all kinds of injury as well as a radiation level to monitor, your inventory has weight and conditions to consider, and every single NPC in the game has a reputation rating with you. There aren't always systems that address these stats directly, but they do represent significant depth to the simulation.
Attention to detail extends to the environments, and it is here that you'll find S.T.A.L.K.E.R.'s greatest strength. For a nearly ten-year-old game, the Zone looks amazing, with crumbling buildings and thick underbrush and rolling clouds blotting out the sun. There's a palpable sense of decay and instability wherever you go, and it only grows more intense as you approach the heart of the Zone. Every dark corner can hide a creature that wants your blood or an anomaly that can rend you in an instant, demanding caution and tense attention even in the daylight hours. And don't get me started on the underground bunkers... some of the most effective horror encounters I've experienced in gaming have come in the subterranean halls of the Zone.
I've spent a lot of time extolling the virtues of S.T.A.L.K.E.R. because they are many, but not without a price. It is an ambitious indie game after all, and that means all sorts of potential glitches and instability whenever you load in. Sometimes the AI breaks down, sometimes items vanish from the ground, and sometimes the thing will just crash when you least expect it. Beyond that there are definitely balance issues with the weapons and combat, exacerbated by missions with no real difficulty curve to them that might send you into a hostile mercenary camp before you find anything more formidable than a sawed-off. The rough translated text might actually be the worst offender, hiding key information and names behind English one step above Google Translate in some cases.
The Zone is a harsh and unforgiving place, and S.T.A.L.K.E.R. exemplifies it right down to the code. It's going to take you a long time and multiple tries to acclimate to its unique style, and turning to modding isn't a bad idea if the base game is just too daunting or janky. But once you come to grips with the combat and start learning the many ways to die in the Zone, you're in for one hell of a ride. S.T.A.L.K.E.R. does immersion and atmosphere better than almost any FPS, presenting you with a rich, frightening, living world that will fight you every step of the way.

I can definitely say
enjoyed this game, but it's hard to say if others will. There's really no way to tell unless you play it for yourself, but if you like brutal shooters, great atmosphere, and spooky nuclear dystopias, this game is for you.
There are a few issues with this game however, but thankfully most of them can be remedied with the large selection of mods available. The biggest issue I had, however, is that I felt the game became a chore to play after a while. I'll chronicle my experience below, which hopefully gives you a good idea of the pros and cons.
Final thoughts: Overall I enjoyed it, but I burned out after a while and felt unsatisfied near the end. If you're not a fan of difficult games this might not be for you (especially if you're a fan of the modern "casual" fps games). However, if you like a challenge and you love games with good atmosphere, I'd give this a try. Hopefully you'll have better motivation to finish it than me.
Note: I used the Zone Reclamation project mod, a few texture mods, and a few sound mods. I only experienced one hard crash, which occurred when I tried to eat bread out of an enemies inventory. Other than that, a few minor hangs but nothing bad.

Completely brimming with bleak atmosphere, STALKER is a very immersive game. The wasteland feels very harsh and unforgiving, and many of the creatures that will be encountered are quite unnerving.
Inventory management is always a concern, but does not feel like too much of a chore. Gunplay requires precision, and on the master difficulty you can ambush and kill enemies just as effectively as they can ambush and kill you.
The game starts with the player feeling very weak, and this can be frustrating as going into every fight at a large disadvantage is rough, and requires liberal use of save files. However, once better equipment is obtained, the tables are turned! The player ends up being much stronger than most of the dangers of the Zone. This relieves a bit of the tension, but it does not trivialize the game's difficulty.
Unfortunately, the story is a bit weak in this game, and many important plot threads are left as side-quests, which could cause a lot of important details to be skipped over unintentionally.

I have had this game for many years now, i have played all of the series and played them again... Vanilla, Modded, Overhauled etc. and never left a review once. So today i'm going to leave my first review on quite possibly not only my favourite STALKER game, but also my favourite game ever.
STALKER is an exceptional game for two reasons, atmosphere and immersion.
It's from 2007, sure it's not PS4 graphics, but neither is skyrim.
Sometimes there are bugs that ruin the experience, but i have only ever encouted them on one play through and a wealth of overhaul mods are available that offer differnt experiences to the table.
However, the game is brutal. With next to no tutorial and unintuitive key binds and mechanics, it's easy for one to start feeling unsure and awkward. The difficulty curve is higher than any other game I've played before. With the game leaving the order of the side mission you take down to you, and the pace you follow the story up to you, you may find yourself unsure of where to go next and what to do.
That said, all these things are what eventually come together to make the game fantastic. You come to master the unintuitive play and mechanics and quicksave becomes your best friend, combat can become tactical and fast paced, or stealth like and tense. The difficulty curve forces you to think instead of run and gun, it forces you to take your time and way up if you really gain more from a raid than the ammo you will use... the only game where ammo really is a valuble item. You start making your own moves without the game telling you where to go and what to do which makes the game feel open and free. All this makes you feel completly immersed in this world.
And the sounds... the darkness... sure the textures are not great but you quickly forget about that once you get a feel for the atmosphere. One part of the game that really had me on edge was very close to the end when you finally have the armour required to enter the high radiation zone and you sit near one of the old plants with almost greyscale vision as winds howel and mutants dawdle the corner to your side.
Honestly a fantastic game and something to not miss out on. This game is worth more than most retail prices games nower days.

This game is amazing, and one of the few that I regard as "full price worthy" even years after its release.
Artwork, Atmosphere, Feel:
The artwork is spot on and a real love letter to Ridley Scotts Alien movies. Every room feels authentic and is full of detail but never feels cluttered or overloaded. And it is not just the bigger areas, even those little dead end hallways that are only there to make the level layout more believable are rich with atmosphere.
Gameplay:
At its core it is a hiding and sneaking game but you also get weapons to fight back. You can't kill the Alien but pretty much everyone else. On top of that is a light crafting system that lets you build distractions, bombs and other little helpers that allow different solutions to a problem. But resources are rare and require additional exploration = more risk to gather.
Another great aspect of the gameplay and this ties in very well with the lvl design is the obfuscation of the engagement areas. A lot of similar games make the mistake that they send you down a linear path with no hiding spots or dark shadowy corners and then all of a sudden you see a room full of them which makes it a clear tell that an enemy will show up and breaks the game apart into safe exploration areas and dangerous engagement spots. This game does it differently, you will often find rooms with conveniently placed hiding spots that would allow a safe route from one shadow to another, a clear tell that an enemy encounter is up, huh? But nope, no one is there. This might sound like a minor detail but it adds so much immersion.
The alien itself doesn't use a fixed patrolling route, rather some sort of clever AI which works pretty well. Only downside to this, and this took me a while to get used to is that you will see it a lot. I would have preferred if it would stay more often in hiding and only come out when it sees a good opportunity to attack you directly, like in the movies.
Overall I would score it a solid 9.5

I almost put this game down early in the piece. In the beginning, for a very long time you will explore the space station in uninterrupted solitude, with a gradually rising feeling of dread. It's an important sequence that does a brilliant job of establishing a sense of place, allowing you time, without fear of attack, to read the text on highly detailed posters, and generally poke about to get an idea of what life on the Sevastopol might have been like prior to the catastrophe that has recently been visited upon it. But you know the game has more. The title promises us an Alien to complement this Isolation.
When the Alien eventually enters the picture it makes up for the time not spent harrassing you by following you around at a distance that suggests it may well be physically magnetised to your person, for about three missions straight. It all becomes insufferably tedious. Despite adoring the game's atmosphere and attention to detail, I felt that the titular Alien, the intended drawcard of the whole affair, was a blight on the experience, because its tenacious nature had transitioned me from admiring the form of the environment to analytically considering no more than its function, and had slowed my progress into new environments to a crawl. After reloading some checkpoint for the nth time, I was ready to just uninstall the thing. But then the alien unexpectedly went on holiday for a while, and I realised that the pacing of the game had been deliberately structured into a series of troughs and peaks, and I thought 'Okay, I can live with that'.
During its hefty playtime you will find times for exploring, times for hiding, times for running, and times for killing. It does a good job of mixing things up to prevent the alien's presence becoming too oppressive.
In addition to the alien, you will encounter two other types of foes: humans, and androids of limited intelligence designed for performing mundane tasks, however something has gone very wrong in their programming. It was this latter enemy that I actually found the most creepy - their body shape is just human enough, and their movement just robotic enough that they venture deep into the uncanny valley. All three enemies require different approaches, however it is a constant that although there are limited combat options available, you are encouraged to avoid violence as far as possible. The alien is so sensitive to sound that if it hears a shot or blast anywhere in the level it will instantly make a beeline to that location, and for the majority of the game your firearms consist of The World's Worst Shotgun And Revolver (I played on hard, and these things emitted the noise of a jet breaking the sound barrier and delivered the force of a flicked pea). The quieter melee option of a maintenance jack to the face is viable, but only situationally as it is slow and only suitable for one-on-one engagement.
Instead of shooting things, you are encouraged to turn various spare parts and salvage into the items you find on blueprints scattered throughout the game. Throw a noisemaker into the corner and make for the exit while the alien investigates the diversion. Lay down an EMP mine to shock a group of androids before smashing them with the jack. Slip through a room of humans with the aid of a smoke bomb. Even though I detest crafting, I found its presence here relatively benign because you will so seldom have need of many of these objects to begin with - I went through the entire game without chucking a single smoke bomb, molotov or flashbang, and used the other items only a scarce handful of times, because the alien is completely impervious to most. The crafting system seems a pointless addition, included only to be trendy, but it could have been so much worse.
The game has a reputation for difficulty, however I can't really agree with it. This may seem an odd thing to say, given the frustration I described earlier, but hear me out. Alien: Isolation requires no twitch reflexes, no combo inputs, no aptitude for puzzle-solving, no resource management, no direction of units, nothing by which we measure the difficulty of a game on any given metric. The only abilities Alien: Isolation requires of the player are the capability to identify clearly designated hiding spots, and the patience to wait within them before resuming their journey to a point marked on their map. I believe the perception of difficulty comes from players' eagerness to progress at a pace out of keeping with the game's rhythm. And to be fair, the game itself encourages this lack of synchronisation.
From the moment you receive it you are told by every second loading screen that the motion detector is your life and to consult it regularly. When I adhered to this advice, I played timidly, looking for a hiding space whenever I saw a blip. That's what I was meant to do, right? The game itself told me as much. As I grew more experienced I realised that that timidity is what had been getting me killed time and again in the early game. The motion detector only works on a horizontal plane, meaning that the alien could be very proximate, yet also oblivious to your presence due to travelling in the overhead network of vents. Therefore, by hiding every time you see a nearby dot on the detector, you may just be giving more time for the enemy to find you. Not a great strategy for self-preservation. A more useful mantra is simply: Keep moving! Around the halfway point I used the motion detector less and instead relied on intuition - sounds in particular provide a reliable indicator of a threat's position.
Alien: Isolation is a very aural experience. You will come to dread the creaking of vents, and feel relief when the familiar repetitive beep of a save point (which I actually found amply portioned, despite others' criticism to the contrary) comes into earshot. Much of the game's scare factor comes not from things you can see per se, but from an expertly crafted atmosphere rife with tension.
Though I felt it struggled to hit its stride at the beginning and dropped the ball towards the conclusion, with a deeply unsatisfying ending and a couple of instances of backtracking for no purpose other than padding, I enjoyed the substantial majority of my time with Alien: Isolation, once I had keyed into what sort of experience it intended to offer me. If you are a fan of the Alien universe, and the first film in particular (the best by a mile in my opinion), I'd encourage you to give this game a look for its production values alone - so much care has gone into doing the source material justice, creating a deliciously retro vision of the future, and providing a cinematic experience that doesn't wrest control of the proceedings away from the player. If you're simply a fan of the genre then it's still worth a play, though it goes without saying that you'll get less from it, because even though the story is self-contained, there are elements of assumed knowledge which will enrich the experience. Alien: Isolation is a fine effort by any measure, however the fact that it's Creative Assembly's first foray outside of the strategy genre makes it exceptionally remarkable.

I purchased this game for three reasons:
1: Love the Alien franchise
2: it was cheap via Humble Bundle and came with all the DLCs
3: Creative Assembly have a reasonably good reputation/track record when it comes to quality, I say reasonably if you take Rome 2 as a diabolical dross of a game.
However what put me off buying this initially was that I am not a stealth player, I love to run, shoot and blow stuff up, if thats what your expecting then this game is not for you. However if your willing to look past that, then this game is excellent. Not completed the Isolation game as of yet, but slowly getting there, and slowly is right. Unlike other Alien based games like Colony Marine or even the AvP games, the Aliens (or Alien in this case) are the feared monsters from the movies again. Stealth is a must and the game plays out very very slowly as a result. The game reminds me a lot of two games specifically, the first is Fallout 4, with the crafting element. Being able to scavange scrap items etc and make tools, tricks and weapons works really well in this game. The other game it reminds me of is Doom 3. I have never soiled myself so much as playing Doom 3 in the dark and using headphones. This game has matched that feeling. There are moments in the game when you know the alien isn't about, or is it? The sound effects and the shadowy effect of the enviroment make this game intense.
I have found very few negatives in the game so far, the main technical one I have is that the game randomly crashes, with no obvious explanation.
The main in game issue I have is the story itself. I like the idea of playing Ripley's daughter, however the game plays out on the backdrop of WY and their decision to close down a long range space station. That story offers no feeling and it slowly becomes annoying. Not sure if this is a bug, but there is a scene were there are a group of armed men and the Alien bypasses them to hunt you down, a slight WTF moment if I ever saw one.
These issues however have not really ruined the game as it might in other gaming experiences, and its fair to say the positives outway the negative. This game brings back the terror of Alien and it reminds the player why Alien is still a movie that has been difficult to beat or better.
In my opinion the game rates a solid 8/10, the niggles take the score down a few notches but considering that Creative Assembly were making an Alien game in the shadow of the controversial Alien: Colonial Marine, they have done an amazing job.

I've been meaning to write something nice about this game for a looong time.
Let that sentence be your TLDR, or read for a while longer if it pleases you.
Old choose your own adventure books were a sort of very early "random" generated adventure games where you would "play" a character in a story that progressed differently depending of your choices. The choices were not open ended, leading either to instant death, progressing in some way, or devious later instant death when you missed something important on an earlier page. The progression was linear, and while it branched somewhat, the roads taken would crystallize into one or two endings, depending on the length and complexity of the adventure. As with any genre of book, game or book/game hybrid there were categories of both comedy, high adventure, gloomy dunkelkeit and of course some smut <3
Some books in the genre were single quest deals leading the player down exotic locales or dark environments. Others came in sets that followed a linear progression between books, each new installment assuming you completed the earlier ones.
This game is very much the first cathegory of adventure book where the story is exotic, strange and stand-alone. The player faces off in space versus a cosmic monstrosity easily dominating them and taunting at their demise. In the nick of time the player is saved by three very strange aliens who introduces themselves as "dark scavengers"; looters of planetary energy, forever traveling and therefore always looting. As their newest member (and the only one who can fight) you are sent down to a nearby world where planetary energy can be harvested. This is where the game begins.
The game is divided into a series of levels that, in turn are divided into a set of "rooms", similar to an adventure book's pages. Each room has a couple of challenges for the player to attempt, yielding loot when successful and damage or other penalties when not. Items aquired can then be used to solve subsequent challenges, awarding the player with an ever larger array of solutions to problems.
And what solutions they are! As for the first set of categories a CYOA could be mentioned to have this game is very much in the comedy section of things. Instances, combat, and even crafting your gear is all permeated with a stellar sense of humour that will have you staring at the screen in disbelief and glee. The world is interesting! The characters inhabiting it are funny! The comical timing is spot on! But aside from being witty, the game is above all else smart.
Now how can I explain that..?
*SEGMENT IS SLIGHT SPOILER OF GAME MECHANIC THAT IS FUN TO DISCOVER FOR YOURSELF*
Well, for starters the game makes the best of its newfound tendency towards the game part of its Book/Game hybrid existance. Say for example that you face of against a bandit and combat ensues. Normally in an adventure game, and in some types of rpg's where the action keyword is absent from its genre title, combat would take place through the taking of turns, opponents slugging each other untill abilities come into play. So too here, but with a twist. Knowing the player can only experience the world through still images, items (used both for combat and environmental encounters) all react to the way a character looks. In his still picture, the bandit is jumping towards you with an axe in hand and with a crazy snarl on his face. In this case, the dentists drill will deal huge amounts of damage since his teeth show, the wind bag will stun him since he is up in the air, and the magnet will take his weapon, weakening him. Of course it would be silly to assume the bandit is always jumping in the air with his mouth open rendering him forever vulnerable to our very situational items. Lucky for us however the game figures its silly rules is better than realism it couldn't fake anyway :>
*END SPOILER*
Long, less spoilery story short; it plays around with genre conventions and mechanics as well as being genuinely humorous.
Dark Scavenger is one of those games where you would like to see more of the world and the characters that inhabits it, but somehow know that to experience them in any other way than this specific game's would somehow spoil the magic. The game never lets itself get old and is surprisingly varied both in terms of difficulty, encounter types and tone. It leaves itself open for an impossible sequel but still somehow feels complete, like an expensive meal where the only regret after finishing it is not being able to have it again.
Its like nothing. Costs basically nothing as well, so don't take my word for it. If you felt even a little compelled to check it out after reading this or the opinion of others I would say go for it! It will have you entertained in that "ah good times" way where you remember it later with a smile.

This game is amazing!! The Art Style / Graphics is hands down beatuiful. Combat is outstanding with the real-time stand alone, but with the turn-based style mixed with real-time delay is perfect. The special effects of each move, and the combinations of functions is simply truely amazing. The story keep me playing until I finished the 1st playthrough. I wanted to know more:  why this was happening, what exactly happened prior the opening of me removing the sword. The level up system is clean, the choice between: passive slots, ability upgrade slots, memory upgrades are nice, since everyone play style is unique to be able to select the one you want to continue doing what you were doing. I myself did memory upgrades so I combine functions    and abused the Jaunt()+Charm() to my benefit.

First of all this game is graphically quite nice, the sound track is good, the narrative is pretty interesting, and the gameplay is high quality - a mixture of Real-Time and Turn-Based play, each with advantages and disadvantages that make sense.  It can get hard later, especially using the Limiters (In Game Difficulty Increases like with Bastion).
Its huge strong point is the Functions - your abilities.  there are quite a few to play with; only 4 can be active in slots... but the rest can be used as a) addons to those actions, or b) passive benefits.
For example; a basic melee skill that does a bit of damage and makes enemies vulnerable to damage ( Crash() ), a long-range narrow attack ( Breach() ) and a invisibility tool ( Mask() ).  By adding Mask() to Breach(), its gains bonus Backstab damage - so you can whack 'em and backstab and get a huge boost of damage - there are huge combinations in the late game.
The New game+ mode lets you carry on where you left off level/function wise back at the start, but its gets more fun - double your function options, get more tactical gameplay, and get a far better challenge.
Overall, I rate this as a pretty damned good game and if you are a fan of Bastion, this is a game that will not disappoint.

Well here goes my review of RoK, hope it helps. Also if you want a serious summary skip to the end paragraph.
First time I ever went on me and a friend started setting up a small wooden base and of course we needed to gather resources, so I set off to firstly locate some food. When I managed to pick up some berries I headed back to base when suddenly an angry man appeared and begin saying something, which I presumed ill natured, softly into his microphone. Without a moment notice this man attacked me so I sprinted through the swamp back to the base. I gave my midget friend, armoured in looted iron armour. a heads up of the situation. He promtly ran to meet the man in CqC(close quaters combat) and dispatched him. Roughly 20 mins later the man returned, only this time with projectile spears and with a friend, however we quickly dispatched these maniacs.
However, the next day the base was ruined and I was dead(when you log off you are still visible). We quickly decided to become outlaws as we seeked a sense of adventure. So we were patrolling the roads when a man sneaked up behind and tied me up with a rope. I quickly told my friend and he followed this mysterious man who had bound me. He took me to his base and put me in a wooden cage when I was still barely clothed. Another man then took out a whip and began whipping me. My friend engaged in combat with these fiends and killed one of them. The other man must have been worried so released me from captivity. However, now me and my friend are engaged in a brutal campaign against the brutal dictator 'Sir Robert' and all his teritories.
All of this has happened in under 6 hours (5.5 hours at time of writing). So quite simply an amazing, although a bit buggy, early access game. Sends a clear message of the standard DayZ and Rust must compete against. Also their appears to be regular game updates, so at the time of writing early access done right. I would however reccomend playing with friends. Can't wait for future updates.

Alien: Isolation - or - Totally Accurate Alien Simulator
This game, man. Firstly, its unbelievably loyal to the first Alien film - aesthetically speaking. (I'm not sure when Rips Sr is supposed to have had this kid, and why she was never mentioned in the film). The way every piece of machinery looks, works and sounds is so bang on that you feel as though you are in the Alien universe. I'm sure its incredible in VR.
The tension created by the encounters with the Alien is unbelievable, especially when you are not someone who gets scared easily. I think there's something about space that really heightens this sense of fear (see also: Dead Space). The game itself is really nicely polished apart from some of the moments in low light and during cutscenes (I felt as though the framerate was quite choppy).
The controls are really tactile (using levers and reloading things like the revolver) and the minigames at terminals, although somewhat cut-and-paste, provide not only some interest to activities that could quickly become boring but also in some moments more tension, especially when you are evading enemies.
The trope of you knowing that things will never be as simple as flicking a switch to get access to somewhere gets played a lot here and there is some back tracking at times, but you do get to know some areas of the ship suprisingly well, both because of the aforementioned linear style but also because you won't get through the game without dying at least once. Probably considerably more times than that.
The Alien AI is very intuitive too. Every time you use one of the items in your box of tricks, it subsequently becomes less effective for the next time. Something I discovered first hand in the closing stages of the game and was chucking everything I had at this thing to leave me alone.
The other NPCs however I would have liked to have had more interaction with, perhaps being able to befriend random civilians who might have rewarded me with a secret keycard to a weapons stash or something.
The crafting system is simple but very well done, decisions about where components are better invested could become quite tricky for someone who is too gadget orientated, although I never had a problem with running out of anything. Two things about the inventory wheel though: it sometimes changed weapons when I didn't want it to and I would have liked to see a description of each item whenever I wanted, rather than only on the crafting screen.
The story I felt while engaging was a little hollow but perhaps this was superfluous given the very clear protagonist/antagonist relationship.

Graphics poorly optimized for my high end rig with an AMD card. Running absolutely terribly when it should not be.
User interface is terrible.
Battlefield AI is a huge step back beyond Shogun 2, how is this possible? The battlefield AI developer should be politely be asked to take his coat and find another job.
Capture points on a battlefield?! Why should we care about an innocuous bit of dirt on the ground?
Removal of family tree. This was the BEST part of the RPG element of total war. Why would you remove this?!
Addition of far too many "special" abilities. Come on. This is total war, not Skyrim.
Naval battles are completely broken. Buttons don't work, units don't do what they are told to do. Glitchy crap.
Cities and sieges are completely underwhelming; I understand the point for having less regularity with sieges, but why no great big city in the background, or a small settlement outside of the main city with a fantastic city in the background? Where is the scope and imagination?!
Unit control is now beyond awful. I never used to have to make hotkeys in order to control my army, now I feel I have to because the control element is terrible.
Skirmishing units still can't skirmish. How many years have we waited for this to be fixed?
Phalanxes, oh look they are not working again.
Ridiculous load times on the campaign map, I don't really want to have to make a sandwich and cup of tea after every turn thank you.
The loss of seasons and one year per turn. Less atmosphere, less RPG element with characters, no tactical planning around when the right time is to fight. The campaign map just looks the same ALL the time. Where is the variety?
Tech tree is broken in its current form. Technology should take a LONG time to acquire, to make it more interesting when you actually get it. Right now, getting legionnaires by 250 BC is frankly, ridiculous.
Battle speed, most battles are over within 2 or 3 minutes! Where is the strategy? Where is the tactics? Another point which proves CA are now targeting the casual gamer who are the completely wrong target audience for these types of games.
No zoom button on the campaign map?
The units are interchangeable pieces, with different skins. Some of which are pretty, some of which are distinctly uninspiring.
Less of the wardogs, flaming pigs, flying elephants, and scuba camels. Can we just get a game that works pretty please?
The lethality of units is so high everyone just dies within 30 seconds. Was this even tested?
The audio is boring and lacklustre. Where is Jeff Van Dyck?! The horrendous monotone voices make me want to disable my audio. I've never had this in any total war game.
The terrible thing is, I could go on! There are so many issues with this game.
I was going to give this a four of ten if the first patch actually fixed some of the issues above, HOWEVER..the first patch does nothing to fix anything I have raised. Therefore a buggy, unpolished, uninspiring, boring, beta game which should never have been released this early gets a two out of ten. Its just an unplayable ball of frustration and mess. What a disappointment and HUGE step back in the series after the fantastic Shogun 2, and I know what I'm talking about with Shogun 2, being one of my most played games to date.

A lot of games are about being a total ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, often taking the role as a faceless, personality-devoid drone, in a dark and dreary world. It is a reason to tire of modern gaming. Papers, Please is about being a total ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, taking the role as a faceless, personality-devoid drone, in a dark and dreary world. It is a reason to cherish modern gaming.
Placed in the role as an immigration control inspector, your job is to apply or decline entry to the fictitious nation of Arstotzka. Carefully checking through each persons documents for inconsistencies gradually becomes a more difficult task as the required paperwork piles up. It's a unique game where the core gameplay experience is essentially administration work and that makes it even more bizarre that it is enjoyable. It helps to have a clever story that builds up around the role you play. You feel as though have the scope to change things in slight ways, but at the same time, each tiny infraction is severely punished. Not only is Arstotzka oppressive to newcomers, residents like yourself must pay high living costs on a very low wage linked to work accuracy. Helping a poorly woman with an invalid entry permit so she can see her son may be the reason your son gets sick. Conversely, taking bribes or being a fascist prick might be the only way your little boy gets to eat tonight! Despite the game world being nothing but the daily newspaper and the cramped work space of your little office, everything you do feels so real and, consequently, important.
Spread over a maximum of 31 days, the main campaign can end in twenty different ways (most of them bad and occuring much earlier) depending on the choices you make and the efficiency with which you do your job. And it's a tough job, but someone's gotta do it. Glory to the Arstotzka!

This is basically someone's community college "games designer" homework.  It's not really a "game" as we see them in the 21st century.   It would have been pretty popular in 1985, though.     Unfortunately the technology industry has bumped up a bit over the last 30 years... and 30 years is about as far as this game is from being acceptable today.
If you treat it like an interactive story, then it's a bit more acceptable, just worse in quality than contemporary interactive stories like the ones from Telltale games (to pick a prominent example).
So, why does this get the thumbs down?
- No options/settings configurable for modern PCs
- Poor quality graphics
- Little to no gameplay
- Compares badly with other games in the genre, even at the same price points
- No, indy developers do not deserve a break just because they're indy developers, bad products are always bad.
Save your time and money.  Whatever you want to do with your time, this isn't it.

Hackers and glitches are common in any early-access title you can buy nowadays. Reign of Kings is no exception, although in fairness, this review was written by the time of the Alpha 10 patch. Nevertheless, these game-breaking glitches and extremely prevelant hacking is ruining what can be at times a fun and enjoyable survival game that is extremely addictive.
PROS:
- Ideal size map (not too big where you see a person every hour or too small where you see one every minute)
- Fun cooperatively, although playing by yourself can be enjoyable if you meet other friendly players
- In-depth crafting system- diffrent tier levels of weapons, building blocks, workbenches etc.
- Intriguing King system where one who takes the throne of the land can tax every person of their materials (creates potential role-playing scenarios if King taxes too high)
- Funny and expansive character creation for an open world survival game (although this leads to people exploiting their character's body size so that they are a midget that cannot be hit in combat)
CONS:
- Game-breaking glitches (as in major fps lag before you enter combat or the plague village, poor collision detection where your character gets stuck on objects like mountains- unable to move because you are lying on your side while you starve to death/slowly die from the plague in the village- you'll see this often if you buy the game at its current state)
- HACKERS- been turned into Shrek or red Shrek so many times (making me stand out in the bush/targeted for being different), been killed by flying glitch 3 times, had hackers storm mine and my neighbours' bases with unlimited trebuchet rounds
- KOS (Kill On Sight) makes the game combat focused, which itself is not the greatest aspect of the game
- If you're Australian, have fun trying to cram into only four offcial servers with 119 other Australians who have the game
Admittedly it is a little unfair to criticise a game on its bugs and hackers when it's only in early Alpha. I'm really only thumbing down this game now so that those indecisive people don't buy the game in its current broken state and give up entirely on the early-access notion. The potential for this game is enormous if the dev team can keep their attention centred on developing the game based off of gamer feedback. I'm desperate to turn this review into a Thumbs Up and will do so if most of the cons are patched up in the next update. For now, I recommend you save your money until the game is discounted or until progress is made on fixing the errors.

This game is amazing!! The Art Style / Graphics is hands down beatuiful. Combat is outstanding with the real-time stand alone, but with the turn-based style mixed with real-time delay is perfect. The special effects of each move, and the combinations of functions is simply truely amazing. The story keep me playing until I finished the 1st playthrough. I wanted to know more:  why this was happening, what exactly happened prior the opening of me removing the sword. The level up system is clean, the choice between: passive slots, ability upgrade slots, memory upgrades are nice, since everyone play style is unique to be able to select the one you want to continue doing what you were doing. I myself did memory upgrades so I combine functions    and abused the Jaunt()+Charm() to my benefit.

First of all this game is graphically quite nice, the sound track is good, the narrative is pretty interesting, and the gameplay is high quality - a mixture of Real-Time and Turn-Based play, each with advantages and disadvantages that make sense.  It can get hard later, especially using the Limiters (In Game Difficulty Increases like with Bastion).
Its huge strong point is the Functions - your abilities.  there are quite a few to play with; only 4 can be active in slots... but the rest can be used as a) addons to those actions, or b) passive benefits.
For example; a basic melee skill that does a bit of damage and makes enemies vulnerable to damage ( Crash() ), a long-range narrow attack ( Breach() ) and a invisibility tool ( Mask() ).  By adding Mask() to Breach(), its gains bonus Backstab damage - so you can whack 'em and backstab and get a huge boost of damage - there are huge combinations in the late game.
The New game+ mode lets you carry on where you left off level/function wise back at the start, but its gets more fun - double your function options, get more tactical gameplay, and get a far better challenge.
Overall, I rate this as a pretty damned good game and if you are a fan of Bastion, this is a game that will not disappoint.

Summation: Don't waste your money if you're frustrated by: Poor aim, numb and clumsy movement, ridiculous stamina drains to perform simple actions, poorly executed martial weaponry tactics; The RPG elements are cool though....
this game series has really tried to bring the difficulty back into gaming, an endeavor i applaud; however the developers accomplished this by poor understanding of basic kinesiology (study of human movement) and the strain the body endures during said motions.
IE I can use the Dagger light attack about Five times before i'm completely out of stamina... that means i would need to rest at least once while making a sammich. seriously?
Yes you can level up stamina and yes i understand it was probably used to balance the game but if you cant make a sandwich with the stamina you start off with then gtfo and stop making games with noodle arm heroes please; games necessarily pursue escapism! make a better game =/.
Further more the aiming system in this game Forces you to use the toggle aim. I mean you *can* fight without the focus but its not the most effective way to fight.
Its as if the makers NEVER spoke to a martial weapons expert; which i'm sure they did not or they would know that wide arc inward attacks uses some of the weakest (smaller by proportion) upper body muscles and there are far more effective but that's not even the main gripe here!
I feel as thought the devs intentionally dumbed down the aiming and precision of the animated attacks to try and scale up the games difficulty; making my fights feel numb and clumsy which really takes away from the whole plot of the game.
Finally the adaptation to the PC was POORLY executed. A LOT of the fighting mechanics require ridiculous button combinations that are counter intuitive; it was as if they asked a console player who has never played on PC before to bind all of his buttons to a mouse and keyboard.
Im not looking for a fight simulator but *If You're Going To Make Fighting Movements Finite With A Stamina Pool And Granulate Player Aiming Then DO IT RIGHT For FORKS Sakes! it feels half a$$ed.

It’s a great strength of Papers Please that it makes the work you do feel dull and monotonous (just like a real border patrol guard) whilst also appealing to a particular part of your puzzle solving brain. It also makes you paranoid like little else. Dare I risk keeping my son’s drawing on the wall with that inspector around?  The game has some irritating issues that I don’t often see addressed, but I won’t list them here. It's more than ready to screw you over at a moment’s notice. Set in a world of hypocritical, xenophobic authority figures, desperate, terrified citizens and refugees, rebels perhaps no better than those they seek to depose and a troubled family just hoping to eat for another day, Papers Please is a harrowing yet brilliant experience, made all the better by its thinly veiled roots in real history.

I bought Dark Parables: The Exiled Prince Collector's Edition during the Christmas Sale and I must say I really enjoyed this Game.
Dark Parables is a nice HO / Point & Click Game Series with Multiple Games and this one is also one of them.
First of all if you havent played the first Dark Parables Game, I strongly recommend going for that one first before playing this Game as they are meant to play in Order.
Dark Parables: The Exiled Prince Collector's Edition comes with a main story which is about 4-5 hours long and a hardcore Adventure Mode that brings you a refreshed yet harder adventure. I personally havent played it but I saw a few screens from a friend of mine.
The Voice Acting was once again very nicely made and the Art Style was absolutely beautiful! Although you couldn't change the resolution, you were able to use the Steam Overlay and also got Trading Cards now.
The Hidden Object Scenes were rather well hidden and the Puzzles were challenging. I personally did like them alot and was surprised how well you can hide something in this game.
The Story was absolutely lovely and reminded me a little bit on my Childhood just in a more Grimm way.
All in all this Game is fantastic, however due to the fact that is rather short I do recommend getting it on Sale rather then for its base price of 10€.
Edit: This Game was for a long time bugged with no Collectors Edition included, however thanks to many people complaining about this issue the developers have resolved it. You are now able to play the Game completely with the Bonus Chapter.
For everybody that has completed this Game before dont worry you wont have to complete it again, for more help just have a look at the forums.

This game in many ways reminds me of Zork minus the art work (now that will date me - Zork as far as I know was the first actual computer game; a text based choice adventure, played on a mainframe, back in the day when one needed punch cards and PCs did not really exist, circa early 1980s).  I digress.  Dark Scavenger is a bit point and click, a bit hidden object, a bit text based D&D choice driven adventure with quite a bit melee mixed in using the crafted weapons, items and allies one has managed to scavenge and a whole lot weird.  Odd characters, even stranger allies, and relatively conceited enemies make this game uniquely interesting.  This game seems simpler then it actually is, and dying can happen easily by making wrong decisions or choices.  Choices really matter, especially in combat where melee attacks are limited to what weapons one has available to use.  Hopefully along the way one has made the correct decisions on who to craft with, where one has looked for items, what information one has managed to gather and what action has been taken in a situation.  As I stated before this game seems far easier then it actually is and requires thought and planning to get through.  Though I did not pay full price, I would have.  The price is worth it for a game that is ... as Monty Python would say ... "and now for something completely different" because it is "completely different".

I cannot recommend this game more highly. It may not be suitable for those who like bells and whistles and constant blood. But for the discerning adventure/rpg enthusiast, Dark Scavanger offers a fresh and satirical take on the genre while casting eyes back to the days of early crpgs.
The mechanics are simple, but beneath the point and click interface interesting choices can be made. Some choices are available depending on whether you have the right weapons, equipment or allies. You acquire these items by finding artifacts as you uncover the mysteries of the planet below. One of three aliens aboard the ship you reside – Kamaho an undead weapons master, Falsen a greenish trickster, and Gazer a mute and very alien alien – will forge the artifact into something unique.
Story and writing are the main selling points of Dark Scavenger. I won’t spoil it by going into detail. Enjoy the humour, quirkiness and silliness of this inventive and imaginative journey that you won’t want to end. I wish more games were like this.

This has to be one of the best horror videogames I've ever played. It's very immersive and it really makes you think. So it's like a strategy horror game as you've got to try your best to avoid the alien. The game has amazing direction, graphics , Voice acting and sound effects.

What can I say? Probably the best Alien game I know of. It truly makes you feel like you are in the Alien universe, everything from the creature itself to the androids and technology you interact with feels just like the original movie.
The attention to detail is amazing, the alien is menacing, your tools and the tech you interact with feels authentic, the music is fantastic and the gameplay organically generates truly cinematic moments.
Example: you are trapped in an area with blairing alarms, you are crawling through an airduct under the floor, you move under some bars, trhough them you see the alien right above you, it's illuminated by the creepy blueish-white light from the lamps in the room and the orange rotating alarm lights behind it, you freeze like a deer in headlights and hold your breath, hoping that he hasn't spotted you because he can and will chase you into vents, he turns around and walks away a few steps, you crawl forward until you are completely hidden from sight, but you still dont dare exhale properly for fear of being overheard.
10/10 would be scared stiff again.
The alien can actually hear you breathing when he walks past your hiding spots, he can also hear the beeping of your motion tracker if you are using it. Also on higher difficulty, he can follow your scent trail. It wont allow him to pinpoint your position, but it will make sure he is in your general visinity most of the time. Also he sometimes resorts to process of elimination and checks all the hiding spots if he saw you run into the room but you hid from sight before he entered it (he runs faster then you btw).
PS. For masochists there is also Nightmare mode. Basically it takes away a lot of your resources (ammo, crafting materials), makes the motion tracker glitchy, makes enemies stronger and ups the alien's aggression and deadliness. Have fun doing the "play through the game without dieing once" achivement on that mode :)
Summary: Great world building, oppressive atmosphere, amazing artstyle and sound design, cinematic gameplay moments and unkillable, relentless alien menace stalking you.
If you are a fan of Aliens you owe it to yourself to experience this, it feels like a redemption after alien 3 and 4 and the mountain of crappy games.

I'm a huge fan of the DeadSpace games. I need to point out that the beginning of the game is a little slow. I had actually stopped playing Alien: Isolation after the first hour of the game because I got so frusterated searching the torch-tool could not figure out the proper door to go through. After a few of my friends said that the game was well-worth the frusteration, I got back on, used a guide to help me out through some of the game, and got hooked IMMEDIATELY.
The game is eerie as it is frightening. The Aliens are everywhere and any kind of noise-even walking too fast- will send the Alien sprinting at 60mph at you! It can get so intense that I through my controller down a few times. I strongly recommend this game. It is so much fun and the storyline is gripping. First off, I have not played Bastion so this is a completely objective review.
I have not yet finished the game when writing this but I feel I'm getting close so why not.
This game screams atmosphere and flows through the story unlike many games I've seen. It's a seamless transition from setup storyline elements to travel to combat to cutscenes and back again. As far as storytelling goes, there is a lot of thought and effort put into this and it shows. Story is a clear motivator for the game and fans of solid, unique storytelling will absolutely love it.
It's real-time action RPG gameplay with pseudo turn-based elements. Combat feels, in a few ways, like Resonance of Fate where combos and position dictate whether you win or lose. It isn't anything ground-breaking but I don't believe people will enjoy this game for its combat system anyway.
The artstyle is beautiful with a watercolored, 1950's advertising feel to it. Paired with amazing audio that's very jazzy it sets a solid foundation for the story to play out. Not to mention that the character you play is a singer who lost her voice. Vocals by Ashley Barret, she was the perfect pick as her sound adds class and sexiness that suits the main character. This coupled with Logan Cunninghams legendary voicework makes for a memorable combination. I cannot stress enough how impressive it is to play something with such a flow to it.
Admittedly I was skeptical in dishing out $20 for this title but the quality is certainly there. Now bear in mind this is probably a one-trick pony in that one playthrough might be enough but that's fine by me because there are a few obscure elements I  may have missed on the first playthrough.
There's plenty of indie titles with the same price point without anything near this level of polish, detail and care. Game devs should pay attention to the structure of this because it hit my sweetspot in all categories. If you need something to pull you away for a day or two I fully recommend Transistor! Thanks and enjoy.

There is definitely a nod to old school RPG games here, but completely reinvented. I have never seen an inventory system like this before, and I was very impressed. When I first saw a youtuber play this game one year ago, I found it to be quite intriguing and very much to my liking. More specifically, the gameplay and art direction. Unfortunately, I did not have the funds to buy the game myself and only bought it a few days ago upon discovering a location to buy steam cards.
After finishing this game, I feel tempted to write a good review for it. Here's a few reasons why:
Unique gameplay: The gameplay of this game is akin to a interactive book combined with a video game with the point and click exploration element added to the mixture. Basically, you click stuff, engage in battles and obtain loot. Loot can be used to craft special items and it also depends on the crafter you choose. Kamaho, the skeleton "warrior" will make weapons for you. Falsen, the green goblin looking guy will create wacky items for you and Gazer, the alien thing will summon or make allies for you. This adds quite a bit of replayability to the game (especially with the new game plus that allows you to keep all your items from your previous run). Choices that you make impact the game in small ways but never really diverge from the main linear plot line of the game. As such, making certain decisions may result in obtaining "extra loot" or just some extra details about the world you are exploring.
Plot: The plot is kinda that a science fiction adventure. You are stranded in space after a battle with a mysterious creature called "Den" and wake up to find yourself in a spaceship with three aliens on board. The aliens request for your help in obtaining fuel to sustain the ship and you somehow find yourself accepting the quest. The rest of the game is just exploring the world to find the mentioned fuel.
Apart from that, the storytelling sometimes takes on a dark humour like tone (with Juno (some random person you meet twice or thrice) lying dead on the floor in the next area with no prior explanation.) which could be quite entertaining to read. Overall, the storytelling is splendidly done to resemble an actual storybook and I find myself having no faults with it.
Art:
The artstyle is simply amazing. It resembles the artstyle of video games in the 1990s while also looking like a picture book. Keep in mind that my opinion about the artstyle is subjective as I really appreciate old school artystyles.
Music:
The music is quite fitting with the battle scenes and the game itself. Not much else to say about it really. (P.S. I can't really good a decent comment about music in general)
The only con I find with this game is that it is a little too short and I would had liked to explore more of this world. Nevertheless, this is still a very good game and I would recommend you to try it.
Rating:
8.5/10

1.3 hrs in and I'm more entertained with it than some other games that I have ten times as much time logged into.
It's a point-n-click game; story is the draw. I'm eager to continue playing. You scrap with "the apex of eternity" in the opening encounter and then wake to find that you've been picked up by Dark Scavengers. They enlist you to find a new power source for their (and now your) ship - they will aid you with equipment. Of course, you find the planet that you intend to drain of resources has a host of issues for you to deal with. The writing/lore is outlandish; the humor isn't forced (not necessarily effective, but it won't exasperate, as many other "quirky" games will).
The art is very fantastic(al); I wish there was a gallery of all the images. That lore; I've yet to figure if the characters/creatures were ideas first and then illustrated, or if they began as doodles and then some background was affixed to further substantiate - a cosmic Zeno Clash is how I'd describe it all (though not nearly as "*puff puff* Bro, wtf.").
The system is interesting:
There are different areas in each Chapter (i.e. Level).
Upon entering a new screen, there is always an event. After the event, you click about the screen on highlighted points of interest; leads to more events.
Sometimes you gain Items from these events; sometimes you can choose to lose(/use) Items (i.e find someone: "My legs are busted, could you have one of your Allies carry me home? (Could you also have another Ally carry my items? (Could you also have another Ally carry my wares?))") - there are choices to be made (usually either good or bad, but sometimes there is a third option); have yet to really come across any consequences (again, 1.3 hrs - a few screens into Chapter 2).
Upon leaving a screen, you're beamed back up into your ship (which you share with three fellow Dark Scavengers). They can convert the items you've found into either Weapons, Items or Allies. Each of these have a certain number of uses before they are depleted; once you make it to a new Chapter, your Health as well as all charges of all equipment are recharged.
DEFINITELY worth the sale price, and I've little doubt it's worth the retail price - length will determine that (there are multiple endings, though, so).
I TOTALLY recommend Dark Scavenger.

This is the first time I've reviewed a game and I'm giving it a negative rating as I felt I ought to let others know that there is a game-breaking glitch that prevents the player from moving past a certain point and therefore makes the game completely unplayable from that point on.
In the "elegant crank" hos, the small silver lever that is supposed to be on the base of the fallen stand (circled in red in the strategy guide) is missing and therefore unable to click on, so one cannot proceed any further as there are no other actions that are possible to complete without finishing this particular hos. This also makes the bonus game impossible to access as it cannot be unlocked without playing through the entire main game first, so the player cannot even console themselves with that!
I checked online and it seems I am not the only one who has this problem but no-one has come up with any solutions and the developer hasn't bothered to fix it either, so the player is left utterly stuck.
I'm so disappointed as up to this point I was really enjoying playing Dark Parables: The Exiled Prince Collector's Edition - the graphics and sound are quite good, the Hidden Object Scenes provide just the right level of challenge, I was looking forward to playing the bonus game and it includes an integrated strategy guide if you get stuck - so I would definitely have given it a thumbs-up had it not been for this glitch, but instead the game has just left me feeling pretty p****ed off as I spent (for me) a ton of money buying this in the dark parables bundle (just buying it individually still would have cost £9.99) I can't even play the game!
So unless or until the developers fix this major issue, Dark Parables: The Exiled Prince Collector's Edition sadly deserves this negative review in my opinion.
[EDIT]
The developers have finally released an update which fixes the game-breaking glitch I discussed above and it now possible to continue the game.
Although I am still in the middle of playing the game and haven't yet completed it, I am now changing my review to give it a positive rating because, as I stated above, the only thing that was preventing me from giving the game a thumbs-up was the aforementioned glitch which has now been fixed!
So unless I find any further major issues (which I will add to this if I do) I firmly believe that this is a great game and deserves an overwhelmingly positive review.

I'm a big fan of games with a strong action-based melee combat system, and that's the main reason Dark Souls II - even more so than its prequel - absolutely got me hooked on. The variety of weapons and attack types, the quality of animations, the numerous different combat styles give a great way to experiment with melee combat and to find your own style.
There are quite a few ways to survive (dodging, blocking, parrying, armoring up, or even going berzerk when the boss is on the brink of death), and soo many more ways to die! But the Souls is not Flappy ♥♥♥♥ing Bird, death has a meaning here, and you seldom feel it was in vain, because you mostly learn from your mistakes. :)
A very strong side of this game is its replayability. I rarely play a game after completing it, but that's not the case with the Souls. 120+ hours, and I haven't even touched the DLC's or PVP yet.
And to contradict those who miss the chance to play co-op with friends: a friend and I have almost finished a complete walkthrough together, side-by-side againts all bosses, mutually summoning each other. It IS possible, just a bit complicated, just like most things with the Souls. :)
The truly dark fantasy setting of this game, its unique narrative and the fine voice acting together delivers a very rich experience story-wise. You will be confused, but so is everyone on this strange land.
And if you're new with the Souls do yourself a favor, and don't ignore the wiki while doing your first playthrough! Doing so won't spare you from spoilers, but will make your journey unnecessarily harder. I believe the wiki is part of the learning curve with this game.
Cons? Well, the Inventory system is a nightmare, and though it is a much better port than the prequel, I still think having a gamepad is a must with this game (but having one worth it anyway). Also, there is this messy case with the upcoming HD version to which you allegedly won't be able to upgrade this version of the game. That, if true, along with the recent news about the upcoming Bloodborne being PS4 exclusive would be a big disappointment. Come on, guys!

What is the Souls series?
The souls series is a series of three games (Demon's Souls, Dark Souls and Dark Souls 2) that are incredibly difficult and challenging. Fight your way through many areas, uncovering the lore and fighting numerous seemingly impossible boss fights and areas.
In my opinion, this game is easier than the first, which some of you may like so take that as you will.
Why is it easier than the first?

PROS:
~Graphics. The game looks pretty good, however, infrequent minor graphical glitches should be expected.
~No Enemy Farming. On the bright side of this point, after several clears of an area, the enemies will stop spawning, allowing you to just walk through that part rather than taking time to clear it and then dying at the end anyway only to restart at the beginning.
~Weapons + Armor. There are some really cool weapons and armor sets in this game, however some weapons are a bit unbalanced in the PvP part of the game.
CONS:
~Tried too hard to live up to DS1. Playing this game, to me, felt like the devs were putting things in there that were unbalanced and gimmicky because they thought it would add some artificial difficulty. They saw that the game was popular because it was hard so they said, "well people though Smaugh and Ornstein were tough, so we'll make 90% of the bosses in this game
sometimes up to ridiculous numbers (Skeleton Lords, Ruin Sentinels, the one room full of a million rolling skeletons)
~Controller. Expecting to be able to dodge on time, or really do anything with the precision this game forces you to develop, with a keyboard and mouse is really an absurd notion. While the keyboard controls are better than the first game, a controller is still 500% recommended.
~No Enemy Farming. On the flip-side of this, you cannot farm enemies in an area for very long because they stop spawning. While farming isn't required, it is certainly helpful if you want to do any of the following:
~Stupid enemy spawns. At times there are uncounterable enemy attacks in which thy fall through the ceiling or break through a wall and instantly attack you. This goes along with the "trying too hard to be hard" point.
~Cheaters. There are a lot of cheaters in PvP and there is no VAC on this game.
~DLC. I can't review the content of the DLC because I do not own any of it (I don't even like the base game), however, when Dark Souls II was announced, the devs said the game would be all-inclusive with no planned paid DLC. Look where we are today.
also talks about the plans devs have to re-release an "HD" version of the game with minor updates that should have been a free patch for owner of this game.
~No Solaire.
TL;DR:
Dark Souls 2 has some new content but pales in comparison to its predecessor because the devs tried to make this game as hard as possible
6/10
FINAL THOUGHTS:
Dark Souls II difficulty is a sales gimmick. Dark Souls was difficult because people weren't used to not having their hand held, and actually having to build skill in a video game. The devs saw that the difficulty was what gained the game popularity, so instead of making a quality game the devs sold out to the "lol this game is so hard look at me guys I can play games like pewdiepie" consumers. Not that tweaking a game to appeal to more people is bad but these games are night and day.

This has to be one of the best horror videogames I've ever played. It's very immersive and it really makes you think. So it's like a strategy horror game as you've got to try your best to avoid the alien. The game has amazing direction, graphics , Voice acting and sound effects.

What can I say? Probably the best Alien game I know of. It truly makes you feel like you are in the Alien universe, everything from the creature itself to the androids and technology you interact with feels just like the original movie.
The attention to detail is amazing, the alien is menacing, your tools and the tech you interact with feels authentic, the music is fantastic and the gameplay organically generates truly cinematic moments.
Example: you are trapped in an area with blairing alarms, you are crawling through an airduct under the floor, you move under some bars, trhough them you see the alien right above you, it's illuminated by the creepy blueish-white light from the lamps in the room and the orange rotating alarm lights behind it, you freeze like a deer in headlights and hold your breath, hoping that he hasn't spotted you because he can and will chase you into vents, he turns around and walks away a few steps, you crawl forward until you are completely hidden from sight, but you still dont dare exhale properly for fear of being overheard.
10/10 would be scared stiff again.
The alien can actually hear you breathing when he walks past your hiding spots, he can also hear the beeping of your motion tracker if you are using it. Also on higher difficulty, he can follow your scent trail. It wont allow him to pinpoint your position, but it will make sure he is in your general visinity most of the time. Also he sometimes resorts to process of elimination and checks all the hiding spots if he saw you run into the room but you hid from sight before he entered it (he runs faster then you btw).
PS. For masochists there is also Nightmare mode. Basically it takes away a lot of your resources (ammo, crafting materials), makes the motion tracker glitchy, makes enemies stronger and ups the alien's aggression and deadliness. Have fun doing the "play through the game without dieing once" achivement on that mode :)
Summary: Great world building, oppressive atmosphere, amazing artstyle and sound design, cinematic gameplay moments and unkillable, relentless alien menace stalking you.
If you are a fan of Aliens you owe it to yourself to experience this, it feels like a redemption after alien 3 and 4 and the mountain of crappy games.

Bastion was all about narration, music and visualisation, storytelling. Transistor is the same, but way more polished, combined with much deeper game mechanics, but you can beat the game in 2-6 hours depends on the style of play. +1-2 hours for reading the lore stuff. So in a nutshell there is only one problem: the game is short.

After 3 years, Supergiant Games brings out its next game. Does it match up?
I think so.
Returning from Bastion is Logan Cunningham, who has a similar role to the Narrator in Bastion. I won't go into deep details but I personally feel his role in this game is better, although it no longer is an original idea to have everything you do be talked over and commented on.
The story in Transistor is presented in an even less hand-holdy way than in Bastion and some additional story is available to unlock through playing the game, which I enjoyed a lot and it encourages experimentation. Red (who you play) felt like a human character from start to finish despite and her relation with the Transistor is exlored well despite the fact that she doesn't talk. The story can be hard to understand, though, and you'll have to do a lot of reading between lines and thinking for yourself to figure it out. It is, at some points, quite vague, although generally not in a bad way.
Gameplay is Top down, Action RPG, Diablo-like hack n slash like Bastion but it also is not. At the core of this game is a function called Turn() that allows you to pause the world and plan out a few moves. With some exceptions, enemies cannot impact what you do during this, but the game feels well-balanced and without Turn() you are dead in the water. Your moves in this game are 4 choosable special attacks, from a simple slash to bombs and blinks. The moves (called functions) can be augmented by putting another function in its upgrade slot. Alternatively, you'll unlock the ability to use your functions as passive abilities. At every Access Point (where you can swap out functions), you can change your setup completely. It feels balanced (some are better than others, but every function has its place). The game encourages experimentation, unlike Bastion (to some extend with the upgradable weapons), and whenever I tried something new I didn't feel like being punished for it at all. If you enjoyed Bastions combat you'll likely enjoy this combat although it is somewhat slower paced and requires less twitch skills but more thinking.
Audio and Visuals I won't go to deep into, but everything looks beautiful and is handdrawn, with the exception of Red and the enemies. While this didn't bother me at all with the enemies, Red's visual (outside of the handdrawn cutscenes) feels somewhat out of place to me. The audio is stellar. More great music from Darren Korb and a few awesome vocal songs make the soundtrack worth a listen to after you're done and the game sounds empower and fit. Voice acting is, unsurprisingly, really great as well.
At some points, the game does get a little slower. At the end, the game almost exclusively throws one enemy type at you, and at times I felt like I was just doing another encounter. For a game that relies so heavily on story some of the parts are surprisingly narrative-light, providing little exposition or character interaction, similar to Bastion. The game is short, as well, but I don't really mind.
That said, it is a great game and I really enjoyed it. It is more than The Next Game by the Creators of Bastion, and deserves everyone's attention.
