If you enjoyed Ragnarok Online and want to play another MMO like it you probably don't need a review. Tree of Savior is very similar, and even improves on a lot of RO's good ideas.
If you never played RO and are curious about ToS, here are the basics: Tree of Savior is a Korean MMO and spiritual successor to the aforementioned Ragnarok Online. It has a anime inspired 2D on 3D artstyle. It looks very good as you can see in the trailer. It is an Action RPG, most closely comparable to something like Diablo. You will either be blowing up large groups of enemies with AoEs, or focusing down one powerful enemy with more strategic single target attacks. They recommend joypad for the best experience, I've just been using keyboard and haven't had any issues.
The game has a very linear quest structure, which makes leveling go by very quickly. The game has a very complex Job system. Every 20-30 levels you will change classes and gain new skills. There are four starting classes, but near infinite possiblities built into each, complemented by the fact that you can build your stats in any way you like as well.
It has all of the modern MMO amenities you would expect: auction house, guilds, instances. I haven't had time to try all of these things, but I did do one instance and it was very pretty fun. The game is packed full of unique features I haven't seen in other MMOs, so if you're someone looking to just try something new you might enjoy Tree of Savior. It's only $10 for early access, and will be free soon.
I must warn you though, the game is a bit of a mess at the moment. Server issues, overpopulation, crashing. Its gotten much better in the past week or so but even if you are starting now expect some issues. I hope they get these problems sorted out before the game goes free to play or it will just get worse. Also be warned that many features are locked to premium members only, which requires real money. Things like trading, selling more than one item on the auction house, and learning multiple skills at the same time. Overturned my sofa cushions, found enough money to buy Dark Scavenger.  Let me tell you how it is:
Picture this if you'd be so kind:  space.  It's unfathomably huge and mostly empty, but you've come across a place where in the background you can see a stream of stars.  Nearby is a sun pounding atoms together to make heavier and heavier elements and putting out the energy of 6 trillion nuclear bombs per second as a by-product.  A few hundred million miles off are some planets; generators of storms guaranteed to instantly pressure cook anything wrought by feeble mortal hands, but only tiny marbleized orbs from your point of view.  This is so real and awesome, you think to yourself.  How could it possibly get any better?  Well, maybe there's a barbarian with a giant axe.  And if that weren't enough, the barbarian is having a no-holds-barred punch-up with a robot micro-universe, the Xenomorph from Alien, and Jesus Christ if he were an alien with a super laser gun.  They are firing rays that go "pew-pew!" and there are explosions and a spaceship and a unicorn runs by!  You cannot believe that this is totally real and you are seeing it!  And what can you even do in the midst of such an amazing scenario?  The only thing a man can do:  swing his rusty sword for 5 damage.
Dark Scavenger is kind of like that, but even better!  This game will take you on an amazing and hilarious adventure with an ultra-simple interface reminiscent of games like Dragon Warrior, Earthbound, and Pokemon.  Of course, without the limitations of old cartridges, Dark Scavenger is free to elaborate on its story and make sure you're never bored.  The graphics are static images, but look quite nice (I don't think the screenshots in Steam did them justice) and despite the simplistic nature of it all Dark Scavenger manages to create a game you'll never forget.
You remember playing those RPGs and getting a little giddy when you finally leveled up and unlocked an awesome sounding new move for your character?  You didn't even care what it did or if you could only do it a couple of times; you totally used that move on the next Level 1 Fuzzy Bunny you came up against.  Dark Scavenger's gameplay manages to capture that feeling in every single encounter.  Rather than leveling up and gaining better hit points or attack prowess, you gain loot.  But instead of simply strapping this loot on to your hurly-burly self, you give it to one of your three allies who will make you a new weapon, item, or ally to call upon.  Every one of these is unique and it never manages to get samey.  And as your allies tease you with what awesome choices lie before you, you'll find yourself in gleeful agony trying to pick your prize.  Each thing has limited uses, but can be used in combat for obvious reasons or choose-your-own-adventure style narrative pieces where having an applicable tool will give you the best rewards or the coolest outcome to your actions.  Thanks to this, nothing is ever useless and you never experience the grind of other RPGs.  Encounters come and go and don't get replayed.  Dark Scavenger is nothing if not perpetually fresh.
So let's say I haven't sold this game to you yet.  Yeah, by passing up on Dark Scavenger, you'll save about 1/24th of what it takes to get a new release that's one of those comittee designed polygon orgies that's like a movie you press buttons to watch.  Or, you could buy this game that has the heart to make you want to replay it years down the line, the balls to ask a couple bucks for a mostly text-driven sci-fi fantasy adventure, and the kind of brain that'll give you disco dancing space goblins if you give it a chance.  I know where I'd rather put half of my lunch money, sir.
Or, if you take the advice of some other reviewers, you could just watch a let's play of Dark Scavenger, since it's one of those games where once you've seen the whole thing there's only minor differences to see.  Fair enough.  But, hey, if you do that and you actually have fun watching, why not buy the game?  For how little it costs on sale, it's basically like buying the devs a beer.  And then maybe they'll make more!

Dark Scavenger is a fairly unique game and represents a hidden gem of the indie scene.  The main focuses of the game are on decision making, story, combat (a more fun version of JRPG combat style), humor, and loot. Loot in this game is not your regular loot, but more on that later.
Each level is composed of multiple areas and (you don't need to visit every one), and each area has interactive objects that you can click on. This procs either combat, dialogue with decisions that have major impact, loot, or combination of those. A clever dialogue option and/or a smart use of your items, yields rewards, but  also keep in mind, if you don't focus on the game, you may get punished as well (don't worry, there is barely any memorization).
Loot has a central part in  the game and after each area transition you get your friends (a skeleton engineer, crazy green alien in a suit, and an alien that can't speak) to make weapons, items or allies out of it. They each explain what loot will you get from them in their own unique way (remember the alien that can't speak?). It's not always obvious what will you get, but that's what makes the game even more interesting.
All in all, Dark Scavenger offers a refreshing experience and a rewarding story if you enjoy games with dialogue options and relatively unique mix of gameplay elements.

I put this game on my wishlist after seeing it on the sidebar and seeing how it looked interesting, it looked like this space game I saw in a magazine when I was a kid (tried looking for the name of the game, but couldn't find it), So I thought I'd eventually buy it down the road expecting it to be a somewhat mediocre game that'll give me a few hours of gameplay. Well, the game went on sale with the Thanksgiving sale, bought it for almost 3 bucks, and stayed up all night playing it, it was that good.
You play an alien that's stranded out in space, who soon comes across a galactic being who wants to consume you. After defeating him you're left to rot in space for years and eventually you're picked up by a group of aliens called the Dark Scavengers who are pretty much intergalactic junkers who invite you to join their crew if you can help them by finding a fuel source for their ship. This leads you to going down to the nearest planet full of your typical medieval fantasy setting including a race of giant masked wrestlers, crazy drunk bandits,  and an armored smart♥♥♥♥♥space raptor with a giant gun who wants you dead.
The story for this game is absolutely amazing. There are constant twists in the story, characters that you get emotionally invested in, and even extremely interesting concepts that get explored. Each character has their own personality and always has you wanting to learn more about them. You'll constantly be laughing at the crazy situations and humorous characters you find yourself interacting with.
Unlike Mass Effect 3, your choices actually matter in this game. You can kill everything you come across right away, or talk to them and get useful items and information or even backstabbed. There's several different endings depending on what you do in the final chapter.
The combat is a bit different from other rpgs. There is no leveling up in this game. Combat is focused around finding objects through battle and having the dark scavengers turn them into either weapons, items, or allies. The vast majority of objects (i'm talking around 95%) have multiple options on what you can turn them into. You may find a bone that you can turn into a weapon that does wind damage, a controller which increases your damage for the next turn, or a zombie ally. You may only choose one of these, and you can't go back on your choice. All items, allies, and weapons have a certain number of uses before they break, and you won't get to use them anymore till they replenish at the start of the next chapter, making it so you have to have a balanced between all 3 categories. The only flaw in this system is that the majority of the time the Dark Scavengers don't give you good hints on what they're about to make for you.
Combat is done with you going first followed by all enemies. You can stun enemies using elements they're weak against, which loses them their turn, allows you to use stuff that's strong vs stun against them the next turn, and refills your healing potion (restores you to full health when you click it). Enemies are even strong vs certain elements which makes them take little damage
Also all weapons, items, and allies have different characteristics. A weapon might be a long bladed weapon or a short blunted staff, or fast strong ally. You may run into an event (events happen regularly) which you need a long bladed weapon to attack with, or you may get stuck in a whirlpool which you need a strong ally to help you out. There are also weapons and allies that effect certain enemies, like ones with their mouths open or enemy with their feet on the ground. This adds a lot of uniqueness to the game.
The game takes about 4 and a half hours to beat, but once you do you get access to New Game Plus. Once you beat it you'll be wishing that there was a sequel to continue the story (which the ending sets up for). I honestly recommend buying this for full price, it's only 5 bucks, but you'll more than get your money's worth.

I think it's probably best to go into this game as a single-player experience that you can play with friends or other randoms online.  And also not to go in expecting something like Skyrim online.  It's definitely an Elder Scrolls game, but it's also definitely not an Elder Scrolls game.
To try to keep it brief, you can pick between one of several Elder Scrolls races and between four classes.  Sounds small, but each class has three skill lines and every character has access to a large number of other skill lines ranging from weapon skills, guild skills, crafting, armor skills, and more.  And every character can mix and match abilities from these trees to their hearts content provided they meet the pre-requisite skill level for the ability.  And then every active skill can be morphed into one of two new versions with additional effects.  So, Sorcerer Orc Tank?  Dragon Knight High Elf Mage?  Nord Support Night Blade?  All possible in a variety of ways and I'm merely scratching the surface here.  You'd probably need a few hundred character slots to get all the combinations down and that's before even considering the champion system for adventuring with level-capped characters to get even more customization options.
As for gameplay itself... well, with recent changes, you can pretty much just go do what you want after the starter area (and maybe even merely after the tutorial).  Wanna quest?  Grind monsters?  Craft?  Look for treasure?  Explore caves?  PvP?  All of them will advance your character and help you level up.  Follow main stories, ignore them, go rob innocents blind, go quest in another faction's zone, whatever.  Pretty much the only thing that won't level you up is chilling in town chatting at other players or roleplaying with them.  I think the only downside is that sometimes the sheer amount of content available is a bit intimidating, which sometimes leaves me feeling indecisive about who to play or where to go with them.
As for the cash shop... well...  you can either buy things directly, including DLC areas, or get ESO Plus membership.  Plus is basically the old MMO subscription model grants you all DLC while membership is active and also gives you free crowns equal to the amount you spent on subbing.  Basically, if you're gonna drop $15 on crowns, just get the membership.  Only downside is the crafting bad and costume re-coloring is only for Plus members, which are features that really should be for everyone, even if in a limited form.  Also, be very careful about how you spend any crowns you get.  Some items in the store have rather insane costs and a few can be obtained in-game cheapy or for free by just asking around, such as becoming a Werewolf.  The store isn't really pay to win, mostly offering some consumables that are easy and fairly cheap to obtain in-game equivalents of.  The biggest changers are DLCs since they give you access to some sets you'd otherwise have to buy off of players and some skill lines that have little to no impact on normal combat.  The biggest loss are the skill points and Sky Shards in the DLC zones, but there's far, far more than enough skill points laying around to max everything you could want on a character.  ...Save maybe maxing all crafting trees on one alt.
I could really go on and on about different nuances, but let's keep it simple and focus on the big things, shall we?  Though, I'll go ahead and say, the game is really beautiful and is what Skyrim really should have looked like.  Also, there is mod support, in true Elder Scrolls fashion, though it is limited mostly to UI enhancements and graphic adjustments... for obvious reasons being an MMO.  Just... use ESOUI over Nexus Mods or the Steam Workshop.  The NMM is great for installing your mods and such, but ESOUI has a far, far, far bigger selection and is often more up to date.
I can definitely recommend picking this game up.  I definitely woulda bought it sooner or later if a friend didn't gift it to me.  Just, remember to treat it more like a single-player game that happens to have lots of other players running about or that your friends can join.  There's definitely some group-focused content, but it's not one of those MMOs where you should expect to be constantly grouping with randoms for most things.  Even still, the community is pretty cool and I've seen some of the most interesting conversations in Zone chat.  If you like Elder Scrolls games but you're willing for an online experience to be different to proper support a MMO rather than just being "Skyrim with other people", then give the game a shot!  If you're unsure, wait for a Steam sale.  It almost always drops in price during those.

Where do I start... this is not a bad game, but certainly not the best RPG ever, as some claim.
There are a lot of haters out there, but as a whole the game is pretty good.
(Just make sure you use a game controller, mouse and keyboard are nearly unusable.)
So why the negative review of it? Well, let's take a look...
(TL:DR at bottom)
Dark Souls(1 and 2) is famous for it's utter unforgiving brutality towards the player. It offers up massive amount of challenge, and doesn't babysit the player.
Unfortunately part of that is that it doesn't tell the player ANYTHING. You don't know what's happening, why you're there, what you need to do, any of it. There's only little hints in the opening. You're cursed, and you want to get rid of the curse. That's all you get.
Now personally I'm a fan of the "let players figure things out for themselves" type of storytelling, but that's usually in a more constructive light. In DS2, if you make a mistake, you die. It's almost like playing a modern version of Dragon's Lair in that respect. Tutorial doorways are covered in a gray mist that looks like it blocks them off, unless you plant your face right into the mist. (A dangerous risk in a game that will kill you any chance it gets.)
As a result I didn't even know there WAS a tutorial until 3 hours in. (They all looked blocked and the path ahead was wide open.)
The game doesn't even offer you a SUGGESTION on where you should be going. So say, when the only NPC that suggests I go anywhere says I should go meet the king, I delightfully set off in the direction of the only thing resembling a palace gate I can see, merrily singing a song while popping open crates and barrels as I go skipping along. Two hours and many respawns later, having only managed to kill the very first mob and dying immediately after (causing everything to respawn) I was informed by a friend that there's a different way I should go first: Down a path on the side of a cliff. Easily missed. Thank you game for making that clear as mud.
Every time you die or tp, it takes a few minutes to walk back. Long, uneventful minutes. You stop at one point to open a gate by pulling a lever. Other than that, it's long hallways, long canals, long stairways, long bridges, etc.
Prepare to spend a lot of time just walking to get back to where you just died. Your character isn't exactly a marathon runner either.
It's Walking Simulator 2014.
I played several hours in the game and I died mostly by:
1. Interface/Camera/Control Issues.
2. Falling.
3. Experimenting.
4. The actual enemies killing me.
I spent a lot more time dying due to issues with the game interface, controls, and camera than I did by these oh so powerful, challenging, over-hyped mobs. The mob fights are actually quite easy, just watch their patterns and dodge where needed. Sure they hurt if you make a mistake, run out of stamina, or you get overrun, but they're simply not hard in and of themselves.
The real challenge comes from grappling with some of the other, less polished bits of the game at the same time. When your game that's supposed to be challenging is so in a large way because of how the game is played, rather than the game itself, that's not something to be commended, it's simply inadequate game design.
The constant restarting and walking back to where you died or TPed from robs you of any sense of progression, really, and after a while you begin to ask yourself. "What's the point?" There doesn't seem to be really anything to gain from going there, and I never given a reason to go one way over another.
Targeting and locking on to enemies is nice, and greatly helps with the duel aspect of the game, when it works. Enemies have to be somewhat close (IE usually within aggro range) to target. Sometimes the game would drop my target at random, or if I get to far away, or go behind something. Ranged enemies it has a terrible time targeting. Also, who maps the camera movement controls and the change target controls to the same stick?
The duel style of combat is nice, but there's some issues in the combat as well. For starters, the animations of your character take quite a while to play out, sometimes non-sensibly. Why is it I can take a broadsword in one hand and swing it full power, and it's a LOT faster to attack, AND recover than swinging the same weapon with both hands? There's a pretty significant amount of idle time after your character swings a weapon before they recover to attack again. What are they doing, taking a tea break?
Also, you run out of stamina insanely fast. Dodge? Chop a large chunk off your stamina. Block? There goes a huge chunk. Swing a weapon? Huge chunk. What happens when you run out of stamina? Well, if you're far enough away to still kite, you wait for it to regen. If you're too close? You'll probably die.
Because while you're character is standing there pondering whether the chicken or egg came first, the enemy does NOT have stamina limits, and can easily string combo after combo at you with very little downtime. This is a frustrating point, where players are held to these arbitrary limits while the enemy is not. It's an unfair, artificial way to make things harder, and it feels as much about the tenth time an enemy is standing over your corpse peeling little bits of your face off the end of their pike which they can effortlessly swing over and over while you didn't have the energy to get out of the way. I get that there needs to be something to keep players from just button mashing to kill enemies, but this feels far too restrictive and saps a lot of the fun from combat.
Weapons wear out faster than tissue paper clothing in a rain storm. You HAVE to have a backup set of weapons in most cases since the ones you have won't last you from campfire to campfire without carrying around repair dust. (Note to the devs: That is NOT a bonfire.)
On the plus side, the game is *mostly* very attractive. The views and areas are very interesting and attractive. Enemies get a bit repetetive after a while, and your character's head is tiny compared to their body, but as a whole it's an immersive, beautiful game. (Another note to devs: You guys clearly have a fetish for wrinkles, and old ladies. Take it easy.)
I love the idea that you're not just mowing down huge groups of enemies as some uber-powered demigod. Each fight has a bit more significance that way. It's like your character actually has to TRY!
Overall there's a lot of fun to be had in the game, and I will be playing it more, but are many little quirks that hold the game back from being it's best. If the game was much less expensive, say half the price it is, I could recommend it. The amount of actual gaming fun vs frustration you'll get for the full cost though, forces me to say I don't.
---------
Here's a quicker summary for the impatient TL:DR people.
PROS:
+ Immersive Graphics and World
+ "Duel Style" Combat
+ Can be a Challenge at times.
+ Doesn't Hold a player's hand,
+ Game Seems Decently Optimized/Runs Well
CONS:
- Plays Terrible on Mouse and Keyboard
- Camera has issues in tight spaces
- Targeting is Fickle.
- Needlessly Long Combat Animations
- Overly Restrictive and Artificially Hard Stamina System
- User Interface is Clunky
- No Simple Way to Compare Armors in Shop (That I could find, anyways.)
- Leveling Up or Custom Tailoring Your Character Stats Requires a PHD
- Many Pricey DLCs Gives the Impression of a Cash Grab
Again, there's really a lot to like in the game, but a lot of stuff that could use more polish.
At times you'll be patting yourself on the back, or screaming obscenities at your monitor, or loathing the game for that really long walk back to the area you just were for the 20th time.
If the price drops into the $30 range, go for it. At full price, I say there's many other things worth your money instead.
Like it or hate it, that's up to you to decide.

Dark souls, oh my dear Dark Souls. How little i initially cared about you. As a hardcore PC gamer im disgusted by the very idea of even holding onto a controller, let alone actually play a game with one. Even after that the horrible PC port actually turned me off Dark Souls 1 completely. But the idea of the Souls games always intrigued me. I was one of the few people who actually enjoyed some of those "I wanna be the guy" Games. In my mind they were challenging, but they were a lot about recollection and planning ahead.
But alas, i didn't play the original Dark Souls. And after the huge disappointment that was Lords of the ♥♥♥♥ers i was kind of turned away from everything Souls-like for a decent amount of time.
But then i noticed Dark Souls 2 was on sale.
Now if you're like me you're always worried whenever you buy a game off of a sale. Cause you never really know what the hell you're getting into. But my fear was increased tenfold when i was booting up Dark Souls 2 for the first time, because i had of course experienced the nightmare that had been Dark Souls on PC. So imagine my very happy self when once i had watched the opening cutscene and got to walk around it happened without a hitch. I was able to walk briskly around like the happiest little puppy in the daycare.
That was when i was greeted by the intro.
Look From Software, i know you haven't got to stretch your cutscene muscles in Demon's souls and Dark souls, but could you maybe not have a cutscene last about 5-10 minutes only for us to make a character and have the cutscene go on for 2 more minutes?
after that i set out into the world, and quickly met my first enemy. An undead warrior wearing what looked to be leather armor. I had of course prior to playing Dark Souls 2, seen a lets play of Dark souls 1. So i knew dodging was an essential part of its combat.
Now, after i had slain my assailant i briskly moved onwards through the tunnels of Things Betwixt, fighting off more undead soldiers as i went along until i came to a hole in the road. I went into my controls to find out what the jump button was, and saw it was bound to F. So i ran forward and immediately fell down because i didn't know how to jump properly.
I then respawned and found to my dismay that my previously handsome knight had somehow caught the Plague, and had therefore turned a very disgusting shade of green. I then also saw that my max health had gone down.
Now, this is a mechanic i don't really like. Cause a lot of the bosses and the areas leading up to them are very much dependent on trying a lot of times to get the hang of their movement and attack patterns. This becomes harder when you're actively punished for your death in a manner that can stick with you for a while.
But that doesn't deter from the awesome combat system though! Every single little bit of Dark Souls seems to be built around the combat. Every single boss is combat focused, when you explore the inevitable thing thats going to be in the way of your progress is enemies that you almost always have to fight, And all of your stat building and upgrades are inevitably going to be focused on fighting enemies. It is very good then, that the combat system is ♥♥♥♥ing awesome. It has this real weight to it that encourages timing and precision. It rewards patience and punished rash decisions. A lot of times the mentality of "Just one more hit," can either land you a close victory or a humiliating defeat.
The exploration is also nice. With plenty of hidden areas to find if you're willing to stray off the beat and path.
All in all this game is great, and while i dont condone the practice of making an HD remaster of it this soon (This being the upcoming redux version From Software are planning) This game is still amazing. Buy it if you can't wait, get the hd remaster once it comes out in the other case.

I cannot recommend this game higher enough. Factorio is a great 2D-isometric sandbox game devoted toward indulging my wildest management fantasies. Now wait, I know I've lost a lot of you right there. Bear with me:
Have you ever straightened a pencil on your desk? Have you ever just been bugged by a crooked picture frame? Have you caught yourself binge watching How It's Made? Factorio is watching a product come to life in front of you. Your interaction with the environment, your equipment, and figuring out how to mesh everything together seamlessly makes it oh so rewarding when the final product rolls off the assembly line.
Do you like survival games with hordes of enemies? Somehow, Factorio manages to wrap two completely different styles of game into one. While you're laying down new belts, you may get attacked by hostile natives bent on destroying your precious creations (and to a greater or lesser extent, yourself). Hole up and hunker down as enemies become increasingly more aggressive. Research brings new opportunities and new weapons, and the feeling of being scared to leave your base only to emerge later armed to the teeth and getting some well-deserved pay back is sublime. Overall, I loved this game. Yeah, occasionally it gets a bit slow as you try and up your production, and while having a simplified tech tree from only 3 real resources, copper, iron, and oil, may seem cool at first, there are some pretty extreme production bottle necks due to the over-reliance on iron ore for most of your items, but that's about my only real criticism.
Pros:
Runs on a potato
Easy to pick up, rewarding to master
That feeling when everything fits together just right
Cons:
Staring at progress bars
Getting overwhelmed
Mid-game learning curve

In 2007, CoD:MW (Call of Duty: Modern Warfare) was released into a community that has a seemingly insatiable lust for more shooter action. They weren't just given another shooter, they were given a game that really pushed the genre considerably. Amazing single player campaign and adrenaline-pumped, fast-paced multiplayer action with perks and weapon sets set the new standard on how these FPS's are done. It left it's mark on gaming as a whole, so a sequel was inevitable and gamers couldn't wait. In fact - according to an eye-witness who works at my local Game Stop - MW2 "...became the best-selling game in history before it was even released", all being pre-orders (of course, #1 sellers are subject to change). Imagine their dissapointment when they got this...
Plot 1/10
..was so convoluted, I can't tell you what it was. Everybody wants everybody dead except the protagonists, and the only solution is...killing everybody. It's a movie written by Michael Bay. That's all I have to say about the plot without spoiling it. If you don't care (which you shouldn't), highlight this big, black box.
The ending also plays out like every other cutscene in the game: "Good job, now let's carry you off and tell you who the kill nex-" CREDITS; THAR'LL BE A SEEQUEL!
Graphics/Sound 8/10
I'll put these in the same category because I don't have much to say about them. MW2's sound and visuals are everything we expect from the series: excellent. The guns, the dust, the lighting, character models are all beautiful, and guns, tanks, explosions all sound great, too; so why an 8/10? Attentive gamers will notice that a majority of this game's voice cast is from Mass Effect. In fact, several things were just "taken" from Mass Effect. For one thing, your CO's voice is the voice of Captain Anderson, and the voice of the general is the voice of Admiral Hackett. Oh, and the general's name? Sheperd.
There's nothing wrong with being inspired, but I call this a lazy, rip off. Infinity Ward wasn't even trying. Maybe I'm just being picky, but this really rubbed me wrong despite Keith David's long career as voice actor for military-esque media.
Gameplay 5/10
Finally, gamers are starting to see the light with the release of CoD:Ghosts. It's the same. Darn. Game. Same rail-shooter scenes, same set pieces, same "set bomb and run away" scene, same door breaching scene, same, same, same. We've been playing the same game since the original Call of Duty in 2003 and before that with the Medal of Honor series. It's been 11 years of the same game. It's time for CoD to die. You run forward, you kill the next thing that moves, and steadily march to the credit roll. Everything about it is so banal; boring to the point of painful. The graphics and sounds aren't enough to mask the bad gameplay and story. A pretty package doesn't make the bad contents good. You've played CoD before. Enough said.
Multiplayer also went downhill with unbalanced weapons and killstreak abilities that broke the game entirely. When you get 3 kills in one life, you get a UAV that reveals all enemies on the radar. However, these streak rewards stacked with one another, so you use the UAV to get a few more kills, and get a chopper. The chopper automatically gets you 5 more kills giving you an AC-130 gunship. Use THAT for a few more kills, you get a nuke that ends the game instantly. Sounds pretty ambitious on pen and paper, but in game it means: first to a 3 kill streak WINS. Hackers also had their way with the game and Infinity Ward/Treyarch/Activision or all three refused to do anything about it. I've heard rumors that the same hacks that worked on MW2 also worked on MW3 and Black Ops. Watching this trend, I believe it.
If you want an example of customer service done RIGHT, let's ask Valve. Some time ago, Steam was glitching up and improperly banning players from accessing MW2. Gabe Newell wrote a personal apology to these gamers, and offered them a free copy of Left 4 Dead 2 (L4D2). While that was generous and very polite, that might have been a bad idea for the poor people that play L4D2, because all the teenage @***holes from this game are now trolling the L4D2 community (as if that game wasn't bad enough.)
The Verdict
Visually, there's little to complain about. MW2 is very realistic by sight and by sound. Some of the settings are creepy with ash blotting out the sun and smoke rising from decimated vehicles and climbing corpses to escape combat. The whole world is going crazy, but they couldn't make the player care less. Traversing the beautiful world is an uphill hike to the credits. Yearly releases also means the community will be widely divided and chopped thinner and thinner with each release, so there's no point in trying to play MP. MW2 is big pass. Maybe get it for 5 bucks and beat it once. Final score: 3/10 Almost no reason to buy it.

What do you get when you mix the Destructibility and variety of weapons from Worms with the Hardcore gameplay of Contra with Action movie heroes from the 80's (Mostly), you get Broforce.
Broforce is a balls to the wall Action sidescroller with fully destructible environments and plenty of gore and dead terorists and aliens along the way.
The plot is fairly basic, you play as the Broforce who are a Paramilitary Organisation made up of all the best Action Heroes of the past 30-40 years and their job is to simply kill all Terrorists and aliens that come in their way therefore liberating all areas on the map.
In terms of Presentation it goes for a very retro look that is still pleasing to the eye, all the Bros look as they should look and all the bad guys and environments explode in very satisfying ways.
The Audio is also top notch with some very powerful weapons along with the gigantic explosions and comedic gibberish yells of your enemies, the soundtrack is also well done.
Gameplay is essentially like most early 90's sidescrollers, you play as 1 of up to 30+ Bros going from one side of the level to the end, killing everything and rescuing hostages along the way.
Those hostages are vital as when you die and you will die often, one of the hostage lives will be spent to bring you back as a random Bro, so you will want to rescue as many as possible since the environment will kill you just as often as the enemies will.
There are a couple of problems that hamper an otherwise terrific game, first problem is that the Online Co-op can get extremely laggy and choppy at certain points making certain players glitch out in the environment or just crash entirely. There are also some areas that are so difficult they will make you want to tear your hair out.
Some of the Bros in the game also feel pretty useless and you will come to rely on a few specific bros to help you beat the levels more easily (If you are lucky to spawn as them).
Overall though Broforce is one of the best Indie games in years and will definitely give you enough value and laughs for the price.

There is very little to complain about when talking about Supergiant's Transistor, it is what I consider to be a very worthy successor to their previous game Bastion, and Transistor on it's own is a brilliant game that I imagine will be a strong contender for my GOTY 2014, much like Bastion was in 2012.
Transistor's gameplay is very interesting, and it works, although there are a few UI elements that could have been somewhat better to make the game just that little bit smoother, such as improving the ability slotting menu. When the player, or "user" as the game refers to you, gets into combat, a small area is cordoned off from the rest of the world, and then enemies and obstacles begin to spawn in, thus beginning the battle sequence. Transistor has two types of combat, and both have their pros and cons for their use, but both are viable means of combat, especially when used in tandem. The first type is the traditional real-time combat that you are used to in most games, where (most of) your 1-4 hotkey skills do not have a cooldown so you can mash the keys to your heart's content, but you are open to attack. The second type is something called "Turn Mode", this mode, often showed off in trailers, stops time and allows you to queue up a set of skills that will be activated in super speed once you exit this mode, often giving most enemies no time to react or move out of the way, but once you activate this mode, almost all of your abilities are put on cooldown, making you a vulnerable target. One other cool aspect of Transistor is the ability to customise your loadouts to suit how you play. Each skill has a basic function when placed in an active slot, and these active slots make up your action bar of 1-4 abilities, once you run out of health, however, one of your 4 equipped skills becomes unusable, until you find another customisation area. These active skills can then be customised with other skills in upgrade slots, improving the effects of that specific skill, allowing it to drastically change the way that active ability functions in combat. One last slot is the passive slot, this allows you to equip a skill and gain a passive ability that can improve the way you fight without using up an ability slot. All this has to be done in the constraints of your "memory", a points system that restricts the player from equipping each and every ability into a slot.
The story for Transistor is really cool, but very vague to begin with. The basic premise of this story is that you play a famous singer known to the player and other characters as Red, but Red's voice has been taken away. You find yourself equipped with a sword containing the personality of a person, and you are fighting against The Process, a mechanical force that is wiping out the city of Cloudbank as well as it's inhabitants. Aside from main plot points, the story is also given to the player through approachable vistas or terminals that offer extra exposition as to what the city was and what is going on now. The story in itself was somewhat predictable, and the last 30 minutes or so were fairly tedious, but it does pay off, and I was satisfied with how it ended. The game itself to around 5-6 hours to playthrough, but there is a new game+ mode for those who want to go through the game again with all unlocked abilities and level up some more.
Graphically, Transistor is just remarkable. The entire game looks like a painting, and it looks gorgeous. Almost every area was just beautiful to look at in one way or another, be it the streets, or the towers, the game was just a visual treat. The only downside to the aesthetics of the game is contained in a minor spoiler that follows, but otherwise, the art department at Supergiant struck gold a second time, and that is just a wonder.
SPOILERS FOLLOW
The audio of Transistor is just fantastic, once again, all praise to Darren Korb and the great vocals of Ashley Barrett as Red. The reason I say this is because as I write this review, I am listening to Transistor's OST, and finding a soundtrack this good is a rare treat. Also, you cant really go without mentioning Logan Cunningham who is the narrator inside of the sword, and he does a wonderful job as well this time around. As opposed to when he played Rucks in Bastion who sounded like he was telling a story, in Transistor the voice is coming in real-time as he talks to Red. The other difference in terms of narration is that as opposed to Bastion, where the narrator was talking about almost everything that the Kid did, in Transistor he only seems to interact with the environment as much as Red did, as well as giving audible hints as to when your Turn mode's cooldown has finished, which was very useful.
During my time playing the game, I did encounter one single bug, but this but was a game breaking one, this bug caused the game to outright crash when the Help passive triggered near the last zone of the game, and caused the game to crash when I fired it's ability. This bug I expect to have been patched by now, however.
Transistor is a brilliant game, and one that is well worth the purchase, regardless of whether or not you enjoyed Bastion. It is honestly one of the best games that I have played in a long while, and I wish Supergiant the best of successes with Transistor.

This game is fantastic. The narrative/presentation style is similar to Bastion in that it drops you immediately into a strange world, and it's up to you to piece together what's going on based on conversations and context.
The game handles similar to Bastion as well, in a sense, though the mechanics are pretty much entirely new (and very creative). The ability system and upgrade system is a breath of fresh air.
Looking forward to seeing what this studio puts out next.

Full disclosure: I got the game for free from the developers, as I am a fellow SF-based developer. I don't think that clouds my judgement, but you can decide for yourself.
The combat is innovative and fun. It starts kind of slow, but once you start getting more and more functions and playing around with the various combinations, it becomes really satisfying. I enjoyed putting together new combos, both in upgrades and in execution order, to deal with the various enemy types. I also liked that the game takes away functions when you die once - this forced me to come up with even more new combos, which was still satisfying! I wanted to share my combos with my friends, such as my stun-cluster-dash. So cool.
My only gripe with the combat is some of the enemies rely on being super-fast to get at you. This can get pretty annoying, especially when you don't have the dash function available. So, keep that dash handy.
I enjoyed the story and atmosphere quite a bit, but I can understand that many would find it pretty vague and unsatisfying. It's never quite clear why things start out the way they did, and I guess some would be bothered by that. Whatever - I enjoy David Lynch movies, so I'm totally AOK with stories that are more about tone than concrete plot. And the tone is quite amazing in this game. The art, music, and dialog establish a juicy sci-fi-noir vibe that is a pleasure to indulge in.
Overall, it starts out a bit slow, but it hooked me soon enough. And I can't wait to play it again in Recursion mode. I beat it once in under 4 hours, so it's a bit on the short side, but for $20 I think that's reasonable. Again, I didn't pay for the game myself, so I can't honestly say how I feel about its length. But I can say that the game doesn't drag itself out, which is important to me as a consumer.

This game looks like it could have been made in the 90's, and that is in no way a bad thing. All the artwork in the game looks like it was hand drawn and the developers use the minimalist static character design in a great and often fantastically funny way. The gaming world seems so focused on graphics nowadays they forget that graphics simply accentuate a game design, they do not make a game great. A great game touches a gamer's emotions and draws them into the world the designer has created. This game will absolutely suck you in and make you chuckle, chortle, guffaw, cackle, snicker, and maybe even regret (there can be some surprisingly dark consequences to your actions in such a light-hearted game.)
So how to describe the game.. I'll start off by saying you will spend most of your time in this game reading. If you don't enjoy reading in your games then I suggest you move on right now. If you do enjoy reading then I highly suggest this zany space opera-esque adventure in which you are a Dark Scavenger! Your spaceship is out of fuel and it is up to you, the courageous Dark Scavenger who will use Your Mother as a meatbag to absorb about a million archer arrows meant for you, in order to save the day! This game plays like an epic game of MadLibs, but instead of just picking random adverbs and adjectives to make a story you will pick from your selection of Weapons, Tools, and Allies to deal with events that pop up, often resulting in laugh out loud situations. How do you get those weapons, tools, and allies you may ask? Well the game is broken into chapters. At the beginning of each chapter you will start with some sort of event in which you choose from a few dialogue choices. After an event ends there is a strong chance you will get some sort of weird object generously called "loot". After the event ends you'll be looking at a map of scenery in which you can point and click on various objects on the map. Clicking on those objects can often trigger events and lead to more loot, so scan that map closely! After you have found everything on that map there will be arrows you click on to lead you along to the next part of the map. After you click the arrow, if you found any loot, you will briefly be whisked away back to your three space alien buddies who happen to be excellent crafters. Lucky you. You will then turn your "loot" over to one of the three crafters and they will offer some sort of funny explanation to what weapon, tool, or ally they will create for you. Now that you have your real loot, what do you do with it? Well when you happen upon an event you are usually given several options of how you wish to deal with it, and are almost always given an option to use a weapon, tool, or ally to help you out. In each chapter of the game you only have X amount of uses of any given weapon, tool, or ally, so choose wisely (I found myself choosing by how funny I thought the result would read!) You do regain the uses in the next chapter though, so don't be afraid of using what you need to use. You'll work your way around the map from room to room in such a manner, gaining loot and power until you reach the end of the chapter where you'll face a boss.
I've had such a blast playing through this game, and there is a New Game + mode so you can go back through the game and hand the loot over to different crafters than you did the first time so there is good replayability. Highly suggested for anyone who would enjoy reading about a wacky sci-fi adventure in which you create funny situations based on your actions in your epic quest for fuel and salvation from an ominous universal being. Worth every penny and I wish there were more adventures like this.

I'm going to keep this VERY short.
For people who want to play a game that reminds you of Ragnarok, is worth it? Yes.
For others who haven't had a chance to play Ragnarok? Probably
Many reviews right now are based on rage alone, which is really sad to see. Here is quick list of Pro's and Con's
Personal Pros:
-Class/Leveling system is well built, promotes diversity.
-Crafting and upgrading seems easy to me.
-Costumes are nice, even though some you have to pay for.
-Grinding is fun, and optional in some situations. ( Grinding for item mats for craft that one hair costume item )
-Devs are active, they came on the chat to reassure players that they work on the game for us.
-Combat is nice and different.
-Controls for me, are perfect. I tried keyboard which felt somewhat smooth, and using my PS4 controller is really nice.
-Graphics are old school, but still look pleasant.
-Some of the more upbeat dungeon music is meh, but most of the music is actually nice to listen to.
-Community is good, no one talks like an elitist. At least, not yet.
Personal Cons:
-At launch, servers were unstable. Sometimes still are, but it'd be foolish not to play based on launch problems.
-The Token, to me is probably the game's biggest flaw. It is the premium subscription membership, and unfortunately blocks a lot of things, like trading, for example.
-Some items are pay to win, it's small but it's there. I personally don't mind, but others will, I did notice that most cash shop items are VERY cheap in comparison to ( as an example ) Maple Story.
-Grinding, even though I like it, others won't. That's why it is both in Pros and Cons.
-Item Diversity, the game is new so it's not that big of a deal, but item diversity is a bit meh.
-Stats, some stats are not explained thoroughly, so some info gathering is needed. This can be countered by reading the ToS Reddit often and making friends who ahve more experience, there's guides too, but the game is missing explanations.
Those are my biggest PERSONAL Pros and Cons.
I've seen so many people give a bad review simply because they reached meta and plowed through content. They played 200 hours of a *free* game, only to *finish* it or get really far ahead and give it a bad review.
Also, server stability on launch week should not make you avoid a game or give it a bad review. If the game is still unstable 2-3 weeks after the full launch, sure it might deserve it, until then....
My 2 cents!

This game is a lot of fun. Most of the other people already posted the PRO and CONS, so I'll just give my opinion. Yes, it has a few problems. Lag issue was mostly solved for me, so far I'm not having any issues. Gold Sellers stopped spamming shout since they tweaked a few things. One thing you need to understand is that we can't trade silver in game, so there's no silver selling. Gold sellers are there for scams. Bots can be a problem, but they'll have to be very creative to bypass the restrictions and ruin the economy (Edit: I can see now that this was very optimistic of me. They'll still need to hunt bots aggressively, and I hope they do.)
Looking at the market restrictions I understand why they did it. If you played Ragnarok Online (and albeit a different game, ToS is similar in many aspects) you'd know that game was infested with bots. They grew so large the staff couldn't contain them. They ruined every aspect of the economy, so much you thought "since everyone is doing it, I might as well do it." The trading and market system in ToS probably has that in mind, and that's why, even though I won't say it's a good thing, it is a design choice that could end up working with some effort. As for tokens, they're as low as 350k right now, maybe they'll drop even more. I hope they will allow some simple form of trading, but I can say that not playing this game only because of that would be your loss.
Tl;DR: Game is a lot of fun, the most fun I had in years in a MMO. And I played most of them. It has flaws, it has grind, but so far it has been worth it. Just play and enjoy. If you're waiting for f2p, that's okay, there'll probably be issues again but you will still have a good time.

In a growing trend of games that set you as a worker in a highly unglamorous and monotonous job role, Papers Please places you as the winner of the labour lottery who has been assigned to tend the new border check office in made up country East Grestin. Your job is to monitor the paper work and make sure only the right people cross the border. While doing this you’ll have to juggle your family life and make sure you meet your daily quota.
The mixture of family and work sets up an uneasy moral compass which may see you denying access to the neediest people who lack the correct paper work. Every time someone slips through the net you are warned and fined and do this too much and you won’t be able to pay for food, rent and medicine for your family. Neglect them for too long and they will die. Fall into dept and the game ends with you being dragged off by officials.
The game has a grim and grey graphical style which perfectly fits the tone of a suspicious and paranoid eastern bloc country. Each morning you walk to work and enter your basic kiosk. A line of silhouetted figures stretches out of the kiosk as far as the eye can see in a never ending parade of people waiting to get across the border. Clicking on the loud speaker summons each person with a depressing sound and they trudge in to see you.
Each day there are new rules and regulations to adhere to. It starts fairly simply with citizens just needing a passport and soon ends up with all manner of paper work ranging from work visas to tickets and diplomatic passes. Each document needs to be checked for details such as dates, gender and validity and cross referenced. This all takes time and you still have that quota to meet each day.
During your checking people will offer you bribes or other incentives to let them through and it’s here that much of the story of game develops. Many things remain untold and you are left to think what happened to the wife you didn’t let pass or the urgent medicine that didn’t have the right documentation.
It won’t be long before body scanners are introduced to check for weapons and contraband and the occasional terrorist attack will also occur. This normally results in the day ending early and even less pay for you to take home to your family.
It’s fair to say that it does take some time for the magic of Papers Please to shine through. The idea of doing a repetitive and monotonous job for hours on end in your spare time may not appeal but it’s the dark and twisted humour that creeps its way into the game that will keep you hooked. It’s also amazing to see how quickly you begin to turn cold to the needs of others in order to save your own skin.
You may start out feeling guilty for turning people away but we found ourselves soon putting up an emotionless wall and quickly denying access to everyone without the correct paperwork. As if to illustrate the point your actions directly have there is a newspaper published at the start of each day which may contain the consequences of your decisions as stories.
Overall, Papers Please is an original and unique take on a kind of point and click adventure. It illustrates how seemingly small decisions can have wide reaching consequences and also acts as a social study on the player and what they are willing to do to make sure things stay in their own interest. It won’t be for everyone but it certainly should be tried by as many people as possible as there is some subtle and really quite clever writing and programming at work here. Once you get the paper stamping bug it’s hard to quit and you’ll always think you can press on further with your next go.
Overall 8/10

Call of Juarez: Gunslinger presents us with the tall tale of Silas Greaves, renowned bounty hunter, unreliable narrator and a man with a score to settle.
The story, seemingly sprung right out of a dime novel, is related to us through the medium of a videogame strongly resembling a graphic novel. This theme is not only apparent in the cutscenes in between chapters, but has clearly influenced the fundamental graphic design of the game itself.
Here, you’ll get to meet and go toe to toe with such legends of the Old West as Billy the Kid, Pat Garret, old man Clanton, Johnny Ringo, John Wesley Hardin, the Daltons, Jesse James, and Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid.
The story – like so many Western stories – is one of revenge and/or redemption. Despite the familiar paths we find ourselves on, the story is quite compelling and strangely profound - I say “strangely” because it works on several different levels. Silas Greaves is more than a superficial gun-toting cowboy, and the story he relates to us, while embellished, is strangely introspective – almost pensive at times.
Thankfully, despite being rather tragic in nature, the story doesn’t take itself too seriously. There’s plenty of humor involved, which makes for a fine balance. The tone is set by the numerous tongue-in-cheek shout-outs to popular culture, the most prominent of which would be the homage to dime novels and the Westerns of yore, of course. Some of these are obvious – think of the mission titles, for example – but others are much more subtle – such as the music in a certain graveyard, or the name of a particular steamboat.
The story takes place across fourteen missions. These are largely linear in nature, but nowhere does it feel very constricting. The environments are beautifully sculpted and not seldom awe-inspiringly beautiful. Same goes for the way the guns have been modeled.
Gameplay is very fun. Even though you only have a limited choice of weapons at your disposal – Ranger, Quick-Shooter, Six-Shooter, and then Shotguns and Rifles and their sawed-off versions, and finally dynamite; they handle quite differently from one another. The game is never boring.
I’m a bit less enamoured with the duel mechanic. It’s somewhat of a challenge, I suppose, and as a way of representing the classic “showdown” it works; but I can’t help but feel it’s a bit too clunky and unwieldy at times.
Apart from the main story, you’ll also find “arcade” and “duel” modes. In the arcade mode, you’re set to go through several of the decors you’ve visited in the story and rack up as high a score as you can manage. In the “duel” mode, you’ll find yourself pitted against your opponents from the story, having to vanquish them consecutively.
There is no multiplayer, but personally I consider that to be a good thing. This game was developed specifically with a single-player experience in mind, and it shows. It’s a thoroughly enjoyable experience.
In the end, this game really is a diamond in the rough. It’s relatively short – the story will take you six to ten hours to play through once, though with the “arcade” and “duel” modes and replayability of the story you’ll likely last a fair bit longer – but that doesn’t really matter. You just keep coming back for more. This game offers the right mix between fun gameplay on the one hand and a compelling story presented in an original fashion, that doesn’t end up taking itself too seriously, on the other.
If you’re into Westerns and/or graphic novels, don’t miss this one. It’s great fun and definitely recommendable. The atmosphere is fantastic. It’s like one of those great Western movies of yesteryear: no matter how many times you’ve viewed them before, you just keep coming back for more.

A great little piece of gaming narrative, a fun and slick corridor shooter, and an absolutely gorgeous piece of visual flair. Gunslinger is an outstanding game (with an outstanding but simple soundtrack, too). If you like first person shooters, and/or the idea of a well told, clever and often humorous wild-west yarn? Pick up Gunslinger. Well worth your time. The Duels are a bit frustrating, but they're perfectly doable and there aren't too many of them.
The gunplay itself is very much in the arcade shooting-gallery style, but encounters are pretty well designed within that space; it's off rails enough that your approach to some of the levels will have a substantial impact on your experience though in yet other levels the only thing separating it from a light-gun arcade game is that you control the character's movement.
That made clear, the game excels in it's genre, is the most visually innovative game I've played in ages, and knows how to tell a story.

In Alien: Isolation, you are in the shoes of Amanda Ripley, a young engineer on a quest to learn more about her mother in a decommissionned space station... which rapidly turns into a game of cat and mouse between you (the mouse) and various lethal dangers. This is probably one of the best survival horror games released in the last few years.
First of all, the setting is incredible, Creative Assembly went the extra mile in recreating the retrofuturistic look of the first two Alien movies when they meticulously crafted Sevastopol station. Every little maintenance panel covered with blinking buttons and every piece of dated yet advanced technology will remind you of the original films. The soundtrack is very much inspired by the film scores, and all the noises, from the creaking bulkheads of the station to the hiss of the alien, will quickly immerse you in an uneasy atmosphere. If you're a fan, you will be absolutely delighted by this fact alone. The director of the soon-to-be-released Alien 5 movie (Neil Blomkamp) actually referenced this game in an interview, saying the artists blew his mind and made him reconsider what he wants his movie to look like.
The gameplay is also a work of art. Where some survival horror games remove weapons from you to make you feel powerless and heighten stress (SOMA, Amnesia, etc.), this one actually gives you a small arsenal of more or less effective guns and melee weapons to use. You might think this trivializes content, and sometimes it does, but there are some threats you will definitely not be able to eliminate through force. Namely, a ruthless alien which will constantly hunt you throughout the game. Where it can end your life swiftly, you are very much limited in what you can do to fight back. Fire will keep it at bay for a short time, flashbangs will stun it, smoke grenades will disorient it, noise will distract it... but you will never be able to kill it.
Another place where Alien: Isolation innovates is the actual AI of the Alien. On higher difficulties, it is hard to predict, and really knows how to keep you on your toes. You will have to adapt your strategies throughout the game as it becomes more aggressive.
The technical aspect is really good as well; textures are high resolution and lighting effects are top notch. The modeling of the enemies is great and the performance is outstanding.
Some drawbacks that professionnal reviewers might point out include the amount of backtracking and the pacing of the game. To me, these were really minor issues, if at all. The backtracking is always justified, and helped make me feel like I was really stuck on this nightmarish station, making my way through the maze of corridors to survive. Besides, the game does a good job of letting you discover new areas in old zones thanks to a set of tools that allow you to progressively open more doors as you upgrade them. As for the pacing, I welcomed sections where the Alien took a backseat. Typically, it was in these parts of the game that I took more time to take in my surroundings, listen to audio tapes, read the information on the public terminals... and there are other dangers than just the Alien in this game.
Overall, Alien: Isolation deserves its place among the greats of the survival horror genre. Creative Assembly did an outstanding job and I can only hope for a sequel to this game.

I had to write this review after the credits rolled. There's no way in hell I could just turn off my PC and go to bed, keeping silent about how extremely satisfied I was by this experience.
This game deserves all of its praise, and more. This was the best horror game I've played since Dead Space, and that game stressed me out so much..I didn't think I could get anymore stressed out by a game. But oh man, I was wrong. I grew up watching the original Alien movie, of course..A huge fan of it. If there's anything I know by heart, it's Star Wars, Alien, Batman, and Zelda. I can't believe just how amazing the atmosphere of this game is. Not only am I actually in the movie Alien, but I have some new toys to play around with..Toys that still retain that certain industrial aesthetic as the movies. So you never really feel like the noisemaker, bolt gun, or door jack are out of place.
This game does incredible fan service and it does it without poking you on the shoulder constantly and whispering "PSSST. Hey, this is Alien.", like we all know some games do.. I could rave about this game forever, and still feel like I haven't given it enough credit. Bu do you know what my most favorite thing about this game is? What made me absolutely fall inlove, and want to keep playing, no matter how much a ♥♥♥♥♥ harde mode is? The atmosphere. This game does atmosphere right. I'm so used to just barging into rooms with an M4A1 pulse rifle in one hand, and an American flag in the other, as I blast away aliens with just enough time to shout random unoriginal things like "DEY SHOULDA WORN LAYERS."
But this game? You're reminded of just how scary a single xenomorph can be. Your weapons aren't going to do anything but♥♥♥♥♥♥it off. You're an average joe..Well, maybe a little more than average, considering Amanda Ripley is a total bad♥♥♥♥♥in this game. You'll be listening for its thuds in the distance, the loud footsteps behind you, the growling ontop of you, as it slinks down from the ceiling.
Oh, and then there are other humans, and maybe a few androids..Meh. Whatever. This game's not about them. Let's get back to the alien. I hate to get technical. Quite frankly, it brings me out of the immersion. But the reason why it's so terrifying is because the AI of the alien is incredible. This thing's completely unpredictable, and it has a mind of its own. This thing doesn't leave you alone on hard(Which is the recommended way to play. And thanks to From Software for not holding my hand). I'd try hiding in vents, only to look behind me and see its big bulbous head. I'd try to distract it with a noisemaker in the room, and then walk out into the hallway, only to turn the corner, and see it walking in my direction. This just isn't scripted, and it makes the game all the more incredible.

I wasn't expecting much from this game based on the Mixed reviews. Nevertheless, a few of us bought it and I rented us a private server just to get to grips with the game. I immediately claimed Kingship and put the taxes on 20% before cutting off my friend's peasant leg with my newly acquired sword of the king.
After a short time butchering every animal we could see (It takes a long time to whip a stag to death), we began crafting some more advanced items. Another friend joined and we built a huge wall to block off the King's castle from peasants. Once we were done I captured one of my friends and hung him in the gallows. For some reason he came back.
Next up was a small competition. Who could fit the most sharp rocks in their orifice slot. The peasants managed 2 or 3 each, but the great king's orifice managed to fit in 5 with plenty of room to spare. The peasants were slaughtered as a reward...
We then moved all of our equipment behind our newly built wall for security and my friends logged off, so I killed them in their sleep before building a trebuchet and knocking down the wall we built.
Overall, the game is brilliant and for such an early Alpha it's more stable than a lot of other Early Access survival games out there.

Reign of Kings is a pretty enjoyable game. I've spent most of my time just playing with friends and doing all sorts of silly things.However, due to it being early-access, there are some blatant problems that come with it.
The most notorious of these problems are hackers. They're everywhere in this game. Avoid official servers at all costs if you want a significantly lower chance of dealing with them.
Another issue is crashing. This game tends to crash a lot for no particular reason. Sometimes your hud will break and you'll crash. Most of the time when you hit "log out" from a server, you'll just crash. When you can't even properly leave a game without crashing, you know your game has problems.
Lag is also a rather large issue. My friends have much better computers than I do and complain about lag as well, so it's not just me. Walking around the world can cause some major lag. Sometimes things wont even render until you stand there for a few minutes. This makes PVP extremely difficult. It usually depends on the server on how much lag you'll get. The official servers seem to be the worst.
There are also a lot of strange miscellaneous issues I've encountered such as falling through walls and not being able to pick up certain items, but nothing too game breaking.
Overall, Reign of Kings is not a bad game by any means. It just needs a lot of work that I hope the developers are willing to put into it. After their last game, I can only hope that they stay commited to this game.

In 2007, CoD:MW (Call of Duty: Modern Warfare) was released into a community that has a seemingly insatiable lust for more shooter action. They weren't just given another shooter, they were given a game that really pushed the genre considerably. Amazing single player campaign and adrenaline-pumped, fast-paced multiplayer action with perks and weapon sets set the new standard on how these FPS's are done. It left it's mark on gaming as a whole, so a sequel was inevitable and gamers couldn't wait. In fact - according to an eye-witness who works at my local Game Stop - MW2 "...became the best-selling game in history before it was even released", all being pre-orders (of course, #1 sellers are subject to change). Imagine their dissapointment when they got this...
Plot 1/10
..was so convoluted, I can't tell you what it was. Everybody wants everybody dead except the protagonists, and the only solution is...killing everybody. It's a movie written by Michael Bay. That's all I have to say about the plot without spoiling it. If you don't care (which you shouldn't), highlight this big, black box.
The ending also plays out like every other cutscene in the game: "Good job, now let's carry you off and tell you who the kill nex-" CREDITS; THAR'LL BE A SEEQUEL!
Graphics/Sound 8/10
I'll put these in the same category because I don't have much to say about them. MW2's sound and visuals are everything we expect from the series: excellent. The guns, the dust, the lighting, character models are all beautiful, and guns, tanks, explosions all sound great, too; so why an 8/10? Attentive gamers will notice that a majority of this game's voice cast is from Mass Effect. In fact, several things were just "taken" from Mass Effect. For one thing, your CO's voice is the voice of Captain Anderson, and the voice of the general is the voice of Admiral Hackett. Oh, and the general's name? Sheperd.
There's nothing wrong with being inspired, but I call this a lazy, rip off. Infinity Ward wasn't even trying. Maybe I'm just being picky, but this really rubbed me wrong despite Keith David's long career as voice actor for military-esque media.
Gameplay 5/10
Finally, gamers are starting to see the light with the release of CoD:Ghosts. It's the same. Darn. Game. Same rail-shooter scenes, same set pieces, same "set bomb and run away" scene, same door breaching scene, same, same, same. We've been playing the same game since the original Call of Duty in 2003 and before that with the Medal of Honor series. It's been 11 years of the same game. It's time for CoD to die. You run forward, you kill the next thing that moves, and steadily march to the credit roll. Everything about it is so banal; boring to the point of painful. The graphics and sounds aren't enough to mask the bad gameplay and story. A pretty package doesn't make the bad contents good. You've played CoD before. Enough said.
Multiplayer also went downhill with unbalanced weapons and killstreak abilities that broke the game entirely. When you get 3 kills in one life, you get a UAV that reveals all enemies on the radar. However, these streak rewards stacked with one another, so you use the UAV to get a few more kills, and get a chopper. The chopper automatically gets you 5 more kills giving you an AC-130 gunship. Use THAT for a few more kills, you get a nuke that ends the game instantly. Sounds pretty ambitious on pen and paper, but in game it means: first to a 3 kill streak WINS. Hackers also had their way with the game and Infinity Ward/Treyarch/Activision or all three refused to do anything about it. I've heard rumors that the same hacks that worked on MW2 also worked on MW3 and Black Ops. Watching this trend, I believe it.
If you want an example of customer service done RIGHT, let's ask Valve. Some time ago, Steam was glitching up and improperly banning players from accessing MW2. Gabe Newell wrote a personal apology to these gamers, and offered them a free copy of Left 4 Dead 2 (L4D2). While that was generous and very polite, that might have been a bad idea for the poor people that play L4D2, because all the teenage @***holes from this game are now trolling the L4D2 community (as if that game wasn't bad enough.)
The Verdict
Visually, there's little to complain about. MW2 is very realistic by sight and by sound. Some of the settings are creepy with ash blotting out the sun and smoke rising from decimated vehicles and climbing corpses to escape combat. The whole world is going crazy, but they couldn't make the player care less. Traversing the beautiful world is an uphill hike to the credits. Yearly releases also means the community will be widely divided and chopped thinner and thinner with each release, so there's no point in trying to play MP. MW2 is big pass. Maybe get it for 5 bucks and beat it once. Final score: 3/10 Almost no reason to buy it.

Transistor - the followup game to Supergiant's Bastion - does exactly what it's pedecessor does. Delivering a polished top down action-RPG with a narrative driven storyline. The game has a pronounced "interactive storybook" feeling resulting from the games total linearity but to be fair the book is pretty damn good.
Logan Cunningham's narration of Bastion was one of the most prominent features of Bastion and in Transistor he fulfills much the same role. Being your ever present companion he lends the game a magical yet melancholy feel. He exposes you to the concept of the world, the story and the characters without overexplaining anything and leaving you to fill in the blanks.
The combat is no slouch either. 16 different moves can be combined or used as passive improvements and tested in the many encounters scattered throughout the storyline. How about firing a blast that scatters into bombs which scatter into more bombs when they explode...and then scatter into even more bombs afterwards - yeah.
The music is really awesome as well and supplements the feel of the whole game perfectly. I'm just in love with the song "The Spine".
A highly imaginitive game, an adult fairy tale, emotionally and intellectually stimulating - the full package. A really enjoyable experience. It just leaves me wondering what Supergiant Games' next storybook is going to be like.
