There is very little to complain about when talking about Supergiant's Transistor, it is what I consider to be a very worthy successor to their previous game Bastion, and Transistor on it's own is a brilliant game that I imagine will be a strong contender for my GOTY 2014, much like Bastion was in 2012.
Transistor's gameplay is very interesting, and it works, although there are a few UI elements that could have been somewhat better to make the game just that little bit smoother, such as improving the ability slotting menu. When the player, or "user" as the game refers to you, gets into combat, a small area is cordoned off from the rest of the world, and then enemies and obstacles begin to spawn in, thus beginning the battle sequence. Transistor has two types of combat, and both have their pros and cons for their use, but both are viable means of combat, especially when used in tandem. The first type is the traditional real-time combat that you are used to in most games, where (most of) your 1-4 hotkey skills do not have a cooldown so you can mash the keys to your heart's content, but you are open to attack. The second type is something called "Turn Mode", this mode, often showed off in trailers, stops time and allows you to queue up a set of skills that will be activated in super speed once you exit this mode, often giving most enemies no time to react or move out of the way, but once you activate this mode, almost all of your abilities are put on cooldown, making you a vulnerable target. One other cool aspect of Transistor is the ability to customise your loadouts to suit how you play. Each skill has a basic function when placed in an active slot, and these active slots make up your action bar of 1-4 abilities, once you run out of health, however, one of your 4 equipped skills becomes unusable, until you find another customisation area. These active skills can then be customised with other skills in upgrade slots, improving the effects of that specific skill, allowing it to drastically change the way that active ability functions in combat. One last slot is the passive slot, this allows you to equip a skill and gain a passive ability that can improve the way you fight without using up an ability slot. All this has to be done in the constraints of your "memory", a points system that restricts the player from equipping each and every ability into a slot.
The story for Transistor is really cool, but very vague to begin with. The basic premise of this story is that you play a famous singer known to the player and other characters as Red, but Red's voice has been taken away. You find yourself equipped with a sword containing the personality of a person, and you are fighting against The Process, a mechanical force that is wiping out the city of Cloudbank as well as it's inhabitants. Aside from main plot points, the story is also given to the player through approachable vistas or terminals that offer extra exposition as to what the city was and what is going on now. The story in itself was somewhat predictable, and the last 30 minutes or so were fairly tedious, but it does pay off, and I was satisfied with how it ended. The game itself to around 5-6 hours to playthrough, but there is a new game+ mode for those who want to go through the game again with all unlocked abilities and level up some more.
Graphically, Transistor is just remarkable. The entire game looks like a painting, and it looks gorgeous. Almost every area was just beautiful to look at in one way or another, be it the streets, or the towers, the game was just a visual treat. The only downside to the aesthetics of the game is contained in a minor spoiler that follows, but otherwise, the art department at Supergiant struck gold a second time, and that is just a wonder.
SPOILERS FOLLOW
The audio of Transistor is just fantastic, once again, all praise to Darren Korb and the great vocals of Ashley Barrett as Red. The reason I say this is because as I write this review, I am listening to Transistor's OST, and finding a soundtrack this good is a rare treat. Also, you cant really go without mentioning Logan Cunningham who is the narrator inside of the sword, and he does a wonderful job as well this time around. As opposed to when he played Rucks in Bastion who sounded like he was telling a story, in Transistor the voice is coming in real-time as he talks to Red. The other difference in terms of narration is that as opposed to Bastion, where the narrator was talking about almost everything that the Kid did, in Transistor he only seems to interact with the environment as much as Red did, as well as giving audible hints as to when your Turn mode's cooldown has finished, which was very useful.
During my time playing the game, I did encounter one single bug, but this but was a game breaking one, this bug caused the game to outright crash when the Help passive triggered near the last zone of the game, and caused the game to crash when I fired it's ability. This bug I expect to have been patched by now, however.
Transistor is a brilliant game, and one that is well worth the purchase, regardless of whether or not you enjoyed Bastion. It is honestly one of the best games that I have played in a long while, and I wish Supergiant the best of successes with Transistor.

Full disclosure: I got the game for free from the developers, as I am a fellow SF-based developer. I don't think that clouds my judgement, but you can decide for yourself.
The combat is innovative and fun. It starts kind of slow, but once you start getting more and more functions and playing around with the various combinations, it becomes really satisfying. I enjoyed putting together new combos, both in upgrades and in execution order, to deal with the various enemy types. I also liked that the game takes away functions when you die once - this forced me to come up with even more new combos, which was still satisfying! I wanted to share my combos with my friends, such as my stun-cluster-dash. So cool.
My only gripe with the combat is some of the enemies rely on being super-fast to get at you. This can get pretty annoying, especially when you don't have the dash function available. So, keep that dash handy.
I enjoyed the story and atmosphere quite a bit, but I can understand that many would find it pretty vague and unsatisfying. It's never quite clear why things start out the way they did, and I guess some would be bothered by that. Whatever - I enjoy David Lynch movies, so I'm totally AOK with stories that are more about tone than concrete plot. And the tone is quite amazing in this game. The art, music, and dialog establish a juicy sci-fi-noir vibe that is a pleasure to indulge in.
Overall, it starts out a bit slow, but it hooked me soon enough. And I can't wait to play it again in Recursion mode. I beat it once in under 4 hours, so it's a bit on the short side, but for $20 I think that's reasonable. Again, I didn't pay for the game myself, so I can't honestly say how I feel about its length. But I can say that the game doesn't drag itself out, which is important to me as a consumer.

Look, I will start out by saying this game has flaws.
It has been well over a year since its release, and Rome 2 has some flaws that never got adequately addressed. The AI still sucks, and there are some mechanics that just don't make sense.
Does that mean I don't enjoy it? Not at all. I actually really like playing this game. It's fun, engaging, and long. It gives me options for development, and mostly just lets me feel like a world conquering badass. Pretend to be Julius Caesar, if he lived 400 years and conquered everything in Europe, North Africa, and the middle east (which he basically did). Be Carthage, and burn Rome to the ground. Play as some country noone has ever heard of and bring everyone else to their knees with your awesomeness.
No, it won't always be challenging. There will be times when you feel like it't too easy to win battles, because you crawled too far ahead of everyone else. But then you watch some elephants waltz through a group of archers who are screaming bloody murder for their lives, chuckle, and keep playing.
I do like this game quite a bit. 8/10, will keep playing for many more hours.

Dark souls, oh my dear Dark Souls. How little i initially cared about you. As a hardcore PC gamer im disgusted by the very idea of even holding onto a controller, let alone actually play a game with one. Even after that the horrible PC port actually turned me off Dark Souls 1 completely. But the idea of the Souls games always intrigued me. I was one of the few people who actually enjoyed some of those "I wanna be the guy" Games. In my mind they were challenging, but they were a lot about recollection and planning ahead.
But alas, i didn't play the original Dark Souls. And after the huge disappointment that was Lords of the ♥♥♥♥ers i was kind of turned away from everything Souls-like for a decent amount of time.
But then i noticed Dark Souls 2 was on sale.
Now if you're like me you're always worried whenever you buy a game off of a sale. Cause you never really know what the hell you're getting into. But my fear was increased tenfold when i was booting up Dark Souls 2 for the first time, because i had of course experienced the nightmare that had been Dark Souls on PC. So imagine my very happy self when once i had watched the opening cutscene and got to walk around it happened without a hitch. I was able to walk briskly around like the happiest little puppy in the daycare.
That was when i was greeted by the intro.
Look From Software, i know you haven't got to stretch your cutscene muscles in Demon's souls and Dark souls, but could you maybe not have a cutscene last about 5-10 minutes only for us to make a character and have the cutscene go on for 2 more minutes?
after that i set out into the world, and quickly met my first enemy. An undead warrior wearing what looked to be leather armor. I had of course prior to playing Dark Souls 2, seen a lets play of Dark souls 1. So i knew dodging was an essential part of its combat.
Now, after i had slain my assailant i briskly moved onwards through the tunnels of Things Betwixt, fighting off more undead soldiers as i went along until i came to a hole in the road. I went into my controls to find out what the jump button was, and saw it was bound to F. So i ran forward and immediately fell down because i didn't know how to jump properly.
I then respawned and found to my dismay that my previously handsome knight had somehow caught the Plague, and had therefore turned a very disgusting shade of green. I then also saw that my max health had gone down.
Now, this is a mechanic i don't really like. Cause a lot of the bosses and the areas leading up to them are very much dependent on trying a lot of times to get the hang of their movement and attack patterns. This becomes harder when you're actively punished for your death in a manner that can stick with you for a while.
But that doesn't deter from the awesome combat system though! Every single little bit of Dark Souls seems to be built around the combat. Every single boss is combat focused, when you explore the inevitable thing thats going to be in the way of your progress is enemies that you almost always have to fight, And all of your stat building and upgrades are inevitably going to be focused on fighting enemies. It is very good then, that the combat system is ♥♥♥♥ing awesome. It has this real weight to it that encourages timing and precision. It rewards patience and punished rash decisions. A lot of times the mentality of "Just one more hit," can either land you a close victory or a humiliating defeat.
The exploration is also nice. With plenty of hidden areas to find if you're willing to stray off the beat and path.
All in all this game is great, and while i dont condone the practice of making an HD remaster of it this soon (This being the upcoming redux version From Software are planning) This game is still amazing. Buy it if you can't wait, get the hd remaster once it comes out in the other case.

Don't let this game's modest price tag fool you, what's offered here for $5 most games don't deliver at double that price. Dark Scavenger is a choose-your-own-adventure JRPG in which the choices you make will directly impact your experience, often making the game either easier or harder and sometimes downright impossible.
Items you find while scavenging can be crafted into 1 of 3 types of gadgets (weapons, items, allies) which usually provide something of value although rarely you'll end up with a bricked gadget which is by all accounts useless. Much of the game's humor is achieved by offering the absurd or unexpected along with the occasional one liner which is tailored to the scene as are most of the dialogs in the game, you won't find any copy pasta here.
Dark Scavenger is all about the choices you make; every battle, every room, and every dialog has the potential to alter your journey forever.

The "no" is for the base price. $5 could buy you a lot better. Its too much for the kind of game Dark Scavenger is. Even getting the game on sale at $2.50 feels a bit like a gyp.  Dark Scavenger, and I know I'm going to get crapped on for saying this, feels and looks a lot like a flash game you could play for free on newgrounds. Hell, you could watch a playthrough start to finish on youtube and not lose much of the experience of actually playing it. There's not much to it.
First: some people keep insisting Dark Scavenger is part jRPG. This is untrue. The closest the game gets to being a traditional jRPG is having menu driven combat and that's it. There's very little RPG about Dark Scavenger. It is almost entirely a choose your own adventure point and click game.
Dark Scavenger is a real one-note game. Its very search about the screen for things to click on, an event triggers, fight maybe, "scavenge" an item, and craft it into equipment to use in events/fights. That's really all it is. Lather, rinse, repeat.There's no real challenge. There are only bad guesses at what to do during an event. The battles themselves are similar in that while you may choose the best weapon or item to use against enemies, luck usually plays role in how effective they are if they work at all.
The sole thing Dark Scavenger has going for it is the writing. What the game lacks in depth, it makes up for with screwy odd-ball over the top writing and art direction which is usually amusing and adds a great deal of charm. Sadly, that's really the only thing Dark Scavenger has that's any good. That's what most of the positive reviews are raving about.

*Summary on bottom*
-THE GOOD:
Smite overall is a very fun game and pretty balanced. It offers great teamwork mechanics along with solid gameplay features that just overall really make the game experience great. If you are someone that likes to be the hero and try to solo everything, this game probably won't be for you and can honestly go from casual to toxic real quick (emphasis on being a team player here). The item build system is simple and straight forward. So long as a good team build is there, and players know the item equip system a win is always possible.
-THE BAD:
Sometimes characters can play outside their intended class (see damage Cabrakan here as a gold example). Rebalancing to the gods that need the rebalancing typically don't really get acknowledged. When you have assassins that can't do damage because they have to run a nearly max defense build, you lose team damage output real quick putting you at a disadvantage. Again to reiterate a win is always possible despite this so it isn't necessarily game breaking per say, it's just more annoying that you have a tank meant to receive damage, 2 shotting all mages and assassins, then 3-4 shotting warriors.
-THE UGLY:
*If you are from console like me* - I moved from console to PC with this game. You cannot tansfer your account over. So all my no lifed diamond god skins, all my time played on console is rendered pretty useless which is really unfortunate because I don't think many people would be willing to regrind again (hence why I have so few hours on here). Despite that, I can still happily recommend this game to new players or to those moving from console, that are comfortable with going through the grind again.

Ahh Smite, one of my favourite games ever! I've played this game since the Beta and it has never stopped being fun for me. Smite brings a refreshing change to the MOBA scene, it is truly unique.
First of all it's strengths. Smite is an action packed MOBA thanks to the third person view which lets you do things other MOBA's cant. Third person view encourages numerous mechanics and tactics such as; Ganks from behind when the enemy won't suspect you, harder to aim skillshots which make the game more competitive, and many others. When I play Smite I feel much closer to the fights and objectives than other MOBA's which use the top down view, which feel more like strategy games to me. Don't get me wrong Smite involves a lot of strategy but it is more than just that.
Another great strength that has kept me coming back are the playable characters, or gods and monsters in Smite's case. These gods are taken from real world religions and mythology and have unique personalities. Hi-Rez makes each god unique and you can truly tell the difference between them, not just at the mechanical level but at the artwork and personal level. Some things that really stand out are the specific taunts some gods have to other gods or monsters that are inspired from ancient lore. This is what Smite has up on other MOBA's. But, it is not without it's flaws.
Smite also has many game modes, 1v1 (Duel), 3v3 (Joust), 4v4 (Siege), and 5v5 (Conquest) and (Arena). All these, with the exception of Duel -which shares the Joust map- have their own maps. Everyday their is a different game mode of the day, which is one of these maps with special rules like reduced cooldowns and infinite mana or 5v5 with all the same god for example. This  allows players to have a variety of options to play which makes it more fun than just one game mode all the time.
Smite has some flaws which could be deterring to anyone looking to play. Some people have a lot against the ranked system but since I don't play ranked I cannot say much for this. All I know is the TP which is the points you earn to rank up, is very confusing. Now balance. If you play online games you are no stranger to overpowered items and characters but Hi-Rez does this a lot. It seems every time a new god comes out it is super strong and if you play ranked you are forced to ban it every game. This usually goes on for about a week then the god is either nerfed until its bad or it is fixed. This happens with items too. Entire seasons of smite have been defined by a few items, such as the season 2 "tank meta" where tank items were crazy strong so the same build was used for 2 different roles at least, every game.
On a more technical level, there are some flaws. Smite is run 32 bit Directx 9, which has been outdated for quite a while. This can cause crashes, in fact I usually get a crash once a day if I play for a couple hours. Performance is also hindered by this, Smite does not take a lot to run, but it could take less if the engine was updated.
TLDR: Very fun game with a few flaws that won't ruin gameplay
Pros:-Action packed third person view
-Characters have cool personalities
-Variety of game modes
Cons:-Ranked System is messy
-Balance issues
-Technical issues
Despite these flaws I highly recommend Smite because of the action packed third person, loveable characters, and the variety of game modes. Thank you for reading!!

As you kill your foes a Concentration bar (Bullit Time) starts to fill up. Overall a very solid FPS with authentic Wild West weapons including a range of Pistols, Shotguns, Rifles & Dynamite.

It does not deliver half as much as fun as a GTA V will, and it was released at the same price. Pro: it runs very smoothly on a mid-end rig, while on the same machine, GTA V will suffer from regular stuttering. And JC3 is very appealing to the eye, too.
As a conclusion, go for it at mid-price or less, but it might not be worth 60 bucks or euros, even though the developers have put a lot of effort in it. It's too repetitive and poor in real content to be satisfying in the long run.

I jumped into this game about 3 weeks ago and have leveled one character to 15 so take this review with that in mind. Is it worth your money. Yes. These things are actually good qualities to many as the questing doesn't hold your hand and the npc scaling means you never run out of enemies to fight. So make your own call. Much love.

I am a post-Tamriel One player, and you can probably see from my playing hours I have spent perhaps way too much time on this game! While I have written a lot of areas for improvement, I would recommend it for a 3 month heavy gaming stint.
Basically the good and the bad
Good:
-ESO allows players a high level of freedom in design of characters (though not nearly as many as some d20 systems). There are so many different builds I would like to try.
-The Community is generally relatively positive and helpful to new players.
-Aesthetically appealing world (not nearly as lovely as the Witcher 3, way better than WoW or Glyph)
-Well thought out quests (better than WoW anyhow)
-Very few serious bugs
-Decent world lore (Delivered in the form of terribly written soporific texts or entertaining PCs)
Mixed Feelings
--ESO Plus Subscription was supposed to come with DLC on a quarterly basis.  I don’t think it has.  It was worth it for me as I am new player, so I received access to DLCs released from the last few years (Orsinium, Thieves Guild, Dark brotherhood, Imperial City).  I haven’t sees a release this past quarter anyhow.
Bad:
-While Tamriel One lets you play the zones and quests of each faction the quests are very much the same here for each group. Some, but very little new quest content.
-there is little sense of accomplishment in levelling up.  All zones are accessible to all players as the game scales to your level ….  Levelling in this sense can seem irrelevant.  But you do get new skills, but no additional firepower behind those skills.  This is a Tamriel One “feature”.  An alternative would be to set up a server or instances where there is no such scaling based on a player’s choice of scaled or not.
-You cannot fully enjoy the game unless you have an ESO Plus subscription. Without a crafting bag that gives you a lot of NECESSARY inventory space, you will be forced to be a choosey looter (Not easy when going through a high paced dungeon with a random group of people), purchase merchant follower (with real money), or give up crafting.  This problem is likely compounded with Homestead that has added a lot of housing items that many people won’t be using.  That means more trips to town to sell them off instead of time adventuring… unless you are a picky looter. It appears that ESO purposely creates inventory problems for the user to force them into a ESO Plus purchase situation: Monster Trophies, Undropable token items, housing, crafting.  The last thing I want to think about when playing a game is inventory management.  Makes it feel too much like work.  At the very least they should provide players with extra inventory to accommodate the homestead associated drops. I have purchased a merchant, a banker and an ESO crafting bag (Via ESO Plus) with real money and still get annoyed.
-Allow inventory to be sorted additionally by sets.
-You need a fairly organized group of 12 players to get the best gear in the game… not good if you don’t want to or have loads of time to invest in game.
-Asia is laggy, and there seems to be no plans for an Asia server.
-GMs either do not exist or do not get involved to spice up the world (I haven’t seen any in my 3 months of play anyhow)

Alien Isolation really captures what made the original Alien film interesting. The Alien is fairly competent, though honestly I would say he's not as scary as I was hoping and is easily gamed. The scenery and retro sci-fi tech is beautiful and sets up a unique visual theme that isn't explored too often in video games. The music and sound effects are excellent, and reminiscent of the original film. Generally it was enjoyable, but I found it got repetitive pretty fast and I started getting annoyed by the setbacks, more fearful of losing my save than I was of the Alien which breaks immersion more than you'd expect.
Pros:
-Beautiful Graphics
-Amazing Music & Sound Effects
-Solid controls and interesting gameplay
-Fearsome enemy
Cons:
-Too many androids and humans
-Alien is too easily scared off and tricked
-Level design gets a little boring, especially near the end
-Characters are okay, but could've been better
On the subject of the save system, I like the idea of having to work for your checkpoint and not being able to save just anywhere since it makes a game way easier. But at the same time the way it was implemented made me more fearful of losing progress and less fearful of the xeno itself.
8/10 = Pretty, but has its flaws. If you like Alien or any of its subsequent films, at least as much as I did, then you will enjoy this game.

This game nails the atmosphere of the Alien universe, which compliments the survival horror genre perfectly. It is evident that the developers placed authenticity before profit by not compromising horror tension and difficulty. The game is simply not easy, but if you are a fan of games like Amnesia: The Dark Descent then you will feel right at home. You are given tools to survive encounter to encounter, but not to run and gun.
With that said, you may find the save system to be extremely frustrating, having to replay stressful segments frequently. There is a great deal of trial, error, and randomization with the Alien AI. If you do not remember to make use of the crafting system and use the tools at your disposal you will find yourself stuck at times with the Alien hugging your proximity. Ultimately, staying stationary will not help you in the long run.
Finally, there is a degree of backtracking, but keep in mind you're on a space ship. The maps provide enough freedom of movement while maintaining a sense of claustrophobia and impending doom.

This is not a review. It would be idiotic to give a game that, as of Alpha 10, lies somewhere between proof-of-concept and pre-alpha, a firm yes or no. if you're considering buying this game because, like me, you watched some entertaining youtube videos (Look up TheDevilDogGamer if you haven't already) and want to join the fun, forget it. The game is buggy, infested with hackers, and has far less depth than you think. I have played for hours and lost every character I've created to server malfunctions before I could get them dressed in leather and build them simple homes. Most servers suffer from awful desync. And that's all fine - I understand the early access program. I didn't pay for a product, I payed to spectate its development. and here are a few of the observations that are making me regret my purchase.
The Game of Thrones medievel political vibe that we all crave - the palace coups, wars, rivalries, and insurrections -  are not possible without a moumental renovation of the game's mechanics and networking. You can claim territory for your clan, but you can't secede. You can't refuse to pay the King's taxes. (Incidentally, that's all the 'king' can do: levy taxes.) But the greatest obstacle is the server structure. The average population is capped at around fourty people, but even if this was raised to 140 or 240 anarchy would be inevitable. There is nothing stopping a guild from reducing a rival's base to rubble with trebuchets while they are asleep or at work. Beyond somehow raising server populations to the thousands or turning the game into an MMO like Eve Online, I don't see a solution to this problem.
I'll restate what I began by saying: the game is still very early in development and much will undountedly be added and changed in a years time, but what little I know about the company doesn't encourage me.
In addition The developers are widely suspected of being incompetant amateurs or simply early-access scammers due to a prior catastrophe which you can learn about with some quick googling. The netcode is not worthy of a first year CS undergrad. For example, weapon values are set client-side, so if you want that driftwood club you spawned with to hit ten times as hard as the King's broadsword you're free to do so.
I suspect this will turn out to be a Rust clone with a medieval skin, but you can never be sure with Early Access. Hold on to your money for now

Wow! What a game! Thrusting you right into the action, Transistor begins with Red and her companion the Transistor; a hybrid magical and technological omnipotent sword. With the Transistor by your side and acting as the narrator, you make your may through CloudBank, a futuristic utopia where everyone has a voice, whether that be what the weather will be, to what food your favorite restaurant will serve that day. But underneath it all something is brewing, and it is up to you to unstir the great storyline that this game has to offer.
The game contains very engaging combat that can either be done on the fly, or via a tactical planning phase where the user is allowed a certain amount of actions per turn. Each mode has their own strengths and weaknesses, but while the planning mode may leave you vulerable for a few seconds after you have had your turn to act, it definitely seems to be better in almost all cases over the on the fly version.
Although the combat in this game is great, Supergiant Games once again proves that they are king when it comes to art direction. The music in the game is a masterpiece, constantly setting the mood of the game as you progress throughout the many streets of CloudBank. This combined with the stellar hand drawn backgrounds and beautiful 2.5D art style makes it pure audio and visual bliss.
Though some may disagree that Supergiant Games have not created a game as good as Bastion, I wholeheartedly disagree. Transistor is something different. Something that cannot be compared to Bastion, and something special that must be experienced by everyone. Get this game, you will NOT regret it.

Interesting combat system, excellent visuals, flaky-bordering-on-tumblr-tier story and dialogue. The build system and Turn-based combat had me hooked from the start, even if the actual difficulty seems to severely underestimate the average player's skill. The difficulty scales extremely slowly, and I daresay a lot of players won't find it challenging before their second playthrough with all 10 limiters active. Even then the skill combinations are poorly planned, making certain combinations extremely OP and others complete duds. Towards the end you will likely find yourself using the same couple of skills as actives and passives, as dps overrules every other conceivable tactic.
Transistor is a gorgeous piece of framework, unfortunately executed without the necessary passion and skill required to create a full-bodied story and a solid gameplay system.
The concept the story builds upon is quite attractive, but Red never receives enough characterization to evoke character immersion or empathy. The narrative is minimalistic; too much so for such a short game. Red's actions are dramatic throughout, escpecially for a city-planner-gone-superstar backdrop, and the player is never truly given the chance to understand and relate. Unfortunate, as the impact of the ending heavily relies on the player's empathy with the main character(s).
The length of the game is disappointing; I spent around 8-10 hours playing the game very slowly to explore as much as possible -most of my recorded time is AFK, to have the music in the background while studying. This brings me to the soundtrack. Darren Korb returns to prove his talent as a composer, unfortunately accompanied by very lackluster vocals. Red, whose voice is supposed to be uniquely extraordinary, sounds like your average youtube starlet or Disney pop star; Not hard on the ears but neither memorable nor suitable for the role or music.
In comparison to Bastion, Transistor is the younger sibling trying to imitate the succesful firstborn but falling short of ambition and expectation. If given more time and love, Transistor could've outshined Bastion, but unfortunately both appear to have been in limited supply.
In conclusion, Transistor is a beautiful, strichtly casual game which I would recommend to those looking for a short adventure. The game would presumably be better received by those with little or no expectations inspired by the wake of Bastion. [5/10]

If you've never played Demon's or Dark Souls then I would say everything below this is irrelevant. Even for those of you who have, the game is still good, especially by the standards we as consumers allow to be set so low for games and their developers nowadays... However for fans of the series who appreciated it on a deeper level than just "It's fun" or "It's hard, but I enjoy a challenge," you may want to read what I have to say, below.
All in all Dark Souls II is a mediocre and ultimately disappointing successor to Dark Souls, no more; no less.
I could go into detail about all of the poor design decisions, the lies and disgusting business practices of FromSoft as well as Bandai Namco, but frankly I don't consider it worth my time.
Before a PC version of this game was available I purchased the collector's edition for Xbox 360.
Within weeks I had put hundreds of hours into the game, completed a handful or two of playthroughs, attempted about 3 dozen times to beat the game without dying or resting at a bonfire in the same playthrough, while still killing all the enemies in my path and PvPed more than I probably did any of those previous things.
Within that same time I beat my first playthrough and felt cheated. Every playthrough afterwards during that left me with the same feeling, as well. It's very common for Developers to exaggerate their games. especially lately, but it's still a bad thing. Maybe had the game not had different directors, had smarter design decisions and help up with all of it's promises, it would be the masterpiece it could have been.
However, that's far from the case and I walk away from the game feeling that it is by far the worst installment in an otherwise phenomenal series.
By the bar some other popular games set, I would say this is a fantastic game and damn near a masterpiece, comparatively.
By the bar me and my expectations for this game as a sequel set, I would say simply out of my overwhelming love for the series that this game is a stain on the franchise.
If Dark Souls is a 9/10, which is about what I consider it, then Dark Souls II would be about a 4/10, in my opinion.

I'm writing this review from the perspective of someone who's played and loved Demon's Souls and Dark Souls 1, so I may be overly critical. After all, that is one hell of a lineage to live up to, so it's hard to be fair. Regardless, here goes:
This game has a lot of flaws that it's predecessors did not have that are difficult to justify. I'll just list them for easy consumption:
1. Enemy Hitboxes: This seems unredeemably broken to me. Many foes will have their animation straight up miss your character, but the game registers that as a hit. This really sucks in a game series where precision and placement have traditionally been very important. Basically you don't ever really know how to defend against certain enemies because there are no visual cues to do so. A wide swing can still take off a chunk of health; a foot stomp that misses you completely will end your adventure right there. This isn't hard in the sense that it's challenging; it's hard in that it's frustrating and feels broken.
2. Enemy Placement: The series has it's share of sneakily-placed opponents, but this game seems to take it to a twisted new level. I don't mind this too much, although it definitely feels cheap that another group of enemies dropped down behind me in a tight corridor for the fiftieth time. Something about this feels very lazy. Instead of the occasional ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥-from-behind trick, this game seemingly elies on placing enemies behind you at the most unpredictable times to enhance difficulty. It's tiresome.
3. Level Design: Damn near every area I've been to so far has a ton of instant-death drops. This is certainly something the series is known for (walking through Blightown required very careful footwork, for example), but those games used this to accentuate difficult areas. In this game, they exist as a matter of course. They are just always there, and instead of serving as an effective means of elevating the tension in select areas, they merely frustrate and impede mobility. It's sort of like a movie about explosions: Explosions are exciting in the climax of a movie, but they get dull quick. Admittedly, I haven't seen the whole game yet, but this is definitely an honest critique of the first few areas.
4. Punishment For Doing Bad: This game punishes the player for failing. When you die, you lose a portion of your max health permanently. This is a twist on the half-health mechanic in the previous games, but whereas those games were apparently balanced around having half-health, this game assumes you will have full health most of the time. And this is simply not true. You will die a lot in this game, and each time you lose a chunk of max health. Eventually you will be stuck at half-health, and you will die even quicker now because most areas are balanced in a way to do a certain amount of damage to a character.
I don't like this mechanic one. Dieing in these games has always been punished fairly severely, and I don't see the need to invent further ways to punish deaths (especially when a lot of them are due to the trial-and-error aspect of traversing cruelly-designed levels). The fact that enemies don't respawn means that one death to many can permanently gimp your character, which would theoretically make it impossible to advance. Both of these new mechanics are terrible additions to the series.
5. Dueling/Swordplay Aspect: This is the most damning miss, in my opinion. The swordplay/whatevery-play just doesn't feel right to me. It's tough to pin down why, because many things have been tweaked slightly and they all change the way the game plays. But they got something wrong, because deuling against monsters is much less fun this time around. It seems like enemies have a much larger pool of stamina than my character, and they seem to stagger me much more often than previous installments. Getting stunned by a axe-blow to the shield is certainly realistic, but it isn't much fun when your character is stuck in the recovery animation for a full second each time that happens.
Careful swordplay is definitely important in this game, but a straight melee build feels very underpowered to me. Some of this is down to the broken hitboxes, and some of it is down to the subtle changes to the basic game mechanics.
I love the Souls series, and I will continue to play this latest entry. But as I go, I can't help but feel like my time would be better spent replaying Demon's Souls again. This is pretty much a big, frustrating letdown.

I started playing this game with the expectation that it would be pretty ridiculous. My expectations were fulfilled, and I still had a lot of fun.
If you like casual, comedic turn-based RPGs that remind you of those choose-your-own-adventure books (decision trees), then you will probably really enjoy this game.
The aesthetics are good - the artstyle is definitely not the best, however, it is stll nice and works well with the overall feel and atmosphere of the game. The music and sounds are decent.
The story is okay, nothing too crazy. Your 3 teammates are available to talk to between missions, each with different personalities. My favorite is the alien who has no mouth, and communicates solely with exaggerated gestures.
The controls are simple - you just need to click your mouse to select options in battle. The beginning of the game puts you in a quick, informative tutorial battle. The learning curve is minimal, and you are not really punished for dying because you can restart at different points and will even have your potion (refills over time) at refilled if you decide to retry your last battle.
During battle, you can use different weapons (durability dicatates how many times you can use it), items, and/or allies to help you succeed. You can also use your fists to attack, which will not reduce any durability from your equipment. Next to your health, a potion that refills over time puts you back to full health can be used.
After you win a battle, your enemies will drop loot. Then, you can choose to explore the area you are in before moving on to a new one. When you explore, many times you will come across an event and have to make decisions - potentially resulting in loss/gain of health, avoiding/not avoiding a battle, or trading/using an item to get a different one (doing this reduces your chosen equipment's durability by 1). I have noticed that when you move on to a new mission all of your items will be restocked and refilled.
When you are done looting and exploring, you can choose to move to any applicable area (left, right, up, or down). After you select an arrow, you will be presented with your ship's room, where you can use your loot and give it to one of 3 crewmembers. This is probably one of the best parts of the game.
Each Dark Scavenger specializes in different things (weapons, items, allies), and they can only be used once per room visit, meaning that you can't simply use all your loot to keep making weapons (if you have more than 1 loot per room visit).
The funniest thing here is that the information your teammates will give you is based on their personality, so you have to decide who to use based on their responses, rather than knowing exactly what will be made. For example, if you have a broken sword loot item and hover over each teammate, they will tell you what they think they can make with it, but the rest is up to your interpreation - since the ally crafter has no mouth, he will use gestures to try to show what he can make with your loot (ex: he holds his arms out like a zombie = zombie ally | he nuzzles against you, making you uncomfortable = an ally that stuns groups).
While exploring, you may be presented with the opportunity to use different things from your inventory (this is almost always the better option than just "going for it"). For example, if you see a boiling pot of liquid, you can either try to scoop the liquid out with your bare hands (resulting in loss of health) or use a container item (ex: a potion or any other applicable item). The game does a good job of deciding what works and what doesn't, and this variety makes playing the game very, very surprising and fun.
If you like casual RPG play with comedic elements, give this game a try.

I would give it a positive recommendation if it was pay to play(monthly pay), but IMCGames decided it was a good idea to release this as a f2p game that features a pay to win premium shop. Prior to the release all we knew was that only cosmetics would be included in that shop.
But now you can buy a token that expires after 30 days. It's similiar to gold membership in other f2p titles such as Aion, which is why I don't recommend this game to f2p players. Without the token you are heavily restricted in terms of multiplayer, which MMOs are all about. Furthermore premium users receive 20% MORE EXP for killing stuff which is a huge advantage especially in a game that heavily favours grinding.
As for gameplay, you won't receive those nostalgic Ragnarok Online feelings. In terms of graphics, yes maybe, but not in terms of gameplay. This game is holding your hands throughout the game, guiding you through zones with linear quests. And after you've cleared all quests and exceeded its level, you'll never look back to that zone again, which is quite disappointing. To be honest I like the diversity in classes, but its annoying to go through the same quests and zones on every single character again.
So as for my conclusion, I can definitely say that if you want an open world MMORPG, you're better off playing the classic Ragnarok Online. As for class and build diversity, I can only recommend Path of Exile instead even though it's more of an online Action RPG than an MMORPG.

Tree of Savior is a fairly decent MMO, but somehow doesn't feel much different to me than Korean MMOs from 10 years ago, like Lineage 2. I don't hate it, but I have, already in fact, recommended to a friend to hold off on getting it. I think one day it COULD be really good, but I don't believe there are any defininig qualities of this game that would get me to recommend leaving a different MMO for this one.
The Bad:
-The biggest weakness to me has to be the story. It is translated fairly well, but even still it's very flat and bland, and unexciting. I'm almost level 50, and I honestly couldn't tell you anything about it....I know you are "The Revelator" or whatever, and you're trying to save everything. That's about where my lore knowledge ends. It was just so dry to me that I stopped caring after about 5 hours in.
-Secondly, as I mentioned above, the game feels very dated. When you come from a game like Elder Scrolls Online that has modern features, this just seems very lacking. You can't trade, crafting is laughable, and there is no other way to progress other than grinding and doing the mindless, monotonous quests. Hell, even Ultima Online handled this whole thing better. ToS makes you feel railroaded, and after 5 hour all of the monsters start looking the same, even the bosses.
-Lastly would be the fact that you can EASILY mess up your character, and most people will tell you it's just better to reroll to fix it. This is ridiculous. They give you NO guidance in-game, guides online are incomplete, and people still have conflicting ideas of what affects what. As a new player, I was terrified to put points into anything, and even after reading countless topics, I am still not sure if my guy will be useless later on. This is 2016, and I'm an adult with a life. I really don't want to put 50 hours into my guy just to find out I need to start over.
The Good:
-The graphics are really pretty.
-The community is friendlier than most MMOs

Alien Isolation really captures what made the original Alien film interesting. The Alien is fairly competent, though honestly I would say he's not as scary as I was hoping and is easily gamed. The scenery and retro sci-fi tech is beautiful and sets up a unique visual theme that isn't explored too often in video games. The music and sound effects are excellent, and reminiscent of the original film. Generally it was enjoyable, but I found it got repetitive pretty fast and I started getting annoyed by the setbacks, more fearful of losing my save than I was of the Alien which breaks immersion more than you'd expect.
Pros:
-Beautiful Graphics
-Amazing Music & Sound Effects
-Solid controls and interesting gameplay
-Fearsome enemy
Cons:
-Too many androids and humans
-Alien is too easily scared off and tricked
-Level design gets a little boring, especially near the end
-Characters are okay, but could've been better
On the subject of the save system, I like the idea of having to work for your checkpoint and not being able to save just anywhere since it makes a game way easier. But at the same time the way it was implemented made me more fearful of losing progress and less fearful of the xeno itself.
8/10 = Pretty, but has its flaws. If you like Alien or any of its subsequent films, at least as much as I did, then you will enjoy this game.

This game nails the atmosphere of the Alien universe, which compliments the survival horror genre perfectly. It is evident that the developers placed authenticity before profit by not compromising horror tension and difficulty. The game is simply not easy, but if you are a fan of games like Amnesia: The Dark Descent then you will feel right at home. You are given tools to survive encounter to encounter, but not to run and gun.
With that said, you may find the save system to be extremely frustrating, having to replay stressful segments frequently. There is a great deal of trial, error, and randomization with the Alien AI. If you do not remember to make use of the crafting system and use the tools at your disposal you will find yourself stuck at times with the Alien hugging your proximity. Ultimately, staying stationary will not help you in the long run.
Finally, there is a degree of backtracking, but keep in mind you're on a space ship. The maps provide enough freedom of movement while maintaining a sense of claustrophobia and impending doom.

Sevastopol station. Never before have I hated a place so much. And that is why this game is great.
The developers absolutely nailed the look and feel of the Alien universe. Some of the crafting and hacking mechanics were a bit lacking but didn't disrupt from the core experience - hiding from 'the Alien' and the many other horrors Sevastapol has on offer.
Not for everyone, but a truly unique, tension filled, and atmospheric experience.

I imagine Papers, Please was constructed around its main action of processing in-game paperwork at a border crossing. Papers, Please doesn't actually have any commentary to make. Validating the paperwork itself is the strongest part here, as you try to do your best in the timed work day. Indeed, more rules are added over time and it is up to each player to physically organize their desk and the placement of documents, but also to mentally process how to approach things. What is the best order (for you?) to check information? Is there enough time during a suspect's body search to do anything useful? The binary choices you make on a personal level are just interesting enough to entice replaying them. Yet, these choices have little payoff, which is true of Papers, Please overall.

Here is my opinion on ESO
Roses
- Massive world to explore.  I still haven't finished exploring the world
- More quests than you can shake a stick at.  Best part is a fair bit of them can be done multiple times.
- Updates and dlc that are actually worth buying
- Probably one of the bigger selling points,  the subscription is optional and no pay wall preventing you from enjoying the game
- The crown store (in game item shop) doesn't sell anything that would fall in to the catagory of "pay to win".  The most useful items in the store imo are the crown store exclusive mounts
-  Earning gold is easy at any level.  I'm 99% positive I made more gold as a level 13 character than I did at max level back in WoW during the days of Warlords
-  While I'm comparing ESO to WoW, dungeons are challenging.  Like Vanilla and BC WoW challenging. Tanks and healers need to be on their A-game here in ESO.
Thorns
-  Presently, there are only 4 classes to choose from, so if having class options is something you can't live without, your gonna be disapointed.  However, they are adding a new class in the new expansion that comes out in June.
-  The biggest thorn for ESO is probably how easy it is to binge play and thus you mighy get burnt out.  Fortunately these burn outs are short lived since new content and in-game events are so frequent that you'll always have something new to do.  For example, the new expansion (Morrowind) will not only add a new class (Warden) but a huge new set of land to explore.
-  The grind gets rough after level 10, but that's kind of the curse that all mmorpgs deal with
All in all, Elder Scrolls Online is by far the most refreshing MMO I've played in a long while.  It's definitely worth buying and it will never let you relapse to playing WoW ever again, that I can promise from personal experience.

I'm revising my review. Well, completely re-writing it, actually. After getting an hour or two into the game, I decided to restart it, using the knowledge I'd already acquired and the suggestion from the commenter below - much appreciated BlueRaja. I feel like an idiot for not realizing my beloved Jaunt, when used as an upgrade, allows that power to be used between planning turns. That has made a HUGE difference, though I do miss it as an active power.
Maybe it's just me, but my restarting the game seems to have made a lot of difference in how I play it and thus, how I enjoy it. I DO enjoy it now, and I'm making sure to take more time to really examine my powers and plan out how to use them best. That also makes a difference - I wasn't respecting just how much damage could be done when you take the time to properly plan out your turns.
I do still think that more could have been done from the outset to let Red defend herself more between turns, but what are you gonna do? It is what it is. I also agree with some other reviewers that more could have been done to break up what is, essentially, a corridor runner mixed with an action RPG and strategy game - corridor running  NEVER makes a game better.
Oh, and that stinking annoying stutter that would happen every few minutes, regardless of whether I was in a battle, in OFFLINE or ONLINE mode in Steam, has evidently been FIXED, thank goodness, at least on my rig.
All-in-all, I'm having a better time now. Do I recommend this game? Well . . . cautiously. I'd say it's an acquired taste, but given there's no other game quite like Transistor - and that's a good thing, mostly - the only way to acquire the taste is to throw down the money and be patient. So for the sake of appearances on Steam, yes, my review has been repolarized to "Yes, I recommend this game."

**This is a review in progress, and will be edited over time. I'm also a noob to the series and skipped the first game, so this is my first go at the series. I'm also basing my review on specific things that peaked my interest throughout my time with the game. More sections will be added and edited as I further my progression through the game. **
Overall Score: 9 out of 10
Story: The game opens with an interesting set of cutscenes which draws the player in right away. The story as a whole seems simple, but interesting enough to hold the attention of the player. It's good enough to peak my further interest into what becomes of my newly created hollow.
**UPDATE** 3/9/15 - I recently completed the story, and I was a bit disappointed by the way the game ended, but I felt as though there was still plenty of incentive to go into NG+ or even make another character.
Gameplay: You MUST use a controller to play the PC version of this game. I spent the first hour or so using my mouse and keyboard and man was it frustratingly hard. The game is very difficult, so prepare for "rinse and repeat repitition." You will die ALOT. The gameplay as a whole is very satisfying, and it feels good to kill an enemy. The game especially rewards you for beating bosses.
*Update* for Gameplay: Now that I have a better idea of how to play the game, the gameplay is highly addicting and very fun. It takes some getting used to, but once you get the hang of it, it is really fun!
Soundtrack: It is very good, and creates a very eerie atmosphere in the game. Because of the eeriness it adds to the amazing experience.
Graphics: The graphics aren't anything mind-blowing, but they help add on to the environment and the overall experience. I run the game on my 4 year old laptop, and it runs at a steady 40-60 fps. The game appears to be intended for consoles, but the PC version is a good port. This game is a gameplay over graphics game, yet it still retains a nice pretty atmosphere.
Noob Awareness: The developers of this game not once took in the idea of helping out players who are new to the game. No tutorial, no game tips (Although player tips are found everywhere), there's no babying involved in this game.
*UPDATE* for noob awareness: It turns out that in the starting area of the game, there is boards with the controls on them and other tips.

I finished the game in eight hours, but by no means am I done with the game. Well into new game plus, I'm still experimenting with the gameplay, finding new combos. Let me explain the gameplay first.
You unlock 16 skills throughout the game. These 16 skills can be used as 4 primary skills, 4 passive skills, and each primary skill can get up to two skills "supporting it" to alter or enhance the skill. Any skill obtained can be put in any of the slots, which allows for an endless array of customization. I'll try to sum up an example-- there's a dash skill. There's also a skill that pulls enemies to the user. So, I use that to support the dash skill. Enemies are now pulled to the location where I dash from. So, I summon a triggerable bomb before I dash. Enemies and the bomb are all drawn into the same location. I use another skill to detonate the bomb from a distance. Enemies drop.
There are many other combinations I haven't touched on, or even discovered. But there is a need to discover these kinds fo clever combos when the enemies get tougher-- and they do. Especially with optional limitiers enabled. These limiters increase damage enemies do, cause more to spawn, as well as a variety of other negative consequences. Never unfair, but always challenging. Think similar to those totems in Bastion.
As for the story-- it's really good. There's enough presented to you to have emotional affects on you, but there's a Dark Souls-esque deal with reading into the "lore" of the game presented through paragraphs of information given to you from abilities, limiters, and etc. It works whether or not you read up on it, but you won't understand the full thing unless you read, most likely. The voiceacting has no flaws that I can call out, every voice-actor is superb. Especially Royce and the narrator. (Which are really half of the game's voice actors, but still.)
The music? It's good. A little subtle most times, I only found myself openly digging the music during combat during an early bossfight, otherwise the music was relatively in the background. However, the more I use limiters that cause battles to become more hectic, the more I notice intense music. Still, it could've been more prominent.
Overall, it's an amazing game. Completely worth the price. Again, I finished the game in eight hours. But there's more to do in the new game plus mode. Enemy spawn locations and patterns are random, there's new elements to the story, and so on.
It's a great game overall, and I see myself putting much more time into it.

Ahh Smite, one of my favourite games ever! I've played this game since the Beta and it has never stopped being fun for me. Smite brings a refreshing change to the MOBA scene, it is truly unique.
First of all it's strengths. Smite is an action packed MOBA thanks to the third person view which lets you do things other MOBA's cant. Third person view encourages numerous mechanics and tactics such as; Ganks from behind when the enemy won't suspect you, harder to aim skillshots which make the game more competitive, and many others. When I play Smite I feel much closer to the fights and objectives than other MOBA's which use the top down view, which feel more like strategy games to me. Don't get me wrong Smite involves a lot of strategy but it is more than just that.
Another great strength that has kept me coming back are the playable characters, or gods and monsters in Smite's case. These gods are taken from real world religions and mythology and have unique personalities. Hi-Rez makes each god unique and you can truly tell the difference between them, not just at the mechanical level but at the artwork and personal level. Some things that really stand out are the specific taunts some gods have to other gods or monsters that are inspired from ancient lore. This is what Smite has up on other MOBA's. But, it is not without it's flaws.
Smite also has many game modes, 1v1 (Duel), 3v3 (Joust), 4v4 (Siege), and 5v5 (Conquest) and (Arena). All these, with the exception of Duel -which shares the Joust map- have their own maps. Everyday their is a different game mode of the day, which is one of these maps with special rules like reduced cooldowns and infinite mana or 5v5 with all the same god for example. This  allows players to have a variety of options to play which makes it more fun than just one game mode all the time.
Smite has some flaws which could be deterring to anyone looking to play. Some people have a lot against the ranked system but since I don't play ranked I cannot say much for this. All I know is the TP which is the points you earn to rank up, is very confusing. Now balance. If you play online games you are no stranger to overpowered items and characters but Hi-Rez does this a lot. It seems every time a new god comes out it is super strong and if you play ranked you are forced to ban it every game. This usually goes on for about a week then the god is either nerfed until its bad or it is fixed. This happens with items too. Entire seasons of smite have been defined by a few items, such as the season 2 "tank meta" where tank items were crazy strong so the same build was used for 2 different roles at least, every game.
On a more technical level, there are some flaws. Smite is run 32 bit Directx 9, which has been outdated for quite a while. This can cause crashes, in fact I usually get a crash once a day if I play for a couple hours. Performance is also hindered by this, Smite does not take a lot to run, but it could take less if the engine was updated.
TLDR: Very fun game with a few flaws that won't ruin gameplay
Pros:-Action packed third person view
-Characters have cool personalities
-Variety of game modes
Cons:-Ranked System is messy
-Balance issues
-Technical issues
Despite these flaws I highly recommend Smite because of the action packed third person, loveable characters, and the variety of game modes. Thank you for reading!!

I bought 'Dark Scavenger', not really expecting too much. I figured it'd be a good way to waste an hour or so, in between more weighty games. However, I was hugely surprised by how good this game actually is.
If you've ever played a 'Lone Wolf' or 'Fighting Fantasy' book, you'll be very familiar with the way the game is played - each "page" (location you visit, chosen by arrows) has an encounter (sometimes multiple) for you to take part in, whether it's a conversation, a fight, or an item to gain via a little puzzle. This harkens back to the early-mid 90s attempts to capture these style of gamebooks on PCs; Dark Scavenger manages to achieve this in a way I've never experienced before.
The game's story follows you, a "Dark Scavenger", a being that can siphon the energy out of planets, and a crew of misfits who find you floating in space. The characters are a wacky bunch, but are also very interesting in spite of their "zany" initial appearances. There are a lot of excellent conversations to be had within the game, and the "dark comedy" tagline it advertises is not a misnomer at all - I've found myself laughing a lot at the various scrapes and events happening to the protagonist.
Graphically, the game is simple yet aesthetically pleasing. There's barely any animation, aside from some flashes when weapons attack and so on. However, this really isn't necessary, as the game manages to get across everything it needs to with the little animation it provides. It still manages to provide exciting combat and fleshed out environments. Likewise, the music and sound effects of the game are apt also. Abandoned areas really feel abandoned due to the subtle sounds, and I defy you to dislike the jaunty battle music!
The battle system is very similar to classic JRPGs like Dragon Warrior or Final Fantasy. You fight alone, but have three options for each attack: 'Weapon' - direct attacks with weapons, 'Item' - use a variety of items with various effects, and 'Ally' - summon one of your many allies to help you out in the combat. Combine this with a huge amount of weapons, items, and allies, each with a limited number of uses, and you have a really varied and interesting battle system, yet one that is simplistic enough to be able to dive right into. Gaining new Weapons/Items/Allies is as simple as finding loot, each piece of which can be crafted into one of the three aforementioned categories. Therefore, you sometimes have to make very crucial decisions - is that one of a kind power-belt better turned into a mega-mace for attacking, an athletics-item, or a strong ally? You only have one, so which will it be?
The bottom line is that this is a very cheap game for what it brings. If you enjoyed the classic adventure/choose-your-own-adventure games from yesteryear, especially Lone-Wolf, then this is the game for you. I planned to play it for an hour or so while I waited for a movie to begin. I never saw that movie - I didn't see why on earth I'd stop playing this game!

To begin with, I was quite skeptical of whether the aliens would actually creep me out much. Best first person survival horror game I've played and I have played a bunch. The reason is because the game does a good job at letting you fight or flee your way to survival, which games like Outlast or Amnesia don't do. Your weapons include a melee weapon, revolver, shotgun, flamethrower (by far the most useful weapon in the game), and a bolt gun. However the ammo is very limited so you won't be able to blow away everything you see, it's only enough to get by certain parts of levels. Also the Alien can hear the noises and one hit kill you at close range so that is highly discouraged. You can also craft helpful tools like molotovs and smoke grenades by salvaging materials from objects and dead bodies. If you decide to flee from danger, you can hide in lockers, vents, underneath tables, etc. Whichever playstyle you choose, the atmosphere is constantly intense and terrifying because of how the Alien stalks you for much of the game. People complain alot about this game and point out many of its flaws, and yes, some of those flaws are evident.  But, none of these flaws ever detracted from my overall experience of the game.  In Papers Please, you play as a border control officer in a made up communist country known as Arstotzka.  Arstotzka has recently opened its walls to let people inside the country, as long as their papers are all authentic.  The game is basically a find the difference game that gets increasingly difficult as the game progresses as you need to check at more than only their passports, but many other documents.  While the gameplay can become somewhat tedious, it works well into the setting and tone of the story as a job like this in real life wouldn't be all that exciting.
Along with the gameplay, a story comes to surface as you continue through the game.  Without spoiling too much, it involves a terrorist organization.  The story, while not unique, is well paced and really makes you want to play until the end to see the ending, which is easier said than done since there are a total of 20 different endings in the game.  However, the best part of Papers Please comes in the form of multiple moral choices that you need to make throughout the campaign.  They could be as small as deciding whether to reunite a couple, despite missing documents to something as big as letting in  terrorist for some extra money.  This is the beauty of this game as you can't always be a nice guy and help ever person who comes to you with a sob story.  This also gives the game alot of replayablility as you can go back and see what the possible outcome may be if you make a different decision on that day.  Overall, Papers Please may not be a game for everyone, but it is a well made game that deserves some praise and for only $9.99, it is worth every cent.

If you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

I'm not usually one for medieval/fantasy MMORPGs, I prefer sci-fi and sim-gaming, which is why it's significant that I enjoy this game.
With a beautifully rendered environment of staggering scale, illuminated by a glorious lighting engine a little akin to Planetside 2, but with actual weather, this game is visually beautiful.  The variety of equipment is great, and scales enough to denote a player's progress, without wandering into ridiculousness as many MMORPGs seem to at higher levels.
The story is surprisingly deep and complex, with lore discoverable in-world in the form of books, scrolls, etc, a very nice touch that adds depth to the gameplay, and thrusts you into immersion, a frequently overlooked, and even avoided element this game thankfully embraces, pulling you into the world.  Indeed, many a night playing ESO, I've glanced away from the computer screen to the window to find that the sun had risen without my realizing.
The characters in the story are likeable and relatable.  Even characters that seem to have no bearing on the story or quests have their own names, and those you speak to have all different voices, of believable voice actors, and distinct personalities.  You find yourself connecting to them, even distraught should they die.  Interactions bear the unmistakable trademark style of Bethesda, which helps make them feel more personal.  You're not clicking a "Next" box in a mission popup, you're conversing them, with a variety of potential responses, and while each one feels like it could use more variety, considering the sheer staggering number of them, the variety they have is quite impressive.
Khajiit are lovely, and my personal favorite.  Anthropomorphic felines make any game better.  My only gripe is plantigrade legs and slightly creepy feet, but this can be overlooked, and the faces are very well rendered, and very extensively customizable in the character creator.  Aside from this, the only issue I have is some lack of customizability in game controller inputs, namely in stick layout, but it's not a big problem.  I switched to third person and use keyboard and mouse, and there's no problem, interactions still appear in first person.
All in all, this is fun and complex game, beautiful and immersive, perfect for an escape from reality.  As pay to buy, it has a relatively low cost, but still lacks the pay to win and pay to glow unpleasantness of full FtP games.  This is the only medieval/fantasy MMORPG I've really taken a serious interest in, and the only one that I find worth playing, having played several, a real masterpiece. If it can drag me off EvE and Star Citizen, it must be.

This is my first review.
It would be prudent to reccomend this game to people who can associate with online messaging and online friends. This game is a simple and free simulator of times when we involed ourselves with such things.
To anyone with memories of "friends" we once spoke with online who have now moved on; emily is away will awaken those emotions once more.
The game is short, maybe about 30 minutes to an hour to complete and consists of 5 chapters. You cannot type, but instead choose predermined options. Emily feels like a real person and the conversations help lead the story. She remembers some options that you choose which leads to different scenrios. The 5 chapters are the passing years of high school to the end of college. The game does a good of showing that time has passed and how much the relationship between you are Emily changes.

I'm revising my review. Well, completely re-writing it, actually. After getting an hour or two into the game, I decided to restart it, using the knowledge I'd already acquired and the suggestion from the commenter below - much appreciated BlueRaja. I feel like an idiot for not realizing my beloved Jaunt, when used as an upgrade, allows that power to be used between planning turns. That has made a HUGE difference, though I do miss it as an active power.
Maybe it's just me, but my restarting the game seems to have made a lot of difference in how I play it and thus, how I enjoy it. I DO enjoy it now, and I'm making sure to take more time to really examine my powers and plan out how to use them best. That also makes a difference - I wasn't respecting just how much damage could be done when you take the time to properly plan out your turns.
I do still think that more could have been done from the outset to let Red defend herself more between turns, but what are you gonna do? It is what it is. I also agree with some other reviewers that more could have been done to break up what is, essentially, a corridor runner mixed with an action RPG and strategy game - corridor running  NEVER makes a game better.
Oh, and that stinking annoying stutter that would happen every few minutes, regardless of whether I was in a battle, in OFFLINE or ONLINE mode in Steam, has evidently been FIXED, thank goodness, at least on my rig.
All-in-all, I'm having a better time now. Do I recommend this game? Well . . . cautiously. I'd say it's an acquired taste, but given there's no other game quite like Transistor - and that's a good thing, mostly - the only way to acquire the taste is to throw down the money and be patient. So for the sake of appearances on Steam, yes, my review has been repolarized to "Yes, I recommend this game."

I finished the game in eight hours, but by no means am I done with the game. Well into new game plus, I'm still experimenting with the gameplay, finding new combos. Let me explain the gameplay first.
You unlock 16 skills throughout the game. These 16 skills can be used as 4 primary skills, 4 passive skills, and each primary skill can get up to two skills "supporting it" to alter or enhance the skill. Any skill obtained can be put in any of the slots, which allows for an endless array of customization. I'll try to sum up an example-- there's a dash skill. There's also a skill that pulls enemies to the user. So, I use that to support the dash skill. Enemies are now pulled to the location where I dash from. So, I summon a triggerable bomb before I dash. Enemies and the bomb are all drawn into the same location. I use another skill to detonate the bomb from a distance. Enemies drop.
There are many other combinations I haven't touched on, or even discovered. But there is a need to discover these kinds fo clever combos when the enemies get tougher-- and they do. Especially with optional limitiers enabled. These limiters increase damage enemies do, cause more to spawn, as well as a variety of other negative consequences. Never unfair, but always challenging. Think similar to those totems in Bastion.
As for the story-- it's really good. There's enough presented to you to have emotional affects on you, but there's a Dark Souls-esque deal with reading into the "lore" of the game presented through paragraphs of information given to you from abilities, limiters, and etc. It works whether or not you read up on it, but you won't understand the full thing unless you read, most likely. The voiceacting has no flaws that I can call out, every voice-actor is superb. Especially Royce and the narrator. (Which are really half of the game's voice actors, but still.)
The music? It's good. A little subtle most times, I only found myself openly digging the music during combat during an early bossfight, otherwise the music was relatively in the background. However, the more I use limiters that cause battles to become more hectic, the more I notice intense music. Still, it could've been more prominent.
Overall, it's an amazing game. Completely worth the price. Again, I finished the game in eight hours. But there's more to do in the new game plus mode. Enemy spawn locations and patterns are random, there's new elements to the story, and so on.
It's a great game overall, and I see myself putting much more time into it.
