Approaching the game objectively as possible,
is a good turn-based RPG that feels as if it was designed to give you the meat-and-potatoes of its genre while forgoing a lot of the fluff turn-based RPGs are known for (grinding, turning in quests, messing around with level progression and so on). You basically run from room to room of each level, beating up enemies, clicking on environment objects, and navigating through chuckle-worthy dialogue, 'scavenging' interesting objects all the while. After each room, you will typically be brought back to your hub to make the scavenged pickings into either a weapon, item, or ally – this is the prize mechanic of the game, though it comes dangerously close to being a gimmick at times. Your crafting buddies give you no clear indication of what they'll make, and although there is certainly fun in this, you can't help but feel a bit cheated by this fairly unforgiving system when you realize that weapon you just made is practically useless.
Thing is, it's hard to take any of the game seriously: between the story, the crafting system, and the writing, it all just feels like the snack-size equivalent of a good time. You go through it and you enjoy it for what it is, but leave with an empty, half-satisfied feeling.

3 minute in-depth review of Dark Scavenger:
Spoiler-free story impressions: Overall story arc is not very intriguing, since most of its depth and detail only becomes apparent during the end screens of the game. The motivation for progression stems from the little side stories and the overall brilliant writting of snippets. If you like bizarre writing along the lines of The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy or anything by Monty Python, you'll love Dark Scavenger.
Graphics: Old-school vibe highly reminiscent of fantasy novel covers of the late 80s and early 90s. It does not look great, but it surely has character.
Sound: The weakest link of the game. The effects are highly repetitive and there is a lack of variety in music. The little there is, is good however.
Gameplay: Adventure point-and-click exploration mixed with classical turn-based RPG combat. The choices you make can influence whether you'll have to fight someone or you might have him/her on your side later on. Nontheless, the combat system gets repetitive later on, since once you figured out the weaknesses of the enemies, you'll stick to specific attack patterns that are most effective.
TL;DR: Dark Scavenger is a bizarre and genuinely funny game with a playtime of roughly 5 hours. Afterwards it also features a New Game Plus mode. Worth the asking price!

I. What. Oh god. My brain. This game. Where do I. What do I. I don't even.
Okay, get a grip. You've seen crazy before. You've read crazy before in books, calm down, this is fine, everything is fine, take the pills, breathe. Relax, relax. Okay, Dark Scavenger - Roleplaying game, mostly a point and click with turn based combat, though without levelling (that's handled with the loot you gain opening up progressively more and more powerful tools as the game progresses), where you play the part of "an human" who for some reason ended up in space, alone, with naught but a spacesuit on. At least, I hope you've a space suit on. You meet a creature called "Den", a big giant spacefaring blob, who beats you up and leaves you for dead.
When you come around you find yourself on a ship home to three alien scavengery sorts, who immediately promote you, you lucky soul, to general gopher, and person who's going to get beaten senseless. In exchange, they agree to convert any loot you find into items that will surely help you to help them keep their rickety little spaceship going. Cue the game proper beginning. You are told that the ship is nearly out of fuel but thankfully the planet nearby happens to have a fuel source, unfortunately, it's in the hands of the bandits. You've been told that you're off to get the fuel, in exchange for your continued passage on the ship, and the services of your three newfound friends.
Mechanically, you move from room to room, represented by static screens with highlighted "hot spots" which bring up text style choose your own adventure style dialogs, depending on what you pick you may end up in combat situations, or you may gain items, or gain life / lose life, or even end up dead. Such is the way of the game, the events are far, far off the insane end of the spectrum, and you'll quickly find that your arsenal will consist of things that shouldn't make sense, whilst fighting things that make no sense.
There is a story in the madness somehow, in so much as your arrival may well change events which are playing out on the planet you've just landed on, but given the madness inherent in what you're playing it's a bit hard to make out all the fine details when you end up creating "your mother" as an ally (no, not a joke, you can summon your mother as an ally, and she stuns all opponents if you're at low health). The best way to enjoy this game is to take it on it's own terms, almost as a Hitchhiker's guide with fighting thrown in, for the ridiculously low price point - it's a steal, and an easy sell in my book, for any RPG fan.
Just don't play this game on any psychoactive or hallucinogenic substances.

Dark scavenger has an unique blend of point and click adventure games with a lot of RPG elements. The visuals is "take it or leave it" but the real stregnth is in it's writing, and characters. Overall, if you are into unique and well written stories, strong characters, and don't care too much about polish dark scavenger is well worth the asking price. But if you are sensitive to presentation dark scavenger's debatable visual style might be a bit off putting.
Strengths:
- Great writing
- Likable characters, even the villains
- Genuine humor
- An interesting concept
Weaknesses:
- Debatable presentation quality
- A niche game, some will really like it, some will hate it

If you expect to be allowed to hunt, though, you are playing the wrong game.The players is being lured into the game much like a hunter would lure a mallard. Imitate familiar sounds, pretend that you're one of them. Just like theHunter pretends to be a Free2Play game, pretending to have a vast world for you to explore, a great many animals to hunt and plenty of tools do hunt with. In reality, your free 2 play account is heavily restricted. After being instructed on how to track and shoot a mule deer, evaluating the kill and rewarding you for it, the game sends you off on your merry journey through the map and laughs diabolically at the fact that you're not allowed to shoot at pretty much anything other than the most basic of prey (expect to shoot lots and lots of mule deer).
Shooting at other animals requires a hunting license, which costs real money and is only temporary. Shooting at certain smaller critters requires a different calibre gun, which also costs real money. Getting the appropriate lure or tracking tools to hunt said critters - you guessed it - costs real money.
To summarise: If you want to do anything remotely fun and interesting, you had better be prepared to spend money on it, because nothing comes free, right?
theHunter is a shining example of how Free2Play should
be done. Not only does it alienate people genuinely interested in the game by restricting their free access to little more than what used to barely qualify as a demo version, it also charges for things that should really be free, or at least cost ingame currency instead.
So, if you want to become a hunter you might as well go and buy yourself some real equipment and shoot up the nearest mole burrow in your neighbourhood - the experience is way more intense and in all likelyhood you might even save a few pennies.
Disclaimer: I have played two hours of theHunter prior to its release on Steam. Don't be fooled by the obligatory 5 minutes of playtime I needed on Steam in order to be allowed to write a review.

So, SMITE. This is a pretty fun MOBA. I have several friends who don't like games like League or DOTA, but love SMITE. Instead of top down, right click to move, this MOBA is third person and WASD to move. If you have MOBA expirence, this game is mostly skillshots. There are a few non-skillshot abilities, but not very many.
Let me start by saying, this game is VERY noob friendly. In league or dota you have to find guides to figure out what items to buy (sort of) or what skills to level, SMITE has default skill setups and item sets that you can automatically level up..
Now, the buisness model. While yes, all gods are 5500 favor (new ones are 11000) you can rent them for 1 day for 300 favor, and earn 300 pretty fast in a day. There are quests you can earn about 1000-2000 favor a week. Also, if you are a new player and refer a friend or two, you both will get boosters (multiplier of favor earned), lots of favor, and even gems (premium currency.) You can also get gems by daily login bonus (takes a week of logins) and you don't NEED to play that day. There are also events every few months where you can earn 200-300 gems (equal to about $6) and other events that give you free chests, skins and more.
There are quite a few gamemodes, I'll sum them up quickly. If you have no moba expirence, you might not understand what some of this is.:
Arena - Pure fighting. No towers or anything - my personal favorite.
Conquest - The main and most popular 5v5 mode (comparable to League's main mode)
Siege - 4v4 mode with a siege monster that spawns, and just walks down a lane to attack a tower.
Joust - 3v3 mode with one tower, and one pheonix.
Assault - 5v5 all random gods.
Duel - Ranked only. 1V1s with ranked into it.
MOTD - Mode of the Day, changes everyday. All kinds of things using current gamemodes and forcing you to play certain gods, or only level certain abilities.
Let's talk about chest, it is not a good idea to buy chests unless you have a lot of money to spend. Most people get the chest exclusives
So... matchmaking... Yeah... it's awful. Not really going to go into it, but you can surely find many many people complain about it by googling it.
Take a look at this really close game:
There are more where it's me on that bad or good team, this is one I screenshotted.
And, God balance. Recently, Hi-Rez has been listening to the community more on god balance, but sometimes buff/nerfs are seemingly random. Like all MOBA games, there are a few group of gods you just want to kill yourself when playing against.
Overall, I put my review on NEUTRAL 5/10. I love this game, believe me. However, the matchmaking and god balance makes me want to die. This game for me is like cocaine. It's bad for you (atleast for me, because the matchmaking is so bad) but very addicting.
TL;DR
Pros
-Fun
-Good time killer
-Generous: they give lots of free premium currency
-Lots of gamemodes (however, you probably won't like every single one)
Cons
-Matchmaking
-God Balance

In soviet Arstotzka, the game plays you!
Explaining the premise of this game really doesn't make you want to buy it: Who would really think that playing a game where you work at a Soviet nation's border station would be challenging, addictive as well as humorous and immersive? Add the fact that this game has the graphics of an early 90's game and it's surprising that anyone has even bought this game. It really is something I've never seen before, even the genre is somewhat hard to describe: It's a "real time puzzle" game combined with roleplaying elements.
The core gameplay consists of checking people's passports and ID's and other various documents before you make the decision of giving entry or turning people away. It is really challenging and fun. And by challenging I mean "makes you want to rip your hair out if you haven't lost it from the stress already", at least with the "no loading allowed" playstyle that I employ.
You have to process people as fast as you can, but making mistakes will also cost you, so you have to balance the speed and the precision. After every day of work, you get to spend your earned money by feeding your family, paying the rent and heating bill, and if things are going well, you can buy upgrades for your toll booth. But there's never enough money for everything after the beginning, unless you're some kind of border guard savant.
It starts off easy: Check if the customer has a passport, if it has expired, if it has been granted in an authorized town and if the person is identifiable from the picture. Foreigners you must turn back. Next day, foreigners are allowed. The next day foreigners and natives both have to have a different kind of extra document to pass and you have to cross-check the information with the passport as well as if the information checks out on it's own.  Before you know it, your desk is cluttered with all sorts of papers and you have to remember three faces of criminals that you can't let pass and a couple of names who you have to pass, while shooting people who try to do terrorist bombings at the border.
You find yourself screaming at the screen: "What?! No way was that entry pass a forgery, you've got to be kidding me! Where the hell is that document? Who was I supposed to let pass and why?!" Things will get desperate soon enough, and maybe you'll let a missing document slide if the customer has some "incentive" to let him/her pass. Oh, stop being so high and mighty, my son was very sick and I needed the money!
The roleplaying is intriguing as well. There are some really desperate people at the border trying to get you to bend the rules and you will be faced with the decision of either doing your job, or the right thing. Dereliction of your duties will first result in notices from your supervisors and then you will get fined, but you find yourself thinking: "She'll get murdered if I decline her Visa, and it's only a 5$ fine if I don't, so maybe I'll do it just this once." You can also team up with different political factions, which have real consequences. There are 20 different endings so the choices matter.
Papers, Please is proof that an excellent game doesn't need a marketable premise or top-notch graphics. On the contrary, it might allow the freedom of focusing on the gameplay aspects that truly make a game great. I know I haven't played this much yet, so this praise is to be taken with a grain of salt, but this might be one of the best games of 2013.

I'm not usually one for medieval/fantasy MMORPGs, I prefer sci-fi and sim-gaming, which is why it's significant that I enjoy this game.
With a beautifully rendered environment of staggering scale, illuminated by a glorious lighting engine a little akin to Planetside 2, but with actual weather, this game is visually beautiful.  The variety of equipment is great, and scales enough to denote a player's progress, without wandering into ridiculousness as many MMORPGs seem to at higher levels.
The story is surprisingly deep and complex, with lore discoverable in-world in the form of books, scrolls, etc, a very nice touch that adds depth to the gameplay, and thrusts you into immersion, a frequently overlooked, and even avoided element this game thankfully embraces, pulling you into the world.  Indeed, many a night playing ESO, I've glanced away from the computer screen to the window to find that the sun had risen without my realizing.
The characters in the story are likeable and relatable.  Even characters that seem to have no bearing on the story or quests have their own names, and those you speak to have all different voices, of believable voice actors, and distinct personalities.  You find yourself connecting to them, even distraught should they die.  Interactions bear the unmistakable trademark style of Bethesda, which helps make them feel more personal.  You're not clicking a "Next" box in a mission popup, you're conversing them, with a variety of potential responses, and while each one feels like it could use more variety, considering the sheer staggering number of them, the variety they have is quite impressive.
Khajiit are lovely, and my personal favorite.  Anthropomorphic felines make any game better.  My only gripe is plantigrade legs and slightly creepy feet, but this can be overlooked, and the faces are very well rendered, and very extensively customizable in the character creator.  Aside from this, the only issue I have is some lack of customizability in game controller inputs, namely in stick layout, but it's not a big problem.  I switched to third person and use keyboard and mouse, and there's no problem, interactions still appear in first person.
All in all, this is fun and complex game, beautiful and immersive, perfect for an escape from reality.  As pay to buy, it has a relatively low cost, but still lacks the pay to win and pay to glow unpleasantness of full FtP games.  This is the only medieval/fantasy MMORPG I've really taken a serious interest in, and the only one that I find worth playing, having played several, a real masterpiece. If it can drag me off EvE and Star Citizen, it must be.

Transistor is probably an afterthought to many gamers out there, but to anyone who has played Bastion, this game is a must buy. To those of you who do not know the majesty of Supergiant games, Bastion and Transistor both share epic qualities that seem to be missing from most games today.
In the simplest way to define Transistor: this is art, truly inspired art. I'm literally at a loss when it comes to reviewing this game. Supergiant manages to pull you into their story and make you feel like you are a part of it. Each character has some unique facet about them that can intrigue the player. Abilities are explained through some fabrication of a character's life. Everything has its mark in Transistor's world. The story is simply magnificent and a main driving point to the game.
As a player, your eyes are met with a glorious palette of colors uniquely blended across the canvas of the game world. Every building, every character, and even every enemy, meshes together in loving unison. Nothing seems out of place and it all looks beautiful. Also, without fail, Supergiant delivers another amazing soundtrack for their game -- to compliment the beautiful scenery and character design, the background music is just as eloquent and wonderous. And to add to the soundtrack even more, the in-game music can be interacted with with the main character. Have you no will to play the game,  the soundtrack alone is worth the price.
As short of a review as this may be, Supergiant did not disappoint -- not even in the slightest. I would highly recommend playing Transistor AND Bastion, if you haven't already. Thanks for your time.
*Disclaimer: This is an opinion, obviously. You do not need to agree :p

The Call of Juarez games and I don't always get along. The first couple games are riddled with flaws, frustrating as hell in certain points, and have some awful pacing at  others. In addition, the story, while good, sometimes dragged in spots.
Call of Juarez: Gunslinger, though, fixes every problem I had with the previous games and adds on layers of fun and innovative storytelling to create a tight and rewarding experience.
The mechanics themselves are as polished as any I've seen in any shooter, with headshots and bullet time ("Concentration") being the key words here. Racking up kills in creative and interesting ways fills your concentration bar, which allows you to slow down time and rack up further and further combos.
All this killing ties into a robust leveling system that has three different sections: Ranger, which is about rifles and long-range shooting; Trapper, whose skills are all about shotguns and dynamite; and the titular Gunslinger, which gives you the power to dual-wield pistols among other perks.
You can mix and match among the three paths, and by game's end should have a hefty majority; in each path there are two legendary weapons to be unlocked, which replace existing varieties and have added bonuses (in addition to being gold and looking awesome).
The levels themselves are well-designed and provide interesting ways of approaching each gunfight, from interactive environments to scattered cover to caches of ammunition and dynamite. They're beautiful, too, with bright colors lending themselves well to the game's cel-shaded art design. The only oddity as far as graphics go is that the game has a black outline around the screen, for no reason as far as I can tell other than artistic choice.
Every few stages there's a duel, which consists of you and one or two other people in a pitched battle to the death. The duel system of previous games was either janky or downright broken, depending on your luck, but here it's been vastly improved; you now have to focus your crosshair on an enemy while simultaneously moving your gun hand closer to your holster, but when your opponent goes to draw, you need only click your mouse to do the same, after which you time it right as your crosshair moves and put your unfortunate enemy in the ground.
The real draw here aside from gunplay is, like the two games before it, the story. A tale of betrayal, murder, and retribution, it's exciting from start to finish and peppered throughout with real-life historical figures, legendary outlaws and brave heroes alike. Twists and turns keep the narrative interesting, and the game's story is relayed to you by the main character, Silas Greaves. As he narrates, details change, causing elements of the levels to disappear and appear at will, and at certain points, even causes time to rewind if a detail was forgotten or left out.
The whole thing makes for a very compelling experience and will keep you entertained as you fight through levels full of both cowboys AND Indians.
Call of Juarez: Gunslinger isn't just a game for Call of Juarez fans, shooter fans, or fans of the Wild West; it's for anyone who appreciates exciting gameplay that rewards skill, a story that keeps things fresh, and a polished and fun experience.

The review balance of this game is about 50-50 at the moment, whether to like or to withdraw it is indeed a difficult question. If one liked Just Cause 2, there is no principal reason not to like Just Cause 3, because it's basically the same game, even almost the same map with a few changes and rotations (for instance the Sky High Club turned into a Sky Fortress), but this is also the big weakness of Just Cause 3. There is nothing new, a missing impact of originality, and the world that was rich and stuffed with cars and people of Panau becomes empty and forelorn named Medici, might be a first impression of this weakness. And even worse, apart from the few game missions and although there are more challenges than in Just Cause 2, one could get the impression that there is almost nothing else to do than visiting graveyards and shrines to doubtfully honor virtually dead people. In fact, more than half of the map is empty, especially the mountain region is totally redundant, whereas it was filled with Fortresses in JC2.
One can, of course, speculate about the reasons for such a mishap: After the success of JC2, members left the team, the remaining workforce was increased , they thought it would be easy, time went by, funds ran out, and then, suddenly, they noticed that there was no innovation in what they were doing except for adjusting their engine to a new generation of GPUs as demanded by the sponsors. Ergo, they clustered together an empty and lifeless sight by slightly changing the map of JC2, named it Medici, added some graves, shrines and in large part monotone challenges here and there to claim it a great game.
Next time, all people that are tired of visiting megalithic graves are warmly invited to expect more of a JC sequel than a mere JC2 copy with a few obtical changes and lots of redundant territory (about 50%, suiting its thumbs up-down voting).

I played this game all the way through on console, and I enjoyed it. I saw it was on sale, bought it even though I already beat it through.
But as a big fan of the Xenomorph I am, most of my enjoyment came from simply how well the game was crafted. And no I'm not talking about the graphics. I'm talking about how the game was made to fit in snug with the timeline of the original movies, and the original universe. It was more on how everything felt like it was 1982. I read some commentary from the devs over at CA. And when coming up with assets for the game, their philosophy was simple. If it looked like it didn't belong in 1982 or couldn't exist at the time, they didn't put it in the game. I'm talking old Commodore PET-looking computers with cathode-ray monochrome character displays, '70s fashion sense, advert posters warning about the dangers of lice, everything just felt so right.
The game itself though, like the way the AI works and how rather than following a bunch of pre-scripted paths and responding primarily to stimuli made the alien really stand out. Getting from one half of the room to the other can be a bit hard, especially when the Alien can actually hear your motion tracker or if you step over a can or something in the room breaks. Along with the fact that the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ wasn't killable all made it a very interesting, and terrifying enemy to go up against.
The story is pretty good. It felt like it belonged with the main series and wasn't just all shoe-horned in just to market a game about the Xeno. It actually had a plot with characters that were aware of what happened in the first movie, the main character was charming and likable while being somewhat admirable for her brave nature, and how all the other characters were scripted to behave how you would expect humans stranded in space without rules or safety to behave.
Overall the game is perfect. 10/10

TL;DR: Challenging but satisfying horror game with (mostly) excellent plot.
What an experience to say the least. If you have watched any sort of sci-fi movies in your life, chances are you know about the Alien franchise. If you have seen the Alien franchise and thought "I wonder how I would feel in that situation", or even if you have just pondered the idea of meeting an alien species, this game is for you. With that said, if you get scared easily, you will not have a good time. This game is (as many described before me) a game of cat and mouse, where you are the mouse. The AI is punishingly difficult (at least on the difficulties I played) with very few mistakes. You are given a fighting chance, as long as you have the patience to utilize everything, and I do mean everything, to your advantage. If you come from games such as Amnesia and want a similar experience, I would say look elsewhere, but maybe give it a try. If you are a newcomer to the horror genre and want an excellent story with the means to make you poop yourself, buy it right now. I have very few complaints about this game, the main one being the ending, which I thought was poorly done given the excellent story preceding it. I recommend playing it at night with no distractions, as they will only make your journey harder.

The strangest thing happened to me...
I have been a fan of Elder Scrolls games since Morrowind and have put more time into this series of games than any other series I have ever played. I am not the biggest fan of MMOs because they can be a bit hokey. When this came out I was uncertain but I decided to give it a whirl because I didn't want to miss out on another installment of my favorite series.
It was okay at first but I kept finding myself walking away from it. I don't know why but it just never stuck. Within the past week I came back to it and allowed it to patch with all of the new updates. I played again for five mintues and was hooked. The combat system is fun and engaging and makes you forget that you are playing an MMO. I play with a controller and it's simple, straightforward, and easy to use which is amazing in and of itself for an MMO.
Now here's the weirdest part: The next day my wife had to do homework on the computer so I fired up the ol' PS3 and popped Skyrim in. I hated it. Seriously. I found myself longing for the environments, combat, and general ease of use that the game designers worked into this puppy. I tried to "summon" my horse in Skyrim and was mad that I had to go tromping around to find Shadowmere (why wouldn't he jump come when I called like Red Dead Redemption, The Witcher 3, or this game?). I went to fight a giant and felt let down that I could fast swap between weapon sets and limited by my choices in combat.
Prior to this experience I wasn't interested in the expansion that they just recently announced that will take players back to Morrowind but now I can't wait.
Kudos to the development team for listening to your fans and keep up the good work. I still hate microtransactions and the general idea of MMO subscription fees but this is still a game well worth playing.

game art - see Transistor
The style, gameplay and last, but not least, soundtrack are all fantastic. With Bastion and Transistor in their stable, there's no wonder why they're called Supergiant. I just finished my first run-though. The game play for Transistor is fantastic and fun. A mix of tactical and real-time attack with each enemy encounter. The soundtrack is eery and full of depth, but it suits the whole story line. The art is, without a doubt gorgeous, as expected. I was hoping for a more elaborate exhibition of the antagonists (but you are given the option to read about each character at terminals within the game).
The story is gripping and depressing. And I love it. I wasn't sure what sort of story I was expecting before the game came out. It was definitely different from what I had initially theorized. I would advise, however, not to let personal expectations get in the way of enjoying the game. I certainly had some reservations when I began playing it, but Supergiant Games had a vision and they did a fantastic job. While there are some similarities to Bastion, this is a different game. Personally, I like the game play in Transistor better, but the story board of Bastion more.
Beautiful animation, battle style that is challenging but VERY fun, great narration, gorgeous soundtrack. The only fault in this game is that there isn't enough of it.

Let me start off by saying I never played Bastion, previous title by SuperGiant Games, I didn't find Bastion appealing but was excited when I saw this gem.
Pros: Transistor is an absolutely georgous game; its so colorful, the backgrounds are absolutely stunning, and the enviroment just feels right for this title. Everything just fits so well. The characters are compelling as you're only fed a little information at the beginning (and for those of you who aren't so interested in game lore Tranistor tucks it away for you to peruse if you're interested rather than cram it into your face) and you learn more about specific people by changing up your combat tactics. Not to mention the soundtrack is awesome, really fills the atmosphere, and the story once it get's rolling will have you entralled!
The combat in this game is extremely enjoyable, theres alot of impact to the hits and graphical effects and sound assets make you really feel like you're doing damage. Where combat get's really interesting is your loadout. Each skill can be used in 3 different ways: Active, modifier, and passive. This means there are tons of combinations and ways to fit each skill to your play style and can really shake up how you appraoch combat. Combat can also take place in a turn styleish manner by executing a planning phase to plan you're attacks and then watch them play out or in a more real time style which is pretty fun(though i found the planning more enjoyable and more effective). I give Transistor respect for incorporating two combat styles. Enemy variety is also great! I found battles mixing in enemy types all the time so fights never became stale, though I cant stand fetch enemies, annoying tossers.
Cons: I found i wasn't sometimes given enough information during fights in certain situations; for example when i attempt to attack and I was only told my attack would be "blocked" I had no idea why, granted this could have been my own fault for not reading something early on but it would have been nice to be reminded if that is the case. I also found when some enemies are close together the life bars for each are not displayed, but thats not a big deal.
Game length will vary for some, I felt if I had not completed alot of the challenge modes it would have been a little too short as I was really getting into the story and was left wanting more, but there is a gamemode + for another run through with your current level and skills.
Overall this was a fantastic game and has really got me looking forward to another SuperGiant game. I loved this game and feel I completely got my money's worth. Ihighly recommend picking it up if you were even considering the game. See you in the country!

Papers, Please is an interesting game. Although at first glance you wouldn't think it, the story has quite a bit of depth and is very intriguing. The game revolves around a few factors; your own family's well being, other people's well being, the government you work for, as well as the rebellion group trying to take down said government. The game is riddled with sections where you must make decisions that will make some factors happy, and others not. Will you let the man's wife in even though she doesn't have her correct papers? Surely if you do, you would be betraying your country, which could result in you getting fined. That fine might make it impossible to feed your family that night. But this guy is a nice guy. Don't break their family apart. The social commentary is phenomenal, and the reoccuring characters such as Jorji make the story very memorable. The game has 20 endings and I'd recommend going for all of them.
Gameplay wise, the game is much more fun and addicting than you'd think. The entire game revolves around checking the entry papers of entrants wishing to cross the border. On the first few days, you check very few details in the passports of entrants. However, that very quickly changes as more and more factors, such as vaccines, entry permits, fingerprints, and contraband become relevant when deciding if someone may enter or not. The game gets hectic as you race againt the clock to ensure you earn the pay you need.
The game uses a pixel based design. That coupled with the very basic sound design may seem like a bad thing for most games, but in this case, it works excellently. It may seem ugly and repulsive at first, but eventually you'll fall in love with the entire style, as the graphics can be seen as part of the story as well.
Papers, Please runs perfectly well. No glitches, no freezing. The game offers both full screen and windowed mode from launch which is great for short bursts of gameplay. The game allows for multiple save tracks. These save games are incorporated in a very cool way, allowing you to resume from any previous day while still creating a brand new track. The achievements all popped without issue.
-The achievement list, although short, allows you to play through the game in many different ways. I would recommend you try for them all, with that said, however, it is highly recommended that you play your first playthrough without any guides, simply make your own decisions for the best possible experience
-Although replaying the story is fun, there is also an endless mode where you can just keep checking papers all day, every day. It is literally heavan.

If you're an ancient history buff then this is the game for you!  The base game itself with various DLC (Which I don't support cutting content but these seem fairly well balanced) is historically accurate to most ends.  What I like best however is the fact that this game leaves the players with the choice to make history however they see fit.  Whether it is smashing Gaulic barbarians with Egytian elephants or having your elite Roman legion hold the last line of deffense, this game is full of opportunity.  I currently play with around 30 different mods installed which add so much more to the game it is almost overwhelming at first.
At launch this game was very poorly managed but it has come a remarkable way since then.  Many issues have been thoroughly ironed out.  If you get this game I would recommend playing vanilla version for a bit then once you start losing interest download some mods from the workshop to get yourself re-immersed in the game.  Mods vary from simple maps to adding entire factions or characters and abilities to the game.  I personally like a little bit of everything for my playstyle.  Some maps, some characters, some new units, some graphical effect enhancers.  This is a very solid game, especially if you like anything history related. :)

The review balance of this game is about 50-50 at the moment, whether to like or to withdraw it is indeed a difficult question. If one liked Just Cause 2, there is no principal reason not to like Just Cause 3, because it's basically the same game, even almost the same map with a few changes and rotations (for instance the Sky High Club turned into a Sky Fortress), but this is also the big weakness of Just Cause 3. There is nothing new, a missing impact of originality, and the world that was rich and stuffed with cars and people of Panau becomes empty and forelorn named Medici, might be a first impression of this weakness. And even worse, apart from the few game missions and although there are more challenges than in Just Cause 2, one could get the impression that there is almost nothing else to do than visiting graveyards and shrines to doubtfully honor virtually dead people. In fact, more than half of the map is empty, especially the mountain region is totally redundant, whereas it was filled with Fortresses in JC2.
One can, of course, speculate about the reasons for such a mishap: After the success of JC2, members left the team, the remaining workforce was increased , they thought it would be easy, time went by, funds ran out, and then, suddenly, they noticed that there was no innovation in what they were doing except for adjusting their engine to a new generation of GPUs as demanded by the sponsors. Ergo, they clustered together an empty and lifeless sight by slightly changing the map of JC2, named it Medici, added some graves, shrines and in large part monotone challenges here and there to claim it a great game.
Next time, all people that are tired of visiting megalithic graves are warmly invited to expect more of a JC sequel than a mere JC2 copy with a few obtical changes and lots of redundant territory (about 50%, suiting its thumbs up-down voting).

This game is hardly worth $30, let alone $40. The game has no challenge; it hands out S-ranks like it's candy. The only hard levels come from the Shadow DLC, which I think strikes the perfect balance. They're easy to complete, but fairly challenging to get an S-rank on.
The Avatar character is a neat concept and genuinely can be fun to play as. Unfortunately, this character's levels are built with modern Sonic in mind (rush forward and hope for the best) with still minimal platforming and some arbitrary moments where you're locked in a room full of harmless enemy robots meant solely to be killed by you.
Modern Sonic's levels are straight boring and have very little gameplay; you can hold the Boost button and jump sometimes and win, and frankly I wish I was exaggerating.
Classic Sonic, shoehorned in so forcefully
, is the worst thing to happen to this game. To preface, I loved the classics and Sonic Mania. A Sonic touted to be "the same as the classics" should, reasonably, play like the classics, right? Is that unreasonable? They somehow made this 3D classic Sonic worse that the Generations one! He feels clunky and falls like a 7-ton weight. He has the weird running speed cap from Sonic 1 (
) and rolling makes him reach insane speeds. His jump starts off at full speed then just suddenly slows down in a weird and unnatural jump arc.
The story seems so rushed and unfinished it makes Sonic '06 look like a cohesive and sensical experience. There are so many plot points that just go unresolved or are resolved by something dumb (
) and it makes the whole thing fall apart. It's the worst story I've ever played and I own Advanced Warfare for god's sake.
The music is where Sonic is usually strongest, right? Well.... Some tracks are standard and repetitive, but some are amazing. The Avatar's music, though being a bit of a genre shift from previous Sonic games, is really good (though seemingly polarizing). The new take on fully-voiced level music with lots of synth surprisingly works. Modern Sonic's music is... meh, I don't hate it and it makes for okay ambiance for a speed game. Classic Sonic's music is... well, it's what you would get if converted Sonic 4's music into a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ electronica midi file. It's real bad. I'm not sure if they were trying to go with a classic style, or what, but it's not good.
Honestly, you'd be spending your money better on the Sonic Generations Collection, it's a better game with actually fun gameplay and even a well-established modding community. And it's $20 at full price!
I should note, a lot of my hours were spent getting some of the level secrets (there are Red Star Rings, some number circle things, and some moon things.) before realizing that they do literally nothing. At all. You don't even unlock Super Sonic or anything. He can only be unlocked through modding. He's a (free) DLC in the console versions though!

Sonic Forces is far from perfect, but it is a very fun and stylish game nevertheless. The gameplay is fast-paced and largely quite thrilling. The visuals are quite beautiful, particularly the levels in the crumbling city setting. The music is consistently catchy and suits the gameplay very well.
Although it's something of a novelty, I really enjoyed being able to create a custom avatar. There are quite a few diverse looks to choose from, and I ended up saving at least a dozen customiezd outfits in my avatar's closet. The inclusion of the avatar character also increased my immersion into the storyline.
There are three notable downsides to the game. Firstly, it is simply too short. I finished the main plot in about six hours, but a more skilled player could have finished in half that time. Secondly, the Star Wars-inspired storyline needed far more fleshing out. The story feels like it's rushing to its conclusion far too quickly. Thirdly, the game was too easy on hard mode. The main challenge here will come from beating your own times and grabbing all of the special rings on each level.
With these downsides noted, I still had a blast playing it. I recommend it to anyone who was enjoyed other 3D Sonic games of recent years. If you didn't enjoy games like Sonic Generations or Sonic Lost World, don't bother.

This game was made by the makers of Bastion, so I had my hopes up. Sadly, while the graphic style and music is gorgeous, the story and gameplay are lacking cohesion. Similar to Bastion the action is controlled from isometric view and has lots of action rpg elements.
There is real time combat and a turn mode, which stops the action and allows you to plan moves, which are then executed. Combat in real time is clunky, as the enemies move much to fast to evade, which forces the player into the turn mode. Consequently the game forces hit and run tactics. Stop the action, move close to the enemy, hit him with a few spells and run out of range. Rinse and repeat.
One of the few good things about combat is the endless combinations of skills you can use. Each of the skills can be used as primary or enhancer of another skill. Sadly, you will end up using the 1-3 heavy hitting spells, without ever experimenting too much.
All in all the developers did not succeed making this a cohesive game. Graphics and sound are great, gameplay and story telling are lacking. So you find yourself walking down pretty hallways without ever caring about the enemies you kill or knowing what exactly happened in this dystopian world.

Papers, Please is an interesting game. Although at first glance you wouldn't think it, the story has quite a bit of depth and is very intriguing. The game revolves around a few factors; your own family's well being, other people's well being, the government you work for, as well as the rebellion group trying to take down said government. The game is riddled with sections where you must make decisions that will make some factors happy, and others not. Will you let the man's wife in even though she doesn't have her correct papers? Surely if you do, you would be betraying your country, which could result in you getting fined. That fine might make it impossible to feed your family that night. But this guy is a nice guy. Don't break their family apart. The social commentary is phenomenal, and the reoccuring characters such as Jorji make the story very memorable. The game has 20 endings and I'd recommend going for all of them.
Gameplay wise, the game is much more fun and addicting than you'd think. The entire game revolves around checking the entry papers of entrants wishing to cross the border. On the first few days, you check very few details in the passports of entrants. However, that very quickly changes as more and more factors, such as vaccines, entry permits, fingerprints, and contraband become relevant when deciding if someone may enter or not. The game gets hectic as you race againt the clock to ensure you earn the pay you need.
The game uses a pixel based design. That coupled with the very basic sound design may seem like a bad thing for most games, but in this case, it works excellently. It may seem ugly and repulsive at first, but eventually you'll fall in love with the entire style, as the graphics can be seen as part of the story as well.
Papers, Please runs perfectly well. No glitches, no freezing. The game offers both full screen and windowed mode from launch which is great for short bursts of gameplay. The game allows for multiple save tracks. These save games are incorporated in a very cool way, allowing you to resume from any previous day while still creating a brand new track. The achievements all popped without issue.
-The achievement list, although short, allows you to play through the game in many different ways. I would recommend you try for them all, with that said, however, it is highly recommended that you play your first playthrough without any guides, simply make your own decisions for the best possible experience
-Although replaying the story is fun, there is also an endless mode where you can just keep checking papers all day, every day. It is literally heavan.

Following the disappoint that was Aliens: Colonial Marines, Sega set out to fix their image, and their franchise with this; Alien: Isolation. The Aliens game series has a long history of being reinvented, with arcade adaptations in the 80’s and early 90’s as well as several Alien V’s Predator (AVP) games. BLUF, Alien: Isolation is a heart pounding and exciting thriller which has done an outstanding job of saving the Alien game franchise.
Alien: Isolation is set after the original 1979 movie Alien, your character is the daughter of Ellen Ripley; Amanda Ripley. Amanda is a rough around the edges mechanic who has been questioning the disappearance of her mother and the commercial spacecraft she crewed, the Nostromo several years previously. Amanda is contacted by the Weyland Yutani Corporation after the Nostromo has been detected by a soon to be decommissioned manufacturing space station, the Sevastopol and offered Amanda the opportunity to investigate before things go wrong and before you know it, you’re being stalked by a seven foot, black lizard alien with a piercing tale and acid for blood (or Xenomorph for the indoctrinated). With limited resources, equipment and supplies, Amanda has to make her way through the Sevastopol with the alien in chase using ventilation shafts and lockers to hide.
The graphics for Alien: Isolation are good, but not ground breaking. After crawling into the 50th locker, I found myself staring at the same graffiti, photos and post-it notes as the previous 49, which may seem a little pedantic but you do spend a lot of time hiding in them. The light and shadow for this game are the better stand out but the crowning glory for this game is the sound (must play surround sound). Every noise seems to be accentuated as you find yourself walking cautiously down a corridor awaiting any sign of distress before you sprint to the closest hiding spot. The story is great, full of suspense and twists with lots of lore to discover throughout the game which explain the events on the Nostromo and Sevastopol.
Although set in a first person format, the game is not a shooter, focused heavily on survival; however there is an infrequent to engage in combat. The crafting mechanics are easy to understand and follow which entices the player to explore as much as possible to become better equipped for what lies ahead. There are a few micro games and challenges as well which include a play through of the events of the Nostromo from the perspective of one of the crew which, although short lived is a lot of fun.
The absolute BEST part of this game is the adaptive AI of the Alien. The Alien learns how you escape/evade it and the methods you use to hide and quickly attunes itself to your play style in an attempt to catch you easier as the game progresses. My advice? Be spontaneous and unpredictable to not build a pattern of activity. The playable area of the Sevastopol is quite large with only a few micro loading screens between particular areas of the game.
Alien: Isolation is a fantastic survival thriller quite unlike anything else.
I give Alien: Isolation the following ratings;
8/10 Story
9/10 Gameplay
7/10 Graphics
10/10 Ambient Sound
8/10 Overall
This game is well suited for those that enjoy the following franchises: Dead Space, Metro, Alien/AVP.

This is a game about the grind. You must feel the grind, live the grind, love the grind. With a current level cap of 250 which will be increased as time goes on, there is a lot of grinding. If you hate running around in circles and killing things for hours on end, then obviously the game isn't for you.
So what if you do love the grind? Well, Tree of Savior proably still isn't the game for you.
There is a lot to like in this game. The anime artstyle is beautiful, the combat and movement are crisp and fun, and there are some unique classes with cool skills. But to experience those moments, you'll have to fight through a lot of issues. The most obvious issues are bugs that have persisted through the Korean launch and through various open betas, some of which are completely game-breaking (I'm looking at you CommanderLoadFail). If you manage to avoid the bugs, fret not for the server lag will drop your framerate the moment you run into any decently populated map.
Assuming you overlook the more obvious issues, then you will be annoyed by the less-visible issues. Leveled a character over dozens of hours into through several classes only to realize that the abilities or spells have zero synergy with your build? Sorry, start a new character. Want to know exactly how your spells/abilities will scale with stats? Sorry, deal with the vague tooltips and spell/ability descriptions. Excited that there are over 80 classes in the game? Sorry, a lot of those classes just aren't viable due to balancing issues.
Then we have the issues that are downright hilarious. Without a premium 30 day token, players are limited to ONE market slot to sell items, in addition to waiting 48 HOURS to retrieve money from item(s) sold on the market. Since you rely on money to not only upgrade your equipment but also make sure your spells and abilities scale in the game, it really feels like the developers are giving non-premium players a giant middle finger.
Oh, and did I mention that after one of the closed betas the developers took away the ability to buyback items that you may have accidently sold to NPCs? Don't worry though, as the list of items you sold at the bottom of the NPC menus just to taunt you just in case you wanted to be reminded of what bad game design looks like.
Even if you spend the money to skip the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t to have an easier experience, there are still things that can't be fixed by real money, like the class balance issues and the unbearable server-side lag. Given the developer's controversial track record in Korea, and how things still aren't fixed despite being relased early in Korea, it's unlikely there will be fixes that the players have been demanding on any reasonable timeframe.
There is a lot of fun to be had in Tree of Savior, but it is hidden behind a lot of bad game design choices that ultimately sour the gameplay experience. Unless you're just craving something to feed your Ragnorok Online nostalgia or just need a good anime-themed grinder, your time and money probably better spent elsewhere.

While I don't agree with some of IMC's business decisions, they'll likely change aspects of the game overtime. Honestly their response is pretty much expected; can't really expect a new MMO to over compensate the amount of resources required when their player base is unknown.
I favor grindy games so I am a bit bias but this is nothing compared to old Ragnarok. I got a character to level 70 in about a week or less and at least 20% of my play time is me falling asleep or watching videos on the side while leaving the game on.
The grind can be almost circumvented if you actually take the time to explore the maps and pick-up the hidden quests. Exploring maps and completing quests rewards you with EXP cards which you can beneficial if you plan properly.
Anyone complaining about the grind in this game is either:
+rediculously high leveled (which is expected anyways, so what the heck?)
+tried to get to hit high levels quickly by "grinding" and burned out
+simply ignored what the game had to offer

Woah boy this game. My view on it shifted so damn much throughout the year but, now that I've actually finished the game, I can finally say my final opinions on Sonic Forces.
Right, let's start:
Pros
- The soundtrack is eargasmic, seriously. Every track made my ears go to the 4th dimension it's amazing. The classic stage tunes definitely sound unfinished and rushed in a way, but I like listening to the various remixes of them (Shoutout to Lil Boulder, they remix the classic themes perfectly).
- Nice graphics. They're not gonna make you feel like you're really there, but they look nice and all the stages have a good look.
- Suitable voice acting. All the voices suit the characters, Matt Mercer works very well as Espio (Even if whenever I hear him I think of Jotaro/McCree).
- It's fun. Blasting through stages as Sonic is fun, swinging around with the avatar is fun, classic sonic
- The avatar. I love making little animal fellas it's good.
Cons:
- The length. Why is this game so short? By the end of the 2-3 hours you feel no emotion towards the game.
- The stages. Sure, 30 stages is a lot but the thing is they ALL take place in the same few areas. Green Hill, Chemical Plant, a city, the Death Egg, Mystic Jungle, Metropolis, and Eggman's fortress. Why? Seaside Hill from Heroes is mentioned by Espio at one point in the game, why don't we go there at all? The world feels so small, which it really shouldn't considering the game follows a worldwide struggle.
- Classic Sonic. He has no reason to be here other than being bait to get classic fans to buy the game. He adds absolutely nothing to the story except saving tails from Chaos 0. Yeah, Chaos ZERO. Tails literally shudders in fear as the weakest form of Chaos approaches him. I guess his battle against Chaos 4 never happened now? Anyway, back to Classic. His gameplay is obviously the weakest in the game. It's off and doesn't hold up to the high standard Mania held him up to.
- The story. It all happens so quickly. Infinite just dissapears somewhere at the end, and he's only explained in Episode Shadow. All the other characters in the Resistance barely get any good moments, they have no reason to be there other than world building, which is fine, but their characters could've had so much growth during this armageddon. Funny enough, Silver actually bothers to fight Infinite, while everyone else is basicallly just there.
- The missed potential. Whoever at Sega thought not having Shadow and Chaos be boss fights needs to be fired. Classic Sonic just defeats Chaos in one hit in the first few minutes and Shadow just roundhouse kicks the Phantom Ruby Shadow later on. Bam, they're gone, just like an angel's kiss. The final Infinite fight is also just a reskin of Metal's fight and the FINAL BOSS is a reskin of Colour's final boss. I'm being serious whoever made these decisions has not made me happy.
- No Big the Cat. Where is he.
Overall, Sonic Forces was a good game, but it could be so much better. I have a lot more bad things to say about this game, but I'll spare you that for now. If you want, get this game when it's cheaper. For now I dont reccomend it. go and buy Sonic Mania or something.

I've been a sonic fan since I played the Sonic Games on the GameCube, Sonic Unleashed and a lot of the games after it was some well done 3d sonic games and are some of the game are in my top 10 favorite games of all time. So when I heard that Sonic Forces was going to be a game like sonic unleashed, a dark story, a new engine, a boost to win title on next-gen consoles, and a fresh coat a paint for the series, I couldn't wait for it! Unfortunately, this game didn't live up to the previous games released along with sonic mania. Heres my review!
Plot: No spoilers for obvious reasons, but to sum things up. Sonic is defeated and apparently "tortured" for 6 months, in that time frame, Eggman takes over 99% of the world, which causes sonic's friends along with your custom character (called Avatar or Rookie) to create a resistance (star wars much?) to stop Eggman and defeat his new creation, Infinite. They later meet back up with tails and classic sonic, coming back from Sonic Mania to complete its story or something? Though this story is interesting, its execution is horrible, and the later parts of the story suck due to the villains being dumb as rocks and a force message about teamwork or something. Not a good way to do a "dark" story, oh and sonic wasn't tortured if he is still happy and go lucky. 3/10
Gameplay: It's split up into three sections, Modern Sonic, Avatar, and Classic Sonic. Modern Sonic is the same boost to win formula as the previous games since sonic unleashed. It's well done, and nice to see again, but I wish it were more of a different take on speedy 3d platforming. The avatar gameplay is decent, you get to make your character and uses his wisp power to get through the level somewhat like the Modern Sonic stages. They're alright, not much, but nice to play. Then we get Classic Sonic... Sigh. Boy, was Classic Sonic wasted. Its just CS from Generations again, and the stages are kinda dull, and it controls awful. They should have removed him and had more stages with the Avatar and Modern Sonic. Speaking of Modern Sonic and Avatar, they have some stages where you play as both trying to get to the end of the level, using double boost at least once during the stage, they're better, but nothing special again. It seems like Sonic Team played it safe with this game, and it backfired severely in they're faces. They should have done a new gameplay style like Sonic Lost World or Mario Oddsey, the boost to win formula should have been retired before this game because it's not 100% fun anymore like Generations or Unleashed. It was still fun, but not as fun as I would have liked. 5/10
Audio: The soundtrack is one of the best in the Sonic series, it's more cinematic, but its also filled with more sonic like music like fist bump and infinite's themes. More songs would be nice though, but still high quality. 9/10
Bosses: Disappointing as well, the mini-bosses are way too easy, and the FInal Boss is also a joke. Take one look at the final boss (if you completed the game) and tell me it's not like the one from Colors and Lost World! 3/10
Summary: Sonic Forces is a huge disappointment for me. The boost to win gameplay is fun, and so is the avatar and double gameplay. The soundtrack is fantastic and is one of the best sonic soundtracks along with sonic mania. However, the story, while it has a good idea, it's not well executed and a huge disappointment, it's not even that dark! Not to mention the Classic Sonic gameplay is pointless and can be removed from the game, and nothing would change. I wish this could have been the game to bring 3d sonic to the next gen, but instead, it has me wishing for more, and for someone else to give this series some justice just like Sonic Mania did. Sega, if you're listening to this, please let someone else make a sonic game, enough of the hedgehog engine, enough of Denuvo DRM and crashes, please have it open world or whatever with no DRM, and something that's not 2d again and helps gives the franchise some new life. Also, P.S. DON'T RUSH IT!

This game was made by the makers of Bastion, so I had my hopes up. Sadly, while the graphic style and music is gorgeous, the story and gameplay are lacking cohesion. Similar to Bastion the action is controlled from isometric view and has lots of action rpg elements.
There is real time combat and a turn mode, which stops the action and allows you to plan moves, which are then executed. Combat in real time is clunky, as the enemies move much to fast to evade, which forces the player into the turn mode. Consequently the game forces hit and run tactics. Stop the action, move close to the enemy, hit him with a few spells and run out of range. Rinse and repeat.
One of the few good things about combat is the endless combinations of skills you can use. Each of the skills can be used as primary or enhancer of another skill. Sadly, you will end up using the 1-3 heavy hitting spells, without ever experimenting too much.
All in all the developers did not succeed making this a cohesive game. Graphics and sound are great, gameplay and story telling are lacking. So you find yourself walking down pretty hallways without ever caring about the enemies you kill or knowing what exactly happened in this dystopian world.

Let's start with Just Cause 2 and Just Cause 3 comparison.
JC2's controls are a bit wacky to begin with, but acceptable. JC3 however has a mediocre controls set for PC.
Graphically, it's obviously better than JC2, but only if you have a decent graphic card. I have GTX 960 2GB, and running JC2 on High setting renders the game beautifully, but that only goes so far. I can only enjoy JC3 gameplay on Low to Medium graphic setting.
Wingsuit, another point goes to JC3.
And this is the most important part of the comparison for these two: vehicle handling. While JC2's vehicle handling is not great, most vehicles are easy to handle and maneuver. In JC3, vehicle handling is worst than any open world games I've played. Not surprised, since Avalanche Studios handed the vehicle handling work to Criterion Games's hired staffs. Remember how most Need for Speed fans complained CG has 'killed' the NFS franchise?
I enjoy playing JC2 and expected the same excitement with JC3. However, JC3 fails to live up to my expectation. And probably because my expectation was too high, I rage quitted.
But let's not fret over my negative review just because I only played for a couple of hours; I've explored so much within these few hours by not gawking at its graphic.
And when my frustration with this game is over, I will play it again. Just not anytime soon.

Bought the game on sale, because a few years ago it was one of these games that got a good portion of attention.
If you want a simple "shoot´em up fps game" search somewhere else, because this game is unforgiving for the unprepared. I don´t go into storytelling, because at this point I didn´t finish it and the parts of the story I saw are somewhat enigmatic.
Game mechanic is as follows:
You are a stalker stranded in the nuclear desaster zone around the Chernobyl Power Plant. You start off with merely a broken pistol and some shirt without ANY bulletproof properties whatsoever. And now: survive.
You have weapons like pistols for the first, and weapons like assault rifles/ shotguns/ sniper rifles for the second slot, grenades and a binocular. Also you can switch your armor to better ones if you find them. On top of that you have 5 slots for artifacts, that push your healing, stop the bleeding of wounds or make you more bulletproof etc. All items lose durability, eg. a weapon with less durability is more prone to misfire, armor loses its resistances.
Inventory management is crucial in this game, your carryweight is 50kg, which sounds a lot at first, but any weapon you carry, any armor you drag around and also artifacts, medikits and ammo (!) have weight, which makes it important to think about what to take from enemies or chests. There are some permanent chests in the game where your loot doesn´t get salvaged, but keep in mind that the runways between them are long.
The FPS part is IMHO well done, your enemies and you have hitboxes, which makes it easy for you (and them) to headshot, BUT: your ammo follows ballistic curves, also (esp. in the beginning) the weapons you find are prone to misfire, you want to use iron sights for slightly better results.
The environment and enemies follow a more or less natural day/ night cycle. Mutants swarm areas and stay in them, bandids raid loners from time to time, and military checkpoints get respawned with new enemies. There are factions to join and random quests to fulfill. The overall atmosphere of the zone is very good executed, there are broken bunkers, abandoned labs or villages and a lot of (mostly antagonistic and mutated) wildlife. Also a lot of other stalkers roam the areas, so there is plenty of room for cheeki breeki :)
The game is quite scary at times, especially the mutated enemies make you crap your pants. The mod-base is HUGE and fulfills a good portion of what this game eventually misses. (I play with the Stalker Complete 2009-mod)
Tl;dr:
Recommended for FPS/RPG hybrid-fans with a good nervous costume. Modifications are abundand, if you like your♥♥♥♥♥being handed to you by invisible Blade 2-vampires, bandids or paramilitary troops in the abandoned zone of the chernobyl power plant I highly recommend it.

Really amazing game, easily one of the best horrors games I've ever played. If you enjoy the Alien films and looking for a new experience and take on the franchise, I can't reccomend this enough.
Pros:
• Game's optimization is fantastic, and the system requirments are super low even though the graphics look phenomenal. I played the game on my rig containing a HD 7750 and a Quad Core i5-6400, and it ran at a solid 60FPS the entire time with no drops in framerate.
• The atmosphere is very well established, and super reminiscint of the classic Alien films. Every corner of the Sevastopol Space Station holds both secrets and horror to behold no matter where you go.
• The story, featuring Amanda Ripley, daughter of Alien series protagonist Ellen Ripley, is chilling, badass, and works perfectly as a piece of Alien series lore.
Follow Amanda as she explores the Sevastopol Space Station, searching for clues on the disappearance of her mother's spaceship and her whereabouts, while evading the danger caused by a Xenomorph terrorizing the station's remaining inhabitants.
• The gameplay is solid, causing the player to rely on stealth and avoiding combat regularly instead of fighting every battle, which I feel is an awesome change in the style that Alien games are played. Enemy A.I. is completely unscripted, allowing enemies to take unique routes and ensure no two playthroughs are exactly the same. Be warned though, certain tricks only work on the Xenomorph before it learns to wise up...
• A wide variety of tools are available for use to avoid situations of any kind, be it the unkillable Xeno, deranged engineers, or killer robots. Add this onto the awesome map design and overall, the experience created by Alien: Isolation is unique and definitely proves itself as an awesome game.
Cons:
• The game doesn't explain some of it's features very well in the tutorials, especially regardinhg the rewire system and terminal use, but with a little know-how and initiative, maybe some internet help, you'll figure it out.
• The crafting system was practical and easy to use, but I couldn't help but feel it felt a little bleak.
• I felt it went on for a little too long and maybe if it was a little shorter, I could've appreciated it more.

I've played this game in the Korean version previously (about 70 hours).
Tree of Savior looks beautiful, sounds great and most of all feels great to play. The game has a solid foundation on most elements. There's a rather large world to explore with many different settings and furry animal sprites and the background music is stunning (although a little out of place in some zones) and the controls feel simple but great. You can jump to dodge attacks and skills, attack jump and overall the hitting animations and skills feel impactful and satisfying. The main appeal is obviously the class system as well as the long-term progression potential in the game, similar to what you'd see in Ragnarok Online.
Unfortunately, the similarities end here. IMC felt like they had to turn most of the leveling experience into humdrum questing, which while not as terribly monotonous as most MMOs due to the variety of activities, is still pretty linear and predictable. There aren't many functional differences between maps either and most of the monster and boss difficulty is laughably easy for most classes. What feels fun at first quickly becomes a very repetitive grind which you have no choice over. Grinding mobs themselves is terrible in this game due to low spawn rates and overall low exp gains compared to dungeons and questing. In turn, this means your whole 'endless level' meme is just a bigger number for the typical endgame you see in most MMOs, which is easily attainable in a month or so of soul crushing quests and dungeons.
The class system, while great in theory feels ultimately pointless most of the time since the content is too easy (or too annoying). Despite the interactive party system the game has very little incentives to actually group up since any group activity can (and is encouraged to) be automatized with dungeon matchmakers... In the end most of the old school feeling of finding parties or grinding with friends is thrown out of the window.
There are also other terrible design decisions, such as the extremely limited trading unless you buy a monthly sub. For a game that encourages experimentation with so many classes it feels odd to not even allow gear transfers between characters unless you pay (and don't forget you'll have to do redo all the quests over again everytime you reroll). The cash shop is mildly pay2win as well and knowing IMC's track record with their previous games, it's only a matter of time until it becomes a massive P2W fest.
In the end, I think this game has great potential and boasts a great baseline of building blocks, but IMC ultimately fails at trying to push the envelope and create something unique out of them and instead settles on creating another dull, forgettable Korean MMO just like Granado Espada. All the modern MMO troupes are back: the humdrum questing, linear leveling experience, little choice on player freedom, extremely streamlined solo content and penalizing just about any form of player interaction doesn't spell a long-term experience. It's also bug ridden some skills and classes don't even work the way they're supposed to, plus the optimization leaves a lot to be desired for a 2.5D game.
While I encourage everyone to try it out once it goes F2P I can't really recommend anyone to pay for EA let alone spending anything in the cash shop.

I consider myself a pretty big Sonic fan, and I have trouble recommending this game even to people who like Sonic. Everything about it is a step back from previous entries in the series. The formula that this game uses was almost perfected by Generations, but Forces manages to take everything good about that game and make it worse in some way.
Movement feels awful; jumps are inconsistent, acceleration is unnatural, and turning is sluggish. Not that it really matters though, because half of the time the levels don't want you moving freely at all. The scripted stages are constantly forcing you down a set path which you have no say over and often take away control entirely. I can't count how many times I put my controller down to watch a scene of Sonic doing something cool instead of making him do something cool, or mindlessly held down the boost button to travel in a straight line with no other input required, or slogged through tedious quick-time events that would be bad enough on their own but made even worse by the fact that they don't require any timing, and often lead to no punishment for failing. It feels like you spend more time watching this game than playing it.
On top of all that, out of the 30 short levels, the Sonic stages are arguably the best out of the three playstyles. However, there are only 7 of them (not including boss fights), and they're anywhere between a minute and two minutes long. I'm not exaggerating at all. Take a look for yourself in this
of
in the game. That's a ridiculously short amount of time spent as Sonic in the latest 3D Sonic game.
As for the other playstyles, there is the custom avatar who plays like Sonic but without boost, a slower homing attack, and spends more time in 2D. They manage to control even worse and unfortunately, you'll be spending most of your time playing as them. You have the option to customize their clothing and give them different weapons, but both end up feeling pointless as I have no interest in OC dress up that doesn't influence gameplay whatsoever, and each weapon is equally capable of wiping every stationary, benign "enemy" on screen. The weapons could have made for a fun, unique combat system that maybe involved swapping gun types mid-stage or levelling them up with experience like in platformers such as Ratchet and Clank, but the whole idea ends up feeling like massive wasted potential.
Lastly, there is Classic Sonic, who if you are familiar with from Generations, plays even more sluggishly, painfully, and inaccuaretly compared to the original Genesis games and the recently released Sonic Mania, which absolutely nails how Sonic should move and feel in 2D. Acceleration and proper physics are nonexistent for Classic Sonic in Forces, and the stages are flat and boring, leaving you with slow, bland, uninspired 2D gameplay that doesn't even come close to matching the quality and fun of the original games or even Generations' Classic Sonic levels. Not to mention the pseudo-chiptune soundfont that attempts to artificially recreate the music of the Genesis, which personally did not bother me but may be downright grating and irritating to others.
The game isn't all bad. The rest of the soundtrack is pretty good, although it uses synth and dubstep-like sound for most tracks which may be off-putting for some. I personally enjoyed the soundtrack, even the vocal songs and lyrics (which are very cheesy, but you know what you're getting yourself into with Sonic music. Take a listen to
, one of the most iconic songs, if you haven't a clue.) The graphics are also superb, making this one of the best-looking Sonic games to date, and I'm happy to say that the whole experience is functionally sound, in that there are no game-breaking glitches or graphical mishaps unlike some other infamously bad Sonic games. The voice acting is surprisingly good, considering the mediocre writing, and the cutscenes are animated decently, but the story... just exists.
The plot is an attempt to return to the "serious" tone ala Sonic Adventure 2 and had loads of potential, but it's ultimately incredibly shallow and never makes an effort to do anything a good story would do, like develop characters, or bother to show you things happening; many crucial plot events are
to you over radio by other characters instead of you seeing them yourself. I guess the writers were never told to show and not tell in elementary school, or the developers just couldn't find the time to work the story into their game in a stronger way.
Sonic Forces feels incomplete, sloppy, and all-around inferior to past games in the series. If you want to blast through 3D levels at high-speed, play Generations or Unleashed. If you want to play as Classic Sonic in updated modern gameplay, play Mania. If you want to dress up your own original character and insert yourself into the story as Sonic's best friend... play Sonic Forces, I guess. To me, the game felt like a 3-4 hour waste of time that I so badly wanted to enjoy, but it never gained its footing and stumbled in almost every aspect from beginning to end. Better luck next time, Sonic Team.
