So what is it with this game?
Well put into easily + quickly to read categories it would look like this:


It is the year so and so in the future and you Amanda Ripley are trying to find your mother (Ellen Ripley from the Alien movies), who went missing after flying a mission for her company, several years ago. Now she is offered the chance to fly over to Sevastopol station, a space station that currently sojourns in the same system, where Ellen Ripley disappeared along with her crew. Said station turns out to be in grave distress, because an alien lifeform is on a killing spree inside. The residents and androids can be quite hostile, too. From there on out this mission becomes a lot more complex, while you sneek and fight your way through the different levels and towers of Sevastopol, to escape this nightmare and find closure...

+Perfect play of light and shadow
+Outstandingly designed space station, very close to the original movies
+Most textures are beautifully made
+Predominantly round objects...
-with some fierce exceptions
+System power per performance is the best; extremely optimised for PC (everything from a gtx 970 onward will allow you to play in 4k (Digital Super Resolution in my case) and that looks plain beautiful!
+Perfect Sound Design ->after some time you can cleary distinguish between the actions of the Alien, by simply listening to it i.e. cruising through the vents
+The music predominantly lives up to the soundtrack of the movies, especially of the first one, with only a few exceptions
+The music changes dynamically, depending on what situation you find yourself in...
-but sometimes makes the suspense unnecessarily great ;)
+The Alien is an unpredictable foe, getting more cunning with every difficulty setting
+The Alien is invincible, which may not appeal to some, but it dramatically improves the experience
+Humans can turn out to be friendly or unfriendly
+The motion tracker allows you to see movements of enemies around you, but it does not by any means guarantee your survival...
-Androids, especially the "Hazard"-Androids, are ridiculously hard to kill, unless you're willing to mobilize a lot of resources or ammunition
+XBOX 360 Controller support
+There are additional modes, which you can obtain through the DLCs:
>Crew Expendable and Lone Survivor let you relive the horrors of the first Alien movie
>Safe Haven puts you in one of the few safe rooms on Sevastopol and from there on you will have to scavange, activate machines and whatnot, while risking your life outside said room, to which you return after each task
>Survivor Mode puts you into a room somewhere on Sevastopol and you'll have to find your way to the goal
+Since the Alien is unpredictable, even veterans will find themselves clutching their wet input device of choice and frantically searching for a way out, or come to behold the face of a deadly adversary as it reveals its shiny teeth
+The Motion Tracker is a useful tool, well unless you play nightmare mode, but it'll make your heart race and may not stop haunting you so very soon...
+The Atmosphere is nothing short of captivating; both visuals and sound help you immerse yourself into the game
+After some time you may deem yourself safe from any threat, but the Alien learns, so especially playing on hard and above, you may not be able to hide in the same place twice...
+This game may not offer you the hot-headed mindless-shooting-vibe of games like Call of Duty, but it certainly let's you explore a thoughtfully constructed space station, while being haunted by a merciless killing machine
+even after countless hours of gameplay it is still worth trying again, or testing your survival abilities in the other modes
Have fun!

This game is by far one of my favorite survival-horror games and i would recommend it to any fans of the alien movies.
Graphics: 8.7/10 I think the graphics are amazing, very reminiscent of the movies, however there is some clipping with the doorways and the aliens tail. Every thing else graphic-wise is solid.
Gameplay: 9.5/10 The alien is amazingly adaptable to ANY situation and/or player. It is unpredictable where it will go at any moment unless you are a veteran of this game. the working joes are arguably the most annoying aspect of this game because they are Very hard to kill for a beginner of the game, especially when being stalked by the alien. The ability to lean out of hiding is a nice feature as well. The crafting system is the part of this game i personally feel conflicted about, like how a molotov costs sensors. The map isn't the best i have seen but it works. sort of. expect to use a few walkthroughs to figure out where you are going.
Audio: 8.5/10 The sound effects are really good, from the footsteps of the alien to the weapon sounds,the sounds in this game are realistic and have minimal bugs. The music is also very good at building up suspense although is a bit overpowering compared to the volume of the rest of the audio. the ambiance is also good at setting the tone of a creepy ship that is in the process of falling to pieces.
Controls: 8/10 This game is best played with a controller, however it has keyboard/mouse support. The controls remind me of your typical console game controls, with a few changes to help with new features such as leaning out of cover.
Overall: 8.6/10 An amazing game by far, you can tell a lot of work went into making this game, I personally got this game on sale for $12.49 however i probably would have saved up for it as well had the sale not happened.

While many of you heard of the atrocious launch that this game (If not be thankful) after over two years worth of patching it is now one of the best total wars currently available (2nd to Medieval 2).
PROS
The Campaign is definatly one of the largest and most detailed in the series covering all of Europe, Middle East, and Northen Africa. The A.I is fairly compentent taking advantage of ambushing and other techniques.
Online Co-op is good allowing you and a friend to play with or against each other in the campaign map.
Steam Workshop support allows for many new unit and balancing mods to be made (I recommend getting some as it helps alot with balancing)
CONS
Vanilla Balancing is very off.  A player controlled Rome can easily overpower any nation at any tier provided they know what there doing. While Carthage (Romes primary rival) is seriously underpowerd until late game and by that time there likely already dead.
The collosion detection is very off in this game when a unit charges they'll typically stop BEFORE actually hitting there target. That and combat consists of just large moshpitting rather than orderly combat.
CONCLUSION: I would recommend this game if it goes on sale for about $20-$30. Hopefully these problems are fixed with the upcoming Total War: Warhammer game

I recently purchased this title and I must say that it's not as buggy as some people have professed. Perhaps I'm reading the older reviews but the game now is quite challenging.
The AI isn't as stupid as some people said and here's why: I attacked the Cimmerians during the winter. An all-out, open field of battle. They laid stakes on the ground as they knew my army was mainly cavalry based. I saw the stakes so I tried luring them away - they didn't give in. Alright, fine. I sent my infantry archers to fire upon them as I snuck around through some trees to flank them. More stakes; dang. I finally found an opening in the stakes after moving the camera around and I sent my cavalry men to charge through the opening. As my men charged through the stakes, it turns out they had a hidden army hidden right behind me in the trees. They laid stakes where the opening was and trapped us into a square. Their men came charging in from all sides and eventually wiped us out.
That was the most exhilarating battle I'd ever encountered. Although I lost years' worth of units, I felt satisfied being bested by a good AI. My hat's off to Creative Assembly for updating their game from a buggy piece of turd to a challenging Total War game.
After playing enough Empire & Napoleon Total War to last me a lifetime, I'm happy they went back into the melee-based Roman era. Nothing feels better than seeing your men charge, sword in hand, to deliver due justice to your invaders. I rate this game 8/10. It loses two points due to a simplified negotiation system.

Best ravioli receipe
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!”

After playing the closed beta of the game and now the Early Head start for founders I find myself having mixed feelings of this game.  While a lot of nostalgia from older games like Ragnarok Online exist in here, and some elements of Final Fantasy Tactics with the art style and job system the game ultimately both fails and delivers on two fronts.
First let's talk about the delivery success.  The art and music in the game is fantasticly well done.  And while the job system does seem to be well thought out and flushed there are severe limitations on what jobs can and cannot do.  Not to mention how long it will take you to get to the desired job class you want.
And now for the fails.  The biggest flaw of this game is it is a grind game.  You will constantly need to grind just to advance through one map and go into the next one where your quest will take you.   There are several instances where one map will be for your level, then suddenly after completing the 5-10 or so quests on that map you have yet to gain a single level and the quests will take you to the next area and that area's monsters jump from say lvl 37 to a level 45 area.  The quests do not give you nearly enough exp to be able to close such a gap, nor does the exp card rewards from the quests.   So plan on grinding out the current map for hours on end just to be able to get close to the next map's area monsters.   Oh and if you don't enjoy grinding, there is no other way for you to level up other then grinding mobs once you've completed all quests in the map area and used all your exp cards so you will be grinding either way.
Other then the exp rate failures or I should say the exp rate and level rate oversight of the developers another issue is the job classes themselves.  While from an outside glance they seem fantasically designed, the truth is a lot of the skills of a class are none essential and quite weak compared to other jobs of a different class or later skills of the same class.   Not to mention the sheer level needed to achieve a desired class.  We'll take the Monk class for example.  It is the 6th ring class for the cleric.  Meaning you must first level up to job class 15 five times in order to be able to pick Monk for your 6th job class.  This does not include the extremely slow leveling of the job class exp, nor the base level character exp into consideration, or even the fact that you may entirely not enjoy the Monk class once you grind your way to it.  Meaning you could have just wasted 100+ hours of your time grinding to a job class that you may all entirely not even enjoy.
This also does not take into consideration the gold spammers that appear in every MMO, the server instability, the fact that if you do play a melee class you are severely punished by the ranged classes when it comes to grinding.   You may be attacking your mob of monsters then suddenly they are all killed by someone off screen or someone on your screen you cannot even see due to server lag, or them simply just not showing up for your game.   The severe limitations of the auction house, no trading between players, or several of the other bug's and issues in the game currently.
All in all if you do enjoy grinding games, you may enjoy Tree of Savior.  However if you do not enjoy gridning to level I clearly advise you to keep your distance from this game.  IMC has a lot to fix and flush out before this is truely a polished title.  And if you do deside to try out Tree of Savior, just be warned that I did warn you about how bad some elements of the game currently are.

This may have been the most unique game I played this year. In Papers, Please, you play a immigration clerk screening immigrants for potential entry into the fictitious country of Arstotzka. Immigrants give you their paperwork and it’s up to you to process and find any discrepancies in their papers.
At the end of the day you’ll have to choose how to spend your very small paycheck - on feeding your family, paying the heat bill, or providing your children their medicine. And you probably won’t have enough money for all of it. You’ll want to process as many immigrants as you can as quickly as possible, because you’re paid by how many you process per day. But you don’t want to go too fast or you may miss a discrepancy in their paperwork and have to pay a fine. It’s kind of a nerve wracking and depressing game to play. But I don’t mean that as a negative criticism of the game, it was clearly designed to invoke those kinds of emotions. You really get the feeling of what it’s like to be a desk clerk doing a menial but stressful job and getting paid next to nothing for it.
It’s an interesting and unique indie game. It’s not my favorite, but it’s certainly different, which is always good.

Not going to lie, I actually enjoy this game quite a lot. I'm really surprised at all the negative reception it has. That's not to say it's flawless, but I'd actually probably say it's my favorite 3D Sonic game.
The worst issues with the game are the classic sonic levels, and a few cheap design issues in other levels, notably the water slide. The classic sonic levels are totally unneeded. Sonic Mania already came out and did it much better. Besides this, it's mostly rehashes anyways.
The story is absolutely terrible and I love it. It reminds me of a Saturday morning kid's cartoon I'd have watched when I was eight or nine. If I was ten years old again I probably would have been super into this game's story. Now I just find it impossible to take seriously and all the cringey dialogue combined with the hilariously bad music just kind of pushes into "So bad it's good" territory and I constantly have a dumb smile on my face. And to clarify, the music is bad in the shlocky dumb typical sonic music sense, it reminds me of playing Metal Gear Revengence and actually made me want to go back and replay it. The main villian is so edgy and the plot is very grimdark and just feels super unfitting which makes the dark stuff even funnier.
On the actual gameplay for modern sonic and the avatar, I don't have much to complain about. Modern Sonic is perhaps a bit too easy since his boost basically lets him steamroll over every level in a minute and a half. The avatar is surprisingly fun with the different weapon types, the grapple hook, and the level design usually works extremely well. A common complaint about Sonic was always that you'd run too fast and you'd end up hitting something you couldn't see which punished you for going too fast. The avatar levels alleviate this since you're unable to move quickly without whatever those treadmill looking things are. So you still get a taste of moving quickly and you're rewarded for it score wise. But you also have platforming so it's not just as easy as holding X/Square to boost.
If you grew up on the adventure games like I did, I'd say this is a fine game to return to the series with. It's not perfect, but it's easily one of the best 3D Sonic games. Though, I would reccomend you wait on a sale, as the content here IMO isn't quite long enough to justify $40. I paid $24 for it and I'm fairly pleased.

The stages were awesome and there were a lot of them, even the classic Sonic stages.  I liked the avatar idea and it was executed very well, even though it made me facepalm during the release trailers.
Changes or concerns I have:
Hard mode is too easy.  I understand, SEGA, that you are trying to introduce younger kids to Sonic games and that's perfectly fine but make a hard mode for the adults/ young adults who are playing the game and have played Sonic games before.  The bosses were the easiest part of the game but they were entertaining.
I was disappointed that at points it felt like I barely needed to make inputs.  I'm not trying to beg here but like please bring drifting back.  Throughout levels there were times when the movement changed to allow sharper turns without a drift.  Every once in a while that was totally needed even if there was a drift; however, drifting allows the player to feel like they're in control.
I'm ok with quicktime events; however, I feel they should have been things like A A B* or like different button presses instead of pressing any button at the correct time. Also, I believe quicktime events should have gotten increasingly harder.
Classic Sonic had a speed cap.
Verdict:
Even with the things I mentioned earlier the game is fun.  I found myself replaying the levels to get an S rank if I didn't the first time.  The graphics are stunning and the character models look super clean.
PS: "True dat" --Tails
PPS: Silver voice cracks every 5 seconds I swear.

tl;dr: Sonic Forces has a great sense of adrenaline paired with a surprisingly great mechanic in creating your own character and you will explore some great level design while listening to amazing electronic bleeps and bloops. And that for the purpose of stopping the probably edgiest character in Sonic history, for a team of cheesy one-note characters. And that in about 4 hours, unless you want to be a completionist in which case this game is a definite reccommendation.
Let me start this review by saying this: I am not really the biggest fan of Jump and Runs, sure I really like some, but I wouldn't call myself a pro. That said, this game made me feel like a Pro... most of the time.
This game has an incredible sense of adrenaline and freedom in it's level design and this is really what drew me to Sonic Forces. Every Grind Section/Obstacle Course/Level has multiple paths and ways to finish the level. This makes Sonic Forces feel like a bigger game then it actually is (sadly with it's short story time of about 4 hours), but if you have fun exploring the vastness of games and especially completing them (which I am far from done yet), then the Level Design shines through.
Especially in levels where you use your own Avatar andI must say, I thought this would be a turn-off, but for me the OC Levels are actually the most fun I had in this game. Customizing your character with clothes and weapons (or "wispons") is really fun, but how you use those wispons in-game change the way you play. There are many to choose from, some let you perform a series of jumps, some let you dash accross rings and enemies, some let you crawl up walls or create your own plattforms, this needless to say adds a ton of replayability to the OC Levels as you can try each level with a different (or even the same weapon) and come up with new ways to finish the course.
And the Soundtrack while you blast through these levels, what can I say about the Soundtrack. It is amazing, but sometimes unfitting for the situation. It's more electronic then previous Sonic OSTs, but whoever decided to make a Hardbass/Eurobeat Mash-up for one of the most dangerous parts in the story deserves a promotion because it fits like a glove and gets the cheeki breeki adrenaline pumping.
But some things will divide people. The story for example is incredibly cheesy, Sonic makes puns like there is no tomorrow, the villain "Infinite" is more edgy then Shadow listening to Linkin Park while ranting about how his parents don't understand him and the story is pretty rushed. That said, this can also be a plus, if you like the in-jokes in the Sonic Boom TV show, this is what you can expect only with a lot more Edge.
I said the level design was for the most part great, there are some parts where you go so fast... that you fall off an edge, bounce off to your death and the Past-Sonic 2D Levels.... where did the polish of Sonic Mania go? Those were really disappointing and actually an unwelcome addition to the game, I would have loved more OC or "Sonic Speed Boost" levels instead of pushing the 2-D Sonic on us, especially because it really can kill the momentum of the entire game at some points. (During the most critical part for 2-D sonics story they push a 1-minute long autoscrolling sequence in a 3 minute level along with a new mechanic that makes you go slow and one of the worst tracks on the OST, this is actually a severe blunder as it leaves you with a bad feeling about the entire point of 2-D Sonic)
The game is also pretty easy, even on Hard Mode that said there are some levels where for some reason you just can't explain why you don't get an S-Rank, when in a lot of levels you feel like you don't deserve one but you get it anyways.

Everytime I think it's over. Everytime I think I did it. It's not done. It will never be done. Let me say this game is so intense that it took me a year and half to finish it.
Let me start with the story. It is good, like really good. This game plays as if you are part of the movies. You are Ripleys daughter Ripley... Ripley 2 is just an awesome character. I really love her personality, she is just like Mom. So around 20 years after the first movie Ripley finds herself on a space station with a xenomorph. The synths are hostile, and so are most of the people. Which does not really make much sense. Regardless the Alien is following you the entire time, and since it is on a big space station it feel like a natural combo of Alien and Aliens.
Graphics look really good on PC as well. A 980ti will play this on Ultra with SMAAx1 at 2160p 60fps and it looks amazing. Everything is well textured and very detailed. The floors show the water streaks from mopping. The smoke effects and fire are very realistic. If it was not for the odd facial animations on people this would be flawless. The colours, the atmosphere, and high detail all add up to a incredibly immersive world.
Sound/music/voice are top notch. I have not played a game where the sound fx and music added so much. From the sounds coming from the ceiling to the heavy foots of the alien, to the screeching violens as you hide, to your breathing and the sirens going off around you. It makes the tensest momments of any movie/game. The voices are all done very well and all in all it is incredible. It is done so well that leaving an area I feel is "safer"my mind say please don't.
The gameplay is another story. You spend most of your time crawling and helpless. You hide, you craw to an area to only find out that way is blocked or the power is down ect... So you back track. Not really what you want to do when your animal assassin is constantly lurking. The sound of it over your head and ready to come down any momment. The fact that guns are worthless since all they do is make noise and noise is bad. Everything is out to get Ripley and I don't know why she keeps going, but that is how I should feel. This is a struggle, and Ripley is almost helpless but just keeps going. There is a lementing forboding feeling of death that is just so intense that it will have you scared and frustrated. I needed to take a break every 30mins to 2hours. Mind you scarey games do NOT typically bother me. Silent Hill, Resident Evil, Dying Light have kind of intense momments but not like this. This is the only game I have ever played and jumped in surprise and fear more times than one or fifty. I will say the back tracking does hurt the pacing of the story, but given the immersion through graphics and sound I found myself pushing through. Your best bet is to hide and take your time, but you will not want to.
Ripley is tough,strong, likable, and doing something that a man would not be able to as well. This is simply the strongest woman in any game. It dawned on me since she is smaller she can fit in areas a typical man could not. This type of thing saves her time and time again. Simply put my 220 pound self would not last long in this situation. My only gipe is it is haunting. The momments I have been through in this game will not leave my memory for as I long as I live. Like a momment I hid behind some crates and its tail almost grazed Ripleys face as it was passing through, or how about jumping into a vent just as it spots me. Getting to a hallway and saying to myself,"I don't want to do this. I don't want to do this. No. No. Oh god it is so close. I will just do it!" This is the norm and not even the worst of it but I don't want to give away any spoilers. This is without adought the most terrifying piece of media I have ever seen and I feel like I have been through it. I will leave you wilth this. The game scared my cat so bad in the first ten minutes I played it she leaves the room whenever she hears the Fox logo start. Oh and you do not even deal with an alien in the first ten minutes... She doesn't know the cat always lives in this series.

So what is it with this game?
Well put into easily + quickly to read categories it would look like this:


It is the year so and so in the future and you Amanda Ripley are trying to find your mother (Ellen Ripley from the Alien movies), who went missing after flying a mission for her company, several years ago. Now she is offered the chance to fly over to Sevastopol station, a space station that currently sojourns in the same system, where Ellen Ripley disappeared along with her crew. Said station turns out to be in grave distress, because an alien lifeform is on a killing spree inside. The residents and androids can be quite hostile, too. From there on out this mission becomes a lot more complex, while you sneek and fight your way through the different levels and towers of Sevastopol, to escape this nightmare and find closure...

+Perfect play of light and shadow
+Outstandingly designed space station, very close to the original movies
+Most textures are beautifully made
+Predominantly round objects...
-with some fierce exceptions
+System power per performance is the best; extremely optimised for PC (everything from a gtx 970 onward will allow you to play in 4k (Digital Super Resolution in my case) and that looks plain beautiful!
+Perfect Sound Design ->after some time you can cleary distinguish between the actions of the Alien, by simply listening to it i.e. cruising through the vents
+The music predominantly lives up to the soundtrack of the movies, especially of the first one, with only a few exceptions
+The music changes dynamically, depending on what situation you find yourself in...
-but sometimes makes the suspense unnecessarily great ;)
+The Alien is an unpredictable foe, getting more cunning with every difficulty setting
+The Alien is invincible, which may not appeal to some, but it dramatically improves the experience
+Humans can turn out to be friendly or unfriendly
+The motion tracker allows you to see movements of enemies around you, but it does not by any means guarantee your survival...
-Androids, especially the "Hazard"-Androids, are ridiculously hard to kill, unless you're willing to mobilize a lot of resources or ammunition
+XBOX 360 Controller support
+There are additional modes, which you can obtain through the DLCs:
>Crew Expendable and Lone Survivor let you relive the horrors of the first Alien movie
>Safe Haven puts you in one of the few safe rooms on Sevastopol and from there on you will have to scavange, activate machines and whatnot, while risking your life outside said room, to which you return after each task
>Survivor Mode puts you into a room somewhere on Sevastopol and you'll have to find your way to the goal
+Since the Alien is unpredictable, even veterans will find themselves clutching their wet input device of choice and frantically searching for a way out, or come to behold the face of a deadly adversary as it reveals its shiny teeth
+The Motion Tracker is a useful tool, well unless you play nightmare mode, but it'll make your heart race and may not stop haunting you so very soon...
+The Atmosphere is nothing short of captivating; both visuals and sound help you immerse yourself into the game
+After some time you may deem yourself safe from any threat, but the Alien learns, so especially playing on hard and above, you may not be able to hide in the same place twice...
+This game may not offer you the hot-headed mindless-shooting-vibe of games like Call of Duty, but it certainly let's you explore a thoughtfully constructed space station, while being haunted by a merciless killing machine
+even after countless hours of gameplay it is still worth trying again, or testing your survival abilities in the other modes
Have fun!

TW: Rome II is probably my favorite Total War game.  Out of all of the Total War games I have played, Rome II is one of the easiest and most simple games (campaign-wise) of the series. For many people its simplicity is one of the problems, but it should actually be something to be attracted to in this game since it makes the game easier to learn.
The game lacks family tree management and certain elements found in earlier games which takes away from some of the experience, but it creates something wonderful instead. Total War: ATTILA was released after this, has more of the features from earlier games (with some removed that are in this game), and is much more difficult while still using the same  map and principles found in Rome II.  Because of this, Rome II serves as a good way to learn the basics before tackling TW:Attila or another game in the series. In many ways, it is better than Napoleon and Empire because the tactics used in those are much different than the rest of the series.
As for the DLC, most of the DLC for Rome 2 is overpriced and some of it should have been included at release. If there is a sale, you should consider getting DLCs that interest you as they do add more depth to the game. Some people may say that the factions included are the same as others or have too few units, but this is only partially correct. The Greek States pack (Athens, Sparta, Epirus) can/will play almost exactly like the included Hellenic factions (Macedon, Massalia, Baktria, etc.) but will not be totally identical with the most obvious differences being in how campaigns progress. If diversity between factions (DLC or not) is not enough, there are plenty of good mods to expand unit rosters and tweak the game.
Overall:
PROS:
+Fun battles
+Good campaigns
+Good entry point to Total War series (ROME II is like TW: ATTILA with training wheels)
+Diversity between factions/cultures
+Steam workshop with many mods
CONS:
-Expensive
-DLC is overpriced
-Lacks more in-depth features of other games in the series
-Thermopylae was nerfed

DISCLAIMER: This review is entirely based on "Launch Early Access" (ignoring anything that happened in the Closed Betas).
What is Tree of Savior?
It is an Action Role Playing Game set in a Massively Multiplayer Online Role Playing -enviroment. Essentially an AMMORPG.
Why is this game an AMMORPG?
Because it has features from ARPG:
- Combat is action driven. You move to avoid hits and use skills that require aiming or positioning. The tempo isn't too challenging and you can easily play the game with a gamepad.
- The game is loot driven. Even in this version of the game there's plenty of different loot to be found both from world drops as well as dungeon bosses. The loot you find lasts quite long as the use of gear is limited by levels starting from 15,40,75... The gear however is not random generated, instead you are looking for the certain drops and crafting recipes.
- Tree of Savior has plenty of monster whacking. Either you are collecting silver (ingame currency), trying to find collectibles (that provide account-wide stat boosts), finding gear (as explained above) or simply grinding those 500 levels (280 currently).
And it has features from MMORPGs:
- It is strongly quest driven. You follow somewhat linear path from zone to zone (there's over 100 zones with different monsters and quests) completing quests and receiving silver and XP cards (Quest XP rewards which you can use when you please). Once you finish a zone you hop to the next one.
- The game has currently 4 servers each of which entails thousands of players and you actually see them ingame. Although there are channels the channels are only opened once there's enough players on the server. As such you will see other players and interact with them. Partying is beneficial and in dungeons it is a must.
- Tree of Savior has instanced dungeons. Although there are debates what the actual function of dungeons are (as they are at the moment limited to 2 entires per day) the instances are a nice change of pace and provide significant XP in order to reduce the grindy part of the game. Later on 90+ the instances become more difficult and provide unique item drops.
- Tree of Savior also carries a form of 'Trinity' where the classes are divided into Damage(Red)/Tank(Blue)/Support(Green) classes. Although it is not as strict as in other MMORPGs because it allow variations and leaves room for skillful gameplay. Playing a Swordsman tank doesn't necessary require you are fully "specced as tank" it only requires that you can control, avoid and when required take some blows.
How is Tree of Savior different from other MMORPGs?
- The 2D/2,5D aspect and the art style is very different from other games and at least for me the style is very appealing. It reminds me of Secret of Mana series namely the last in the series called Legend of Mana. The bosses look fantastic and even small monsters have nice details in them. Pets are goshdarn cute and this comes from someone who generally barfs  at cuteness. It fits the game however.
- Class system. Now this is the make or break part of the game. Either you absolutely LOVE IT or HATE IT. There's no middle ground with the class system.
1) Eventually there will be 80 classes. At the moment there's more than plenty 50+ or so. The classes are divided into ranks and you character can have three "circles" of certain class at most. Meaning if you really really want to be a Swordsman you can pick the Swordsman class from the start and then 2 times at any rank up. Until you reach "3rd Circle" with is the maximum. In the next rank up you'll need to select another class. You don't have to always go for the "3rd Circle" 1-2 is more tha enough. You could for example be a Swordsman(Rank1)-Swordsman(Rank2)-Swordsman(Rank3)-Highlander(Rank1)-... or Swordsman(R1)-Highlander(R1)-Highlander(R2)-Highlander(R3)-... or Swordsman(R1)-Highlander(R1)-Swordsman(R2)-Highlander(R2)-... Once you reach R7 (eventually R10) your character will become this supreme mixed martial arts master that kicks butt in many a different ways. Nothing you have learned is pointless, instead your skillbar is formed through the selection of your classes.
2) However the game requires you to plan ahead. There's no resetting your chosen classes and it is entirely possible to screw up your character with poor synergies. You will need read forums/websites to get a general grasp of things in order to build a decent character. This said it is not _that_ difficult and once you get hang of the system it really becomes Child's Play
has many tools that help you understand the game). The class system in Tree of Savior has a lot of potential and allows you to make your "own class" but it also requires you to understand the game and its' mechanics. Which makes the game _difficult to get started with_. Of course you can YOLO into the fray and accept that your first character might not become the Savior of the Tree ;)
Reasons to play/buy Tree of Savior:
1) You've enjoyed Ragnarok Online. (Stop reading and start playing!)
2) You enjoy different, new and refreshing classes in MMORPGs. Pirate class that literally makes your party a group of bandits? Chronomancer that reverts the flow of time and spawns monster that were killed earlier? Druid that changes the terrain in order to change into their foes and use their abilities? Thamathurgist that enlarges a monster making it give more rewards, or increases your damage by making your hand double in size? Linker that forms chains between monsters causing them to share the damage taken? This list goes on and the classes not yet added to game will feature even more suprising abilities...
3) You love the art direction of the game.
4) You enjoy quest/mob grinding.
5) You love games that have longterm goals and not everything is given out as welfare.
6) You respect a company that listens to its' fans and fixes big problems ASAP.
7) You just want a decent F2P AMMORPG (Goes F2P April 28th).
Reasons to avoid this game as if it were the plague:
1) You don't enjoy quest/mob grinding.
2) You want everything not tomorrow but yesterday.
3) You have no patience to do background work for a game. This isn't your average pick up and play punch club.
4) You hate the art style.
5) ARPG / MMORPG are not your "thing".
6) You read this review fully and are still undecided.
P.S The game does have some "wierd" design choices in regards to auction house/trading/dungeons but these are certainly work-in-progress and IMC has already fixed some of the issues that players were unhappy about (for example monster spawn rate).

I'll start first by saying that I played this game initially on PS4 when it released on console. I played ESO on console for about a year and a half. Eventually I quit, not due to ESO, just sick of the console experience. Once I built my pc, I told myself "DO NOT BUY ESO AGAIN." There are some bugs and inbalances here and there (like with all games of this size). And after experiencing some of the same bugs over and over on console, I needed a break. I decided to play other games on PC for a few months.
Well after sometime, I could NOT resist the urge to plunge back into the world that this game provides. For me, the PVP experience and the community are more than enough to keep me coming back for more. I now have 200+ hours logged on the PC version, not the mention the countless hours I spent on the console version.
The game is a MMO with the Elder Scrolls world laid on top of it. And I love that. The world itself is down right beautiful. There is so much to do from Crafting, Farming, Bank system, Guilds and Guild Traders to make money. All the weapon and armor sets you could ever want to farm or craft yourself.
The PVE portion is vast and fun. But for me, the PVP is where I spend majority of my time. And finding an active and fun guild makes a world a difference. Small-Scale PVP "Battlegrounds" are coming soon with the Morrowind Expansion (which you must buy seperately and NO Eso+ subscription will not get your Morrowind).
If you are thinking about this buying this game, ask yourself:
Do I enjoy MMOS?
Do I enjoy crafting?
Do I enjoy being social?
Do I enjoy PVP?
If those are a yes, try it out! If you are jumping over from other MMORPGs, please do. You won't be dissappointed. If you are new MMOs, try it! The community is great and can help with anything you need to know.
You can spend as little or as much time as you'd like playing ESO, and You will enjoy it.
Personally, I don't see myself quitting this game for a long time. I'm enjoying everytime I log on. There's always something to do. Something to work towards. Gold to earn. Skills to hone. Enemies to fight. And If you find yourself amongst like-minded people in a Guild, it makes it all that much sweeter.
EDIT: 800+ hours in. Still love this game. Sure, it still has some issues. But finding a great guild anf having a blast in pvp and trials, it's still incredibly addicting and fun.

I like this game a lot, definitely one of my favorites. If you rush through the campaign expect 4-6hrs of gameplay, but much much more if you are someone who goes for 100% completion. Once you complete the game you can create new Avatars to rank up for wardrobe purposes and achievements. There are 30 levels (including bosses) and each has a distinct feel with some repeated ones that are played through using a different main character (Burst Sonic, Classic Sonic, or your Avatar). Also there are missions that after completing certain requirements unlock more clothing/wispons (weapons) for your Avatar.
Factoring in getting S rank, all the collectables, completing secret stages and ranking up Avatars not to mention the daily missions that can give score multipliers this game does come packed with replayablity, it's a game not meant to be binged through but maybe play a little bit at a time and strive for that 100% completion.
The biggest downside is the classic levels, aside from feeling a little out of place the reliance of a joystick when using a gamepad can create some frustration if you are not precise. Although in due time I expect to play through them without trouble I find the pacing compared to the burst sonic/avatar stages unpleasant.
Overall, I say I really like this game and put it next to Sonic Generations as definitely in my top 5.

I went in to this game hearing a lot of mixed things about its quality but I wound up really liking it. The shorter levels fixed my biggest complaint with the end game of Generations where the stages dragged on too long. The avatar stages aren't as great as the rest of the game but nowere near "bad" like I was hearing.
Overall I liked my time with this game, short and sweet with a goofy plot, a real good followup to Generations and a step in the right direction from Lost World.

Ok so as a disclaimer: I generally like the 3D Sonic games. There are obvious exceptions to this like Sonic '06, but I don't want to live in a world where Sonic '06 is the bar that Sonic Team is going for. I thought Unleashed was okay and Generations was pretty good.
Performance: I expected a little better from the game. I would like to think that an i7-7700K, 16GB RAM, and a GTX 1070 would be enough to get me at least 60fps, but apparently not. Some levels in this game chug like crazy, even when running on the lowest graphic settings. Granted I am running the game in 4k; but if I can get rock solid 60fps from Generations then I'd like to think that would also be achievable here too, especially when this game doesn't look *that* much better than Generations.
Level design: A regression for sure. Modern Sonic levels basically have no platforming sections at all, the game frequently takes control away from you (my favourite was when control was taken away so that Sonic could go around a corner. I mean
), and the levels are short. REALLY short. The shortness is exacerbated by the frequency in which control is removed from the player or sections that are basically on rails.
The custom avatar levels are probably some of the better offerings here, with a customisable weapon that is obviously there to encourage replayability. Problem is that you start off with the best weapon in the game (flamethrower). I did try to experiment with the other weapons available, but they were either less powerful than what I already had, or made me lose control (the drill weapon once sent me flying miles off in to the distance where I then fell to my death).
There aren't many boss fights in the game. I guess Infinite the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ is supposed to be the main villain, but all of his fights play out more or less the same. In fact there are a lot of bosses that just involve boosting + homing attacks to win.
There is some free "Episode Shadow" DLC which is like three levels long. One of those levels is probably an example of one of the better levels in the game, but otherwise you're not missing a whole lot if you give it a miss. The game recycles levels A LOT, so I hope you like the few that are here.
Control: at best, it is worse than Generations, at worst it is inconsistent, or at least it doesn't feel consistent. I actually went back and played Generations just to try and validate these feelings, and sure enough for some reason in Generations I feel like I have good control of the character, but not so in Forces.
Story: Ughhhh. Yeah feel free to ignore most of this. I'm not going to sit here and pretend that Sonic games have expertly crafted stories but this is pretty dreadful. I'm guessing Sega really went overboard and let an actual 12 year old design and write the lines for Infinite the edgelord. He is just the most dreadful character. Most of the plot is told in the level select menu as two characters just talking to each other.
Conclusion: Why did I buy this? Because I liked Generations and kind of hoped this would be similar. It is not. Do not buy this. Go and buy/replay Generations instead if you have a hankering for a 3D Sonic game. I can't in good conscience recommend this unless it's on sale and very cheap. Like less-than $15 cheap.

Introduction:
Paperwork, the worst kind of work you will ever face once you get a job, it's boring, tedious and can make a man/woman insane. So how can a game about paperwork be one of the BEST games I've ever played?!
It's a game that requires a good eye for detail, patience and vigilance (no slacking!) This is a game that is both simple and complex at the same time.
PROS:
+ Immersive: - Unlike other games where you feel detached from the characters, Papers, Please will really really make you feel like you're there making a difference.
+ Consequence based Story: - The story, if you look at it from a distance, is simple. Yet each and every decision you make affects the overall story. The morality system in this game is one of the best I've seen as of late.
+ Simple but effective Artstyle: - It's pixel art but it does the job well in conveying it's message. Most people would appreciate its simplicity.
+ Surprisingly complex mechanic: - The game is not a simple approve and reject kind of thing. Each and every aspect of the unique immigrants who tries to enter needs to be inspected (from the face, the name, the weight, height, place of origin etc.). The game WILL know if you missed something and promptly gives you a citation for it.
CONS:
- Story is a bit short: - It would have been best if the story was stretched out more than it did. Although an endless mode is unlocked, I still think more side stories, more in-game events and more time could have been added. It has a lengthy gameplay, don't get me wrong.
- Needs more sound: - The base music in this game is good and does its job well. I do feel they should add a wee bit more. Not a whole orchestra, but an alternative to the usual thing.
CONCLUSION:
"Don't Judge a Game because of it's graphics" is a phrase that would wholly apply to Papers, Please.
It's a great game for a good price and a good re-playability and experience value.
MUST HAVE.

Papers, Please is one of 2013's new cult classics and I'd say for good reason. You play the role of an inspector at the border checkpoint of two fictional Soviet sattelite states. The game itself is pretty simple. You look over doucments and look for anything out of place. As you progress there are more things you have to look out for, and eventually you will have the choice to arrest and even defend your checkpoint with a sniper rifle and a tranq gun. Game Informer put it well. There is just something oddly satisfying about locking up a terrorist or finding something wrong with someones passport. The game also gives a good look into what sattelite states were like in the 1980's. Overall I think Papers is a good game, albeit short. While the game is short (the entire game takes place within just thirty one days), there are twenty possible endings so the replay value certainly is there. If you got ten bucks lying around, and you like puzzles and games that present you with moral decisions, then Papers, Please is definitely a good choice to spend that ten bucks on.

This game is by far one of my favorite survival-horror games and i would recommend it to any fans of the alien movies.
Graphics: 8.7/10 I think the graphics are amazing, very reminiscent of the movies, however there is some clipping with the doorways and the aliens tail. Every thing else graphic-wise is solid.
Gameplay: 9.5/10 The alien is amazingly adaptable to ANY situation and/or player. It is unpredictable where it will go at any moment unless you are a veteran of this game. the working joes are arguably the most annoying aspect of this game because they are Very hard to kill for a beginner of the game, especially when being stalked by the alien. The ability to lean out of hiding is a nice feature as well. The crafting system is the part of this game i personally feel conflicted about, like how a molotov costs sensors. The map isn't the best i have seen but it works. sort of. expect to use a few walkthroughs to figure out where you are going.
Audio: 8.5/10 The sound effects are really good, from the footsteps of the alien to the weapon sounds,the sounds in this game are realistic and have minimal bugs. The music is also very good at building up suspense although is a bit overpowering compared to the volume of the rest of the audio. the ambiance is also good at setting the tone of a creepy ship that is in the process of falling to pieces.
Controls: 8/10 This game is best played with a controller, however it has keyboard/mouse support. The controls remind me of your typical console game controls, with a few changes to help with new features such as leaning out of cover.
Overall: 8.6/10 An amazing game by far, you can tell a lot of work went into making this game, I personally got this game on sale for $12.49 however i probably would have saved up for it as well had the sale not happened.

Was looking forward to this game after seeing it delayed for a pc port.  The mouse input was still the worst I have EVER seen in any game, ever. There really seems to be no effort put into it, now they are releasing a completely different version of this and screwing everyone over.

The bad:
Dated Console graphics. Even on max settings, this game looks like its from 2010. Very low poly count on everything from terrain, objects and characters.
Horrid level design. Not only are the levels serious gated and filled with invisible walls and barriers, the layout and flow of the areas is just awful. I easily walked into the EXIT of 3 different areas before I found the ENTRANCE to those areas. Which was odd, because you read messages by players saying "Watch out for XYZ" only, you are going in reverse so XYZ isnt there. Scripted events dont see to trigger if you dont go in from the right direction. The first game seemed to have more direction to it, this game seems to think that putting you blindfolded into a maze for no reason, is awesome.
Frustrating controls. Yes, I played this game with a 360 controller. I also tried keyboard/mouse (which was worse). Half of this games "challenge" isnt from learning boss fights, or where traps are. Its from fighting the ridiculous, buggy, glitchy, awkward controls. They are very unintuitive, and often times you find yourself fighting with them just to move in the right direction, or perform the task you want. Whoever thought making "Jump" as a sequence of holding down dash, while pushing down on one of the analog sticks (ie: L3) was a good idea, should be fired from game development.
Annoying sound. Aside from the music, the sound in this game is just irritating. Walking through any grass sounds like someone is ripping sheets of paper next to your ear. Most combat sounds are sudden and out of place, and VERY unrealistic sounding. You will hear creatures growl or moan and it sounds like they are right next to you, only they are not. Even the voice acting is subpar (not awful, just rather meh).
Co-op stupidity. Again, whatever "game" designer had the bright idea to do co-op the way they do in this game, needs to be removed from the industry. Its just a lesson in being let down and irritation. There is ZERO reason for it, aside from some game designer trying to leave their mark by implimenting an idea that simply shouldnt have made it past the design table.
The good.
Pretty much any of the "good" aspects of this game are watered down versions of the first game. It feels like you are eating leftovers from a great meal the previous night, that didnt reheat very well.
Even for the 15 dollars I paid for this game, I just dont enjoy it enough to keep playing it. I dont feel driven to beat the challenge like I did with the first one, and nearly all of the gameplay elements just annoy me, rather than that well known "ARgh!!! I WILL beat this guy" frustration that made the first one fun. The first one left me wanting to know and see what comes next, this game only makes me not care what comes next.

Transistor throws the player in an unique artistic sci fi world, where your main task is to fight through the enemy lines called "the process". You play the game from a top down view with a simple 4 button active skill system and you can move around with WASD or by simply clicking with the cursor on the ground. But what sounds like done a thousand times, becomes very special very soon.
One of the specialties of the game is an ability called Turn. You can activate it via the space button and you can chain up movements and abilities, positioning you right where you want to be. Your moves are then executed at an accelerated speed compared to the normal combat. But after that your abilities are all in cool down for some time until the Turn is recharged, unless you invest to build around it.
However, you can also fight without the Turn system. Depending on your fighting style, enemy type and your build you might prefer the Turn based combat or the simple point and click combat similar but not the same as games like the Diablo series or Path of Exile.
For me the thing that makes Transistor stand out is the build system. You have access to a variety of skills, called functions and slot them in up to 4 active slots. Each active slot has a passive slot to modify the function. You can unlock additional upgrades further down the road, including passive slots that either effect your functions further or give you additional passive properties in the form of trigger effects or constant passive bonuses. On each save point, called access point, you can redesign your build. And they are plentiful distributed throughout the game.
Experimenting with builds is really much fun and opens up a lot of possibilities. But having many options doesn't necessarily mean they all make sense. And while this may be the case for some combinations (at least I couldn't make them work), most of the possibilities can be highly effective. I for example went from a damage over time tank/self heal build over an insane spike damage build to a build, where I make the process my ally for some seconds and add a self heal effect when they are close to me.
If you then lose all your life, you will lose one of your 4 active function. That is called overload. When you have no function left any more, you are officially defeated. Basically with 4 functions equipped you have 3 additional lives until you finally die and restart at the last access point. But you might not have all 4 active functions equipped due to limitations like the memory space (MEM) each function takes up in active and passive slots.
In addition to the functions, you can apply limiters. There are different limiters who let you earn more experience but also increase the difficulty, making the process spawn in higher numbers, deal more damage or let you overload more functions when your life bar hits 0 and more. This allows you to edit the kind of difficulty to have a higher experience gain. I currently play the game a 2nd time and have all limiters applied, giving me a big experience bonus but making the game significantly more difficult.
The world is very romantic, dreamy and at times dark, although ***deleted for spoiling reasons***. The game is accompanied by a narrator trapped in your sword, called transistor, and beautiful visuals and music. Over all this creates a very enchanting atmosphere while you venture through a very lonely city, however, you never feel quite alone. I for myself could not find a stopping point, on which I should take a break and that let me to discover one main weak point of the game. The story is very short and you can expect to finish the game in one or two nights. The story is linear, as far as I can tell, and therefor it doesn't give much incentive to try it again, unless you want to try out other builds, what can make the experience of the game indeed very very different, especially with the limiters.
- unique skill and combat system
- beautiful story telling
- graphics and sound form an elegant atmosphere
- very short story
- lacking introduction in gameplay mechanics

Basically, this is Bastion with a "software" theme. The art and music are outstanding, though very similar to Bastion, as is the attention to detail.
There are loads and loads of programming references, which I found absolutely delightful, being a software engineer.
You don't have to be a software engineer to enjoy the game, though. Like Bastion, the game is perfectly accessible to anyone. It's been described as an RPG-lite, but there's plenty of gameplay complexity. The combat is a mix between ARPG and TBS.
There are even a few "puzzles" (game calls them "tests") thrown in, where you are challenged to win a fight by utilizing your abilities in specific ways. These tests are a way of educating you on the combat mechanics.
There's plenty of strategy involved, including the ability to make combat more difficult in exchange for a small exp bonus. I played at effectively the highest difficult setting and enjoyed the challenge. I'm probably going to continue through the second playthrough for additional challenge.
The first playthrough is fairly short, but never feels tedious, either. The second playthrough can be taken to extend play time by quite a bit. I like the game length. Some might complain about the price point, but I think it's fair for a quality indie title like this.
There are stability issues at the moment, but they are rapidly being patched, so I expect those to mostly be resolved soon. I mainly encountered problems with the optional "tests" deadlocking (?) and requiring manual process termination. Glancing at the forums, this seems to be related to the online features, which are understandably more difficult to test prior to release, so it's not exactly fair to ask "don't these people test their game?"
Also, there's not much character development and no real character interaction (though there's plenty of good voiceover). Some might miss that, but it didn't bother me. The focus is on atmosphere. I liked the way the game slowly revealed the backstory and made you work for some of it - revealing character biographies if you used your abilities in different ways.
I liked the story, though I may be biased given the theme :)
In conclusion, I highly recommend this.
Disclaimer: I only played 30 minutes into Bastion so far, so I'm not very qualified to compare the two titles. (Yeah, I know, I'll get around to finishing it eventually)

I have yet to see a more seemless integration between gameplay and story than found in Transistor. The metaphors are as endless as the fun and just as colorful as the artwork.
Transistor is a thinking person's game as it creates puzzles through combat, atmostphere through prose and deep story through seemless gameplay.
To me, the best games either create more games or are too complex to ever describe to a layman of video games. Transistor is the latter, but I humbly suggest everyone picking it up and humming along with Red for an unforgettable experience.

After playing through the story and using the recursion mode I can safely say that Supergiant Games has done it again. After Bastion I felt that whatever game they would make next would get overhyped, and Transistor did. But the thing is that it lived up to it's hype.
The gameplay is a unique mix of real time and turn based combat that blend perfectly together. The upgrade system is so mindblowingly amazing that you will want to keep trying new combinations. The Limiter system works like the Idols from Bastion and adds a whole other level of difficulty into the game. They also include challenges that provide a fun distraction from the story and they also provide the greatest award ever: the soundtrack.
The soundtrack is just amazing. I have yet to see a developer that can make a better sountrack than Supergiant can. The mix of songs is great. The vocal ones, sung by the main character Red, are all connected to the story and make moments in the game beutiful, especially the ending.
The voice acting also deserves an A+. Logan Cunningham, the voice of Rucks in Bastion, comes back and blesses us with narrating the game through the Transistor. All the characters that speak are so well voice acted that you will wonder why other games do not have this amount of quality in them.
The story in Transistor deserves some kind of award. The amount of storytelling put into this game is overwhelming. From picking up tidbits of information from the OVC terminals to putting functions() in an active slot, upgrade slot, or passive slot so you can upgrade more of those character bios that are masterfully written. The ending is beutiful but does leave some questions lingering in your head.
In reality the only thing bringing this game down is that the counter on the ball resets when you do Recursion mode.
10/10

Overall, I do recommend this game. It's fun, and despite what some people are saying, the game does have some challenge to it. If you want a hard time, do all the extra missions. Some of them will have you pulling hairs out trying to get that perfect run.
Boost Formula is at its best here, exploration is rewarded, for the few extra paths offered, and the custom character is by far the best part of the game. A little more variety in races and abilities would've been kind of cool, but the system as is, is solid fun.
Now, to the negatives
And almost all of them revolve around the story and its execution.
So many plotholes, so much wasted story potential, and so much unnecessary edge. I love the Sonic Franchise, and Forces is a perfectly serviceable game.
It's just a shame to realize that THIS was Sonic's chance to stop being a byword, and to grow into something new. Only a few tweaks here and there, and this could have easily been a 10/10.
The phantom ruby was utterly indecisive in what it was supposed to be and what powers it had.
Tails was an uncharacteristically scared and worthless brat on camera
The few dark moments that could have made a compelling story were delivered in the most boring ways possible (See: White text and black screen explaining how everything went to heck. Would've been infinitely better to have a short 15 second or so clip of Eggman laughing his portly posterior off as his phantom forces bowl through multiple cities and towns), and then immediately contradicted in the next cutscene (SONIC IS ALIVE!! No really, I didn't spoil it for you if you haven't got past the first cutscene. They tell you immediately afterwards)
Infinite couldn't be bothered to remember our own OC on 3 separate occasions in a row (1 cutscene, the fight with him, and then the cutscene after).
The fact that the oc has their own phantom ruby is almost completely glossed over except for at the very end and then we break it.
Infinite gets replaced as the final boss by ANOTHER big robot with arms, and his backstory was horrifically bland and under developed.
From a technical standpoint, I only have one thing of note: Watch your platforming because Sonic, Classic, and the OC have very limited horizontal momentum in the air and on the ground. It made for so many moments of rage.
This game could've been UTTERLY amazing.
As it is, it's okay.
The fact that the Super Sonic transformation has to be DOWNLOADED SEPARATELY should raise some eyebrows, though.
You know, the super all powerful gems that the Doctor has always been after. The ones that POWER MACHINERY, grant wishes, and give the user super powers? Things the leaders of Forces would know about and would seek out in force after Sonic's demise?
I recommend Sonic Forces for the gameplay.
The story, however, is just good for some cheap laughs and for the occassional one-liners that strike gold.

TL;DR: It's a cat and mouse game... and you are not the cat!
Alien: Isolation is the first person survival horror, so don't expect to run around with a pulse rifle shooting hundreds of monsters. Alien: Isolation is a little different, it focuses on the first movie, Ridley Scott’s Alien.
As Amanda Ripley, your goal is to use the darkness and crawlspaces to avoid detection by humans, androids and alien alike as you slowly piece together events, find out what happened to Ellen Ripley and get off the station. The whole story is scary, exciting and strong, with some surprising twists.
Though gun use is not essential you are granted one early on, however it is just a handgun with very limited ammo which you quickly learn is not as useful as one would hope, rather ineffective against the androids and pointless to use against the Alien, making more noise than necessary which in turn attracts even more enemies. Instead there is a decent selection of tools to use to your advantage, many of which make a noise or other type of distraction to spare you a few lifesaving moments by using it to your advantage to attract and distract enemies.
Fans of the film will certainly be pleased with the overall presentation, the game being littered with movie references. Halls of the space station ravaged by the preceding fights, crates left without purpose, doors waiting patiently to hiss open, the chattering robots and old green pixelated display screens, lots of brown leather jackets and clinical white corridors and of course the towering black death that is the Alien, never looking better!
Overall verdict:
Highly recommended!

After spending more than 45 hours on this game, I have to say it's one of the best and SCARIEST games I've ever played. Throughout almost the entire game, there's a feeling of constant, terrifying tension and dread, as you have no idea where the Alien is or when it will pop up. But not only is it the Alien you have to worry about, but the HUGE uncertainty of the other NPC characters on board the ship. Some could be nice and helpful and give you items you need to craft vital items, whereas some, as soon as you're seen, will try and kill you and loot your items.
Some of the negative things about the game were:
1. The Alien's VERY annoying AI pattern
When you're trying to fix an elevator, or get a security card needed to open a door, you're BOUND to run into the Alien and have to hide. But the problem with this is that you would (at times) only have literally a three second window to escape. Sometimes, instead of it being scary, it became very annoying, with the fact that you would just keep dying, and dying, and dying, over and over again. Soon enough, I found that I wasn't even scared by that one specific point anymore because of the amount of times I've had to repeat it, and that it simply became annoying.
2. The game's EXTREMELY LONG length
Although it is very entertaining, with so much to do throughout the entire game, one thing that wasn't a good thing about the game was it's enormous length. In the first part of the game, and someway to the end, it became very intense and scary and it was good. The ending was also AMAZING and that really added to the already amazing game. But around almost the entire middle of the game was literally just trying to get into elevators, but they need security cards, you get the security card, but then while riding it, the elevator breaks, and you have to take detour, after detour, after detour, and eventually, you start to think "WHEN WILL THIS GAME END". It's fresh at the start, and amazing towards the finish, but the meat in between seems to just drag on, and on, and on, quickly running out of ideas, and just making the game seem exhausting to play, which is not a good thing when you want people to ENJOY the game, not feel like it's a chore.
My verdict: I would recommend it to a friend that enjoys having the♥♥♥♥♥♥scared out of them HEAPS, but also a friend that doesn't mind the length of the game.

Papers, Please is a prime example that a game does not need a big budget to be great.
Who would've though stamping papers in a border checkpoint box could be fun? The game has a very original concept and it does an amazing job of making a very mundane task appear thrilling and exciting. You start out as an immigration officer working in a border checkpoint of a communist country. The pay is abysmal and you have to provide for your whole family. When money's short, do you take bribes to keep you family fed and warm, or do you sacrifice their well-being for your own moral high ground? The game is full of such decisions that have long-lasting effects. The game starts with a simple task of checking entrant's passports then starts adding more and more rules to remember. Making more than two mistakes means you get fined, which can quicly drive you bankrupt. These challenges only make the gameplay more compelling though and you start to develop a sense of pride for your job. The constant narrative implications your actions have make for a very thrilling experience from the beginning to end.
The retro visual style of the game fits perfectly and adds a certain atmosphere to it that enhances the narrative setting. The soundtrack may be small in quantity, but the few tracks set the communist theme amazingly well.
The only real issue I had while playing this game was the repetitive nature of the gameplay, which I started to notice towards the end of the game. It is but a small blemish on an otherwise wonderful experience however.

TL:DR;
A game that was well ahead of its time, technically and thematically, and has an active modding community and positive reviews to this very day. Highly recommend checking this out, no matter what genre you're a fan of; there really is something here for everyone.
FACTS:
Released in 2007
Inspired "[by] the popular science fiction novella Roadside Picnic by Boris and Arkady Strugatsky and the 1979 Andrei Tarkovsky film Stalker that was loosely based on it, as well as Stalker, the film's subsequent novelization by the original authors. -Wikipedia, sue me
METACRITIC: 82, 8.4 User Score
Hell, even IGN gave it an 8.2. (and they were whining about the technical limitations of an open-world FPS RPG made by indie developers in 200-and-flipping-7, and how the almost non-existent cutscenes were "badly compressed" despite the fact that Half Life proved you don't need cutscenes for a story to be told well.)
________________________________________________________________________________
What the hell CANT you say about STALKER? Its critically renowned, a cult classic, STILL has an active modding community almost 9 years later, helped jumpstart the open-world RPG FPS genre mixture, has one of the most haunting and memorable atmospheres I've ever experienced in any form of media (and I'm a fan of horror) AND your crumb-filled, burnt-smelling toaster can run it now!
Raving over a personal favorite of mine aside, whatever you don't initially like about this game, you'll come to like. What you won't come to like, you can mod out, or, in (a surprisingly large amount) some cases, in. Some things just can't be fixed however.
Yes, it is open world.
Yes, there are fences and loading screens between areas.
Yes, it has an in-depth story, chock full of lore,personality, dark humor, and some pretty mature themes.
Yes, most of it is behind walls of text that instead of reading, you'd rather be AH NUUUU CHEEKI BREEKI-ing the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of mutants.
Yes, there are not a lot of guns.
Yes, you can mod more in / mod them to feel better/more realistic.
Yes, it can be buggy/glitchy/graphically dated.
Yes, the fans have solved all three problems (mostly).
Basically, pretty much any problem you have with the game can be solved by either sucking it up (which, in gaming, you shouldn't really be expected to), mod it in/out, or learn to love it.
While it certainly has it cons, this is the one game I'm willing to overlook the glaring problems it has in favor of the spectacularly good parts of it.

And what it does right? Oh, it does it so... sooooooo right.
