Transistor throws the player in an unique artistic sci fi world, where your main task is to fight through the enemy lines called "the process". You play the game from a top down view with a simple 4 button active skill system and you can move around with WASD or by simply clicking with the cursor on the ground. But what sounds like done a thousand times, becomes very special very soon.
One of the specialties of the game is an ability called Turn. You can activate it via the space button and you can chain up movements and abilities, positioning you right where you want to be. Your moves are then executed at an accelerated speed compared to the normal combat. But after that your abilities are all in cool down for some time until the Turn is recharged, unless you invest to build around it.
However, you can also fight without the Turn system. Depending on your fighting style, enemy type and your build you might prefer the Turn based combat or the simple point and click combat similar but not the same as games like the Diablo series or Path of Exile.
For me the thing that makes Transistor stand out is the build system. You have access to a variety of skills, called functions and slot them in up to 4 active slots. Each active slot has a passive slot to modify the function. You can unlock additional upgrades further down the road, including passive slots that either effect your functions further or give you additional passive properties in the form of trigger effects or constant passive bonuses. On each save point, called access point, you can redesign your build. And they are plentiful distributed throughout the game.
Experimenting with builds is really much fun and opens up a lot of possibilities. But having many options doesn't necessarily mean they all make sense. And while this may be the case for some combinations (at least I couldn't make them work), most of the possibilities can be highly effective. I for example went from a damage over time tank/self heal build over an insane spike damage build to a build, where I make the process my ally for some seconds and add a self heal effect when they are close to me.
If you then lose all your life, you will lose one of your 4 active function. That is called overload. When you have no function left any more, you are officially defeated. Basically with 4 functions equipped you have 3 additional lives until you finally die and restart at the last access point. But you might not have all 4 active functions equipped due to limitations like the memory space (MEM) each function takes up in active and passive slots.
In addition to the functions, you can apply limiters. There are different limiters who let you earn more experience but also increase the difficulty, making the process spawn in higher numbers, deal more damage or let you overload more functions when your life bar hits 0 and more. This allows you to edit the kind of difficulty to have a higher experience gain. I currently play the game a 2nd time and have all limiters applied, giving me a big experience bonus but making the game significantly more difficult.
The world is very romantic, dreamy and at times dark, although ***deleted for spoiling reasons***. The game is accompanied by a narrator trapped in your sword, called transistor, and beautiful visuals and music. Over all this creates a very enchanting atmosphere while you venture through a very lonely city, however, you never feel quite alone. I for myself could not find a stopping point, on which I should take a break and that let me to discover one main weak point of the game. The story is very short and you can expect to finish the game in one or two nights. The story is linear, as far as I can tell, and therefor it doesn't give much incentive to try it again, unless you want to try out other builds, what can make the experience of the game indeed very very different, especially with the limiters.
- unique skill and combat system
- beautiful story telling
- graphics and sound form an elegant atmosphere
- very short story
- lacking introduction in gameplay mechanics

Basically, this is Bastion with a "software" theme. The art and music are outstanding, though very similar to Bastion, as is the attention to detail.
There are loads and loads of programming references, which I found absolutely delightful, being a software engineer.
You don't have to be a software engineer to enjoy the game, though. Like Bastion, the game is perfectly accessible to anyone. It's been described as an RPG-lite, but there's plenty of gameplay complexity. The combat is a mix between ARPG and TBS.
There are even a few "puzzles" (game calls them "tests") thrown in, where you are challenged to win a fight by utilizing your abilities in specific ways. These tests are a way of educating you on the combat mechanics.
There's plenty of strategy involved, including the ability to make combat more difficult in exchange for a small exp bonus. I played at effectively the highest difficult setting and enjoyed the challenge. I'm probably going to continue through the second playthrough for additional challenge.
The first playthrough is fairly short, but never feels tedious, either. The second playthrough can be taken to extend play time by quite a bit. I like the game length. Some might complain about the price point, but I think it's fair for a quality indie title like this.
There are stability issues at the moment, but they are rapidly being patched, so I expect those to mostly be resolved soon. I mainly encountered problems with the optional "tests" deadlocking (?) and requiring manual process termination. Glancing at the forums, this seems to be related to the online features, which are understandably more difficult to test prior to release, so it's not exactly fair to ask "don't these people test their game?"
Also, there's not much character development and no real character interaction (though there's plenty of good voiceover). Some might miss that, but it didn't bother me. The focus is on atmosphere. I liked the way the game slowly revealed the backstory and made you work for some of it - revealing character biographies if you used your abilities in different ways.
I liked the story, though I may be biased given the theme :)
In conclusion, I highly recommend this.
Disclaimer: I only played 30 minutes into Bastion so far, so I'm not very qualified to compare the two titles. (Yeah, I know, I'll get around to finishing it eventually)

I have yet to see a more seemless integration between gameplay and story than found in Transistor. The metaphors are as endless as the fun and just as colorful as the artwork.
Transistor is a thinking person's game as it creates puzzles through combat, atmostphere through prose and deep story through seemless gameplay.

After playing through the story and using the recursion mode I can safely say that Supergiant Games has done it again. After Bastion I felt that whatever game they would make next would get overhyped, and Transistor did. But the thing is that it lived up to it's hype.
The gameplay is a unique mix of real time and turn based combat that blend perfectly together. The upgrade system is so mindblowingly amazing that you will want to keep trying new combinations. The Limiter system works like the Idols from Bastion and adds a whole other level of difficulty into the game. They also include challenges that provide a fun distraction from the story and they also provide the greatest award ever: the soundtrack.
The soundtrack is just amazing. I have yet to see a developer that can make a better sountrack than Supergiant can. The mix of songs is great. The vocal ones, sung by the main character Red, are all connected to the story and make moments in the game beutiful, especially the ending.
The voice acting also deserves an A+. Logan Cunningham, the voice of Rucks in Bastion, comes back and blesses us with narrating the game through the Transistor. All the characters that speak are so well voice acted that you will wonder why other games do not have this amount of quality in them.
The story in Transistor deserves some kind of award. The amount of storytelling put into this game is overwhelming. From picking up tidbits of information from the OVC terminals to putting functions() in an active slot, upgrade slot, or passive slot so you can upgrade more of those character bios that are masterfully written. The ending is beutiful but does leave some questions lingering in your head.
In reality the only thing bringing this game down is that the counter on the ball resets when you do Recursion mode.

If I had to use only one word to describe this game, it would be Beautiful.
The artistry and the music is just levels above to what I'm used to from video games. For example, take a look at the poster on the top page with Red and the Sword. She could have been put in some sort of badass pose brandishing it at a robot horde or swinging it above her head with explosions in the background but take a good look. She's holding it close to her, embracing it even as if it were dear to her which in my opinion brings amazing character to both her and the Sword, characterizing it as something with a soul rather than objectifying it as just a weapon. And that's just the poster for the game.
The music for Transistor is just amazing, nothing from what I'd expect from a video game. It adds a soul to the game which most lack, both the singer (Ashley Barrett) and the songwriter (Darren Korb) have incredible talent that it's not uncommon for me to just stop playing for a second and listen, I highly suggest listening to a song or two (The Spine, We All Become) by itself and all of their songs for this game are posted up on Youtube, hosted by the gaming company themselves. If this motivates just one person to buy the soundtrack, I'll be happy.
To me, it feels like the gameplay itself wasn't up to par with the rest of the game, and even then I still have a really good time playing it. It's an action/turn-based RPG hybrid with a unique style of combining attacks. The Functions(attacks) in game that you get have three posibilities: the first is as a main attack, the second adds its characteristics to an attack and the third is as a character buff. There's so many different ways to play this game it's crazy, however something I feel holds this game back a little is the enemy variety. There's only a handful of enemies and as you progress they get recycled and given some sort of ability to make it more difficult/interesting, which it does, but it feels kinda lazy at the same time. That's honestly the only gripe I have with the game, and it's a small one at that. The game is a little on the short side but I'd rather have an awesome time for 6 hours rather than a game I have to tredge through for 12.
Long story short: Buy the game, buy the soundtrack. We need more games like this one.

There are a lot of negative reviews on this game, and I would say they are right, more or less.
However, I will still recommend you try out this game because the game is still in very early phase of development. Features will be changed, bugs will be fixed and issues will be addressed. My review will base on these premises.
+++++PROS+++++
- Great art style
- Really great music
- Diversed character builds and progression
- Unique class system
- Non-targeting action fighting
- Low grinding curve, with a quest-based + exploration progression (who says this is a grinding game has no clue what they are doing)
- Developers do listen to the community
+++++CONS+++++
- Some features are locked behind subscription token (although token can be bought using in-game currency) including peer-to-peer trading.
- Unbalanced classes and skills in PvP (hopefully this will be adjusted in future)
- Really restricted market system (hopefully this will be changed in future, or else many people would quit)
- Slow character progression (your skill only get 1% stronger each time you learn the mastery)

I recently wrote a comment on facebook describing my opinion on the game.
After I wrote it I realized it makes a great review, so I decided to post it as my review. It is not the typical "Pros and Cons" review which makes it different, and more of a journey of how I felt as I played, so I thought I'd use it to contribute to anyone confused about the game if it helps
Personally my score is varying between 4 and 6 out of 10, so I give it a 5 or 5.5 out of 10
Below is the review
"the gameplay feels reminiscent of a fancier Sonic Dash. It has the same gameplay mechanics and feel of a mobile game. It has many more issues but that's the first main issue that hits you. You don't feel in control sonic at all. When Sonic Lost world came, it wasn't for PC at first. i don't have a console so I didn't get to play it. Sonic Dash came out on the phone and had one of the Sonic Lost world bosses. I played it so much out of boredom that when Sonic Lost World came to PC, as SLOW as it was, the first thing I noticed is how beautiful it feels to be in control of the character again. When I played Sonic Forces it was the opposite feeling. There was an extreme "on rails" feeling that is hard to describe until u try it yourself. In any sonic game.. if u slow down and explore u always find that it is possible to do so. Here if u slow down the character can't do anything.. it's as if u interrupted the on rails system and he is stuck in place. Over that, sonic feels heavy, slow and nerfed down (Except when dashing but again, on rails more than any sonic game ever made) and the custom character has all the physics fixed in comparison, like somehow the custom character and shadow ARE sonic, and sonic is the side character.
What makes it feel like a mobile game even more is stuff like making super sonic a DLC. Not only does a game feel like an on rails Android or Iphone game, it even has the marketing sensibilities of a mobile game. It almost feels as if the Mobile game marketing team in Sega were deeply responsible for all the decisions in the game, like nerfing down Sonic and Classic sonic on purpose to make the player feel the urge to pay the extra 2 dollars for super sonic. Super sonic feels like how sonic should have been, but still less fast and still feels heavier than any sonic game ever released.
The story is amazing. The custom character is amazing and making him or her is amazing. You feel a sense of high in every cutscene even the ending, followed by a sense of DEEP disappointment when the level starts. Unless you are a new generation gamer that plays MOSTLY casual mobile games, making it hard for u to distinguish an on rails mobile game from an ACTUAL sonic game, u might not notice how flawed the game is. But as someone that played ALMOST every sonic game out there.. the feeling was MORE limited and less enjoyable than even Sonic Lost World in my opinion. Best Story ever. Worst Gameplay Ever, medium music (makes u fall in love with the custom avatar music then disappoints u with badly made classic sonic music)"
An extra note regarding the music: it was too tinny and more retro than even classic sonic games. It felt very Sonic 4 which didn't' make sense because supposedly Classic Sonic came straight from the Sonic Mania dimension, so it made more sense that his music would be funky 90's style pop music like Mania as he is not from the past, but from another dimension.
I will attach also in the comments a message I sent to Aaron Webber from Sega's Public Relations team about the game that I also sent to customer support and was completely ignored. I feel it was ignored because all Sega staff seems have signed an agreement to never talk bad about the game so Sega can keep depending on fans that blindly love anything Sonic and use that for their marketing advantage. Since the message I sent them was completely overlooked, I am putting it in the comments in public in case it helps ppls opinion feel heard or in case it feels relatable.
My personal opinion. Wait it out. Wait till all the DLCs come out. Give it a year. Wait for it and the DLC's to be 20$ or less then buy it. Don't waste money like I did and just try it for yourself on December 2018 if you really need to know why it doesn't feel right. Maybe you enjoy it, but at least u wont' feel u wasted 40$. The story is great after all.
Edit:
Due to the message being too big to fit in the review OR the comments, attached below is a google drive link containing the message that was overlooked that I sent to both Aaron Webber from Sonic PR and SEGA Customer Support in case anyone is interested <3

TLDR
This is a message for all sonic fans that try to see the good in all of this, those who thought Sonic Lost World was good and all the detractors are haters like me: there is a reason so many people say this game sucks.
Everything about this game was poised to make for another great sonic game, but then someone dropped the ball.
Whoever's idea it was to make the level design department for Forces so small that not a single level lasts for more than two minutes, every level is linear and constantly takes control away in a clear effort to hide unfinished portions, and bosses are so bland that even the surprisingly good final boss battle has to have a third phase that basically repeats Colors and Lost World, absolutely needs to be either fired, or whoever made the decision to make the department so small needs to be fired.
The graphics are superb, the avatar gameplay and customization is genius, and there were a lot of little moments that had me smiling. But it was such a letdown. Sonic Team needs to be reorganized, or someone needs to be fired.

No more room in hell is a free zombie survival horror game.
This game is not just your average zombie survival game. Your character isn't immune, he isn't special. He is an civilian trying to survive, you can get infected and after some time you will turn into one of them, effectivly hindering your teammates or even catching them on suprise. And yes, you will die, a lot. Some of my friends get bored after one match and I can see why.
The game has got a rather big skill factor that you will see when you play the game more. It's very well made and it feels extremely rewarding to complete a rather hard map. But when you start you have mostly have no idea what to do. You will die, and die, and die again. It's boring to lose and lose again. But if you stick long enough you will see what you are capable off.
The main game has 2 modes, NMO and NMS, lets start with NMO.
NMO is a mode that is based around objectives, usally it's the left 4 dead style. Keep on moving until the end. But this game makes objectives random per game. On the same map you could be walking in a different section and doing different objectives then you did last time. Reducing repetitveness from this mode.
NMS on the other hand is more about defending
while searching for weapons and suplies as the waves come at you. This is possible to do solo but this mode will be A LOT more easy if you got a friend or more to help you out. I think this mode is harder then NMO because you are more dependend on your team. You can't just run away if everything fails. You got a zone to protect.
Now to the soundtrack in this game. It's a solid 10/10 for a free game and It is AMAZING. The soundtrack will fill you with despair, horror, but also hope when near the end. The soundtrack surely makes the atmosphere better by a big step.
tl;dr
This has to be one of the best free to play games here on steam. It feels very realistic and it's skill based. It has 2 modes which are both very fun to do and repetitveness is played out by placing different objectives on the same map. It's a must get and I recommend this to everyone that hasn't tried it out yet or didn't gave it a second chance.

All in all, this isn't a bad pick up, especially for free.
However, out of necessity for a gameplay review, it's not worth much more than free - and that's perfectly fine.
On the first playthrough, the narrative is compelling and choices definitely matter... it's after the first playthrough where things start falling apart.
It becomes cascadingly clear that, as with many (if not all) 'choices matter' titles there is actually very little deviation from plot points across playthroughs representing different choices.  Is that a crime? Not necessarily, at least for a free game.  Though I feel it must be pointed out - if only to throw in an objective opinion.
So why the positive review?  The game does wonders in conveying emotion and even themes and morals if the player is looking for it.  Standard $60 titles are picked up for their playability.  Indie releases such as this are picked up for their impact on the player.  Without sounding too pretentious, I enjoy a game infinitely more if it successfully incorporates meaning and intent seamlessly into it.
So yes, its worth the playthrough, but not because it's bringing new life to the 'choices matter' genre.

There will be several instances where, throughout gameplay, you will yell out, "I do not have enough room to do all of this." -- and this is exactly the game's purpose. Working for a totalitarian government is not supposed to be easy, nor is it supposed to be accomodating -- in fact, it is simply exhausting. It feels like work, it is work, and by the end of your day, you feel more and more broken down. The first rejection was hard, then the 500 more just become a statistic; their faces become blurs; their stories become muddled; your morals become bland. Their pleading for your mercy only becomes time wasted to accumulate enough money to feed your family for the day, if they are still alive that is. Friends are murdered, families grow sickly, and the innocent with nothing more than a typo on their passport are hauled away to a place only God knows of. "Papers, Please" is nothing short of brilliant, where you will be stunned as to how a pixeleated game could conjure such visceral emotions out of you -- thereby also realizing that effective storytelling is never a matter of graphics.

TL:DR;
A game that was well ahead of its time, technically and thematically, and has an active modding community and positive reviews to this very day. Highly recommend checking this out, no matter what genre you're a fan of; there really is something here for everyone.
FACTS:
Released in 2007
Inspired "[by] the popular science fiction novella Roadside Picnic by Boris and Arkady Strugatsky and the 1979 Andrei Tarkovsky film Stalker that was loosely based on it, as well as Stalker, the film's subsequent novelization by the original authors. -Wikipedia, sue me
METACRITIC: 82, 8.4 User Score
Hell, even IGN gave it an 8.2. (and they were whining about the technical limitations of an open-world FPS RPG made by indie developers in 200-and-flipping-7, and how the almost non-existent cutscenes were "badly compressed" despite the fact that Half Life proved you don't need cutscenes for a story to be told well.)
________________________________________________________________________________
What the hell CANT you say about STALKER? Its critically renowned, a cult classic, STILL has an active modding community almost 9 years later, helped jumpstart the open-world RPG FPS genre mixture, has one of the most haunting and memorable atmospheres I've ever experienced in any form of media (and I'm a fan of horror) AND your crumb-filled, burnt-smelling toaster can run it now!
Raving over a personal favorite of mine aside, whatever you don't initially like about this game, you'll come to like. What you won't come to like, you can mod out, or, in (a surprisingly large amount) some cases, in. Some things just can't be fixed however.
Yes, it is open world.
Yes, there are fences and loading screens between areas.
Yes, it has an in-depth story, chock full of lore,personality, dark humor, and some pretty mature themes.
Yes, most of it is behind walls of text that instead of reading, you'd rather be AH NUUUU CHEEKI BREEKI-ing the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of mutants.
Yes, there are not a lot of guns.
Yes, you can mod more in / mod them to feel better/more realistic.
Yes, it can be buggy/glitchy/graphically dated.
Yes, the fans have solved all three problems (mostly).
Basically, pretty much any problem you have with the game can be solved by either sucking it up (which, in gaming, you shouldn't really be expected to), mod it in/out, or learn to love it.
While it certainly has it cons, this is the one game I'm willing to overlook the glaring problems it has in favor of the spectacularly good parts of it.

When I first started playing this game I honestly thought very little of it. A free to play hunting game just didn't sound fun to me. I was dead wrong. The moment you get your first kill is the moment you learn to love this game. It's a game that requires patience. You have to be mindful of the noise you make, how visible you are and even the wind direction, as animals can easily smell you if you're not careful. You have to listen out for calls, track them by marks and droppings, and then when you find it, you need to get a clean, painless kill. The game doesn't punish you for not killing the animal in a single shot outright, but if you wound the target instead of killing it, you can expect a few minutes of having to track a panicked animal, instead of being able to harvest it immediately and move on.
The selection of weapons as you begin the game is terribly limited. A single rifle, which can be upgrated with a subscription to a basic shotgun and a revolver handgun. But as you play, and if you're willing to put a bit of money into it (and support the devs, they're nice folk!), your options grow vastly. Several varieties of rifles, shotguns, handguns, bows/crossbows and muzzle loaders can be bought, along with a huge variety of ammunitions. Shotguns can have buckshot, birdshot or slugs, for an example.
Not only that, but the gear and equipment you can get is fantastic as well. A variety of different outfits with different stats that'll help you against different prey. Urine spreys and lures to attract prey. Wind indicators and ground blinds. Camping gear, climbing gear, first aid kits. There's a lot of selection in regards to what you can bring along with you. It helps too that the game is gorgeous. It's not 'next gen', but it's pretty. The maps are huge. You can wander around for literally hours stalking prey and constantly be seeing new and interesting terrain. The land makes such a huge difference to how you hunt as well, how you approach your prey and whether or not you get seen or not.
The only downside is that, well, it's "free to play". Sort of. The game has a mix of subscription fees and micropayments, and some may find that distasteful. There are those that want one or the other; if you're buying stuff for micropayments, then you shouldn't need a monthly payment. If you're paying monthly, then you shouldn't need micropayments.  The subscription does give you a few items and the basic guns you need to hunt every animal in the game, mind you, but if you want variety in your weapons or looks, you'll likely need to pull out the credit card; again. And yet, I don't really personally mind. This is a niche title and the developer needs to be funded if the game is to survive. A nice way (or at least an optimistic way) of thinking of it is to look at it like a sort of kickstarter. You fund the game, and you get rewarded.
Still, like I said, I can easily recommend this game. I'm not a hunter. I'm primarily an RPG / strategy / Dota 2 player. Yet I just absolutely adore this game. Every hunt is so satisfying, and it has these really nice ups and downs, where you go from tensely stalking your prey, to just relaxing and wandering the woods seeking the next. Plus. It's free to check out! What've you got to lose? :)

This game's gotten a bad rap - not entirely undeservedly - but as someone who's been steeped in this series since early childhood, somehow Forces has become one of my favourite Sonic games to replay and revisit. As a complete precaution to skeptical buyers: your initial playthrough won't be anything remarkable. It's nothing but a step down from Generations and a salvage from Lost World.
Awkwardly tight, almost binary controls will feel out of place in a series so long focused on momentum and fluid motion, and short, gimmick-driven levels will leave you wanting. This is where I think most people stop when they give the game a middling to lacking score.
If you're willing to put in the time, though, the replay-value on display here is incredibly satisfying. Every stiff aspect of the controls will eventually click as predictable and hyper-responsive tools to complete levels as efficiently as possible, be it for those elusive S-Ranks, the time-attack missions, pure score to level up your avatar character, or hunting down the fifteen main collectibles in every stage. The short length of levels suddenly becomes relief that numerous retries of a stage won't eat up too much of your time, though I could certainly have done with a few longer stages as well.
Options and variety really are the focus here, especially in the Avatar stages. Every major level accommodates every weapon you can chose from, and if you ever give the speedrunning community a glance you'll start seeing uses for Drill that, even if unintended, basically add a whole other layer to the experience. Steam says I've played this for 40 hours (seemed longer) and only now am I starting to feel fatigue at going back through familiar terrain.
The only real area I haven't actively looked to replay has been Classic Sonic's levels. There's very few of them and they're underwhelming to say the least. I hope we get a break from him next game around, maybe to make room for more Modern or secondary-character stages, but even so I had fun enough hunting down the collectibles.
Overall well-worth the full price I paid, though if all of the above sounds like a workload-investment instead of an exciting discovery, I'd give this a pass until a decent sale.

"Sonic Forces exists" is a general summary of how I feel about this game.  I neither find it amazing, nor offensive, it just exists.  Don't get me wrong there are segments of the game I found enjoyable and other bits frustrating but overall it's a mostly average game.  Sonic Team definitely tried to harken back to the Adventure era in overall tone for the game as it's overall grittier, granted it doesn't get as gritty as say Shadow the Hedgehog, it gets close though. Also, I can't help but feel that Shadow would have been a more fitting lead for this title.
Like I said, the story is a lot grittier than recent entries getting close to Shadow the Hedgehog, which is a shame it doesn't because I find the grittiness in Shadow the Hedgehog downright hilarious at times with moments like Shadow straight up killing Dr. Eggman or Sonic on certain endings, alas this isn't Shadow the Hedgehog though.  Dr. Eggman takes over the world with his new creation dubbed "Infinite", who is a jackal whom Shadow called weak and he got so triggered by it he subjected himself to Dr. Eggman, allowing him to be used as the test subject for the Phantom Ruby (introduced in Sonic Mania).  Fused with the Phantom Ruby, Infinite has the ability to create realistic illusions of previous enemies amongst other things.  Anyway this caused trouble for ol' Sonic and the gang which leads to Dr. Eggman sucessfully taking over the world.  Seemingly inspired by the Archie and SatAM on this front, a resistance is formed to combat Dr. Eggman and reclaim their world.  This sounds like overall it should work, but due to how the game is structured it ends up being fairly disjointed in execution leading to a messy a story, which you can't even laugh at for being hilarious bad like some previous entries.
Overall it plays like a more awkward version of Sonic Generations, Modern Sonic controls probably the best he has in this set up due to being built off Sonic Lost World, however he lacks drifting which I hurts the design of one level in particular, if he only he could drift though.  The Avatar plays like a worse version of Modern as it's slowed down and relies on the use of Wispons which if you're going for completion probably means replaying levels multiple times for completionists.  Team is a mix of Modern and Avatar which uh... it works I guess.  Classic Sonic is the worst offender though, while not controlling as bad as Sonic 4 Ep 1, he controls considerably worse than he did in Generations (there's apparently a mod though fixes this issues, so you might want to use that while playing.)
Due to being modified from Lost World rather than Generations (I really have no idea why Sega did this), the levels are noticably considerably shorter than previous entries.  This wouldn't be so bad I don't think if it had a proper act structure for the games zones and was designed around it but it ultimately comes off as extremely disjointed due to this... which hurts several stages especially ones that overall aren't bad but end up ending just right when it's getting really good (this especially happens with Modern Sonic).
The music in Forces soundtrack is all over the damn place, there are some tracks that are pretty good (none are particularly amazing though) and then there are tracks that are downright earbleeding terrible (most of the Avatar stages).  Infinite's main theme though (which is only used in a cutscene) is hilariously edgy though, and the main theme Fist Bump, much like this game kinda exists.  The best the music gets is probably the orchestral pieces during the menus and cutscenes followed up by most of Modern Sonic's and the Tag stages.  Classic Sonic's are very uninspired Genesis-esque tracks which is really bizzare considering Naofumi Hayata composed a few of these tracks too.
It's on par with Sonic Unleashed and Sonic Generations I guess.  (Sometimes looking worse though)
Again, this game isn't particularly too bad, but it isn't great either.  If you're wanting to pick this up wait for at least a 50% off sale or an overall price drop, and then you too can experience perhaps one of the most average entries in the Sonic series.  It's honestly kind of a shame it isn't a trainwreck though, cause then I could have probably gotten some enjoyment out of it's terribleness like I do with the majority of the Adventure era titles.
I feel like I should mention, that if anyone gets this game Episode Shadow (hopefully it remains free) is while super short at least has some more enjoyable parts than the main game I feel (even if they are retooled levels from the main game :X), and the remixes from Sonic Adventure 2 and Shadow the Hedgehog used here are probably better than most of the games soundtrack.  So if you do happen to pick this game I definitely recommend playing through Episode Shadow.

I stress the first missions because after a while you do become accustomed to being grusomely mauled by the Xenomorph or strangled to death by a malfunctioning android. That being said I am still enjoying it very much; I find myself intentionally putting it down for days at a time so that it's still at least somewhat scary when I come back to it.
The story is interesting enough. The graphics are beautiful and the audio is horrifyingly on point. I recommend it if you can get it on sale.

So just to start off, I will say I've always been a scaredy cat when it comes to survival horror games and I generally avoid them.
That being said, I saw a friend play this game and fell in love with it. The whole concept of survival while being actively hunted by something that you can't just overpower and kill is aMAZING. The game forces you to use stealth and a limited amount of supplies to traverse enemies and obstacles as you duck, weave and go slow/stealthlike through areas. It also forces you to stay engaged by limiting your knowledge of whats near you to the motion tracker, which isn't always accurate, and the audio cues, without which you will probably die over and over and over.
I don't think it got repetitive, and it had a substantial campaign mode, it took me about 20 hours to complete on the hardest difficulty. The last 2 missions are pretty lackluster, at that point the tools you have let you kind of cheat the level (I still tried to play stealthy), but nonetheless was satisfying.
The graphics are in line with current games in my opinion and the whole "lo-fi" thing people associate with the alien movies is captured extremely well.
The horror aspect is actually surprisingly just right for me. I liked to play at night and with a little lighting so I kind of get that "heeby-jeebies" feeling whenever the game starts to build the sound up, or I know the alien is nearby and I can hear her moving. There are also many points in the game where there is information necessary but you have to disengage your character from the "active" mode, to read a computer screen or perform a task, and you're not technically "immune" or "impervious" to dying while performing the tasks, which in my opinion makes it that much more scary and awesome.
I really really really hope they continue the story, the cliffhangar ending (as all alien movies do) is leaving me wanting more.
Definite buy, even if its not on a steam sale. Well worth it.

Superb game. The 'Stardew Valley' of the MMOs. Due to it's art style it is a very pleasurable place to spend time. I've found the community very friendly, unlike other MMOs - if you speak to people, they speak back (rather than continuing grinding before running off whilst completely ignoring you) and have teamed up with strangers to complete some quests together fairly regularly. Perhaps it's the pretty world rubbing off on them, I don't know.
I would say it is fairly simplified and easy to learn by comparison to other MMOs also, which is a plus for me as I can not always be bothered to read pages upon pages of wiki game sites to learn some baffling system or to progress whilst always feeling like I'm missing out on something. Despite it's simplification, I would say there is enough depth and plenty of world to explore. The amount of classes and skill mixing and matching is huge also, which is something I love in games of this type - making a character that is truly mine.
Highly recommended - a lovely world to spend your time in. Love it.

The thing about Transistor is, while being from the same studio that made Bastion, it is NOT Bastion, per se. They share similar game mechanics, as well as the way story is presented at time, but they are wholly different thematically in art, music, narrative, and design.
This is not a bad thing.
In fact, the fact Transistor is not a copy of Bastion shows that Supergiant Games is being creative and reinventing on top of what worked as well as experimenting with new styles. This creativity lends itself into crafting Transistor into a wonderful game.
The gameplay is similar to Bastion's, exscept there is a new mechanic called "Turn()" that allows you to pause time and plan moves accordingly. It brings in a strategic element that allows you to decide how you'll deal with enemies. This is especially helpful in close combat areas, as the usage of a function like "Vault()" can save you in the nick of time.
The story and narrative are cryptic for sure, but can be pieced together. The fact that they don't give you all the details, and let's you come to your own conclusions, brings about an interesting anbiguity that actual lends itself to the narrative of the world. Furthermore, the personalities of the characters, though mostly just glimpses, were all different and varied. This is especially apparent when reading about them after obtaining different functions.
The art and music are what really solidify this game. The art direction is fantastic, utilizing sharp edges yet soft painterly textures in a contradictory yet appealing aesthetic. There are even design homages to Gustav Klimt in there! The world created breathes its own life as it moves and shifts. The music brings its own meaning and sets the tone for the areas or encounters in the game. Both lend itself into creating an engrossing atmosphere that really enhances what's going on on screen.
The only glitch I encountered was upon loading the game and playing the first 5 minutes on launch day; my screen stayed on black after entering a tunnel to go to a new area. I believe this has been fixed in the latest patch. Furthermore, some enemy AI may not react despite being close to them for a good five to ten seconds, but I did not find this detrimental to my experience with the game.
The comparisons to Bastion are unavoidable, but this game is not Bastion, and is its own game. Overall, Transistor is a wonderful indie title from Supergiant Games, and I recommend it to all who enjoyed Bastion and Supergiant Games' work on it, as well as to those who enjoy turn based strategy games with fantastic art and music.

Ok, where to start. It's probably one of my favorite games of all time. Based on the book 'Roadside Picnic', which also inspired the Stalker movie from 1979. You're a Stalker, basically a looter that roams around the Zone, the area of exclusion where the Chernobyl incident in '86 happened, although the game is set in an alternative reality.
In the Zone you'll find anomalies, artifacts, Stalkers, bandits, the army, mutants, vodka, Warsaw pact weapons, bugs and glitches.
The game is mainly a FPS, even though it has a relevant weapon and gear progression. You can make some decision in the dialogues here and there, but it's nothing too major in most of the cases.
The gunplay/weapon mechanics is really solid, with somewhat realistic ballistics, but it takes a while to get used to it. Gun variety is also good, from your good 'ol Makarov pistol to the futuristic FN F2000. The AI of the enemies is decent, not too dumb but neither too frustratingly hard, at least generally.
But the part where the game really shines is the atmosphere. The areas feels organic, nothing feels out of place and once you overcome the feel of being lost and fear the Zone becomes the comfiest place imaginable. There's nothing more comfy than sitting around in a camp surrounded by a bonfire with your fellow Stalkers, hearing the hilarious conversations in russian and playing guitar songs.
The storyline it's interesting and with a few twists here and there, but don't expect the game to be story heavy.
The vanilla experience is good, though it can be somewhat clunky at times and buggy, and here it's where the mods come in. After the first playthrough of vanilla + bugfixes and grafix mod you can start taking a look on other bigger ones. AMK Mod is probably the definitive STALKER SoC experience, a must play. Other amazing mods are Autumn Aurora, LURK and if you're feeling hardcore, Zone of Alignation.
All that said, the game has some issues like the slow start, occasional bugs that can appear even with the unofficial fixes, lack of transport to move quickly between areas... But once you get into it and start feeling immersed, you'll forgive almost all of them. Definitely a future classic.
Last few notes about the game:
With mods it looks really good and on the lowest settings you can run it on a toaster. It's very recommended to play on master difficulty and to disable the crosshair. Installing big mods it's easy, but when you try to install small ones and try to merge them with other ones it can be a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ The sequel (actually prequel) Clear Sky is the worst game in the series. So if you go through the game and want more you can skip to Call of Pripyat or replay the game with mods.

Sonic Forces had three level designers, as opposed to Generations' (on sale now go buy it its one of the best Sonic title in the past 10 years and GOTY for whatever year it was released in) 12 or so level designers, many of which were veterans from previous titles. Here we have two new guys who don't know what's going on and one guy who's last Sonic game was Sonic Lost World, which was....
. It was....a game I wouldn't go out of my way to buy or force myself to play unless I'm a Sonic fan (which I am). It's a few levels above this game, but not something incredible.
The problem with Forces is automation (game plays itself) and Sonic Team's weird sort of bipolar disorder with the franchise. I couldn't imagine Nintendo making a new Mario game and telling all its veteran designers to "take the year off, we got Neil the intern to work on this one". There's no consistency on this franchise which is weird because it IS their flagship. It's a revolving door in terms of designers which is why you get such drastic quality shifts. My theory is that Sega uses the Sonic franchise as a testing ground for interns and new employees because they know the games will sell anyway.
Whatever the case, the level design in this game is all automation. It's one of those "press right to finish level" cases where half the level is all set pieces where the title plays itself a la Sonic Colors, only that Sonic Colors had variety and other factors to carry it through. There are a few moments of brilliance where I start having faith in the interns, like one small segment in death egg where I have to quickly react to to take the quicker paths that lead to the red rings in the level (5 in each collect them all limited time run). In this other level which I forget cause its Sonic Forces, I'm sliding down a water slide, but you can easily fall off the edges and bumping into any enemies that are with you lead to their deaths but also move you an adequate amount to provide a challenge in not falling off. There are three other slides above and below you so you might fall to a slide slightly underneath you and not die, which means you have a linear level but with challenge and plenty of movement.
Sadly the level lasts a minute and 20 or so seconds.
Most levels last under 2 minutes, they're generally shorter but some might go for maybe 3 minutes. Not necessarily due to challenge but mostly due to elements that are there to stretch the level out. Such as placing 10 enemies in a circle, requiring you to home (sp?) in on all of them (press A repeatedly while the game plays itself) which will lead to an opening to continue the level afterwards.
I don't mind automation if its done like the lightning wisp power up, which allows you to automatically follow a string of rings even if they're suspended in the air. They're typically a path in and of themselves that lead to a lot of coin and a quicker route. Even though the game is playing itself while you hold Y, getting to this segment requires (usually) quick timing to not run past the rings that you can latch on to and staying alert when the 'ring path' runs out and the level requires you to hit some enemies to get closer to the other 'ring path' that will allow you to continue on with this aerial segment. The point is, give me a challenge other than pressing forward. At least require me to be
.
I will say that the game allows you to customize a playable avatar, and the amount of customization is really something. I know its pre-set costumes and clothing items, but the massive amount of items and being able to see them in cutscenes and levels without it looking like s*it (clipping, items oddly out of place) put a smile on my face.
I didn't mention classic sonic stages because....eh. The music sounds like dogsh*t in his levels. Don't know why. All they did in Generations was make the tempo of the songs slower for his stages and basically re-arrange the songs. But they didn't equate "Classic Sega Genesis music" with "dogsh*t" so I dunno. I guess the composers in this game thought if its old it has to sound like dogsh*t?
Gameplay on his levels is 'better' but only because you can't have 2D levels play themselves. I mean, they pulled it off with some levels which is mindblowing. But otherwise his prescenece here does nothing and is just there to tie into Mania.
The best I could say is that it's a mediocre game. It's a budget title that isn't worth more than 20 dollars; recommendations are for titles you go out of your way to tell people to play. A thumbs down doesn't mean a game is
, it means it doesn't leave enough of an impression to start evangelizing for the title and telling others to play it. Like Deus Ex. Just go buy Sonic Generations
again

Techland are an odd company that seem to only be able to make good or bad games with no in-between. The latest Dead Island is bad Techland and pretty much just a cash grab with no improvements over the original and in some cases worse with features removed. I can gladly say though that this is good Techland. Very good actually. CoJ: Gunslinger is a top-notch western shooter with great stylised graphics with awesome pacing that make you want to continue until the very end.
You play as Silas Greaves, an aging bounty hunter looking to get his last kill. On his way to do so, he stops by a bar and recounts tales of his past and deeds to the locals. In his tales he tells of famous outlaws he either partnered with or killed but some of the locals aren't convinced as Silas isn't the most focused story-teller which is made apparant through actual gameplay.
As Silas narrates, he will sometimes get details wrong or Patrons of the bar will tell the story how they think it is such as an early section where Silas has to face against a sherrif in a one on one gun dual but in actuallity, Silas just gets knocked out and arrested. Another notable instance is a section where Silas explains a plan he had that you play out but he then says he did something else so you then play an alternate route. It's a concept that isn't overly used and when it is, it's a nice surprise and to great effect.
As a bounty hunter of the Wild West, you have access to a unfortunately small arsenal consisting of pistols, rifles and shotguns but that only extends to saw-off versions of the latter. I personally saw very little use for the shotgun as it pays to be more accurate as enemies can be taken down with a well placed shot to the head which also earns you a better score. By shooting enemies with more skillful shots, you earn a higher score for each and by killing enemies in quick succession, you can combo your score even higher with each kill multiplaying. This gains you access to a skill tree where you can unlock new abilties such as dual weilding to slowing down time to the more traditional such as more ammo.
Last but by no means least is Dual mode in which you face an enemy in a quick draw. During this, you have to use the WASD keys (or left stick on a controller) to keep your hand hovering over your gun and the mouse (right stick) to aim your gun at the enemy. While it's confusing at first, I certainly got the hang of it but it took much longer than what really felt nessessary as you have to try and split your vision between your hand and your aim.
As a downloadable game baring the Call of Juarez name, it can be easy to see why anyone would pass this up. The last game in the series was awful but thankfully Techland graced us with a game that really should be taken notice of, not avoided.

So let me get something straight: I do not agree with the many things that are currently in the game. I am not white knighting IMC nor am I giving them a pass for this being Early Access.
I am, however, willing to stick by a game that is fun. Tree of Savior IS a fun game if we're putting aside all the glaring issues that you see in the many reviews here. I would just like to state that many MMORPGs have had rough launches. One game that reminds me of this launch is Diablo 3 if anyone remembers that. Launch was horrendous, riddled with login errors, had terrible end-game and leveling and the actual gear was a mess. Don't even get me started on the ridiculous Auction House. It's essentially the same mistake that Tree of Savior made, they crippled the concept of trading. However, Blizzard addressed the concerns of their playerbase, removed the Auction House, started making slow and steady steps towards a better game. I have been monitoring the official Tree of Savior forums and IMC's responses to the playerbase and I have to say that although there can be a lack of communication, THEY ARE TRYING. They have been fixing issues and working around the clock to deliver a good experience and have definitely been on the right track. It will take time, please be patient with them, but I have to say that all these negative reviews ARE JUSTIFIED. IMC has done this to themselves. They deserve all the negative backlash for their poor design choices, lack of proper foresight and just terrible management of the launch overall. However, I can understand that not all good games start off as such and I am willing to be patient with IMC to see where this game goes.
TL;DR IMC messed up big time and deserve all the negativity, but they are absolutely taking the right steps in communicating, addressing and fixing issues slowly. Step by step, they ARE working towards a better game. Patience is key with this game.
PROS
--------
+ Breath-taking Art
+ Excellent music
+ Highly intuitive and complex class system that really gives you endless customization
+ They rebalanced the leveling process and made it smoother
+ Controller support, mouse support and keyboard controls are smooth
+ IMC is taking proper measures to ensure a stable game
+ Very good fansites that provide plenty of information about classes, items, monsters, etc, including Skill/Stat simulators
+ All the CONS listed below are things that CAN (and most likely will due to the pressure from the playerbase) be fixed
CONS
--------
- Extremely limited Auction House
- Overpriced Token (Premium Subscription)
- No F2P Trading whatsoever, P2P trading limited to 30/month (This is the biggest con by far)
- Stat system is incredibly linear and the game is almost entirely gear dependent
- Progression can be confusing and frustrating if you have not done extensive research
- Dungeon entry limit is too strict; Two entries per day for F2P users is too harsh

Have you ever wanted to work in security customs and border control? Have you ever wanted to be responsible for controlling who comes in and out of your country? This game simulates just that. It may use cheap 2D, 16 color graphics, but in a way, a game like this doesn't need to be fancy. All you have to do is make sure you follow regulations, make sure all citizens have the proper papers, make sure they have followed the guide lines (Expiration Date, proper photo, correct city information, etc.) Make sure no one passes that are not allowed in the country. This game tests your ability to remember rules and watch for inconsistant information on documents. If you think you would make a good borders patrol, then test your knowledge and skill with this game. It starts easy, but you have to remember more as you progress through the game. You not only have to watch for face versus photo and expiration date, but you also have to remember which cities are valid places to get papers as well as checking to make sure all fields are filled in. How well you work determines how much money you make to help your family. This is not so different from real life. Work well and do your job correctly, your family will be well taken care of. If you screw up, you and your family will be out in the cold.

The thing about Transistor is, while being from the same studio that made Bastion, it is NOT Bastion, per se. They share similar game mechanics, as well as the way story is presented at time, but they are wholly different thematically in art, music, narrative, and design.
This is not a bad thing.
In fact, the fact Transistor is not a copy of Bastion shows that Supergiant Games is being creative and reinventing on top of what worked as well as experimenting with new styles. This creativity lends itself into crafting Transistor into a wonderful game.
The gameplay is similar to Bastion's, exscept there is a new mechanic called "Turn()" that allows you to pause time and plan moves accordingly. It brings in a strategic element that allows you to decide how you'll deal with enemies. This is especially helpful in close combat areas, as the usage of a function like "Vault()" can save you in the nick of time.
The story and narrative are cryptic for sure, but can be pieced together. The fact that they don't give you all the details, and let's you come to your own conclusions, brings about an interesting anbiguity that actual lends itself to the narrative of the world. Furthermore, the personalities of the characters, though mostly just glimpses, were all different and varied. This is especially apparent when reading about them after obtaining different functions.
The art and music are what really solidify this game. The art direction is fantastic, utilizing sharp edges yet soft painterly textures in a contradictory yet appealing aesthetic. There are even design homages to Gustav Klimt in there! The world created breathes its own life as it moves and shifts. The music brings its own meaning and sets the tone for the areas or encounters in the game. Both lend itself into creating an engrossing atmosphere that really enhances what's going on on screen.
The only glitch I encountered was upon loading the game and playing the first 5 minutes on launch day; my screen stayed on black after entering a tunnel to go to a new area. I believe this has been fixed in the latest patch. Furthermore, some enemy AI may not react despite being close to them for a good five to ten seconds, but I did not find this detrimental to my experience with the game.
The comparisons to Bastion are unavoidable, but this game is not Bastion, and is its own game. Overall, Transistor is a wonderful indie title from Supergiant Games, and I recommend it to all who enjoyed Bastion and Supergiant Games' work on it, as well as to those who enjoy turn based strategy games with fantastic art and music.

I'll be blunt; this game is fun for the general audience, but dissapointing for long-time Sonic fans. I can only reccomend this game to other Sonic fans, Speed-runners, Completionists, or kids wanting to make their own character.
And now, a brief list of pros and cons:
Pros
- Pressentation
The graphics are amazing, the music is pretty great, and the story isn't perfect, but the writing between characters is the best we've gotten from the series in a while. There are also quick time events that aren't really challenging in any way, but they do add a good amount of visual flare.
- Custom Hero
Without a doubt the best part of the game. There are so many customization options and the Wispons (the gadgets) add a lot of replay value to the gameplay.
- Modern Sonic
He's fast, powerful, and can team up with your custom hero on certain levels. But I should mention that his controls are not made for tight platforming in this game (this goes for the custom hero too.)
- Episode Shadow
After 11 years, Shadow's back in action. He plays just like Sonic, but also has a prequel story with 3 levels all to himself, which are some of the best in the game. You can even play as him in most of Sonic's levels.
- Replay Value
After the main story, you can spend some time completing missions to unlock more outfits for your hero. The ranking system makes it feel great when you play through a level flawlessly enough to get an S Rank without having to be a master at the game. And of course, it's a Sonic game, so speed runners can relish in time trial missions and trying to beat their best times.
Cons
- Classic Sonic
You want to talk about a complete downgrade from Sonic Generations? Look no further than Classic Sonic. His controls are heavy and stiff, making his platforming sections a complete chore, his speed power up lasts for a pathetically short time, he can't stay underwater as long as he could in previous games, and to top it off, he's completely forced into the story.
- Level Design
Definitely, the weakest part of the game. Most levels feel too short, half of Modern Sonic's are extremely linear, there is a small variety of enemies, and towards the end, there are some really cheap moments of trial and error.
- Length
This game is about as long as Sonic Generations, but with the shorter levels, it ends up feeling so disconnected as a whole.
I'm not sure if it's really worth $40, so wait for a sale or price drop if you're curious.
EDIT: Well, it's January 2018 so let me save you the trouble: The Super Sonic DLC isn't worth the $2. It should have been in the full game and even so, it barely adds much replay value for both Sonics.

There have been many hunting simulators on the pc and in my youth I do remember playing a few. Then, they were more ambitious and less refined. Today, theHunter stands as a full experience with graphics to match. It is a massively multiplayer online game which is completely free to play. It borrows from games like second life but is all about the complete hunting experience. This isn't like a game you setup on top of your tv and blast bucks flying at you in technicolor. This is a game which has taken strives to create a realistic simulation of a real hunting experience.
You start by designing your character and signing up for another source of lifelong emails. The game allows you to explore the entire reservation and hunt rabbits and mule deals. The are other players to interact with and If you're wanting to upgrade to the full experience, you will have to purchase the proper license. Beware, your steam coins will start jingling. So that begs the question. Is it worth it?
The game's graphics are very up to date and beyond beautiful. On the highest settings I see a game that completely is devoted to simulating a real hunting experience. The sounds are crisp with extreme attention to detail. Animals have real sounds, branches break with a real crispiness. The guns are real with a big verity of gadgets and equipment to use on your hunt.

Although the experience is totally immersive, the free version is a little more like a demo. The limitations of only being able to hunt mule deer and cottontail rabbits really make the free version become old quick. There are a lot of expansions and editions, but reviewing strictly the free portion it is beautiful but limited. If you're looking for a genuine hunting simulator, I totally recommend it. If you're a little bored and looking for a consistent long lasting free experience you might have to look elsewhere.

Um I don't exactly know what to say about Papars, Please. After playing for one run through and about 1 hour and a half I don't really think this is a good game. There is certainly potential in this game. While simple it was engaging to play border security- it was almost like a detective sitting at the desk. Not to mention it offers a unique perspective on the effects of authoritarian regimes (like the USSR) on average everyday people. But there are to many issues for this to be a good experience. For one the way you examine paperwork is unwieldy and given that your on the clock (you have til 6:00 til your shift is over) time wasted going back and forth between ever increasing pieces of paperwork becomes iritating and impossible to see errors or mismatching information. I understand that this is an attempt to simulate reality but this doesn't really bring anything to a videogame's experience. Literally this games need "Less Papers, Please". I will perhaps give Papers, Please further attempts but I don't see myself getting anything more out of this game.

The newest title from indie developer Supergiant Games, Transistor is the story of Red, a famous singer in the city of Cloudbank, and the Transistor, the massive sword she swings around. Red has had her voice taken and the Transistor is looking to regain his body.
The game is a beautifully sublime mixture of both real-time and turn-based combat. The system allows for you to rapid-fire abilities by taking on the attacking animations and their timing or to forgo that in favor of activiting your Turn() and being able to plot out your attacks and movement. It takes a bit of getting used to but it an incredibly clean system once you're used to it and it plays like a dream. With about a dozen abilities to choose from and being able to combine them in active, utility, and passive slots, the combat has a lot of room for variation.
The art is in the style the Supergiant is now known for: every backdrop, every character, every enemy, everything within the game is an absolutely breathtakingly beautifully made piece of hand-drawn art. The subtle electric lights that give an eerie blue glow to the city are just beautiful and sorrowful at the same time.
The sounds. Dear god, the sounds. I don't even think that I really need to say much. It's done by the brilliant Darren Korb, who was also responsible for the Bastion soundtrack and sound design. I've had the OST on for the last few days and it just never gets old. Every piece of music from the game is brilliant. It goes from relaxing and cheerful sounding to deep, resonating, and sorrowful from track to track. It's a perfect reflection of the game. Ashley Barrett lends her vocal talents once again with this amazing sound track. Her voice is such a sublime mixture of gripping and haunting in the soundtrack and it's so easy to lose yourself in the music.
I don't know how much more praise I can give this game. Supergiant Games has outdone themselves once again. If this is their standard for their games, I can see myself buying anything and everything from them from here on out. 10/10.

Another good game from Bastion creators Supergiant. Not without flaws though, and not up to the high bar the group set previously with Bastion. Combat is weighted too heavily on use of Turn() movements, and it is straight up impossible to beat the game in only real time combat, unlike what Supergiant said during events like PAX. The game is far more linear than it should be, with almost no splitting off. Additionally, you are given a lot of customization with how you use your skills, but it will always boil down to what does the most burst damage at the time, since you can only effectively fight in Turn(). As such, it has very little replayability, since there is not going to be any variance in order of area completion or how you play the game, unlike Bastion. Lastly, enemies to far, far too much damage, the other reason open combat outside of Turn() isn't feasible. After the halfway point of game, most enemies will take well over half your HP in one attack or combo, and the AI is exceptionally aggressive and tracks movement during thier shots.
Despite all this negatively, the game is still good. Art style is great, story is unusual but interesting, music is solid (though personally find it inferior to Bastion's western styling) and gameplay is mostly enjoyable. It may not be exceptional, but it's still above the average of most AAA releases these days.

If you have the cash to spare, absolutely pick this up.

This game is a piece of art. The style of art fits so perfectly with the mode of the game. It is a great experience. The combat is tactical but also exciting. While the story and voice acting and lore all make you, the player, attracted to the game and it keeps your eye on it.

Transistor, much like any other great piece of fictional work, will likely be discussed for days to come.  To say anything about the story would ruin the experience for anyone.
The gameplay, which can be discussed, attempts for a healthy blend between Bastion's real time action combat and the 'time freezing' turn based mechanics of other RPG titles.  Combat does a solid job staying intense and fresh throughout the initial 5-8 hour playthrough, feeding the player just enough new tools to experiment with much like Bastion.
But what you will and others will remember of this game is its commitment to quality presentation much like it's predecessor.  Artwork, sound and story design all blend perfectly into an unforgettable gameplay experience that will leave a significant impact on you for days to come...  Or even weeks depending on your enjoyment of the game.
Likely to be a contender for Game of the Year, Transistor should NOT be missed and is proof that these more independent companies like Supergiant are definitely capable of producing the kind of sleeper hits the indie scene attempts but often fails to put out.  They practice what they preach and when so many other groups can't even pull that off, they have earned my loyalty and purchase of future titles.

Examples for why I do not recommend this game:
GLITCHES
The second boss of the endgame veteran trial Hel Ra Citadel in Craglorn splits your group of 12 into parties of 6 to fight two bosses at once (commonly referred to as top and bottom boss), if one side wipes the other enrages, it's a neat mechanic, but if the group fighting bottom boss does not kill their boss first try, the lower boss resets but does not respawn, leaving the top group permanently enraged, requiring a reset to reattempt.  This trial has been in game for more than a year and this still hasn't been fixed.  For reference, the first boss you have to re-kill is the 6 armed stone guy in the  screenshots.
I personally have game crashes on average AT LEAST once every 2 days, sometimes 3 to 4 crashes in 5 hours of playtime.
PvP
It's nice to have fights of 50-100 people fighting to capture/defend keeps, but you might change your opinion when the framerate drops to 5 FPS, or the fact that with the drop of Homestead people become invisible (not rendering) and kill you without being able to see them, this goes both ways but it's very disappointing.
Cheating/Exploits
The only permanent actions I've seen against people is a forum ban when they bad mouth the devs on there.  Get caught using cheat engine? 3-day ban.  Lag-spiking in Cyrodiil PvP?  Have yet to see actions on that.
Upcoming content/ESO+ subscription
In Quarter 3 they are releasing "a dungeon-based DLC", and beginning Q2, "Chapter's" annually.  Basically a zone the size of Wrothgar, (another DLC, but included with ESO+ subscription, or purchasable with $30 in Crown's, the Real Money currency for the game) but also including a class and the games 6th trial.  This Chapter will NOT be purchasable with crowns or included in the subscription.  you need to pay $40 if you already own the game, or $60, and you get the base game, but none of the extra content in Gold Edition.
I complain about this because for $15 per month you get 1500 crowns to spend, so you cannot get this content just by being subscribed.
ZoS has plans for Q4, but the only description right now is "content-based"
TL;DR In-game bugs are game breaking and have existed un-patched for well over a year, support is awful at best.  End game is stagnant.  When it works, it's a pretty game, buy it for $10, enjoy the 3 main questlines, then dump this game.

Total War: Rome II is an intense and fun real-time tactical combat game wrapped in an overall decent strategy package. Creative Assembly continually strives to add depth to the campaign and empire building aspects of their series, and though not every change and feature in TW: R2 rings as true in practice as it does in theory, the game is definitely in a state that is not only playable, but worthy of the Total War name. You will not find deep economic or diplomatic gameplay here, but the city management and grand military strategy are enough to keep you going that extra turn. Not to mention that next turn, you’re going to be laying siege to that big walled city with thousands of men on either side, where the game allows you, in true Total War form, to plan out your favorite military tactics and watch it unfold on an epic scale. With solid animations, off-the-charts unit variety, great design, and sweet historical quotes on the loading screen, this game does many things right. Unfortunately, all flash and no substance makes Caesar a dull boy. Save this one for those lazy weekends!
Amazing for someone who enjoys large scale historical RTS games

Take just about everything that made Total War shogun 2 special; The gripping campaign, authentic and exciting battles, addicting gameplay and swiftly through that out the window for a complete step backwards in game quality.
Major con's
Battles - Still buggy as hell, they're rather ugly with a terrible art style (saving private ryan wannabe), awful animations and alot of lazy cut corners like siege towers being magically pushed by the force rather than man, or ladders being slightly different siege towers.
Campaign - Uglier than Shogun 2, less depth, less investment. The province system is an abomination, because it further reduces depth and encourages blitzkrieg and full region ownership not by borders, chokepoints or geographic reasons but because you will be penalized for owning Sparta when Athens is islamic, leading to endless revolts and issues because of problems out of your control. Only good thing; Public order isn't an instant revolt anymore.
Multiplayer - 100% step backwards, almost all the features from Shogun 2 have simply been thrown out.
Visuals - Again, this game is not nearly as pretty as the screenshots promise. Not only does the game very rarely capture the epic skill of there PR team's talent for cherry-picking, there are several video's of pre-release footage showing very promising footage, promising even more in the future at the same time, then the general process of "Optimisation" occured where the game was severely visualy degraded and dumbed down, based on the "Super super early code we're way way pre-alpha" footage of the historical battle of carthage vs the Release version that was bait-switched on launch.
Conclusion; Don't buy unless below 20$. I've come along way from a naive total war fan initially buying and playing the game for the first 300 hours, overlooking it's flaws and living in denial that this game isn't a complete failure. But then I listen to Reynold Sanity and real critics of this game, that pointed out the utterly apparent flaws and absurdity of defending the game, and I've come full circle to become an grizzled, tired and grumpy arm chair general looking upon future titles with a cynical eye, as I see more corners being cut and more anti consumer activity occuring.

In a word: Fascinating. This game is so ridiculously simple at first, but it spirals rapidly within a matter of a few in-game days (about an hour of play or less). The elegance and minimalism of the retro graphics is a perfect backdrop for this multi-ending little paper-stamping adventure. You are a border checkpoint inspector, charged with allowing only sanctioned entrants into the fictional country of Arstotzka‎, run by a totalitarian regime of the 1980's. Each decision will affect you in some way, whether it increases your daily stipend through stipend or bribe, get you cited and penalized (causing you to be docked pay) or puts you squarely in the middle of international intrigue, possibly at the cost of your life or the lives of your family members.
If you are a highly detail-oriented person, like me, you will find the early stages of this game a snap. But watch out...and keep your finger in the digitally rendered rulebook!

Finally, my cold-hearted perspective on customer service that I've formed from years in sales can be put to use. Glory to Arstotzka. Bring all of your damned papers or something to exchange for not having them, lest you be detained/denied - unless your name is Jarji and you look like a Russian Mario <3

PGMENTUM requires good reflexes and a steady focus in order to complete the levels. You play as a rectangular block that can adjust between 3 colours; Red, blue and green. You’ll need to go through other blocks that are placed vertically, and in order to pass them your block must match the colour of the incoming block.
It’s minimalistic in challenge and can easily be compared to the (infamous) Flappy Bird. I dislike the concept for its repetitive nature, and unchanging goal. I flew by the first 3 levels on the first go. AFter player it another 3 times, I no longer felt motivated to try again, if all I’m going to encounter is the same 3-potential colour blocks again … and again …
To add to this concept, the developers could have added other features such as:
1) A new colour unlocked in the later levels
2) A Steam Leaderboard feature, so that it can establish its competitive aspect better.
3) Perks and items that can aid you. For instance, you could unlock an item that can be used to change all the colours of the blocks to one for a small period of time. Or an item that slows the speed of the incoming blocks. There can even be an ability that has your block auto-correct it’s colour to the next few blocks before falling back to your control.
A lot could be done for option 3) that would make the game more enjoyable. It offering a small reward for players, which if I may also point out, is something the game doesn’t give. There was so much potential for this game to be more than just a simple test-your-reaction game. The developers had blown it, though, and decided to publish it as complete. It’s due to that, that I would not recommend playing PIGMENTUM. Especially if you are a colour blinded individual.
(I have no comment on its graphics or audio in this review, as it is basically everything you see in the trailer. It’s either bland, or non-existent, excluding the BG.)

Transistor is a sci-fi action adventure game with a combat system that's a mix of hack & slash and turn-based. You get about 20 "functions" which can each be used in three roles: firstly as a combat skill, secondly as an upgrade for skills, and thirdly as a passive that effects all skills and combat. You can install and uninstall these functions as much as you like, giving you lots of flexibility. As you level up you also get the choice to use limiters, which buff your enemies. These are optional, so you can challenge yourself however you see fit.
The only thing this game needs is more content. However, you can replay the game retaining all your skills and level from the previous playthrough, and there are special arenas that test your skill.
Definitely worth checking out.
