Super Giant Games: making grown men cry like little girls since 2011.
The first thing you must account for when playing this game is that it is not Bastion. The developers have created a new experience and it should not be criticized for being a different style of game from their former work. The approach that the developers have taken this time have meant that this game is not for everyone.
The game has amazing, well thought out music, in addition Supergiant Games have heavily improved upon the art style of Bastion by adding well implemented modern graphical effects. The game drew me in immediately as the genre greatly appeals to me, the immersion will definitely vary by the player. An understated accomplishment of the developers, is that they have managed to successfully create a second game of the same genre without repetition. The world, story and themes are vastly different from Bastion and I truly appreciate the details of the story.
From what I've seen people raise three main arguments against the game:
-The story is confusing and uninspired.
-Combat is unappealing.
-Slow progression
This time around the story is agreeably cryptic as #$^& and a more human approach was taken to the narration. I would compare it to braid in the way that you are left to solve the jigsaw that is the story-line, however unlike braid you are given all the pieces. Everything in this game is explained through details in the world alongside some conclusions of your own. I understand a wide portion of the player base was distraught with the ending, (SPOILERS to theme ahead) as it wasn't directly satisfying, though if you truly investigate the world you will understand it could not have ended any other way (end of SPOILERS).
I find the only legitimate argument to be made against this game is with the combat. The system is a unique integration of real time and turn based combat, the system has one issue in my opinion and that is the time while your turn ability is recharging. This just felt incredibly restrictive, an interesting trade off but definitely not justifiable in terms of good game design. The rest of the combat was still up to par as there were some interesting play style choices to be made that were well balanced.
After having raised these few issues some would say that the game is only worth an 8 or 9 out of 10. However at the end of my first play-through and even in my second I was in awe of the masterful emotional reaction that Supergiant managed to evoke from me. Transistor is another experience I wont forget, 10/10.

The only thing Transistor shares with Bastion is the artistic and narration style. The game tries to involve strategy with the use of a planning sequence you can activate. It will execute a certain number of moves in an instant, so planning ahead is encouraged. Although that "strategy" is kind of lost once you gain access to more diverse functions (moves). The world of Transistor outshines its story. Cloudbank is a very interesting city and will appeal to any fan of sci-fi world building. Story wise it is fragmented and at times lifeless, but it has its charms and leads to a satisfying conclusion. The soundtrack is soothing and there are some tracks that stand out similar to Bastion. Graphically it looks great and has the same storybook feel as Bation.
A definite recommend, but non-fans of Bastion might want to wait on a sale.
Beautiful game, love the art and the subtle story-telling mechanics. Solid and challenging gameplay that rewards you for experimentation and creativity. Worth every dollar.

Great game.  Mostly it was emotional.  Everything that Supergiant got right with Bastion was multiplied times ten.  The voice acting is amazing, so much more personal than Bastion, and continues to immerse.  The OST is not as diverse, but overall better themed and works more to the feel of the game.  The songs with vocals are phenomenal, and normally vocals turn me right off.
Now the combat, which is what makes up the vast majority of the game is really neat.  Supergiant opted to experiment and hit the ball right out of the park.  Only four abilites can be on your bar at once, but extra abilities can be used to fill either buff slots to the active abilities or as passives on your character, and with 16 abilities, this leads to lots and lots of customization that the game encourages you to play around with, as having the ability in each function unlocks codex entries about the people in town.  And then the Turn() system is pretty cool.  It's a way of mixing up the whole idea of turn-based vs real-time combat.  Basically, you can either run around, using abilities in real-time, which puts you at a disadvantage, or you pause, queue up a bunch of abilities, use them with super speed, but then are extremely vulnerable for a few seconds afterwards.  The goal is to destroy enemies before you go vulnerable.  It works really well, and gets incredibly fun when the game starts throwing large groups of enemies that all require different strategies to take down.
Anyways, the gameplay is innovative and fun, the story insanely emotional, for $20 there is zero reason not to play this game (yes I know it will be cheap on sale at some point, ♥♥♥♥ off).

The Avatar ends up getting the best tracks, with lots of vocal pop songs, although some of them don't fit the stage they are in like Guardian Rock
Sonic Forces is split into three characters for its short 3-4 hour campaign, with Modern Sonic, Classic Sonic, and the Avatar recieving 1 stage between 7 locales, plus boss battles and 2 tag team levels with Modern Sonic and the Avatar teaming up.
For all characters, controls are concerningly bad. Sonic Generations wasn't perfect with Modern and Classic Sonic but they controlled fine, even Unleashed was fine but Sonic Forces decides to absolutely destroy this making all three characters having extremely akward jumps, making midair control challenging, and everyone far too heavy making platforming hell. The amount of jank when going fast with the Avatar when switching speeds is unreal.
Modern Sonic's level design can be an absolute joke, levels are very straightfoward and non-threating. Sonic can boost foward by pressing and holding the X button after obtaining boost from White Wisp Capsule scattered frequently through stages or by defeating enemies. The boost makes sonic travel super fast plus making all enemies die on contact. Levels switch between 3D and 2D in certain points, with most platforming happening in the 2D sections. Sonic can instantly dispatch an enemy with a homing attack, which can sometimes fail to function on faraway tagrets. 2D levels ususally have an upper and lower pathway with the upper pathway being faster and the lower pathway being more punishing, but 3D sections require little skill besides switching lanes, and using the homing attack. Sonic's double jump is almost useless due to its pathetic jump height. Drifting is removed, a major good mechanic introduced in Sonic Unleashed has been removed, cutting down on complexity. The Lightspeed Dash is also absent, the Wall Jump is used in one stage as the Avatar, and sliding is used like twice in the whole campaign. Tag Team stages combine both Modern Sonic and the Avatar's abilities, with double boost sections introduced where the player mashes X and the duo rush off in a scripted segment, even if you fail the mashing segement you the duo still rushes off albeit with a stumble.
Classic Sonic in Sonic Generations tried a different take on his gameplay, with the incrediable overpowered, but incrediebly fun and useful Spindash. Forces throws this out, alongside Classic's alright controls from generations. Jumping is exessively heavy, landing jumps is a pain. Jank is fully present in Classic Sonic with springs popping out of no where to kill your midair momentum. Classic Sonic's gameplay is in 2D, and he jump to reach higher ground and kill robots, he can curl into a ball and some slopes to gain incredible unnatural feeling hight, and can hold perform a Drop Dash by holding the jump button in the air for a certain amount of time and when he hits te ground Classic gains a large amount of speed.
The Spindash is activated by crouching and mashing the jump button, but doesn't have much speed and much use, but at least it destroys enemies. Unfortunately the Ghost Town is the only stage that feels like the Drop Dash and Spin Dash were built around.
The Avatar plays similarly to Modern Sonic just without a boost and double jump, allowing for more interesting level design involving more platforming. Wispons are used as weapons and one can be equipped ranging from a flamethrower to a all-consuming gun that shoots black wholes that sucks everything in. There are 7 weapons in total, and can be upgraded by clearing challenges, and half of these are useful and fun to use, the others break pace and are akward to use. Wisp capsules are found in stages, and if holding a weapon corresponding to the right Wisp in the capsule when touched, the Avatar can use a new skill for a short time ranging from infinite arched jumps or dashing on a trial of rings. Enemies are found en mass in Avatar stages, proposing little threat with each weapon destroying enemies in a single hit. Each Avatar type out of 7 has a small benefit such as starting with rings from a death, or having a wider pickup radius. The Avatar has a wide array of customisations with outfits and 3 different variations in the same species, with 500 parts, with plenty of colours to choose from. Parts are unlocked via challenges, which involve clearing extra stages unlocked by collecting Ring Rings, time trials, S-Ranks and a wide variety of other challenges.
Collectables are in each non-Boss stage (and even in some Bosses), and consist of first collecting Red Rings, then collecting Number Rings that mut be collected in the right order, then finally for a third playthrough sliver moon rings that must be collected in successesion quickly. Bosses are passable, with them being inoffensive, but fun. The final boss does have some rather unfair segements that result in instant death, but I'll live with 1/7 bosses being unfair.
Sonic Forces is a medicore platformer that tries to focus on far too many things in its short runtime, while never getting anything just right and satisfying. Get this on a cheap sale, or play Sonic Generations + the Unleashed Project or Sonic Colours.

Its Just Cause 2 but with more everything!  Its just what you would want and the new stuff that is added is fun, which is what this game is suppose to be.  I could tell that the optimization was not perfect still, but my GTX 960 could handle everything at high at 30-50 FPS and medium at 60 FPS.  I had a few minor drops during big explosions but nothing major.  I did encounter 2 crashes after a few hours of play though which look to be the main issue now.
My first 10 hours were spent just enjoying the awesome world they dropped you in.  I drive, flew, glided, and blew up things all across this world and all of it was just fun to do.  Which is what I think the game is best described as, a big, fun sand box.
After getting used to it, all of the actions on foot feel perfect; shooting, gliding, moving, grappling, it all felt good and smooth.  The new wing suit is easily my favorite thing and feels perfect but has a bit of learning curve to use well.  Grappling feels the same if not better than just cause 2 which is great since its a big part of the game.
Vehicles on the other hand felt off with some more than others.  Driving felt odd but once I got use to it I was able to do the race challenges without too much trouble.  Its not racing physics but still fine unless its motorcycles.  It could just be me but I felt that I never could fuller control where I was going with a motorcycle.  The controls felt stiff and unresponsive at times.
Flying was better but only with a controller.  Flying with keyboard and mouse is near impossible in my opinion. Flying is still fun though.  Helicopters though, tend to just move very odd when trying to make small, precise turns.  High speed is fine but when hovering and trying to shoot, i'm just glad we have unlimited ammo....
Over all I think the game delivers what it set out to and is worth it for anyone looking for this kind of game.

Its pure arcade action with some minor RPG elements and the game rewards you for being extremely quicky AND accuracte in the gunfights you will be taking part in.
You will also learn a thing or two about the Old West by finding "Nuggets of Truth" that provide you with information about the various criminals you will be chasing along with historical conflicts in the Wild West.
